# ORDER MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 3 — State Machines, Transition Rules & Operational Gates

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The Order Domain is not merely a collection of records.

It is a controlled business process.

Every order progresses through a finite number of officially recognized business states.

Each state has:

- business meaning
- ownership
- required validations
- allowed transitions
- blocked transitions
- required approvals
- mandatory operational evidence
- audit implications

No system implementation may permit state changes outside this canon.

The state machine becomes one of the permanent business contracts of GiftHatkeOS.

---

# 3.2 Principles

The Order Lifecycle shall be:

Deterministic.

At every moment:

An order has exactly one current lifecycle state.

The next possible states are fully defined.

No undefined transition may exist.

---

Core Principles

### Single Source of Truth

State exists only once.

Never infer state from multiple flags.

---

### Explicit Transitions

Every movement must be intentional.

No hidden transitions.

No automatic status rewriting.

---

### Traceability

Every transition creates:

- timestamp
- actor
- reason
- evidence
- audit entry

History is immutable.

---

### Operational Safety

Business gates prevent movement when mandatory work has not been completed.

---

# 3.3 Master Order Lifecycle

The official lifecycle consists of:

Draft

↓

Quotation

↓

Pending Approval

↓

Confirmed

↓

Production Planning

↓

Ready for Production

↓

In Production

↓

Quality Inspection

↓

Ready to Dispatch

↓

Dispatched

↓

Delivered

↓

Closed

Alternative paths:

Cancelled

On Hold

Returned

Refunded

Archived

These are controlled exception states.

---

# 3.4 State Definitions

## Draft

Purpose

Internal working document.

Customer commitment has not occurred.

Characteristics

May be edited freely.

Inventory not reserved.

Production not scheduled.

Financial documents absent.

Exit Conditions

Quotation generated

or

Order confirmed directly.

---

## Quotation

Purpose

Commercial proposal.

Characteristics

Price finalized.

Products finalized.

Customer reviewing.

Allowed Operations

Modify pricing.

Modify products.

Regenerate quotation.

Approve.

Reject.

Convert.

---

## Pending Approval

Purpose

Internal authorization required.

Typical Reasons

High discount.

Corporate account.

Large value.

Custom pricing.

Blocked customer.

Required Approval

Sales Manager

or

Finance

or

Business Owner

depending on policy.

---

## Confirmed

Meaning

Customer commitment exists.

Business now owns delivery responsibility.

System Effects

Order number locked.

Financial obligation begins.

Production becomes eligible.

Inventory reservation permitted.

Planning allowed.

---

## Production Planning

Purpose

Operational scheduling.

Planning Activities

Machine allocation.

Material verification.

Resource assignment.

Capacity balancing.

Expected completion estimation.

---

## Ready for Production

Meaning

Everything required is available.

Checklist

Artwork approved.

Materials available.

Machine assigned.

Operator assigned.

Personalization verified.

Payments satisfy business policy.

Only after passing all operational gates may production begin.

---

## In Production

Meaning

Manufacturing officially started.

Allowed Activities

Laser.

Printing.

Assembly.

Packaging.

Inspection preparation.

Critical Rule

Editing commercial information prohibited.

---

## Quality Inspection

Purpose

Business quality verification.

Possible Results

Pass

Fail

Rework Required

Conditional Approval

Only successful quality verification may release dispatch.

---

## Ready to Dispatch

Meaning

Production complete.

QC approved.

Packaging complete.

Shipping labels available.

Courier booking allowed.

---

## Dispatched

Meaning

Custody transferred.

Evidence Required

Courier.

Tracking.

Dispatch timestamp.

Dispatch operator.

Carrier details.

---

## Delivered

Meaning

Courier confirms successful delivery.

Business Outcome

Order fulfilled.

---

## Closed

Meaning

Business process completed.

Requirements

No pending financial issues.

No open support cases.

No returns.

No disputes.

Order becomes read-only.

---

# 3.5 Exception States

## On Hold

Purpose

Temporary operational suspension.

Reasons

Customer requested.

Payment issue.

Artwork pending.

Inventory unavailable.

Management decision.

Resume requires explicit authorization.

---

## Cancelled

Allowed Before

Production commitment.

or

Management override.

Mandatory Fields

Reason.

Actor.

Timestamp.

Refund policy outcome.

---

## Returned

Only after delivery.

Return authorization mandatory.

Inventory handling required.

---

## Refunded

Financial process completed.

Requires Finance approval.

Linked financial documents mandatory.

---

## Archived

Historical storage.

Read-only.

Immutable.

---

# 3.6 Official Transition Matrix

| Current State | Allowed Next States |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Draft | Quotation, Confirmed, Cancelled |
| Quotation | Pending Approval, Confirmed, Cancelled |
| Pending Approval | Confirmed, Cancelled, Quotation |
| Confirmed | Production Planning, On Hold, Cancelled |
| Production Planning | Ready for Production, On Hold |
| Ready for Production | In Production |
| In Production | Quality Inspection |
| Quality Inspection | Ready to Dispatch, In Production, On Hold |
| Ready to Dispatch | Dispatched |
| Dispatched | Delivered |
| Delivered | Closed, Returned |
| Returned | Refunded, Closed |
| Refunded | Closed |
| On Hold | Previous Operational State |
| Closed | Archived |

No other transitions are permitted.

---

# 3.7 Forbidden Transitions

The following transitions are permanently prohibited:

Draft

→ Delivered

Confirmed

→ Delivered

Quotation

→ Production

Ready for Production

→ Closed

Production

→ Draft

Delivered

→ Production

Archived

→ Editable

Closed

→ Production

Cancelled

→ Production

Refunded

→ Production

Any prohibited transition requires creation of a new order or an authorized corrective process rather than altering lifecycle history.

---

# 3.8 Operational Gates

State progression is governed by mandatory business gates. A gate validates that all required operational evidence exists before an order can advance.

## Commercial Gate

Required before **Confirmed**:
- Customer identity verified.
- Pricing finalized.
- Products and quantities validated.
- Taxes calculated.
- Required approvals completed.

## Payment Gate

Required before production when payment policy demands:
- Deposit or full payment received as defined by business rules.
- Payment reference recorded.
- Outstanding exceptions explicitly approved.

## Personalization Gate

Required before **Ready for Production**:
- Artwork approved.
- Customer personalization complete.
- Assets validated.
- Final production proof accepted when applicable.

## Material Gate

Required before **Ready for Production**:
- Required inventory available or reserved.
- Procurement exceptions resolved.
- Material substitutions approved.

## Capacity Gate

Required before **In Production**:
- Machine assigned.
- Operator assigned.
- Production slot scheduled.
- Estimated completion established.

## Quality Gate

Required before **Ready to Dispatch**:
- QC checklist completed.
- Mandatory inspections passed.
- Rework closed.
- Packaging approved.

## Dispatch Gate

Required before **Dispatched**:
- Shipping address verified.
- Courier selected.
- Labels generated.
- Tracking number issued.

## Financial Closure Gate

Required before **Closed**:
- Financial reconciliation complete.
- Refunds resolved.
- Outstanding balances cleared.
- Credit notes finalized if applicable.

---

# 3.9 Transition Authority

Every state transition must identify the authorized actor. Authorization is determined by role and business policy rather than implementation technology.

Each transition records:
- Initiating actor.
- Role at the time of transition.
- Transition timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business reason.
- Supporting approvals where required.

Delegated authority, emergency overrides, and policy-based approvals are handled through the security and governance canon defined in later stages.

---

# 3.10 State Integrity Rules

The lifecycle model enforces the following permanent integrity constraints:

- An order may occupy only one lifecycle state at any instant.
- State changes are atomic and either complete fully or not at all.
- Every successful transition generates an immutable audit record.
- Failed transition attempts may be logged for security and operational analysis but do not modify lifecycle history.
- Historical states remain preserved and cannot be rewritten.
- Business evidence supporting completed transitions remains linked for audit purposes.

---

# 3.11 Operational Outcome

This state machine defines the permanent operational behavior of the GiftHatkeOS Order Domain.

It serves as the authoritative lifecycle specification for:
- SMP1 standalone implementation.
- Future Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0.
- ERP9 and ERP10 implementation.
- Mobile applications.
- AI-driven operational assistance.
- Reporting and analytics.
- Workflow automation.
- Compliance and audit.

The business lifecycle described here is technology-independent and remains stable even as implementation platforms evolve.

# ORDER MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 4 — API Contracts & Domain Services

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The Order Domain is exposed to the rest of the enterprise through a well-defined collection of business services.

These services represent business capabilities—not implementation details.

The Canon deliberately avoids prescribing:

- programming languages
- REST
- GraphQL
- RPC
- databases
- queues
- frameworks

Instead, it defines the permanent business contracts that every future implementation must honor.

Whether the platform is:

- Apps Script
- Java
- .NET
- Go
- Python
- Node.js
- Cloud Native
- AI-assisted
- Mobile-first

the business behavior remains identical.

---

# 4.2 Service Philosophy

The Order Domain is responsible only for order-related business behavior.

It does **not** own:

- inventory balances
- production execution
- accounting
- shipping operations
- CRM activities

Instead it coordinates these domains through published contracts.

Core principles:

- High cohesion.
- Loose coupling.
- Explicit ownership.
- Stable contracts.
- Technology independence.
- Business-first design.

---

# 4.3 Domain Service Landscape

The Order Domain exposes the following canonical business services.

## Order Creation Service

Responsible for:

- Draft creation.
- Customer association.
- Product association.
- Initial pricing.
- Default business policies.
- Initial validation.

Output:

A valid Draft Order.

---

## Order Configuration Service

Responsible for:

- Products.
- Quantities.
- Variants.
- Personalization references.
- Discounts.
- Taxes.
- Delivery preferences.
- Internal notes.

---

## Pricing Service

Responsible for:

- Product pricing.
- Discount rules.
- Promotional adjustments.
- Corporate pricing.
- Tax computation.
- Final payable amount.

Must never perform payment processing.

---

## Quotation Service

Responsible for:

- Quote generation.
- Quote revision.
- Quote approval workflow.
- Quote expiration.
- Quote conversion.

---

## Approval Service

Responsible for:

Business approvals including:

- High-value orders.
- Manual discounts.
- Policy exceptions.
- Corporate authorization.
- Escalation workflow.

---

## Order Confirmation Service

Responsible for:

Transition into Confirmed.

Triggers:

- Business commitments.
- Commercial validation.
- Downstream orchestration.

---

## Planning Service

Responsible for:

- Production planning request.
- Operational readiness.
- Capacity coordination.
- Material readiness coordination.

---

## Fulfilment Coordination Service

Coordinates:

- Production.
- Inventory.
- Shipping.

The Order Domain never performs these activities itself.

---

## Dispatch Coordination Service

Coordinates:

- Shipping request.
- Courier assignment.
- Dispatch readiness.

---

## Closure Service

Responsible for:

Business completion.

Ensures:

- Delivery complete.
- Financial completion.
- Operational completion.

---

## Audit Service

Responsible for:

Immutable history.

Tracks:

- state changes
- approvals
- modifications
- actors
- timestamps
- operational evidence

---

# 4.4 Domain Ownership Matrix

| Capability | Owning Domain |
|------------|---------------|
| Order Lifecycle | Order |
| Quote Management | Order |
| Pricing Coordination | Order |
| Customer Master | Customer |
| Inventory Balance | Inventory |
| Manufacturing | Production |
| Courier Operations | Shipping |
| Accounting | Finance |
| Marketing | CRM |
| Reports | Reporting |

Ownership is exclusive.

Cross-domain modification is prohibited.

---

# 4.5 Canonical Business Operations

The Order Domain publishes a stable catalog of business operations.

Illustrative operations include:

### Draft Operations
- Create Draft
- Read Draft
- Update Draft
- Delete Draft (policy controlled)
- Duplicate Draft

### Configuration Operations
- Add Product
- Remove Product
- Update Quantity
- Update Variant
- Apply Discount
- Attach Personalization
- Assign Sales Representative

### Pricing Operations
- Recalculate Pricing
- Validate Taxes
- Refresh Promotions

### Quote Operations
- Generate Quote
- Revise Quote
- Send Quote
- Expire Quote
- Convert Quote

### Approval Operations
- Submit Approval
- Approve
- Reject
- Escalate
- Withdraw

### Confirmation Operations
- Confirm Order
- Cancel Confirmation
- Revalidate Before Confirmation

### Planning Operations
- Request Planning
- Verify Material Readiness
- Verify Capacity
- Lock Planning

### Fulfilment Operations
- Release to Production
- Hold Production
- Resume Production
- Request Dispatch

### Completion Operations
- Mark Delivered
- Close Order
- Archive Order

---

# 4.6 Commands and Queries

The Canon separates operations into two categories.

## Commands

Commands change business state.

Examples:

- Create Order.
- Confirm Order.
- Cancel Order.
- Hold Order.
- Close Order.

Commands:

- perform validation
- enforce policy
- create audit entries
- trigger business events

---

## Queries

Queries never modify business state.

Examples:

- Find Order.
- Search Orders.
- Order Timeline.
- Customer Order History.
- Pending Orders.
- Orders Awaiting Approval.

Queries are read-only.

---

# 4.7 Validation Contract

Every command executes canonical business validation before state changes occur.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

Examples:

- Required fields.
- Valid identifiers.
- Mandatory customer.
- Product existence.

---

### Commercial Validation

Examples:

- Pricing complete.
- Tax calculated.
- Discount policy satisfied.
- Approval thresholds met.

---

### Operational Validation

Examples:

- Inventory readiness.
- Personalization completeness.
- Artwork approval.
- Production eligibility.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

Examples:

- Transition allowed.
- State compatible.
- Previous gate satisfied.
- Required approvals complete.

---

### Security Validation

Examples:

- Actor authorized.
- Role permitted.
- Approval authority valid.
- Delegation active.

---

# 4.8 Transaction Boundaries

A business command is treated as one logical transaction.

Either:

Everything succeeds

or

Nothing changes.

Partial completion is not permitted.

For example:

Confirm Order performs:

- validation
- state transition
- audit recording
- business event publication

If any required step fails, the transaction is considered unsuccessful and the order remains in its prior valid state.

---

# 4.9 Idempotency Canon

Certain business commands must be safe to repeat without producing duplicate business outcomes.

Examples include:

- Confirm Order.
- Generate Dispatch Request.
- Archive Order.
- Close Order.

If the same command is received multiple times after successful completion, the resulting business state remains unchanged and duplicate downstream effects are prevented.

---

# 4.10 Concurrency Canon

Multiple users may work with the same order.

The Canon requires controlled concurrency.

Rules include:

- Prevent conflicting updates to the same business data.
- Detect stale edits before committing changes.
- Reject or reconcile simultaneous modifications according to business policy.
- Preserve auditability of every accepted change.

The implementation mechanism is technology-specific; the business rule is permanent.

---

# 4.11 Error Classification

Business services classify outcomes into consistent categories.

## Validation Errors

Business data violates required rules.

Examples:
- Missing customer.
- Invalid quantity.
- Required personalization absent.

## Policy Errors

Business policy prevents the requested action.

Examples:
- Discount exceeds authority.
- Approval required.
- Payment prerequisite not met.

## Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition is not permitted.

Examples:
- Attempting dispatch before quality approval.
- Closing an order that has not been delivered.

## Dependency Errors

A required collaborating domain cannot satisfy its contract.

Examples:
- Inventory reservation unavailable.
- Production scheduling rejected.
- Shipping service temporarily unavailable.

## System Errors

Unexpected technical failures outside business logic.

Business services expose these distinctly from business rule violations.

---

# 4.12 Business Invariants

The following conditions remain true regardless of implementation technology:

- Every order has a unique business identity.
- Lifecycle transitions follow the certified state machine.
- Financial totals remain internally consistent.
- Audit history is immutable.
- Customer ownership is preserved.
- Product configuration reflects the approved commercial agreement.
- Every completed command leaves the order in a valid business state.
- Every rejected command leaves the prior business state unchanged.

---

# 4.13 Cross-Domain Service Contracts

The Order Domain collaborates with other enterprise domains through explicit business contracts.

| Domain | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| CRM | Lead conversion, opportunity context, sales ownership |
| Customer | Customer identity, billing and delivery information |
| Inventory | Material availability, reservation status |
| Production | Planning readiness, manufacturing progress |
| Personalization | Artwork, assets, proofs, customization status |
| Finance | Payments, invoices, refunds, credit notes |
| Shipping | Courier assignment, tracking, delivery confirmation |
| Reporting | Operational metrics and analytical views |
| Notification | Customer and internal communications |
| AI Services | Decision support, recommendations, anomaly detection (advisory only unless explicitly authorized by policy) |

Each domain remains responsible for its own business rules while honoring these shared contracts.

---

# 4.14 Service Governance

All Order Domain services are governed by the following permanent principles:

- Contracts are versioned and backward-compatible wherever practical.
- Changes to business behavior require governance approval and documentation.
- Consumers depend on published business contracts, not internal implementation.
- Service responsibilities remain stable even if technology platforms change.
- Business semantics take precedence over technical optimization.

---

# 4.15 Stage 4 Certification

The API Contracts & Domain Services Canon establishes the permanent business service architecture for the Order Domain.

It defines:

- Domain responsibilities.
- Service boundaries.
- Canonical business operations.
- Command/query separation.
- Validation contracts.
- Transaction principles.
- Idempotency expectations.
- Concurrency rules.
- Error taxonomy.
- Cross-domain collaboration.
- Governance standards.

This specification becomes the authoritative business contract for all future implementations, including:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile applications
- AI capabilities
- External integrations
- Future enterprise expansion

The business architecture remains permanent. Technology may evolve, but every implementation must conform to the canonical business contracts defined in this stage.

# ORDER MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 5 — Permissions, Roles & Security Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Order Domain contains commercially sensitive, operationally critical, and financially significant business information.

Its security model must ensure that:

- the right people perform the right actions,
- at the right time,
- with the appropriate authority,
- under complete accountability.

Security is not treated as a technical feature but as a permanent business governance framework.

This Canon defines the business authorization model that every future implementation must enforce, regardless of technology.

---

# 5.2 Security Philosophy

The Order Domain is governed by the following principles:

### Least Privilege

Every user receives only the permissions necessary to perform their business responsibilities.

No role is granted broad access for convenience.

---

### Business Need

Access is granted because of business responsibility, not organizational status.

A senior employee does not automatically receive unrestricted operational access.

---

### Explicit Authorization

Every business operation requires an explicit permission.

No action is implicitly allowed.

---

### Separation of Duties

Critical business processes are divided among different authorities to reduce fraud, error, and operational risk.

---

### Complete Accountability

Every business action is attributable to a single accountable actor.

Anonymous or untraceable changes are prohibited.

---

### Policy Before Technology

Security decisions are based on business policy.

Technology implements policy; it does not define it.

---

# 5.3 Authorization Layers

Authorization is evaluated across multiple layers.

## Layer 1 — Identity

The actor must have a verified enterprise identity.

Examples:
- Employee
- Contractor
- Partner
- Service Account
- AI Agent (future)

---

## Layer 2 — Role

The actor is assigned one or more approved business roles.

---

## Layer 3 — Permissions

The assigned role grants explicit permissions.

---

## Layer 4 — Business Context

Additional contextual conditions may apply, such as:

- Company
- Branch
- Department
- Sales territory
- Customer ownership
- Order value
- Business unit

---

## Layer 5 — Operational State

Certain actions are only permitted when the order is in specific lifecycle states.

Example:

A production operator cannot modify pricing while an order is **In Production**.

---

## Layer 6 — Policy Rules

Enterprise policies may impose further restrictions, including:

- Approval thresholds.
- Time-based controls.
- Delegation windows.
- Temporary emergency access.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Business Roles

The Canon defines logical business roles rather than job titles.

## Sales Executive

Responsibilities:

- Create quotations.
- Configure orders.
- Update customer-facing information.
- Submit approvals.

Cannot:

- Approve restricted discounts.
- Override financial controls.
- Close completed orders.

---

## Sales Manager

Responsibilities:

- Approve quotations.
- Approve discounts within policy.
- Escalate commercial exceptions.
- Monitor sales activity.

Cannot:

- Alter financial postings.
- Modify production completion records.

---

## Customer Success Executive

Responsibilities:

- Track order progress.
- Communicate with customers.
- Update non-commercial communication notes.
- Coordinate follow-ups.

Cannot:

- Change pricing.
- Cancel confirmed orders.
- Modify production data.

---

## Production Planner

Responsibilities:

- Schedule production.
- Allocate resources.
- Validate readiness.
- Release work to manufacturing.

Cannot:

- Modify customer agreements.
- Edit financial values.

---

## Production Operator

Responsibilities:

- Execute manufacturing.
- Record production progress.
- Report completion.
- Submit quality requests.

Cannot:

- Edit commercial information.
- Approve refunds.
- Cancel orders.

---

## Quality Inspector

Responsibilities:

- Perform inspections.
- Record quality outcomes.
- Approve or reject production quality.
- Request rework.

Cannot:

- Modify customer pricing.
- Alter production history.

---

## Inventory Manager

Responsibilities:

- Reserve materials.
- Release reservations.
- Resolve stock conflicts.
- Confirm material availability.

Cannot:

- Modify quotations.
- Close orders.

---

## Dispatch Coordinator

Responsibilities:

- Prepare shipments.
- Assign couriers.
- Generate tracking.
- Confirm dispatch.

Cannot:

- Modify production history.
- Change commercial terms.

---

## Finance Executive

Responsibilities:

- Record payments.
- Process refunds.
- Validate invoices.
- Manage financial completion.

Cannot:

- Alter production records.
- Change customer artwork.

---

## Finance Manager

Responsibilities:

- Approve financial exceptions.
- Approve refunds above threshold.
- Authorize credit adjustments.

---

## Operations Manager

Responsibilities:

- Resolve operational bottlenecks.
- Authorize operational exceptions.
- Coordinate cross-functional execution.

---

## Business Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Configure business policies.
- Manage operational reference data.
- Assign roles (subject to governance).

Cannot:

- Rewrite audit history.
- Alter completed business evidence.

---

## System Administrator

Responsible only for technical platform administration.

Does not automatically receive unrestricted business authority.

Business permissions remain policy-controlled.

---

## Auditor

Read-only access to:

- history
- approvals
- lifecycle
- audit evidence
- business records

Cannot modify business information.

---

# 5.5 Permission Taxonomy

Permissions are organized by business capability.

## Order Permissions

Examples:

- Create Order
- Read Order
- Update Order
- Cancel Order
- Confirm Order
- Close Order
- Archive Order

---

## Quote Permissions

- Create Quote
- Revise Quote
- Convert Quote
- Expire Quote

---

## Pricing Permissions

- Modify Price
- Apply Discount
- Override Discount
- Override Tax (policy-controlled)

---

## Approval Permissions

- Submit Approval
- Approve
- Reject
- Escalate
- Delegate Approval

---

## Production Permissions

- Schedule Production
- Release Production
- Record Progress
- Complete Production

---

## Quality Permissions

- Perform Inspection
- Record Failure
- Approve Quality
- Require Rework

---

## Dispatch Permissions

- Prepare Shipment
- Generate Tracking
- Confirm Dispatch

---

## Finance Permissions

- Record Payment
- Issue Refund
- Generate Invoice
- Approve Credit Note

---

## Administrative Permissions

- Configure Policies
- Manage Roles
- Manage Reference Data
- Assign Delegations

---

# 5.6 Separation of Duties (SoD)

Certain combinations of authority must never reside with the same actor during a single business process.

Examples:

- A user who approves a high-value discount cannot approve the related refund.
- A production operator cannot approve their own quality inspection.
- A finance approver cannot modify the originating quotation after approval.
- A user assigning roles cannot approve their own elevated access request.
- A dispatcher cannot confirm delivery without delivery evidence where policy requires independent confirmation.

These controls reduce fraud, error, and conflicts of interest.

---

# 5.7 Approval Authority Matrix

Approval authority is determined by business policy, including:

- Order value.
- Discount percentage.
- Customer classification.
- Payment terms.
- Contract type.
- Exception category.

Policies define thresholds rather than individuals, allowing organizational changes without altering the Canon.

---

# 5.8 Delegation

Delegation supports planned absences while preserving accountability.

Delegations must specify:

- Delegating authority.
- Delegate.
- Scope of authority.
- Effective start.
- Effective end.
- Business justification.

Delegated actions remain traceable to both the delegate and the original authority.

---

# 5.9 Data Visibility Canon

Access to data follows business responsibility.

Examples:

Sales Executive:
- Own customers and assigned orders.

Sales Manager:
- Team-level visibility.

Production:
- Operational data required for manufacturing.

Finance:
- Financial data relevant to accounting.

Auditor:
- Historical records without modification rights.

Visibility may be constrained by:

- Company.
- Branch.
- Department.
- Territory.
- Business unit.
- Customer ownership.

---

# 5.10 Field-Level Security

Some business fields require stronger protection than the order record itself.

Examples include:

- Cost price.
- Margin.
- Internal profitability.
- Discount justification.
- Approval comments.
- Financial adjustments.
- Refund reasons.
- Internal audit notes.

Permissions may grant access to the order while restricting specific fields.

---

# 5.11 Sensitive Operations

The following operations require elevated authorization or additional controls:

- High-value discount overrides.
- Cancellation after production has started.
- Refunds above policy threshold.
- Manual lifecycle overrides.
- Customer data correction after invoicing.
- Financial adjustments affecting completed orders.
- Emergency reopening of closed orders.

Such actions require documented justification and enhanced auditing.

---

# 5.12 Emergency ("Break-Glass") Access

In exceptional circumstances, temporary elevated access may be granted.

Requirements:

- Authorized approval.
- Time limitation.
- Recorded justification.
- Enhanced audit logging.
- Automatic expiry.
- Post-event review.

Emergency access is never a substitute for routine operational permissions.

---

# 5.13 AI and Service Account Governance

Future AI agents, integrations, and service accounts operate under the same business governance model as human users.

Rules include:

- Explicit identity.
- Assigned role.
- Limited permissions.
- Traceable actions.
- Policy-based authority.
- Human oversight where required.

No automated actor receives unrestricted authority by default.

---

# 5.14 External Partner Security

Third-party integrations and business partners interact through controlled business contracts.

Access is limited to the minimum required scope and may be restricted by:

- Operation type.
- Data domain.
- Customer relationship.
- Company.
- Time window.
- Contractual agreement.

---

# 5.15 Audit and Non-Repudiation

Every protected business action records:

- Actor identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state (if applicable).
- Operation performed.
- Business justification (where required).
- Related approvals.
- Source channel or integration.

These records form an immutable audit trail supporting compliance, investigations, and operational review.

---

# 5.16 Security Governance

The security model is governed by the following permanent principles:

- Permissions are business-defined and technology-independent.
- Roles aggregate permissions but do not redefine business policy.
- Authorization decisions are deterministic and auditable.
- Changes to security policy follow formal governance.
- Backward compatibility is preserved where feasible.
- Security evolves through controlled policy updates rather than ad hoc implementation changes.

---

# 5.17 Stage 5 Certification

The Permissions, Roles & Security Canon establishes the permanent governance framework for the Order Domain.

It defines:

- Enterprise security principles.
- Layered authorization.
- Canonical business roles.
- Permission taxonomy.
- Separation of duties.
- Approval authority.
- Delegation rules.
- Data visibility.
- Field-level protection.
- Sensitive operation controls.
- Emergency access governance.
- AI and integration authorization.
- External partner security.
- Audit and non-repudiation.
- Long-term security governance.

This Canon is the authoritative business security blueprint for all future implementations, including:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile applications.
- AI capabilities.
- External enterprise integrations.
- Future multi-company and multi-tenant expansion.

The business security architecture defined here is permanent. Future technologies must implement these governance rules without altering the certified business model.

# ORDER MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 6 — Events, Automations & Integration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Order Domain does not operate in isolation.

Every meaningful business action creates consequences across the enterprise.

For example:

- A confirmed order affects Production.
- A payment affects Finance.
- A dispatch affects Shipping.
- A completed delivery affects Reporting.
- A cancellation affects Inventory.

Rather than tightly coupling domains together, the enterprise communicates through **business events** and **business service contracts**.

This Canon defines the permanent event-driven business architecture for the Order Domain.

It specifies **what business facts are communicated**, **when they are communicated**, and **how collaborating domains respond**, independent of implementation technology.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A business event represents an immutable statement that something of business significance has occurred.

Examples:

- "Order Confirmed"
- "Production Released"
- "Payment Recorded"
- "Shipment Dispatched"

An event is **not**:

- a user interface action,
- a database trigger,
- a programming callback,
- or a transport protocol.

It is a permanent business fact.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

Every event must satisfy the following principles:

### Business Meaning

Each event describes a completed business occurrence.

---

### Immutability

Once published, an event is never modified.

Corrections are represented by new events.

---

### Single Publication

A business occurrence results in one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented by policy.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Business identity.
- Timestamp.
- Originating actor or service.
- Related business entity.
- Correlation identifier.
- Business context.

---

### Technology Independence

Events describe business semantics rather than implementation details.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Order Events

The Order Domain publishes a stable catalog of business events.

## Commercial Events

- Order Draft Created
- Order Updated
- Quote Generated
- Quote Revised
- Quote Approved
- Quote Rejected
- Order Confirmed
- Order Cancelled
- Order Reopened (policy-controlled)

---

## Approval Events

- Approval Requested
- Approval Granted
- Approval Rejected
- Approval Delegated
- Approval Escalated

---

## Planning Events

- Planning Requested
- Capacity Allocated
- Materials Verified
- Ready for Production

---

## Production Events

- Production Released
- Production Started
- Production Paused
- Production Resumed
- Production Completed

---

## Quality Events

- Inspection Started
- Inspection Passed
- Inspection Failed
- Rework Requested
- Rework Completed

---

## Dispatch Events

- Dispatch Requested
- Shipment Prepared
- Shipment Dispatched
- Tracking Assigned

---

## Delivery Events

- Delivery Confirmed
- Delivery Exception Reported
- Customer Acceptance Recorded

---

## Financial Events

- Payment Received
- Invoice Generated
- Refund Requested
- Refund Approved
- Refund Completed

---

## Closure Events

- Order Closed
- Order Archived

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Events are published only after the associated business action has been successfully completed.

Examples:

- "Order Confirmed" is published only after confirmation has been accepted by business rules.
- "Shipment Dispatched" is published only after custody has transferred to the carrier.
- "Order Closed" is published only after all closure gates have been satisfied.

Failed or rejected operations do not publish completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Each event follows a controlled lifecycle:

1. Business action requested.
2. Validation completed.
3. Business transaction committed.
4. Audit record created.
5. Canonical event published.
6. Authorized consumers process the event.
7. Monitoring confirms processing status.

This sequence ensures that published events always represent committed business facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Business events may be consumed by other enterprise domains.

Examples include:

| Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|--------|--------------------------|
| Order Confirmed | Production, Inventory, Finance, Reporting |
| Ready for Production | Production |
| Production Completed | Quality, Dispatch |
| Shipment Dispatched | Shipping, Customer Communication, Reporting |
| Delivery Confirmed | Finance, Reporting, Customer Success |
| Order Closed | Reporting, Analytics, Archive |

Consumers act on the event according to their own business responsibilities while preserving domain ownership.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every event communicates sufficient business information to identify and understand the occurrence.

Canonical elements include:

- Event identity.
- Event type.
- Business entity identity.
- Correlation identifier.
- Event timestamp.
- Business actor.
- Business role.
- Company or business unit.
- Lifecycle state.
- Business reason (where applicable).

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded from the Canon.

---

# 6.9 Business Automation Principles

Automation supports business execution but does not replace business policy.

Every automation must be:

- deterministic,
- auditable,
- reversible where appropriate,
- governed by policy,
- observable.

Automations never bypass mandatory approvals or operational gates.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Automations

Illustrative automations include:

### Commercial

- Generate quotation document.
- Notify customer after quotation approval.
- Schedule quotation expiration reminder.

---

### Operational

- Request inventory reservation after order confirmation.
- Initiate production planning.
- Generate production work package.
- Notify planner of material shortages.

---

### Quality

- Create quality inspection task after production completion.
- Escalate repeated inspection failures.

---

### Dispatch

- Generate shipment documentation.
- Request courier booking.
- Notify customer with tracking information.

---

### Financial

- Generate invoice after policy-defined milestone.
- Notify finance of overdue payment.
- Trigger refund workflow after approval.

---

### Closure

- Archive completed orders according to retention policy.
- Publish business intelligence metrics.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Canon recognizes two collaboration patterns:

## Orchestration

A coordinating business service directs a sequence of business activities across multiple domains.

Suitable for:

- complex approval flows,
- fulfillment coordination,
- closure processes.

---

## Choreography

Independent domains respond to published business events according to their own responsibilities.

Suitable for:

- notifications,
- reporting,
- analytics,
- customer communications.

The chosen pattern depends on business responsibility, not technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The Order Domain integrates with other enterprise domains through published business contracts.

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|--------|------------------|
| CRM | Lead conversion and sales context |
| Customer | Customer identity and contact information |
| Personalization | Artwork, assets, proof approval |
| Inventory | Material reservation and availability |
| Production | Manufacturing planning and execution |
| Finance | Payments, invoicing, refunds |
| Shipping | Shipment preparation and delivery |
| Reporting | Operational and executive analytics |
| Notification | Internal and customer communications |
| AI Services | Recommendations, forecasting, anomaly detection |

The Order Domain requests or publishes business information but does not assume ownership of another domain's data.

---

# 6.13 External Enterprise Integrations

The Canon supports controlled integration with external systems, including:

- E-commerce platforms.
- Marketplaces.
- Payment providers.
- Courier networks.
- Accounting platforms.
- CRM systems.
- Manufacturing equipment.
- AI decision-support services.
- Government and compliance services where applicable.

External systems interact only through governed business contracts.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Business failures are classified and handled consistently.

Examples:

### Validation Failure

The requested action violates business rules.

No event is published.

---

### Dependency Failure

A collaborating domain cannot complete its responsibility.

Business policy determines whether to:

- retry,
- wait,
- escalate,
- or compensate.

---

### Communication Failure

Business completion has occurred, but an integration channel is temporarily unavailable.

The event remains pending for controlled delivery according to enterprise policy.

---

### Policy Failure

Required approvals or operational gates are not satisfied.

Business progression stops until the condition is resolved.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries are governed by business policy.

Repeated attempts must not create duplicate business outcomes.

Where partial cross-domain activity has occurred, compensation follows explicit business rules rather than silently reversing history.

Compensation actions create new business events and remain fully auditable.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Business events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Existing event semantics remain stable.
- Changes preserve backward compatibility where feasible.
- Deprecated events remain supported during defined transition periods.
- Consumers adopt new versions through controlled migration.

---

# 6.17 Observability

Enterprise operations require visibility into event processing.

Monitoring includes:

- Event publication status.
- Consumer processing status.
- Processing failures.
- Retry activity.
- Escalations.
- Latency trends.
- Business throughput.

Operational monitoring supports reliability without changing business semantics.

---

# 6.18 Integration Security

Business integrations follow the enterprise security model established in Stage 5.

Requirements include:

- Authenticated identities.
- Authorized operations.
- Auditable interactions.
- Controlled data exposure.
- Principle of least privilege.
- Policy-governed access.

Security remains consistent across internal and external integrations.

---

# 6.19 Governance

The event architecture is governed by the following permanent principles:

- Events represent completed business facts.
- Event definitions are business-owned.
- Integrations depend on published contracts.
- Automation respects business policy.
- Domain ownership remains explicit.
- Cross-domain collaboration remains loosely coupled.
- All event evolution follows controlled governance.

---

# 6.20 Stage 6 Certification

The Events, Automations & Integration Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Order Domain.

It defines:

- Business event philosophy.
- Canonical event catalog.
- Event publication rules.
- Event lifecycle.
- Consumer responsibilities.
- Automation principles.
- Orchestration and choreography models.
- Cross-domain integration.
- External enterprise contracts.
- Failure handling.
- Retry and compensation.
- Event versioning.
- Observability.
- Integration security.
- Governance standards.

This Canon is the authoritative integration blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile applications.
- AI services.
- Marketplace and partner integrations.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The business event architecture defined here is permanent. Future technologies may change transport mechanisms, messaging platforms, or implementation patterns, but every implementation must preserve the certified business events, governance rules, and integration contracts defined in this Canon.

# ORDER MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 7 — UI & UX Canon

---

# 7.1 Purpose

The Order Domain is the operational center of GiftHatkeOS.

Its user experience must enable employees to execute business processes accurately, efficiently, and consistently across every supported platform.

This Canon defines the permanent business interaction model for the Order Domain. It is independent of any specific technology, framework, device, or visual design system.

The Canon specifies **how users interact with the business**, not how software is implemented.

---

# 7.2 UX Philosophy

The Order Domain user experience is governed by the following principles:

### Business First

Interfaces are designed around business workflows rather than technical structures.

---

### Role-Oriented

Each user sees the information and actions required for their business responsibilities.

---

### Progressive Disclosure

Present essential information first.

Advanced details are available when needed without overwhelming the user.

---

### Context Preservation

Users should remain within their current business context whenever possible.

Navigation should minimize unnecessary context switching.

---

### Predictability

The same business action always behaves consistently.

---

### Efficiency

Common tasks require the fewest practical interactions while preserving business controls.

---

### Transparency

Users understand:

- Current order state.
- Available actions.
- Required approvals.
- Pending operational work.
- Next business steps.

---

# 7.3 Information Architecture

The Order Domain is organized into consistent business workspaces.

Primary workspaces include:

- Order Dashboard
- Order List
- Order Workspace
- Customer Context
- Commercial Information
- Production Context
- Financial Context
- Shipping Context
- Activity Timeline
- Attachments
- Audit History
- Reports

Each workspace serves a distinct business purpose and avoids duplication of responsibility.

---

# 7.4 Navigation Model

Navigation follows a hierarchical structure:

Enterprise Navigation

↓

Order Module

↓

Business Workspace

↓

Business Context

↓

Specific Business Task

Users should never be required to understand technical implementation details to complete business operations.

---

# 7.5 Order Dashboard

The dashboard provides an operational overview rather than detailed editing.

Typical content includes:

- Orders awaiting confirmation.
- Orders awaiting approval.
- Orders ready for production.
- Orders in production.
- Quality exceptions.
- Dispatch queue.
- Delayed orders.
- Today's operational workload.
- Key performance indicators.
- Recent activity.

The dashboard emphasizes monitoring and prioritization.

---

# 7.6 Order List Workspace

The list workspace is the primary operational control surface.

Capabilities include:

- Search.
- Filter.
- Sort.
- Group.
- Saved views.
- Bulk operations (policy-controlled).
- Quick previews.
- Status indicators.
- Assignment visibility.

List presentation must scale from small businesses to enterprise volumes without altering business behavior.

---

# 7.7 Order Workspace

The Order Workspace is the authoritative environment for a single order.

It consolidates all relevant business information while maintaining clear domain boundaries.

Recommended sections include:

- Order Summary
- Customer Information
- Products & Configuration
- Pricing & Commercial Details
- Personalization
- Production Readiness
- Production Status
- Quality Status
- Shipping Information
- Financial Summary
- Activity Timeline
- Documents & Attachments
- Audit History

Each section displays information owned by its respective business domain.

---

# 7.8 Contextual Command Model

Available actions are determined by:

- Order lifecycle state.
- User role.
- Permissions.
- Business policy.
- Operational readiness.

Examples:

Draft:
- Edit.
- Add products.
- Generate quote.
- Delete (policy-controlled).

Confirmed:
- Submit to planning.
- Place on hold.
- View approvals.

Ready for Production:
- Release to production.

In Production:
- Record progress.
- Pause.
- Complete production.

Ready to Dispatch:
- Prepare shipment.
- Generate tracking.

Closed:
- View only.
- Archive (if authorized).

Unavailable actions should be hidden or clearly disabled with explanatory guidance.

---

# 7.9 Search and Discovery

Search is a primary navigation mechanism.

Users should locate orders using business-oriented criteria, including:

# ORDER MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 8 — Reporting & Business Intelligence Canon

---

# 8.1 Purpose

The Order Domain is the primary source of operational intelligence within GiftHatkeOS.

Every quotation, confirmation, production milestone, dispatch, delivery, cancellation, and closure contributes to the organization's understanding of business performance.

The purpose of Reporting & Business Intelligence is not merely to display numbers, but to transform business activity into actionable information for operational, tactical, and strategic decision-making.

This Canon defines the permanent reporting architecture for the Order Domain, independent of reporting tools, databases, visualization platforms, or analytics technologies.

---

# 8.2 Reporting Philosophy

Enterprise reporting is governed by the following principles:

### Single Version of Business Truth

All reports derive from the certified Order Domain and its governed business events.

Conflicting calculations are prohibited.

---

### Decision-Oriented

Reports exist to support business decisions rather than simply presenting data.

Every metric should answer a business question.

---

### Role-Relevant

Different business roles require different levels of information.

Executives require strategic insight.

Operational teams require actionable worklists.

---

### Traceable

Every reported figure must be traceable to its originating business records and audit history.

---

### Consistent

Business definitions remain identical across all reports.

An "Order Confirmed" means the same thing everywhere in the enterprise.

---

# 8.3 Reporting Layers

The reporting architecture is organized into four logical layers.

## Operational Reporting

Supports day-to-day execution.

Examples:

- Orders awaiting approval.
- Production queue.
- Dispatch queue.
- Overdue deliveries.

---

## Tactical Reporting

Supports departmental management.

Examples:

- Team performance.
- Sales conversion.
- Capacity utilization.
- Order aging.

---

## Strategic Reporting

Supports executive leadership.

Examples:

- Revenue trends.
- Customer growth.
- Business profitability.
- Operational efficiency.
- Service-level achievement.

---

## Analytical Reporting

Supports long-term planning.

Examples:

- Seasonality.
- Product demand.
- Customer lifetime value.
- Production forecasting.
- Resource planning.

---

# 8.4 Canonical KPI Framework

The Order Domain defines enterprise-standard Key Performance Indicators (KPIs).

## Commercial KPIs

- Total quotations.
- Quote conversion rate.
- Average quotation value.
- Average order value.
- Sales by representative.
- Sales by channel.
- Corporate vs. retail mix.
- Discount utilization.

---

## Operational KPIs

- Orders created.
- Orders confirmed.
- Orders awaiting production.
- Orders in production.
- Orders dispatched.
- Orders delivered.
- Orders closed.
- Orders on hold.
- Orders cancelled.

---

## Time-Based KPIs

- Quote response time.
- Approval turnaround time.
- Planning duration.
- Production cycle time.
- Quality inspection duration.
- Dispatch preparation time.
- Delivery lead time.
- Total order lifecycle duration.

---

## Quality KPIs

- First-pass quality rate.
- Rework percentage.
- Inspection failure rate.
- Production defect trends.
- Customer quality complaints.

---

## Financial KPIs

- Revenue.
- Outstanding payments.
- Refund volume.
- Credit adjustments.
- Margin (subject to authorization).
- Average revenue per order.

---

## Customer KPIs

- Repeat customers.
- Customer retention.
- Customer response time.
- Order satisfaction indicators.
- Complaint frequency.

---

# 8.5 Business Dimensions

Reports may analyze Order Domain information across standardized business dimensions.

Examples include:

- Date.
- Customer.
- Sales representative.
- Product.
- Product category.
- Branch.
- Company.
- Business unit.
- Territory.
- Channel.
- Campaign.
- Corporate account.
- Production facility.
- Delivery region.

Business dimensions remain stable across implementations.

---

Focus:

- Revenue.

- Enterprise trends.

- Quote pipeline.

Focus:

- Production readiness.

Focus:

---

## Dispatch Dashboard

Focus:

- Dispatch queue.

---

## Finance Dashboard

Focus:

- Revenue.

---

## Customer Success Dashboard

Examples:

- Awaiting Artwork.
- Awaiting Inventory.
- Ready for Production.
- Production Delayed.
- Awaiting Quality Inspection.
- Ready for Dispatch.
- Delivery Exceptions.
- Refund Pending.

Operational queues are prioritized by business urgency.

---

The reporting architecture preserves historical business information for long-term analysis.

Capabilities include:

- Year-over-year comparison.
- Month-over-month trends.
- Seasonal demand analysis.
- Historical production efficiency.
- Customer purchasing history.
- Business growth tracking.

Historical reports are based on immutable business records.

---

# 8.12 Security and Reporting

Reporting respects the security model established in Stage 5.

# 8.13 Data Quality

The value of reporting depends on the quality of business data.

- Verified master data.

Reports identify data quality issues but do not silently compensate for them.

# 8.14 AI and Business Intelligence

- Identifying anomalies.

- Explaining KPI changes.
- Recommending actions.
- Summarizing business performance.

AI-generated insights remain advisory unless enterprise policy explicitly authorizes automated business decisions.

---

# 8.15 Governance

The reporting architecture follows permanent governance principles:

- Business metrics are centrally defined.
- Calculations are standardized.
- Reports remain traceable.
- Historical records are preserved.
- KPI evolution follows controlled governance.
- Security applies equally to operational and analytical views.
- Reporting never changes operational business data.

---

The Reporting & Business Intelligence Canon establishes the permanent analytical architecture for the Order Domain.

- Reporting layers.

- Executive analytics.

Future reporting technologies may change visualization, storage, or analytical engines, but every implementation must preserve the certified business definitions, KPI semantics, governance rules, and decision-support principles established by this Canon.

## Stage 9 — Migration, Testing & Acceptance Canon

---

# 9.1 Purpose

The Order Domain is a business-critical capability. Any migration, enhancement, or replacement of its implementation must preserve certified business behavior.

This Canon defines the permanent framework for:

- Business migration.
- Validation.
- Verification.
- Testing.
- Acceptance.

- ERP9
- ERP10
- Future platform upgrades.
- Disaster recovery environments.
- Multi-company deployments.

---

# 9.2 Migration Philosophy

Migration is governed by one fundamental principle:

> **Business behavior is preserved; implementation may change.**

The objective of migration is not redesign but faithful reproduction of certified business capabilities.

Migration activities must maintain:

- Business semantics.
- Lifecycle rules.
- Approval policies.
- Security model.
- Reporting definitions.
- Audit integrity.
- Integration contracts.

---

# 9.3 Migration Scope

Migration covers:

### Business Configuration

- Order policies.
- Approval thresholds.
- Lifecycle configuration.
- Business calendars.
- Reference data.

---

### Master Data

- Customers.
- Products.
- Price lists.
- Tax rules.
- Shipping methods.
- Sales territories.

---

### Transactional Data

- Draft orders.
- Active orders.
- Completed orders.
- Cancelled orders.
- Historical orders.

---

### Business Documents

- Quotations.
- Invoices.
- Artwork references.
- Shipping documentation.
- Quality records.

---

### Audit Information

- State transitions.
- Approvals.
- Comments.
- Attachments.
- Business events.

---

### Reporting Structures

- KPI definitions.
- Historical metrics.
- Analytical dimensions.
- Saved operational views.

---

# 9.4 Migration Principles

Every migration follows these permanent principles.

## Completeness

All required business information is migrated.

No business-critical records are omitted.

---

## Accuracy

Migrated information must match certified source records.

---

## Traceability

Every migrated record can be traced back to its origin.

---

## Repeatability

Migration procedures produce consistent outcomes when repeated.

---

## Verifiability

Migration results are measurable and independently validated.

---

## Reversibility

Where practical, migration supports controlled rollback or recovery procedures.

---

# 9.5 Data Mapping Canon

Every migrated element has an explicit business mapping.

Mappings define:

- Source business entity.
- Target business entity.
- Business meaning.
- Transformation rules.
- Validation rules.
- Exception handling.

Implicit or undocumented mappings are prohibited.

---

# 9.6 Validation Gates

Migration progresses through formal validation gates.

## Gate 1 — Structural Validation

Confirms:

- Required entities exist.
- Mandatory relationships are preserved.
- Business identities remain unique.

---

## Gate 2 — Data Validation

Confirms:

- Values are complete.
- Required fields populated.
- Business constraints satisfied.

---

## Gate 3 — Lifecycle Validation

Confirms:

- Order states remain valid.
- Transition history preserved.
- State machine integrity maintained.

---

## Gate 4 — Security Validation

Confirms:

- Roles.
- Permissions.
- Delegations.
- Ownership.
- Visibility rules.

---

## Gate 5 — Integration Validation

Confirms:

- Cross-domain references remain valid.
- Event relationships preserved.
- Business contracts satisfied.

---

## Gate 6 — Reporting Validation

Confirms:

- KPI calculations unchanged.
- Historical reports consistent.
- Business dimensions preserved.

---

# 9.7 Testing Strategy

Testing verifies business correctness rather than implementation technology.

The testing hierarchy consists of:

### Business Rule Testing

Validation of business policies.

Examples:

- Discount approvals.
- Lifecycle transitions.
- Cancellation policy.

---

### Domain Service Testing

Validation of business operations.

Examples:

- Order confirmation.
- Quote conversion.
- Dispatch readiness.

---

### Workflow Testing

Validation of complete business processes.

Examples:

- Quote to cash.
- Order to delivery.
- Return and refund.

---

### Integration Testing

Validation of collaboration between enterprise domains.

Examples:

- CRM to Order.
- Order to Production.
- Order to Finance.
- Order to Shipping.

---

### Regression Testing

Verification that certified business behavior remains unchanged after modification.

Regression suites become part of the permanent certification process.

---

### Performance Testing

Verification that business processes operate within agreed operational expectations without compromising correctness.

---

### Security Testing

Verification of:

- Authorization.
- Role enforcement.
- Separation of duties.
- Sensitive data protection.
- Audit recording.

---

### Disaster Recovery Testing

Verification that business continuity procedures preserve certified business behavior following recovery.

---

# 9.8 Acceptance Criteria

A business capability is accepted only when:

- Functional requirements satisfied.
- Business policies enforced.
- Lifecycle integrity preserved.
- Security validated.
- Audit complete.
- Reports accurate.
- Integrations verified.
- Performance acceptable.
- Documentation updated.
- Business owners approve.

Technical completion alone is insufficient.

---

# 9.9 Business Acceptance Testing (BAT)

Business Acceptance Testing is conducted by business stakeholders rather than development teams.

BAT validates:

- Real business workflows.
- Operational usability.
- Policy compliance.
- End-user readiness.
- Business outcomes.

Successful BAT is required before production certification.

---

# 9.10 User Acceptance Testing (UAT)

Representative users validate that the implementation supports day-to-day operational responsibilities.

Typical participants include:

- Sales.
- Customer Success.
- Production.
- Inventory.
- Dispatch.
- Finance.
- Operations.
- Management.

UAT focuses on operational execution rather than implementation details.

---

# 9.11 Certification Gates

Every Order Domain implementation progresses through formal certification stages.

## Functional Certification

Business capabilities complete.

---

## Integration Certification

Cross-domain collaboration validated.

---

## Security Certification

Authorization model verified.

---

## Operational Certification

Production workflows validated.

---

## Reporting Certification

Business intelligence confirmed.

---

## Business Certification

Business owners formally approve operational readiness.

Only after Business Certification may the implementation proceed to production use.

---

# 9.12 Exception Management

Migration and testing exceptions are classified and managed through controlled governance.

Categories include:

- Data discrepancies.
- Business policy conflicts.
- Security exceptions.
- Integration failures.
- Performance concerns.
- Documentation gaps.

Each exception requires:

- Classification.

- Resolution plan.
- Approval where required.
- Audit recording.

---

# 9.13 Documentation Requirements

Every certified implementation maintains documentation covering:

- Business architecture.
- Configuration.
- Migration mappings.
- Test evidence.
- Acceptance records.
- Operational procedures.
- Release notes.
- Known limitations (if any).

Documentation forms part of the certification evidence.

---

# 9.14 Governance

Migration and certification are governed by the following permanent principles:

- Business continuity takes precedence over technical convenience.
- Certified behavior is preserved across implementations.
- Testing validates business outcomes.
- Acceptance is business-owned.
- Certification is evidence-based.
- Changes follow controlled governance.
- Historical certification records remain permanently available.

---

# 9.15 Stage 9 Certification

The Migration, Testing & Acceptance Canon establishes the permanent quality assurance and certification framework for the Order Domain.

It defines:

- Migration philosophy.
- Migration scope.
- Data mapping principles.
- Validation gates.
- Testing hierarchy.

- Business Acceptance Testing.

# PRODUCTION & MANUFACTURING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation & Business Scope

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The Production & Manufacturing Domain is responsible for transforming an approved customer order into a completed physical product that conforms to commercial commitments, engineering specifications, quality standards, and delivery expectations.

It represents the operational execution engine of GiftHatkeOS.

While the Order Domain governs **what the business promises**, the Production Domain governs **how the business fulfills that promise**.

The Production Domain is therefore responsible for:

- Manufacturing planning.
- Production execution.
- Work coordination.
- Resource utilization.
- Manufacturing traceability.
- Operational visibility.
- Production completion.

It is **not** responsible for:

- Sales.
- Commercial negotiation.
- Customer relationship management.
- Accounting.
- Shipping execution.
- Inventory ownership.

Those responsibilities remain within their respective enterprise domains.

---

# 1.2 Mission

The mission of the Production Domain is to ensure that every approved order is manufactured:

- correctly,
- consistently,
- efficiently,
- safely,
- on time,
- and with complete operational traceability.

Success is measured not only by production volume but by reliability, quality, predictability, and customer fulfillment.

---

# 1.3 Domain Vision

The Production Domain provides a standardized manufacturing framework capable of supporting:

- Single-machine workshops.
- Multi-machine production floors.
- Personalized manufacturing.
- Batch production.
- Make-to-order manufacturing.
- Future semi-automated production.
- Future AI-assisted scheduling.
- Future smart factory environments.

The business architecture remains constant while manufacturing technologies evolve.

---

# 1.4 Business Objectives

The Production Domain exists to achieve the following business objectives:

### Fulfillment

Transform confirmed customer demand into completed products.

---

### Predictability

Provide accurate planning, scheduling, and completion expectations.

---

### Efficiency

Optimize utilization of:

- Machines.
- Operators.
- Materials.
- Time.
- Production capacity.

---

### Quality

Ensure manufacturing output satisfies approved quality standards before release.

---

### Traceability

Maintain complete visibility into:

- What was produced.
- Who produced it.
- When it was produced.
- How it was produced.
- Which resources were used.

---

### Continuous Improvement

Generate operational intelligence that supports process optimization without compromising business integrity.

---

# 1.5 Domain Boundaries

The Production Domain owns:

- Production planning.
- Manufacturing work execution.
- Work sequencing.
- Machine allocation.
- Operator assignment.
- Manufacturing progress.
- Production completion.
- Operational traceability.

The Production Domain does **not** own:

- Customer master data.
- Commercial pricing.
- Inventory valuation.
- Procurement.
- Financial accounting.
- Shipping.
- Human resource management.

---

# 1.6 Business Responsibilities

The Production Domain is responsible for:

### Planning

Preparing work for manufacturing.

---

### Scheduling

Determining production sequence and timing.

---

### Execution

Managing manufacturing operations.

---

### Resource Coordination

Assigning:

- Machines.
- Operators.
- Workstations.
- Production lines.

---

### Operational Monitoring

Tracking progress from release through completion.

---

### Production Evidence

Capturing manufacturing records required for audit, quality, and operational analysis.

---

### Manufacturing Completion

Formally declaring production complete and releasing the order to subsequent business processes.

---

# 1.7 Core Business Principles

The Production Domain operates under the following permanent principles.

### Customer Commitment First

Production fulfills confirmed customer commitments.

Manufacturing never begins without an authorized business trigger.

---

### Controlled Execution

Every manufacturing activity follows an approved operational workflow.

Unauthorized production is prohibited.

---

### Standardized Work

Operational procedures are standardized while allowing controlled product-specific variations.

---

### Traceable Manufacturing

Every production activity is attributable to:

- Order.
- Product.
- Machine.
- Operator.
- Time.
- Business event.

---

### Capacity Awareness

Production planning respects available manufacturing capacity and operational constraints.

---

### Quality Before Completion

Manufacturing completion requires successful quality validation according to enterprise policy.

---

### Continuous Visibility

Production status is continuously observable by authorized business stakeholders.

---

# 1.8 Manufacturing Scope

The Canon supports multiple manufacturing models, including:

### Make-to-Order (MTO)

Manufacture begins only after order confirmation.

This is the primary model for personalized products.

---

### Configure-to-Order (CTO)

Standard components with configurable customer-specific options.

---

### Batch Production

Groups of similar work executed together for operational efficiency.

---

### Prototype Production

Limited-run manufacturing for validation or customer approval.

---

### Rework

Controlled correction of products that fail quality requirements.

---

### Future Manufacturing Models

The architecture accommodates future expansion without altering core business principles.

---

# 1.9 Business Inputs

The Production Domain receives governed inputs from collaborating domains.

Typical inputs include:

From Order:

- Confirmed order.
- Product configuration.
- Delivery commitments.

From Personalization:

- Artwork.
- Customer assets.
- Production proof approvals.

From Inventory:

- Material availability.
- Reserved stock.
- Component readiness.

From Planning:

- Capacity allocation.
- Work priorities.

The Production Domain validates operational readiness before commencing work.

---

# 1.10 Business Outputs

The Production Domain produces governed outputs for the enterprise.

Examples include:

- Production release.
- Manufacturing progress.
- Completion confirmation.
- Machine utilization records.
- Labor activity.
- Quality handover.
- Dispatch readiness.
- Production metrics.
- Audit evidence.

These outputs become inputs for Quality, Shipping, Finance, and Reporting.

---

# 1.11 Enterprise Relationships

The Production Domain collaborates with:

| Domain | Relationship |
|---------|--------------|
| Order | Receives authorized production requests and fulfillment priorities |
| Personalization | Receives approved artwork and customization specifications |
| Inventory | Confirms material availability and consumption |
| Quality | Transfers completed work for inspection and disposition |
| Shipping | Releases finished goods for dispatch preparation |
| Finance | Supplies production milestones that may trigger financial events |
| Reporting | Provides operational metrics, throughput, and efficiency data |
| Notification | Generates production-related communications and alerts |
| AI Services | Supplies manufacturing data for recommendations, forecasting, and anomaly detection |

Ownership remains explicit. Production collaborates with these domains but does not assume responsibility for their business data.

---

# 1.12 Business Success Measures

The Production Domain contributes to enterprise success through measurable outcomes, including:

- On-time production completion.
- Schedule adherence.
- Throughput.
- Capacity utilization.
- First-pass quality rate.
- Rework percentage.
- Manufacturing lead time.
- Order fulfillment performance.
- Resource productivity.
- Production predictability.

The precise calculations are defined in the Reporting & Business Intelligence Canon while the business meaning is established here.

---

# 1.13 Long-Term Architectural Principles

The Production Domain is designed to remain valid across future evolution of the enterprise.

It supports:

- Additional manufacturing facilities.
- Multiple production lines.
- Distributed operations.
- Automated equipment.
- Robotics.
- IoT-enabled machines.
- AI-assisted scheduling.
- Predictive maintenance.
- Digital work instructions.

These future capabilities extend the certified architecture rather than replacing it.

---

# 1.14 Stage 1 Certification

The **Production & Manufacturing Enterprise Canon — Stage 1** establishes the permanent business foundation for the Production Domain.

It defines:

- Domain purpose.
- Mission.
- Vision.
- Business objectives.
- Domain boundaries.
- Core responsibilities.
- Manufacturing principles.
- Supported production models.
- Business inputs and outputs.
- Enterprise relationships.
- Success measures.
- Long-term architectural direction.

This Stage becomes the authoritative business foundation for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile manufacturing applications.
- AI-assisted manufacturing.
- Future smart factory capabilities.
- Enterprise expansion.

The Production Domain is hereby established as the permanent business capability responsible for converting certified customer commitments into controlled, traceable, and high-quality manufacturing outcomes.
