# QUALITY MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 4 — API Contracts & Domain Services

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The Quality Management Domain exposes its business capabilities through a stable set of **domain services**.

These services represent permanent business responsibilities—not REST APIs, SDKs, messaging protocols, database procedures, or implementation technologies.

Whether the future implementation uses:

- Apps Script
- Java
- .NET
- Go
- Python
- Node.js
- Cloud-native architecture
- Microservices
- Event-driven platforms
- AI orchestration
- Smart factory platforms

the business service contracts remain unchanged.

This Canon establishes the permanent service architecture for the Quality Management Domain.

---

# 4.2 Service Philosophy

The Quality Domain owns:

- Inspection governance.
- Quality standards.
- Non-conformance management.
- Quality disposition.
- Corrective and Preventive Actions (CAPA).
- Quality evidence.
- Quality analytics.

It does **not** own:

- Manufacturing execution.
- Inventory ownership.
- Procurement.
- Customer agreements.
- Shipping execution.
- Financial accounting.

The domain collaborates with those business areas through governed contracts.

Every service shall:

- Represent one business capability.
- Preserve explicit ownership.
- Enforce certified quality rules.
- Produce auditable outcomes.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 4.3 Service Landscape

The Quality Management Domain publishes the following canonical business services.

| Service | Business Responsibility |
|----------|-------------------------|
| Quality Standards Service | Govern enterprise quality standards |
| Inspection Planning Service | Define inspection plans and requirements |
| Inspection Execution Service | Execute governed inspections |
| Quality Evidence Service | Manage inspection evidence |
| Disposition Service | Issue official quality decisions |
| Non-Conformance Service | Manage quality deviations |
| CAPA Service | Govern corrective and preventive actions |
| Rework Governance Service | Coordinate rework authorization and verification |
| Supplier Quality Service | Evaluate supplier quality performance |
| Audit Service | Preserve quality history and audit records |
| Quality Intelligence Service | Publish enterprise quality metrics |

---

# 4.4 Quality Standards Service

## Purpose

Maintains the enterprise catalog of approved quality standards.

Responsibilities:

- Create quality standards.
- Review quality standards.
- Approve quality standards.
- Activate quality standards.
- Retire quality standards.

The service governs business standards rather than operational inspection activities.

---

# 4.5 Inspection Planning Service

Coordinates inspection preparation.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Inspection Plans.
- Define inspection scope.
- Assign inspection checklists.
- Define sampling methods.
- Define evidence requirements.
- Establish approval requirements.

The service standardizes inspection planning across the enterprise.

---

# 4.6 Inspection Execution Service

Coordinates governed inspection activities.

Responsibilities include:

- Start inspection.
- Record measurements.
- Record observations.
- Complete inspection.
- Submit for evaluation.

The service performs inspections but does not independently authorize product acceptance.

---

# 4.7 Quality Evidence Service

Maintains supporting inspection evidence.

Examples include:

- Inspection photographs.
- Measurement records.
- Test reports.
- Calibration references.
- Inspection notes.
- Customer-specific verification records.

Evidence remains permanently linked to inspection history.

---

# 4.8 Disposition Service

Issues official quality decisions.

Examples:

- Accept.
- Reject.
- Rework Required.
- Quarantine.
- Further Investigation Required.

Only this service may authorize official quality disposition.

---

# 4.9 Non-Conformance Service

Coordinates enterprise quality deviations.

Responsibilities:

- Register Non-Conformance.
- Classify issue.
- Assess impact.
- Assign ownership.
- Monitor resolution.
- Close issue.

The service governs investigation without executing manufacturing corrections.

---

# 4.10 CAPA Service

Coordinates continuous improvement.

Responsibilities:

- Register CAPA.
- Approve CAPA.
- Plan implementation.
- Verify effectiveness.
- Close CAPA.

Corrective and Preventive Actions remain independently governed.

---

# 4.11 Rework Governance Service

Coordinates Quality-owned rework governance.

Responsibilities:

- Create Rework Request.
- Approve rework.
- Monitor completion.
- Schedule verification.
- Approve successful verification.

Production performs rework.

Quality certifies successful completion.

---

# 4.12 Supplier Quality Service

Coordinates supplier quality evaluation.

Responsibilities:

- Evaluate supplier quality.
- Record supplier performance.
- Track supplier quality history.
- Recommend supplier improvement.
- Support supplier qualification.

Commercial supplier ownership remains within the Inventory & Procurement Domain.

---

# 4.13 Audit Service

Maintains immutable quality history.

Examples:

- Inspection history.
- Dispositions.
- CAPA history.
- Non-Conformance history.
- Rework history.
- Quality evidence.
- Audit findings.

Historical quality records remain append-only.

---

# 4.14 Quality Intelligence Service

Publishes governed enterprise quality information.

Responsibilities include:

- Quality KPIs.
- Defect trends.
- Inspection performance.
- Supplier quality metrics.
- CAPA effectiveness.
- Executive quality intelligence.

This service supports Reporting while preserving Quality ownership.

---

# 4.15 Canonical Business Operations

The domain publishes a stable catalog of business operations.

### Quality Standards

- Create Standard.
- Review Standard.
- Approve Standard.
- Activate Standard.
- Retire Standard.

---

### Inspection

- Create Inspection.
- Assign Inspector.
- Start Inspection.
- Record Evidence.
- Complete Inspection.
- Evaluate Inspection.

---

### Disposition

- Accept Product.
- Reject Product.
- Request Rework.
- Quarantine Product.
- Close Inspection.

---

### Non-Conformance

- Register Issue.
- Classify Issue.
- Assign Issue.
- Resolve Issue.
- Close Issue.

---

### CAPA

- Register CAPA.
- Approve CAPA.
- Implement CAPA.
- Verify Effectiveness.
- Close CAPA.

---

### Rework

- Create Rework Request.
- Approve Rework.
- Verify Rework.
- Close Rework.

---

### Supplier Quality

- Evaluate Supplier.
- Record Supplier Performance.
- Recommend Improvement.

---

### Audit

- Record Audit Finding.
- Assign Finding.
- Verify Resolution.
- Close Finding.

---

# 4.16 Commands and Queries

Business services are divided into two categories.

## Commands

Commands modify business state.

Examples:

- Start Inspection.
- Register Non-Conformance.
- Issue Disposition.
- Approve CAPA.

Commands:

- Validate policy.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish business events.

---

## Queries

Queries never modify business state.

Examples:

- Inspection Status.
- Quality Standard.
- Non-Conformance History.
- CAPA Status.
- Supplier Quality History.

Queries remain read-only.

---

# 4.17 Validation Framework

Every command performs mandatory validation.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

- Inspection exists.
- Standard exists.
- Product reference valid.
- Required evidence references valid.

---

### Operational Validation

- Required inspection assigned.
- Evidence complete.
- Measurements complete.
- Required approvals available.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

- Requested transition permitted.
- Operational gates satisfied.
- Business sequence preserved.

---

### Security Validation

- Authorized inspector.
- Required permissions.
- Separation of duties enforced.
- Delegation valid where applicable.

---

### Policy Validation

- Inspection policy.
- Sampling policy.
- CAPA policy.
- Supplier quality policy.
- Regulatory policy where applicable.

---

# 4.18 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical quality transaction.

Example:

Issue Quality Disposition:

- Validate inspection completion.
- Validate evidence.
- Validate approval requirements.
- Record disposition.
- Update inspection lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish business event.

If any required step fails, the quality record remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.19 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Complete Inspection.
- Issue Disposition.
- Register CAPA.
- Close Non-Conformance.
- Verify Rework.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate business outcomes.

---

# 4.20 Concurrency

Multiple users may participate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Inspectors.
- Quality managers.
- Production supervisors.
- CAPA coordinators.
- Auditors.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled updates.
- Prevention of inconsistent quality decisions.
- Preservation of audit integrity.

---

# 4.21 Error Classification

Quality services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Business information incomplete.

---

### Inspection Errors

Examples:

- Missing evidence.
- Required measurement absent.
- Inspection not assigned.

---

### Quality Policy Errors

Examples:

- Unauthorized disposition.
- Missing approval.
- Invalid sampling policy.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition prohibited.

---

### Dependency Errors

Collaborating domain unable to satisfy business contract.

Examples:

- Production not completed.
- Inventory unavailable for inspection.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Business failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

# 4.22 Cross-Domain Contracts

The Quality Domain collaborates with:

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Production | Receive completed work and communicate quality disposition |
| Inventory & Procurement | Coordinate inspection status for inbound materials and inventory release |
| Shipping | Release accepted products for dispatch preparation |
| Finance | Supply quality-related information supporting governed financial processes where applicable |
| Reporting | Publish quality intelligence |
| Notification | Generate inspection and quality alerts |
| AI Services | Supply inspection data for predictive quality, anomaly detection, and continuous improvement |

Ownership boundaries remain explicit.

---

# 4.23 Service Governance

The Quality service architecture follows permanent principles:

- Stable business contracts.
- Explicit domain ownership.
- Backward-compatible evolution where feasible.
- Consistent business semantics.
- Technology-independent implementation.
- Controlled governance of service changes.

---

# 4.24 Stage 4 Certification

The **Quality Management Enterprise Canon — Stage 4** establishes the permanent business service architecture for the Quality Management Domain.

It defines:

- Service landscape.
- Domain service responsibilities.
- Canonical business operations.
- Command and query separation.
- Validation framework.
- Transaction boundaries.
- Idempotency.
- Concurrency principles.
- Error taxonomy.
- Cross-domain collaboration.
- Service governance.

This Canon becomes the authoritative quality service blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile quality applications.
- AI-assisted inspection.
- Smart factory quality systems.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The Quality service architecture defined here is permanent. Future quality management platforms, computer vision systems, AI inspection engines, automation technologies, and cloud architectures may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified business services, operational semantics, validation rules, and governance established by this Canon. memcite

# QUALITY MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 5 — Permissions, Roles & Security Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Quality Management Domain protects one of the enterprise's most critical responsibilities: determining whether materials, components, work-in-progress, and finished products satisfy approved business and quality requirements.

An incorrect quality decision may result in:

- Defective products reaching customers.
- Unnecessary rejection of acceptable products.
- Production disruption.
- Regulatory non-compliance.
- Warranty claims.
- Financial loss.
- Loss of customer trust.

This Canon establishes the permanent governance model for authorization, accountability, inspection independence, quality evidence protection, and quality decision integrity.

The security model is business-driven and technology-independent.

---

# 5.2 Security Philosophy

Quality operations follow these permanent principles.

### Independent Quality Authority

Quality decisions remain independent from Production, Procurement, and Shipping.

Operational pressure must never override governed quality decisions.

---

### Evidence-Based Decisions

Every quality decision is supported by objective business evidence.

---

### Accountability

Every inspection, disposition, and CAPA activity has one accountable business actor.

---

### Least Privilege

Users receive only the permissions required to perform their quality responsibilities.

---

### Separation of Duties

Critical quality decisions require independent authority.

---

### Immutable Quality History

Historical inspection records, evidence, and dispositions remain permanently protected.

---

# 5.3 Authorization Layers

Authorization is evaluated through multiple business layers.

## Layer 1 — Identity

Verified identity:

- Employee.
- Quality contractor.
- External auditor.
- Supplier quality representative.
- Service account.
- Future AI inspection agent.

---

## Layer 2 — Business Role

Every actor performs work through an approved enterprise role.

---

## Layer 3 — Permissions

Roles grant explicit quality capabilities.

---

## Layer 4 — Operational Context

Authorization may depend upon:

- Company.
- Manufacturing site.
- Product family.
- Inspection type.
- Supplier.
- Regulatory scope.
- Business unit.

---

## Layer 5 — Business State

Certain actions are permitted only during specific lifecycle states.

Example:

Only completed inspections may receive an official Quality Disposition.

---

## Layer 6 — Policy Controls

Additional governance may depend upon:

- Safety-critical products.
- Regulatory requirements.
- High-value customer orders.
- Controlled product categories.
- Customer-specific quality agreements.
- Enterprise approval thresholds.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Quality Roles

## Quality Director

Responsibilities:

- Enterprise quality governance.
- Quality strategy.
- Regulatory oversight.
- Approval of quality policies.
- Escalation authority.

Cannot:

- Modify production history.
- Alter financial records.

---

## Quality Manager

Responsibilities:

- Inspection governance.
- Quality approvals.
- CAPA oversight.
- Audit management.
- Continuous improvement.

Cannot:

- Modify manufacturing execution records.

---

## Quality Supervisor

Responsibilities:

- Daily inspection coordination.
- Inspector assignments.
- Operational quality monitoring.
- Inspection workload management.

Cannot:

- Override enterprise quality policy without authorization.

---

## Quality Inspector

Responsibilities:

- Execute inspections.
- Record measurements.
- Collect quality evidence.
- Submit inspection results.

Cannot:

- Override approved Quality Standards.
- Independently change enterprise quality policies.

---

## CAPA Coordinator

Responsibilities:

- Corrective Action coordination.
- Preventive Action coordination.
- Effectiveness reviews.
- CAPA reporting.

Cannot:

- Modify historical inspection evidence.

---

## Supplier Quality Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Supplier quality evaluation.
- Supplier inspections.
- Supplier performance monitoring.
- Supplier improvement coordination.

Cannot:

- Modify procurement contracts.

---

## Quality Auditor

Responsibilities:

- Internal audits.
- Compliance verification.
- Audit findings.
- Governance assessment.

Cannot:

- Modify operational quality records during audit activities.

---

## Laboratory Technician (where applicable)

Responsibilities:

- Laboratory testing.
- Measurement recording.
- Technical analysis.
- Test evidence generation.

Cannot:

- Issue final Quality Disposition unless authorized.

---

## Operations Manager

Responsibilities:

- Review enterprise quality performance.
- Coordinate operational improvements.
- Approve business escalations where applicable.

Cannot:

- Override certified quality decisions.

---

## Quality Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Quality reference data.
- Inspection templates.
- Quality Standards maintenance.
- Configuration administration.

Cannot:

- Alter certified inspection history.

---

## Auditor

Read-only access to:

- Inspection history.
- Quality evidence.
- CAPA records.
- Audit findings.
- Non-Conformance history.
- Quality metrics.

No modification authority.

---

# 5.5 Permission Taxonomy

Permissions are organized by business capability.

## Quality Standards

- Create Standard.
- Review Standard.
- Approve Standard.
- Activate Standard.
- Retire Standard.

---

## Inspection

- Create Inspection.
- Assign Inspection.
- Perform Inspection.
- Record Evidence.
- Complete Inspection.

---

## Quality Disposition

- Issue Acceptance.
- Issue Rejection.
- Request Rework.
- Quarantine Product.
- Close Inspection.

---

## Non-Conformance

- Register Non-Conformance.
- Classify Issue.
- Assign Issue.
- Resolve Issue.
- Close Issue.

---

## CAPA

- Register CAPA.
- Approve CAPA.
- Implement CAPA.
- Verify Effectiveness.
- Close CAPA.

---

## Supplier Quality

- Evaluate Supplier.
- Record Supplier Performance.
- Recommend Supplier Improvement.

---

## Audit

- Create Audit Finding.
- Assign Audit Finding.
- Verify Resolution.
- Close Audit Finding.

---

## Administration

- Configure Quality Policies.
- Maintain Inspection Templates.
- Maintain Reference Data.

---

# 5.6 Separation of Duties (SoD)

Critical quality activities are intentionally divided.

Examples:

- A Quality Inspector cannot approve the Quality Standard against which they are performing inspections when policy requires independent approval.
- A Quality Inspector cannot approve their own CAPA effectiveness review if enterprise policy requires independent verification.
- A Production Supervisor cannot issue an official Quality Disposition for work they supervised unless enterprise governance explicitly permits it.
- A CAPA Coordinator cannot independently close a CAPA when effectiveness verification requires a separate reviewer.
- A Quality Administrator cannot alter inspection history while maintaining Quality Standards.

These controls reduce operational bias, error, fraud, and compliance risk.

---

# 5.7 Approval Authority

Business policy determines approval authority.

Examples requiring elevated approval include:

- Safety-critical product acceptance.
- Major Non-Conformances.
- High-impact CAPA.
- Supplier suspension recommendations.
- Regulatory deviations.
- Quality policy exceptions.
- Controlled product releases.

Approval authority is governed by policy rather than individual identity.

---

# 5.8 Delegation

Temporary delegation supports business continuity.

Delegations specify:

- Delegating authority.
- Delegate.
- Authorized scope.
- Effective period.
- Business justification.

Delegated quality activities remain fully auditable.

---

# 5.9 Data Visibility

Quality information is visible according to business responsibility.

Examples:

Quality Inspector:

- Assigned inspections.
- Related evidence.
- Assigned Non-Conformances.

Quality Supervisor:

- Inspection workload.
- Team performance.
- Operational quality status.

Quality Manager:

- Enterprise quality information.
- CAPA.
- Supplier quality.
- Audit status.

Executive:

- Strategic quality intelligence.

Auditor:

- Historical quality records.

Visibility may additionally be restricted by:

- Company.
- Manufacturing site.
- Product category.
- Regulatory program.
- Customer agreement.
- Business unit.

---

# 5.10 Field-Level Security

Certain quality information requires elevated authorization.

Examples:

- Regulatory observations.
- Customer complaint investigations.
- Root cause analyses.
- CAPA effectiveness evaluations.
- Supplier audit comments.
- Internal quality assessments.
- Controlled product specifications.
- Sensitive laboratory measurements.

Access to an Inspection does not automatically grant access to every field.

---

# 5.11 Sensitive Operations

Examples include:

- Retroactive quality disposition.
- Reopening closed inspections.
- Overriding mandatory inspection requirements.
- Closing a Major Non-Conformance without approved resolution.
- Modifying Quality Standards after activation.
- Deleting quality evidence where enterprise policy permits.
- Releasing quarantined products by exception.

These operations require documented justification, elevated authorization, and enhanced audit controls.

---

# 5.12 Emergency ("Break-Glass") Access

Emergency access may be granted only under exceptional operational circumstances.

Requirements include:

- Authorized approval.
- Time-limited duration.
- Recorded business justification.
- Enhanced audit logging.
- Automatic expiration.
- Mandatory post-event review.

Emergency authority never becomes permanent operational authority.

---

# 5.13 Inspection Integrity

Inspection governance follows certified business controls.

Policies require:

- Qualified inspectors.
- Approved Inspection Plans.
- Controlled evidence collection.
- Independent evaluation where required.
- Protected inspection history.
- Controlled Quality Disposition.
- Verified CAPA closure.

Inspection integrity protects enterprise quality decisions from operational bias.

---

# 5.14 AI and Automation Governance

Future AI inspection systems, computer vision platforms, autonomous measurement systems, and quality recommendation engines operate under the same governance principles as human actors.

Requirements include:

- Explicit identity.
- Assigned business role.
- Limited authority.
- Full auditability.
- Policy-based permissions.
- Human oversight where required.

Automation enhances inspection capability without redefining certified quality governance.

---

# 5.15 Audit and Non-Repudiation

Every protected quality activity records:

- Actor identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous lifecycle state.
- New lifecycle state.
- Inspection reference.
- Product or material reference.
- Business justification (where required).
- Related approvals.
- Supporting evidence references.

Audit records are immutable and support compliance, regulatory review, customer assurance, and continuous improvement.

---

# 5.16 Security Governance

The Quality security model follows these permanent governance principles:

- Quality permissions are business-defined.
- Inspection independence is preserved.
- Roles aggregate permissions without redefining quality policy.
- Authorization decisions are deterministic and auditable.
- Sensitive quality operations require enhanced controls.
- Security evolves only through controlled governance.
- Implementation technologies enforce—but never redefine—the certified security model.

---

# 5.17 Stage 5 Certification

The **Quality Management Enterprise Canon — Stage 5** establishes the permanent security and authorization framework for the Quality Management Domain.

It defines:

- Quality security philosophy.
- Layered authorization model.
- Canonical business roles.
- Permission taxonomy.
- Separation of duties.
- Approval authority.
- Delegation.
- Data visibility.
- Field-level protection.
- Sensitive quality operations.
- Emergency access governance.
- Inspection integrity.
- AI and automation governance.
- Audit and non-repudiation.
- Security governance.

This Canon becomes the authoritative security blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile quality applications.
- AI-assisted inspection.
- Smart factory quality systems.
- Future enterprise quality expansion.

The security architecture defined here is permanent. Future Quality Management Systems (QMS), computer vision platforms, AI inspection technologies, laboratory systems, and automation frameworks must implement these governance principles without altering the certified business security model. memcite

---

# QUALITY MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 6 — Events, Automations & Integration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Quality Management Domain is the enterprise's authoritative source of truth for inspection outcomes, quality decisions, non-conformance management, and continuous improvement.

Every significant quality activity generates business events that coordinate downstream enterprise operations.

Examples include:

- Inspection completed.
- Product accepted.
- Product rejected.
- Rework required.
- CAPA initiated.
- Supplier quality issue detected.

These events synchronize enterprise behavior while preserving Quality's independent authority.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Quality Management Domain.

It defines:

- Business events.
- Event publication rules.
- Automation governance.
- Cross-domain orchestration.
- Integration boundaries.

It intentionally avoids prescribing messaging technologies, middleware, or implementation patterns.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A Quality event represents a completed business fact.

Examples:

- Inspection Assigned.
- Inspection Completed.
- Quality Disposition Issued.
- Non-Conformance Registered.
- CAPA Approved.
- Rework Verified.

Events communicate **what has occurred**, not **how software processed it**.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business occurrence.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve business semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Quality Domain follows these permanent principles.

### Business Significance

Only meaningful quality activities become canonical business events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed business occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through business governance.

---

### Immutable History

Published events are never modified.

Corrections are represented through subsequent business events.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Quality events originate only from the Quality Management Domain.

No collaborating domain may publish quality events on its behalf.

---

### Auditability

Each event records:

- Event identity.
- Timestamp.
- Inspection reference.
- Product or material reference.
- Business actor.
- Business role.
- Correlation identifier.
- Related Work Order, Purchase Order, or Material (where applicable).

---

# 6.4 Canonical Quality Events

## Quality Standard Events

- Quality Standard Created.
- Quality Standard Approved.
- Quality Standard Activated.
- Quality Standard Superseded.
- Quality Standard Retired.

---

## Inspection Events

- Inspection Planned.
- Inspector Assigned.
- Inspection Started.
- Inspection Completed.
- Inspection Closed.

---

## Evidence Events

- Quality Evidence Recorded.
- Measurement Recorded.
- Inspection Evidence Verified.

---

## Disposition Events

- Product Accepted.
- Product Rejected.
- Rework Required.
- Product Quarantined.
- Product Released After Approved Exception (policy-controlled).

---

## Non-Conformance Events

- Non-Conformance Detected.
- Non-Conformance Validated.
- Non-Conformance Classified.
- Non-Conformance Closed.

---

## CAPA Events

- CAPA Registered.
- CAPA Approved.
- CAPA Implementation Started.
- CAPA Verified.
- CAPA Closed.

---

## Rework Events

- Rework Requested.
- Rework Approved.
- Rework Completed by Production.
- Rework Successfully Verified.

---

## Supplier Quality Events

- Supplier Quality Issue Detected.
- Supplier Improvement Requested.
- Supplier Quality Review Completed.

---

## Audit Events

- Audit Finding Recorded.
- Audit Finding Assigned.
- Audit Finding Verified.
- Audit Finding Closed.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Business events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding business activity.

Examples:

- **Inspection Completed** is published only after required evidence and evaluation are complete.
- **Product Accepted** is published only after an official Quality Disposition has been issued.
- **CAPA Closed** is published only after effectiveness verification has succeeded.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Quality event follows the same sequence:

1. Business request received.
2. Business validation completed.
3. Quality transaction committed.
4. Audit record created.
5. Canonical event published.
6. Authorized consumers process the event.
7. Monitoring records processing outcomes.

Published events therefore represent authoritative business facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Quality events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Quality Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|---------------|--------------------------|
| Product Accepted | Inventory & Procurement, Shipping, Reporting |
| Product Rejected | Production, Reporting, Notification |
| Rework Required | Production, Reporting |
| Inspection Completed | Reporting, Notification |
| Non-Conformance Detected | Production, CAPA Analytics, Notification |
| CAPA Approved | Production, Inventory & Procurement, Reporting |
| Supplier Quality Issue Detected | Inventory & Procurement, Reporting |
| Product Quarantined | Inventory & Procurement, Shipping |
| Audit Finding Closed | Reporting, Governance |

Consumer domains respond to Quality events without assuming ownership of quality business rules.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every Quality event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event identity.
- Event type.
- Inspection reference.
- Product reference.
- Material reference (where applicable).
- Work Order reference (where applicable).
- Supplier reference (where applicable).
- Business actor.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Company.
- Correlation identifier.
- Business reason (where applicable).

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Quality Automation Principles

Automation improves operational efficiency while respecting certified quality governance.

Every automation must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Observable.
- Reversible where appropriate.

Automation must never bypass:

- Inspection requirements.
- Quality approvals.
- Regulatory controls.
- Security policies.
- Operational gates.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Quality Automations

Examples include:

### Inspection

- Automatically schedule required inspections after Production completion.
- Recommend inspectors based on qualifications and workload.
- Notify inspectors of pending assignments.

---

### Non-Conformance

- Escalate critical defects immediately.
- Suggest defect classifications based on approved taxonomy.
- Detect recurring quality issues requiring investigation.

---

### CAPA

- Recommend Corrective Actions using historical effectiveness data.
- Notify responsible owners of approaching CAPA deadlines.
- Escalate overdue effectiveness reviews.

---

### Supplier Quality

- Notify Procurement of declining supplier quality performance.
- Recommend supplier audits when thresholds are exceeded.

---

### Production Support

- Notify Production when rework has been authorized.
- Notify Production immediately after successful rework verification.

---

### Shipping Support

- Release accepted products for dispatch preparation.
- Prevent shipment of rejected or quarantined products.

---

### Reporting

- Refresh quality dashboards.
- Update defect trends.
- Publish enterprise quality KPIs.

---

### Notifications

- Notify management of major Non-Conformances.
- Alert Quality Managers of overdue inspections.
- Notify Operations of critical customer-impacting quality issues.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Quality Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized quality governance is required.

Examples:

- Inspection execution.
- Quality Disposition.
- CAPA approval.
- Rework verification.

---

## Choreography

Used where independent domains respond to Quality events.

Examples:

- Reporting.
- Notifications.
- Inventory release.
- Shipping preparation.
- AI recommendations.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The Quality Management Domain integrates with other enterprise domains through governed business contracts.

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Production | Receive completed work, communicate dispositions, govern rework |
| Inventory & Procurement | Control inspection status for materials and inventory release |
| Shipping | Release accepted products for dispatch preparation and prevent shipment of rejected products |
| Finance | Supply quality-related information supporting governed financial processes where applicable |
| Reporting | Publish quality intelligence |
| Notification | Generate inspection and quality alerts |
| AI Services | Supply inspection data for predictive quality, anomaly detection, and continuous improvement |

Each domain remains independently governed.

---

# 6.13 External Integrations

The Canon supports future integration with:

- Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS).
- Computer Vision inspection platforms.
- Coordinate Measuring Machines (CMM).
- Industrial vision systems.
- Digital measurement equipment.
- Regulatory compliance systems.
- Customer quality portals.
- Supplier quality portals.
- Smart factory platforms.
- Industrial IoT quality monitoring.

These integrations consume or publish certified business events without redefining Quality business semantics.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Quality failures are categorized consistently.

### Validation Failure

Business prerequisites are not satisfied.

No completion event is published.

---

### Operational Failure

Inspection or quality activity cannot proceed.

Examples:

- Required evidence missing.
- Measurement equipment unavailable.
- Inspection interrupted.

---

### Dependency Failure

A collaborating domain cannot satisfy its business contract.

Examples:

- Production not completed.
- Material unavailable.
- Required documentation missing.

---

### Communication Failure

Business completion occurred but downstream notification or integration is temporarily unavailable.

Events remain pending for governed delivery.

---

### Policy Failure

Business rules prevent operational progression.

Examples:

- Required approval missing.
- Regulatory restriction.
- Inspector qualification requirements not met.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries follow controlled business policy.

Repeated processing must never create:

- Duplicate inspections.
- Duplicate Quality Dispositions.
- Duplicate CAPA records.
- Duplicate Non-Conformance records.

Where business compensation is required, corrective actions generate new business events while preserving historical accuracy.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Quality events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Stable business semantics.
- Backward compatibility where feasible.
- Managed deprecation.
- Controlled consumer migration.

Business meaning remains consistent across versions.

---

# 6.17 Observability

The enterprise monitors Quality event processing through:

- Event publication status.
- Consumer processing status.
- Processing latency.
- Failed deliveries.
- Retry activity.
- Inspection throughput.
- Defect event volume.
- CAPA effectiveness trends.
- Quality exception frequency.

Observability supports operational reliability without altering business behavior.

---

# 6.18 Integration Security

Quality integrations comply with the Security Canon.

Requirements include:

- Authenticated identities.
- Authorized operations.
- Least privilege.
- Controlled data exposure.
- Full auditability.
- Policy-based access.

Internal and external integrations follow identical governance principles.

---

# 6.19 Governance

The event architecture follows these permanent principles:

- Quality events represent completed business facts.
- Event definitions are owned by the Quality Management Domain.
- Automation respects quality policy.
- Integrations consume certified business contracts.
- Domain ownership remains explicit.
- Cross-domain collaboration remains loosely coupled.
- Event evolution follows controlled governance.

---

# 6.20 Stage 6 Certification

The **Quality Management Enterprise Canon — Stage 6** establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Quality Management Domain.

It defines:

- Quality event philosophy.
- Canonical event catalog.
- Event publication rules.
- Event lifecycle.
- Event consumers.
- Automation principles.
- Orchestration and choreography.
- Cross-domain integration.
- External quality integration.
- Failure handling.
- Retry and compensation.
- Event versioning.
- Observability.
- Integration security.
- Governance standards.

This Canon becomes the authoritative integration blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile quality applications.
- AI-assisted inspection.
- Smart factory quality systems.
- Future enterprise quality expansion.

The event-driven quality architecture defined here is permanent. Future Quality Management Systems, laboratory platforms, computer vision technologies, AI inspection engines, industrial automation, and cloud infrastructures may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified business events, operational semantics, governance rules, and integration contracts established by this Canon. memcite

# QUALITY MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 7 — UI & UX Canon

---

# 7.1 Purpose

The Quality Management Domain is the enterprise's operational center for inspection, verification, quality governance, and continuous improvement.

Its user experience must enable inspectors, laboratory personnel, quality engineers, supervisors, managers, auditors, and executives to perform quality activities accurately, consistently, and independently while maintaining complete business traceability.

This Canon defines the permanent business interaction model for the Quality Domain.

It is independent of:

- Programming language.
- User interface framework.
- Desktop or mobile platform.
- Laboratory hardware.
- Inspection equipment.
- Computer vision systems.
- AI technologies.
- Visual design systems.

It specifies **how quality work is experienced**, not how software is implemented.

---

# 7.2 Quality UX Philosophy

The Quality experience follows seven permanent principles.

### Evidence-Centric

The primary object of interaction is the **Inspection** supported by objective evidence.

Quality decisions are driven by verified observations rather than subjective judgment.

---

### Independent Evaluation

The interface preserves Quality's independence from Production and other operational domains.

Users evaluate products against standards—not operational pressure.

---

### Minimal Cognitive Load

Inspectors should focus on evaluation rather than software navigation.

Only information relevant to the current inspection context is presented.

---

### Immediate Business Feedback

Every quality action provides immediate confirmation or a clear business explanation when an action cannot proceed.

---

### Continuous Traceability

Every inspection, measurement, disposition, and corrective action is visible through a permanent operational timeline.

---

### Safety Before Speed

The interface prevents unauthorized or policy-violating quality decisions.

---

### Consistent Enterprise Experience

Inspection workspaces follow standardized interaction patterns across all products, facilities, and inspection types.

---

# 7.3 Information Architecture

The Quality Domain is organized into specialized business workspaces.

Primary workspaces include:

- Quality Dashboard
- Inspection Queue
- Inspection Workspace
- Quality Standards
- Inspection Plans
- Quality Evidence
- Non-Conformance Management
- CAPA Workspace
- Rework Verification
- Supplier Quality
- Audit Management
- Quality Timeline
- Quality Intelligence

Each workspace serves one clearly defined quality responsibility.

---

# 7.4 Navigation Model

Navigation follows the quality lifecycle rather than technical modules.

```text id="qm-stage7-nav"
Enterprise Navigation
        │
        ▼
Quality Module
        │
        ▼
Operational Workspace
        │
        ▼
Inspection Context
        │
        ▼
Quality Activity
```

Users navigate according to quality responsibilities rather than implementation structure.

---

# 7.5 Quality Dashboard

The dashboard provides a real-time enterprise view of quality operations.

Typical content includes:

### Inspection Health

- Pending inspections.
- Active inspections.
- Completed inspections.
- Overdue inspections.
- Awaiting disposition.

---

### Quality Performance

- First-pass acceptance.
- Defect trends.
- Rework volume.
- CAPA status.
- Supplier quality performance.

---

### Operational Alerts

- Critical Non-Conformances.
- Escalated CAPA.
- Inspection delays.
- Supplier quality risks.
- Regulatory concerns.

---

### Productivity

- Inspection throughput.
- Inspector workload.
- Average inspection duration.
- Quality response times.

The dashboard supports operational awareness and management rather than transaction entry.

---

# 7.6 Inspection Workspace

The Inspection Workspace is the primary operational record for each inspection.

Recommended sections include:

### Inspection Summary

- Inspection identity.
- Inspection type.
- Product or material.
- Related Work Order or Purchase Order.
- Inspection status.

---

### Inspection Checklist

- Required inspection steps.
- Completion status.
- Outstanding activities.

---

### Quality Characteristics

- Measured values.
- Tolerances.
- Pass/fail evaluation.

---

### Evidence

- Photographs.
- Measurement records.
- Test results.
- Inspector observations.

---

### Non-Conformances

- Recorded issues.
- Severity.
- Impact.
- Linked defects.

---

### Disposition

- Proposed decision.
- Required approvals.
- Final Quality Disposition.

---

### Timeline

Complete quality history.

---

### Audit

Business evidence and governance history.

---

# 7.7 Quality Standards Workspace

Quality Standards are maintained within a dedicated governance workspace.

Capabilities include:

- Standard creation.
- Version comparison.
- Review workflow.
- Approval history.
- Applicability management.
- Revision timeline.

Historical standards remain accessible for previously completed inspections.

---

# 7.8 CAPA Workspace

Corrective and Preventive Actions are managed within a dedicated workspace.

Capabilities include:

- CAPA registration.
- Root cause documentation.
- Action planning.
- Responsibility assignment.
- Progress monitoring.
- Effectiveness verification.
- Closure governance.

This workspace emphasizes long-term quality improvement rather than immediate operational resolution.

---

# 7.9 Contextual Command Model

Available actions depend upon:

- Inspection lifecycle state.
- Business role.
- Security permissions.
- Regulatory context.
- Operational readiness.

Examples:

Planned Inspection:

- Assign Inspector.

Assigned Inspection:

- Start Inspection.

Inspection In Progress:

- Record Evidence.
- Record Measurements.
- Pause Inspection (where policy permits).

Evidence Complete:

- Evaluate Inspection.

Evaluation Complete:

- Issue Quality Disposition.

Non-Conformance Assigned:

- Begin Investigation.

CAPA Approved:

- Start Implementation.

Unavailable actions are hidden or disabled with business explanations.

---

# 7.10 Search and Discovery

Enterprise search supports business-oriented discovery.

Users search using:

- Inspection.
- Product.
- Material.
- Work Order.
- Purchase Order.
- Quality Standard.
- Non-Conformance.
- CAPA.
- Supplier.
- Inspector.
- Audit Finding.
- Quality Disposition.

Search behavior remains consistent across future implementations.

---

# 7.11 Filtering and Saved Views

Illustrative filters include:

- Pending Inspection.
- Awaiting Disposition.
- Critical Defects.
- Rework Required.
- CAPA Overdue.
- Supplier Quality Issues.
- Audit Findings.
- High-Risk Products.
- Regulatory Inspections.
- Escalated Issues.

Users may save operational views according to enterprise governance.

---

# 7.12 Data Entry Standards

Quality data entry follows permanent business standards.

Requirements include:

- Immediate business validation where appropriate.
- Mandatory field indicators.
- Controlled quality terminology.
- Protection against accidental data loss.
- Preservation of entered information during recoverable interruptions.

Validation messages explain quality policy rather than technical errors.

---

# 7.13 Visual Business Indicators

The interface communicates quality state through standardized indicators.

Examples:

- Planned.
- Assigned.
- In Progress.
- Awaiting Evidence.
- Awaiting Disposition.
- Accepted.
- Rejected.
- Rework Required.
- Quarantined.
- CAPA Active.
- Audit Pending.

Visual indicators complement explicit business information.

---

# 7.14 Quality Timeline

Every Inspection and Non-Conformance contains a chronological business timeline.

Typical entries include:

- Inspection created.
- Inspector assigned.
- Evidence recorded.
- Measurements completed.
- Disposition issued.
- Non-Conformance created.
- CAPA initiated.
- Rework requested.
- Rework verified.
- Issue closed.

The timeline becomes the permanent operational narrative for quality activities.

---

# 7.15 Collaboration

Quality collaboration includes:

- Inspector notes.
- Quality engineering comments.
- Root cause discussions.
- CAPA coordination.
- Supplier communication records.
- Audit observations.

Collaboration supplements—but never replaces—formal approvals, audit records, or business events.

---

# 7.16 Quality Documents

Typical quality documents include:

- Quality Standards.
- Inspection Plans.
- Test reports.
- Measurement reports.
- Laboratory results.
- Inspection photographs.
- CAPA documentation.
- Audit reports.
- Regulatory records.
- Customer quality documentation.

The Canon governs business relationships rather than document storage technology.

---

# 7.17 Notifications

Quality notifications include:

- Inspection assigned.
- Inspection overdue.
- Critical Non-Conformance detected.
- CAPA approved.
- CAPA overdue.
- Rework required.
- Rework verified.
- Supplier quality issue.
- Audit finding assigned.
- Regulatory inspection due.

Notifications improve operational awareness without bypassing quality governance.

---

# 7.18 Productivity Features

Enterprise productivity is supported through:

- Guided inspection workflows.
- Quick evidence capture.
- Barcode and QR identification readiness.
- Camera integration readiness.
- Bulk assignment (policy-controlled).
- Saved layouts.
- Context-sensitive actions.
- Mobile inspection workflows.
- Offline inspection readiness with governed synchronization.

Productivity enhancements must never bypass inspection validation or operational gates.

---

# 7.19 Accessibility

Quality interfaces shall support inclusive operation.

Business requirements include:

- Keyboard accessibility.
- Touch-friendly interaction for tablets and inspection devices.
- High-contrast presentation.
- Screen-reader compatibility for administrative workspaces.
- Non-color-dependent status communication.
- Consistent interaction patterns.

Accessibility is treated as a quality requirement.

---

# 7.20 Localization

Quality interfaces support:

- Multiple languages.
- Regional date and time formats.
- Number formats.
- Measurement units.
- Local regulatory terminology where required.

Localization changes presentation only—not certified quality behavior.

---

# 7.21 Responsive Experience

The Quality Domain supports:

- Desktop workstations.
- Shop-floor tablets.
- Rugged handheld inspection devices.
- Laboratory workstations.
- Mobile quality applications.
- Future wearable inspection devices.

Business rules remain identical across all form factors.

---

# 7.22 AI-Assisted Quality Operations

Future AI capabilities may assist by:

- Recommending inspection priorities.
- Detecting visual defects.
- Identifying measurement anomalies.
- Predicting defect trends.
- Suggesting CAPA based on historical effectiveness.
- Highlighting regulatory risks.
- Summarizing inspection performance.

AI recommendations remain advisory unless enterprise policy explicitly authorizes automated execution.

---

# 7.23 Performance Expectations

The quality interface shall:

- Respond promptly.
- Prevent duplicate submissions.
- Preserve inspection context.
- Clearly indicate long-running quality activities.
- Display current inspection status accurately.
- Support continuous quality operations.

Performance optimizations must never compromise quality integrity.

---

# 7.24 UX Governance

The Quality experience follows permanent governance principles.

- Quality workflows take precedence over visual design.
- Inspection terminology is standardized.
- Navigation reflects quality responsibilities.
- Interfaces remain consistent across implementations.
- New capabilities extend certified interaction patterns.
- Productivity improvements preserve quality governance.

---

# 7.25 Stage 7 Certification

The **Quality Management Enterprise Canon — Stage 7** establishes the permanent user experience architecture for the Quality Management Domain.

It defines:

- Quality UX philosophy.
- Information architecture.
- Navigation model.
- Dashboard and operational workspaces.
- Contextual command model.
- Inspection, CAPA, and Quality Standards workspaces.
- Search and filtering.
- Data entry standards.
- Visual business indicators.
- Timeline and collaboration.

This Canon becomes the authoritative interaction blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**

The Quality Management user experience defined here is permanent. Future Quality Management Systems, laboratory platforms, computer vision technologies, AI-assisted inspection tools, and smart factory interfaces may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified business workflows, operational semantics, governance principles, and interaction patterns established by this Canon. memcite

# QUALITY MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 8 — Reporting & Quality Intelligence Canon

---

# 8.1 Purpose

The Quality Management Domain is the enterprise's authoritative source of intelligence regarding product quality, process capability, supplier performance, inspection effectiveness, and continuous improvement.

Every quality activity contributes to enterprise knowledge.

Examples include:

- Every inspection contributes to product quality trends.
- Every Non-Conformance improves defect analysis.
- Every CAPA contributes to process improvement.
- Every supplier quality issue influences procurement decisions.
- Every audit finding strengthens enterprise governance.

The purpose of Reporting & Quality Intelligence is to transform operational quality data into measurable business insight that improves:

- Product quality.
- Manufacturing stability.
- Customer satisfaction.
- Supplier performance.
- Operational efficiency.
- Regulatory compliance.
- Enterprise decision-making.

This Canon defines the permanent reporting architecture for the Quality Management Domain independent of reporting tools, databases, dashboards, or analytics technologies.

---

# 8.2 Reporting Philosophy

Quality intelligence follows these permanent principles.

### Single Source of Quality Truth

All reports derive from certified inspections, dispositions, Non-Conformances, CAPA records, audit findings, and governed business events.

Conflicting quality calculations are prohibited.

---

### Decision Support

Every report exists to support operational or strategic business decisions.

Reports answer business questions rather than merely displaying metrics.

---

### Actionable Intelligence

Reports identify:

- Quality risks.
- Improvement opportunities.
- Defect patterns.
- Supplier quality trends.
- CAPA effectiveness.
- Operational bottlenecks.

---

### Traceability

Every reported figure is traceable to certified quality records.

---

### Consistency

Business definitions remain identical across the enterprise.

For example, a "First-Pass Acceptance Rate" has the same business meaning in every report.

---

# 8.3 Reporting Layers

Quality reporting is organized into four enterprise layers.

## Operational Reporting

Supports day-to-day inspection activities.

Examples:

- Pending inspections.
- Active inspections.
- Inspection workload.
- Open Non-Conformances.

---

## Tactical Reporting

Supports quality management.

Examples:

- CAPA progress.
- Defect categories.
- Supplier quality.
- Rework trends.
- Inspector productivity.

---

## Strategic Reporting

Supports executive decision-making.

Examples:

- Enterprise quality performance.
- Customer complaint trends.
- Cost of poor quality.
- Supplier risk.
- Regulatory readiness.

---

## Analytical Reporting

Supports long-term optimization.

Examples:

- Root cause trends.
- Process capability.
- Seasonal quality variation.
- Product quality improvement.
- Predictive quality analytics.

---

# 8.4 Canonical Quality KPIs

The Quality Domain defines enterprise-standard KPIs.

## Inspection KPIs

- Planned inspections.
- Completed inspections.
- Overdue inspections.
- Inspection cycle time.
- Inspection throughput.
- Inspection completion rate.

---

## Product Quality KPIs

- First-pass acceptance rate.
- Product rejection rate.
- Rework rate.
- Scrap recommendation rate.
- Product conformance rate.

---

## Non-Conformance KPIs

- Open Non-Conformances.
- Closed Non-Conformances.
- Average resolution time.
- Critical defect frequency.
- Repeat defect rate.

---

## CAPA KPIs

- Open CAPA.
- Closed CAPA.
- CAPA effectiveness rate.
- Average implementation time.
- Overdue CAPA.

---

## Supplier Quality KPIs

- Incoming acceptance rate.
- Supplier defect rate.
- Supplier corrective action completion.
- Supplier audit performance.
- Supplier quality trend.

---

## Audit KPIs

- Audit findings.
- Findings resolved.
- Overdue findings.
- Compliance rate.
- Audit completion rate.

---

## Operational KPIs

- Quality response time.
- Rework turnaround time.
- Inspection backlog.
- Escalation frequency.
- Regulatory issue frequency.

---

# 8.5 Business Dimensions

Quality reports analyze information across standardized business dimensions.

Examples:

- Date.
- Company.
- Manufacturing site.
- Product.
- Product family.
- Material.

- Quality Standard.

- CAPA category.
- Audit program.

Business dimensions remain stable across future implementations.

Historical quality records remain immutable.

# SHIPPING & FULFILLMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation & Business Scope

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The Shipping & Fulfillment Domain governs the controlled preparation, packaging, dispatch, transportation coordination, delivery confirmation, and post-dispatch management of customer orders.

Its purpose is not merely to send parcels.

Its mission is to ensure that every approved customer order is fulfilled accurately, securely, efficiently, and traceably according to the enterprise's operational commitments.

Shipping therefore functions as an independent business capability responsible for transforming approved finished products into successfully delivered customer orders.

---

# 1.2 Mission

The Shipping & Fulfillment Domain exists to ensure that products accepted by the Quality Management Domain are packaged, dispatched, transported, delivered, and, where necessary, returned in accordance with approved business policies.

It provides confidence that:

- Customers receive the correct products.
- Packaging protects products during transportation.
- Carrier commitments are managed.
- Shipment status remains visible.
- Delivery evidence is preserved.
- Returns are governed.
- Fulfillment performance continuously improves.

---

# 1.3 Domain Vision

The Shipping Domain supports organizations ranging from a single workshop dispatching a few parcels per day to a distributed multi-company enterprise operating across multiple warehouses and carriers.

The architecture supports:

- Personalized product fulfillment.
- Domestic shipping.
- International shipping.
- Multi-warehouse fulfillment.
- Multiple carrier integrations.
- Omnichannel fulfillment.
- Marketplace fulfillment.
- Franchise fulfillment.
- AI-assisted logistics planning.
- Future autonomous logistics technologies.

Business semantics remain constant while logistics technologies evolve.

---

# 1.4 Business Objectives

The Shipping Domain pursues the following permanent objectives.

### Accurate Fulfillment

Every shipment accurately reflects the approved customer order.

---

### Controlled Dispatch

Only approved products may enter the shipping process.

---

### Delivery Reliability

Customers receive products according to governed business commitments.

---

### Shipment Traceability

Every shipment remains visible throughout its lifecycle.

---

### Customer Protection

Packaging, handling, and delivery processes preserve product integrity.

---

### Continuous Improvement

Shipping performance contributes to ongoing enterprise optimization.

---

# 1.5 Domain Boundaries

The Shipping & Fulfillment Domain owns:

- Shipment planning.
- Packing operations.
- Packaging governance.
- Shipment creation.
- Carrier assignment.
- Dispatch.
- Shipment tracking.
- Delivery confirmation.
- Return initiation.
- Reverse logistics coordination.
- Shipping documentation.
- Delivery evidence.

The domain does **not** own:

- Customer agreements.
- Order pricing.
- Manufacturing.
- Inventory ownership.
- Quality approval.
- Financial accounting.
- Customer support case management.

Ownership remains explicit.

---

# 1.6 Business Responsibilities

The Shipping Domain is responsible for:

### Fulfillment Preparation

Preparing approved customer orders for shipment.

---

### Packaging Governance

Ensuring products are packed according to approved packaging standards.

---

### Carrier Coordination

Selecting and coordinating shipping providers.

---

### Shipment Execution

Managing dispatch and transportation initiation.

---

### Shipment Visibility

Providing shipment status throughout the delivery lifecycle.

---

### Delivery Confirmation

Recording successful delivery evidence.

---

### Reverse Logistics

Coordinating returns, failed deliveries, and return shipments.

---

### Shipping Intelligence

Providing enterprise insight into shipping performance, carrier reliability, fulfillment efficiency, and delivery outcomes.

---

# 1.7 Core Business Principles

The Shipping Domain follows these permanent principles.

### Ship Only Approved Products

Products enter fulfillment only after successful completion of certified upstream business processes.

---

### Accurate Fulfillment

Shipment contents match approved customer commitments.

---

### Standardized Packaging

Packaging follows approved enterprise standards.

---

### Controlled Carrier Selection

Carrier assignment follows governed business policies.

---

### Continuous Traceability

Every shipment remains traceable from packing through final delivery or return.

---

### Customer-Centric Delivery

Shipping decisions prioritize fulfillment quality while respecting enterprise operational policies.

---

# 1.8 Supported Fulfillment Models

The architecture supports multiple fulfillment models.

### Standard Shipping

Normal parcel fulfillment.

---

### Express Shipping

Priority fulfillment with accelerated carrier services.

---

### Marketplace Fulfillment

Integration with marketplace logistics networks.

---

### Multi-Warehouse Fulfillment

Shipment sourcing from multiple warehouse locations.

---

### Partial Shipment

Orders fulfilled through multiple coordinated shipments.

---

### International Shipping

Cross-border fulfillment with applicable documentation and compliance.

---

### Future Fulfillment Models

The architecture accommodates future logistics models, autonomous delivery systems, and evolving carrier technologies without altering certified business behavior.

---

# 1.9 Business Inputs

The Shipping Domain receives governed inputs from collaborating domains.

Examples include:

From Order Management:

- Approved customer order.
- Shipping address.
- Customer delivery preferences.

From Inventory & Procurement:

- Product availability.
- Warehouse allocation.

From Production:

- Completed manufacturing work.

From Quality Management:

- Approved Quality Disposition.

The Shipping Domain validates shipment readiness before initiating fulfillment.

---

# 1.10 Business Outputs

The Shipping Domain produces governed outputs including:

- Shipment records.
- Packaging records.
- Carrier assignments.
- Tracking information.
- Dispatch confirmations.
- Delivery confirmations.
- Return requests.
- Reverse logistics records.
- Shipping performance metrics.
- Audit evidence.

These outputs support Finance, Reporting, Customer Service, Inventory, and enterprise governance.

---

# 1.11 Enterprise Relationships

The Shipping Domain collaborates with:

| Domain | Relationship |
|---------|--------------|
| Order Management | Receives approved customer commitments and delivery information |
| Inventory & Procurement | Coordinates product allocation and warehouse release |
| Production & Manufacturing | Receives completed products where direct shipment applies |
| Quality Management | Receives products approved for shipment |
| Finance | Supplies shipping-related business information supporting governed financial processes |
| Reporting | Provides enterprise shipping intelligence |
| Notification | Generates dispatch and delivery notifications |
| AI Services | Supplies logistics data for optimization, routing, demand prediction, and carrier analysis |

Each collaborating domain retains ownership of its own business responsibilities.

---

# 1.12 Business Success Measures

The Shipping Domain contributes to enterprise success through measurable outcomes including:

- On-time shipment rate.
- On-time delivery rate.
- Shipment accuracy.
- Packaging quality.
- Carrier performance.
- Delivery success rate.
- Return rate.
- Shipping cost efficiency.
- Average fulfillment cycle time.
- Customer delivery satisfaction.

Detailed calculations are defined in the Reporting & Business Intelligence Canon; the business meaning is established here.

---

# 1.13 Long-Term Architectural Principles

The Shipping Domain is designed to remain valid across future enterprise evolution.

The architecture supports:

- Multiple fulfillment centers.
- Multi-company logistics.
- Carrier ecosystems.
- International trade.
- Smart warehouses.
- Autonomous logistics.
- AI-assisted routing.
- Predictive fulfillment.
- Robotics-assisted packing.
- Future logistics technologies.

These capabilities extend the certified business architecture without altering its semantics.

---

# 1.14 Stage 1 Certification

The **Shipping & Fulfillment Enterprise Canon — Stage 1** establishes the permanent business foundation for the Shipping & Fulfillment Domain.

It defines:

- Domain purpose.
- Mission.
- Vision.
- Business objectives.
- Domain boundaries.
- Core responsibilities.
- Shipping principles.
- Supported fulfillment models.
- Business inputs and outputs.
- Enterprise relationships.
- Success measures.
- Long-term architectural direction.

This Stage becomes the authoritative business foundation for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile shipping applications.
- AI-assisted logistics.
- Smart warehouse fulfillment.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The Shipping & Fulfillment Domain is hereby established as the permanent enterprise capability responsible for governing shipment preparation, packaging, dispatch, transportation coordination, delivery confirmation, reverse logistics, and enterprise fulfillment across the GiftHatkeOS business architecture. memcite

|---------|---------|
| Shipment | Represents a customer fulfillment commitment |
| Shipment Line | Individual fulfilled order item |
| Package | Physical shipment container |
| Packaging Standard | Defines approved packaging requirements |
| Packing Activity | Represents packaging execution |
| Carrier | Logistics service provider |
| Carrier Service | Specific delivery service offered by a carrier |
| Carrier Assignment | Assignment of shipment to a carrier service |
| Dispatch | Official release of a shipment to transportation |
| Tracking Event | Recorded shipment movement |
| Delivery Confirmation | Evidence of successful delivery |
| Delivery Exception | Records delivery issues |
| Return Request | Customer or operational return initiation |
| Return Shipment | Physical return movement |
| Reverse Logistics Case | Governs return processing |
| Shipping Document | Commercial and transportation documentation |
| Shipping Evidence | Proof supporting shipping activities |
| Fulfillment Exception | Operational shipping issue |

---

# 2.4 Shipment

## Purpose

Represents the enterprise commitment to fulfill an approved customer order through one or more physical deliveries.

A Shipment governs logistics execution—it does not replace the original customer order.

---

### Responsibilities

- Shipment identity.
- Related customer order.
- Fulfillment scope.
- Shipping priority.
- Destination.
- Operational status.
- Fulfillment history.

---

# 2.5 Shipment Line

Represents an individual product or quantity fulfilled within a Shipment.

Responsibilities include:

- Product reference.
- Variant.
- Quantity.
- Fulfillment status.
- Associated package.

Shipment Lines enable partial fulfillment while preserving customer order integrity.

---

# 2.6 Package

Represents the physical container prepared for transportation.

Examples:

- Corrugated shipping box.
- Protective carton.
- Tube package.
- Document envelope.
- Multi-package shipment.

Responsibilities include:

- Package identity.
- Dimensions.
- Weight.
- Packaging materials.
- Contents.
- Handling instructions.

A Package exists independently of any specific carrier technology.

---

# 2.7 Packaging Standard

Defines approved packaging requirements.

Examples include:

- Box type.
- Cushioning requirements.
- Protective films.
- Fragile handling.
- Moisture protection.
- Branding requirements.
- Sustainability requirements.

Packaging Standards govern how products are prepared—not which products are shipped.

---

# 2.8 Packing Activity

Represents execution of physical packaging.

Typical information includes:

- Responsible operator.
- Packaging completion.
- Packaging verification.
- Time completed.
- Packaging evidence.

Packing Activities establish operational accountability.

---

# 2.9 Carrier

Represents an approved logistics provider.

Examples include:

- National courier.
- International express carrier.
- Postal operator.
- Freight provider.
- Internal delivery fleet.

Carrier commercial management remains outside the Shipping Domain.

---

# 2.10 Carrier Service

Represents a governed shipping service offered by a Carrier.

Examples:

- Standard delivery.
- Express delivery.
- Same-day delivery.
- Economy shipping.
- International priority.

Carrier Services define delivery characteristics rather than contractual relationships.

---

# 2.11 Carrier Assignment

Represents the governed allocation of a Shipment to a specific Carrier Service.

Responsibilities include:

- Carrier.
- Service level.
- Assignment reason.
- Assignment time.
- Operational constraints.

Carrier Assignment precedes physical dispatch.

---

# 2.12 Dispatch

Represents official release of a Shipment into transportation.

Typical information includes:

- Dispatch timestamp.
- Dispatch location.
- Responsible operator.
- Carrier handover.
- Dispatch evidence.

Dispatch transfers operational responsibility from enterprise fulfillment to transportation.

---

# 2.13 Tracking Event

Represents a recorded logistics milestone.

Examples:

- Collected by carrier.
- In transit.
- At sorting facility.
- Out for delivery.
- Delivery attempted.
- Delivered.
- Returned.

Tracking Events record logistics history without modifying Shipment ownership.

---

# 2.14 Delivery Confirmation

Represents governed evidence that delivery has been completed.

Examples include:

- Recipient confirmation.
- Carrier confirmation.
- Digital signature.
- Delivery photograph.
- Timestamp.
- GPS verification where supported.

Delivery Confirmation closes the transportation objective while preserving permanent traceability.

---

# 2.15 Delivery Exception

Represents a deviation from expected delivery execution.

Examples:

- Customer unavailable.
- Address issue.
- Damaged shipment.
- Lost shipment.
- Weather delay.
- Customs delay.
- Carrier operational issue.

Delivery Exceptions describe operational disruptions without assigning responsibility.

---

# 2.16 Return Request

Represents formal initiation of a return process.

Typical information includes:

- Related Shipment.
- Return reason.
- Customer request.
- Operational request.
- Return authorization status.

Return Requests initiate reverse logistics without executing the physical return.

---

# 2.17 Return Shipment

Represents the physical transportation of returned goods.

Responsibilities include:

- Return tracking.
- Carrier.
- Package.
- Expected arrival.
- Return status.

---

# 2.18 Reverse Logistics Case

Represents governed management of returned products.

Examples include:

- Customer return.
- Failed delivery.
- Warranty return.
- Quality return.
- Carrier damage.

The Reverse Logistics Case coordinates investigation and resolution while preserving cross-domain ownership.

---

# 2.19 Shipping Document

Represents formal documentation supporting fulfillment.

Examples include:

- Packing list.
- Shipping label.
- Commercial invoice.
- Customs documentation.
- Carrier manifest.
- Delivery receipt.

The Shipping Domain governs document relationships rather than storage technology.

---

# 2.20 Shipping Evidence

Represents supporting operational evidence.

Examples include:

- Packing photographs.
- Dispatch photographs.
- Carrier receipt.
- Delivery proof.
- Packaging verification.
- Shipment weight verification.

Evidence supports auditability, compliance, and customer dispute resolution.

---

# 2.21 Fulfillment Exception

Represents an operational issue affecting shipment execution.

Examples:

- Packaging failure.
- Carrier rejection.
- Missing shipment contents.
- Incorrect shipment.
- Dispatch interruption.
- Tracking inconsistency.

Fulfillment Exceptions drive operational investigation and corrective action.

---

# 2.22 Entity Relationships

The Shipping Domain follows explicit ownership relationships.

```text
Customer Order
        │
        ▼
Shipment
        │
 ┌──────┼───────────────┐
 ▼      ▼               ▼
Shipment Line      Package      Carrier Assignment
                     │                 │
                     ▼                 ▼
             Packing Activity    Carrier Service
                     │                 │
                     └──────────┬──────┘
                                ▼
                           Dispatch
                                │
                                ▼
                         Tracking Events
                                │
                   ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                   ▼                         ▼
         Delivery Confirmation     Delivery Exception
                                             │
                                             ▼
                                      Return Request
                                             │
                                             ▼
                                      Return Shipment
                                             │
                                             ▼
                                  Reverse Logistics Case
```

This hierarchy separates fulfillment planning, physical packaging, transportation, delivery, and reverse logistics while preserving complete business traceability.

---

# 2.23 Domain Ownership Matrix

| Business Capability | Owning Domain |
|----------------------|---------------|
| Shipment Management | Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Packaging Governance | Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Carrier Assignment | Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Dispatch | Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Delivery Tracking | Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Reverse Logistics | Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Customer Commitments | Order Management |
| Inventory Ownership | Inventory & Procurement |
| Manufacturing Execution | Production & Manufacturing |
| Product Acceptance | Quality Management |
| Financial Accounting | Finance |

Ownership boundaries are permanent and enforced through certified business contracts.

---

# 2.24 Business Integrity Rules

The Shipping & Fulfillment Domain enforces the following invariants:

- Every Shipment references an approved Customer Order.
- Every Shipment contains one or more Shipment Lines.
- Every Shipment is associated with at least one Package before Dispatch.
- Every Package complies with an approved Packaging Standard where required by policy.
- Every Dispatch references a valid Carrier Assignment.
- Every Delivery Confirmation references one Shipment.
- Every Return Shipment references an approved Return Request.
- Reverse Logistics Cases remain traceable to the originating Shipment.
- Shipping history is append-only and never rewritten.
- Delivery Exceptions and Fulfillment Exceptions create additional business records rather than altering historical events.

These rules preserve enterprise fulfillment integrity independent of implementation technology.

---

# 2.25 Stage 2 Certification

The **Shipping & Fulfillment Enterprise Canon — Stage 2** establishes the permanent business model for the Shipping & Fulfillment Domain.

It defines:

- Canonical fulfillment entities.
- Entity responsibilities.
- Stable business identities.
- Ownership boundaries.
- Entity relationships.
- Shipment model.
- Packaging model.
- Carrier model.
- Dispatch model.
- Tracking model.
- Reverse logistics model.
- Business integrity constraints.

This Domain Model becomes the authoritative shipping specification for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile shipping applications.
- AI-assisted logistics.
- Smart warehouse fulfillment.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The business entities defined here constitute the permanent fulfillment vocabulary of GiftHatkeOS and must be preserved across all future implementations. memcite
