# FINANCE & ACCOUNTING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 2 — Domain Model & Business Entities

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The Finance & Accounting Domain is governed by a certified business model that defines every financial object used throughout the enterprise.

These entities represent permanent business concepts—not database tables, software classes, accounting software modules, APIs, or implementation artifacts.

They establish the enterprise financial vocabulary of GiftHatkeOS and remain stable regardless of implementation technology.

Every implementation—including **SMP1**, **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**, **ERP9**, **ERP10**, mobile finance applications, AI-assisted accounting, autonomous finance systems, and future enterprise platforms—must preserve these business entities and their certified meanings.

---

# 2.2 Entity Principles

Every Finance entity follows these permanent principles.

### Single Business Responsibility

Each entity owns one clearly defined financial concept.

Examples:

- A **Customer Invoice** represents a governed claim against a customer.
- A **Journal Entry** represents an accounting event.
- A **Payment** represents the settlement of a financial obligation.

Responsibilities are never shared across entities.

---

### Stable Business Identity

Each entity possesses a permanent business identity independent of implementation technology.

Business identity is immutable.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Every entity has one owning business domain.

Cross-domain updates occur only through certified business contracts.

---

### Lifecycle Governance

Every financial entity follows a governed lifecycle with controlled transitions.

---

### Auditability

Every financial record, adjustment, approval, and settlement remains permanently traceable.

---

# 2.3 Entity Landscape

The Finance & Accounting Domain consists of the following canonical business entities.

| Entity | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| Financial Transaction | Represents a governed financial business event |
| Journal Entry | Records balanced accounting movements |
| Journal Line | Individual debit or credit posting |
| General Ledger Account | Represents a governed accounting account |
| Accounting Period | Defines financial reporting boundaries |
| Fiscal Year | Governs annual financial reporting |
| Customer Invoice | Represents customer billing |
| Supplier Invoice | Represents supplier obligations |
| Accounts Receivable Item | Represents outstanding customer obligations |
| Accounts Payable Item | Represents outstanding supplier obligations |
| Payment | Represents receipt or disbursement of funds |
| Payment Allocation | Associates payments with financial obligations |
| Tax Record | Represents tax obligations and calculations |
| Cost Allocation | Represents assignment of operational costs |
| Budget | Represents planned financial allocation |
| Budget Line | Individual planning allocation |
| Financial Adjustment | Represents governed financial corrections |
| Financial Document | Governs financial documentation |
| Financial Evidence | Supporting operational or statutory evidence |
| Financial Exception | Represents controlled accounting or settlement issues |

---

# 2.4 Financial Transaction

## Purpose

Represents the financial consequence of an approved business event.

Examples include:

- Sale.
- Purchase.
- Payment.
- Refund.
- Tax recognition.
- Cost recognition.
- Adjustment.

Responsibilities include:

- Financial identity.
- Source business event.
- Transaction type.
- Financial amount.
- Currency.
- Accounting status.

---

# 2.5 Journal Entry

Represents an official accounting event.

Responsibilities include:

- Journal identity.
- Accounting period.
- Posting date.
- Approval status.
- Financial purpose.

A Journal Entry records accounting intent—not commercial activity.

---

# 2.6 Journal Line

Represents one debit or credit posting within a Journal Entry.

Responsibilities include:

- Ledger account.
- Debit amount.
- Credit amount.
- Currency.
- Cost center where applicable.
- Business reference.

Journal Lines collectively satisfy enterprise accounting balance requirements.

---

# 2.7 General Ledger Account

Represents a governed accounting classification.

Examples include:

- Cash.
- Bank.
- Accounts Receivable.
- Accounts Payable.
- Revenue.
- Cost of Goods Sold.
- Inventory.
- Tax Payable.
- Operating Expenses.

The Chart of Accounts governs enterprise accounting without depending upon implementation technology.

---

# 2.8 Accounting Period

Defines a governed financial reporting period.

Responsibilities include:

- Period identity.
- Opening date.
- Closing date.
- Period status.
- Reporting readiness.

Accounting Periods govern posting eligibility.

---

# 2.9 Fiscal Year

Represents one governed financial reporting year.

Responsibilities include:

- Fiscal year identity.
- Reporting boundaries.
- Closing status.
- Historical integrity.

---

# 2.10 Customer Invoice

Represents a governed financial claim against a customer.

Responsibilities include:

- Invoice identity.
- Customer.
- Invoice date.
- Due date.
- Invoice amount.
- Tax.
- Outstanding balance.
- Settlement status.

Commercial pricing originates outside the Finance Domain.

---

# 2.11 Supplier Invoice

Represents an approved supplier financial obligation.

Responsibilities include:

- Supplier.
- Invoice amount.
- Due date.
- Tax.
- Payment status.
- Outstanding balance.

Supplier procurement remains governed by the Inventory & Procurement Domain.

---

# 2.12 Accounts Receivable Item

Represents money owed by a customer.

Responsibilities include:

- Customer obligation.
- Due amount.
- Outstanding amount.
- Aging status.
- Collection status.

---

# 2.13 Accounts Payable Item

Represents money owed to a supplier.

Responsibilities include:

- Supplier obligation.
- Due amount.
- Outstanding amount.
- Aging status.
- Payment readiness.

---

# 2.14 Payment

Represents the movement of funds.

Examples include:

- Customer payment.
- Supplier payment.
- Refund.
- Adjustment payment.

Responsibilities include:

- Payment identity.
- Amount.
- Currency.
- Payment method.
- Settlement status.
- Financial references.

---

# 2.15 Payment Allocation

Represents the governed association between Payments and financial obligations.

Examples:

- One payment settling multiple invoices.
- Multiple payments settling one invoice.
- Partial settlements.
- Credit allocations.

Payment Allocation preserves accurate settlement history.

---

# 2.16 Tax Record

Represents governed tax recognition.

Examples include:

- GST.
- VAT.
- Sales tax.
- Withholding tax.
- Future jurisdiction-specific taxes.

Tax Record responsibilities include:

- Tax category.
- Tax amount.
- Tax basis.
- Reporting status.

The business model remains jurisdiction-neutral.

---

# 2.17 Cost Allocation

Represents assignment of operational costs.

Examples include:

- Manufacturing.
- Shipping.
- Departments.
- Cost centers.
- Projects.
- Business units.

Cost Allocation supports profitability analysis without changing operational ownership.

---

# 2.18 Budget

Represents planned financial allocation.

Responsibilities include:

- Budget identity.
- Fiscal period.
- Organizational scope.
- Approval status.
- Planning assumptions.

---

# 2.19 Budget Line

Represents one planned financial allocation within a Budget.

Examples include:

- Department budgets.
- Cost center budgets.
- Operational spending.
- Capital expenditure.
- Marketing allocation.

---

# 2.20 Financial Adjustment

Represents governed correction of financial information.

Examples include:

- Credit notes.
- Debit notes.
- Accounting corrections.
- Period adjustments.
- Accrual adjustments.

Historical records remain preserved.

---

# 2.21 Financial Document

Represents formal financial documentation.

Examples include:

- Invoices.
- Credit notes.
- Debit notes.
- Statements.
- Payment receipts.
- Tax reports.
- Financial statements.

The Canon governs business relationships rather than storage technology.

---

# 2.22 Financial Evidence

Represents supporting evidence.

Examples include:

- Payment confirmations.
- Bank confirmations.
- Tax documentation.
- Adjustment approvals.
- Audit evidence.
- Supporting calculations.

Evidence supports statutory compliance and enterprise governance.

---

# 2.23 Financial Exception

Represents an operational issue affecting financial processing.

Examples include:

- Payment mismatch.
- Posting failure.
- Tax discrepancy.
- Bank reconciliation issue.
- Approval conflict.
- Currency variance.

Financial Exceptions initiate controlled investigation and resolution.

---

# 2.24 Entity Relationships

The Finance Domain follows explicit ownership relationships.

```text id="finance-stage2-model"
Operational Business Event
            │
            ▼
   Financial Transaction
            │
            ▼
      Journal Entry
            │
     ┌──────┴──────┐
     ▼             ▼
Journal Line   Tax Record
     │
     ▼
General Ledger
     │
     ▼
Customer Invoice ──────┐
                        │
Supplier Invoice ───────┤
                        ▼
                    Payment
                        │
                        ▼
              Payment Allocation
                        │
                        ▼
              Financial Adjustment
                        │
                        ▼
             Financial Documents
                        │
                        ▼
              Financial Evidence
```

This hierarchy separates commercial events, accounting recognition, settlement, reporting, and supporting evidence while preserving complete financial traceability.

---

# 2.25 Domain Ownership Matrix

| Business Capability | Owning Domain |
|----------------------|---------------|
| Financial Transactions | Finance & Accounting |
| General Ledger | Finance & Accounting |
| Customer Invoicing | Finance & Accounting |
| Accounts Receivable | Finance & Accounting |
| Accounts Payable | Finance & Accounting |
| Payment Processing | Finance & Accounting |
| Tax Accounting | Finance & Accounting |
| Budgeting | Finance & Accounting |
| Financial Reporting | Finance & Accounting |
| Customer Orders | Order Management |
| Inventory Quantities | Inventory & Procurement |
| Manufacturing Execution | Production & Manufacturing |
| Product Acceptance | Quality Management |
| Shipment Execution | Shipping & Fulfillment |

Ownership boundaries are permanent and enforced through certified business contracts.

---

# 2.26 Business Integrity Rules

The Finance & Accounting Domain enforces the following invariants:

- Every Financial Transaction references an approved originating business event.
- Every Journal Entry contains one or more Journal Lines.
- Every Journal Entry satisfies balanced accounting principles before posting.
- Every Journal Line references a valid General Ledger Account.
- Every Customer Invoice belongs to one governed customer.
- Every Supplier Invoice belongs to one governed supplier.
- Every Payment Allocation references valid financial obligations.
- Every Tax Record is associated with a governed financial transaction.
- Financial history is append-only and never rewritten.
- Financial Adjustments create new accounting records rather than modifying historical postings.

These rules preserve enterprise financial integrity independent of implementation technology.

---

The **Finance & Accounting Enterprise Canon — Stage 2** establishes the permanent business model for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

# FINANCE & ACCOUNTING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 3 — State Machines, Transition Rules & Operational Gates

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The Finance & Accounting Domain governs how financial obligations, accounting records, payments, taxation, budgeting, and period management progress through controlled business lifecycles.

Financial records are not simple data entries.

They are governed business commitments with legal, statutory, operational, and audit consequences.

Every financial entity progresses through certified lifecycle states.

Every transition passes mandatory financial control gates.

Every posting becomes part of the permanent financial history of the enterprise.

This Canon establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for:

- Financial Transactions.
- Journal Entries.
- Customer Invoices.
- Supplier Invoices.
- Payments.
- Accounts Receivable.
- Accounts Payable.
- Budgets.
- Financial Adjustments.
- Accounting Periods.

These lifecycle contracts are implementation-independent and become permanent business architecture.

---

# 3.2 Lifecycle Philosophy

Financial lifecycle management follows these principles.

### Single Financial State

Every governed financial entity exists in one authoritative business state at any point in time.

---

### Explicit State Progression

State transitions occur only through approved financial business actions.

---

### Financial Control Gates

Business validation precedes every lifecycle transition.

---

### Auditability

Every transition records:

- Timestamp.
- Actor.
- Business role.
- Financial reason.
- Supporting evidence.
- Related approvals.
- Accounting period.

---

### Immutable Financial History

Financial history is append-only.

Corrections generate governed accounting adjustments rather than modifying historical financial records.

---

# 3.3 Financial Transaction Lifecycle

Every Financial Transaction follows a governed lifecycle.

```text id="finance-stage3-transaction"
Initiated
    │
Validated
    │
Approved
    │
Recognized
    │
Posted
    │
Settled
    │
Closed
```

Exception states:

- Rejected.
- Cancelled (where permitted by policy before posting).
- Reversed.
- Under Investigation.

---

### Initiated

Financial consequence identified.

Awaiting validation.

---

### Validated

Business rules satisfied.

---

### Approved

Required financial authorization completed.

---

### Recognized

Financial obligation officially recognized.

---

### Posted

Journal successfully posted.

---

### Settled

Associated financial obligation fulfilled where applicable.

---

### Closed

Financial lifecycle completed.

Historical integrity preserved.

---

# 3.4 Journal Entry Lifecycle

```text id="finance-stage3-journal"
Draft
   │
Validated
   │
Approved
   │
Posted
   │
Closed
```

Exception states:

- Rejected.
- Reversed.

Posted Journal Entries remain immutable.

---

# 3.5 Customer Invoice Lifecycle

```text id="finance-stage3-arinvoice"
Draft
   │
Approved
   │
Issued
   │
Outstanding
   │
Partially Paid
   │
Paid
   │
Closed
```

Exception states:

- Cancelled.
- Disputed.
- Written Off.

---

# 3.6 Supplier Invoice Lifecycle

```text id="finance-stage3-apinvoice"
Received
   │
Validated
   │
Approved
   │
Outstanding
   │
Scheduled
   │
Paid
   │
Closed
```

Exception states:

- Rejected.
- Disputed.

---

# 3.7 Payment Lifecycle

```text id="finance-stage3-payment"
Initiated
   │
Authorized
   │
Processed
   │
Allocated
   │
Completed
```

Exception states:

- Failed.
- Reversed.
- Cancelled.

---

# 3.8 Budget Lifecycle

```text id="finance-stage3-budget"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Active
   │
Closed
```

Exception states:

- Rejected.
- Superseded.

---

# 3.9 Financial Adjustment Lifecycle

```text id="finance-stage3-adjustment"
Requested
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Posted
   │
Closed
```

Exception states:

- Rejected.

Financial Adjustments never overwrite original accounting records.

---

# 3.10 Accounting Period Lifecycle

```text id="finance-stage3-period"
Planned
   │
Open
   │
Restricted
   │
Closing
   │
Closed
```

Exception state:

- Reopened (only through governed enterprise authorization).

---

# 3.11 Official Transition Matrix

Examples include:

| Current State | Allowed Next States |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Initiated Transaction | Validated |
| Validated | Approved |
| Approved | Recognized |
| Recognized | Posted |
| Posted | Settled |
| Settled | Closed |
| Draft Journal | Validated |
| Validated Journal | Approved |
| Approved Journal | Posted |
| Posted Journal | Closed |
| Draft Invoice | Approved |
| Approved Invoice | Issued |
| Issued Invoice | Outstanding |
| Outstanding | Partially Paid / Paid |
| Partially Paid | Paid |
| Paid | Closed |
| Draft Budget | Reviewed |
| Reviewed | Approved |
| Approved | Active |
| Active | Closed |
| Planned Accounting Period | Open |
| Open | Restricted |
| Restricted | Closing |
| Closing | Closed |

Transitions outside certified pathways are prohibited.

---

# 3.12 Forbidden Transitions

Examples include:

Draft Journal

→ Closed

Draft Invoice

→ Paid

Initiated Payment

→ Completed

Draft Budget

→ Active

Planned Accounting Period

→ Closed

Recognized Financial Transaction

→ Initiated

Operational control gates prevent these invalid transitions.

---

# 3.13 Financial Control Gates

Financial progression is governed through mandatory business gates.

## Recognition Gate

Before Recognition:

- Approved operational event exists.
- Financial rules satisfied.
- Currency validated.
- Required references complete.

---

## Posting Gate

Before Posting:

- Balanced accounting confirmed.
- General Ledger accounts validated.
- Accounting Period open.
- Required approvals complete.

---

## Invoice Issue Gate

Before Issued:

- Customer or supplier validated.
- Amount confirmed.
- Tax calculation completed.
- Commercial approval satisfied.

---

## Payment Gate

Before Processed:

- Payment authorization complete.
- Banking information validated.
- Outstanding obligation confirmed.

---

## Budget Activation Gate

Before Active:

- Budget approved.
- Fiscal period valid.
- Organizational scope confirmed.

---

## Period Closing Gate

Before Closed:

- Outstanding postings resolved.
- Reconciliations complete.
- Financial reports generated.
- Required approvals completed.

---

# 3.14 Operational Authority

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Responsible actor.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business justification.
- Financial references.
- Supporting approvals.

Financial transitions are never anonymous.

---

# 3.15 Financial Outcome Model

Every Financial Transaction concludes with one governed accounting outcome.

Canonical outcomes include:

- Successfully Posted.
- Successfully Settled.
- Reversed.
- Written Off (where policy permits).
- Closed.

These outcomes govern downstream reporting while preserving Finance ownership.

---

# 3.16 Parallel Financial Activities

Enterprise operations may execute multiple financial activities simultaneously.

Examples:

- Multiple invoices.
- Multiple journal postings.
- Multiple payment allocations.
- Parallel budgeting.
- Concurrent tax calculations.

Business rules require:

- One authoritative lifecycle state per entity.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Conflict prevention.
- Complete financial traceability.

---

# 3.17 Exception Escalation

Examples requiring escalation:

- Large payment variance.
- Unbalanced journal.
- Duplicate payment detection.
- Tax discrepancy.
- Period closing failure.
- Fraud investigation.
- Unauthorized financial adjustment.

Escalations generate governed financial events while preserving Finance ownership.

---

# 3.18 State Integrity Rules

The Finance & Accounting Domain enforces the following invariants:

- Every Financial Transaction has one authoritative lifecycle state.
- Every posted Journal Entry remains immutable.
- Every Customer Invoice references one governed customer.
- Every Supplier Invoice references one governed supplier.
- Every Payment references governed financial obligations.
- Every Accounting Period governs posting eligibility.
- Closed financial records remain immutable.
- Financial Adjustments preserve historical accounting.
- Financial history is append-only.

---

# 3.19 Stage 3 Certification

The **Finance & Accounting Enterprise Canon — Stage 3** establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

It defines:

- Financial Transaction lifecycle.
- Journal Entry lifecycle.
- Customer Invoice lifecycle.
- Supplier Invoice lifecycle.
- Payment lifecycle.
- Budget lifecycle.
- Financial Adjustment lifecycle.
- Accounting Period lifecycle.
- Official transition matrix.
- Forbidden transitions.
- Financial control gates.
- Outcome governance.
- Parallel financial processing.
- Escalation rules.
- State integrity constraints.

This lifecycle becomes the authoritative operational model for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile finance applications.
- AI-assisted accounting.
- Enterprise financial platforms.
- Future enterprise financial operations.

The Finance & Accounting lifecycle defined here is permanent. Future ERP platforms, accounting engines, banking integrations, AI financial systems, cloud accounting technologies, and autonomous finance solutions may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified business states, transition rules, financial control gates, and governance established by this Canon. memcite

# FINANCE & ACCOUNTING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 4 — API Contracts & Domain Services

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The Finance & Accounting Domain exposes its business capabilities through a stable set of **domain services**.

These services represent permanent financial business responsibilities—not REST APIs, SDKs, messaging protocols, middleware, stored procedures, or implementation technologies.

Whether the future implementation uses:

- Apps Script
- Java
- .NET
- Go
- Python
- Node.js
- Cloud-native architecture
- Microservices
- Event-driven platforms
- AI accounting assistants
- Autonomous financial platforms

the business service contracts remain unchanged.

This Canon establishes the permanent service architecture for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

---

# 4.2 Service Philosophy

The Finance Domain owns:

- Financial recognition.
- Accounting.
- Invoicing.
- Accounts Receivable.
- Accounts Payable.
- Payments.
- General Ledger.
- Tax accounting.
- Budgeting.
- Financial reporting support.

It does **not** own:

- Customer orders.
- Inventory operations.
- Manufacturing.
- Quality approval.
- Shipment execution.

The domain collaborates with those business areas through governed business contracts.

Every service shall:

- Represent one financial capability.
- Preserve explicit ownership.
- Enforce certified accounting rules.
- Produce auditable outcomes.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 4.3 Service Landscape

The Finance & Accounting Domain publishes the following canonical business services.

| Service | Business Responsibility |
|----------|-------------------------|
| Financial Transaction Service | Govern financial recognition |
| General Ledger Service | Govern accounting postings |
| Journal Management Service | Govern journal entries |
| Accounts Receivable Service | Govern customer financial obligations |
| Accounts Payable Service | Govern supplier financial obligations |
| Invoicing Service | Govern customer and supplier invoicing |
| Payment Service | Govern payment processing and allocation |
| Tax Management Service | Govern tax calculations and reporting |
| Budget Management Service | Govern budgeting and financial planning |
| Cost Allocation Service | Govern operational cost distribution |
| Financial Intelligence Service | Publish financial performance metrics |
| Audit Service | Preserve immutable financial history |

---

# 4.4 Financial Transaction Service

## Purpose

Maintains enterprise financial recognition.

Responsibilities:

- Create Financial Transaction.
- Validate Financial Transaction.
- Recognize Financial Transaction.
- Close Financial Transaction.
- Reverse Financial Transaction (where policy permits).

The service governs business financial identity rather than accounting software implementation.

---

# 4.5 General Ledger Service

Coordinates enterprise accounting.

Responsibilities include:

- Maintain Chart of Accounts.
- Validate ledger accounts.
- Post accounting entries.
- Maintain ledger balances.
- Govern posting rules.

The General Ledger remains the authoritative accounting foundation.

---

# 4.6 Journal Management Service

Maintains enterprise Journal Entries.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Journal Entry.
- Validate Journal Entry.
- Approve Journal Entry.
- Post Journal Entry.
- Reverse Journal Entry.
- Close Journal Entry.

Journal governance preserves financial integrity.

---

# 4.7 Accounts Receivable Service

Coordinates customer financial obligations.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Receivable.
- Update Receivable.
- Record customer payments.
- Manage outstanding balances.
- Monitor aging.
- Close Receivable.

Commercial customer relationships remain governed outside the Finance Domain.

---

# 4.8 Accounts Payable Service

Coordinates supplier financial obligations.

Responsibilities include:

- Register Supplier Invoice.
- Approve supplier obligations.
- Schedule payments.
- Record supplier payments.
- Manage outstanding balances.
- Close Payable.

Supplier procurement remains governed outside this service.

---

# 4.9 Invoicing Service

Coordinates enterprise invoicing.

Responsibilities include:

- Generate Customer Invoice.
- Generate Supplier Invoice.
- Issue Invoice.
- Cancel Invoice (where policy permits).
- Credit Invoice.
- Debit Invoice.

Only this service governs financial invoice lifecycle behavior.

---

# 4.10 Payment Service

Coordinates movement of funds.

Responsibilities:

- Register Payment.
- Authorize Payment.
- Allocate Payment.
- Complete Payment.
- Reverse Payment (where policy permits).

Payment settlement remains fully traceable.

---

# 4.11 Tax Management Service

Coordinates enterprise taxation.

Responsibilities:

- Calculate tax.
- Validate tax.
- Record tax.
- Generate tax reports.
- Support statutory submissions.

Tax legislation is applied through localization without changing certified financial behavior.

---

# 4.12 Budget Management Service

Coordinates enterprise budgeting.

Responsibilities:

- Create Budget.
- Review Budget.
- Approve Budget.
- Activate Budget.
- Revise Budget.
- Close Budget.

Budget governance supports financial planning without modifying operational ownership.

---

# 4.13 Cost Allocation Service

Coordinates assignment of operational costs.

Responsibilities:

- Allocate manufacturing costs.
- Allocate shipping costs.
- Allocate departmental expenses.
- Allocate project costs.
- Allocate overhead.

Cost allocation supports profitability analysis and managerial reporting.

---

# 4.14 Financial Intelligence Service

Publishes governed financial information.

Responsibilities include:

- Revenue KPIs.
- Profitability metrics.
- Cash flow indicators.
- Budget performance.
- Financial trends.
- Executive financial analytics.

This service supports Reporting while preserving Finance ownership.

---

# 4.15 Audit Service

Maintains immutable financial history.

Examples:

- Financial Transaction history.
- Journal history.
- Invoice history.
- Payment history.
- Tax history.
- Budget history.
- Financial Adjustment history.

Historical financial records remain append-only.

---

# 4.16 Canonical Business Operations

The domain publishes a stable catalog of business operations.

### Financial Transactions

- Create Financial Transaction.
- Validate Financial Transaction.
- Recognize Financial Transaction.
- Close Financial Transaction.

---

### Journals

- Create Journal Entry.
- Validate Journal Entry.
- Approve Journal Entry.
- Post Journal Entry.
- Reverse Journal Entry.

---

### Accounts Receivable

- Create Receivable.
- Record Customer Payment.
- Allocate Payment.
- Close Receivable.

---

### Accounts Payable

- Register Supplier Invoice.
- Approve Supplier Invoice.
- Record Supplier Payment.
- Close Payable.

---

### Invoicing

- Generate Customer Invoice.
- Generate Supplier Invoice.
- Issue Invoice.
- Credit Invoice.

---

### Payments

- Register Payment.
- Authorize Payment.
- Allocate Payment.
- Complete Payment.

---

### Budgeting

- Create Budget.
- Approve Budget.
- Activate Budget.
- Revise Budget.

---

### Tax

- Calculate Tax.
- Record Tax.
- Generate Tax Report.

---

### Cost Allocation

- Allocate Cost.
- Reallocate Cost (where policy permits).

---

# 4.17 Commands and Queries

Business services are divided into two categories.

## Commands

Commands modify financial state.

Examples:

- Post Journal.
- Issue Invoice.
- Complete Payment.
- Activate Budget.

Commands:

- Validate policy.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish business events.

---

## Queries

Queries never modify financial state.

Examples:

- Invoice Status.
- Ledger Balance.
- Payment History.
- Budget Status.
- Tax Summary.

Queries remain read-only.

---

# 4.18 Validation Framework

Every command performs mandatory validation.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

- Ledger account exists.
- Customer exists.
- Supplier exists.
- Accounting period valid.
- Currency supported.

---

### Financial Validation

- Balanced accounting.
- Valid invoice amounts.
- Outstanding obligation exists.
- Budget limits respected where policy requires.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

- Requested transition permitted.
- Financial gates satisfied.
- Business sequence preserved.

---

### Security Validation

- Authorized financial role.
- Required permissions.
- Delegation valid.
- Separation of duties enforced where applicable.

---

### Policy Validation

- Accounting policy.
- Tax policy.
- Budget policy.
- Payment policy.
- Regulatory policy where applicable.

---

# 4.19 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical financial transaction.

Example:

Post Journal Entry:

- Validate journal.
- Validate ledger accounts.
- Validate accounting period.
- Confirm balanced posting.
- Record journal.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish business event.

If any required step fails, the Journal Entry remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.20 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Post Journal.
- Complete Payment.
- Issue Invoice.
- Allocate Payment.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate financial outcomes.

---

# 4.21 Concurrency

Multiple users may participate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Accountants.
- Finance managers.
- Accounts Receivable clerks.
- Accounts Payable clerks.
- Controllers.
- Auditors.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled updates.
- Prevention of inconsistent financial state.
- Preservation of audit integrity.

---

# 4.22 Error Classification

Financial services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Financial information incomplete.

---

### Accounting Errors

Examples:

- Unbalanced journal.
- Invalid ledger account.
- Closed accounting period.

---

### Payment Errors

Examples:

- Payment mismatch.
- Insufficient settlement information.
- Allocation conflict.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition prohibited.

---

### Dependency Errors

Collaborating domain unable to satisfy business contract.

Examples:

- Shipment not completed.
- Operational approval pending.
- Missing originating business event.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Business failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

# 4.23 Cross-Domain Contracts

The Finance Domain collaborates with:

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Receive approved commercial commitments and pricing events |
| Inventory & Procurement | Receive purchasing and inventory valuation events |
| Production & Manufacturing | Receive manufacturing cost events |
| Quality Management | Receive quality valuation events where applicable |
| Shipping & Fulfillment | Receive fulfillment completion and logistics cost events |
| Reporting | Publish financial intelligence |
| Notification | Generate financial communications |
| AI Services | Supply financial data for forecasting, anomaly detection, and planning |

Ownership boundaries remain explicit.

---

# 4.24 Service Governance

The Finance service architecture follows permanent principles:

- Stable business contracts.
- Explicit domain ownership.
- Backward-compatible evolution where feasible.
- Consistent financial semantics.
- Technology-independent implementation.
- Controlled governance of service changes.

---

# 4.25 Stage 4 Certification

The **Finance & Accounting Enterprise Canon — Stage 4** establishes the permanent business service architecture for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

It defines:

- Service landscape.
- Domain service responsibilities.
- Canonical business operations.
- Command and query separation.
- Validation framework.
- Transaction boundaries.
- Idempotency.
- Concurrency principles.
- Error taxonomy.
- Cross-domain collaboration.
- Service governance.

This Canon becomes the authoritative finance service blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile finance applications.
- AI-assisted accounting.
- Enterprise financial platforms.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The Finance & Accounting service architecture defined here is permanent. Future ERP platforms, accounting engines, banking integrations, AI financial systems, cloud accounting technologies, and autonomous finance solutions may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified business services, financial semantics, validation rules, transaction boundaries, and governance established by this Canon. memcite

# FINANCE & ACCOUNTING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 5 — Permissions, Roles & Security Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Finance & Accounting Domain governs the enterprise's monetary assets, statutory obligations, accounting records, and financial reporting.

Financial errors or unauthorized actions can result in:

- Financial loss.
- Fraud.
- Regulatory penalties.
- Tax non-compliance.
- Incorrect financial statements.
- Audit failures.
- Loss of stakeholder confidence.

This Canon establishes the permanent governance model for financial authorization, accounting integrity, approval controls, treasury operations, and statutory compliance.

The security model is business-driven and technology-independent.

---

# 5.2 Security Philosophy

Finance operations follow these permanent principles.

### Financial Integrity

Every financial record accurately reflects an approved business event.

---

### Accountability

Every financial action has one accountable business actor.

---

### Least Privilege

Users receive only the permissions required for their financial responsibilities.

---

### Separation of Duties

Critical financial activities are intentionally divided across independent roles.

---

### Controlled Financial Authority

High-impact financial actions require explicit approval according to enterprise policy.

---

### Immutable Financial History

Historical accounting records remain permanently protected.

---

# 5.3 Authorization Layers

Authorization is evaluated through multiple business layers.

## Layer 1 — Identity

Verified identity:

- Employee.
- Accountant.
- Finance manager.
- Controller.
- Auditor.
- External accounting advisor.
- Banking integration.
- Future AI financial agent.

---

## Layer 2 — Business Role

Every actor performs work through an approved finance role.

---

## Layer 3 — Permissions

Roles grant explicit financial capabilities.

---

## Layer 4 — Operational Context

Authorization may depend upon:

- Company.
- Business unit.
- Department.
- Currency.
- Accounting period.
- Cost center.
- Legal entity.

---

## Layer 5 — Business State

Certain actions are permitted only during specific financial lifecycle states.

Example:

Only **Approved** Journal Entries may be posted.

---

## Layer 6 — Policy Controls

Additional governance may depend upon:

- Monetary thresholds.
- Tax jurisdiction.
- High-value payments.
- Regulatory requirements.
- Period closing status.
- Delegated authority limits.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Finance Roles

## Chief Financial Officer (CFO)

Responsibilities:

- Enterprise financial governance.
- Financial strategy.
- Regulatory oversight.
- Treasury governance.
- Executive financial approval.

Cannot:

- Modify historical accounting records outside governed adjustment processes.

---

## Finance Manager

Responsibilities:

- Daily financial operations.
- Accounting supervision.
- Financial approvals.
- Budget governance.

Cannot:

- Override enterprise accounting policy.

---

## Financial Controller

Responsibilities:

- Financial controls.
- Journal approval.
- Period closing.
- Financial reconciliation.

Cannot:

- Modify operational business events owned by other domains.

---

## General Accountant

Responsibilities:

- Journal preparation.
- Ledger maintenance.
- Reconciliations.
- Financial adjustments.

Cannot:

- Independently approve high-risk financial activities beyond delegated authority.

---

## Accounts Receivable Officer

Responsibilities:

- Customer invoicing.
- Payment allocation.
- Collections.
- Receivable management.

Cannot:

- Approve supplier payments.

---

## Accounts Payable Officer

Responsibilities:

- Supplier invoice processing.
- Payment preparation.
- Vendor settlements.

Cannot:

- Approve customer credit adjustments beyond delegated authority.

---

## Treasury Officer

Responsibilities:

- Banking operations.
- Cash movement.
- Payment execution.
- Liquidity management.

Cannot:

- Modify approved accounting entries.

---

## Budget Manager

Responsibilities:

- Budget planning.
- Budget revisions.
- Financial planning coordination.

Cannot:

- Post accounting transactions solely through budget authority.

---

## Finance Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Chart of Accounts.
- Tax configuration.
- Financial reference data.
- Accounting configuration.

Cannot:

- Modify immutable financial history.

---

## Internal Auditor

Read-only access to:

- Financial records.
- Journals.
- Payments.
- Adjustments.
- Audit history.
- Period closing evidence.

No modification authority.

---

# 5.5 Permission Taxonomy

Permissions are organized by business capability.

## Financial Transactions

- Create Financial Transaction.
- Approve Financial Transaction.
- Reverse Financial Transaction.
- Close Financial Transaction.

---

## Journals

- Create Journal.
- Validate Journal.
- Approve Journal.
- Post Journal.
- Reverse Journal.

---

## Accounts Receivable

- Create Customer Invoice.
- Record Customer Payment.
- Allocate Customer Payment.
- Write Off Receivable (policy-controlled).

---

## Accounts Payable

- Register Supplier Invoice.
- Approve Supplier Invoice.
- Schedule Payment.
- Record Supplier Payment.

---

## Payments

- Register Payment.
- Authorize Payment.
- Execute Payment.
- Reverse Payment.

---

## Tax

- Calculate Tax.
- Approve Tax Adjustments.
- Generate Tax Reports.

---

## Budgeting

- Create Budget.
- Review Budget.
- Approve Budget.
- Revise Budget.
- Close Budget.

---

## Administration

- Maintain Chart of Accounts.
- Maintain Financial Configuration.
- Maintain Reference Data.

---

# 5.6 Separation of Duties (SoD)

Critical financial activities are intentionally divided.

Examples:

- The user preparing a Journal Entry should not independently approve and post the same entry when enterprise policy requires independent review.
- An Accounts Payable Officer prepares supplier payments, while payment authorization may require a Finance Manager or Treasury Officer based on policy.
- A Treasury Officer executes approved payments but does not redefine the underlying accounting treatment.
- A Finance Administrator maintains financial configuration but cannot alter historical financial postings.
- Internal Auditors review financial activity but do not participate in operational accounting decisions.

These controls reduce fraud risk, operational error, and regulatory exposure.

---

# 5.7 Approval Authority

Business policy determines approval authority.

Examples requiring elevated approval include:

- High-value customer refunds.
- High-value supplier payments.
- Manual journal adjustments affecting closed periods.
- Budget revisions exceeding delegated limits.
- Period closing.
- Period reopening.
- Write-offs above policy thresholds.
- Tax adjustments with statutory impact.

Approval authority is governed by enterprise policy rather than individual identity.

---

# 5.8 Delegation

Temporary delegation supports operational continuity.

Delegations specify:

- Delegating authority.
- Delegate.
- Authorized financial scope.
- Effective period.
- Business justification.

Delegated financial activities remain fully auditable.

---

# 5.9 Data Visibility

Financial information is visible according to business responsibility.

Examples:

Accounts Receivable Officer:

- Customer invoices.
- Customer payments.
- Receivable aging.

Accounts Payable Officer:

- Supplier invoices.
- Supplier payments.
- Payable aging.

General Accountant:

- Journals.
- Ledger balances.
- Reconciliations.

Finance Manager:

- Enterprise financial operations.
- Budgets.
- Financial performance.

Executive:

- Strategic financial intelligence.

Auditor:

- Historical financial records.

Visibility may additionally be restricted by:

- Company.
- Legal entity.
- Department.
- Cost center.
- Currency.
- Accounting period.

---

# 5.10 Field-Level Security

Certain financial information requires elevated authorization.

Examples:

- Banking account identifiers.
- Treasury instructions.
- Tax identification details.
- Executive compensation-related accounting.
- Fraud investigation notes.
- Confidential financial adjustments.
- Sensitive commercial pricing references where policy requires.

Access to a financial record does not automatically grant access to every field.

---

# 5.11 Sensitive Operations

Examples include:

- Posting journals into restricted periods.
- Reopening closed accounting periods.
- Reversing posted journals.
- Writing off receivables.
- Executing high-value payments.
- Modifying tax configuration.
- Manual ledger adjustments.
- Emergency payment processing.

These operations require documented justification, elevated authorization, and enhanced audit controls.

---

# 5.12 Emergency ("Break-Glass") Access

Emergency access may be granted only under exceptional business circumstances.

Requirements include:

- Authorized approval.
- Time-limited duration.
- Recorded business justification.
- Enhanced audit logging.
- Automatic expiration.
- Mandatory post-event review.

Emergency authority never becomes permanent operational authority.

---

# 5.13 Financial Integrity Controls

Financial governance follows certified business controls.

Policies require:

- Approved originating business events.
- Balanced accounting.
- Controlled Journal posting.
- Authorized payments.
- Governed tax recognition.
- Approved financial adjustments.
- Controlled accounting period management.

Financial integrity protects enterprise assets and statutory compliance.

---

# 5.14 AI and Automation Governance

Future AI accounting systems, treasury automation, intelligent reconciliation engines, autonomous financial assistants, and predictive planning platforms operate under the same governance principles as human actors.

Requirements include:

- Explicit identity.
- Assigned business role.
- Limited authority.
- Full auditability.
- Policy-based permissions.
- Human oversight where required.

Automation enhances Finance without redefining certified financial governance.

---

# 5.15 Audit and Non-Repudiation

Every protected financial activity records:

- Actor identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous lifecycle state.
- New lifecycle state.
- Financial references.
- Journal reference where applicable.
- Accounting period.
- Business justification (where required).
- Related approvals.
- Supporting evidence references.

Audit records are immutable and support statutory compliance, financial assurance, regulatory review, internal governance, and external audits.

---

# 5.16 Security Governance

The Finance security model follows these permanent governance principles:

- Financial permissions are business-defined.
- Roles aggregate permissions without redefining accounting policy.
- Authorization decisions are deterministic and auditable.
- Sensitive financial operations require enhanced controls.
- Security evolves only through controlled governance.
- Implementation technologies enforce—but never redefine—the certified financial security model.

---

# 5.17 Stage 5 Certification

The **Finance & Accounting Enterprise Canon — Stage 5** establishes the permanent security and authorization framework for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

It defines:

- Finance security philosophy.
- Layered authorization model.
- Canonical finance roles.
- Permission taxonomy.
- Separation of duties.
- Approval authority.
- Delegation.
- Data visibility.
- Field-level protection.
- Sensitive financial operations.
- Emergency access governance.
- Financial integrity controls.
- AI and automation governance.
- Audit and non-repudiation.
- Security governance.

This Canon becomes the authoritative security blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile finance applications.
- AI-assisted accounting.
- Enterprise financial platforms.
- Future enterprise financial expansion.

The security architecture defined here is permanent. Future ERP platforms, accounting engines, banking networks, AI financial technologies, cloud accounting infrastructures, and autonomous finance systems must implement these governance principles without altering the certified business security model. memcite

# FINANCE & ACCOUNTING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 6 — Events, Automations & Integration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Finance & Accounting Domain is the enterprise's authoritative source of truth for financial recognition, accounting postings, receivables, payables, payments, taxation, budgeting, and statutory financial reporting.

Every significant financial activity generates governed business events that synchronize the enterprise while preserving Finance ownership.

Examples include:

- Customer Invoice Issued.
- Journal Posted.
- Payment Received.
- Supplier Payment Completed.
- Accounting Period Closed.
- Budget Approved.

These events coordinate enterprise behavior while maintaining financial integrity.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

It defines:

- Business events.
- Event publication rules.
- Financial automations.
- Cross-domain orchestration.
- Integration boundaries.

It intentionally avoids prescribing messaging technologies, middleware, event brokers, APIs, or implementation patterns.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A Finance event represents a completed financial business fact.

Examples:

- Journal Posted.
- Customer Invoice Issued.
- Payment Allocated.
- Tax Recorded.
- Accounting Period Closed.

Events communicate **what has occurred**, not **how software processed it**.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed financial occurrence.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve accounting semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Finance Domain follows these permanent principles.

### Financial Significance

Only meaningful financial activities become canonical business events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed financial occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through business governance.

---

### Immutable History

Published events are never modified.

Corrections are represented through subsequent governed financial events.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Finance events originate only from the Finance & Accounting Domain.

No collaborating domain may publish Finance events on its behalf.

---

### Auditability

Each event records:

- Event identity.
- Timestamp.
- Financial reference.
- Journal reference where applicable.
- Customer or supplier reference where applicable.
- Accounting period.
- Business actor.
- Business role.
- Correlation identifier.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Finance Events

## Financial Transaction Events

- Financial Transaction Created.
- Financial Transaction Recognized.
- Financial Transaction Posted.
- Financial Transaction Reversed.
- Financial Transaction Closed.

---

## Journal Events

- Journal Created.
- Journal Approved.
- Journal Posted.
- Journal Reversed.

---

## Customer Invoice Events

- Customer Invoice Generated.
- Customer Invoice Issued.
- Customer Invoice Paid.
- Customer Invoice Written Off.

---

## Supplier Invoice Events

- Supplier Invoice Registered.
- Supplier Invoice Approved.
- Supplier Invoice Paid.

---

## Payment Events

- Payment Registered.
- Payment Authorized.
- Payment Processed.
- Payment Allocated.
- Payment Completed.
- Payment Reversed.

---

## Tax Events

- Tax Calculated.
- Tax Recorded.
- Tax Adjustment Approved.

---

## Budget Events

- Budget Created.
- Budget Approved.
- Budget Activated.
- Budget Revised.
- Budget Closed.

---

## Accounting Period Events

- Accounting Period Opened.
- Accounting Period Restricted.
- Accounting Period Closed.
- Accounting Period Reopened.

---

## Financial Exception Events

- Financial Exception Reported.
- Financial Exception Escalated.
- Financial Exception Resolved.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Business events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding financial activity.

Examples:

- **Journal Posted** is published only after balanced accounting validation succeeds and the posting is committed.
- **Customer Invoice Issued** is published only after invoice approval and issuance are complete.
- **Payment Completed** is published only after payment execution and allocation are successfully recorded.
- **Accounting Period Closed** is published only after all required closing controls are completed.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Finance event follows the same sequence:

1. Business request received.
2. Financial validation completed.
3. Financial transaction committed.
4. Audit record created.
5. Canonical event published.
6. Authorized consumers process the event.
7. Monitoring records processing outcomes.

Published events therefore represent authoritative financial facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Finance events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Finance Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|---------------|--------------------------|
| Customer Invoice Issued | Order Management, Reporting, Notification |
| Customer Invoice Paid | Order Management, Reporting, Customer Service |
| Supplier Invoice Approved | Inventory & Procurement, Reporting |
| Payment Completed | Reporting, Notification |
| Journal Posted | Reporting |
| Budget Approved | Reporting |
| Accounting Period Closed | Reporting, Executive Governance |
| Financial Exception Escalated | Reporting, Notification |
| Tax Recorded | Reporting |
| Financial Transaction Reversed | Reporting, Audit |

Consumer domains respond to Finance events without assuming ownership of financial rules.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every Finance event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event identity.
- Event type.
- Financial Transaction reference.
- Journal reference where applicable.
- Invoice reference where applicable.
- Customer or supplier reference where applicable.
- Accounting period.
- Company.
- Currency.
- Business actor.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation identifier.
- Business reason where applicable.

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Finance Automation Principles

Automation improves operational efficiency while respecting certified financial governance.

Every automation must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Observable.
- Reversible where appropriate.

Automation must never bypass:

- Financial approval.
- Accounting validation.
- Double-entry integrity.
- Tax controls.
- Period controls.
- Security policies.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Finance Automations

Examples include:

### Financial Recognition

- Automatically recognize financial consequences of approved operational events according to enterprise policy.
- Validate accounting readiness before posting.

---

### Journals

- Suggest journal templates.
- Validate balancing.
- Detect duplicate postings.
- Flag abnormal accounting entries.

---

### Accounts Receivable

- Generate invoices from approved commercial events.
- Schedule payment reminders.
- Escalate overdue receivables.
- Recommend collection priorities.

---

### Accounts Payable

- Route supplier invoices through approval workflows.
- Schedule payments according to policy.
- Detect duplicate supplier invoices.
- Alert users to approaching payment deadlines.

---

### Payments

- Match incoming payments to outstanding obligations where enterprise policy permits.
- Detect allocation conflicts.
- Notify treasury of failed payment execution.

---

### Tax

- Calculate tax according to certified localization rules.
- Validate tax completeness.
- Prepare statutory reporting data.

---

### Budgeting

- Monitor budget consumption.
- Notify responsible managers when thresholds are reached.
- Highlight significant variances.

---

### Reporting

- Refresh financial dashboards.
- Update profitability metrics.
- Publish executive KPIs.
- Refresh budget analytics.

---

### Notifications

- Notify approvers of pending financial approvals.
- Notify customers of invoice issuance where policy requires.
- Notify finance teams of payment failures.
- Alert management to financial exceptions or period-closing risks.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Finance Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized financial governance is required.

Examples:

- Journal approval.
- Payment authorization.
- Budget approval.
- Accounting period closing.

---

## Choreography

Used where independent domains respond to Finance events.

Examples:

- Reporting.
- Notifications.
- AI services.
- Executive dashboards.
- Customer communications.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The Finance & Accounting Domain integrates with other enterprise domains through governed business contracts.

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Receive approved commercial commitments and communicate financial outcomes where appropriate |
| Inventory & Procurement | Receive purchasing events and provide supplier settlement information |
| Production & Manufacturing | Receive manufacturing cost events |
| Quality Management | Receive valuation-related quality events where policy requires |
| Shipping & Fulfillment | Receive fulfillment completion events and shipping cost information |
| Reporting | Publish certified financial intelligence |
| Notification | Generate governed financial communications |
| AI Services | Supply financial data for forecasting, anomaly detection, planning, and optimization |

Each domain remains independently governed.

---

# 6.13 External Integrations

The Canon supports future integration with:

- Banking systems.
- Payment gateways.
- Tax authority platforms.
- Electronic invoicing networks.
- Enterprise ERP platforms.
- Treasury systems.
- Financial planning systems.
- External audit tools.
- Regulatory reporting systems.
- Future AI financial platforms.

These integrations consume or publish certified business events without redefining Finance business semantics.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Financial failures are categorized consistently.

### Validation Failure

Financial prerequisites are not satisfied.

No completion event is published.

---

### Operational Failure

Financial activity cannot proceed.

Examples:

- Unbalanced journal.
- Invalid accounting period.
- Missing approval.

---

### Dependency Failure

A collaborating domain cannot satisfy its business contract.

Examples:

- Shipment not completed.
- Source operational event unavailable.
- Missing valuation information.

---

### Communication Failure

Financial completion occurred but downstream notification or integration is temporarily unavailable.

Events remain pending for governed delivery.

---

### Policy Failure

Business rules prevent financial progression.

Examples:

- Closed accounting period.
- Approval threshold exceeded.
- Tax validation failure.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries follow controlled financial policy.

Repeated processing must never create:

- Duplicate journals.
- Duplicate invoices.
- Duplicate payments.
- Duplicate accounting postings.

Where financial compensation is required, corrective accounting activities generate new governed financial events while preserving historical accuracy.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Finance events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Stable financial semantics.
- Backward compatibility where feasible.
- Managed deprecation.
- Controlled consumer migration.

Business meaning remains consistent across versions.

---

# 6.17 Observability

The enterprise monitors Finance event processing through:

- Event publication status.
- Consumer processing status.
- Posting latency.
- Payment completion times.
- Failed financial operations.
- Retry activity.
- Period closing progress.
- Budget processing.
- Financial exception frequency.

Observability supports operational reliability without altering financial behavior.

---

# 6.18 Integration Security

Finance integrations comply with the Security Canon.

Requirements include:

- Authenticated identities.
- Authorized operations.
- Least privilege.
- Controlled financial data exposure.
- Full auditability.
- Policy-based access.

Internal and external integrations follow identical governance principles.

---

# 6.19 Governance

The event architecture follows these permanent principles:

- Finance events represent completed financial facts.
- Event definitions are owned by the Finance & Accounting Domain.
- Automation respects financial policy.
- Integrations consume certified business contracts.
- Domain ownership remains explicit.
- Cross-domain collaboration remains loosely coupled.
- Event evolution follows controlled governance.

---

# 6.20 Stage 6 Certification

The **Finance & Accounting Enterprise Canon — Stage 6** establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

It defines:

- Finance event philosophy.
- Canonical event catalog.
- Event publication rules.
- Event lifecycle.
- Event consumers.
- Automation principles.
- Orchestration and choreography.
- Cross-domain integration.
- External financial integration.
- Failure handling.
- Retry and compensation.
- Event versioning.
- Observability.
- Integration security.
- Governance standards.

This Canon becomes the authoritative integration blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Mobile finance applications.
- AI-assisted accounting.
- Enterprise financial platforms.
- Future enterprise financial expansion.

The event-driven finance architecture defined here is permanent. Future ERP platforms, banking networks, payment ecosystems, tax authority integrations, AI financial technologies, and cloud accounting infrastructures may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified business events, financial semantics, governance rules, and integration contracts established by this Canon. memcite

# FINANCE & ACCOUNTING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 7 — UI & UX Canon

---

# 7.1 Purpose

The Finance & Accounting Domain is the enterprise's operational center for accounting, receivables, payables, treasury, budgeting, taxation, financial control, and statutory reporting.

Its user experience must enable accountants, finance managers, controllers, treasury officers, accounts receivable specialists, accounts payable specialists, auditors, executives, and future AI financial assistants to perform financial activities accurately, consistently, and independently while maintaining complete financial traceability.

This Canon defines the permanent business interaction model for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

It is independent of:

- Programming language.
- User interface framework.
- Desktop or mobile platform.
- Banking technologies.
- Tax authority systems.
- ERP vendors.
- AI technologies.
- Visual design systems.

It specifies **how financial work is experienced**, not how software is implemented.

---

# 7.2 Finance UX Philosophy

The Finance experience follows seven permanent principles.

### Financial Truth First

The primary object of interaction is the **Financial Record**.

Every interface exists to support accurate financial representation of approved business events.

---

### Business Before Accounting Mechanics

Users interact through meaningful financial responsibilities rather than technical accounting structures.

Operational complexity is hidden where appropriate without reducing financial control.

---

### Minimal Cognitive Load

Financial professionals focus on accounting decisions rather than software navigation.

Only information relevant to the current financial activity is presented.

---

### Immediate Business Feedback

Every financial action provides immediate confirmation or a clear business explanation when an action cannot proceed.

---

### Continuous Traceability

Every posting, approval, payment, adjustment, and reconciliation appears within a permanent financial timeline.

---

### Financial Safety Before Speed

The interface prevents unauthorized, inconsistent, or policy-violating financial actions.

---

### Consistent Enterprise Experience

All finance workspaces follow standardized interaction patterns across companies, currencies, tax regimes, and future technologies.

---

# 7.3 Information Architecture

The Finance Domain is organized into specialized business workspaces.

Primary workspaces include:

- Finance Dashboard
- Financial Transactions
- General Ledger
- Journal Management
- Customer Invoicing
- Accounts Receivable
- Supplier Invoicing
- Accounts Payable
- Treasury
- Banking
- Tax Management
- Budget Management
- Cost Accounting
- Financial Adjustments
- Accounting Period Management
- Financial Intelligence
- Audit & Compliance

Each workspace serves one clearly defined financial responsibility.

---

# 7.4 Navigation Model

Navigation follows financial responsibilities rather than software modules.

```text id="finance-stage7-nav"
Enterprise Navigation
        │
        ▼
Finance Module
        │
        ▼
Operational Workspace
        │
        ▼
Financial Context
        │
        ▼
Financial Activity
```

Users navigate according to accounting and financial responsibilities rather than implementation structure.

---

# 7.5 Finance Dashboard

The dashboard provides a real-time enterprise view of financial operations.

Typical content includes:

### Financial Health

- Revenue.
- Gross profit.
- Net profit.
- Cash position.
- Accounts Receivable.
- Accounts Payable.

---

### Financial Performance

- Budget utilization.
- Outstanding invoices.
- Collections.
- Supplier payments.
- Financial close progress.

---

### Operational Alerts

- Overdue receivables.
- Pending approvals.
- Payment failures.
- Tax deadlines.
- Accounting period closing risks.

---

### Productivity

- Journals awaiting approval.
- Payments awaiting authorization.
- Outstanding reconciliations.
- Budget reviews.
- Financial exceptions.

The dashboard supports operational awareness and financial management rather than transaction entry.

---

# 7.6 Financial Transaction Workspace

The Financial Transaction Workspace is the primary operational record for financial recognition.

Recommended sections include:

### Financial Summary

- Financial Transaction identity.
- Originating business event.
- Transaction type.
- Currency.
- Current lifecycle state.

---

### Accounting

- Journal Entry.
- Ledger accounts.
- Debit/Credit summary.
- Accounting period.

---

### Commercial References

- Customer.
- Supplier.
- Invoice references.
- Payment references.

---

### Tax

- Tax category.
- Tax calculation.
- Tax status.

---

### Settlement

- Outstanding balance.
- Payment allocations.
- Settlement progress.

---

### Timeline

Complete financial history.

---

### Audit

Accounting evidence and governance history.

---

# 7.7 Journal Management Workspace

Journal activities are managed within a dedicated workspace.

Capabilities include:

- Journal preparation.
- Validation.
- Approval.
- Posting.
- Reversal.
- Historical review.

Historical Journal Entries remain permanently available.

---

# 7.8 Treasury Workspace

Treasury operations are managed within a dedicated workspace.

Capabilities include:

- Bank account overview.
- Payment processing.
- Cash position.
- Payment approvals.
- Liquidity monitoring.
- Banking history.

Treasury execution remains governed by certified financial controls.

---

# 7.9 Contextual Command Model

Available actions depend upon:

- Financial lifecycle state.
- Business role.
- Security permissions.
- Accounting period status.
- Regulatory context.

Examples:

Draft Journal:

- Validate Journal.

Validated Journal:

- Approve Journal.

Approved Journal:

- Post Journal.

Outstanding Customer Invoice:

- Allocate Payment.

Authorized Payment:

- Execute Payment.

Open Accounting Period:

- Post Financial Transactions.

Closing Accounting Period:

- Execute Period Closing.

Unavailable actions are hidden or disabled with business explanations.

---

# 7.10 Search and Discovery

Enterprise search supports business-oriented discovery.

Users search using:

# FINANCE & ACCOUNTING ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 8 — Reporting & Financial Intelligence Canon

---

# 8.1 Purpose

The Finance & Accounting Domain is the enterprise's authoritative source of truth for financial performance, profitability, liquidity, taxation, budgeting, statutory reporting, and executive financial intelligence.

Every governed financial activity contributes to enterprise knowledge.

Examples include:

- Every customer invoice contributes to revenue analysis.
- Every supplier invoice contributes to procurement cost intelligence.
- Every journal posting contributes to financial reporting.
- Every payment contributes to cash-flow analysis.
- Every budget contributes to financial planning.
- Every accounting period contributes to historical financial performance.

The purpose of Reporting & Financial Intelligence is to transform governed financial records into actionable business insight that supports:

- Executive decision-making.
- Financial planning.
- Regulatory compliance.
- Operational control.
- Strategic growth.
- Enterprise sustainability.

This Canon defines the permanent reporting architecture for the Finance & Accounting Domain independent of reporting platforms, databases, visualization tools, or analytics technologies.

---

# 8.2 Reporting Philosophy

Financial intelligence follows these permanent principles.

### Single Source of Financial Truth

All reports derive from certified financial transactions, journals, invoices, payments, tax records, budgets, accounting periods, and governed financial events.

Conflicting financial calculations are prohibited.

---

### Decision Support

Every report exists to support financial or business decisions.

Reports answer business questions rather than merely presenting numbers.

---

### Actionable Intelligence

Reports identify:

- Revenue opportunities.
- Cost drivers.
- Cash-flow risks.
- Budget variances.
- Collection priorities.
- Profitability trends.
- Compliance concerns.

---

### Traceability

Every reported figure is traceable to certified financial records.

---

### Consistency

Business definitions remain identical across the enterprise.

For example, "Net Profit" has one certified business definition regardless of report or implementation.

---

# 8.3 Reporting Layers

Financial reporting is organized into four enterprise layers.

## Operational Reporting

Supports day-to-day accounting operations.

Examples:

- Outstanding invoices.
- Payments awaiting allocation.
- Journals awaiting approval.
- Open accounting periods.

---

## Tactical Reporting

Supports finance management.

Examples:

- Accounts Receivable aging.
- Accounts Payable aging.
- Cash-flow analysis.
- Budget monitoring.
- Tax obligations.

---

## Strategic Reporting

Supports executive decision-making.

Examples:

- Revenue performance.
- Profitability.
- Liquidity.
- Financial health.
- Capital allocation.
- Enterprise financial performance.

---

## Analytical Reporting

Supports long-term optimization.

Examples:

- Revenue trends.
- Margin analysis.
- Customer profitability.
- Supplier cost trends.
- Budget forecasting.
- Cash-flow forecasting.

---

# 8.4 Canonical Financial KPIs

The Finance Domain defines enterprise-standard KPIs.

## Revenue KPIs

- Gross Revenue.
- Net Revenue.
- Revenue Growth.
- Average Order Revenue.
- Revenue by Business Unit.

---

## Profitability KPIs

- Gross Profit.
- Gross Margin.
- Operating Profit.
- Net Profit.
- EBITDA (where enterprise policy applies).

---

## Liquidity KPIs

- Cash Balance.
- Cash Inflow.
- Cash Outflow.
- Operating Cash Flow.
- Free Cash Flow.

---

## Accounts Receivable KPIs

- Outstanding Receivables.
- Collection Rate.
- Average Collection Period.
- Receivable Aging.
- Overdue Receivables.

---

## Accounts Payable KPIs

- Outstanding Payables.
- Average Payment Period.
- Payment Compliance.
- Supplier Payment Aging.

---

## Budget KPIs

- Budget Utilization.
- Budget Variance.
- Department Budget Performance.
- Capital Expenditure Performance.

---

## Tax KPIs

- Tax Liability.
- Tax Paid.
- Tax Variance.
- Tax Filing Status.

---

## Operational Finance KPIs

- Journal Processing Time.
- Financial Close Duration.
- Reconciliation Completion Rate.
- Financial Exception Rate.
- Posting Accuracy.

---

# 8.5 Business Dimensions

Financial reports analyze information across standardized business dimensions.

Examples:

- Date.
- Fiscal Year.
- Accounting Period.
- Company.
- Legal Entity.
- Department.
- Cost Center.
- Business Unit.
- Customer.
- Supplier.
- Product Category.
- Currency.
- Tax Category.
- Project.
- Region.

Business dimensions remain stable across future implementations.

---

The Canon defines standard enterprise dashboards.

## Executive Financial Dashboard

Displays:

- Revenue.
- Profitability.
- Cash position.
- Budget performance.
- Enterprise financial health.

---

## Revenue Dashboard

Displays:

- Sales revenue.
- Customer revenue.
- Revenue trends.

- Revenue by region.

---

Displays:

- Cash position.

---

## Budget Dashboard

Displays:

- Budget utilization.

---

- Outstanding supplier obligations.

- Cash requirements.

---

## Tax Dashboard

Displays:

- Tax obligations.

---

## Financial Close Dashboard

Displays:

Financial intelligence includes prioritized operational queues.

Examples:

- Invoices Awaiting Issue.
- Payments Awaiting Authorization.
- Outstanding Receivables.
- Supplier Payments Due.
- Budget Reviews.
- Tax Filing Activities.
- Period Closing Tasks.
- Financial Exceptions.

Operational queues support real-time enterprise execution.

---

# 8.8 Historical Financial Analysis

Historical financial information supports:

- Profitability analysis.
- Cash-flow trends.
- Budget performance.
- Revenue forecasting.
- Cost optimization.
- Customer profitability.
- Supplier performance.
- Financial planning.

Historical accounting records remain immutable.

---

# 8.9 Forecasting Inputs

The Finance Domain provides certified inputs for forecasting.

Examples:

- Revenue.
- Cash flow.
- Expenses.
- Budget utilization.
- Accounts Receivable.
- Accounts Payable.
- Working capital.
- Profitability.

Forecasting consumes financial information but never modifies accounting records.

Financial intelligence proactively identifies:

- Budget overruns.
- Cash shortages.

- Tax deadlines.

- Reconciliation issues.

Authorized users may create custom analytical views using certified:

- Time periods.

- Preserve KPI definitions.

- Maintain traceability.
- Protect sensitive financial information.

# 8.12 Security and Reporting

Financial reporting follows the Security Canon.

- Strategic financial intelligence.

Sensitive financial information remains governed by business policy.

---

# 8.13 Data Quality

Financial reporting depends upon high-quality financial records.

The Canon requires:

- Complete financial history.
- Balanced accounting.
- Accurate journal postings.
- Valid payment history.
- Controlled tax records.
- Consistent financial terminology.
- Reliable budget information.

Reports identify data quality concerns rather than concealing them.

---

# 8.14 AI and Financial Intelligence

Future AI capabilities may:

- Predict revenue.
- Forecast cash flow.
- Detect accounting anomalies.
- Recommend budget adjustments.
- Predict collection risk.
- Explain KPI changes.
- Identify profitability opportunities.
- Recommend financial improvements.

AI remains advisory unless enterprise policy explicitly authorizes automated execution.

---

# 8.15 Governance

Financial reporting follows permanent governance principles.

- KPIs are centrally governed.
- Financial calculations remain standardized.
- Historical records remain immutable.
- Reports remain traceable.
- Security applies equally to reporting.
- New metrics follow controlled governance.
- Reporting never changes accounting records.

---

# 8.16 Stage 8 Certification

The **Finance & Accounting Enterprise Canon — Stage 8** establishes the permanent reporting and intelligence architecture for the Finance & Accounting Domain.

It defines:

- Reporting philosophy.
- Reporting layers.
- Canonical financial KPIs.
- Business dimensions.
- Standard enterprise dashboards.
- Operational work queues.

- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**

The reporting architecture defined here is permanent.
