# NOTIFICATION, COMMUNICATION & COLLABORATION ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 5 — Communication Governance, Collaboration & Security Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Notification, Communication & Collaboration Domain establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for business communications, collaboration, messaging, alerts, approval communications, delivery, confidentiality, and communication security.

Unlike operational domains that govern business transactions, this domain governs **how enterprise information is communicated, who may communicate it, who may receive it, how collaboration occurs, and how communication remains secure, traceable, and business-appropriate**.

It is the authoritative enterprise communication governance layer for every certified GiftHatkeOS domain.

This Canon defines the permanent business architecture for:

- Business communications.
- Notifications.
- Collaboration.
- Conversations.
- Communication security.
- Delivery governance.
- Approval communications.
- Escalation.
- Confidentiality.
- AI-assisted communication.
- Communication audit.

It intentionally avoids prescribing messaging protocols, encryption technologies, collaboration software, email providers, or communication infrastructure.

---

# 5.2 Enterprise Communication Philosophy

Enterprise communication follows eight permanent principles.

### Communication Originates from Business

Enterprise communication exists because of certified business activities.

Communication never becomes a substitute for business execution.

---

### One Business Communication Intent

Each business event generates one authoritative communication intent.

Multiple delivery channels may fulfill that intent according to enterprise policy.

---

### Right Information to the Right Audience

Enterprise communication is targeted.

Recipients receive only communication relevant to their responsibilities, organizational scope, and approved authority.

---

### Collaboration with Accountability

Enterprise collaboration remains business-focused and attributable.

Every contribution has a responsible enterprise identity.

---

### Confidentiality by Business Need

Communication visibility is governed by business responsibility rather than technical capability.

---

### Explainable Communication

Recipients understand:

- Why they received a communication.
- Which business event originated it.
- Which action (if any) is expected.

---

### Traceability

Every governed communication remains attributable to:

- Business event.
- Enterprise identity.
- Organizational context.
- Delivery channel.
- Time.
- Communication history.

---

### Technology Independence

Communication governance remains stable while communication platforms evolve.

---

# 5.3 Enterprise Communication Model

Communication decisions evaluate multiple business dimensions.

## Layer 1 — Business Event

Originating business occurrence.

Examples:

- Order approved.
- Production completed.
- Invoice overdue.

---

## Layer 2 — Communication Intent

Purpose of communication.

Examples:

- Inform.
- Request approval.
- Escalate.
- Warn.
- Collaborate.

---

## Layer 3 — Audience

Approved recipients.

Examples:

- Sales Executive.
- Warehouse Team.
- Finance Manager.
- Executive Leadership.
- Customer.
- Supplier.

---

## Layer 4 — Communication Policy

Enterprise communication rules.

Examples:

- Confidentiality.
- Delivery timing.
- Escalation.
- Retention.

---

## Layer 5 — Delivery

Approved communication channels.

Examples:

- In-app notification.
- Email.
- Push notification.
- SMS.
- External collaboration platform.

---

## Layer 6 — Communication Audit

Permanent enterprise communication history.

Communication succeeds only after all required governance layers are satisfied.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Communication Roles

The Notification Domain governs communication responsibilities.

Illustrative roles include:

## Communication Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Communication governance.
- Template administration.
- Communication policy oversight.

---

## Collaboration Moderator

Responsibilities:

- Collaboration governance.
- Conversation management.
- Workspace standards.

---

## Announcement Publisher

Responsibilities:

- Enterprise announcements.
- Executive communications.
- Organization-wide messaging.

---

## Notification Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Notification governance.
- Delivery policies.
- Recipient routing.

---

## Escalation Coordinator

Responsibilities:

- Escalation governance.
- Escalation monitoring.
- Resolution coordination.

---

## Communication Auditor

Responsibilities:

- Communication history.
- Delivery evidence.
- Collaboration audit.
- Policy compliance.

Cannot modify communication history.

---

## AI Communication Administrator

Responsibilities:

- AI-generated communication governance.
- AI communication quality.
- AI communication accountability.

Cannot bypass enterprise communication policy.

---

# 5.5 Communication Classification

Enterprise communications are categorized according to business purpose.

## Informational

Examples:

- Order confirmed.
- Production completed.
- Inventory replenished.

---

## Action Required

Examples:

- Approval requested.
- Quality review.
- Financial validation.

---

## Warning

Examples:

- Low inventory.
- Delivery delay.
- Budget threshold exceeded.

---

## Critical

Examples:

- Security incident.
- Production outage.
- Compliance breach.
- Executive escalation.

---

## Collaborative

Examples:

- Team discussion.
- Customer clarification.
- Supplier coordination.

Classification determines governance behavior rather than delivery technology.

---

# 5.6 Confidentiality Model

Enterprise communication follows controlled visibility.

Examples:

### Public Enterprise

Visible to all enterprise personnel according to policy.

---

### Departmental

Visible only within approved organizational boundaries.

---

### Restricted

Visible only to specifically authorized participants.

---

### Executive

Visible only to executive governance.

---

### Confidential

Visible only to explicitly authorized enterprise identities.

Confidentiality follows business responsibility rather than communication platform capabilities.

---

# 5.7 Approval Communication Governance

Approval communication supports enterprise governance.

Requirements include:

- Clear business context.
- Decision request.
- Responsible approver.
- Organizational scope.
- Supporting references.
- Escalation policy.
- Audit evidence.

Approval communication does not perform approvals; it communicates governed approval workflows owned by other domains.

---

# 5.8 Escalation Governance

Escalation preserves enterprise responsiveness.

Examples:

- Unanswered approval.
- Production delay.
- Customer complaint.
- Financial exception.
- Executive notification.

Escalations define:

- Trigger.
- Responsible recipients.
- Escalation path.
- Business priority.
- Resolution expectations.
- Audit history.

---

# 5.9 Collaboration Governance

Enterprise collaboration follows governed principles.

Requirements include:

- Business context.
- Accountable participants.
- Conversation ownership.
- Organizational scope.
- Permanent communication history.

Collaboration supports business execution without replacing formal governance.

---

# 5.10 Delivery Governance

Enterprise delivery follows governed business policy.

Considerations include:

- Recipient preferences where permitted.
- Mandatory delivery rules.
- Business priority.
- Escalation requirements.
- Communication timing.
- Delivery confirmation where required.

Delivery channels may vary while communication intent remains unchanged.

---

# 5.11 AI-Assisted Communication

AI communication remains governed.

Examples include:

- Communication summaries.
- Executive digests.
- Suggested responses.
- Operational recommendations.
- Translation assistance.
- Conversation summaries.

AI-generated communication:

- References certified business context.
- Identifies itself according to enterprise policy.
- Remains reviewable where required.
- Preserves communication auditability.

---

# 5.12 Sensitive Communications

Examples include:

- Executive decisions.
- Financial approvals.
- Security incidents.
- Identity governance.
- Personnel communications.
- Legal notices.
- Strategic announcements.

Sensitive communications require enhanced confidentiality, delivery governance, and complete audit evidence.

---

# 5.13 Communication Audit and Non-Repudiation

Every protected communication records:

- Business event.
- Enterprise identity.
- Organizational context.
- Timestamp.
- Delivery channel.
- Communication classification.
- Delivery outcome.
- Related approvals where applicable.

Communication history is immutable and supports enterprise governance, regulatory obligations where applicable, dispute resolution, internal assurance, external audits, and long-term organizational accountability.

---

# 5.14 Enterprise Communication Standards

The Notification, Communication & Collaboration Domain follows these permanent principles:

- Communications originate from governed business events.
- Conversations remain accountable.
- Delivery follows enterprise policy.
- Confidentiality follows business need.
- Collaboration remains traceable.
- AI communications remain governed.
- Communication history remains immutable.
- Communication governance evolves only through approved enterprise governance.

---

# 5.15 Stage 5 Certification

The **Notification, Communication & Collaboration Enterprise Canon — Stage 5** establishes the permanent enterprise communication governance framework.

It defines:

- Enterprise communication philosophy.
- Multi-layer communication model.
- Canonical communication roles.
- Communication classification.
- Confidentiality model.
- Approval communication governance.
- Escalation governance.
- Collaboration governance.
- Delivery governance.
- AI-assisted communication governance.
- Sensitive communication handling.
- Communication audit and non-repudiation.
- Enterprise communication standards.

This Canon becomes the authoritative communication governance blueprint for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Enterprise communication platforms.
- Mobile collaboration applications.
- AI communication services.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The enterprise communication architecture defined here is permanent. Future messaging platforms, collaboration suites, email providers, AI communication systems, push notification services, enterprise digital workplaces, and communication technologies may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified business communication semantics, governance principles, confidentiality model, collaboration standards, and audit framework established by this Canon. memcite

# NOTIFICATION, COMMUNICATION & COLLABORATION ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 6 — Events, Automations & Integration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Notification, Communication & Collaboration Domain governs enterprise-wide communication events, notification delivery, collaboration activities, approval communications, escalations, announcements, and communication policies.

Unlike operational domains that publish business transaction events, this domain publishes **communication governance events** that coordinate enterprise messaging and collaboration while preserving the ownership of the originating business events.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Notification, Communication & Collaboration Domain.

It defines:

- Communication business events.
- Event publication rules.
- Communication automations.
- Cross-domain orchestration.
- Enterprise collaboration integration.
- Delivery integration boundaries.

It intentionally avoids prescribing messaging brokers, email providers, collaboration platforms, SMS gateways, push services, AI messaging technologies, or middleware.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A Communication event represents a completed communication business fact.

Examples include:

- Notification Published.
- Announcement Delivered.
- Conversation Opened.
- Approval Communication Created.
- Escalation Triggered.

Events communicate **completed communication outcomes**, not technical delivery operations.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business communication.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise communication semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Notification Domain follows these permanent principles.

### Communication Significance

Only meaningful communication activities generate canonical business events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed communication occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable Communication History

Published communication events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Communication events originate only from the Notification, Communication & Collaboration Domain.

Operational domains continue to own the originating business events.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event identity.
- Timestamp.
- Communication reference.
- Originating business event.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Business role.
- Correlation identifier.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Communication Events

## Notification Events

- Notification Created.
- Notification Validated.
- Notification Scheduled.
- Notification Published.
- Notification Delivered.
- Notification Archived.

---

## Alert Events

- Alert Detected.
- Alert Published.
- Alert Acknowledged.
- Alert Resolved.
- Alert Escalated.

---

## Communication Events

- Communication Drafted.
- Communication Approved.
- Communication Sent.
- Communication Completed.

---

## Conversation Events

- Conversation Opened.
- Message Added.
- Participant Invited.
- Conversation Resolved.
- Conversation Closed.

---

## Approval Communication Events

- Approval Request Created.
- Approval Reminder Sent.
- Approval Communication Escalated.
- Approval Communication Closed.

---

## Announcement Events

- Announcement Approved.
- Announcement Published.
- Announcement Withdrawn.

---

## Delivery Events

- Delivery Queued.
- Delivery Attempted.
- Delivery Successful.
- Delivery Failed.
- Delivery Retried.

---

## Communication Policy Events

- Policy Proposed.
- Policy Approved.
- Policy Published.
- Policy Retired.

---

## Collaboration Workspace Events

- Workspace Created.
- Workspace Updated.
- Workspace Archived.

---

## Communication Exception Events

- Communication Exception Detected.
- Communication Exception Escalated.
- Communication Exception Resolved.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Communication events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding communication activity.

Examples:

- **Notification Published** is emitted only after recipients, communication policy, and delivery preparation are validated.
- **Conversation Opened** is emitted only after the collaboration context and participants are established.
- **Announcement Published** is emitted only after governance approval.
- **Delivery Successful** is emitted only after communication reaches its intended destination according to enterprise policy.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Communication event follows the same sequence:

1. Business communication initiated.
2. Governance validation completed.
3. Communication transaction completed.
4. Communication audit recorded.
5. Canonical communication event published.
6. Authorized consumers process the event.
7. Monitoring records processing outcomes.

Published events therefore represent authoritative communication facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Communication events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Communication Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Notification Published | All certified business domains |
| Notification Delivered | Originating business domain |
| Alert Published | Order Management, Inventory & Procurement, Production & Manufacturing, Quality Management, Shipping & Fulfillment, Finance & Accounting |
| Approval Reminder Sent | Originating approval workflow |
| Conversation Opened | Related operational domain |
| Announcement Published | All enterprise domains |
| Communication Policy Published | All communication components |
| Delivery Failed | Notification Service, Escalation Service |
| Communication Exception Escalated | Executive Governance, Identity, Security & Administration |

Consumers respond to communication events without assuming ownership of communication governance.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every communication event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event identity.
- Event type.
- Communication reference.
- Originating business event.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Recipient scope.
- Organizational context.
- Communication classification.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation identifier.
- Governance reference.

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Communication Automation Principles

Automation improves enterprise communication while respecting certified governance.

Every automation must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Observable.
- Repeatable.

Automation must never bypass:

- Communication governance.
- Required approvals.
- Confidentiality rules.
- Organizational scope.
- Delivery policy.
- Audit requirements.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Communication Automations

Examples include:

### Notification Automation

- Deliver notifications according to communication policy.
- Group related notifications where enterprise policy permits.
- Detect duplicate notifications.
- Archive completed notifications.

---

### Approval Automation

- Send approval reminders.
- Escalate overdue approval communications.
- Notify alternate approvers according to policy.
- Close completed approval communications.

---

### Collaboration Automation

- Notify participants of new messages.
- Summarize long conversations.
- Highlight unresolved discussions.
- Archive inactive conversations according to retention policy.

---

### Delivery Automation

- Retry failed delivery according to policy.
- Select alternative approved delivery channels.
- Detect repeated delivery failures.
- Record delivery outcomes.

---

### Escalation Automation

- Trigger escalation after governed thresholds.
- Notify escalation recipients.
- Track escalation progress.
- Close resolved escalations.

---

### AI Communication Automation

- Generate executive summaries.
- Recommend recipients.
- Suggest communication templates.
- Translate communications where approved.
- Detect communication anomalies.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Notification Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized communication governance is required.

Examples:

- Notification delivery.
- Approval reminders.
- Escalation workflows.
- Announcement publication.

---

## Choreography

Used where independent domains respond to communication events.

Examples:

- Order Management reacting to delivery confirmations.
- Finance responding to payment reminder outcomes.
- Reporting tracking communication metrics.
- AI Services summarizing collaboration activity.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than implementation technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The Notification Domain integrates with every certified enterprise domain through governed business contracts.

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Communicate commercial events |
| Inventory & Procurement | Communicate inventory and procurement events |
| Production & Manufacturing | Communicate manufacturing events |
| Quality Management | Communicate quality events |
| Shipping & Fulfillment | Communicate fulfillment events |
| Finance & Accounting | Communicate financial events |
| Reporting & Business Intelligence | Publish analytical alerts and executive summaries |
| Identity, Security & Administration | Communicate governance and security events |
| AI Services | Assist communication generation, summarization, translation, and prioritization |

Each collaborating domain remains independently governed.

---

These integrations consume or publish certified communication events without redefining enterprise communication governance.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Communication failures are categorized consistently.

### Validation Failure

Communication prerequisites are not satisfied.

No completion event is published.

---

### Delivery Failure

Communication could not reach the intended recipient.

Governed retry or escalation policies determine subsequent action.

---

### Policy Failure

Communication violates enterprise communication policy.

Publication is prevented until governance requirements are satisfied.

---

### Dependency Failure

A collaborating domain cannot satisfy its business contract.

Examples:

- Originating business event unavailable.
- Identity unavailable.
- Recipient resolution unavailable.

---

### Communication Failure

Technical delivery infrastructure temporarily unavailable.

Business communication intent remains preserved for governed recovery.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries follow controlled enterprise policy.

Repeated processing must never create:

- Duplicate notifications.
- Duplicate announcements.
- Duplicate approval requests.
- Duplicate escalation records.
- Duplicate communication history.

Where correction is required, new communication events preserve historical accountability while superseding previous communication outcomes according to enterprise governance.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Communication events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Stable business semantics.
- Backward compatibility where practical.
- Managed deprecation.
- Controlled consumer migration.

Business meaning remains consistent across versions.

# 7.1 Purpose

The Notification, Communication & Collaboration Domain provides the enterprise experience for notifications, collaboration, messaging, approvals, alerts, announcements, and business communication.

Unlike operational workspaces that execute transactions, communication workspaces exist to ensure that the **right people receive the right information at the right time, understand the business context, collaborate effectively, and complete required business actions**.

This Canon defines the permanent user experience architecture for enterprise communication.

It is independent of:

- Email platforms.
- Collaboration software.
- Chat applications.
- Mobile notification frameworks.
- Messaging providers.

It specifies **how enterprise communication is experienced**, not how communication software is implemented.

# 7.2 Communication UX Philosophy

Enterprise communication follows eight permanent principles.

### Business Context Before Conversation

Every communication begins with the business event that generated it.

Users immediately understand:

- Why the communication exists.
- Which business process it relates to.
- Which action, if any, is expected.

---

### Action-Oriented Communication

Communications should guide users toward appropriate business decisions rather than simply delivering information.

### Progressive Disclosure

Users first see essential information.

Additional communication history, supporting documents, discussions, and audit details are available when needed.

---

### Collaboration Around Business Objects

Conversations are anchored to governed business entities such as:

- Orders.
- Purchase requests.
- Production jobs.
- Quality inspections.
- Shipments.
- Financial approvals.
- Reports.
- Administrative actions.

Conversations never become isolated from enterprise business context.

---

### Communication Without Noise

Enterprise communication minimizes unnecessary interruptions.

High-priority information is distinguished from routine updates.

---

### Consistent Enterprise Experience

Every communication workspace follows identical interaction patterns across the enterprise.

---

### Explainable Communication

Users always understand:

- Who sent the communication.
- Which business event originated it.
- Why they received it.
- Which action is expected.

---

### Technology Independence

Business communication remains consistent across future communication technologies.

# DOCUMENT & DIGITAL ASSET MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation & Business Scope

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The **Document & Digital Asset Management Domain** establishes the permanent enterprise architecture for managing business documents, digital assets, engineering files, customer personalization assets, operational evidence, marketing resources, legal records, and enterprise knowledge artifacts.

Unlike operational domains that execute business transactions, this domain governs **how enterprise information is created, organized, versioned, secured, referenced, retained, and made available throughout its lifecycle**.

It is the enterprise's authoritative source for document and digital asset governance.

Its purpose is **not** to own operational business processes.

Its purpose is to ensure that every governed document and digital asset remains authentic, traceable, version-controlled, securely accessible, and permanently linked to the business context that created or uses it.

Examples include:

- Customer-uploaded personalization files.
- Product artwork.
- Laser engraving designs.
- Acrylic cutting vectors.
- Product photographs.
- Production job packets.
- Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs).
- Work instructions.
- Contracts.
- Purchase documents.
- Quotations.
- Invoices.
- Quality inspection reports.
- Certificates.
- Financial documents.
- HR forms.
- Marketing assets.
- Brand guidelines.
- Training materials.
- Enterprise knowledge documents.

Every future implementation must preserve these business responsibilities independently of storage technologies or file systems.

---

# 1.2 Mission

The Document & Digital Asset Management Domain exists to ensure that every enterprise document and digital asset remains governed, discoverable, version-controlled, secure, auditable, and continuously available throughout its certified business lifecycle.

---

The architecture supports organizations ranging from a single personalized manufacturing workshop to globally distributed enterprises operating across:

- Marketing teams.

## Stage 2 — Domain Model & Business Entities

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The Document & Digital Asset Management Domain is governed by a permanent enterprise information model that defines every document-related and asset-related business object within GiftHatkeOS.

These entities represent **business concepts**, not files stored on disks, cloud storage objects, folders, databases, repositories, content management systems, or vendor-specific document technologies.

Whether future implementations use:

- Apps Script
- Standalone GiftHatkeOS

- Cloud object storage

# 2.2 Entity Principles

Every document-related entity follows these permanent principles.

### Single Responsibility

Each entity owns one enterprise responsibility.

Examples:

- A **Document** represents one governed business document.
- A **Digital Asset** represents one governed media or production asset.
- A **Document Version** represents one certified revision.
- A **Retention Policy** governs document preservation.

Responsibilities are never shared.

### Stable Business Identity

Every document entity possesses a permanent enterprise identity independent of storage technology.

### Explicit Ownership

Every entity has one governing domain owner.

Operational domains reference documents but do not own document governance.

### Governance

Every document entity follows enterprise approval, lifecycle governance, version control, auditability, and controlled evolution.

---

### Traceability

Every document and digital asset remains fully traceable throughout its lifecycle.

# DOCUMENT & DIGITAL ASSET MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 3 — State Machines, Transition Rules & Operational Gates

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The Document & Digital Asset Management Domain governs the complete lifecycle of enterprise documents, digital assets, document versions, asset versions, templates, collections, archive records, retention policies, and document governance.

Every governed document and digital asset progresses through certified business states.

These states ensure that enterprise information remains:

- Governed.
- Authentic.
- Version-controlled.
- Traceable.
- Auditable.
- Business-approved.
- Technology-independent.

This Canon establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for:

- Documents.
- Digital Assets.
- Document Versions.
- Asset Versions.
- Document Templates.
- Asset Collections.
- Archive Records.
- Retention Policies.
- Access Policies.

---

# 3.2 Lifecycle Philosophy

Document lifecycle management follows permanent principles.

### Single Authoritative State

Every governed document exists in exactly one official lifecycle state.

---

### Controlled Progression

State transitions occur only through approved business actions.

---

### Governance Gates

Every transition passes mandatory governance validation before becoming effective.

---

### Traceability

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business justification.
- Related approvals where applicable.
- Audit references.

---

### Immutable Historical Record

Historical document and asset records remain permanently preserved.

Corrections generate new governed versions rather than rewriting history.

---

# 3.3 Document Lifecycle

Every Document follows the certified lifecycle.

```text id="document-stage3-document"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Published
   │
Archived
```

Exceptional states include:

- Rejected.
- Withdrawn.
- Superseded.

---

### Draft

Document created but not yet approved.

---

### Reviewed

Business review completed.

---

### Approved

Certified as the authoritative business version.

---

### Published

Available for governed enterprise use.

---

### Archived

Retained according to retention policy.

---

# 3.4 Digital Asset Lifecycle

```text id="document-stage3-asset"
Captured
    │
Processed
    │
Approved
    │
Production Ready
    │
Archived
```

Exceptional states:

- Rejected.
- Obsolete.

This lifecycle is especially important for personalized manufacturing assets.

---

# 3.5 Document Version Lifecycle

```text id="document-stage3-version"
Created
    │
Validated
    │
Certified
    │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Replaced.
- Withdrawn.

Only one Document Version may be Effective at a time.

---

# 3.6 Asset Version Lifecycle

```text id="document-stage3-assetversion"
Uploaded
    │
Edited
    │
Customer Approved
    │
Production Approved
```

Exceptional states:

- Rejected.
- Superseded.

GiftHatke manufacturing preserves every historical artwork revision.

---

# 3.7 Document Template Lifecycle

```text id="document-stage3-template"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Published
```

Exceptional states:

- Retired.
- Superseded.

Templates standardize document creation.

---

# 3.8 Retention Policy Lifecycle

```text id="document-stage3-retention"
Proposed
     │
Reviewed
     │
Approved
     │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Replaced.
- Retired.

Retention policies remain centrally governed.

---

# 3.9 Archive Lifecycle

```text id="document-stage3-archive"
Active
   │
Eligible
   │
Archived
```

Exceptional states:

- Restored.
- Destroyed (only where enterprise policy and applicable legal or regulatory requirements explicitly permit).

Archive history remains permanently traceable.

---

# 3.10 Official Transition Matrix

Examples include:

| Current State | Allowed Next States |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Draft Document | Reviewed |
| Reviewed Document | Approved |
| Approved Document | Published |
| Published Document | Archived |
| Captured Asset | Processed |
| Processed Asset | Approved |
| Approved Asset | Production Ready |
| Created Version | Validated |
| Validated Version | Certified |
| Certified Version | Effective |
| Draft Template | Reviewed |
| Reviewed Template | Approved |
| Approved Template | Published |

Transitions outside certified pathways are prohibited.

---

# 3.11 Forbidden Transitions

Examples include:

Draft Document

→ Published

Captured Asset

→ Production Ready

Created Version

→ Effective

Draft Template

→ Published

Proposed Retention Policy

→ Effective

Operational governance prevents these invalid transitions.

---

# 3.12 Governance Gates

Every lifecycle progression passes mandatory business gates.

## Document Publication Gate

Before Published:

- Business review completed.
- Required approvals complete.
- Metadata validated.
- Classification assigned.
- Access policy established.

---

## Asset Production Gate

Before Production Ready:

- Asset quality verified.
- Required approvals complete.
- Production compatibility confirmed.
- Correct version certified.

For GiftHatke personalization assets, customer approval is required whenever enterprise policy specifies it.

---

## Version Certification Gate

Before Effective:

- Previous version superseded where appropriate.
- Version lineage validated.
- Audit evidence recorded.

---

## Template Publication Gate

Before Published:

- Enterprise review complete.
- Business terminology validated.
- Governance approval completed.

---

## Retention Policy Effectiveness Gate

Before Effective:

- Governance approval completed.
- Legal review completed where applicable.
- Organizational impact assessed.

---

# 3.13 Operational Authority

Every document transition records:

- Responsible Enterprise Identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business justification.
- Related approvals.

Document transitions are never anonymous.

---

# 3.14 Business Outcomes

Every governed document concludes with one authoritative outcome.

Canonical outcomes include:

- Published.
- Production Ready.
- Effective.
- Archived.
- Superseded.
- Withdrawn.

These outcomes preserve enterprise information integrity.

---

# 3.15 Parallel Activities

Enterprise document management supports concurrent work.

Examples:

- Multiple reviewers.
- Parallel document drafting.
- Simultaneous asset editing.
- AI-assisted classification.
- Marketing asset creation.
- Production artwork revision.

Business rules require:

- One authoritative lifecycle state per governed entity.
- Controlled versioning.
- Conflict prevention.
- Complete historical preservation.

---

# 3.16 Exception Escalation

Examples requiring governed escalation include:

- Missing approvals.
- Version conflicts.
- Unauthorized modifications.
- Missing personalization assets.
- Broken business references.
- Retention policy violations.
- Classification conflicts.
- Asset corruption.

Escalations generate governed document events while preserving Document Domain ownership.

---

# 3.17 State Integrity Rules

The Document & Digital Asset Management Domain enforces the following invariants:

- Every Document has one authoritative lifecycle state.
- Every Digital Asset has one authoritative lifecycle state.
- Only one Document Version is Effective at any given time.
- Only one Production Approved Asset Version is authoritative for a manufacturing activity.
- Every Published Document remains historically traceable.
- Every Archive Record preserves historical accountability.
- Every Retention Policy follows governed lifecycle transitions.
- Document history remains append-only.

---

# 3.18 GiftHatke Personalization Lifecycle

For personalized manufacturing, customer artwork follows an additional certified lifecycle.

```text id="document-stage3-personalization"
Customer Upload
        │
Quality Review
        │
Design Preparation
        │
Proof Generated
        │
Customer Approved
        │
Production Approved
        │
Manufacturing Released
        │
Archived
```

This lifecycle permanently links customer-uploaded assets with:

- Personalization Intake.
- Artwork revisions.
- Customer approval.
- Production release.
- Manufactured product.

This ensures complete manufacturing traceability and protects against accidental use of obsolete artwork.

---

# 3.19 Lifecycle Governance

The lifecycle architecture follows permanent principles.

- Every state has defined business meaning.
- Every transition is governed.
- Version history remains immutable.
- Customer-approved assets remain identifiable.
- Published documents remain authoritative.
- Historical versions remain preserved according to retention policy.
- Business semantics remain independent of storage technology.

---

# 3.20 Stage 3 Certification

The **Document & Digital Asset Management Enterprise Canon — Stage 3** establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for the Document & Digital Asset Management Domain.

It defines:

- Document lifecycle.
- Digital Asset lifecycle.
- Document Version lifecycle.
- Asset Version lifecycle.
- Template lifecycle.
- Retention lifecycle.
- Archive lifecycle.
- Official transition matrix.
- Forbidden transitions.
- Governance gates.
- Business outcomes.
- Parallel document activities.
- Exception escalation.
- State integrity constraints.
- GiftHatke personalization artwork lifecycle.

This lifecycle becomes the authoritative operational model for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Enterprise document management platforms.
- Digital asset management systems.
- AI document intelligence.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The Document & Digital Asset Management lifecycle defined here is permanent. Future document repositories, cloud storage technologies, digital asset management platforms, AI knowledge systems, engineering content platforms, and enterprise content ecosystems may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified lifecycle states, transition rules, governance gates, version semantics, and document management principles established by this Canon. memcite

# 4.17 Commands and Queries

## Commands

Commands modify document state.

Examples:

- Publish Document.
- Approve Asset.
- Certify Version.
- Archive Document.

Commands:

- Validate governance.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish business events.

---

## Queries

Queries never modify document state.

Examples:

- Document Details.
- Version History.
- Asset Library.
- Metadata.
- Archive Contents.
- Related Business References.

Queries remain read-only.

---

# 4.18 Validation Framework

Every command performs mandatory validation.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

- Document exists.
- Asset exists.
- Template exists.
- Metadata profile exists.

---

### Business Validation

- Business reference valid.
- Classification assigned.
- Required metadata complete.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

- Requested transition permitted.
- Governance gates satisfied.
- Version integrity maintained.

---

### Policy Validation

- Retention policy.
- Access policy.
- Classification policy.
- Confidentiality policy.

---

### Governance Validation

- Required approvals.
- Business ownership.
- Document standards.
- Organizational policy.

---

# 4.19 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical document transaction.

Example:

Publish Document:

- Validate metadata.
- Validate approvals.
- Validate classification.
- Activate version.
- Record audit.
- Publish document event.

If any required step fails, the Document remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.20 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Publish Document.
- Archive Document.
- Certify Version.
- Apply Retention Policy.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate governed documents or duplicate version history.

---

# 4.21 Concurrency

Multiple participants may collaborate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Technical writers.
- Designers.
- Marketing teams.
- Production engineers.
- Quality inspectors.
- AI document assistants.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled versioning.
- Preservation of authoritative versions.
- Complete document history.

---

# 4.22 Error Classification

Document services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Document information incomplete.

---

### Metadata Errors

Examples:

- Missing classification.
- Missing required metadata.
- Invalid metadata values.

---

### Governance Errors

Examples:

- Missing approval.
- Retention conflict.
- Confidentiality violation.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition prohibited.

---

### Dependency Errors

Collaborating domain unable to satisfy business contract.

Examples:

- Related Order unavailable.
- Production Job unavailable.
- Enterprise Identity unavailable.

---

### Asset Errors

Examples:

- Asset unavailable.
- Unsupported governed asset state.
- Missing production-ready version.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Business failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

The Document Domain collaborates with:

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Customer documents and order assets |
| Inventory & Procurement | Supplier documents and material records |
| Production & Manufacturing | Engineering drawings and production assets |

- Explicit domain ownership.

- Consistent document semantics.

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Document & Digital Asset Management Domain establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for business documents, digital assets, engineering files, customer personalization assets, knowledge resources, legal records, operational evidence, document security, retention, and long-term information stewardship.

Unlike operational domains that govern business transactions, this domain governs **how enterprise information is created, classified, approved, secured, versioned, retained, shared, archived, and ultimately governed throughout its lifetime**.

It is the authoritative enterprise information governance layer for every certified GiftHatkeOS domain.

This Canon defines the permanent business architecture for:

- Document governance.
- Digital asset governance.
- Version governance.
- Information classification.
- Document security.
- Access governance.
- Retention governance.
- Archive governance.
- AI-assisted document governance.
- Enterprise knowledge governance.

It intentionally avoids prescribing storage technologies, document repositories, cloud platforms, file systems, OCR engines, AI platforms, or search technologies.

# 5.2 Enterprise Information Philosophy

Enterprise information governance follows eight permanent principles.

### Information Exists to Support Business

Documents and digital assets support certified business execution.

They never replace certified business transactions.

---

### One Authoritative Information Source

Every governed document and asset has one authoritative enterprise identity.

---

### Business Context Preservation

Every document permanently retains its originating business context.

Future implementations must never separate business information from the business entities that created or use it.

---

### Version Integrity

Enterprise users always know which version is authoritative.

Historical revisions remain preserved according to enterprise governance.

---

### Confidentiality by Business Need

Information visibility follows certified business responsibility rather than storage capabilities.

---

### Explainable Information

Users understand:

- What the document represents.
- Which business process created it.
- Which version is authoritative.
- Why they have access.

---

### Traceability

Every document and asset remains attributable to:

- Business event.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Version history.
- Approval history.
- Audit history.

---

### Technology Independence

Business information governance remains stable while storage technologies evolve.

# 5.3 Enterprise Information Model

Information governance evaluates multiple business layers.

- Marketing.

---

## Layer 4 — Governance

Enterprise information policy.

Examples:

- Approval.
- Retention.
- Confidentiality.
- Access.
- Archival.

---

## Layer 5 — Lifecycle

Business lifecycle state.

Examples:

- Draft.
- Published.
- Production Ready.
- Archived.

---

## Layer 6 — Audit

Permanent enterprise information history.

Information becomes authoritative only after all required governance layers are satisfied.

---

- Document governance.

- Template governance.

---

- Compliance verification.

Cannot modify historical audit records.

---

## AI Knowledge Administrator

Responsibilities:

- AI document governance.
- AI-assisted classification.
- AI-assisted knowledge organization.

Cannot bypass enterprise governance.

Examples:

---

### Departmental

Visible only within approved organizational boundaries.

---

### Restricted

Visible only to specifically authorized participants.

---

### Executive

Visible only to executive governance.

---

### Confidential

Visible only to explicitly authorized enterprise identities.

Confidentiality follows business responsibility rather than storage platform capabilities.

Retention decisions follow enterprise governance rather than storage limitations.

# DOCUMENT & DIGITAL ASSET MANAGEMENT ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 6 — Events, Automations & Integration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Document & Digital Asset Management Domain governs enterprise documents, digital assets, document versions, asset versions, metadata, templates, retention, archives, and enterprise knowledge.

Unlike operational domains that publish business transaction events, this domain publishes **document governance events** that communicate the lifecycle of enterprise information while preserving ownership of the originating business entities.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Document & Digital Asset Management Domain.

It defines:

- Document business events.
- Asset business events.
- Event publication rules.
- Information automations.
- Cross-domain orchestration.
- Enterprise integration boundaries.
- AI document integration.

It intentionally avoids prescribing document repositories, cloud storage providers, content delivery systems, OCR technologies, AI platforms, or middleware.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A Document event represents a completed enterprise information fact.

Examples include:

- Document Published.
- Asset Approved.
- Version Certified.
- Archive Completed.
- Retention Policy Activated.

Events communicate **completed information governance outcomes**, not storage operations.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business activity.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise information semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Document Domain follows permanent principles.

### Information Significance

Only meaningful document governance activities generate canonical business events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed information occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable Information History

Published events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Document events originate only from the Document & Digital Asset Management Domain.

Operational domains continue to own the business entities that reference the information.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event identity.
- Timestamp.
- Document or Asset reference.
- Related business entity.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Business role.
- Correlation identifier.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Document Events

## Document Events

- Document Created.
- Document Reviewed.
- Document Approved.
- Document Published.
- Document Archived.
- Document Restored.

---

## Digital Asset Events

- Asset Registered.
- Asset Classified.
- Asset Approved.
- Production Asset Released.
- Asset Archived.

---

## Version Events

- Version Created.
- Version Validated.
- Version Certified.
- Effective Version Activated.
- Version Superseded.

---

## Template Events

- Template Drafted.
- Template Approved.
- Template Published.
- Template Retired.

---

## Metadata Events

- Metadata Assigned.
- Metadata Updated.
- Metadata Validated.

---

## Archive Events

- Archive Initiated.
- Archive Completed.
- Archive Restored.

---

## Retention Events

- Retention Policy Proposed.
- Retention Policy Approved.
- Retention Policy Activated.
- Retention Action Executed.

---

## Access Governance Events

- Access Granted.
- Access Updated.
- Access Revoked.

---

## Knowledge Events

- Knowledge Article Published.
- Knowledge Article Updated.
- Knowledge Article Retired.

---

## Document Exception Events

- Version Conflict Detected.
- Missing Metadata Detected.
- Retention Violation Detected.
- Unauthorized Access Detected.
- Asset Integrity Exception Detected.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Document events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding governance activity.

Examples:

- **Document Published** is emitted only after approvals, metadata validation, classification, and governance checks are complete.
- **Production Asset Released** is emitted only after the production-ready asset has been certified.
- **Version Certified** is emitted only after version integrity has been verified.
- **Archive Completed** is emitted only after archive validation succeeds.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Document event follows the same sequence:

1. Information governance activity initiated.
2. Governance validation completed.
3. Information transaction completed.
4. Audit recorded.
5. Canonical document event published.
6. Authorized consumers process the event.
7. Monitoring records processing outcomes.

Published events therefore represent authoritative information facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Document events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Document Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|----------------|--------------------------|
| Document Published | All certified business domains |
| Production Asset Released | Production & Manufacturing |
| Effective Version Activated | Referencing business domain |
| Archive Completed | Records Management, Reporting & Business Intelligence |
| Knowledge Article Published | Notification, Communication & Collaboration, AI Services |
| Retention Policy Activated | Identity, Security & Administration, Compliance functions |
| Access Granted | Identity, Security & Administration |
| Version Conflict Detected | Production, Quality Management, Executive Governance |

Consumers respond to document events without assuming ownership of document governance.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every document event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event identity.
- Event type.
- Document or Asset reference.
- Related business entity.
- Version reference.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Classification.
- Organizational context.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation identifier.
- Governance reference.

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Information Automation Principles

Automation improves enterprise information governance while respecting certified policies.

Every automation must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Observable.
- Repeatable.

Automation must never bypass:

- Approval requirements.
- Version governance.
- Confidentiality policies.
- Retention governance.
- Access governance.
- Audit requirements.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Information Automations

Examples include:

### Document Automation

- Apply metadata recommendations.
- Detect duplicate documents.
- Validate document completeness.
- Archive obsolete documents according to policy.

---

### Asset Automation

- Generate thumbnails.
- Classify uploaded assets.
- Detect duplicate artwork.
- Validate production asset packages.

---

### Version Automation

- Detect version conflicts.
- Notify referencing domains of new effective versions.
- Preserve historical versions.
- Prevent multiple effective versions.

---

### Knowledge Automation

- Recommend related knowledge articles.
- Identify outdated procedures.
- Detect documentation gaps.
- Suggest cross-references.

---

### Retention Automation

- Monitor retention schedules.
- Notify upcoming archive actions.
- Detect retention violations.
- Initiate governed archive workflows.

---

### AI Information Automation

- Summarize documents.
- Generate metadata suggestions.
- Recommend classifications.
- Identify similar assets.
- Extract knowledge relationships.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Document Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized information governance is required.

Examples:

- Version certification.
- Archive execution.
- Retention policy enforcement.
- Metadata validation.

---

## Choreography

Used where independent domains respond to information events.

Examples:

- Production consuming new artwork.
- Quality referencing updated inspection procedures.
- Notification attaching published documents.
- AI Services indexing new knowledge assets.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than implementation technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The Document Domain integrates with every certified enterprise domain through governed business contracts.

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Customer documents and personalization assets |
| Inventory & Procurement | Supplier documentation |
| Production & Manufacturing | Engineering drawings and production assets |
| Quality Management | Inspection evidence and compliance documents |
| Shipping & Fulfillment | Shipping documentation |
| Finance & Accounting | Financial documents |
| Reporting & Business Intelligence | Published reports and executive documents |
| Identity, Security & Administration | Access governance and compliance |
| Notification, Communication & Collaboration | Document attachments and shared assets |
| AI Services | Knowledge indexing, summarization, classification, and semantic search |

Each collaborating domain remains independently governed.

---

# 6.13 External Integrations

The Canon supports future integration with:

- Enterprise document repositories.
- Cloud storage providers.
- Digital asset management platforms.
- Enterprise content management systems.
- Knowledge management platforms.
- OCR and intelligent document processing systems.
- Computer vision platforms.
- AI knowledge graphs.
- Future enterprise content ecosystems.

These integrations consume or publish certified document events without redefining enterprise information governance.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Information failures are categorized consistently.

### Validation Failure

Document governance prerequisites are not satisfied.

No completion event is published.

---

### Version Failure

Version integrity cannot be established.

Certification is prevented.

---

### Governance Failure

Document violates enterprise governance.

Publication is prevented until requirements are satisfied.

---

### Dependency Failure

A collaborating domain cannot satisfy its business contract.

Examples:

- Related Order unavailable.
- Production Job unavailable.
- Enterprise Identity unavailable.

---

### Repository Failure

Storage technology temporarily unavailable.

Business information intent remains preserved for governed recovery.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries follow controlled enterprise policy.

Repeated processing must never create:

- Duplicate documents.
- Duplicate versions.
- Duplicate archive records.
- Duplicate retention actions.
- Duplicate audit history.

Where correction is required, new document events preserve historical accountability while superseding previous outcomes according to enterprise governance.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Document events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Backward compatibility where practical.

- Controlled consumer migration.

Business meaning remains consistent across versions.

# 6.17 Observability

The enterprise monitors information processing through:

- Search effectiveness.

- Consumer processing status.

Observability supports enterprise information governance without changing business semantics.

Document integrations comply with the Identity, Security & Administration Canon.

# 7.2 Enterprise Information UX Philosophy

### Business Context Before File

Users first understand **why** an information resource exists before interacting with the document or asset itself.

# WORKFLOW, PROCESS AUTOMATION & ORCHESTRATION ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 2 — Domain Model & Business Entities

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain is governed by a permanent enterprise process model that defines every workflow-related business object within GiftHatkeOS.

These entities represent **business concepts**, not workflow engines, BPM products, orchestration frameworks, task schedulers, automation software, queues, or implementation technologies.

Whether future implementations use:

- Apps Script
- Standalone GiftHatkeOS
- BPMN-based workflow engines
- Enterprise BPM platforms
- Low-code automation platforms
- Event-driven orchestration engines
- AI orchestration services
- Robotic process automation (RPA)
- Workflow schedulers
- Future enterprise automation technologies

the certified business entities remain unchanged.

They define the permanent enterprise workflow vocabulary of GiftHatkeOS.

---

# 2.2 Entity Principles

Every workflow-related entity follows these permanent principles.

### Single Responsibility

Each entity owns one enterprise process responsibility.

Examples:

- A **Business Process** represents one governed enterprise process.
- A **Workflow Instance** represents one execution of that process.
- A **Human Task** represents one accountable work assignment.
- An **Automation Rule** represents one governed automation decision.

Responsibilities are never shared.

---

### Stable Business Identity

Every workflow entity possesses a permanent enterprise identity independent of execution technology.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Every entity has one governing domain owner.

Operational domains participate in workflows but do not own workflow governance.

---

### Governance

Every workflow entity follows enterprise approval, lifecycle governance, auditability, and controlled evolution.

---

### Traceability

Every workflow entity remains fully traceable throughout its lifecycle.

---

# 2.3 Entity Landscape

The Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain consists of the following canonical entities.

| Entity | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| Business Process | Represents one governed enterprise process |
| Workflow Definition | Represents the certified blueprint for a process |
| Workflow Instance | Represents one execution of a workflow |
| Process State | Represents the current lifecycle state of a workflow |
| Human Task | Represents one accountable work assignment |
| System Task | Represents one automated execution step |
| Decision Point | Represents a governed business decision |
| Business Rule | Represents one certified decision rule |
| Automation Rule | Represents one certified automation policy |
| SLA Policy | Governs deadlines and expected completion |
| Timer | Represents scheduled workflow actions |
| Escalation Rule | Governs workflow escalation behavior |
| Process Exception | Represents workflow deviations |
| Workflow Audit Record | Represents immutable workflow history |
| Process Template | Represents reusable workflow patterns |
| Orchestration Contract | Defines cross-domain workflow coordination |
| Process Milestone | Represents a major business checkpoint |

---

# 2.4 Business Process

## Purpose

Represents one governed enterprise business process.

Examples include:

- Order Fulfillment.
- Purchase Approval.
- Production Planning.
- Customer Personalization.
- Product Return.
- Employee Onboarding.

Responsibilities include:

- Business objective.
- Participating domains.
- Governance.
- Lifecycle.
- Auditability.

---

# 2.5 Workflow Definition

Represents the certified blueprint describing how a Business Process is executed.

Responsibilities include:

- Activities.
- Sequence.
- Decision points.
- Participants.
- Business rules.
- Exception paths.

Workflow Definitions remain stable while individual Workflow Instances execute independently.

---

# 2.6 Workflow Instance

Represents one execution of a Workflow Definition.

Examples:

- Order #10248 fulfillment.
- Purchase Request #481 approval.
- Customer Artwork Approval for Order GH-24051.

Each Workflow Instance preserves its own execution history.

---

# 2.7 Process State

Represents the current lifecycle state of a Workflow Instance.

Examples:

- Created.
- Running.
- Waiting.
- Escalated.
- Completed.
- Cancelled.

Only one authoritative Process State exists at any given time.

---

# 2.8 Human Task

Represents one accountable activity assigned to an enterprise participant.

Examples:

- Review artwork.
- Approve purchase.
- Inspect finished product.
- Confirm shipment.
- Validate invoice.

Human Tasks always identify:

- Responsible role.
- Responsible enterprise identity.
- Related workflow.
- Due expectations.

---

# 2.9 System Task

Represents one automated workflow activity.

Examples:

- Generate invoice.
- Create production job.
- Publish notification.
- Archive completed workflow.
- Calculate production schedule.

System Tasks execute according to certified automation governance.

---

# 2.10 Decision Point

Represents a governed business decision within a workflow.

Examples:

- Customer approved artwork?
- Inventory available?
- Quality passed?
- Payment confirmed?
- Executive approval required?

Decision Points preserve explicit business reasoning.

---

# 2.11 Business Rule

Represents one certified business decision rule.

Examples:

- Production begins only after artwork approval.
- Shipment requires successful quality inspection.
- Financial approval required above configured authority limits.
- Customer notification required after dispatch.

Business Rules govern workflow behavior rather than implementation logic.

---

# 2.12 Automation Rule

Represents one governed automation policy.

Examples:

- Automatically notify customer after shipment.
- Automatically archive completed workflow.
- Automatically assign production queue.
- Automatically generate packing documentation.

Automation Rules never bypass enterprise governance.

---

# 2.13 SLA Policy

Represents enterprise expectations for workflow completion.

Examples:

- Artwork proof within one business day.
- Purchase approval within defined governance targets.
- Production planning within approved operational timelines.
- Customer response reminder after configured waiting period.

SLA Policies define business expectations rather than technical timers.

---

# 2.14 Timer

Represents a scheduled workflow action.

Examples:

- Reminder interval.
- Approval deadline.
- Escalation trigger.
- Archive eligibility review.
- Scheduled workflow checkpoint.

Timers support workflow governance without owning business decisions.

---

# 2.15 Escalation Rule

Represents governed workflow escalation.

Examples:

- Approval overdue.
- Customer proof awaiting response.
- Production blocked.
- Shipment delay.
- Financial review overdue.

Escalation Rules maintain business responsiveness.

---

# 2.16 Process Exception

Represents deviations from certified workflow execution.

Examples:

- Missing approval.
- Conflicting business rule.
- Inventory unavailable.
- Document missing.
- Production interruption.
- External dependency unavailable.

Every Process Exception requires governed handling and audit evidence.

---

# 2.17 Workflow Audit Record

Represents immutable workflow history.

Examples:

- Workflow started.
- Human Task assigned.
- Decision recorded.
- Automation executed.
- Workflow completed.

Workflow Audit Records remain append-only.

---

# 2.18 Process Template

Represents reusable workflow patterns.

Examples:

- Two-stage approval.
- Multi-level approval.
- Customer review cycle.
- Quality inspection flow.
- Executive approval workflow.

Templates standardize enterprise processes without owning business execution.

---

# 2.19 Orchestration Contract

Represents the certified agreement governing cooperation between enterprise domains.

Examples:

- Order → Production.
- Production → Quality.
- Quality → Shipping.
- Shipping → Finance.
- Document → Production.
- Notification → Workflow.

Orchestration Contracts preserve explicit domain ownership.

---

# 2.20 Process Milestone

Represents a major business checkpoint within a workflow.

Examples:

- Customer confirmed order.
- Artwork approved.
- Manufacturing started.
- Quality accepted.
- Shipment dispatched.
- Order completed.

Milestones provide measurable progress while preserving workflow history.

---

        │
        ▼

        ▼
Workflow Instance

        ▼
Process State

 ┌──────┼────────────┐
 ▼      ▼            ▼
Human  System   Decision
Task    Task      Point
          │
          ▼
     Business Rule

This model separates workflow coordination, task execution, decision governance, automation, and auditability while preserving explicit enterprise responsibilities.

# WORKFLOW, PROCESS AUTOMATION & ORCHESTRATION ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 3 — State Machines, Transition Rules & Operational Gates

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain governs the complete lifecycle of enterprise business processes, workflow definitions, workflow instances, human tasks, system tasks, decision points, automation rules, SLA policies, process milestones, and orchestration contracts.

Every governed workflow progresses through certified business states.

These states ensure that enterprise processes remain:

- Governed.
- Predictable.
- Traceable.
- Auditable.
- Business-approved.
- Recoverable.
- Technology-independent.

This Canon establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for:

- Business Processes.
- Workflow Definitions.
- Workflow Instances.
- Human Tasks.
- System Tasks.
- Decision Points.
- Automation Rules.
- SLA Policies.
- Escalation Rules.
- Process Exceptions.

---

# 3.2 Lifecycle Philosophy

Workflow lifecycle management follows permanent principles.

### Single Authoritative State

Every governed workflow entity exists in exactly one official lifecycle state.

---

### Controlled Progression

State transitions occur only through approved business actions.

---

### Governance Gates

Every transition passes mandatory governance validation before becoming effective.

---

### Traceability

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business justification.
- Related approvals where applicable.
- Audit references.

---

### Immutable Workflow History

Historical workflow records remain permanently preserved.

Corrections generate new governed transitions rather than rewriting history.

---

# 3.3 Business Process Lifecycle

Every Business Process follows the certified lifecycle.

```text id="workflow-stage3-process"
Defined
    │
Approved
    │
Active
    │
Retired
```

Exceptional states include:

- Suspended.
- Withdrawn.

---

### Defined

Business process documented but not yet certified.

---

### Approved

Business governance completed.

---

### Active

Authoritative process available for enterprise execution.

---

### Retired

Process no longer initiated but preserved for historical reference.

---

# 3.4 Workflow Definition Lifecycle

```text id="workflow-stage3-definition"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Certified
   │
Published
```

Exceptional states:

- Superseded.
- Withdrawn.

Only certified Workflow Definitions may initiate Workflow Instances.

---

# 3.5 Workflow Instance Lifecycle

```text id="workflow-stage3-instance"
Created
    │
Running
    │
Waiting
    │
Completed
```

Exceptional states:

- Cancelled.
- Escalated.
- Failed.

Waiting represents a governed pause for external input, approvals, timers, or dependent business activities.

---

# 3.6 Human Task Lifecycle

```text id="workflow-stage3-human"
Assigned
    │
Accepted
    │
In Progress
    │
Completed
```

Exceptional states:

- Reassigned.
- Cancelled.
- Escalated.

Every Human Task preserves enterprise accountability.

---

# 3.7 System Task Lifecycle

```text id="workflow-stage3-system"
Queued
   │
Executing
   │
Completed
```

Exceptional states:

- Retried.
- Failed.
- Cancelled.

System Tasks follow certified automation governance.

---

# 3.8 Decision Point Lifecycle

```text id="workflow-stage3-decision"
Pending
   │
Evaluated
   │
Resolved
```

Exceptional states:

- Deferred.
- Escalated.

Decision Points preserve explicit business reasoning.

---

# 3.9 Automation Rule Lifecycle

```text id="workflow-stage3-automation"
Defined
    │
Validated
    │
Activated
```

Exceptional states:

- Suspended.
- Retired.

Automation Rules remain centrally governed.

---

# 3.10 SLA Policy Lifecycle

```text id="workflow-stage3-sla"
Proposed
     │
Reviewed
     │
Approved
     │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Replaced.
- Retired.

SLA Policies define business expectations rather than implementation timing.

---

# 3.11 Official Transition Matrix

Examples include:

| Current State | Allowed Next States |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Defined Process | Approved |
| Approved Process | Active |
| Active Process | Retired |
| Draft Workflow Definition | Reviewed |
| Reviewed Workflow Definition | Certified |
| Certified Workflow Definition | Published |
| Created Workflow Instance | Running |
| Running Workflow Instance | Waiting, Completed |
| Assigned Human Task | Accepted |
| Accepted Human Task | In Progress |
| In Progress Human Task | Completed |
| Queued System Task | Executing |
| Executing System Task | Completed |

Transitions outside certified pathways are prohibited.

---

# 3.12 Forbidden Transitions

Examples include:

Defined Process

→ Active

Draft Workflow Definition

→ Published

Created Workflow Instance

→ Completed

Assigned Human Task

→ Completed

Queued System Task

→ Completed

Operational governance prevents these invalid transitions.

---

# 3.13 Governance Gates

Every lifecycle progression passes mandatory business gates.

## Workflow Publication Gate

Before Published:

- Business review completed.
- Participating domains validated.
- Business rules verified.
- Governance approval completed.

---

## Workflow Execution Gate

Before Running:

- Workflow Definition certified.
- Required business context available.
- Required participants identified.
- Dependencies satisfied.

---

## Human Task Assignment Gate

Before Assigned:

- Responsible role identified.
- Enterprise Identity resolved.
- Required authority confirmed.
- Supporting business context available.

---

## Automation Activation Gate

Before Activated:

- Business rules validated.
- Governance approval completed.
- Audit requirements verified.

Automation activation never bypasses enterprise governance.

---

## SLA Effectiveness Gate

Before Effective:

- Governance approval completed.
- Organizational expectations defined.
- Escalation rules validated.

---

# 3.14 Operational Authority

Every workflow transition records:

- Responsible Enterprise Identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business justification.
- Related approvals.

Workflow transitions are never anonymous.

---

# 3.15 Business Outcomes

Every governed workflow concludes with one authoritative outcome.

Canonical outcomes include:

- Completed.
- Cancelled.
- Failed.
- Escalated.
- Suspended.
- Retired.

These outcomes preserve enterprise process integrity.

---

# 3.16 Parallel Workflow Activities

Enterprise workflows support concurrent execution.

Examples:

- Multiple approval branches.
- Parallel manufacturing activities.
- Concurrent quality inspections.
- Simultaneous document preparation.
- AI-assisted task recommendations.

Business rules require:

- One authoritative Process State per Workflow Instance.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Conflict prevention.
- Complete execution history.

---

# 3.17 Exception Escalation

Examples requiring governed escalation include:

- Missed SLA.
- Missing approval.
- Inventory unavailable.
- Customer proof overdue.
- Production interruption.
- Shipping delay.
- Financial review overdue.
- Cross-domain dependency failure.

Escalations generate governed workflow events while preserving Workflow Domain ownership.

---

# 3.18 State Integrity Rules

The Workflow Domain enforces the following invariants:

- Every Workflow Instance has one authoritative Process State.
- Every Human Task belongs to one Workflow Instance.
- Every System Task belongs to one Workflow Instance.
- Every Decision Point follows certified Business Rules.
- Every Published Workflow Definition remains historically traceable.
- Every Automation Rule follows governed activation.
- Workflow history remains append-only.
- Workflow audit remains immutable.

---

# 3.19 GiftHatke Personalized Manufacturing Workflow Lifecycle

For personalized manufacturing, the certified workflow follows:

```text id="workflow-stage3-personalization"
Customer Order
        │
        ▼
Personalization Intake
        │
        ▼
Artwork Preparation
        │
        ▼
Proof Review
        │
        ▼
Customer Approval
        │
        ▼
Production Release
        │
        ▼
Manufacturing
        │
        ▼
Quality Inspection
        │
        ▼
Packaging
        │
        ▼
Shipping
        │
        ▼
Order Completed
```

Each stage remains governed by its owning business domain while the Workflow Domain coordinates overall execution.

---

# 3.20 Lifecycle Governance

The workflow lifecycle architecture follows permanent principles.

- Every state has defined business meaning.
- Every transition is governed.
- Workflow history remains immutable.
- Human accountability remains explicit.
- Automation remains policy-driven.
- Parallel execution remains controlled.
- Business semantics remain independent of workflow technology.

---

# 3.21 Stage 3 Certification

The **Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Enterprise Canon — Stage 3** establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for the Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain.

It defines:

- Business Process lifecycle.
- Workflow Definition lifecycle.
- Workflow Instance lifecycle.
- Human Task lifecycle.
- System Task lifecycle.
- Decision Point lifecycle.
- Automation Rule lifecycle.
- SLA Policy lifecycle.
- Official transition matrix.
- Forbidden transitions.
- Governance gates.
- Business outcomes.
- Parallel workflow activities.
- Exception escalation.
- State integrity constraints.
- GiftHatke personalized manufacturing workflow lifecycle.

This lifecycle becomes the authoritative operational model for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Enterprise workflow platforms.
- Business process management systems.
- AI-assisted orchestration.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration lifecycle defined here is permanent. Future workflow engines, orchestration platforms, BPM systems, automation technologies, AI workflow assistants, and enterprise process platforms may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified lifecycle states, transition rules, governance gates, orchestration semantics, and workflow management principles established by this Canon. memcite

# WORKFLOW, PROCESS AUTOMATION & ORCHESTRATION ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 4 — API Contracts & Domain Services

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain provides the enterprise with a stable set of **business workflow services** that govern business processes, workflow execution, task management, orchestration, business rules, automation, SLAs, escalations, and workflow governance.

These services represent **permanent business capabilities**.

They do **not** prescribe:

- BPM engines.
- Workflow frameworks.
- Automation platforms.
- Task schedulers.
- Queue technologies.
- Event buses.
- Low-code products.
- Process orchestration products.
- AI workflow engines.
- Cloud workflow services.

Those technologies may evolve.

The certified business services defined by this Canon remain permanent.

---

# 4.2 Service Philosophy

The Workflow Domain owns:

- Business Processes.
- Workflow Definitions.
- Workflow Instances.
- Human Tasks.
- System Tasks.
- Business Rules.
- Automation Rules.
- SLA Policies.
- Workflow Exceptions.
- Workflow Audit.
- Orchestration Contracts.

It does **not** own:

- Orders.
- Inventory.
- Production.
- Documents.
- Notifications.
- Finance.
- Enterprise identities.

Operational domains own business execution.

The Workflow Domain governs process coordination.

Every business service must:

- Represent one enterprise responsibility.
- Preserve business ownership.
- Enforce certified workflow governance.
- Produce auditable outcomes.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 4.16 Canonical Business Operations

The domain publishes a stable catalog of business operations.

- Create Process.

- Retire Process.

### Workflow Execution
