# 4.17 Commands and Queries

Business services are divided into two categories.

## Commands

Commands modify workflow state.

Examples:

- Start Workflow.
- Complete Task.
- Activate Rule.
- Execute Automation.

Commands:

- Validate governance.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish workflow events.

---

## Queries

Queries never modify workflow state.

Examples:

- Workflow Status.
- Task Queue.
- SLA Dashboard.
- Process History.
- Exception List.

Queries remain read-only.

---

# 4.18 Validation Framework

Every command performs mandatory validation.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

- Workflow exists.
- Process exists.
- Task exists.
- Rule exists.

---

### Business Validation

- Business prerequisites satisfied.
- Responsible participant identified.
- Dependencies available.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

- Requested transition permitted.
- Governance gates satisfied.
- Workflow integrity maintained.

---

### Policy Validation

- Automation policy.
- SLA policy.
- Escalation policy.
- Business rule policy.

---

### Governance Validation

- Required approvals.
- Business ownership.
- Organizational policy.
- Audit requirements.

---

# 4.19 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical workflow transaction.

Example:

Start Workflow:

- Validate Process Definition.
- Validate Participants.
- Validate Business Context.
- Create Workflow Instance.
- Record Audit.
- Publish Workflow Started event.

If any required step fails, the Workflow remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.20 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Start Workflow.
- Complete Workflow.
- Execute Automation.
- Publish Process.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate Workflow Instances, duplicate Human Tasks, duplicate milestones, or duplicate workflow history.

---

# 4.21 Concurrency

Multiple participants may collaborate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Parallel approvals.
- Concurrent production planning.
- Multiple quality inspectors.
- Cross-functional reviews.
- AI-assisted routing recommendations.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Preservation of authoritative workflow state.
- Complete execution history.

---

# 4.22 Error Classification

Workflow services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Workflow prerequisites not satisfied.

---

### Business Rule Errors

Business policy prevents execution.

---

### Governance Errors

Missing approvals or authorization.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition prohibited.

---

### Dependency Errors

Participating domain unable to satisfy business contract.

Examples:

- Order unavailable.
- Production unavailable.
- Document unavailable.
- Identity unavailable.

---

### SLA Errors

Deadline exceeded or governance expectation violated.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Business failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

The Workflow Domain collaborates with:

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Coordinate customer processes |
| Inventory & Procurement | Coordinate material availability |
| Production & Manufacturing | Coordinate manufacturing execution |
| Quality Management | Coordinate inspection workflows |
| Shipping & Fulfillment | Coordinate fulfillment |
| Finance & Accounting | Coordinate financial approvals |
| Reporting & Business Intelligence | Workflow analytics |

| Notification, Communication & Collaboration | Workflow notifications and communications |
| Document & Digital Asset Management | Workflow-dependent documents and digital assets |
| AI Services | Routing, prioritization, optimization, and decision support |

Operational ownership remains explicit.

# 4.25 Service Governance

The Workflow service architecture follows permanent principles.

- Stable business contracts.
- Explicit domain ownership.
- Controlled evolution.
- Consistent workflow semantics.
- Technology-independent implementation.
- Governance-first orchestration.

# WORKFLOW, PROCESS AUTOMATION & ORCHESTRATION ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 5 — Workflow Governance, Automation Governance & Enterprise Control Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for business workflows, process automation, orchestration, human tasks, system tasks, business rules, service levels, process exceptions, and cross-domain execution.

Unlike operational domains that govern business data, this domain governs **how enterprise work is coordinated, monitored, controlled, and continuously improved while preserving explicit ownership of every participating business domain**.

This Canon defines the permanent business architecture for:

- Workflow governance.
- Automation governance.
- Human task governance.
- Business rule governance.
- Process governance.
- SLA governance.
- Escalation governance.
- Exception governance.
- AI-assisted workflow governance.
- Enterprise orchestration governance.

It intentionally avoids prescribing workflow engines, BPM platforms, orchestration software, automation frameworks, or implementation technologies.

---

# 5.2 Enterprise Workflow Philosophy

Enterprise workflow governance follows eight permanent principles.

### Work Exists to Achieve Business Outcomes

Workflows coordinate certified business activities.

They never redefine business ownership.

---

### One Authoritative Workflow Definition

Every governed business process has one authoritative workflow definition.

---

### Explicit Responsibility

Every workflow activity has one accountable owner.

Automation never removes accountability.

---

### Controlled Automation

Automation accelerates business execution without bypassing governance.

---

### Explainable Processes

Enterprise participants understand:

- Why a workflow exists.
- Who owns each activity.
- Why automation occurred.
- Why a decision was taken.
- Why a task was assigned.

---

### Enterprise Visibility

Workflow execution remains observable from initiation through completion.

---

### Traceability

Every workflow activity remains attributable to:

- Business Process.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Workflow history.
- Audit history.

---

### Technology Independence

Workflow governance remains stable while automation technologies evolve.

---

# 5.3 Enterprise Workflow Governance Model

Workflow governance evaluates six enterprise layers.

## Layer 1 — Business Process

Defines enterprise intent.

Examples:

- Order Fulfillment.
- Purchase Approval.
- Manufacturing Execution.

---

## Layer 2 — Workflow

Coordinates enterprise execution.

Examples:

- Workflow Definition.
- Workflow Instance.
- Human Task.

---

## Layer 3 — Decision

Applies certified business rules.

Examples:

- Approval decision.
- Inventory decision.
- Quality decision.

---

## Layer 4 — Automation

Executes governed automation.

Examples:

- Automatic notifications.
- Automatic task assignment.
- Automatic workflow routing.

---

## Layer 5 — Governance

Applies:

- SLA.
- Escalation.
- Exception handling.
- Organizational policy.

---

## Layer 6 — Audit

Maintains permanent enterprise workflow history.

Workflow execution becomes authoritative only after all required governance layers are satisfied.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Governance Roles

The Workflow Domain governs process coordination responsibilities.

Illustrative roles include:

## Workflow Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Workflow definitions.
- Process governance.
- Workflow configuration.

---

## Process Owner

Responsibilities:

- Business outcomes.
- Workflow performance.
- Governance compliance.

---

## Automation Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Automation governance.
- Automation validation.
- Automation lifecycle.

Cannot modify business ownership.

---

## Workflow Auditor

Responsibilities:

- Workflow history.
- SLA compliance.
- Governance verification.

Cannot modify historical workflow records.

---

## AI Workflow Administrator

Responsibilities:

- AI workflow recommendations.
- AI routing governance.
- AI decision explainability.

Cannot bypass certified governance.

---

# 5.5 Workflow Classification

Enterprise workflows are categorized according to business purpose.

## Operational

Examples:

- Manufacturing.
- Inventory replenishment.
- Shipping.

---

## Approval

Examples:

- Purchase approval.
- Artwork approval.
- Executive approval.

---

## Customer

Examples:

- Lead conversion.
- Personalization approval.
- Complaint resolution.

---

## Administrative

Examples:

- User provisioning.
- Policy review.
- Compliance workflow.

---

## Knowledge

Examples:

- SOP publication.
- Documentation review.
- Training approval.

Classification determines governance behavior rather than implementation technology.

---

# 5.6 Automation Governance

Enterprise automation follows controlled principles.

Automation may:

- Route work.
- Assign tasks.
- Calculate priorities.
- Schedule reminders.
- Generate notifications.
- Synchronize workflow state.

Automation may **not**:

- Bypass approvals.
- Override business ownership.
- Suppress audit history.
- Ignore enterprise policies.
- Modify workflow history.

Automation remains subordinate to governance.

---

# 5.7 Human Task Governance

Human work follows permanent standards.

Every Human Task records:

- Responsible role.
- Assigned Enterprise Identity.
- Business context.
- Due expectations.
- Workflow relationship.
- Completion evidence.

Tasks remain accountable throughout their lifecycle.

---

# 5.8 SLA Governance

Service Level governance evaluates:

- Expected completion.
- Reminder thresholds.
- Escalation thresholds.
- Compliance measurement.
- Historical performance.

SLAs represent business expectations rather than technical timers.

---

# 5.9 Exception Governance

Workflow exceptions remain governed.

Examples:

- Missing approvals.
- Production delays.
- Customer inactivity.
- Inventory shortages.
- Financial review delays.
- Cross-domain dependency failures.

Every exception requires:

- Classification.
- Business impact assessment.
- Responsible owner.
- Resolution tracking.
- Permanent audit evidence.

---

# 5.10 AI-Assisted Workflow Governance

AI assistance remains governed.

Examples include:

- Workflow prioritization.
- Task recommendations.
- SLA risk prediction.
- Intelligent routing.
- Resource recommendations.
- Process optimization.
- Exception prediction.

AI-generated recommendations:

- Remain explainable.
- Preserve business ownership.
- Respect enterprise governance.
- Support human decision-making.

---

# 5.11 GiftHatke Manufacturing Workflow Governance

For personalized manufacturing, workflow governance additionally protects:

- Customer personalization approvals.
- Artwork revision control.
- Production release authorization.
- Manufacturing sequencing.
- Quality inspection completion.
- Packaging readiness.
- Shipping authorization.

Every personalized manufacturing workflow preserves:

- Customer reference.
- Order reference.
- Artwork reference.
- Production reference.
- Quality reference.
- Delivery reference.

This guarantees manufacturing consistency while preserving complete workflow accountability.

---

# 5.12 Sensitive Workflow Governance

Certain workflows require enhanced governance.

Examples include:

- Financial approvals.
- Executive approvals.
- Customer data handling.
- HR workflows.
- Manufacturing intellectual property.
- Legal review.
- Compliance investigations.

Sensitive workflows require strengthened authorization, auditability, separation of duties where applicable, and controlled escalation.

---

# 5.13 Audit and Non-Repudiation

Every governed workflow records:

- Business process.
- Workflow Instance.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Task history.
- Decision history.
- Automation history.
- SLA history.
- Exception history.

Workflow history is immutable and supports enterprise governance, dispute resolution, internal assurance, external audits where applicable, regulatory compliance where required, and long-term organizational accountability.

---

# 5.14 Enterprise Workflow Standards

The Workflow Domain follows these permanent principles.

- Processes remain business-driven.
- Automation remains governed.
- Human accountability remains explicit.
- Workflow definitions remain authoritative.
- AI remains accountable.
- Workflow history remains immutable.
- Governance evolves only through approved enterprise processes.

---

# 5.15 Stage 5 Certification

The **Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Enterprise Canon — Stage 5** establishes the permanent enterprise governance framework for the Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain.

It defines:

# WORKFLOW, PROCESS AUTOMATION & ORCHESTRATION ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 6 — Events, Automations & Integration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain governs enterprise process coordination, workflow execution, business rules, automation, human tasks, system tasks, SLAs, exceptions, and cross-domain orchestration.

Unlike operational domains that publish business transaction events, this domain publishes **workflow orchestration events** that communicate the progression of enterprise business processes while preserving ownership of the underlying business entities.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Workflow Domain.

It defines:

- Workflow business events.
- Process orchestration events.
- Event publication rules.
- Enterprise workflow automation.
- Cross-domain choreography.
- Integration boundaries.
- AI-assisted workflow integration.

It intentionally avoids prescribing workflow engines, message brokers, event buses, BPM products, orchestration platforms, or implementation technologies.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A Workflow event represents a completed enterprise process fact.

Examples include:

- Workflow Started.
- Human Task Assigned.
- Approval Completed.
- Workflow Escalated.
- Process Completed.

Events communicate **completed orchestration outcomes**, not technical execution details.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business activity.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise workflow semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Workflow Domain follows permanent principles.

### Process Significance

Only meaningful workflow activities generate canonical business events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed workflow occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable Process History

Published events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Workflow events originate only from the Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain.

Operational domains continue to own the business entities coordinated by those workflows.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event identity.
- Timestamp.
- Workflow reference.
- Related business entity.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Business role.
- Correlation identifier.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Workflow Events

## Business Process Events

- Process Defined.
- Process Approved.
- Process Activated.
- Process Retired.

---

## Workflow Events

- Workflow Started.
- Workflow Paused.
- Workflow Resumed.
- Workflow Completed.
- Workflow Cancelled.

---

## Human Task Events

- Task Created.
- Task Assigned.
- Task Accepted.
- Task Completed.
- Task Reassigned.

---

## System Task Events

- System Task Queued.
- System Task Started.
- System Task Completed.
- System Task Failed.

---

## Decision Events

- Decision Requested.
- Decision Evaluated.
- Decision Approved.
- Decision Rejected.

---

## Automation Events

- Automation Triggered.
- Automation Completed.
- Automation Suspended.
- Automation Resumed.

---

## SLA Events

- SLA Monitoring Started.
- SLA Warning Issued.
- SLA Breach Detected.
- SLA Compliance Recorded.

---

## Escalation Events

- Escalation Triggered.
- Escalation Assigned.
- Escalation Resolved.

---

## Workflow Exception Events

- Workflow Blocked.
- Dependency Failure Detected.
- Approval Timeout Detected.
- Exception Resolved.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Workflow events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding governance activity.

Examples:

- **Workflow Started** is emitted only after the Workflow Instance has been successfully created and validated.
- **Task Assigned** is emitted only after responsibility has been established.
- **Automation Completed** is emitted only after governed automation finishes successfully.
- **Workflow Completed** is emitted only after all mandatory business milestones have been achieved.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Workflow event follows the same sequence:

1. Workflow activity initiated.
2. Governance validation completed.
3. Workflow transaction completed.
4. Audit recorded.
5. Canonical workflow event published.
6. Authorized consumers process the event.
7. Monitoring records processing outcomes.

Published events therefore represent authoritative workflow facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Workflow events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Workflow Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|----------------|--------------------------|
| Workflow Started | Reporting & Business Intelligence |
| Task Assigned | Notification, Communication & Collaboration |
| Decision Approved | Participating business domain |
| Workflow Completed | Reporting & Business Intelligence, Finance & Accounting (where applicable) |
| SLA Breach Detected | Identity, Security & Administration, Executive Governance |
| Automation Completed | Participating business domains |
| Escalation Triggered | Notification, Communication & Collaboration |
| Exception Resolved | Originating business domain |

Consumers respond to workflow events without assuming ownership of workflow governance.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every workflow event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event identity.
- Event type.
- Workflow reference.
- Process reference.
- Related business entity.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation identifier.
- Governance reference.

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Workflow Automation Principles

Automation improves enterprise process execution while respecting certified policies.

Every automation must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Observable.
- Repeatable.

Automation must never bypass:

- Required approvals.
- Human accountability.
- Business rules.
- SLA governance.
- Exception governance.
- Audit requirements.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Workflow Automations

Examples include:

### Task Automation

- Assign tasks.
- Send reminders.
- Detect overdue work.
- Suggest task reassignment.

---

### Workflow Automation

- Start dependent workflows.
- Advance completed workflows.
- Synchronize workflow milestones.
- Archive completed workflow history.

---

### SLA Automation

- Monitor deadlines.
- Generate warnings.
- Trigger governed escalations.
- Measure compliance.

---

### Process Intelligence Automation

- Detect bottlenecks.
- Recommend optimizations.
- Predict workflow delays.
- Suggest workload balancing.

---

### AI Workflow Automation

- Recommend routing.
- Recommend prioritization.
- Explain workflow state.
- Predict completion.
- Detect anomalies.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Workflow Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized coordination is required.

Examples:

- Order Fulfillment.
- Manufacturing.
- Artwork Approval.
- Executive Approval.

---

## Choreography

Used where domains respond independently to workflow events.

Examples:

- Notification after approval.
- Reporting after completion.
- Document publication after workflow completion.
- AI analytics after workflow execution.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than implementation technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The Workflow Domain integrates with every certified enterprise domain through governed business contracts.

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Commercial workflow coordination |
| Inventory & Procurement | Material availability workflows |
| Production & Manufacturing | Manufacturing orchestration |
| Quality Management | Inspection workflows |
| Shipping & Fulfillment | Fulfillment orchestration |
| Finance & Accounting | Financial approvals |
| Reporting & Business Intelligence | Workflow analytics |
| Identity, Security & Administration | Authorization and organizational routing |
| Notification, Communication & Collaboration | Workflow communications |
| Document & Digital Asset Management | Workflow-dependent documents and approvals |
| AI Services | Workflow intelligence and optimization |

Each collaborating domain remains independently governed.

---

# 6.13 External Integrations

The Canon supports future integration with:

- BPM suites.
- Enterprise workflow engines.
- Automation platforms.
- Event-driven orchestration frameworks.
- AI workflow assistants.
- Robotic process automation platforms.
- Low-code orchestration platforms.
- Future enterprise workflow ecosystems.

These integrations consume or publish certified workflow events without redefining enterprise workflow governance.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Workflow failures are categorized consistently.

### Validation Failure

Workflow prerequisites are not satisfied.

No completion event is published.

---

### Business Rule Failure

Workflow violates certified business policy.

Execution is prevented.

---

### Dependency Failure

A participating domain cannot satisfy its business contract.

Examples:

- Order unavailable.
- Production unavailable.
- Document unavailable.
- Identity unavailable.

---

### SLA Failure

Workflow exceeds governed expectations.

Escalation may occur according to policy.

---

### Engine Failure

Execution technology temporarily unavailable.

Business workflow intent remains preserved for governed recovery.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries follow controlled enterprise policy.

Repeated processing must never create:

- Duplicate Workflow Instances.
- Duplicate Human Tasks.
- Duplicate Process Milestones.
- Duplicate workflow history.
- Duplicate audit records.

Where correction is required, new workflow events preserve historical accountability while superseding previous outcomes according to enterprise governance.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Workflow events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Stable business semantics.
- Backward compatibility where practical.
- Managed deprecation.
- Controlled consumer migration.

Business meaning remains consistent across versions.

---

# 6.17 Observability

The enterprise monitors workflow execution through:

- Workflow completion.
- Task assignment.
- SLA compliance.
- Automation performance.
- Exception frequency.
- Escalation trends.
- Cross-domain coordination.
- Consumer processing status.

Observability supports enterprise workflow governance without changing business semantics.

---

# 6.18 Integration Security

Workflow integrations comply with the Identity, Security & Administration Canon.

Requirements include:

- Authenticated identities.
- Authorized workflow participation.
- Least privilege.
- Controlled workflow visibility.
- Full auditability.

Internal and external workflow integrations follow identical governance principles.

---

Each milestone publishes certified workflow events while preserving ownership of the participating business domains.

---

# 6.20 Stage 6 Certification

The **Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Enterprise Canon — Stage 6** establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration Domain.

It defines:

- Workflow event philosophy.

- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**

# MASTER DATA MANAGEMENT (MDM) ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation & Business Scope

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The **Master Data Management (MDM) Domain** establishes the permanent enterprise architecture for governing shared business reference data across the entire GiftHatkeOS Enterprise Canon.

Unlike operational domains that create business transactions, the MDM Domain governs the **authoritative business entities that are referenced by multiple enterprise domains**.

It does **not** own:

- Customer Orders.
- Purchase Orders.
- Production Jobs.
- Shipments.
- Invoices.
- Payments.
- Workflow Instances.

Instead, it governs the enterprise master records that those transactions depend upon.

The MDM Domain is the authoritative source for:

- Customer Master.
- Supplier Master.
- Product Master.
- Material Master.
- Equipment Master.
- Warehouse & Location Master.
- Organizational Master.
- Reference Catalogs.
- Classification Standards.
- Enterprise Reference Data.

---

# 1.2 Mission

The Master Data Management Domain exists to ensure that every certified enterprise domain operates using **consistent, trusted, governed, and authoritative business reference data**.

---

# 1.3 Domain Vision

The architecture supports organizations ranging from a single personalized manufacturing workshop to globally distributed enterprises operating across:

- Multiple companies.
- Manufacturing facilities.
- Warehouses.
- Distribution centers.
- Retail operations.
- Franchise networks.
- International subsidiaries.
- AI-assisted enterprises.

The architecture supports:

- Centralized master data.
- Federated stewardship.
- Multi-company governance.
- Enterprise-wide synchronization.
- Cross-domain consistency.
- AI-assisted master data quality.

Business semantics remain stable while implementation technologies evolve.

---

# 1.4 Business Objectives

The Master Data Management Domain pursues the following permanent objectives.

### One Enterprise Truth

Every master record has one authoritative enterprise identity.

---

### Consistency

Every certified domain references identical master information.

---

### Data Quality

Master data remains accurate, complete, and governed.

---

### Controlled Change

Master data evolves through approved governance.

---

### Enterprise Reuse

Master data is shared rather than duplicated.

---

### Long-Term Stability

Reference data remains stable while operational transactions continue independently.

---

# 1.5 Domain Boundaries

The Master Data Management Domain owns:

- Customer Master.
- Supplier Master.
- Product Master.
- Material Master.
- Service Master.
- Equipment Master.
- Warehouse Master.
- Location Master.
- Unit of Measure Master.
- Currency Master.
- Tax Master.
- Organizational Master.
- Classification Catalogs.
- Reference Lists.
- Master Data Governance Policies.
- Master Data Stewardship.

The domain does **not** own:

- Orders.
- Procurement transactions.
- Manufacturing execution.
- Financial postings.
- Shipping activities.
- Workflow execution.
- Documents.
- Communications.

Operational domains consume master data but do not govern enterprise master definitions.

---

# 1.6 Business Responsibilities

The Master Data Management Domain is responsible for:

### Master Governance

Maintaining enterprise master records.

---

### Data Stewardship

Managing ownership and quality of master information.

---

### Reference Standardization

Standardizing enterprise reference values.

---

### Synchronization Governance

Coordinating master data consistency across certified domains.

---

### Classification Governance

Managing enterprise taxonomies and classifications.

---

### Master Data Quality

Maintaining completeness, consistency, uniqueness, and accuracy.

---

# 1.7 Core Business Principles

The domain follows these permanent principles.

### Master Data Exists to Support Business

Master data enables certified enterprise operations.

It never replaces operational transactions.

---

### One Authoritative Record

Every governed master entity has one authoritative enterprise record.

---

### Explicit Stewardship

Every master entity has one accountable steward.

---

### Shared Enterprise Asset

Master data is an enterprise asset rather than departmental property.

---

### Traceability

Every master record remains attributable to:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Governance history.
- Version history.
- Audit history.

---

### Technology Independence

Master data governance remains stable while implementation technologies evolve.

---

# 1.8 Supported Master Data Categories

The architecture supports:

### Party Master

Examples:

- Customers.
- Suppliers.
- Business Partners.

---

### Product Master

Examples:

- Finished Goods.
- Semi-Finished Goods.
- Services.
- Product Families.

Examples:

- Customer Segments.

---

### AI Knowledge Master

- Classification dictionaries.
- Controlled vocabularies.
- Enterprise taxonomies.
- Semantic reference catalogs.

From Order Management:

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The Master Data Management (MDM) Domain is governed by a permanent enterprise information model that defines every master data business object within GiftHatkeOS.

the certified business entities remain unchanged.

# 2.2 Entity Principles

Every master data entity follows these permanent principles.

### Single Responsibility

Each entity governs one enterprise reference responsibility.

Examples:

- A **Customer Master** represents one authoritative customer identity.
- A **Product Master** represents one authoritative product definition.
- A **Material Master** represents one authoritative material specification.

Responsibilities are never shared.

### Stable Enterprise Identity

Every master entity possesses one permanent enterprise identity independent of implementation technology.

---

### Explicit Stewardship

Every master entity has one accountable business steward.

---

### Governance

Every master entity follows enterprise lifecycle governance, approval, auditability, and controlled evolution.

---

### Traceability

Every master entity remains fully traceable throughout its lifecycle.

# MASTER DATA MANAGEMENT (MDM) ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 3 — State Machines, Transition Rules & Operational Gates

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The Master Data Management (MDM) Domain governs the complete lifecycle of enterprise master records, classifications, reference catalogs, stewardship assignments, governance policies, and enterprise reference standards.

Every governed master entity progresses through certified business states.

These states ensure that enterprise reference information remains:

- Governed.
- Consistent.
- Traceable.
- Auditable.
- Business-approved.
- Recoverable.
- Technology-independent.

This Canon establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for:

- Customer Master.
- Supplier Master.
- Product Master.
- Product Variants.
- Material Master.
- Equipment Master.
- Warehouse Master.
- Organization Master.
- Classification Master.
- Reference Catalogs.
- Governance Policies.
- Stewardship Assignments.

---

# 3.2 Lifecycle Philosophy

Master data lifecycle management follows permanent principles.

### Single Authoritative State

Every governed master entity exists in exactly one official lifecycle state.

---

### Controlled Evolution

Master data changes occur only through approved governance.

---

### Governance Gates

Every lifecycle transition passes mandatory business validation before becoming effective.

---

### Traceability

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business justification.
- Related approvals.
- Audit references.

---

### Immutable History

Historical master records remain permanently preserved.

Corrections generate governed revisions rather than rewriting historical information.

---

# 3.3 Master Record Lifecycle

Every enterprise master entity follows the certified lifecycle.

```text id="mdm-stage3-master"
Proposed
    │
Reviewed
    │
Approved
    │
Active
```

Exceptional states include:

- Suspended.
- Deprecated.
- Archived.

---

### Proposed

Master information has been requested but is not yet enterprise-approved.

---

### Reviewed

Business stewardship has validated the proposed information.

---

### Approved

Governance approval has been completed.

---

### Active

The master record becomes the authoritative enterprise reference.

---

### Suspended

Temporarily unavailable for new business use while historical references remain valid.

---

### Deprecated

Scheduled for replacement by another governed master record.

---

### Archived

Retained only for historical and audit purposes.

---

# 3.4 Product Variant Lifecycle

```text id="mdm-stage3-variant"
Defined
    │
Validated
    │
Released
```

Exceptional states:

- Deprecated.
- Archived.

Only Released variants may be referenced by operational transactions.

---

# 3.5 Classification Lifecycle

```text id="mdm-stage3-classification"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Published
```

Exceptional states:

- Withdrawn.
- Superseded.

Published classifications become enterprise standards.

---

# 3.6 Reference Catalog Lifecycle

```text id="mdm-stage3-reference"
Draft
   │
Validated
   │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Replaced.
- Archived.

Reference catalogs remain centrally governed.

---

# 3.7 Stewardship Assignment Lifecycle

```text id="mdm-stage3-steward"
Assigned
    │
Accepted
    │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Reassigned.
- Retired.

Every master entity always has an accountable steward.

---

# 3.8 Master Data Policy Lifecycle

```text id="mdm-stage3-policy"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Replaced.
- Retired.

Policies govern master data behavior throughout the enterprise.

---

# 3.9 Official Transition Matrix

Examples include:

| Current State | Allowed Next States |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Proposed | Reviewed |
| Reviewed | Approved |
| Approved | Active |
| Active | Suspended, Deprecated |
| Suspended | Active, Archived |
| Deprecated | Archived |
| Draft Classification | Reviewed |
| Reviewed Classification | Published |
| Draft Reference Catalog | Validated |
| Validated Reference Catalog | Effective |
| Assigned Steward | Accepted |
| Accepted Steward | Effective |

Transitions outside certified pathways are prohibited.

---

# 3.10 Forbidden Transitions

Examples include:

Proposed

→ Active

---

Draft Classification

→ Published

---

Draft Reference Catalog

→ Effective

---

Assigned Steward

→ Effective

---

Approved

→ Archived

Operational governance prevents these invalid transitions.

---

# 3.11 Governance Gates

Every lifecycle progression passes mandatory business gates.

## Master Record Activation Gate

Before Active:

- Duplicate validation completed.
- Required attributes complete.
- Steward assigned.
- Business approval completed.

---

## Product Release Gate

Before Released:

- Product definition approved.
- Product Variant validated.
- Classification assigned.
- Units of Measure verified.
- Tax references validated.

---

## Classification Publication Gate

Before Published:

- Governance review completed.
- Terminology validated.
- Cross-domain compatibility confirmed.

---

## Reference Catalog Activation Gate

Before Effective:

- Governance approval completed.
- Referencing domains validated.
- Duplicate prevention completed.

---

## Stewardship Effectiveness Gate

Before Effective:

- Responsible business owner confirmed.
- Organizational assignment validated.
- Governance acceptance completed.

---

# 3.12 Operational Authority

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Responsible Enterprise Identity.
- Business role.
- Timestamp.
- Previous state.
- New state.
- Business justification.
- Governance approvals.

Master data transitions are never anonymous.

---

# 3.13 Business Outcomes

Every governed master entity concludes with one authoritative outcome.

Canonical outcomes include:

- Active.
- Suspended.
- Deprecated.
- Archived.
- Replaced.

These outcomes preserve enterprise reference integrity.

---

# 3.14 Parallel Governance

Enterprise master data supports concurrent governance activities.

Examples:

- Product review.
- Tax validation.
- Classification review.
- AI quality assessment.
- Steward review.

Business rules require:

- One authoritative lifecycle state.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Conflict prevention.
- Complete governance history.

---

# 3.15 Duplicate Prevention

Master data integrity requires proactive duplicate prevention.

Examples:

- Duplicate Customer.
- Duplicate Supplier.
- Duplicate Product.
- Duplicate Material.
- Duplicate Classification.

Potential duplicates require steward review before activation.

---

# 3.16 Change Control

Master records evolve through controlled governance.

Examples:

- Customer address updates.
- Product specification revisions.
- Material attribute updates.
- Organizational restructuring.
- Tax classification changes.

Changes preserve:

- Historical values.
- Audit history.
- Business traceability.
- Cross-domain consistency.

---

# 3.17 State Integrity Rules

The MDM Domain enforces the following invariants:

- Every master entity has one authoritative lifecycle state.
- Every Active master record has an assigned steward.
- Every Product Variant belongs to one Product Master.
- Every Published Classification remains historically traceable.
- Every Effective Reference Catalog follows approved governance.
- Every governance policy follows approved lifecycle progression.
- Master data history remains append-only.

---

# 3.18 GiftHatke Manufacturing Master Lifecycle

For personalized manufacturing, the certified master lifecycle includes:

```text id="mdm-stage3-gifthatke"
Material Proposed
        │
        ▼
Material Approved
        │
        ▼
Product Variant Released
        │
        ▼
Production Equipment Validated
        │
        ▼
Warehouse Activated
        │
        ▼
Operational Manufacturing Ready
```

This guarantees that manufacturing always references governed master data before operational execution begins.

---

# 3.19 Lifecycle Governance

The MDM lifecycle architecture follows permanent principles.

- Every state has defined business meaning.
- Every transition is governed.
- Stewardship remains explicit.
- Master history remains immutable.
- Duplicate prevention remains mandatory.
- Governance precedes operational usage.
- Business semantics remain independent of implementation technology.

---

# 3.20 Stage 3 Certification

The **Master Data Management Enterprise Canon — Stage 3** establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for the Master Data Management Domain.

It defines:

- Master Record lifecycle.
- Product Variant lifecycle.
- Classification lifecycle.
- Reference Catalog lifecycle.
- Stewardship lifecycle.
- Master Data Policy lifecycle.
- Official transition matrix.
- Forbidden transitions.
- Governance gates.
- Business outcomes.
- Parallel governance.
- Duplicate prevention.
- Change control.
- State integrity constraints.
- GiftHatke manufacturing master lifecycle.

This lifecycle becomes the authoritative operational model for:

- **SMP1** (Standalone Migration Programme)
- **Standalone GiftHatkeOS Version 1.0**
- **ERP9**
- **ERP10**
- Enterprise MDM platforms.
- Product Information Management systems.
- Customer Data Platforms.
- AI-assisted master data governance.
- Future enterprise expansion.

The Master Data Management lifecycle defined here is permanent. Future MDM platforms, PIM suites, semantic catalogs, enterprise reference hubs, AI master data assistants, and data governance technologies may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified lifecycle states, transition rules, governance gates, stewardship principles, and master data management semantics established by this Canon. memcite

# MASTER DATA MANAGEMENT (MDM) ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 4 — API Contracts & Domain Services

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The Master Data Management (MDM) Domain provides the enterprise with a stable set of **business master data services** that govern enterprise reference information, master records, classifications, stewardship, data quality, synchronization, and enterprise-wide reference consistency.

These services represent **permanent business capabilities**.

They do **not** prescribe:

- MDM software.
- Product Information Management (PIM) platforms.
- Customer Data Platforms (CDP).
- Supplier Information Management (SIM) systems.
- Databases.
- APIs.
- Data synchronization technologies.
- Integration middleware.
- AI master data platforms.

Those technologies may evolve.

The certified business services defined by this Canon remain permanent.

---

# 4.2 Service Philosophy

The MDM Domain owns:

- Customer Master.
- Supplier Master.
- Product Master.
- Material Master.
- Equipment Master.
- Warehouse Master.
- Organization Master.
- Classification Master.
- Reference Catalogs.
- Stewardship Assignments.
- Master Data Policies.

It does **not** own:

- Orders.
- Procurement transactions.
- Production Jobs.
- Financial postings.
- Documents.
- Workflow execution.
- Communications.

Operational domains own business execution.

The MDM Domain governs enterprise reference information.

Every business service must:

- Represent one enterprise responsibility.
- Preserve master data ownership.
- Enforce certified governance.
- Produce auditable outcomes.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 4.3 Service Landscape

The Master Data Management Domain publishes the following canonical business services.

| Service | Business Responsibility |
|----------|-------------------------|

| Audit Service | Preserve immutable master data history |

---

# 4.4 Customer Master Service

## Purpose

Maintains enterprise Customer Master records.

Responsibilities include:

- Register Customer.
- Review Customer.

- Activate Customer.
- Suspend Customer.
- Archive Customer.

The service governs enterprise customer definitions rather than customer transactions.

---

# 4.5 Supplier Master Service

Maintains Supplier Master records.

Responsibilities include:

- Register Supplier.

- Suspend Supplier.
- Archive Supplier.

Procurement transactions reference Supplier Master.

---

# 4.6 Product Master Service

Coordinates Product Master governance.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Product.
- Maintain Product.
- Release Product.
- Manage Product Variants.
- Retire Product.

Products remain enterprise reference assets.

---

# 4.7 Material Master Service

Maintains enterprise Material definitions.

Responsibilities include:

- Register Material.
- Approve Material.
- Classify Material.
- Update Material.
- Retire Material.

Production, Procurement, Inventory, and Quality consume Material Master.

---

# 4.8 Equipment Master Service

Coordinates enterprise Equipment definitions.

Responsibilities include:

- Register Equipment.
- Activate Equipment.
- Maintain Equipment.
- Retire Equipment.

Equipment governance supports manufacturing planning and reporting.

---

# 4.9 Organization Master Service

Coordinates organizational reference information.

Responsibilities include:

- Maintain Companies.
- Maintain Departments.
- Maintain Business Units.
- Maintain Cost Centers.
- Maintain Organizational Relationships.

Organizational changes remain centrally governed.

---

# 4.10 Classification Service

Coordinates enterprise classifications.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Classification.
- Publish Classification.
- Retire Classification.
- Validate Classification Usage.

Classification standards remain enterprise-wide.

---

# 4.11 Reference Catalog Service

Coordinates enterprise reference lists.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Catalog.
- Publish Catalog.
- Update Catalog.
- Retire Catalog.

Reference catalogs eliminate duplicated enterprise configuration.

---

# 4.12 Stewardship Service

Coordinates accountable ownership.

Responsibilities include:

- Assign Steward.
- Reassign Steward.
- Validate Stewardship.
- Record Stewardship History.

Stewardship remains explicit.

# 4.13 Data Quality Service

Coordinates enterprise master data quality.

# 4.14 Synchronization Service

Coordinates enterprise reference consistency.

Responsibilities include:

- Publish Master Updates.
- Synchronize Domains.
- Detect Synchronization Failures.
- Resolve Consistency Issues.

Synchronization preserves one enterprise truth.

# 4.15 Audit Service

Maintains immutable master data history.

Examples:

- Master record created.
- Steward assigned.
- Product released.
- Classification published.
- Reference catalog updated.
- Master archived.

Master Data Audit remains append-only.

# 4.16 Canonical Business Operations

The domain publishes a stable catalog of business operations.

### Customer Master

- Register Customer.
- Activate Customer.
- Suspend Customer.

---

### Supplier Master

- Register Supplier.
- Approve Supplier.

---

### Product Master

- Create Product.
- Release Product.
- Retire Product.

---

### Material Master

- Register Material.
- Classify Material.

---

### Classification

- Publish Classification.
- Retire Classification.

---

### Reference Catalog

- Publish Catalog.
- Update Catalog.

---

### Stewardship

- Assign Steward.
- Reassign Steward.

---

### Data Quality

- Detect Duplicates.
- Measure Quality.

---

# 4.17 Commands and Queries

Business services are divided into two categories.

## Commands

Commands modify master data.

Examples:

- Register Product.
- Publish Classification.
- Assign Steward.
- Activate Customer.

Commands:

- Validate governance.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish master data events.

---

## Queries

Queries never modify master data.

Examples:

- Customer Lookup.
- Product Lookup.
- Material Search.
- Classification Lookup.
- Steward Assignment.
- Master Quality Dashboard.

Queries remain read-only.

---

# 4.18 Validation Framework

Every command performs mandatory validation.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

- Master exists.
- Classification exists.
- Reference catalog exists.
- Steward exists.

---

### Business Validation

- Duplicate prevention.
- Required attributes complete.
- Cross-domain compatibility.
- Business ownership confirmed.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

- Requested transition permitted.
- Governance gates satisfied.
- Master integrity maintained.

---

### Policy Validation

- Naming standards.
- Stewardship policies.
- Quality policies.
- Classification policies.

---

### Governance Validation

- Required approvals.
- Steward assignment.
- Organizational policy.
- Audit requirements.

---

# 4.19 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical master data transaction.

Example:

Activate Product:

- Validate Product.
- Validate Variants.
- Validate Classification.
- Validate Units of Measure.
- Activate Product.
- Record Audit.
- Publish Product Activated event.

If any required step fails, the Product remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.20 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Register Customer.
- Activate Product.
- Publish Classification.
- Assign Steward.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate master records, duplicate classifications, duplicate stewardship assignments, or duplicate audit history.

---

# 4.21 Concurrency

Multiple stewards may collaborate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Product review.
- Tax validation.
- Classification review.
- AI quality recommendations.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Preservation of authoritative master data.
- Complete governance history.

---

# 4.22 Error Classification

Master Data services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Master prerequisites not satisfied.

---

### Business Rule Errors

Enterprise governance prevents requested action.

---

### Governance Errors

Missing approvals or stewardship.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition prohibited.

---

### Synchronization Errors

Referencing domains cannot achieve enterprise consistency.

Examples:

- Product referenced by obsolete classification.
- Warehouse unavailable.
- Organization reference invalid.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Business failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

# 4.23 Cross-Domain Contracts

The Master Data Management Domain collaborates with:

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Customer and product references |
| Inventory & Procurement | Supplier, warehouse, and material references |
| Production & Manufacturing | Equipment, material, and product references |

| Shipping & Fulfillment | Customer and location references |

| Identity, Security & Administration | Stewardship and organizational governance |
| Notification, Communication & Collaboration | Reference-based communications |
| Document & Digital Asset Management | Enterprise classifications and metadata |
| Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration | Workflow participant and reference resolution |
| AI Services | Semantic knowledge, quality recommendations, and reference intelligence |

Operational ownership remains explicit.

---

# 4.24 GiftHatke Manufacturing Master Services

For personalized manufacturing, the domain additionally provides specialized master services.

Examples include:

- Maintain Acrylic Color Catalog.
- Maintain Wood Material Catalog.

- Maintain Courier Reference Catalog.

These services preserve enterprise manufacturing consistency while remaining independent of implementation technologies.

---

# 4.25 Service Governance

The Master Data service architecture follows permanent principles.

- Stable business contracts.
- Explicit stewardship.
- Controlled evolution.
- Consistent enterprise semantics.
- Technology-independent implementation.
- Governance-first reference management.

---

# MASTER DATA MANAGEMENT (MDM) ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 5 — Master Data Governance, Stewardship & Enterprise Quality Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Master Data Management (MDM) Domain establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for master records, reference catalogs, classifications, enterprise taxonomies, stewardship, synchronization, data quality, and long-term reference information stewardship.

Unlike operational domains that govern business transactions, this domain governs **the authoritative enterprise reference data upon which every certified business domain depends**.

This Canon defines the permanent business architecture for:

- Master data governance.
- Stewardship governance.
- Data quality governance.
- Classification governance.
- Reference data governance.
- Synchronization governance.
- Change governance.
- AI-assisted master data governance.
- Enterprise reference stewardship.

It intentionally avoids prescribing MDM platforms, PIM software, CDP products, databases, synchronization middleware, or implementation technologies.

---

# 5.2 Enterprise Master Data Philosophy

Enterprise master data governance follows eight permanent principles.

### Reference Data Exists to Support Business

Master data enables certified enterprise operations.

It never replaces operational transactions.

---

### One Enterprise Truth

Every governed master entity has one authoritative enterprise record.

---

### Explicit Stewardship

Every master entity has one accountable business steward.

---

### Enterprise Asset

Master data belongs to the enterprise rather than individual departments.

---

### Explainable Reference Data

Enterprise users understand:

- What the master record represents.
- Why it exists.
- Who owns it.
- Why it is authoritative.
- Why changes occurred.

---

### Enterprise Consistency

Every certified domain references identical master information.

---

### Traceability

Every master entity remains attributable to:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Governance history.
- Stewardship history.
- Audit history.

---

### Technology Independence

Master data governance remains stable while implementation technologies evolve.

---

# 5.3 Enterprise Governance Model

Master data governance evaluates six enterprise layers.

## Layer 1 — Business Concept

Defines enterprise intent.

Examples:

- Customer.
- Product.
- Supplier.
- Material.

---

## Layer 2 — Master Entity

Represents authoritative enterprise reference information.

Examples:

- Customer Master.
- Product Master.
- Material Master.

---

## Layer 3 — Classification

Applies enterprise taxonomy.

Examples:

- Product category.
- Customer segment.
- Material family.
- Supplier classification.

---

## Layer 4 — Stewardship

Assigns accountable ownership.

Examples:

- Product Steward.
- Customer Steward.
- Material Steward.

---

## Layer 5 — Governance

Applies:

- Approval.
- Quality validation.
- Synchronization.
- Lifecycle control.

---

## Layer 6 — Audit

Maintains permanent enterprise master history.

Master data becomes authoritative only after all required governance layers are satisfied.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Governance Roles

The MDM Domain governs enterprise reference responsibilities.

Illustrative roles include:

## Master Data Administrator

# MASTER DATA MANAGEMENT (MDM) ENTERPRISE CANON
## Stage 6 — Events, Synchronization & Integration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The Master Data Management (MDM) Domain governs enterprise master records, reference catalogs, classifications, stewardship, synchronization, and authoritative enterprise reference information.

Unlike operational domains that publish business transaction events, this domain publishes **master data governance events** that communicate authoritative changes to enterprise reference information while preserving ownership of the underlying master entities.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Master Data Management Domain.

It defines:

- Master data business events.
- Synchronization events.
- Event publication rules.
- Enterprise synchronization automation.
- Cross-domain propagation.
- Integration boundaries.
- AI-assisted master data integration.

It intentionally avoids prescribing message brokers, event buses, middleware, MDM platforms, integration products, or implementation technologies.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A Master Data event represents a completed enterprise reference fact.

Examples include:

- Customer Activated.
- Product Released.
- Material Approved.
- Classification Published.
- Steward Assigned.

Events communicate **completed governance outcomes**, not technical synchronization operations.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business activity.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise master data semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Master Data Management Domain follows permanent principles.

### Reference Significance

Only meaningful master data governance activities generate canonical business events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed master data occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable Reference History

Published events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Master data events originate only from the Master Data Management Domain.

Operational domains continue to own the business transactions that reference those master entities.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event identity.
- Timestamp.
- Master entity reference.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Business role.
- Correlation identifier.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Master Data Events

## Customer Events

- Customer Proposed.
- Customer Approved.
- Customer Activated.
- Customer Suspended.
- Customer Archived.

---

## Supplier Events

- Supplier Registered.
- Supplier Approved.
- Supplier Activated.
- Supplier Suspended.

---

## Product Events

- Product Created.
- Product Released.
- Product Deprecated.
- Product Archived.

---

## Material Events

- Material Registered.
- Material Approved.
- Material Activated.

---

## Classification Events

- Classification Drafted.
- Classification Published.
- Classification Retired.

---

## Reference Catalog Events

- Catalog Published.
- Catalog Updated.
- Catalog Retired.

---

## Stewardship Events

- Steward Assigned.
- Steward Reassigned.
- Stewardship Validated.

---

## Synchronization Events

- Synchronization Started.
- Synchronization Completed.
- Synchronization Failed.
- Synchronization Recovered.

---

## Master Data Quality Events

- Duplicate Detected.
- Duplicate Resolved.
- Quality Threshold Achieved.
- Quality Degradation Detected.

---

## Governance Exception Events

- Governance Conflict Detected.
- Invalid Reference Detected.
- Policy Violation Detected.
- Synchronization Exception Detected.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Master Data events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding governance activity.

Examples:

- **Customer Activated** is emitted only after governance approval and activation are complete.
- **Product Released** is emitted only after all required validations succeed.
- **Classification Published** is emitted only after enterprise governance approval.
- **Synchronization Completed** is emitted only after governed synchronization finishes successfully.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Master Data event follows the same sequence:

1. Master governance activity initiated.
2. Governance validation completed.
3. Master transaction completed.
4. Audit recorded.
5. Canonical master data event published.
6. Authorized consumers process the event.
7. Monitoring records processing outcomes.

Published events therefore represent authoritative enterprise reference facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Master Data events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Master Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|--------------|--------------------------|
| Customer Activated | Order Management, Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Supplier Approved | Inventory & Procurement |
| Product Released | Order Management, Production & Manufacturing, Quality Management |
| Material Activated | Inventory & Procurement, Production & Manufacturing |
| Classification Published | Document & Digital Asset Management, Reporting & Business Intelligence |
| Steward Assigned | Identity, Security & Administration |
| Synchronization Completed | All certified enterprise domains |
| Duplicate Resolved | Reporting & Business Intelligence, AI Services |

Consumers respond to master data events without assuming ownership of master governance.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every master data event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event identity.
- Event type.
- Master entity reference.
- Entity category.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Organizational context.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation identifier.
- Governance reference.

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Synchronization Automation Principles

Synchronization improves enterprise consistency while respecting certified governance.

Every synchronization activity must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Observable.
- Repeatable.

Synchronization must never bypass:

- Steward approval.
- Governance validation.
- Quality rules.
- Audit requirements.
- Cross-domain consistency validation.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Synchronization Automations

Examples include:

### Master Distribution

- Publish customer updates.
- Publish product updates.
- Publish supplier updates.
- Publish material updates.

---

### Quality Automation

- Detect duplicates.
- Validate completeness.
- Monitor consistency.
- Recommend corrections.

---

### Classification Automation

- Publish taxonomy updates.
- Detect obsolete classifications.
- Recommend new classifications.

---

### Synchronization Recovery

- Detect synchronization failures.
- Retry synchronization.
- Validate recovery.
- Report unresolved conflicts.

---

### AI Master Data Automation

- Recommend duplicate merges.
- Suggest classifications.
- Predict data quality issues.
- Recommend stewardship actions.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The MDM Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized governance is required.

Examples:

- Product release.
- Customer activation.
- Steward assignment.
- Classification publication.

---

## Choreography

Used where independent domains respond to master data events.

Examples:

- Orders referencing new customers.
- Production referencing released products.
- Documents referencing updated classifications.
- AI services indexing new master entities.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than implementation technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The MDM Domain integrates with every certified enterprise domain through governed business contracts.

| Domain | Business Purpose |
|---------|------------------|
| Order Management | Customer and product references |
| Inventory & Procurement | Supplier, material, and warehouse references |
| Production & Manufacturing | Product, equipment, and material references |
| Quality Management | Product and specification references |
| Shipping & Fulfillment | Customer and location references |
| Finance & Accounting | Organization, currency, and tax references |
| Reporting & Business Intelligence | Enterprise dimensions and hierarchies |
| Identity, Security & Administration | Stewardship and organizational governance |
| Notification, Communication & Collaboration | Reference-based communications |
| Document & Digital Asset Management | Metadata, classifications, and enterprise taxonomies |
| Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration | Participant and reference resolution |
| AI Services | Semantic reference knowledge and quality intelligence |

Each collaborating domain remains independently governed.

---

# 6.13 External Integrations

The Canon supports future integration with:

- Enterprise MDM platforms.
- Product Information Management systems.
- Customer Data Platforms.
- Supplier Information Management systems.
- ERP reference hubs.
- AI knowledge graphs.
- Semantic catalogs.
- Enterprise integration platforms.
- Future enterprise master data ecosystems.

These integrations consume or publish certified master data events without redefining enterprise master data governance.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Master data failures are categorized consistently.

### Validation Failure

Master governance prerequisites are not satisfied.

No completion event is published.

---

### Quality Failure

Reference information fails enterprise quality standards.

Activation is prevented.

---

### Synchronization Failure

Cross-domain consistency cannot be achieved.

Recovery follows governed synchronization policy.

---

### Dependency Failure

A collaborating domain cannot satisfy its business contract.

Examples:

- Organization unavailable.
- Classification unavailable.
- Steward unavailable.

---

### Platform Failure

Implementation technology temporarily unavailable.

Business reference intent remains preserved for governed recovery.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries follow controlled enterprise policy.

Repeated processing must never create:

- Duplicate master records.
- Duplicate classifications.
- Duplicate stewardship assignments.
- Duplicate synchronization history.
- Duplicate audit records.

Where correction is required, new master data events preserve historical accountability while superseding previous outcomes according to enterprise governance.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Master data events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Stable business semantics.
- Backward compatibility where practical.
- Managed deprecation.
- Controlled consumer migration.

Business meaning remains consistent across versions.

---

# 6.17 Observability

The enterprise monitors master data governance through:

- Master activation.
- Synchronization success.
- Duplicate detection.
- Quality improvements.
- Stewardship activity.
- Classification changes.
- Synchronization failures.
- Consumer processing status.

Observability supports enterprise master data governance without changing business semantics.

---

# 6.18 Integration Security

Master data integrations comply with the Identity, Security & Administration Canon.

Requirements include:

- Authenticated identities.
- Authorized stewardship.
- Least privilege.
- Controlled master data visibility.
- Full auditability.

Internal and external integrations follow identical governance principles.

---

The event-driven master data architecture defined here is permanent. Future MDM suites, PIM platforms, enterprise reference hubs, semantic knowledge systems, AI master data assistants, and data governance technologies may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified master data events, governance semantics, synchronization principles, integration contracts, quality controls, and end-to-end traceability established by this Canon. memcite

# 1.1 Purpose

The **Integration, APIs & Enterprise Connectivity Domain** establishes the permanent enterprise architecture for governed communication between certified business domains, external systems, partner platforms, AI services, and future enterprise ecosystems.

Unlike operational domains that own business capabilities, this domain governs **how certified business capabilities communicate while preserving domain ownership, enterprise integrity, and long-term interoperability**.

It does **not** own:

- Inventory.
- Production.
- Finance.
- Documents.

Instead, it governs the contracts through which those domains exchange business information.

- Event contracts.
- Enterprise messaging.
- Domain interoperability.
- External connectivity.
- Version compatibility.
- Enterprise integration security.
- Enterprise communication standards.

# 2.2 Entity Principles

Every integration entity follows these permanent principles.

### Single Responsibility

Each entity governs one enterprise communication responsibility.

Examples:

- An **API Contract** represents one governed business interface.
- An **Event Contract** represents one governed business event.
- A **Service Contract** represents one governed enterprise capability.

Responsibilities are never shared.

---

### Stable Enterprise Identity

Every communication entity possesses one permanent enterprise identity independent of implementation technology.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Every communication entity has one owning business domain.

---

### Governance

Every communication entity follows enterprise lifecycle governance, versioning, approval, auditability, and controlled evolution.

---

### Traceability

Every communication entity remains fully traceable throughout its lifecycle.

---

The Integration Domain consists of the following canonical entities.

| API Contract | Represents one governed business interface |
| Service Contract | Represents one enterprise service capability |
| Event Contract | Represents one governed enterprise event |

# 2.4 API Contract

## Purpose

Represents one authoritative enterprise business interface.

Responsibilities include:

- Business capability definition.
- Contract ownership.
- Input semantics.
- Output semantics.
- Version governance.

An API Contract defines business meaning rather than transport technology.

# 2.5 Service Contract

Represents one governed enterprise service capability.

Responsibilities include:

- Business responsibility.
- Service ownership.
- Operational semantics.
- Contract stability.

Consumers depend upon Service Contracts rather than internal implementations.

---

# 2.6 Event Contract

Represents one enterprise business event.

Examples:

- Order Created.
- Product Released.
- Workflow Completed.
- Customer Activated.

Event Contracts standardize enterprise communication while preserving business ownership.

---

# 2.7 Command Contract

Represents governed business requests that modify enterprise state.

Examples:

- Create Order.
- Approve Product.
- Start Workflow.
- Activate Customer.

Commands preserve enterprise governance.

---

# 2.8 Query Contract

Represents read-only enterprise requests.

Examples:

- Customer Lookup.
- Product Search.
- Workflow Status.
- Inventory Availability.

Queries never modify enterprise state.

---

# 2.9 Integration Policy

Represents enterprise communication governance.

Examples:

- Authentication policy.
- Version policy.
- Retry policy.
- Timeout policy.
- Availability policy.

Policies govern enterprise communication behavior.

---

# 2.10 Version Definition

Represents controlled evolution of enterprise contracts.

Responsibilities include:

- Version identity.
- Compatibility.
- Deprecation.
- Migration guidance.

Version governance protects long-term interoperability.

---

# 2.11 Consumer Registration

Represents authorized consumers of enterprise contracts.

Examples:

- Order Management.
- Production.
- Finance.
- External partner.
- AI service.

Consumer registrations preserve explicit communication accountability.

---

# 2.12 Provider Registration

Represents the owning business domain for enterprise contracts.

Examples:

- Master Data Management.
- Workflow Domain.
- Finance Domain.

Provider ownership remains explicit.

---

# 2.13 Message Definition

Represents governed enterprise business messages.

Examples:

- Customer reference.
- Product reference.
- Workflow notification.
- Financial approval.

Messages remain technology-independent.

---

# 2.14 Endpoint Definition

Represents logical communication entry points.

Examples:

- Order Service.
- Product Service.
- Customer Service.
- Workflow Service.

Endpoint Definitions describe business interfaces rather than implementation addresses.

---

# 2.15 Integration Profile

Represents reusable enterprise communication patterns.

Examples:

- Request/Response.
- Publish/Subscribe.
- Command/Event.
- Batch Synchronization.

Profiles standardize enterprise integration behavior.

---

# 2.16 Compatibility Rule

Represents governed contract compatibility.

Examples:

- Backward compatibility.
- Deprecation policy.
- Version coexistence.
- Consumer migration.

Compatibility preserves enterprise continuity.

---

# 2.17 Connectivity Policy

Represents enterprise communication standards.

Examples:

- Availability requirements.
- Reliability expectations.
- Authentication requirements.
- Encryption standards.

Connectivity policies remain implementation-independent.

---

# 2.18 Integration Audit Record

Represents immutable enterprise communication history.

Examples:

- Contract published.
- Version released.
- Consumer registered.
- Compatibility verified.
- Integration approved.

Audit history remains append-only.

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The **Integration, APIs & Enterprise Connectivity Domain** governs the complete lifecycle of enterprise communication contracts, APIs, services, events, integration policies, compatibility rules, consumer registrations, and provider registrations.

Every governed communication entity progresses through certified business states.

These states ensure that enterprise integrations remain:

- Governed.
- Stable.
- Backward compatible where practical.
- Traceable.
- Auditable.
- Business-approved.
- Recoverable.
- Technology-independent.

This Canon establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for:

- API Contracts.
- Service Contracts.
- Event Contracts.
- Command Contracts.
- Query Contracts.
- Integration Policies.
- Version Definitions.
- Consumer Registrations.
- Provider Registrations.
- Connectivity Policies.

---

# 3.2 Lifecycle Philosophy

Enterprise integration lifecycle management follows permanent principles.

### Single Authoritative State

Every governed communication entity exists in exactly one official lifecycle state.

---

### Controlled Evolution

Enterprise contracts evolve only through approved governance.

---

### Governance Gates

Every lifecycle transition passes mandatory business validation before becoming effective.

---

### Traceability

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Contract Version.
- Previous State.
- New State.
- Business Justification.
- Related Approvals.
- Audit References.

---

### Immutable History

Historical communication contracts remain permanently preserved.

Contract revisions create governed new versions rather than rewriting historical definitions.

---

# 3.3 API Contract Lifecycle

Every enterprise API Contract follows the certified lifecycle.

```text id="integration-stage3-api"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Published
```

Exceptional states include:

- Deprecated.
- Retired.
- Archived.

---

### Draft

Business contract under definition.

---

### Reviewed

Technical and business governance completed.

---

### Approved

Enterprise governance approved the contract.

---

### Published

Contract becomes officially available for certified consumers.

---

### Deprecated

Scheduled for replacement by a governed successor.

---

### Retired

No longer available for new integrations while preserving historical compatibility.

---

### Archived

Retained exclusively for governance and audit purposes.

---

# 3.4 Service Contract Lifecycle

```text id="integration-stage3-service"
Defined
   │
Validated
   │
Operational
```

Exceptional states:

- Suspended.
- Retired.

Only Operational services may participate in enterprise integrations.

---

# 3.5 Event Contract Lifecycle

```text id="integration-stage3-event"
Defined
   │
Validated
   │
Published
```

Exceptional states:

- Deprecated.
- Archived.

---

```text id="integration-stage3-policy"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Replaced.
- Retired.

Integration policies govern enterprise communication.

---

# 3.7 Consumer Registration Lifecycle

```text id="integration-stage3-consumer"
Requested
     │
Validated
     │
Authorized
```

Exceptional states:

- Suspended.
- Revoked.

---

# 3.8 Version Lifecycle

```text id="integration-stage3-version"
Planned
    │
Released
    │
Supported
```

Exceptional states:

# INTEGRATION, APIs & ENTERPRISE CONNECTIVITY CANON

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The **Integration, APIs & Enterprise Connectivity Domain** governs enterprise communication, APIs, service contracts, event contracts, interoperability, messaging, synchronization, and external connectivity.

Unlike operational domains that publish business events related to their own business responsibilities, this domain governs **how enterprise communication itself is coordinated, synchronized, monitored, versioned, and managed across certified business domains**.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven communication architecture for the Integration Domain.

It defines:

- Communication events.
- Enterprise messaging.
- Synchronization orchestration.
- Event publication rules.
- Integration monitoring.
- Cross-domain coordination.
- External connectivity.
- AI-assisted communication intelligence.

It intentionally avoids prescribing message brokers, event buses, ESBs, API gateways, middleware, streaming platforms, or implementation technologies.

---

# 6.2 Event Philosophy

A Communication Event represents a completed enterprise communication activity.

Examples include:

- API Published.
- Consumer Authorized.
- Version Released.
- Compatibility Verified.
- Integration Registered.

Communication events represent **completed governance outcomes**, not low-level transport operations.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business communication activity.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise communication semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Integration Domain follows permanent principles.

### Communication Significance

Only meaningful enterprise communication activities generate canonical communication events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed communication occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable Communication History

Published events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed communication events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Communication events originate only from the Integration Domain.

Operational domains continue to own business events related to their own business capabilities.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event Identity.
- Timestamp.
- Contract Reference.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Provider Domain.
- Consumer Domain.
- Correlation Identifier.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Communication Events

## API Events

- API Drafted.
- API Approved.
- API Published.
- API Deprecated.
- API Retired.

---

## Service Events

- Service Registered.
- Service Activated.
- Service Suspended.
