# 4.10 Policy Management Service

Coordinates enterprise policies.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Policy.
- Review Policy.
- Approve Policy.
- Activate Policy.
- Retire Policy.

Policies govern enterprise behavior.

---

# 4.11 Configuration Version Service

Coordinates configuration evolution.

Responsibilities include:

- Create Version.
- Validate Version.
- Certify Version.
- Release Version.
- Archive Version.

Version services preserve enterprise configuration continuity.

---

# 4.12 Configuration Coordination Service

Coordinates enterprise-wide configuration synchronization.

Responsibilities include:

- Synchronize Business Domains.
- Coordinate Rule Activation.
- Manage Configuration Dependencies.
- Resolve Configuration Conflicts.
- Publish Configuration Status.

Coordination maintains enterprise behavioral consistency.

---

# 4.13 Configuration Audit Service

Maintains immutable configuration history.

Examples:

- Configuration approved.
- Feature enabled.
- Rule activated.
- Policy updated.
- Version released.
- Conflict resolved.

Configuration Audit remains append-only.

---

# 4.14 Canonical Business Operations

The domain publishes a stable catalog of business operations.

### Configuration Management

- Activate Configuration.
- Retire Configuration.
- Publish Configuration.

---

### Feature Management

- Enable Feature.
- Disable Feature.

---

### Rule Management

- Activate Rule.
- Replace Rule.

---

### Decision Management

- Publish Decision Table.
- Retire Decision Table.

---

### Policy Management

- Activate Policy.
- Retire Policy.

---

### Configuration Coordination

- Synchronize Configuration.
- Resolve Configuration Conflict.

---

# 4.15 Commands and Queries

Business services are divided into two categories.

## Commands

Commands modify enterprise configuration governance.

Examples:

- Activate Configuration.
- Enable Feature.
- Activate Rule.
- Publish Decision Table.

Commands:

- Validate governance.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish configuration events.

---

## Queries

Queries never modify enterprise configuration.

Examples:

- Configuration Lookup.
- Rule Search.
- Feature Status.
- Policy View.
- Version History.

Queries remain read-only.

---

# 4.16 Validation Framework

Every command performs mandatory validation.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

- Configuration exists.
- Rule exists.
- Policy exists.
- Version exists.

---

### Business Validation

- Ownership confirmed.
- Business objectives satisfied.
- Required evidence complete.
- Dependencies resolved.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

- Requested transition permitted.
- Governance gates satisfied.
- Configuration integrity maintained.

---

### Policy Validation

- Configuration Policy.
- Rule Policy.
- Feature Policy.
- Version Policy.

---

### Governance Validation

- Required approvals.
- Business ownership.
- Configuration evidence.
- Audit requirements.

---

# 4.17 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical configuration transaction.

Example:

Activate Configuration:

- Validate Configuration.
- Validate Dependencies.
- Validate Version.
- Activate Configuration.
- Record Audit.
- Publish Configuration Activated event.

If any required step fails, the Configuration remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.18 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Activate Configuration.
- Enable Feature.
- Publish Decision Table.
- Activate Policy.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate Configurations, duplicate Rules, duplicate Policies, duplicate Versions, or duplicate Audit history.

---

# 4.19 Concurrency

Multiple governance teams may collaborate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Business governance.
- Compliance review.
- Security review.
- AI rule analysis.
- Executive approval.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Preservation of authoritative configuration evidence.
- Complete governance history.

---

# 4.20 Error Classification

Configuration services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Configuration prerequisites not satisfied.

---

### Business Rule Errors

Enterprise governance prevents requested action.

---

### Governance Errors

Missing approvals or ownership.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition prohibited.

---

### Dependency Errors

Required configuration dependencies unavailable.

---

### Configuration Errors

Enterprise configuration conflicts requiring intervention.

Examples:

- Feature dependency missing.
- Rule conflict.
- Policy inconsistency.
- Version incompatibility.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Business configuration failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

The Configuration Domain collaborates with every certified enterprise domain.

| Order Management | Commercial configuration |
| Inventory & Procurement | Inventory policies |

| Integration, APIs & Enterprise Connectivity | Integration configuration |
| Enterprise Monitoring, Observability & Operations | Monitoring thresholds |
| Enterprise Scheduling, Time & Resource Management | Scheduling rules |

Configuration ownership remains explicit.

# 4.23 Service Governance

The Configuration service architecture follows permanent principles.

- Explicit business ownership.
- Controlled configuration evolution.
- Consistent enterprise business semantics.
- Technology-independent implementation.
- Governance-first enterprise adaptability.

The **Enterprise Configuration, Feature Management & Business Rules Canon — Stage 4** establishes the permanent business service architecture for the Configuration Domain.

# ENTERPRISE CONFIGURATION, FEATURE MANAGEMENT & BUSINESS RULES CANON
## Stage 5 — Enterprise Governance, Configuration Stewardship & Policy Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Configuration, Feature Management & Business Rules Domain** establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for configuration management, business rules, feature rollout, policy administration, decision logic, validation governance, calculation governance, configuration stewardship, and long-term business adaptability.

Unlike operational domains that govern business transactions, this domain governs **how enterprise behavior is safely configured, versioned, approved, and evolved while preserving business ownership, auditability, and operational consistency**.

This Canon defines the permanent business architecture for:

- Configuration governance.
- Rule stewardship.
- Policy governance.
- Feature governance.
- Version governance.
- Decision governance.
- Validation governance.
- Calculation governance.
- AI-assisted configuration governance.
- Enterprise adaptability governance.

It intentionally avoids prescribing configuration stores, rule engines, feature-flag frameworks, policy engines, AI platforms, or implementation technologies.

---

# 5.2 Enterprise Configuration Philosophy

Enterprise configuration governance follows eight permanent principles.

### Configuration Exists to Support Business

Configuration enables controlled business adaptability.

It never replaces business ownership.

---

### Authoritative Configuration

Every active configuration represents one governed enterprise business decision.

---

### Explicit Configuration Stewardship

Every configuration capability has one accountable business steward.

---

### Enterprise Consistency

Business behavior remains consistent across every certified domain.

---

### Explainable Configuration

Enterprise users understand:

- What is configured.
- Why configuration exists.
- Business impact.
- Dependencies.
- Governance ownership.

---

### Controlled Evolution

Business behavior evolves through governed enterprise processes.

---

### Traceability

Every configuration entity remains attributable to:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Configuration Steward.
- Governance History.
- Audit History.

---

### Technology Independence

Configuration governance remains stable while implementation technologies evolve.

---

# 5.3 Enterprise Governance Model

Configuration governance evaluates six enterprise layers.

## Layer 1 — Business Capability

Defines enterprise business purpose.

Examples:

- Manufacturing.
- Finance.
- Scheduling.
- Shipping.

---

## Layer 2 — Configuration

Represents authoritative business behavior.

Examples:

- Configuration Profile.
- Business Rule.
- Feature Flag.
- Policy Definition.

---

## Layer 3 — Business Standards

Applies enterprise behavior expectations.

Examples:

- Validation Rules.
- Calculation Rules.
- Decision Tables.
- Compliance Policies.

---

## Layer 4 — Stewardship

Assigns accountable ownership.

Examples:

- Configuration Steward.
- Rule Steward.
- Policy Owner.

---

## Layer 5 — Governance

Applies:

- Validation.
- Approval.
- Version control.
- Conflict resolution.

---

## Layer 6 — Audit

Maintains permanent configuration history.

Business behavior becomes authoritative only after all required governance layers are satisfied.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Governance Roles

The Configuration Domain governs enterprise behavior responsibilities.

Illustrative roles include:

## Configuration Administrator

Responsibilities:

- Enterprise configuration governance.
- Version administration.
- Configuration quality.

---

## Configuration Steward

Responsibilities:

- Configuration ownership.
- Configuration quality.
- Business consistency.
- Cross-domain coordination.

---

## Rule Steward

Responsibilities:

- Business rules.
- Decision logic.
- Validation consistency.

---

## Policy Owner

Responsibilities:

- Enterprise policies.
- Compliance.
- Governance alignment.

---

## Configuration Auditor

- Governance verification.
- Configuration evidence.
- Policy compliance review.

Cannot modify historical audit records.

---

## AI Configuration Administrator

Responsibilities:

- AI configuration recommendations.
- Rule optimization.
- Feature rollout analysis.

Cannot bypass certified governance.

# 5.5 Configuration Classification

- Operational parameters.

- Approval thresholds.

---

## Feature Management

- Feature rollout.
- Pilot deployment.
- Progressive enablement.

---

- Security.

Classification determines governance behavior rather than implementation technology.

Enterprise configuration stewardship follows controlled principles.

Configuration Stewards may:

- Review configuration.
- Approve configuration changes.
- Coordinate rollout.
- Recommend optimization.
- Ensure business consistency.

Configuration Stewards may **not**:

- Bypass governance.
- Override required approvals.
- Alter historical configuration.
- Ignore policy conflicts.
- Override business ownership.

Stewardship remains accountable and transparent.

---

# 5.7 Configuration Quality Governance

Enterprise configuration quality follows permanent standards.

Every governed configuration capability is evaluated for:

- Configuration accuracy.
- Rule consistency.
- Policy alignment.
- Version quality.
- Feature rollout safety.
- Decision integrity.

Configuration quality remains measurable throughout the configuration lifecycle.

---

# 5.8 Version Governance

Enterprise version governance evaluates:

- Active version.
- Candidate version.
- Rollback readiness.
- Version compatibility.
- Business continuity.

Version governance preserves enterprise operational confidence across independently governed domains.

---

# 5.9 Change Governance

Examples:

- New pricing model.

- Regional compliance update.
- New AI-assisted feature.

- Impact assessment.
- Dependency assessment.
- Permanent audit evidence.

---

# 5.10 AI-Assisted Configuration Governance

AI assistance remains governed.

Examples include:

- Feature rollout recommendations.
- Policy consistency analysis.
- Configuration conflict prediction.
- Version compatibility analysis.

AI-generated recommendations:

- Respect enterprise governance.

# 5.13 Audit and Non-Repudiation

# ENTERPRISE CONFIGURATION, FEATURE MANAGEMENT & BUSINESS RULES CANON
## Stage 6 — Configuration Events, Enterprise Synchronization & Cross-Domain Coordination Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Configuration, Feature Management & Business Rules Domain** governs enterprise configuration, business rules, feature management, decision logic, policy administration, and controlled business adaptability.

Unlike operational domains that publish business events related to transactional execution, this domain governs **how enterprise configuration decisions themselves are communicated, synchronized, coordinated, and governed across every certified business domain**.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven configuration architecture for the Configuration Domain.

It defines:

- Configuration events.
- Business rule publication.
- Feature rollout events.
- Policy synchronization.
- Configuration publication rules.
- Cross-domain configuration visibility.
- Configuration version coordination.
- AI-assisted configuration intelligence.

It intentionally avoids prescribing event buses, message brokers, rule engines, feature-flag platforms, policy engines, cloud configuration services, or implementation technologies.

---

# 6.2 Configuration Event Philosophy

A Configuration Event represents a completed enterprise configuration decision.

Examples include:

- Configuration Activated.
- Feature Enabled.
- Rule Published.
- Policy Approved.
- Version Released.

Configuration events communicate **completed business configuration facts**, not intermediate configuration activities.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed configuration decision.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise configuration semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Configuration Domain follows permanent principles.

### Configuration Significance

Only meaningful enterprise configuration activities generate canonical configuration events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed configuration occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable Configuration History

Published configuration events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed configuration events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Configuration events originate only from the Configuration Domain.

Operational business domains continue to own business events related to their own responsibilities.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event Identity.
- Timestamp.
- Configuration Reference.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Correlation Identifier.
- Configuration Context.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Configuration Events

## Configuration Events

- Configuration Created.
- Configuration Reviewed.
- Configuration Approved.
- Configuration Activated.
- Configuration Retired.
- Configuration Archived.

---

## Feature Events

- Feature Defined.
- Feature Approved.
- Feature Enabled.
- Feature Disabled.
- Feature Retired.

---

## Rule Events

- Rule Validated.
- Rule Approved.
- Rule Activated.
- Rule Replaced.
- Rule Retired.

---

## Policy Events

- Policy Reviewed.
- Policy Approved.
- Policy Activated.
- Policy Replaced.

---

## Version Events

- Version Created.
- Version Certified.
- Version Released.
- Version Withdrawn.

---

## Dependency Events

- Dependency Established.
- Dependency Updated.
- Dependency Removed.

---

## Governance Events

- Configuration Audit Completed.
- Compliance Review Completed.
- Configuration Conflict Resolved.

---

## AI Configuration Events

- AI Rule Recommendation Generated.
- AI Feature Rollout Recommended.
- AI Configuration Optimization Published.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Configuration events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding configuration activity.

Examples:

- **Configuration Activated** is emitted only after governance approval is complete.
- **Feature Enabled** is emitted only after rollout validation succeeds.
- **Rule Activated** is emitted only after business-rule validation is complete.
- **Version Released** is emitted only after certification.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Configuration Event follows the same sequence:

1. Configuration activity initiated.
2. Configuration validation completed.
3. Configuration transaction completed.
4. Audit recorded.
5. Canonical configuration event published.
6. Authorized stakeholders process the event.
7. Enterprise configuration records updated.

Published events therefore represent authoritative enterprise configuration facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Configuration events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Configuration Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Configuration Activated | Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration |
| Feature Enabled | Order Management, Production & Manufacturing |
| Rule Activated | Finance & Accounting, Shipping & Fulfillment |
| Policy Activated | Identity, Security & Administration |
| Version Released | Enterprise Monitoring, Observability & Operations |
| Dependency Updated | Integration, APIs & Enterprise Connectivity |
| Configuration Audit Completed | Reporting & Business Intelligence |
| AI Configuration Optimization Published | Operations & Business Leadership |

Consumers respond to configuration events without assuming ownership of enterprise configuration governance.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every configuration event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event Identity.
- Event Type.
- Configuration Reference.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Configuration Category.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation Identifier.
- Governance Reference.

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Configuration Synchronization Principles

Enterprise configuration synchronization improves organizational consistency while respecting certified governance.

Every synchronization activity must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Traceable.
- Repeatable.

Synchronization must never bypass:

- Configuration governance.
- Business ownership.
- Audit requirements.
- Configuration validation.
- Enterprise configuration consistency.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Configuration Automations

Examples include:

### Configuration Synchronization

- Publish approved configuration.
- Synchronize active business rules.
- Update configuration repositories.

---

### Feature Rollout Automation

- Enable approved features.
- Coordinate phased rollout.
- Validate rollout completion.

---

### Rule Automation

- Publish approved rules.
- Synchronize decision tables.
- Validate configuration consistency.

---

### Version Automation

- Release certified versions.
- Archive superseded versions.
- Notify dependent domains.

---

### AI Configuration Automation

- Predict configuration conflicts.
- Recommend rule optimization.
- Recommend feature rollout sequencing.
- Forecast configuration impact.

---

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Configuration Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized configuration governance is required.

Examples:

- Feature rollout.
- Enterprise policy activation.
- Configuration version release.
- Business-rule publication.

---

## Choreography

Used where independent domains respond to configuration events.

Examples:

- Workflow adapting after Rule Activated.
- Monitoring updating thresholds after Configuration Activated.
- Scheduling consuming new Time Policies.
- AI learning from configuration outcomes.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than implementation technology.

---

# 6.12 Integration Boundaries

The Configuration Domain coordinates enterprise behavior across every certified enterprise domain.

|---------|-----------------------|
| Order Management | Commercial behavior |
| Inventory & Procurement | Inventory rules |
| Production & Manufacturing | Manufacturing configuration |

| Shipping & Fulfillment | Shipping behavior |

| Master Data Management | Reference-data governance |
| Integration, APIs & Enterprise Connectivity | Integration behavior |
| Enterprise Monitoring, Observability & Operations | Monitoring thresholds |
| Enterprise Scheduling, Time & Resource Management | Scheduling rules |
| AI Services | AI governance |

Each collaborating domain remains independently governed.

---

# 6.13 External Configuration

The Canon supports future integration with:

- Enterprise configuration platforms.
- Business rule engines.
- Feature management systems.
- Policy management platforms.
- AI configuration services.
- Decision management suites.
- Enterprise governance platforms.
- Future configuration technologies.

These integrations consume or publish certified configuration events without redefining enterprise configuration governance.

---

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

Configuration failures are categorized consistently.

### Validation Failure

Configuration prerequisites are not satisfied.

No completion event is published.

---

### Configuration Failure

Business configuration objectives cannot be achieved.

Recovery follows governed configuration policy.

---

### Dependency Failure

Required configuration dependencies are unavailable.

Examples:

- Missing rule.
- Missing policy.
- Missing version.
- Missing feature dependency.

---

### Governance Failure

Required approvals or policy validations are incomplete.

---

### Platform Failure

Implementation technology temporarily unavailable.

Business configuration intent remains preserved for governed recovery.

---

# 6.15 Retry and Compensation

Retries follow controlled enterprise policy.

Repeated processing must never create:

- Duplicate Configurations.
- Duplicate Rules.
- Duplicate Features.
- Duplicate Versions.
- Duplicate Configuration Events.
- Duplicate Audit Records.

Where correction is required, new configuration events preserve historical accountability while superseding previous configuration outcomes according to enterprise governance.

---

# 6.16 Event Versioning

Configuration events evolve through controlled governance.

Rules include:

- Stable business semantics.
- Backward compatibility where practical.
- Managed deprecation.
- Controlled configuration migration.

Business meaning remains consistent across versions.

---

# 6.17 Configuration Observability

The enterprise monitors configuration governance through:

- Configuration activation.
- Feature rollout.
- Rule publication.
- Version release.
- Dependency management.
- Policy evolution.
- Configuration quality.
- Enterprise adaptability.

Configuration observability supports enterprise governance without changing business semantics.

---

# 6.18 Configuration Security

Enterprise configuration complies with the **Identity, Security & Administration Canon**.

Requirements include:

- Authenticated configuration identities.
- Authorized configuration visibility.
- Least privilege.
- Controlled configuration evidence.
- Complete auditability.

Internal and external configuration visibility follows identical governance principles.

Future rule engines, feature management platforms, policy systems, AI configuration assistants, enterprise configuration ecosystems, and business decision technologies may evolve, but every implementation must preserve the certified configuration events, governance semantics, synchronization principles, configuration contracts, security framework, and end-to-end traceability established by this Canon. memcite

# ENTERPRISE SEARCH, KNOWLEDGE & INFORMATION RETRIEVAL CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation & Business Scope

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Search, Knowledge & Information Retrieval Domain** establishes the permanent enterprise architecture for discovering, indexing, organizing, ranking, retrieving, governing, and presenting enterprise knowledge across every certified domain within GiftHatkeOS.

Unlike operational domains that execute business activities or manage business records, this domain governs **how enterprise information is found, understood, related, and securely accessed while preserving ownership within the originating business domains**.

It does **not** own:

- Orders.
- Inventory.
- Production records.
- Finance records.
- Documents.
- Master data.
- Business workflows.
- Operational monitoring.

Instead, it provides the authoritative enterprise capability that enables users, workflows, reporting systems, and AI services to discover and retrieve governed enterprise knowledge regardless of where that information originates.

The Search Domain is the enterprise authority for:

- Enterprise Search.
- Knowledge Discovery.
- Information Retrieval.
- Search Index Governance.
- Search Ranking.
- Metadata Indexing.
- Semantic Search.
- Knowledge Relationships.
- Search Personalization.
- Federated Search.
- Enterprise Knowledge Graphs.
- AI-assisted Enterprise Retrieval.

---

# 1.2 Mission

The Search Domain exists to ensure that every authorized enterprise user, workflow, integration, and AI capability can **locate the right enterprise information at the right time with the appropriate level of governance, relevance, security, and explainability**.

---

# 1.3 Domain Vision

The architecture supports organizations ranging from a single personalized manufacturing workshop to globally distributed enterprises operating across:

- Multiple companies.
- Manufacturing plants.
- Warehouses.
- Retail operations.
- Franchise networks.
- Regional business units.
- Knowledge-intensive organizations.
- AI-assisted enterprises.

The architecture supports:

- Enterprise-wide search.
- Unified knowledge discovery.
- Secure information access.
- AI-assisted retrieval.
- Federated enterprise knowledge.
- Context-aware search.
- Explainable search results.
- Continuous knowledge evolution.

Business meaning remains stable while search technologies evolve.

---

# 1.4 Business Objectives

The Search Domain pursues the following permanent objectives.

### Universal Enterprise Discovery

Authorized users can discover enterprise knowledge regardless of where it resides.

---

### Trusted Information Retrieval

Search returns governed enterprise information rather than uncontrolled data.

---

### Explainable Search

Enterprise users understand:

- Why results appear.
- How relevance was determined.
- Information ownership.
- Information freshness.
- Applicable governance.

---

### Knowledge Accessibility

Enterprise knowledge remains discoverable while respecting security and business ownership.

---

### AI-Ready Retrieval

Enterprise knowledge supports future AI reasoning through governed retrieval.

---

### Technology Independence

Search governance remains stable while search technologies evolve.

---

# 1.5 Domain Boundaries

The Search Domain owns:

- Search Indexes.
- Search Catalogs.
- Search Metadata.
- Search Profiles.
- Search Ranking Policies.
- Search Queries.
- Saved Searches.
- Search Relevance Models.
- Knowledge Relationships.
- Search Audit.
- Retrieval Policies.
- Search Personalization.

The domain does **not** own:

- Business records.
- Documents.
- Images.
- Orders.
- Inventory.
- Production.
- Finance.
- Master Data.
- Business workflows.

Ownership remains with the originating certified domains.

---

# 1.6 Business Responsibilities

The Search Domain is responsible for:

### Enterprise Search Governance

Maintaining enterprise search standards.

---

### Knowledge Discovery

Supporting enterprise-wide information discovery.

---

### Search Relevance

Delivering useful business search results.

---

### Search Security

Ensuring information is discoverable only by authorized users.

---

### Knowledge Relationships

Connecting related enterprise information across domains.

---

### Continuous Search Improvement

Supporting enterprise knowledge accessibility through governed evolution.

---

# 1.7 Core Business Principles

The domain follows these permanent principles.

### Search Exists to Support Business

Search improves enterprise decision-making.

It never replaces business ownership.

---

### Authoritative Retrieval

Every search result represents governed enterprise information.

---

### Explainable Relevance

Enterprise users understand:

- Why information appears.
- Business context.
- Ownership.
- Confidence.
- Related information.

---

### Enterprise Consistency

Search follows standardized enterprise definitions.

---

### Traceability

Every search activity remains attributable to:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Search Context.
- Retrieval History.
- Governance History.

---

### Technology Independence

Search governance remains stable while implementation technologies evolve.

---

# ENTERPRISE SEARCH, KNOWLEDGE & INFORMATION RETRIEVAL CANON
## Stage 2 — Domain Model & Business Entities

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Search, Knowledge & Information Retrieval Domain** is governed by a permanent enterprise search model that defines every search and knowledge business object within the GiftHatkeOS Enterprise Canon.

These entities represent **business search concepts**, not implementation artifacts such as search indexes, inverted indexes, vector databases, embeddings, search engine collections, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch indexes, SQL full-text indexes, graph databases, AI retrieval engines, or cloud search services.

Whether future implementations use:

- Apps Script
- Standalone GiftHatkeOS
- Elasticsearch
- OpenSearch
- Apache Solr
- PostgreSQL Full-Text Search
- Google Cloud Search
- Microsoft Search
- Azure AI Search
- Pinecone
- Weaviate
- Milvus
- Neo4j
- AI Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
- Future enterprise search technologies

the certified business entities remain unchanged.

They define the permanent enterprise search vocabulary of GiftHatkeOS.

---

# 2.2 Entity Principles

Every search entity follows these permanent principles.

### Single Responsibility

Each entity governs one business responsibility.

Examples:

- A **Search Index** represents one governed searchable knowledge space.
- A **Knowledge Asset** represents one discoverable enterprise information object.
- A **Search Query** represents one governed retrieval request.

Responsibilities are never shared.

---

### Stable Enterprise Identity

Every search entity possesses one permanent enterprise identity independent of implementation technology.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Every search entity has one accountable owning business domain.

Search ownership never transfers to the Search Domain.

---

### Governance

Every search entity follows enterprise lifecycle governance, approval, auditability, security, and controlled evolution.

---

### Traceability

Every search entity remains fully traceable throughout its lifecycle.

---

# 2.3 Entity Landscape

The Search Domain consists of the following canonical entities.

| Entity | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| Search Index | Represents one governed searchable knowledge space |
| Knowledge Asset | Represents one discoverable enterprise information object |
| Search Query | Represents one enterprise retrieval request |
| Search Result | Represents one governed retrieval outcome |
| Search Profile | Represents personalized search behavior |
| Search Collection | Represents a logical grouping of searchable assets |
| Metadata Definition | Represents governed search metadata |
| Search Ranking Policy | Represents enterprise relevance rules |
| Knowledge Relationship | Represents semantic relationships between assets |
| Saved Search | Represents reusable enterprise search definitions |
| Search Session | Represents one governed retrieval interaction |
| Retrieval Policy | Represents search authorization and governance |
| Search Version | Represents governed search evolution |
| Search Audit Record | Represents immutable search history |

---

# 2.4 Search Index

## Purpose

Represents one governed enterprise searchable knowledge space.

Responsibilities include:

- Search scope.
- Indexed business categories.
- Governance.
- Search ownership.
- Retrieval behavior.

A Search Index defines enterprise discoverability rather than technical indexing structures.

---

# 2.5 Knowledge Asset

Represents one discoverable enterprise information object.

Examples include:

- Order.
- Customer.
- SOP.
- Manufacturing drawing.
- Invoice.
- Product specification.
- Policy.
- Training article.

Ownership remains with the originating business domain.

---

# 2.6 Search Query

Represents one governed enterprise retrieval request.

Examples:

- Search customer.
- Search laser jobs.
- Search GST rules.
- Search production SOPs.
- Search shipping policies.

Search Queries describe business intent independent of search technology.

---

# 2.7 Search Result

Represents one governed retrieval outcome.

Each Search Result includes:

- Business relevance.
- Ownership.
- Retrieval context.
- Security eligibility.
- Confidence explanation.

Search Results represent business retrieval rather than ranking algorithms.

---

# 2.8 Search Profile

Represents enterprise search preferences.

Examples:

- Preferred language.
- Preferred business domains.
- Saved filters.
- Personal relevance preferences.
- Accessibility preferences.

Search Profiles personalize retrieval without changing enterprise governance.

---

# 2.9 Search Collection

Represents logical enterprise search organization.

Examples:

- Manufacturing Knowledge.
- Financial Knowledge.
- Policies.
- Customer Records.
- Technical Documentation.

Collections simplify enterprise discovery.

---

# 2.10 Metadata Definition

Represents governed searchable metadata.

Examples:

- Department.
- Product category.
- Customer.
- Date.
- Manufacturing line.
- Region.
- Business owner.

Metadata improves enterprise discovery.

---

# 2.11 Search Ranking Policy

Represents enterprise relevance governance.

Examples:

- Exact match preference.
- Business priority weighting.
- Freshness preference.
- Security filtering.
- Domain relevance.

Ranking Policies govern business relevance independent of implementation algorithms.

---

# 2.12 Knowledge Relationship

Represents semantic enterprise relationships.

Examples:

- Order references Product.
- SOP references Machine.
- Policy governs Workflow.
- Customer related to Orders.
- Manufacturing Job references Material.

Knowledge Relationships support enterprise understanding.

---

# 2.13 Saved Search

Represents reusable enterprise retrieval definitions.

Examples:

- Daily production exceptions.
- Pending approvals.
- Overdue manufacturing jobs.
- High-value customers.

Saved Searches improve enterprise productivity.

---

# 2.14 Search Session

Represents one governed enterprise retrieval interaction.

A Search Session preserves:

- Search intent.
- Query history.
- Retrieved knowledge.
- Navigation context.
- Audit information.

Sessions improve enterprise search continuity.

---

# 2.15 Retrieval Policy

Represents governed enterprise search authorization.

Examples:

- Executive search permissions.
- Finance visibility.
- Manufacturing visibility.
- Regional restrictions.
- AI retrieval permissions.

Retrieval Policies protect enterprise information.

---

# 2.16 Search Version

Represents governed evolution of enterprise search.

Examples:

- Ranking revision.
- Metadata enhancement.
- Search policy update.
- Knowledge graph improvement.

Versions preserve search evolution.

---

# 2.17 Search Audit Record

Represents immutable enterprise search history.

Examples:

- Search executed.
- Saved Search created.
- Ranking policy updated.
- Metadata modified.
- Retrieval policy approved.

Search Audit remains append-only.

---

# ENTERPRISE SEARCH, KNOWLEDGE & INFORMATION RETRIEVAL CANON
## Stage 3 — State Machines, Knowledge Lifecycles & Search Governance Gates

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Search, Knowledge & Information Retrieval Domain** governs the complete lifecycle of searchable knowledge, search indexes, search collections, search profiles, metadata definitions, ranking policies, retrieval policies, saved searches, search sessions, knowledge relationships, and enterprise search governance.

Every governed search entity progresses through certified business states.

These states ensure enterprise knowledge remains:

- Governed.
- Discoverable.
- Explainable.
- Traceable.
- Auditable.
- Business-approved.
- Recoverable.
- Technology-independent.

This Canon establishes the permanent lifecycle architecture for:

- Search Indexes.
- Knowledge Assets (search lifecycle only; ownership remains with source domains).
- Search Collections.
- Metadata Definitions.
- Search Ranking Policies.
- Retrieval Policies.
- Search Profiles.
- Saved Searches.
- Search Versions.
- Knowledge Relationships.

---

# 3.2 Lifecycle Philosophy

Enterprise search lifecycle management follows permanent principles.

### Single Authoritative State

Every governed search entity exists in exactly one official lifecycle state.

---

### Controlled Knowledge Evolution

Enterprise search evolves only through approved governance.

---

### Governance Gates

Every lifecycle transition passes mandatory validation before becoming effective.

---

### Traceability

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Previous State.
- New State.
- Business Justification.
- Related Evidence.
- Governance Approvals.
- Audit References.

---

### Immutable Search History

Historical search decisions remain permanently preserved.

Search revisions create governed new versions rather than rewriting historical search behavior.

---

# 3.3 Search Index Lifecycle

Every enterprise Search Index follows the certified lifecycle.

```text id="search-stage3-index"
Draft
   │
Validated
   │
Approved
   │
Active
   │
Optimized
```

Exceptional states include:

- Suspended.
- Retired.
- Archived.

---

### Draft

Search scope under preparation.

---

### Validated

Search structure and governance verified.

---

### Approved

Business governance approves enterprise use.

---

### Active

Index participates in enterprise discovery.

---

### Optimized

Search quality improved while preserving business semantics.

---

### Suspended

Temporarily unavailable through governance.

---

### Retired

Permanently removed from operational discovery.

---

### Archived

Retained exclusively for governance and audit.

---

# 3.4 Knowledge Asset Search Lifecycle

Knowledge Assets retain their own lifecycle within their originating domains.

The Search Domain governs only discoverability.

```text id="search-stage3-knowledge"
Discovered
     │
Indexed
     │
Searchable
     │
Referenced
```

Exceptional states:

- Hidden.
- Deindexed.

The underlying business record remains governed by its owning domain.

---

# 3.5 Search Ranking Policy Lifecycle

```text id="search-stage3-ranking"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Suspended.
- Replaced.
- Retired.

Only **Effective** ranking policies govern enterprise relevance.

---

# 3.6 Retrieval Policy Lifecycle

```text id="search-stage3-policy"
Draft
   │
Reviewed
   │
Approved
   │
Effective
```

Exceptional states:

- Replaced.
- Retired.

Retrieval Policies govern enterprise search authorization.

---

# 3.7 Search Version Lifecycle

```text id="search-stage3-version"
Created
    │
Validated
    │
Certified
    │
Released
```

Exceptional states:

- Rejected.
- Withdrawn.

Released versions become the authoritative search baseline.

---

# 3.8 Saved Search Lifecycle

```text id="search-stage3-saved"
Created
    │
Validated
    │
Shared
```

Exceptional states:

- Disabled.
- Deleted.

Shared Saved Searches become reusable enterprise knowledge assets.

---

# 3.9 Official Transition Matrix

Examples include:

| Current State | Allowed Next States |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Draft Search Index | Validated |
| Validated Search Index | Approved |
| Approved Search Index | Active |
| Active Search Index | Optimized |
| Draft Ranking Policy | Reviewed |
| Reviewed Ranking Policy | Approved |
| Approved Ranking Policy | Effective |
| Draft Retrieval Policy | Reviewed |
| Reviewed Retrieval Policy | Approved |
| Approved Retrieval Policy | Effective |
| Created Search Version | Validated |
| Validated Search Version | Certified |
| Certified Search Version | Released |

Transitions outside certified pathways are prohibited.

---

# 3.10 Forbidden Transitions

Examples include:

Draft Search Index

→ Active

---

Draft Ranking Policy

→ Effective

---

Created Search Version

→ Released

---

Hidden Knowledge Asset

→ Referenced

---

Retired Search Index

→ Draft

Enterprise governance prevents these invalid transitions.

---

# 3.11 Governance Gates

Every lifecycle progression passes mandatory business gates.

## Search Approval Gate

Before **Approved**:

- Business scope confirmed.
- Metadata validated.
- Security verified.
- Search documentation complete.

---

## Search Activation Gate

Before **Active**:

- Index certified.
- Retrieval policies approved.
- Ranking policy validated.
- Business readiness confirmed.

---

## Ranking Activation Gate

Before **Effective**:

- Ranking validation completed.
- Relevance verified.
- Business impact approved.

---

## Retrieval Policy Gate

Before **Effective**:

- Authorization reviewed.
- Security verified.
- Compliance confirmed.

---

## Search Version Release Gate

Before **Released**:

- Regression validation complete.
- Documentation finalized.
- Executive approval completed.

---

# 3.12 Search Authority

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Responsible Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Timestamp.
- Previous State.
- New State.
- Business Justification.
- Governance Approvals.

Enterprise search transitions are never anonymous.

---

# 3.13 Business Outcomes

Every governed search entity concludes with one authoritative outcome.

Canonical outcomes include:

- Active.
- Effective.
- Searchable.
- Released.
- Optimized.
- Retired.
- Archived.

These outcomes preserve enterprise search integrity.

# 3.14 Parallel Governance

Enterprise search supports concurrent governance activities.

Examples:

- Search quality review.
- Metadata review.
- Security review.
- AI ranking analysis.

# 3.18 GiftHatke Manufacturing Search Lifecycle

For personalized manufacturing, the certified search lifecycle includes:


# 4.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Search, Knowledge & Information Retrieval Domain** provides the enterprise with a stable set of **business search services** that govern enterprise discovery, knowledge indexing, metadata management, search relevance, semantic retrieval, authorization-aware search, enterprise knowledge relationships, and cross-domain information retrieval.

These services represent **permanent business capabilities**.

They do **not** prescribe:

- Search engines.

It does **not** own:

Commands:

- Validate governance.

- Ownership confirmed.

---

### Governance Validation

- Audit requirements.

# 4.17 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical search transaction.

Example:

Activate Search Index:

- Validate Search Index.
- Validate Metadata.
- Validate Retrieval Policies.
- Activate Search Index.
- Record Audit.
- Publish Search Index Activated event.

If any required step fails, the Search Index remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.18 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Activate Search Index.
- Register Knowledge Asset.
- Save Search.
- Activate Ranking Policy.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate Search Indexes, duplicate Metadata Definitions, duplicate Ranking Policies, duplicate Retrieval Policies, or duplicate Search Audit history.

---

# 4.19 Concurrency

Multiple enterprise teams may collaborate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Business governance.
- Metadata review.
- Security review.
- AI search optimization.
- Executive search governance.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Preservation of authoritative search evidence.
- Complete governance history.

Search services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Search prerequisites not satisfied.

---

### Authorization Errors

---

### Governance Errors

Missing approvals or governance requirements.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

---

### Search Errors

Enterprise search cannot satisfy business intent.

Examples:

- Missing metadata.
- Incomplete indexing.
- Knowledge relationship unavailable.
- Ranking conflict.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Business search failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Search, Knowledge & Information Retrieval Domain** establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for search management, knowledge discovery, information retrieval, metadata governance, semantic relationships, relevance management, retrieval authorization, search stewardship, and long-term enterprise knowledge accessibility.

Unlike operational domains that govern business transactions or source records, this domain governs **how enterprise information is discovered, retrieved, secured, ranked, and continuously improved while preserving ownership within the originating business domains**.

This Canon defines the permanent business architecture for:

- Enterprise search governance.
- Knowledge stewardship.
- Metadata governance.
- Search relevance governance.
- Retrieval authorization governance.
- Knowledge relationship governance.
- Search quality governance.
- AI-assisted retrieval governance.
- Enterprise information accessibility governance.

It intentionally avoids prescribing search engines, vector databases, graph databases, retrieval frameworks, AI assistants, or implementation technologies.

---

# 5.2 Enterprise Search Philosophy

Enterprise search governance follows eight permanent principles.

### Search Exists to Support Business

Search enables better enterprise decisions.

It never replaces ownership of enterprise information.

---

### Authoritative Retrieval

Every search result represents governed enterprise knowledge.

---

### Explicit Knowledge Stewardship

Every searchable knowledge asset has one accountable business steward.

---

### Enterprise Consistency

Search behavior remains consistent across every certified domain.

---

### Explainable Retrieval

Enterprise users understand:

- Why a result appears.
- Business relevance.
- Information ownership.
- Confidence.
- Applicable governance.

---

### Controlled Evolution

Enterprise search evolves through governed business processes.

---

### Traceability

Every search activity remains attributable to:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Knowledge Steward.
- Governance History.
- Retrieval History.

---

### Technology Independence

Search governance remains stable while implementation technologies evolve.

# 5.3 Enterprise Governance Model

Enterprise search governance evaluates six enterprise layers.

## Layer 1 — Business Knowledge

Defines enterprise business meaning.

Examples:

- Orders.
- Manufacturing.
- Finance.
- Policies.
- SOPs.

---

## Layer 2 — Discoverability

Represents searchable enterprise information.

Examples:

- Search Index.

- Knowledge Relationship.

---

## Layer 3 — Search Standards

Applies enterprise search expectations.

Examples:

- Metadata standards.

- Retrieval policies.
- Search taxonomy.

---

## Layer 4 — Stewardship

Assigns accountable ownership.

Examples:

- Knowledge Steward.
- Metadata Steward.
- Search Administrator.

---

## Layer 5 — Governance

Applies:

- Validation.
- Approval.
- Security.
- Quality.
- Continuous improvement.

---

## Layer 6 — Audit

Maintains permanent enterprise search history.

Knowledge becomes enterprise-searchable only after all required governance layers are satisfied.

---

# ENTERPRISE SEARCH, KNOWLEDGE & INFORMATION RETRIEVAL CANON
## Stage 6 — Search Events, Knowledge Synchronization & Cross-Domain Coordination Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Search, Knowledge & Information Retrieval Domain** governs enterprise discovery, knowledge indexing, metadata management, semantic relationships, retrieval authorization, search relevance, and information accessibility.

Unlike operational domains that publish business events related to transactions, this domain governs **how enterprise knowledge changes are communicated, synchronized, indexed, related, secured, and made discoverable across every certified business domain**.

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the Search Domain.

It defines:

- Search events.
- Knowledge indexing events.
- Metadata synchronization.
- Search publication rules.
- Cross-domain discoverability.
- Search version coordination.
- AI-assisted knowledge synchronization.

It intentionally avoids prescribing event buses, search engines, message brokers, vector databases, knowledge graphs, AI retrieval frameworks, or implementation technologies.

---

# 6.2 Search Event Philosophy

A Search Event represents a completed enterprise search or knowledge-governance occurrence.

Examples include:

- Knowledge Indexed.
- Metadata Updated.
- Search Index Activated.
- Ranking Policy Released.
- Search Version Published.

Search events communicate **completed enterprise knowledge facts**, not intermediate indexing activities.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business occurrence.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise search semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The Search Domain follows permanent principles.

### Knowledge Significance

Only meaningful enterprise search activities generate canonical events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed search occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable Search History

Published search events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

Search events originate only from the Search Domain.

Operational domains continue to own events related to their own business responsibilities.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event Identity.
- Timestamp.
- Knowledge Reference.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Correlation Identifier.
- Search Context.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Search Events

## Search Index Events

- Search Index Created.
- Search Index Validated.
- Search Index Activated.
- Search Index Suspended.
- Search Index Retired.

---

## Knowledge Events

- Knowledge Registered.
- Knowledge Indexed.
- Knowledge Reindexed.
- Knowledge Hidden.
- Knowledge Deindexed.

---

## Metadata Events

- Metadata Defined.
- Metadata Updated.
- Metadata Retired.

---

## Search Query Events

- Search Executed.
- Saved Search Created.
- Saved Search Shared.

---

## Ranking Events

- Ranking Policy Approved.
- Ranking Policy Activated.
- Ranking Policy Replaced.

---

## Retrieval Events

- Retrieval Authorized.
- Retrieval Denied.
- Retrieval Policy Updated.

---

## Governance Events

- Search Audit Completed.
- Metadata Validation Completed.
- Search Quality Review Completed.

---

## AI Search Events

- AI Knowledge Recommendation Generated.
- AI Relationship Discovered.
- AI Search Optimization Published.

---

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

Search events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding business activity.

Examples:

- **Knowledge Indexed** is emitted only after indexing governance succeeds.
- **Search Index Activated** is emitted only after governance approval is complete.
- **Ranking Policy Activated** is emitted only after relevance validation succeeds.
- **Retrieval Authorized** is emitted only after authorization evaluation.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every Search Event follows the same sequence:

1. Search activity initiated.
2. Validation completed.
3. Business transaction completed.
4. Audit recorded.
5. Canonical Search Event published.
6. Authorized stakeholders process the event.
7. Enterprise search records updated.

Published events therefore represent authoritative enterprise knowledge facts.

---

# 6.7 Event Consumers

Search events are consumed by collaborating enterprise domains.

| Search Event | Typical Consumer Domains |
|--------------|--------------------------|
| Knowledge Indexed | AI Services |
| Metadata Updated | Reporting & Business Intelligence |
| Search Index Activated | Workflow, Process Automation & Orchestration |
| Ranking Policy Activated | Enterprise Monitoring, Observability & Operations |
| Retrieval Authorized | Identity, Security & Administration |
| Search Version Published | Integration, APIs & Enterprise Connectivity |
| Search Audit Completed | Executive Governance |
| AI Search Optimization Published | Business Leadership |

Consumers respond to search events without assuming ownership of enterprise knowledge.

---

# 6.8 Event Payload Principles

Every Search Event communicates sufficient business context for downstream processing.

Canonical elements include:

- Event Identity.
- Event Type.
- Knowledge Reference.
- Enterprise Identity.
- Business Domain.
- Search Category.
- Timestamp.
- Correlation Identifier.
- Governance Reference.

Implementation-specific metadata is intentionally excluded.

---

# 6.9 Knowledge Synchronization Principles

Enterprise search synchronization improves organizational knowledge consistency while respecting certified governance.

Every synchronization activity must be:

- Deterministic.
- Auditable.
- Policy-driven.
- Traceable.
- Repeatable.

Synchronization must never bypass:

- Business ownership.
- Retrieval authorization.
- Metadata governance.
- Search validation.
- Enterprise search consistency.

---

# 6.10 Canonical Search Automations

Examples include:

### Knowledge Synchronization

- Publish searchable knowledge.
- Refresh metadata.

# 6.11 Orchestration vs. Choreography

The Search Domain supports both collaboration models.

## Orchestration

Used where centralized search governance is required.

Examples:

- Enterprise indexing.
- Ranking policy activation.
- Retrieval policy deployment.
- Search version release.

---

## Choreography

Used where independent domains respond to Search Events.

Examples:

- AI Services consuming Knowledge Indexed.
- Reporting updating metadata statistics.
- Workflow discovering new knowledge.
- Monitoring consuming Search Quality events.

The collaboration model is determined by business ownership rather than implementation technology.

# 5.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Artificial Intelligence, Decision Intelligence & Autonomous Operations Domain** establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for artificial intelligence, decision support, autonomous operations, enterprise memory, AI safety, explainability, human oversight, agent collaboration, and long-term organizational intelligence.

Unlike operational domains that govern business transactions or source information, this domain governs **how artificial intelligence may reason, recommend, predict, coordinate, learn, and assist while preserving enterprise accountability, regulatory compliance, and business ownership.**

# 5.2 Enterprise AI Philosophy

Enterprise AI governance follows eight permanent principles.

### AI Exists to Augment Human Capability

Artificial Intelligence improves enterprise effectiveness.

It never replaces enterprise responsibility.

---

### Humans Remain Accountable

Business accountability always remains with authorized enterprise personnel.

AI recommendations never transfer legal, financial, operational, or governance responsibility.

---

### Explainability Before Automation

Enterprise users understand:

- Why AI reached a conclusion.
- Supporting evidence.
- Business assumptions.
- Confidence.
- Applicable governance.

---

### Trusted Enterprise Knowledge

AI reasons only from governed enterprise information.

---

### Enterprise Consistency

AI follows certified enterprise definitions across every business domain.

### Controlled Evolution

Enterprise AI evolves through governed business processes.

---

### Traceability

Every AI activity remains attributable to:

- Enterprise Identity.
- AI Agent.
- Human Supervisor.
- Enterprise Memory.
- Governance History.
- Audit History.

---

### Technology Independence

AI governance remains stable while AI technologies evolve.

Defines trusted enterprise information.

---

## Layer 5 — Enterprise Governance

Applies:

- AI Policies.
- Safety Rules.
- Security.
- Compliance.
- Risk management.

---

## Layer 6 — Audit

Maintains immutable AI history.

---

## Layer 7 — Continuous Improvement

Enterprise learning continuously improves AI governance while preserving certified business semantics.

## Stage 6 — AI Events, Enterprise Memory Synchronization & Cross-Domain Intelligence Coordination Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Artificial Intelligence, Decision Intelligence & Autonomous Operations Domain** governs enterprise intelligence, AI reasoning, enterprise memory, decision support, recommendations, predictions, autonomous coordination, explainability, and AI governance.

Unlike operational domains that publish events describing business transactions, this domain governs **how enterprise intelligence, AI reasoning, enterprise memory, and autonomous coordination are communicated, synchronized, audited, and governed across every certified enterprise domain.**

This Canon establishes the permanent event-driven architecture for the AI Domain.

It defines:

- AI Events.
- Enterprise Memory Events.
- Decision Intelligence Events.
- Recommendation Events.
- Prediction Events.
- AI Governance Events.
- Agent Coordination Events.
- Cross-domain intelligence synchronization.
- AI lifecycle events.

It intentionally avoids prescribing event buses, message brokers, orchestration platforms, AI frameworks, foundation models, or implementation technologies.

---

# 6.2 AI Event Philosophy

An AI Event represents a completed enterprise intelligence occurrence.

Examples include:

- Recommendation Generated.
- Prediction Published.
- AI Agent Activated.
- Human Approval Recorded.
- Enterprise Memory Updated.

AI Events communicate **completed enterprise intelligence facts**, not intermediate reasoning activities.

Every event must:

- Represent a completed business occurrence.
- Be immutable.
- Be traceable.
- Preserve enterprise AI semantics.
- Remain technology-independent.

---

# 6.3 Event Principles

The AI Domain follows permanent principles.

### Business Significance

Only meaningful enterprise intelligence activities generate canonical AI Events.

---

### Single Publication

Each completed intelligence occurrence generates one canonical event.

Duplicate publication is prevented through governance.

---

### Immutable AI History

Published AI Events are never modified.

Corrections generate subsequent governed events while preserving historical accountability.

---

### Explicit Ownership

AI Events originate only from the AI Domain.

Operational domains continue to own events related to their own business responsibilities.

---

### Traceability

Each event records:

- Event Identity.
- Timestamp.
- Enterprise Identity.
- AI Agent.
- Human Supervisor.
- Business Domain.
- Correlation Identifier.
- Enterprise Context.

---

# 6.4 Canonical AI Events

## AI Agent Events

- AI Agent Registered.
- AI Agent Validated.
- AI Agent Activated.
- AI Agent Suspended.
- AI Agent Retired.

---

## Enterprise Memory Events

- Enterprise Memory Captured.
- Enterprise Memory Verified.
- Enterprise Memory Updated.
- Enterprise Memory Archived.

---

## Recommendation Events

- Recommendation Approved.
- Recommendation Rejected.

- Evidence Attached.

---

## AI Learning Events

- Learning Opportunity Identified.
- Recommendation Quality Improved.
- Enterprise Memory Refined.

# 6.5 Event Publication Rules

AI Events are published only after successful completion of the corresponding business activity.

Examples:

- **Recommendation Generated** is emitted only after enterprise reasoning completes.
- **Human Approval Recorded** is emitted only after governance approval is complete.
- **Prediction Published** is emitted only after prediction validation succeeds.
- **Enterprise Memory Updated** is emitted only after governance verification.

Validation failures do not generate completion events.

---

# 6.6 Event Lifecycle

Every AI Event follows the same sequence:

1. Intelligence activity initiated.
2. Enterprise context gathered.
3. Validation completed.
4. Business transaction completed.
5. Audit recorded.
6. Canonical AI Event published.
7. Authorized enterprise domains process the event.
8. Enterprise intelligence history updated.

Published events therefore represent authoritative enterprise intelligence facts.

---

|-----------|--------------------------|

Consumers respond to AI Events without assuming ownership of enterprise intelligence.

- Timestamp.

# 6.14 Failure Handling Principles

# 3.2 Lifecycle Philosophy

Enterprise customer lifecycle management follows permanent principles.

### Single Authoritative State

Every governed customer entity exists in exactly one official lifecycle state.

---

### Controlled Relationship Evolution

Customer relationships evolve through governed business processes.

---

### Governance Gates

Every lifecycle transition passes mandatory business validation.

---

### Traceability

Every lifecycle transition records:

- Enterprise Identity.
- Customer Account.
- Responsible Employee.
- Previous State.
- New State.
- Business Justification.
- Supporting Evidence.
- Governance Approvals.
- Audit References.

---

### Immutable Relationship History

Changes create new governed relationship events rather than rewriting enterprise history.

# 3.3 Lead Lifecycle

Every Lead follows the certified lifecycle.

```text id="crm-stage3-lead"
Captured
    │
Qualified
    │
Assigned
    │
Engaged
    │
Converted
```

Exceptional states include:

- On Hold.
- Disqualified.
- Lost.
- Archived.

---

### Captured

Initial inquiry received.

---

### Qualified

Business opportunity verified.

---

### Assigned

Ownership allocated.

---

### Engaged

Customer relationship initiated.

---

### Converted

Lead becomes a governed Customer Account and/or Opportunity.

---

### On Hold

Awaiting future activity.

---

### Disqualified

Lead does not meet business criteria.

---

### Lost

Opportunity not pursued successfully.

---

### Archived

Retained exclusively for audit and historical analysis.

---

# 3.4 Customer Account Lifecycle

```text id="crm-stage3-account"
Created
   │
Verified
   │
Active
   │
Preferred
```

Exceptional states:

- Suspended.
- Dormant.
- Closed.
- Archived.

Customer Accounts remain active until governed business closure.

---

# 3.5 Opportunity Lifecycle

```text id="crm-stage3-opportunity"
Identified
     │
Qualified
     │
Proposed
     │
Negotiation
     │
Won
```

Exceptional states:

- Lost.
- Withdrawn.
- Archived.

Won Opportunities transition into operational fulfillment governed by the Order Management Domain.

```text id="crm-stage3-case"
Opened
   │
Assigned
   │
In Progress
   │
Resolved
   │
Closed
```

Exceptional states:

- Escalated.
- Reopened.
- Cancelled.

# 3.7 Customer Success Plan Lifecycle

```text id="crm-stage3-success"
Planned
   │
Approved
   │
Active
   │
Completed
```

Exceptional states:

- Suspended.
- Cancelled.

Success Plans evolve through governed customer engagement.

---

# 3.8 Loyalty Program Lifecycle

```text id="crm-stage3-loyalty"
Designed
   │
Approved
   │
Active
```

Exceptional states:

- Suspended.
- Retired.

Examples include:

| Current State | Allowed Next States |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Captured Lead | Qualified |
| Qualified Lead | Assigned |
| Assigned Lead | Engaged |
| Engaged Lead | Converted |
| Created Account | Verified |
| Verified Account | Active |
| Active Account | Preferred |
| Identified Opportunity | Qualified |
| Qualified Opportunity | Proposed |
| Proposed Opportunity | Negotiation |
| Negotiation | Won or Lost |

Transitions outside certified pathways are prohibited.

→ Converted

---

Created Account

→ Preferred

---

Opened Case

→ Closed

---

Identified Opportunity

→ Won

---

Archived Customer Account

→ Created

Enterprise governance prevents these invalid transitions.

# 3.11 Governance Gates

Before **Qualified**:

- Contact information validated.
- Customer intent identified.
- Minimum relationship information available.

Before **Assigned**:

---

Before **Negotiation**:

- Commercial review completed.
- Pricing governance satisfied.
- Business approvals recorded.

---

## Customer Success Gate

Before **Active Success Plan**:

- Customer objectives documented.
- Success metrics defined.
- Ownership confirmed.

- Redeem Rewards.

---

# 4.16 Commands and Queries

Business services are divided into two categories.

## Commands

Commands modify customer relationships.

Examples:

- Capture Lead.
- Update Customer Account.
- Resolve Customer Case.
- Award Loyalty Benefits.

Commands:

- Validate governance.
- Update lifecycle.
- Record audit.
- Publish CRM events.

---

## Queries

Queries never modify customer relationships.

Examples:

- View Customer Timeline.
- Retrieve Customer Journey.
- View Opportunity.
- View Relationship Intelligence.
- View Communication History.

Queries remain read-only.

---

# 4.17 Validation Framework

Every command performs mandatory validation.

Validation categories include:

### Structural Validation

- Customer exists.
- Contact exists.
- Opportunity exists.
- Case exists.

---

### Business Validation

- Customer identity valid.
- Business ownership confirmed.
- Required information available.
- Relationship context sufficient.

---

### Lifecycle Validation

- Requested transition permitted.
- Governance gates satisfied.
- Relationship integrity maintained.

---

### Privacy Validation

- Customer consent.
- Communication preferences.
- Applicable privacy policies.

---

### Governance Validation

- Required approvals.
- Security compliance.
- Audit requirements.
- Business ownership.

---

# 4.18 Transaction Boundaries

Every business command represents one logical CRM transaction.

Example:

Convert Lead:

- Validate Lead.
- Validate Customer information.
- Create Customer Account.
- Create Contact.
- Update Lead status.
- Record Audit.
- Publish Lead Converted event.

If any required step fails, the Lead remains in its previous valid business state.

---

# 4.19 Idempotency

Certain commands must be repeat-safe.

Examples:

- Register Customer.
- Convert Lead.
- Merge Customer Accounts.
- Record Customer Interaction.

Repeated requests must never create duplicate customer relationships, duplicate contacts, duplicate opportunities, duplicate cases, or duplicate CRM audit history.

---

# 4.20 Concurrency

Multiple enterprise teams may collaborate simultaneously.

Examples:

- Sales.
- Customer Service.
- Manufacturing.
- Finance.
- Customer Success.

Business rules require:

- Conflict detection.
- Controlled synchronization.
- Preservation of authoritative customer information.
- Complete relationship history.

---

# 4.21 Error Classification

CRM services classify failures consistently.

### Validation Errors

Business prerequisites not satisfied.

---

### Authorization Errors

Operation prohibited by enterprise policy.

---

### Governance Errors

Missing approvals or governance requirements.

---

### Lifecycle Errors

Requested transition prohibited.

---

### Relationship Errors

Examples:

- Duplicate customer.
- Invalid customer ownership.
- Opportunity conflict.
- Customer merge conflict.
- Missing relationship context.

---

### System Errors

Unexpected technical failures.

Relationship failures remain distinguishable from technical failures.

---

The Customer Experience Domain collaborates with every certified enterprise domain.

# 5.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Experience, CRM & Relationship Management Domain** establishes the enterprise-wide governance model for customer relationships, customer lifecycle management, customer success, customer privacy, customer communications, relationship intelligence, omnichannel engagement, customer loyalty, and long-term customer value.

Unlike operational domains that fulfill customer orders or manage production activities, this domain governs **how customer relationships are acquired, maintained, protected, expanded, and continuously improved while preserving enterprise accountability, customer trust, privacy, and long-term business value.**

This Canon defines the permanent business architecture for:

- Customer governance.
- Customer ownership.
- Customer privacy.
- Customer stewardship.
- Customer Success.
- Relationship intelligence.
- Customer satisfaction.
- Loyalty governance.

It intentionally avoids prescribing CRM platforms, customer engagement software, marketing automation systems, communication technologies, or implementation methods.

# 5.2 Customer Relationship Philosophy

Enterprise CRM governance follows eight permanent principles.

### Relationships Before Revenue

Long-term customer relationships take precedence over isolated commercial transactions.

---

### Customer Trust

Every customer interaction strengthens enterprise trust.

---

### One Enterprise Relationship

Customers experience one enterprise regardless of department, channel, or employee.

---

### Customer Ownership

Every customer relationship has accountable enterprise ownership.

---

### Privacy by Design

Customer information is governed according to enterprise privacy policies and applicable legal requirements.

---

### Continuous Customer Success

Customer relationships continue after sales are completed.

---

### Enterprise Consistency

Customer governance follows identical principles across every certified domain.

---

### Technology Independence

Customer governance remains stable while CRM technologies evolve.

# 5.3 Enterprise Governance Model

Enterprise customer governance evaluates seven enterprise layers.

## Layer 1 — Customer Identity

Defines trusted customer identity.

Examples:

- Customer Accounts.
- Contacts.
- Relationship ownership.

---

## Layer 2 — Customer Context

Defines governed relationship information.

Examples:

- Communication history.
- Previous orders.
- Preferences.
- Customer Journey.
- Customer Cases.

---

## Layer 3 — Relationship Intelligence

Provides:

- Customer insights.
- Segmentation.
- Loyalty indicators.
- Relationship health.

---

## Layer 4 — Customer Success

Coordinates:

- Customer objectives.
- Long-term value.
- Relationship development.

---

## Layer 5 — Enterprise Governance

Applies:

- Privacy.
- Customer policies.
- Consent management.
- Security.
- Relationship ownership.

---

## Layer 6 — Audit

Maintains immutable customer relationship history.

---

## Layer 7 — Continuous Improvement

Enterprise learning continuously improves customer relationships while preserving certified governance.

---

- Long-term customer value.
- Success planning.
- Customer retention.

---

## Customer Service Manager

Responsibilities:

- Case governance.

- Escalation management.
- Customer satisfaction.

---

## Privacy Steward

Responsibilities:

- Customer privacy.
- Consent management.
- Data governance.
- Regulatory compliance.

---

## CRM Auditor

- Audit validation.
- Privacy compliance.
- Customer history review.

Cannot modify historical CRM records.

---

## Active Customer Relationships

---

---
