# ENTERPRISE ANALYTICS, REPORTING INTELLIGENCE & PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT CANON
## Stage 2 — Performance Entity Model, KPI Architecture & Enterprise Measurement Structure Canon

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Domain** requires a permanent entity model that defines the structures used to represent enterprise measurement, performance targets, scorecards, analytical dimensions, variances, forecasts, reviews, and decision-support intelligence.

Stage 1 established:

- Domain scope.
- Performance philosophy.
- KPI governance principles.
- Enterprise measurement hierarchy.
- Cross-domain ownership boundaries.

Stage 2 now establishes the canonical information architecture for performance management.

The objective is to ensure that enterprise measurement remains:

- Consistent.
- Governed.
- Traceable.
- Comparable.
- Explainable.
- Technology-independent.

A dashboard is only a presentation layer.

The enterprise performance architecture exists beneath it.

---

# 2.2 Performance Entity Principles

Every performance entity follows permanent principles.

---

## Business Meaning Before Calculation

Every measure must have an understandable business definition.

---

## Ownership Before Publication

Every critical KPI requires accountable ownership.

---

## Source Before Result

Every measure must trace to governed source information.

---

## Target Before Variance

Performance deviation requires an approved comparison basis.

---

## Context Before Interpretation

Numbers require dimensional and temporal context.

---

## Version Before Historical Comparison

Material changes to calculations must preserve historical interpretability.

---

## Evidence Before Executive Use

Critical performance information must be auditable.

---

# 2.3 Canonical Performance Entity Landscape

The permanent entity architecture includes:

| Entity | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Enterprise Objective | Defines desired enterprise outcome |
| Strategic Goal | Defines strategic direction |
| Performance Objective | Defines measurable business expectation |
| Metric | Represents a measurable observation |
| KPI | Represents critical performance |
| KPI Definition | Defines KPI business meaning |
| KPI Owner | Defines accountability |
| KPI Formula | Defines calculation |
| KPI Source Mapping | Links KPI to authoritative information |
| Measurement Record | Stores observed result |
| Measurement Period | Defines time context |
| Performance Target | Defines expected result |
| Performance Threshold | Defines interpretation boundaries |
| Variance Record | Represents difference from expectation |
| Performance Dimension | Defines analytical context |
| Scorecard | Groups performance measures |
| Dashboard Definition | Defines visual performance experience |
| Performance Review | Records structured management review |
| Performance Action | Converts insight into accountable action |
| Performance Issue | Represents material deviation |
| Root Cause Record | Records performance cause analysis |
| Forecast | Represents expected future performance |
| Scenario | Represents modeled future conditions |
| Benchmark | Represents comparison reference |
| Performance Trend | Represents change over time |
| Performance Insight | Represents analytical interpretation |
| Performance Recommendation | Represents suggested action |
| Performance Risk | Represents risk to objectives |
| KPI Certification Record | Records KPI approval and validity |
| Performance Audit Record | Preserves performance governance evidence |

---

# 2.4 Enterprise Objective Entity

## Purpose

Represents a high-level desired enterprise outcome.

Examples:

- Profitable growth.
- Reliable fulfillment.
- Excellent customer experience.
- Scalable production.
- Strong operational control.

An Enterprise Objective should contain:

- Objective ID.
- Name.
- Description.
- Owner.
- Effective period.
- Status.

---

# 2.5 Strategic Goal Entity

## Purpose

Translates an Enterprise Objective into strategic direction.

Example:

```text id="strategic-goal-example"
Enterprise Objective:
Reliable Fulfillment

↓

Strategic Goal:
Reduce Order-to-Dispatch Time
```

Strategic Goals connect leadership intent with measurable performance.

---

# 2.6 Performance Objective Entity

## Purpose

Defines a measurable expectation connected to a strategic or operational goal.

Example:

```text id="performance-objective"
Strategic Goal:
Reduce Order-to-Dispatch Time

↓

Performance Objective:
Improve average fulfillment cycle while maintaining quality
```

A Performance Objective may link to multiple KPIs.

---

# 2.7 Metric Entity

## Purpose

Represents a measurable business observation.

Examples:

- Orders received.
- Orders completed.
- Revenue.
- Production minutes.
- Customer complaints.
- Material shortages.

A Metric contains:

- Metric ID.
- Business definition.
- Unit.
- Source.
- Frequency.
- Owner.

Metrics are building blocks.

Not all Metrics are KPIs.

---

# 2.8 KPI Entity

## Purpose

Represents a governed measure of important business performance.

A KPI contains:

- KPI ID.
- Name.
- Business definition.
- Owner.
- Objective relationship.
- Calculation.
- Unit.
- Source mappings.
- Frequency.
- Target.
- Thresholds.
- Status.
- Certification.

---

# 2.9 KPI Definition Entity

## Purpose

Preserves the business meaning of the KPI.

Example:

```text id="kpi-definition-example"
KPI:
On-Time Dispatch Rate

Definition:
Percentage of eligible orders dispatched within the committed dispatch deadline.
```

The definition must distinguish:

- Included records.
- Excluded records.
- Time basis.
- Calculation logic.
- Business interpretation.

---

# 2.10 KPI Owner Entity

## Purpose

Defines accountability for KPI meaning and performance interpretation.

The KPI Owner may be:

- Department leader.
- Domain owner.
- Business manager.
- Executive owner.

The owner is responsible for:

- Definition approval.
- Target approval within authority.
- Interpretation.
- Performance review.
- Improvement accountability.

---

# 2.11 KPI Formula Entity

## Purpose

Defines calculation logic.

Example:

```text id="kpi-formula-example"
On-Time Dispatch Rate

=

Orders Dispatched On Time
÷
Eligible Orders
×
100
```

A formula should record:

- Numerator.
- Denominator.
- Filters.
- Exclusions.
- Rounding.
- Unit.
- Calculation version.

---

# 2.12 KPI Source Mapping Entity

## Purpose

Links KPI calculations to authoritative enterprise information.

Example:

```text id="kpi-source-map"
KPI:
On-Time Dispatch Rate

Source Domain:
Order Management
Shipping & Fulfillment

Source Fields:
Order ID
Committed Dispatch Date
Actual Dispatch Date
Order Status
```

This creates performance lineage.

---

# 2.13 Measurement Record Entity

## Purpose

Represents an observed value for a Metric or KPI.

Contains:

- Measurement ID.
- Metric/KPI.
- Period.
- Actual value.
- Calculation version.
- Source snapshot or references where appropriate.
- Status.
- Certification state.

---

# 2.14 Measurement Period Entity

## Purpose

Defines the time context of performance.

Examples:

- Daily.
- Weekly.
- Monthly.
- Quarterly.
- Annual.
- Rolling 7 days.
- Rolling 30 days.
- Fiscal period.

The Measurement Period ensures comparable performance analysis.

---

# 2.15 Performance Target Entity

## Purpose

Defines expected business performance.

Contains:

- Target ID.
- KPI.
- Target value.
- Target type.
- Effective period.
- Owner.
- Approval.
- Version.

Target types may include:

- Minimum.
- Maximum.
- Exact.
- Range.
- Growth rate.
- Milestone.

---

# 2.16 Performance Threshold Entity

## Purpose

Defines performance interpretation bands.

Example:

```text id="threshold-example"
KPI:
On-Time Dispatch

Healthy:
≥ 95%

Watch:
90–94.99%

At Risk:
80–89.99%

Critical:
< 80%
```

Thresholds must be governed business rules.

They should not exist solely for visual dashboard coloring.

---

# 2.17 Variance Record Entity

## Purpose

Represents difference between actual and comparison basis.

Variance types may include:

- Actual vs Target.
- Actual vs Forecast.
- Actual vs Prior Period.
- Actual vs Benchmark.
- Actual vs Budget.

Contains:

- Actual.
- Comparison value.
- Absolute variance.
- Percentage variance.
- Materiality.
- Interpretation status.

---

# 2.18 Performance Dimension Entity

## Purpose

Defines the business context across which performance may be analyzed.

Canonical dimensions may include:

- Time.
- Customer.
- Product.
- Product category.
- Channel.
- Department.
- Location.
- Supplier.
- Employee role.
- Order type.
- Production method.

Dimensions must align with governed master and business data.

---

# 2.19 Dimensional Hierarchy

Dimensions may contain hierarchies.

Example:

```text id="product-dimension"
Product Family

↓

Product

↓

Variant

↓

SKU
```

Another example:

```text id="time-dimension"
Year

↓

Quarter

↓

Month

↓

Week

↓

Day
```

Hierarchies support drill-down without redefining underlying measures.

---

# 2.20 Scorecard Entity

## Purpose

Groups related KPIs according to business responsibility.

A Scorecard contains:

- Scorecard ID.
- Name.
- Owner.
- Audience.
- KPIs.
- Display order.
- Review frequency.
- Effective period.

Examples:

- Executive Scorecard.
- Production Scorecard.
- Sales Scorecard.
- Customer Experience Scorecard.

---

# 2.21 Executive Scorecard Structure

A future GiftHatke Executive Scorecard may include:

```text id="executive-scorecard"
Growth

Customer

Sales

Operations

Production

Quality

Inventory

Finance

People

Risk
```

Each section should contain only decision-relevant KPIs.

---

# 2.22 Dashboard Definition Entity

## Purpose

Defines how performance information is presented.

Contains:

- Dashboard name.
- Audience.
- KPIs.
- Filters.
- Dimensions.
- Refresh expectations.
- Access requirements.

A Dashboard Definition is separate from KPI ownership.

Changing a chart does not change KPI meaning.

---

# 2.23 Performance Review Entity

## Purpose

Records structured evaluation of business performance.

Contains:

- Review period.
- Participants.
- Scorecard.
- Major variances.
- Findings.
- Decisions.
- Actions.
- Risks.
- Follow-up.

Examples:

- Daily Operations Review.
- Weekly Production Review.
- Monthly Business Review.
- Quarterly Strategic Review.

---

# 2.24 Performance Action Entity

## Purpose

Converts intelligence into accountable execution.

Contains:

- Action.
- Related KPI.
- Owner.
- Due state.
- Priority.
- Status.
- Expected impact.
- Completion evidence.

---

# 2.25 Performance Issue Entity

## Purpose

Represents material deviation requiring investigation.

Examples:

- Production throughput below target.
- Customer complaints above threshold.
- Margin deterioration.
- Shipping delays.

Contains:

- Issue severity.
- KPI.
- Business impact.
- Owner.
- Investigation status.

---

# 2.26 Root Cause Record Entity

## Purpose

Preserves evidence explaining why performance deviated.

Potential categories include:

- Process.
- People capability.
- Material.
- Equipment.
- Data.
- Supplier.
- Customer dependency.
- Technology.
- Policy.
- External factor.

Root Cause Records should distinguish verified causes from hypotheses.

---

# 2.27 Forecast Entity

## Purpose

Represents expected future performance.

Examples:

- Revenue forecast.
- Order volume forecast.
- Production demand forecast.
- Inventory requirement forecast.

A Forecast records:

- Forecast period.
- Model or method.
- Input sources.
- Forecast value.
- Confidence or range where appropriate.
- Creation date.
- Version.

---

# 2.28 Scenario Entity

## Purpose

Represents a modeled alternative future condition.

Examples:

- 20% order growth.
- Supplier disruption.
- New production machine.
- Festival-season demand spike.
- Price increase.

Scenario analysis allows:

```text id="scenario-model"
Assumption

↓

Business Model

↓

Expected Performance

↓

Risk / Opportunity

↓

Management Decision
```

A Scenario is not a forecast unless explicitly designated.

---

# 2.29 Benchmark Entity

## Purpose

Defines a performance comparison reference.

Benchmarks may be:

- Historical.
- Internal.
- Industry.
- Competitor-derived where legitimately available.
- Strategic target.

Benchmark source and validity must be recorded.

---

# 2.30 Performance Trend Entity

## Purpose

Represents changes in performance across time.

Examples:

- Revenue increasing.
- Rework declining.
- Fulfillment deteriorating.
- Customer response improving.

Trend records may identify:

- Direction.
- Magnitude.
- Duration.
- Volatility.

---

# 2.31 Performance Insight Entity

## Purpose

Represents a meaningful interpretation derived from performance information.

Example:

```text id="performance-insight-example"
Observation:
Order-to-dispatch time increased by 18%.

Insight:
Increase is concentrated in personalized acrylic products and correlates with production backlog.
```

Insights should preserve evidence and lineage.

---

# 2.32 Performance Recommendation Entity

## Purpose

Represents a proposed management action.

Examples:

- Increase production capacity.
- Review supplier lead times.
- Adjust reorder points.
- Improve personalization intake validation.

Recommendations may originate from:

- Managers.
- Analysts.
- AI systems.
- Continuous improvement processes.

They remain recommendations until approved.

---

# 2.33 Performance Risk Entity

## Purpose

Represents a threat to achieving an objective or KPI target.

Examples:

- Material shortage risk.
- Production bottleneck.
- High return rate.
- Margin deterioration.
- Customer-response backlog.

Performance Risk links analytics with risk management.

---

# 2.34 KPI Certification Record Entity

## Purpose

Records formal approval of KPI definitions.

Contains:

- KPI.
- Definition version.
- Formula version.
- Source mappings.
- Owner.
- Approver.
- Effective date.
- Certification status.

Critical KPIs should not become authoritative without certification.

---

# 2.35 Performance Audit Record Entity

## Purpose

Preserves performance-governance history.

Examples:

- KPI definition changes.
- Target changes.
- Formula changes.
- Source changes.
- Scorecard changes.
- Certification actions.

Historical KPI interpretation must remain reconstructable.

---

# 2.36 Performance Entity Relationship Model

The certified architecture is:

```text id="performance-entity-topology"
Enterprise Objective

↓

Strategic Goal

↓

Performance Objective

↓

KPI

↓

Formula + Source Mapping

↓

Measurement

↓

Target

↓

Variance

↓

Insight

↓

Action

↓

Performance Improvement
```

---

# 2.37 KPI Lifecycle States

The canonical KPI lifecycle is:

```text id="kpi-lifecycle"
Proposed

↓

Defined

↓

Validated

↓

Certified

↓

Active

↓

Reviewed

↓

Revised / Retired

↓

Archived
```

Only **Certified / Active** KPIs should be treated as authoritative enterprise measures.

---

# 2.38 Metric Lifecycle

Metrics follow:

```text id="metric-lifecycle"
Identified

↓

Defined

↓

Mapped to Source

↓

Validated

↓

Active

↓

Reviewed

↓

Retired
```

Metrics can remain useful even when they are not KPIs.

---

# 2.39 Target Lifecycle

Targets follow:

```text id="target-lifecycle"
Proposed

↓

Business Justified

↓

Approved

↓

Effective

↓

Measured

↓

Reviewed

↓

Revised / Closed
```

Past targets must remain historically visible.

---

# 2.40 Scorecard Lifecycle

Scorecards follow:

```text id="scorecard-lifecycle"
Designed

↓

Reviewed

↓

Approved

↓

Published

↓

Used

↓

Reviewed

↓

Updated / Retired
```

Scorecards should evolve without rewriting historical KPI results.

---

# 2.41 Measure Aggregation Model

Measures may be aggregated according to defined rules.

Examples:

- Sum.
- Average.
- Median.
- Count.
- Percentage.
- Minimum.
- Maximum.
- Weighted average.

Aggregation must preserve correct business meaning.

For example:

A percentage KPI often cannot be safely averaged across groups without appropriate weighting.

---

# 2.42 Derived Metric Architecture

Derived Metrics result from other measures.

Example:

```text id="derived-metric"
Revenue

-

Direct Cost

=

Gross Margin
```

Derived metrics require:

- Component lineage.
- Formula.
- Versioning.
- Ownership.

---

# 2.43 Composite KPI Architecture

A Composite KPI combines several performance dimensions.

Example:

```text id="composite-kpi"
Operational Health Index

=

Fulfillment
+
Quality
+
Production
+
Inventory Reliability
```

Composite KPIs require careful governance.

They must remain explainable and should not conceal individual weak areas.

---

# 2.44 KPI Dependency Architecture

KPIs may depend on other KPIs.

Example:

```text id="kpi-dependencies"
Customer Satisfaction

↑

On-Time Delivery

↑

Production Throughput

↑

Material Availability
```

Dependency mapping supports causal performance analysis.

---

# 2.45 Leading-Lagging Relationship Model

The Canon supports explicit relationships between leading and lagging indicators.

Example:

```text id="leading-lagging-example"
Production Backlog
Leading Indicator

↓

Dispatch Delay
Lagging Operational Outcome

↓

Customer Complaint Rate
Lagging Customer Outcome
```

This helps management intervene earlier.

---

# 2.46 KPI Ownership Matrix

Each critical KPI requires:

| Governance Dimension | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Business Owner | Mandatory |
| Definition | Mandatory |
| Formula | Mandatory |
| Source | Mandatory |
| Target | Where applicable |
| Frequency | Mandatory |
| Certification | Critical KPIs |
| Review Cycle | Mandatory |
| Audit History | Mandatory |

---

# 2.47 Cross-Domain KPI Architecture

Some KPIs are inherently cross-domain.

Example:

## Perfect Order Rate

May depend on:

- Orders.
- Production.
- Quality.
- Shipping.
- Customer outcome.

The KPI must have one clear enterprise owner while preserving source-domain authority.

---

# 2.48 Shared Metric Governance

Different domains may use the same metric.

Example:

**Revenue**

may appear in:

- Finance.
- Sales.
- Executive reporting.
- Marketing analysis.

There must not be four conflicting definitions of revenue.

Finance remains authoritative for financial meaning.

Other domains consume the certified measure.

---

# 2.49 KPI Granularity

A KPI may be measured at different granularities:

- Enterprise.
- Department.
- Location.
- Channel.
- Product family.
- Product.
- Team.
- Process.

Granularity must be appropriate to the business question.

---

# 2.50 Measurement Snapshot Model

Where historical reproducibility matters, measurement may preserve a snapshot or reproducible reference to source state.

This supports answering:

> Why did the dashboard show this value at that time?

Without historical reproducibility, past management decisions become difficult to audit.

---

# 2.51 Real-Time vs Periodic Measures

Metrics may be:

## Real-Time / Near Real-Time

Examples:

- Current production backlog.
- Open orders.
- Active incidents.

## Periodic

Examples:

- Monthly revenue.
- Quarterly margin.
- Annual customer retention.

The required freshness must be defined per metric.

---

# 2.52 Performance Materiality

Not every variance requires management intervention.

Materiality may depend on:

- Absolute size.
- Percentage deviation.
- Business impact.
- Duration.
- Strategic importance.

A small percentage deviation in a highly critical KPI may matter more than a large deviation in a low-value metric.

---

# 2.53 Performance Severity

Performance Issues may be categorized:

- Informational.
- Watch.
- At Risk.
- Critical.

Severity is determined by business rules, not merely chart appearance.

---

# 2.54 Data Quality Relationship

Each KPI should be able to expose source Data Trust context.

Example:

```text id="kpi-data-trust"
KPI:
Inventory Accuracy

Performance Value:
94%

Source Information Trust:
UNDER REVIEW
```

Management should know when a performance value is based on uncertain underlying information.

---

# 2.55 KPI Confidence State

A KPI may have states such as:

- Certified.
- Certified With Data Condition.
- Preliminary.
- Under Review.
- Invalid.

This prevents uncertain values from appearing identical to fully certified measures.

---

# 2.56 Forecast Confidence

Forecasts may include:

- Confidence range.
- Model reliability.
- Input quality.
- Assumptions.

Forecast uncertainty must remain visible.

---

# 2.57 Scenario Assumption Entity Relationship

Scenarios must preserve their assumptions.

Example:

```text id="scenario-assumptions"
Scenario:
Diwali Demand Surge

Assumptions:
+35% orders
Same production capacity
Current supplier lead times

↓

Projected Outcome:
Production backlog risk
```

If assumptions change, the scenario result must be recalculated.

---

# 2.58 GiftHatke Core KPI Architecture

For GiftHatke, a canonical enterprise performance structure may include:

## Growth

- Order growth.
- Revenue growth.
- Repeat customer growth.

## Commercial

- Conversion rate.
- Average order value.
- Channel revenue.
- Discount rate.

## Customer

- Response time.
- Complaint rate.
- Repeat purchase rate.

## Personalization

- Personalization completeness.
- Approval turnaround time.
- Personalization-related rework.

## Production

- Jobs completed.
- Throughput.
- Cycle time.
- Rework.

## Quality

- First-pass quality.
- QC rejection.
- Defect rate.

## Inventory

- Material availability.
- Inventory accuracy.
- Shortage frequency.

## Fulfillment

- On-time dispatch.
- Order-to-dispatch time.

## Finance

- Revenue.
- Gross margin.
- Contribution profitability.

---

# 2.59 GiftHatke Personalized Order Performance Model

A personalized order may contribute to several measures.

```text id="gift-order-performance"
Customer Order

↓

Personalization Complete?

↓

Production Started

↓

Production Completed

↓

QC Passed

↓

Dispatched

↓

Delivered

↓

Customer Outcome
```

Potential KPIs arise at each stage.

This allows performance analysis across the complete value chain.

---

# 2.60 GiftHatke On-Time Dispatch KPI Example

Canonical definition example:

```text id="gift-otd-kpi"
KPI:
On-Time Dispatch Rate

Owner:
Operations

Numerator:
Eligible Orders Dispatched On or Before Committed Dispatch Date

Denominator:
All Eligible Orders Due for Dispatch

Sources:
Order Management
Shipping & Fulfillment

Dimensions:
Product
Channel
Order Type
Time

Review:
Daily / Weekly / Monthly
```

The exact operational target may evolve.

The governance structure remains permanent.

---

# 2.61 GiftHatke Personalization Readiness KPI

Example:

```text id="personalization-readiness-kpi"
KPI:
Production-Ready Personalization Rate

Purpose:
Measure percentage of production-due orders with complete approved personalization information before production start.
```

This KPI can reveal customer-intake and order-quality weaknesses before they create manufacturing rework.

---

# 2.62 GiftHatke Rework KPI

Rework may be categorized by cause:

- Personalization error.
- Production error.
- Material defect.
- Machine issue.
- Customer change.
- Quality failure.

This enables the enterprise to distinguish:

```text id="rework-analysis"
Rework Count

from

Why Rework Happened
```

Cause classification is essential for meaningful improvement.

---

# 2.63 GiftHatke Executive Performance Architecture

A future executive scorecard may connect:

```text id="gift-executive-map"
Revenue Growth

Customer Conversion

Average Order Value

Order Backlog

Production Throughput

First-Pass Quality

On-Time Dispatch

Inventory Availability

Gross Margin

Customer Experience
```

The goal is a concise view of enterprise health.

---

# 2.64 GiftHatke Channel Dimension

Performance may be segmented across channels such as:

- Shopify.
- Amazon.
- Flipkart.
- Meesho.
- Offline sales.
- Corporate/B2B.
- Other future channels.

Channel dimensions must use governed master/reference data rather than inconsistent free-text labels.

---

# 2.65 GiftHatke Product Performance Dimension

Performance analysis may drill down through:

```text id="gift-product-performance"
Product Category

↓

Product Family

↓

Product

↓

Variant

↓

SKU
```

This enables profitability, demand, quality, and operational analysis by product structure.

---

# 2.66 GiftHatke Customer Dimension

Customer performance may analyze:

- New vs returning.
- Consumer vs corporate.
- Channel origin.
- Location.
- Customer segment.

Sensitive profiling must remain governed by privacy and ethical boundaries.

---

# 2.67 Auditability Architecture

A critical performance value must be reconstructable through:

```text id="performance-auditability"
Dashboard Value

↓

Measurement Record

↓

KPI Version

↓

Formula

↓

Source Mapping

↓

Source Data

↓

Authoritative Domain
```

This is the permanent foundation of trusted executive analytics.

---

# 2.68 KPI Versioning

Material KPI definition changes create a new version.

Examples:

- Formula changed.
- Exclusion rule changed.
- Source changed.
- Measurement frequency changed.

Historical periods should retain the KPI definition applicable at that time.

---

# 2.69 Target Versioning

Targets may change due to:

- New business strategy.
- Capacity expansion.
- Seasonality.
- New operating model.

Historical target comparisons remain preserved.

---

# 2.70 Metric Retirement

Metrics may be retired when:

- No longer useful.
- Superseded.
- Business process removed.
- Better measure replaces them.

Retirement should preserve:

- Definition.
- Historical values.
- Reason.
- Replacement where applicable.

---

# 2.71 KPI Retirement

A KPI may be retired when it no longer represents a material business objective.

Retirement must not delete historical performance.

---

# 2.72 Performance Governance Boundary With Human Capital

Employee and team information may contribute to performance analysis.

However, individual workforce evaluation remains governed by the Human Capital Domain.

This Domain must not become an uncontrolled employee surveillance mechanism.

Operational performance should prioritize:

- Process capability.
- Workload.
- Capacity.
- Business outcome.

---

# 2.73 Performance Governance Boundary With Finance

Financial KPIs must preserve Finance as the authoritative owner of:

- Revenue definition.
- Expense definition.
- Margin definition.
- Profit definition.
- Accounting treatment.

Analytics may calculate and present certified financial measures.

It cannot redefine accounting meaning.

---

# 2.74 Performance Governance Boundary With AI

AI may create:

- Forecasts.
- Insights.
- Recommendations.
- Anomaly alerts.

These must be represented separately from certified actual performance.

Canonical distinction:

```text id="performance-ai-states"
Actual
Verified Business Fact

Forecast
Expected Future Result

Insight
Analytical Interpretation

Recommendation
Suggested Action
```

These information types must never be confused.

---

# 2.75 SMP1 Entity Preservation Requirement

During SMP1, the new standalone runtime must be able to preserve or reconstruct certified existing reporting measures.

The migration must maintain:

- Source identifiers.
- Business timestamps.
- Relationships.
- Financial values.
- Production statuses.
- Order states.

Without these, historical performance continuity would be damaged.

---

# 2.76 Standalone v1.0 Measurement Foundation

Standalone v1.0 should provide a durable foundation for:

- KPI calculations.
- Historical measurements.
- Event-based metrics.
- Analytical dimensions.
- Auditability.
- Future forecasting.

The architecture should enable performance capability without forcing business workflow redesign.

---

# 2.77 ERP9 Measurement Integration

ERP9 additions must declare where relevant:

- New metrics.
- Potential KPIs.
- Analytical dimensions.
- Performance events.

This ensures Settings and Master Data expansion remains measurable.

---

# 2.78 ERP10 Performance Certification

ERP10 final business certification should validate:

- Critical KPI definitions.
- Data sources.
- Scorecards.
- Performance visibility.
- Historical consistency.
- Executive usability.

---

# 2.79 Permanent Performance Entity Standards

The Domain permanently follows:

- Objective before KPI.
- Meaning before formula.
- Owner before publication.
- Source before measurement.
- Target before variance.
- Context before comparison.
- Version before historical analysis.
- Cause before corrective action.
- Data Trust before judgment.
- Evidence before executive certification.

---

# ENTERPRISE ANALYTICS, REPORTING INTELLIGENCE & PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT CANON
## Stage 3 — Performance Lifecycle, Review Cadence & Enterprise Management Operating Model Canon

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Domain** requires a permanent operating model defining how enterprise performance is:

- Planned.
- Measured.
- Reviewed.
- Interpreted.
- Escalated.
- Improved.
- Re-certified.

Stages 1–2 established:

- Domain scope.
- Performance philosophy.
- KPI governance.
- Performance entities.
- Measurement architecture.
- Target and scorecard structures.

Stage 3 now defines how those entities operate together as a continuous enterprise management system.

The objective is to ensure that performance management becomes:

- Continuous.
- Accountable.
- Evidence-based.
- Cross-domain.
- Action-oriented.
- Improvement-driven.

Performance measurement must not end at dashboard visibility.

It must connect:

```text id="performance-operating-model"
Objective

↓

Measurement

↓

Review

↓

Interpretation

↓

Decision

↓

Action

↓

Improvement

↓

Re-Measurement
```

---

# 3.2 Performance Management Lifecycle

The certified enterprise performance lifecycle is:

```text id="enterprise-performance-lifecycle"
Business Objective Defined

↓

Performance Objective Established

↓

KPI Defined

↓

Target Approved

↓

Measurement Activated

↓

Performance Observed

↓

Variance Evaluated

↓

Review Conducted

↓

Action Decided

↓

Improvement Executed

↓

Outcome Re-Measured

↓

Performance Model Reviewed
```

Every strategic or material operational KPI should exist within this lifecycle.

---

# 3.3 Objective Formation Lifecycle

Performance management begins with business purpose.

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="objective-formation"
Enterprise Need

↓

Business Objective

↓

Responsible Owner

↓

Expected Outcome

↓

Performance Objective

↓

Measurement Requirement
```

The organization should not create KPIs simply because data is available.

Measurement must follow business intent.

---

# 3.4 KPI Introduction Lifecycle

New KPIs follow:

```text id="kpi-introduction"
Measurement Need Identified

↓

KPI Proposed

↓

Business Definition Created

↓

Owner Assigned

↓

Formula Defined

↓

Source Mapping Verified

↓

Target Defined

↓

Validation

↓

Certification

↓

Operational Use
```

No critical KPI should become authoritative through informal dashboard creation alone.

---

# 3.5 KPI Activation Requirements

Before activation, a critical KPI should have:

- Business purpose.
- Owner.
- Definition.
- Formula.
- Source.
- Measurement frequency.
- Target where applicable.
- Thresholds.
- Certification status.

If source information is not trusted, the KPI must clearly indicate that condition.

---

# 3.6 Measurement Lifecycle

The certified measurement lifecycle is:

```text id="measurement-lifecycle"
Measurement Due

↓

Source Information Retrieved

↓

Data Trust Evaluated

↓

Calculation Executed

↓

Validation Applied

↓

Measurement Recorded

↓

Performance State Determined

↓

Published to Authorized Consumers
```

The measurement process itself must remain traceable.

---

# 3.7 Measurement Frequency Governance

Measures may operate at different frequencies.

Examples:

## Real-Time / Near Real-Time

Used for:

- Production backlog.
- Active orders.
- Current incidents.
- Immediate operational capacity.

## Daily

Used for:

- Orders received.
- Orders dispatched.
- Production throughput.
- Customer response backlog.

## Weekly

Used for:

- Operations performance.
- Production trends.
- Sales pipeline.
- Inventory risk.

## Monthly

Used for:

- Revenue.
- Margin.
- Customer performance.
- Management scorecards.

## Quarterly / Annual

Used for:

- Strategic progress.
- Enterprise objectives.
- Capability maturity.

Frequency must reflect decision need.

More frequent measurement is not automatically better.

---

# 3.8 Performance Observation

Performance observation answers:

> What actually happened?

Observed performance must remain separate from interpretation.

Example:

```text id="observation-vs-interpretation"
FACT:
On-Time Dispatch = 84%

INTERPRETATION:
Performance below target due to production backlog
```

The second statement requires evidence.

---

# 3.9 Target Comparison Lifecycle

Actual performance is evaluated against:

- Approved target.
- Threshold.
- Forecast.
- Previous period.
- Benchmark.

Canonical comparison:

```text id="target-comparison"
Actual Performance

↓

Comparison Basis

↓

Variance

↓

Materiality

↓

Performance Status
```

---

# 3.10 Performance Status Model

Performance may be classified as:

- On Track.
- Watch.
- At Risk.
- Critical.
- Not Assessable.

**Not Assessable** should be used when:

- Data quality is insufficient.
- Source systems are incomplete.
- KPI calculation failed.

A missing or unreliable value must not automatically be interpreted as poor performance.

---

# 3.11 Variance Management Lifecycle

The permanent variance lifecycle is:

```text id="variance-management"
Variance Identified

↓

Materiality Evaluated

↓

Owner Notified

↓

Context Reviewed

↓

Cause Investigated

↓

Response Determined

↓

Action Assigned

↓

Outcome Monitored
```

---

# 3.12 Materiality Assessment

Variance significance may depend on:

- Magnitude.
- Duration.
- Customer impact.
- Financial impact.
- Operational impact.
- Strategic importance.
- Risk.

A single threshold alone may not define business materiality.

---

# 3.13 Root-Cause Analysis Operating Model

Material deviations require structured investigation.

Canonical process:

```text id="root-cause-operating-model"
Performance Deviation

↓

Evidence Collection

↓

Contributing Factors

↓

Hypothesis

↓

Validation

↓

Root Cause

↓

Corrective Action
```

Possible cause categories include:

- Customer input.
- Process.
- Workforce capability.
- Material.
- Supplier.
- Equipment.
- Data quality.
- Technology.
- Capacity.
- External dependency.

---

# 3.14 Cause vs Symptom Governance

Performance management must distinguish cause from symptom.

Example:

```text id="cause-symptom"
SYMPTOM:
Late Dispatch

Possible Causes:
Production delay
Missing personalization
Material shortage
QC rework
Logistics issue
```

Treating symptoms as causes weakens improvement quality.

---

# 3.15 Performance Review Operating Model

Performance Reviews convert measurement into management action.

Every structured review should consider:

- Current performance.
- Targets.
- Variances.
- Trends.
- Risks.
- Root causes.
- Open actions.
- Forecast.
- Decisions.

---

# 3.16 Daily Operational Review

Purpose:

Manage immediate execution.

Typical scope:

- Open orders.
- Production backlog.
- Delays.
- Material shortages.
- Customer blockers.
- Shipping exceptions.

Output:

- Immediate priorities.
- Owners.
- Escalations.

---

# 3.17 Weekly Performance Review

Purpose:

Identify emerging patterns.

May review:

- Sales.
- Orders.
- Production.
- Quality.
- Inventory.
- Fulfillment.
- Customer issues.

Output:

- Improvement actions.
- Cross-domain coordination.
- Risk escalation.

---

# 3.18 Monthly Business Review

Purpose:

Assess broader business performance.

Typical areas:

- Revenue.
- Margin.
- Growth.
- Customer performance.
- Operational efficiency.
- Production.
- Inventory.
- Workforce capacity.
- Strategic risks.

Output:

- Management decisions.
- Target review.
- Resource decisions.
- Improvement priorities.

---

# 3.19 Quarterly Strategic Review

Purpose:

Evaluate progress against strategic objectives.

May include:

- Strategic KPIs.
- Growth.
- Profitability.
- Capability maturity.
- Investments.
- Major risks.
- Strategic initiatives.

Output:

- Strategic adjustment.
- Resource allocation.
- Initiative changes.
- Future priorities.

---

# 3.20 Annual Performance Review

Purpose:

Evaluate enterprise performance across the full operating year.

May include:

- Strategic achievement.
- Financial results.
- Customer growth.
- Operational maturity.
- Capability development.
- Risk performance.

Annual review provides input into future strategic planning.

---

# 3.21 Review Cadence Governance

The Canon defines the existence of appropriate review cadences.

It does not require every KPI to be discussed every day.

The rule is:

```text id="review-cadence"
Performance Criticality

+

Decision Frequency

+

Business Impact

=

Review Cadence
```

---

# 3.22 Performance Review Authority

Different review levels have different authority.

## Operational Manager

May:

- Reprioritize immediate work.
- Assign corrective tasks.
- Escalate constraints.

## Domain Owner

May:

- Approve domain-level improvements.
- Review KPI interpretation.
- Manage operational targets within authority.

## Executive Leadership

May:

- Adjust strategic targets.
- Allocate resources.
- Approve major changes.

Authority remains explicit.

---

# 3.23 Performance Action Lifecycle

The certified action lifecycle is:

```text id="performance-action-lifecycle"
Issue / Opportunity

↓

Action Proposed

↓

Owner Assigned

↓

Expected Outcome Defined

↓

Action Approved

↓

Execution

↓

Progress Monitored

↓

Outcome Measured

↓

Closed / Escalated
```

Actions must link back to the performance issue they address.

---

# 3.24 Performance Action Requirements

A meaningful action should define:

- Action.
- Owner.
- Priority.
- Due state.
- Related KPI.
- Expected impact.
- Status.
- Completion evidence.

Actions without ownership are not management controls.

---

# 3.25 Corrective vs Preventive Action

The Domain distinguishes:

## Corrective Action

Addresses an existing performance problem.

Example:

Resolve current material shortage.

## Preventive Action

Reduces likelihood of future problems.

Example:

Introduce reorder-point controls.

Mature performance management emphasizes prevention.

---

# 3.26 Performance Escalation

Performance issues escalate based on:

- Severity.
- Duration.
- Cross-domain impact.
- Customer impact.
- Financial exposure.
- Strategic importance.

Canonical escalation:

```text id="performance-escalation"
Operational Owner

↓

Domain Manager

↓

Cross-Domain Management

↓

Executive Leadership
```

---

# 3.27 Cross-Domain Performance Coordination

Many enterprise outcomes require multiple domains.

Example:

```text id="cross-domain-performance"
On-Time Delivery

depends on

Order Accuracy
+
Personalization Readiness
+
Material Availability
+
Production
+
Quality
+
Shipping
```

No single domain should be blamed automatically for a cross-domain outcome.

Performance management must identify contributing dependencies.

---

# 3.28 Performance Dependency Management

Each material KPI may identify upstream dependencies.

Example:

```text id="performance-dependency"
Gross Margin

depends on

Revenue
+
Product Cost
+
Production Cost
+
Discounting
+
Shipping Cost
```

Dependency visibility improves root-cause analysis.

---

# 3.29 Performance Risk Operating Model

Performance risks follow:

```text id="performance-risk"
Risk Identified

↓

Affected Objective / KPI

↓

Likelihood Assessed

↓

Impact Assessed

↓

Owner Assigned

↓

Mitigation

↓

Monitoring

↓

Closed / Accepted
```

Performance Risk management supports proactive management.

---

# 3.30 Forecast Operating Model

Forecasting follows:

```text id="forecast-operating-model"
Historical Information

+

Current Conditions

+

Assumptions

↓

Forecast Model

↓

Expected Performance

↓

Management Review

↓

Updated Forecast
```

Forecasts should be refreshed when significant assumptions change.

---

# 3.31 Rolling Forecasts

Future performance systems may use rolling forecasts.

Examples:

- Next 4 weeks.
- Next 3 months.
- Next 12 months.

Rolling forecasts allow management to continually update expectations rather than relying solely on static annual plans.

---

# 3.32 Scenario Management

Scenario analysis follows:

```text id="scenario-operating-model"
Business Question

↓

Assumptions

↓

Scenario Created

↓

Performance Modeled

↓

Risk / Opportunity Analyzed

↓

Decision
```

Examples:

- Festival demand surge.
- New marketplace launch.
- Equipment failure.
- Supplier disruption.
- Capacity expansion.

---

# 3.33 Scenario Governance

Scenarios must clearly display:

- Assumptions.
- Data sources.
- Model version.
- Forecast period.
- Uncertainty.

A scenario must never be displayed as actual performance.

---

# 3.34 Benchmarking Operating Model

Benchmarking follows:

```text id="benchmark-operating-model"
Performance Measure

↓

Valid Comparison Identified

↓

Context Normalized

↓

Difference Evaluated

↓

Learning Opportunity
```

Comparisons must be contextually meaningful.

---

# 3.35 Target Review Lifecycle

Targets may require revision when:

- Strategy changes.
- Capacity changes.
- Business conditions change.
- Historical target is unrealistic.
- Process improvement raises expectations.

Lifecycle:

```text id="target-review"
Existing Target

↓

Performance History

↓

Business Context

↓

Review

↓

Retain / Revise

↓

New Version
```

Target changes must not rewrite historical performance interpretation.

---

# 3.36 KPI Review Lifecycle

KPIs require periodic review to determine:

- Is the measure still meaningful?
- Does the formula remain valid?
- Are sources authoritative?
- Does the KPI still influence decisions?
- Should it be revised or retired?

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="kpi-review"
Active KPI

↓

Review

↓

Retain
or
Revise
or
Retire
```

---

# 3.37 Metric Rationalization

The enterprise should periodically identify:

- Duplicate metrics.
- Unused metrics.
- Conflicting metrics.
- Vanity metrics.
- Obsolete measures.

The goal is not maximum metric count.

The goal is useful measurement.

---

# 3.38 Performance Governance Against Vanity Metrics

A metric becomes questionable when it:

- Has no owner.
- Has no decision consequence.
- Has no clear interpretation.
- Exists only because it looks impressive.

The Canon explicitly rejects dashboard quantity as a measure of analytics maturity.

---

# 3.39 Performance Data Quality Control

Before performance review, the platform should evaluate:

- Source completeness.
- Data Trust.
- Calculation success.
- Refresh status.
- Known data issues.

Example:

```text id="performance-data-quality"
KPI:
Production Throughput

Value:
127 jobs

Data Trust:
Trusted

Refresh:
Current

Calculation:
Certified
```

---

# 3.40 Preliminary Performance

Some measures may temporarily be preliminary.

Examples:

- Month-end finance before close.
- Incomplete shipping updates.
- Pending reconciliations.

Preliminary information must be visibly identified.

---

# 3.41 Performance Certification States

Measurement may have states:

- Preliminary.
- Validated.
- Certified.
- Certified With Conditions.
- Invalidated.

This prevents management from treating incomplete data as final fact.

---

# 3.42 Performance Correction

If a historical measurement is found incorrect:

```text id="performance-correction"
Incorrect Measurement Identified

↓

Cause Verified

↓

Correct Value Calculated

↓

Correction Approved

↓

Measurement Updated / Superseded

↓

Audit History Preserved
```

Silent historical rewriting is prohibited for critical measurements.

---

# 3.43 Performance Restatement

Material financial or executive measures may require formal restatement.

Restatement should record:

- Original value.
- Corrected value.
- Reason.
- Affected periods.
- Approver.
- Timestamp.

---

# 3.44 Operational Performance vs Individual Performance

This Domain primarily measures enterprise and process performance.

Individual employee performance remains governed by the Human Capital Domain.

Examples of appropriate operational analysis:

- Team capacity.
- Queue backlog.
- Process cycle time.
- Coverage gaps.

Individual surveillance must not become a hidden default.

---

# 3.45 Performance Improvement Lifecycle

Continuous improvement follows:

```text id="performance-improvement"
Performance Gap

↓

Root Cause

↓

Improvement Opportunity

↓

Change Implemented

↓

Performance Re-Measured

↓

Effect Verified

↓

Successful Practice Standardized
```

---

# 3.46 Improvement Effectiveness

An improvement action is not complete merely because the task was executed.

It must answer:

> Did performance actually improve?

The platform should compare:

- Baseline.
- Post-change performance.
- Expected outcome.
- Actual outcome.

---

# 3.47 Lessons Learned

Performance reviews should preserve useful lessons such as:

- Causes of recurring delay.
- Successful operational changes.
- Failed interventions.
- Seasonal patterns.
- Supplier impacts.

These lessons integrate with enterprise knowledge systems.

---

# 3.48 Performance Knowledge Preservation

The enterprise should preserve:

- Why a KPI was created.
- Why targets changed.
- Why performance deteriorated.
- Which action fixed the problem.
- Which assumptions were wrong.
- Which operating practices worked.

This converts performance history into organizational memory.

---

```text id="gift-production-delay"

Root Cause

↓

Action
```

This prevents treating all production delays as identical.

---

# 3.54 GiftHatke Rework Review

Rework must be analyzed by cause.

Potential categories:

- Incorrect customer input.
- Incorrect data capture.
- Design error.
- Production error.
- Equipment issue.
- Material defect.
- Quality rejection.
- Customer-requested change.

This provides actionable improvement intelligence.

---

# 3.55 GiftHatke Inventory Shortage Review

When shortages affect production:

```text id="gift-inventory-shortage"
Material Shortage

↓

Affected Jobs Identified

↓

Supplier / Procurement Status

↓

Root Cause

↓

Immediate Recovery

↓

Reorder / Planning Improvement
```

# 3.56 GiftHatke Customer Performance Review

Customer Experience review may evaluate:

- Response time.
- Open complaints.
- Resolution time.
- Repeat customers.
- Personalization blockers.
- Order cancellation reasons.

---

# 3.57 GiftHatke Financial Performance Review

Financial review may include:

- Revenue.
- Gross margin.
- Product profitability.
- Channel profitability.
- Cost trends.

Finance retains authoritative financial meaning.

---

# 3.58 GiftHatke Product Performance Review

Product performance may analyze:

- Sales.
- Revenue.
- Margin.
- Rework.

- Material requirements.

- Improve product.
- Reprice.
- Promote.
- Reduce complexity.
- Retire.

# 3.59 Performance Alerts

Performance events may generate alerts when:

- Threshold crossed.
- Critical KPI deteriorates.
- Forecast predicts target miss.
- Data becomes untrusted.
- Performance action becomes overdue.

Alerts should be actionable.

---

# 3.60 Alert Fatigue Governance

The enterprise must avoid excessive low-value alerts.

Alerts should be based on:

- Materiality.
- Role.
- Severity.
- Required action.

A system producing constant alarms becomes less effective.

---

# 3.61 Performance Workflow Coordination

Performance actions may integrate with the certified Workflow Domain.

Example:

```text id="performance-workflow"
Critical KPI Variance

↓

Performance Issue

↓

Investigation Workflow

↓

Action Assignment

↓

Completion

↓

Re-Measurement
```

Performance Management owns the performance context.

Workflow owns process execution capability.

---

# 3.62 Performance Event Coordination

Important events may include:

- KPI Threshold Breached.
- Performance Review Completed.
- Performance Action Created.
- Target Revised.
- Forecast Updated.
- KPI Certified.

These events will be formally expanded in Stage 6.

---

# 3.63 AI-Assisted Performance Review

AI may assist reviews by:

- Summarizing changes.
- Identifying unusual trends.
- Suggesting possible causes.
- Comparing periods.
- Forecasting risks.
- Drafting review summaries.

AI output must distinguish:

- Fact.
- Inference.
- Forecast.
- Recommendation.

---

# 3.64 AI Root-Cause Boundary

AI may propose likely causes.

It must not present correlation as confirmed causation without evidence.

Human review remains required for material root-cause conclusions.

---

# 3.65 Automated Performance Actions

Future systems may automate low-risk responses.

Examples:

- Generate review task.
- Notify KPI owner.
- Refresh forecast.
- Open investigation workflow.

High-impact actions such as:

- Major resource reallocation.
- Pricing changes.
- Employee consequences.
- Financial commitments.

require appropriate authority.

---

# 3.66 Performance Operating Model Observability

The enterprise should monitor:

- Measurement failures.
- Stale KPIs.
- Missed reviews.
- Unowned actions.
- Overdue actions.
- Calculation errors.
- Data Trust degradation.
- Repeated unresolved variances.

The performance system itself must remain operationally healthy.

---

SMP1 must preserve the historical context required for performance continuity.

This includes:

- Business timestamps.
- Entity relationships.
- Status history.
- Financial values.
- Production history.
- Order history.
- Customer relationships.

```text id="smp1-performance-continuity"

Standalone Migration
```

# 3.68 SMP1 Reporting Equivalence

Existing certified operational reports should remain functionally equivalent through migration before advanced redesign.

SMP1 should prioritize:

- Correctness.
- Continuity.
- Reconciliation.
- Business usability.

# 3.69 Standalone v1.0 Operating Foundation

Standalone v1.0 should support future performance management through:

- Reliable event timestamps.
- Historical state.
- Stable IDs.
- Governed metrics.
- Performance actions.
- Audit history.

This foundation enables richer analytics later.

- Executive visibility.

- Data Trust.

# 3.72 Permanent Operating Principles

The Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Domain permanently follows:

- Objective before measurement.
- Measurement before judgment.
- Data Trust before interpretation.
- Variance before reaction.
- Cause before correction.
- Ownership before action.

# ENTERPRISE ANALYTICS, REPORTING INTELLIGENCE & PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT CANON
## Stage 4 — Performance Services, KPI Execution & Enterprise Analytics Service Architecture Canon

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Domain** requires a permanent service architecture that converts certified KPI definitions, measurement rules, targets, analytical dimensions, review cadences, and performance governance into executable enterprise capability.

Stages 1–3 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Performance entity architecture.
- KPI structure.
- Measurement lifecycle.
- Review operating model.
- Performance actions and improvement cycles.

Stage 4 defines the services responsible for:

- KPI execution.
- Metric calculation.
- Target management.
- Variance detection.
- Scorecard generation.
- Performance review support.
- Forecasting.
- Performance risk detection.
- Insight generation.
- Improvement tracking.
- Performance certification.
- Executive intelligence.

The objective is to ensure enterprise performance management operates as a governed system rather than a collection of disconnected reports and spreadsheets.

---

# 4.2 Performance Service Philosophy

The Domain follows permanent execution principles.

---

## Definition Before Calculation

A KPI must have certified meaning before a service calculates it.

---

## Trusted Source Before Measurement

Measurement must originate from governed enterprise information.

---

## Deterministic Logic Before Interpretation

Actual performance calculation must remain reproducible.

---

## Target Before Variance

Deviation requires a governed comparison basis.

---

## Context Before Insight

Performance values require period, dimension, and business context.

---

## Evidence Before Certification

Authoritative KPI values must be traceable.

---

## Human Authority Before Management Automation

Automation may calculate, detect, and recommend.

Accountable business owners retain decision authority.

---

# 4.3 Canonical Performance Service Landscape

The permanent service architecture includes:

| Service | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Performance Objective Service | Govern measurable objectives |
| Metric Registry Service | Manage enterprise metrics |
| KPI Management Service | Govern KPI definitions |
| KPI Certification Service | Validate authoritative KPIs |
| KPI Calculation Service | Execute KPI calculations |
| Measurement Service | Record performance observations |
| Performance Period Service | Govern analytical time periods |
| Target Management Service | Govern expected performance |
| Threshold Management Service | Interpret performance states |
| Variance Analysis Service | Identify deviations |
| Performance Dimension Service | Govern analytical dimensions |
| Scorecard Service | Organize accountable KPI views |
| Dashboard Composition Service | Assemble role-based performance views |
| Performance Review Service | Govern management reviews |

# 4.4 Performance Objective Service

## Purpose

Maintains the link between strategy and measurable performance.

Capabilities:

- Create Performance Objective.
- Link to Strategic Goal.
- Assign owner.
- Define effective period.
- Link KPIs.
- Review objective status.
- Retire objective.

Canonical relationship:

```text id="objective-service-flow"
Enterprise Objective

↓

Strategic Goal

↓

Performance Objective

↓

KPIs
```

No KPI should exist entirely disconnected from business purpose when classified as strategically critical.

---

# 4.5 Metric Registry Service

## Purpose

Provides the authoritative registry of enterprise metrics.

Capabilities:

- Register metric.
- Define business meaning.
- Assign owner.
- Define unit.
- Link authoritative source.
- Define measurement frequency.
- Version metric.
- Retire metric.

The Metric Registry prevents multiple teams from unknowingly creating conflicting measures for the same concept.

## Purpose

Govern the lifecycle of enterprise KPIs.

Capabilities:

- Propose KPI.
- Define KPI.
- Assign owner.
- Link business objective.
- Define formula.
- Map sources.
- Define target and threshold requirements.
- Version KPI.
- Review KPI.
- Retire KPI.

The service preserves the canonical lifecycle:

```text id="kpi-management-service"
Proposed

↓

Defined

↓

Validated

↓

Certified

↓

Active

↓

Reviewed

↓

Revised / Retired
```

# 4.7 KPI Certification Service

## Purpose

Determines whether a KPI is fit to become an authoritative enterprise measure.

Certification verifies:

- Business definition.
- Ownership.
- Formula.
- Source mapping.
- Data Trust.
- Measurement frequency.
- Target context.
- Auditability.

Certification outcomes may include:

- Certified.
- Certified With Conditions.
- Rejected.
- Requires Remediation.

# 4.8 KPI Calculation Service

## Purpose

Executes deterministic performance calculations.

Responsibilities:

- Retrieve governed source information.
- Apply certified KPI formula.
- Apply filters.
- Apply exclusions.
- Aggregate correctly.
- Record calculation version.
- Generate measurement result.

Example:

```text id="kpi-calculation-service"
Certified KPI

↓

Authoritative Sources

↓

Formula

↓

Filters / Exclusions

↓

Calculation

↓

Measurement Record
```

The service must not silently change business logic.

# 4.9 Metric Calculation Service

Metrics may be:

- Direct measures.
- Derived measures.
- Aggregated measures.
- Ratios.
- Rates.
- Percentages.

The calculation architecture must preserve correct aggregation semantics.

Examples:

### Direct

Orders received = Count of eligible orders.

### Derived

Gross Margin = Revenue − Cost.

### Ratio

Conversion Rate = Converted Leads ÷ Eligible Leads.

## Purpose

Creates and manages actual observed performance records.

Capabilities:

- Generate measurement.
- Associate period.
- Associate dimensions.
- Record actual value.
- Record source lineage.
- Record calculation version.
- Assign confidence/certification state.
- Correct or supersede measurement.

Measurements become enterprise historical evidence.

Before publication, measurements may be validated for:

- Source availability.
- Data Trust.
- Calculation completeness.
- Required dimensions.
- Valid period.
- Formula version.
- Duplicate execution.

Invalid measurements must not silently appear as certified performance.

# 4.37 Commands and Queries Separation

State-changing actions are separated from read operations.

## Commands

Examples:

- CertifyKPI.
- ApproveTarget.
- CreatePerformanceAction.
- CorrectMeasurement.
- CompletePerformanceReview.

## Queries

Examples:

- GetKPI.
- GetMeasurement.
- GetScorecard.
- GetVariance.
- GetPerformanceTrend.
- GetExecutiveSummary.

This separation improves:

- Auditability.
- API clarity.
- Security.
- Testing.
- Reliability.

# 4.38 Validation Architecture

Performance services validate:

## KPI Validation

- Definition exists.
- Owner exists.
- Formula valid.
- Sources mapped.

## Data Validation

- Sources available.
- Data Trust acceptable.

## Calculation Validation

- Formula executed correctly.
- Aggregation valid.

## Period Validation

- Measurement period is valid.

## Target Validation

- Target applicable to the period.

## Governance Validation

- Required authority exists.

## Evidence Validation

- Calculation can be reconstructed.

# 4.39 Transaction Boundary — KPI Certification

Canonical transaction:

```text id="kpi-certification-transaction"
KPI Proposed

↓

Business Definition Verified

↓

Owner Verified

↓

Formula Validated

↓

Source Mapping Verified

↓

Data Trust Evaluated

↓

Certification Decision

↓

Audit Record
```

Partial certification must not leave the KPI appearing authoritative.

---

# 4.40 Transaction Boundary — Measurement Publication

```text id="measurement-publication"
Source Data Retrieved

↓

Trust Check

↓

Calculation

↓

Validation

↓

Measurement Stored

↓

Status Assigned

↓

Authorized Publication
```

Publication must occur only after required validation.

---

# 4.41 Idempotency

Repeated calculations or service calls must not unintentionally create:

- Duplicate measurements.
- Duplicate performance issues.
- Duplicate actions.
- Duplicate reviews.
- Duplicate certifications.

Measurement identity may include:

- KPI.
- Period.
- Dimension set.
- Calculation version.

---

# 4.42 Concurrency Governance

Multiple systems or users may simultaneously:

- Recalculate KPI.
- Change target.
- Complete review.
- Correct source data.
- Publish dashboard.

Concurrency controls must preserve:

- KPI version.
- Measurement integrity.
- Target applicability.
- Audit history.

A KPI must never be calculated partly under two conflicting formula versions.

---

# 4.43 Late-Arriving Data

Some enterprise information may arrive after initial measurement.

Examples:

- Shipping confirmation.
- Marketplace settlement.
- Financial adjustment.
- Customer outcome.

The service architecture must support:

```text id="late-arriving-data"
Initial Measurement

↓

Late Data Arrives

↓

Materiality Evaluated

↓

Measurement Recalculated if Required

↓

New Version / Restatement

↓

Audit Preserved
```

---

# 4.44 Missing Data Handling

Missing source information may result in:

- Not Assessable.
- Preliminary.
- Certified With Conditions.

The system must not automatically interpret missing data as zero unless the KPI definition explicitly requires it.

---

# 4.45 Performance Failure Classification

Failures include:

## Source Failure

Required business data unavailable.

## Data Trust Failure

Underlying information is unreliable.

## Calculation Failure

Formula cannot execute.

## Mapping Failure

Required source relationship missing.

## Target Failure

No valid comparison basis.

## Forecast Failure

Prediction cannot be generated reliably.

## Publication Failure

Measurement exists but cannot be delivered.

## Platform Failure

Underlying analytics service unavailable.

Failures must remain observable.

---

# 4.46 Retry Architecture

Safe retries may apply to:

- KPI calculation.
- Dashboard generation.
- Forecast generation.
- Notification.
- Measurement publication.

Retries must remain idempotent.

They must not create duplicate performance state.

---

# 4.47 Performance Caching

Future standalone architecture may cache performance results for faster access.

Caching must preserve:

- Calculation version.
- Measurement period.
- Data freshness.
- Invalidation rules.

A stale cache must not appear indistinguishable from current certified performance.

---

# 4.48 Performance Freshness

Every material performance result should have understandable freshness.

Possible states:

- Real-Time.
- Current.
- Delayed.
- Stale.
- Unknown.

Freshness requirements vary by KPI.

Monthly profitability need not operate at second-level latency.

Production backlog may require much faster updates.

---

# 4.49 Performance Access Governance

Not every performance value is appropriate for every user.

Access depends on:

- Role.
- Business responsibility.
- Data classification.
- Source information sensitivity.

Examples:

- Executive financial performance may be restricted.
- Employee personal-performance data may require stronger controls.
- Operational queue metrics may be broadly available internally.

Security Domain owns access enforcement.

# 4.69 SMP1 Service Preservation Requirement

- Query APIs.
- Materialized views.
- Caches.
- Event-driven metrics.
- Warehousing.
- Semantic models.

```text id="smp1-performance-services"
New Technical Analytics Architecture

≠

New Business KPI Meaning
```

# 4.70 SMP1 Historical Measurement Requirement

Migration must preserve sufficient information to reconstruct:

- Historical order performance.
- Production performance.
- Financial performance.
- Customer performance.
- Inventory performance.

If a KPI cannot be reconstructed because required historical information was discarded, the standalone migration has damaged enterprise intelligence.

- Failed KPI calculations.
- Stale measurements.
- Missing sources.
- Invalid mappings.
- Delayed refresh.
- Failed forecasts.

# 4.75 Service-Level Quality Principles

Performance services should maintain:

## Correctness

Values reflect certified rules.

## Reproducibility

Historical results can be reconstructed.

## Timeliness

Information arrives when needed.

## Consistency

Equivalent measures agree.

## Explainability

Users understand calculation and interpretation.

## Availability

Critical management information remains accessible.

# 4.76 Permanent Service Standards

The Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Domain permanently follows:

- Objective before measurement.
- Definition before calculation.
- Ownership before certification.
- Trusted source before publication.
- Correct aggregation before visualization.
- Target before variance.
- Materiality before escalation.
- Root cause before recommendation.
- Evidence before restatement.
- Human authority before autonomous management action.
