# ENTERPRISE ANALYTICS, REPORTING INTELLIGENCE & PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT CANON
## Stage 9 — Performance Migration, Historical Reconciliation, Validation, Testing & Enterprise Analytics Certification Canon

---

# 9.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Domain** requires a permanent assurance architecture proving that enterprise performance history, KPI definitions, targets, measurements, scorecards, analytical relationships, and executive intelligence remain valid whenever systems, reporting platforms, databases, or runtimes change.

Stages 1–8 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Performance entity architecture.
- Measurement lifecycle.
- KPI services.
- Performance governance.
- Event coordination.
- Executive and management experiences.
- Predictive and optimization intelligence.

Stage 9 defines the permanent framework for:

- Performance migration.
- Historical continuity.
- KPI reconciliation.
- Measurement validation.
- Scorecard verification.
- Forecast continuity.
- analytical testing.
- business acceptance.
- performance certification.

The central principle is:

> Performance history must survive platform evolution without silently changing the meaning of the business.

---

# 9.2 Performance Migration Philosophy

Enterprise analytics migration follows permanent principles.

---

## Meaning Before Dashboard Migration

Recreating a visual dashboard is insufficient if KPI meaning changes.

---

## KPI Definition Before Historical Calculation

Historical values must be interpreted using the appropriate KPI version.

---

## Source Continuity Before Performance Continuity

Required source information must survive migration.

---

## Reconciliation Before Acceptance

Old and new platform outputs must be compared.

---

## Historical Context Before Optimization

Advanced analytics must not destroy or obscure prior performance meaning.

---

## Evidence Before Certification

Performance equivalence must be proven.

---

## Business Acceptance Before Authority Transfer

Technical teams alone cannot certify enterprise performance meaning.

---

# 9.3 Migration Scope

Performance migration may include:

- KPI definitions.
- Metric definitions.
- KPI formulas.
- Source mappings.
- Measurement history.
- Targets.
- Thresholds.
- Scorecards.
- Dashboard definitions.
- Analytical dimensions.
- Performance reviews.
- Performance actions.
- Performance issues.
- Root-cause records.
- Forecasts.
- Scenarios.
- Benchmarks.
- Insights.
- Performance risks.
- Audit evidence.

---

# 9.4 Performance Migration Inventory

Before migration, the enterprise creates a governed inventory.

Each object may record:

- Performance object ID.
- Name.
- Type.
- Owner.
- Current version.
- Source system.
- Data dependencies.
- Historical range.
- Certification status.
- Target system.
- Migration method.
- Validation approach.

No critical KPI should migrate without explicit identification.

---

# 9.5 KPI Migration Mapping

Every critical KPI requires source-to-target mapping.

Mapping should preserve:

- KPI identity.
- Business definition.
- Formula.
- Owner.
- Source mappings.
- dimensions.
- targets.
- thresholds.
- historical measurements.
- certification state.

Example:

```text id="kpi-migration-map"
Apps Script KPI:
On-Time Dispatch

↓

Standalone KPI:
On-Time Dispatch

Business Meaning:
UNCHANGED

Formula:
UNCHANGED

Sources:
Mapped to Standalone Order + Shipping Data

Historical Measurements:
Preserved / Reconstructed
```

---

# 9.6 KPI Semantic Equivalence

Migration must prove that target KPI meaning is semantically equivalent.

A KPI is not equivalent merely because:

- It has the same name.
- It uses similar fields.
- Results look approximately correct.

Semantic equivalence requires:

- Same business population.
- Same inclusions.
- Same exclusions.
- Same time basis.
- Same formula.
- Same units.
- Same interpretation.

---

# 9.7 KPI Version Preservation

Historical KPI versions must survive.

Example:

```text id="kpi-version-preservation"
KPI v1
2025–2026

↓

Historical Measurements

KPI v2
2027 onward

↓

New Measurements
```

Migration must not recalculate history using a newer formula unless explicit governed restatement is approved.

---

# 9.8 Metric Migration

Metrics require validation of:

- Definition.
- Unit.
- Source.
- aggregation.
- dimensional relationships.
- historical values.

Derived metrics require preservation of formula lineage.

---

# 9.9 Measurement Migration

Historical measurements should preserve:

- KPI.
- KPI version.
- period.
- dimensions.
- actual value.
- source context.
- certification state.
- timestamp.

Where measurement history can be reliably recalculated from preserved source data, the enterprise may reconstruct it.

The reconstruction must be identifiable.

---

# 9.10 Original vs Reconstructed Measurements

The target system must distinguish where material:

- Original certified measurement.
- migrated measurement.
- reconstructed historical measurement.
- restated measurement.

This prevents reconstructed history from masquerading as original recorded evidence.

---

# 9.11 Target Migration

Targets must preserve:

- Value.
- type.
- effective period.
- owner.
- approval.
- version.

Migration must not apply current targets retroactively to historical periods.

---

# 9.12 Threshold Migration

Thresholds must retain:

- effective dates.
- interpretation.
- versions.

Example:

If a KPI was considered healthy above 90% historically and later changed to 95%, the old period must preserve the old interpretation where applicable.

---

# 9.13 Scorecard Migration

Scorecards require preservation of:

- Name.
- owner.
- audience.
- KPI membership.
- layout intent where materially relevant.
- review cadence.
- historical version.

Visual redesign is permitted.

Business composition must remain controlled.

---

# 9.14 Dashboard Migration

Dashboard migration validates:

- KPI correctness.
- filters.
- dimensions.
- time periods.
- access controls.
- freshness indicators.
- Data Trust status.

Visual equivalence is not mandatory.

Business-information equivalence is.

---

# 9.15 Analytical Dimension Migration

Dimensions may include:

- Product.
- channel.
- customer.
- supplier.
- location.
- department.
- time.

Migration must preserve dimension identity and hierarchy.

Example:

```text id="dimension-migration"
Product Family

↓

Product

↓

Variant

↓

SKU
```

Broken hierarchies can invalidate analytical comparisons.

---

# 9.16 Historical Time Continuity

Migration must preserve:

- event timestamps.
- measurement dates.
- fiscal periods.
- calendar interpretation.
- timezone context where relevant.

Incorrect time conversion can corrupt performance history.

---

# 9.17 Performance Data Baseline

Before migration, critical performance outputs should be captured as a certified baseline.

The baseline may include:

- KPI values.
- scorecards.
- historical trends.
- target values.
- key dimensional cuts.
- executive summaries.

This becomes the reference for reconciliation.

---

# 9.18 Performance Reconciliation Framework

Canonical reconciliation:

```text id="performance-reconciliation"
Certified Legacy Performance

↓

Standalone Calculation

↓

Comparison

↓

Difference Identified

↓

Cause Classified

↓

Correction / Approval

↓

Certification
```

---

# 9.19 Reconciliation Outcomes

Differences may be classified as:

- Exact Match.
- Expected Technical Difference.
- Approved Business Transformation.
- Legacy Defect Corrected.
- Migration Defect.
- Unexplained Difference.

Unexplained differences in critical KPIs block certification.

---

# 9.20 Numerical Tolerance Governance

Some calculations may exhibit minor technical differences due to:

- Rounding.
- decimal precision.
- time-boundary handling.

Tolerance must be:

- Defined.
- justified.
- documented.

Tolerance must never be used to hide meaningful performance discrepancies.

---

# 9.21 Historical Trend Reconciliation

Migration should verify not only point values but also:

- Trend direction.
- period comparisons.
- seasonality.
- rolling calculations.
- year-over-year comparisons.

A platform producing similar current KPI values but incorrect history is not fully equivalent.

---

# 9.22 Cross-Domain KPI Reconciliation

Cross-domain KPIs require source reconciliation across all contributing domains.

Example:

```text id="cross-domain-reconciliation"
On-Time Delivery

Order Data ✓

Personalization Data ✓

Production Data ✓

Quality Data ✓

Shipping Data ✓

↓

KPI Reconciliation
```

A missing dependency invalidates the final KPI.

---

# 9.23 Financial KPI Reconciliation

Financial performance receives stronger verification.

Examples:

- Revenue.
- gross margin.
- contribution margin.
- profitability.

Finance must validate authoritative financial meaning.

Differences require formal explanation.

---

# 9.24 Order Performance Reconciliation

May validate:

- Order volume.
- order cycle time.
- backlog.
- status distributions.
- fulfillment readiness.

---

# 9.25 Production Performance Reconciliation

May validate:

- Throughput.
- backlog.
- production cycle.
- rework.
- capacity-related measures.

---

# 9.26 Quality Performance Reconciliation

May validate:

- First-pass quality.
- rejection.
- defects.
- rework.

Underlying Quality Domain definitions must remain preserved.

---

# 9.27 Inventory Performance Reconciliation

May validate:

- Availability.
- stock accuracy.
- shortages.
- turnover or aging where used.

---

# 9.28 Customer Performance Reconciliation

May validate:

- complaint rate.
- response time.
- repeat purchase.
- resolution.

Customer identity continuity is essential for historical comparison.

---

# 9.29 Sales Performance Reconciliation

May validate:

- Conversion.
- AOV.
- channel revenue.
- pipeline metrics.

---

# 9.30 Personalization Performance Reconciliation

For GiftHatke, this is especially important.

Potential measures:

- Personalization completeness.
- approval turnaround.
- missing asset rate.
- personalization-related rework.

Migration must preserve the relationship between:

- Customer.
- asset.
- order.
- production.

---

# 9.31 GiftHatke End-to-End Order Reconciliation

Canonical test:

```text id="gift-e2e-performance-reconciliation"
Historical Order

↓

Customer

↓

Personalization

↓

Production

↓

QC

↓

Shipping

↓

Finance

↓

Reconstructed End-to-End Performance
```

This proves cross-domain performance continuity.

---

# 9.32 Migration Test Levels

The permanent assurance model includes:

1. KPI Definition Testing.
2. Formula Testing.
3. Source Mapping Testing.
4. Measurement Testing.
5. Dimensional Testing.
6. Historical Trend Testing.
7. Scorecard Testing.
8. Dashboard Testing.
9. Cross-Domain Integration Testing.
10. Forecast/Scenario Testing.
11. Security Testing.
12. Business Acceptance Testing.

---

# 9.33 KPI Definition Testing

Validates:

- Name.
- definition.
- inclusions.
- exclusions.
- owner.
- unit.
- period logic.

---

# 9.34 Formula Testing

Formula testing uses controlled input cases.

Example:

```text id="formula-test"
Eligible Orders:
100

On-Time Orders:
92

Expected KPI:
92%
```

The target implementation must return the expected result.

---

# 9.35 Boundary Testing

KPIs should be tested around:

- period boundaries.
- midnight.
- month end.
- year end.
- leap dates where applicable.
- timezone conversions.

Boundary errors can create subtle reporting defects.

---

# 9.36 Null & Missing Data Testing

Validates how formulas behave when:

- source data missing.
- denominator zero.
- dimension missing.
- status incomplete.

Missing data must not silently become zero unless certified formula logic requires it.

---

# 9.37 Aggregation Testing

Validates:

- Sum.
- count.
- average.
- weighted average.
- rate.
- ratio.
- percentage.

Particular attention is required for percentages and ratios.

Example:

```text id="aggregation-warning"
Average of Department Percentages

≠

Always Correct Enterprise Percentage
```

The correct weighting must be used.

---

# 9.38 Dimensional Testing

Validates filtering and drill-down by:

- product.
- channel.
- time.
- supplier.
- location.
- customer segment.

Totals should reconcile appropriately with lower-level views.

---

# 9.39 Scorecard Testing

Validates:

- Correct KPIs.
- correct target periods.
- status.
- ordering.
- permissions.
- freshness.

---

# 9.40 Dashboard Testing

Validates presentation does not alter business interpretation.

Checks include:

- Labels.
- filters.
- comparison periods.
- drill-down.
- data freshness.
- preliminary/certified state.

---

# 9.41 Review Workflow Testing

Validates:

- Review schedule.
- scorecard preparation.
- decision capture.
- action creation.
- action ownership.
- follow-up.

---

# 9.42 Performance Event Testing

Validates events such as:

- KPI Certified.
- Threshold Breached.
- Performance Action Created.
- Forecast Risk Identified.

Testing covers:

- Ordering.
- deduplication.
- retry.
- consumer synchronization.

---

# 9.43 Forecast Migration Testing

Forecast migration should distinguish whether historical forecasts are:

- Preserved as recorded.
- migrated.
- recalculated.

Original forecasts should not be rewritten based on knowledge of future actual outcomes.

---

# 9.44 Forecast Accuracy Continuity

Historical forecasts may be compared against actual outcomes after migration to ensure forecast-performance history survives.

---

# 9.45 Scenario Migration Testing

Scenarios require preservation of:

- Assumptions.
- model version.
- input context.
- output.

Without assumptions, historical scenario results lose meaning.

---

# 9.46 Predictive Model Validation

Where predictive models exist, migration validation may include:

- Model version.
- feature/input mapping.
- expected output distribution.
- confidence behavior.
- performance metrics.

Model migration must not silently alter analytical meaning.

---

# 9.47 AI Intelligence Validation

AI-assisted analytics require testing for:

- Source grounding.
- distinction between fact and inference.
- hallucination resistance.
- access controls.
- auditability.
- confidence communication.

---

# 9.48 Performance Security Testing

Validates:

- Role access.
- sensitive financial views.
- workforce analytics.
- executive scorecards.
- exports.
- API access.

The standalone platform must not broaden sensitive analytics access accidentally.

---

# 9.49 Performance Privacy Testing

Where analytics uses customer or employee information:

- Minimum necessary exposure.
- segmentation rules.
- access context.
- privacy boundaries.

must remain preserved.

---

# 9.50 Performance Testing

Performance infrastructure itself should be tested for:

- Dashboard load.
- KPI calculation time.
- drill-down.
- scorecard generation.
- large-period queries.
- historical trend retrieval.

Technical speed must not compromise correctness.

---

# 9.51 Volume Testing

Standalone analytics should be validated against realistic and future data volumes.

Areas include:

- Orders.
- customers.
- production jobs.
- events.
- measurements.
- historical periods.

---

# 9.52 Concurrent Usage Testing

Multiple users may simultaneously:

- Load dashboards.
- run reports.
- refresh KPIs.
- conduct reviews.

The system must preserve consistent measurements under concurrency.

---

# 9.53 Failure-Recovery Testing

Tests may simulate:

- Data-source unavailable.
- calculation service failure.
- event delivery failure.
- dashboard cache failure.
- partial refresh.
- forecast service failure.

Recovery must preserve integrity.

---

# 9.54 Cache Validation

If standalone architecture uses caching:

Testing verifies:

- Correct invalidation.
- freshness.
- version awareness.
- target changes.
- KPI changes.

A stale cached KPI must not appear certified as current.

---

# 9.55 Business Acceptance Testing

Business users must validate real management scenarios.

Examples:

- Review today's orders.
- identify production bottleneck.
- inspect fulfillment KPI.
- drill into delayed orders.
- conduct Monthly Business Review.
- compare revenue to target.
- identify product profitability.
- create performance action.

---

# 9.56 Executive Acceptance Testing

Leadership should validate:

- Executive scorecard clarity.
- materiality.
- cross-domain visibility.
- strategic KPI meaning.
- drill-down where required.
- trust indicators.
- decision usefulness.

---

# 9.57 Manager Acceptance Testing

Managers validate:

- Domain scorecards.
- operational KPIs.
- action tracking.
- review workflows.
- root-cause analysis.

---

# 9.58 Analyst Acceptance Testing

Analysts validate:

- Dimensions.
- calculations.
- trend behavior.
- source traceability.
- drill-down.
- reconciliation.

---

# 9.59 KPI Owner Acceptance

Every critical KPI Owner should confirm:

- Definition.
- source.
- formula.
- target context.
- historical continuity.

---

# 9.60 Certification Gates

The permanent performance certification gates are:

---

## Gate 1 — Inventory Certification

Critical performance objects identified.

---

## Gate 2 — KPI Definition Certification

Business definitions preserved.

---

## Gate 3 — Formula Certification

Calculations validated.

---

## Gate 4 — Source Mapping Certification

Authoritative information mapped.

---

## Gate 5 — Historical Reconciliation Certification

Historical values reconciled.

---

## Gate 6 — Dimension Certification

Drill-down structures verified.

---

## Gate 7 — Scorecard Certification

Role-specific scorecards validated.

---

## Gate 8 — Security Certification

Performance access controlled.

---

## Gate 9 — Operational Acceptance

Managers validate operational use.

---

## Gate 10 — Executive Acceptance

Leadership validates enterprise decision usefulness.

---

# 9.61 Performance Certification States

Migration outcome may be:

- Fully Certified.
- Certified With Controlled Exceptions.
- Not Certified.

Critical unresolved semantic or reconciliation defects block full certification.

---

# 9.62 Exception Management

Performance migration exceptions may include:

- Missing historical data.
- unavailable original formula.
- legacy KPI inconsistency.
- broken source lineage.
- unreconstructable period.
- dashboard-only metric with no formal definition.

Each exception requires:

- ID.
- description.
- impact.
- owner.
- treatment.
- approval.
- certification consequence.

---

# 9.63 Legacy KPI Cleanup

Migration may reveal legacy metrics that should not become part of the standalone authoritative architecture.

Candidates include:

- Duplicate KPIs.
- unused metrics.
- vanity metrics.
- undocumented metrics.
- unsupported calculations.

These may be retired through governance.

They must not disappear silently if historically material.

---

# 9.64 SMP1 Mandatory Performance Assurance

Stage 9 applies directly to **SMP1**.

The Apps Script ERP remains the certified reference baseline for existing business behavior.

SMP1 must prove that the standalone platform preserves:

- Existing report meaning.
- core KPI logic.
- historical information required for reporting.
- domain relationships.
- operational status interpretation.
- financial integrity.

---

```text id="smp1-performance-migration"

Performance Inventory

↓
```

# 9.66 SMP1 Evidence Lock

SMP1 must not declare analytics migration successful merely because:

- New dashboards render.
- queries execute.
- charts look similar.
- totals appear close.

Certification requires evidence of:

- Definition equivalence.
- formula equivalence.
- source lineage.
- historical continuity.
- reconciliation.
- business acceptance.

---

# 9.67 SMP1 Historical Preservation Priority

Historical information necessary for future performance intelligence should be preserved wherever available.

Examples:

- Order created dates.
- production start/completion.
- shipping dates.
- customer relationships.
- payment values.
- product history.

If a historical field never existed, the migration must document the gap rather than fabricate it.

```text id="smp1-performance-cutover"
Reference Baseline

Business Acceptance

Standalone Performance Platform
Authoritative

↓

Apps Script
Historical Certification Reference
```

Standalone v1.0 performance certification should verify:

- Critical operational reports.
- KPI correctness.
- historical continuity.
- role-based views.
- Data Trust indicators.
- executive usability where implemented.

Advanced predictive capability is not required for baseline equivalence unless explicitly included.

ERP9 should begin only after standalone certification according to the locked roadmap.

New ERP9 data and settings should integrate with the certified KPI and analytical architecture rather than creating isolated reporting logic.

- Executive scorecard completeness.

- source.
- target.

- actual result.
- difference.
- decision.

Future auditors must be able to understand why the target platform was accepted.

The Domain permanently follows:

- Meaning before migration.
- KPI version before recalculation.
- source continuity before performance continuity.
- historical context before redesign.
- reconciliation before cutover.

# ENTERPRISE ANALYTICS, REPORTING INTELLIGENCE & PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT CANON
## Stage 10 — Final Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Certification Canon

---

# 10.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Analytics, Reporting Intelligence & Performance Management Domain** is hereby consolidated into one final authoritative enterprise specification.

Stages 1–9 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Performance entity architecture.
- KPI and metric governance.
- Performance lifecycle.
- KPI execution services.
- Performance authority.
- Event coordination.
- Executive and management experiences.
- Predictive intelligence.
- Performance migration and assurance.

Stage 10 formally certifies the Domain as the permanent GiftHatkeOS architecture for enterprise measurement, management performance, executive intelligence, and performance-driven improvement.

The Domain exists to ensure that enterprise performance remains:

- Meaningful.
- Governed.
- Owned.
- Traceable.
- Comparable.
- Explainable.
- Actionable.
- Historically consistent.
- Decision-relevant.
- Auditable.

---

# 10.2 Final Canon Mission

The permanent mission of the Domain is:

> Convert trusted enterprise information into governed performance measures, meaningful management intelligence, accountable decisions, and continuous business improvement.

The Domain must enable the enterprise to answer:

- What happened?
- What is happening now?
- Why did it happen?
- What is likely to happen?
- What requires attention?
- Which actions should management consider?
- Did those actions improve the business?

---

# 10.3 Certified Permanent Principles

The Domain permanently follows:

- Objective before KPI.
- Meaning before metric.
- Definition before dashboard.
- Owner before publication.
- Trusted data before judgment.
- Target before variance.
- Context before comparison.
- Root cause before blame.
- Balanced performance before local optimization.
- Evidence before certification.
- Forecast uncertainty before certainty.
- Recommendation before action.
- Human accountability before autonomous management.

---

# 10.4 Certified Domain Boundary

The Domain permanently owns:

- Enterprise KPI governance.
- Metric architecture.
- Performance targets.
- Thresholds.
- Enterprise scorecards.
- Performance measurement.
- Variance management.
- Performance reviews.
- Executive performance management.
- Performance actions.
- Trend intelligence.
- Forecasting.
- Scenario analysis.
- Performance Risk.
- Predictive performance intelligence.
- Performance optimization.
- Executive Intelligence.
- Performance certification.

It does **not** replace source-domain ownership.

Canonical model:

```text
Operational Business Domains
        ↓
Authoritative Business Information
        ↓
Data Governance
        ↓
Performance Management
        ↓
Reporting & BI
        ↓
Management Decision
```

- material shortages.

- aggregated.
- ratios.
- rates.

- effective period.
- owner.
- approval.
- version.

Targets may be:

- Minimum.
- maximum.
- exact.
- range.
- growth rate.
- milestone.

Retrospective manipulation of targets to make poor performance appear acceptable is prohibited.

- workload.

- equipment.

- system design.

before concluding that individual behavior caused the performance outcome.


Important KPIs should therefore use balancing measures and counter-metrics where needed.

# ENTERPRISE REVENUE MANAGEMENT, PRICING & COMMERCIAL INTELLIGENCE CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation & Enterprise Commercial Economics Scope

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain** establishes the permanent enterprise architecture responsible for how the organization:

- Defines prices.
- Governs discounts.
- Protects margins.
- Structures commercial offers.
- Evaluates deal economics.
- Manages channel pricing.
- Applies pricing exceptions.
- Measures revenue quality.
- Optimizes commercial outcomes.
- Uses pricing and revenue intelligence responsibly.

The goal is not merely to increase sales.

The goal is to build a disciplined system that ensures the enterprise sells:

- At the right price.
- To the right customer.
- Through the right channel.
- With the right margin.
- Under the right commercial controls.

---

# 1.2 Domain Mission

The permanent mission of the Domain is:

> Govern enterprise pricing, commercial terms, discounting, revenue quality, and deal economics so that growth remains profitable, controlled, explainable, and strategically aligned.

This Domain converts commercial activity from ad hoc pricing into governed economic decision making.

---

# 1.3 Commercial Economics Philosophy

The Domain follows permanent principles.

---

## Value Before Discount

Price should reflect customer value and business economics before discounting is considered.

---

## Margin Before Volume

Additional sales volume is not automatically beneficial if profitability is destroyed.

---

## Governance Before Exception

Price exceptions must remain controlled.

---

## Segmentation Before Uniform Pricing

Different markets, channels, customer types, and commercial contexts may legitimately require different pricing structures.

---

## Transparency Before Commercial Complexity

Pricing structures should remain understandable and auditable.

---

## Revenue Quality Before Revenue Vanity

Revenue should be evaluated alongside:

- Margin.
- discount.
- cost.
- returns.
- fulfillment burden.
- payment quality.

---

## Evidence Before Optimization

Commercial recommendations require trusted economic information.

---

## Human Authority Before Autonomous Pricing

AI may recommend pricing actions.

Critical pricing authority remains governed.

---

# 1.4 Domain Objectives

The Domain permanently supports:

- Pricing consistency.
- Margin protection.
- Revenue growth.
- Commercial flexibility.
- Deal profitability.
- Discount governance.
- Promotion control.
- Channel economics.
- Customer-segment pricing.
- Revenue optimization.
- Commercial forecasting.
- Pricing intelligence.
- Executive commercial visibility.

---

# 1.5 Domain Boundary

The Domain permanently owns:

- Pricing architecture.
- Price lists.
- price books.
- pricing rules.
- discount structures.
- promotion economics.
- pricing exceptions.
- commercial approval thresholds.
- deal economics.
- margin protection.
- revenue-quality analysis.
- commercial intelligence.
- pricing optimization.
- channel commercial economics.

It does **not** replace:

- Finance.
- Sales.
- Product.
- Marketing.
- Customer Experience.
- Tax governance.

Canonical separation:

```text
Product
Defines What Is Sold

↓

Finance
Defines Authoritative Financial Meaning

↓

Revenue Management
Defines Commercial Economics

↓

Sales / Commerce
Executes the Commercial Transaction
```

---

# 1.6 Relationship With Finance

Finance remains authoritative for:

- Revenue recognition.
- accounting treatment.
- costs.
- gross margin definitions.
- tax accounting.
- profitability statements.

Revenue Management governs:

- Commercial pricing.
- discounting.
- price floors.
- deal economics.
- pricing policy.
- commercial margin protection.

Canonical rule:

```text
Commercial Price
→ Revenue Management

Accounting Revenue
→ Finance
```

The two must remain connected but distinct.

---

# 1.7 Relationship With Sales

Sales owns:

- Customer-facing selling.
- opportunity progression.
- negotiation.
- deal execution.

Revenue Management governs:

- Allowed pricing.
- discount authority.
- deal profitability.
- commercial exceptions.

Sales must not create uncontrolled pricing policy through individual negotiation.

---

# 1.8 Relationship With Product

Product owns:

- Product definition.
- variants.
- lifecycle.
- positioning.
- product structure.

Revenue Management owns commercial pricing structures attached to those products.

Example:

```text
Product:
Personalized Acrylic LED Lamp

↓

Price Architecture:
Retail Price
Marketplace Price
Corporate Price
Promotional Price
```

---

# 1.9 Relationship With Marketing

Marketing may propose:

- Promotions.
- campaign discounts.
- coupon strategies.
- acquisition incentives.

Revenue Management evaluates:

- Margin impact.
- price integrity.
- channel conflict.
- campaign economics.

Marketing does not independently redefine permanent pricing architecture.

---

# 1.10 Relationship With Customer Experience

Customer Experience may require:

- Service credits.
- goodwill discounts.
- recovery offers.

These remain subject to controlled commercial authority.

Customer recovery must not become an uncontrolled discount channel.

---

# 1.11 Relationship With Tax & Compliance

Pricing may interact with:

- GST.
- VAT.
- marketplace tax treatment.
- regional pricing obligations.
- promotional-disclosure rules.

Tax and Legal authorities remain authoritative for statutory interpretation.

Revenue Management ensures commercial structures correctly consume those rules.

---

# 1.12 Core Enterprise Capabilities

The permanent capability landscape includes:

| Capability | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Price Management | Govern sell prices |
| Price Book Management | Organize pricing structures |
| Price Rule Management | Apply pricing logic |
| Customer Pricing | Support customer-specific terms |
| Channel Pricing | Govern marketplace/channel economics |
| Discount Management | Control discount structures |
| Promotion Pricing | Govern campaign economics |
| Price Exception Management | Control deviations |
| Commercial Approval Management | Govern authority thresholds |
| Margin Protection | Prevent uneconomic selling |
| Deal Economics | Evaluate transaction profitability |
| Commercial Terms Management | Govern non-price deal terms |
| Revenue Quality Management | Evaluate quality of revenue |
| Commercial Forecasting | Project commercial outcomes |
| Pricing Intelligence | Analyze pricing performance |
| Revenue Optimization | Improve profitable growth |
| Pricing Audit | Preserve commercial evidence |

---

# 1.13 Revenue Architecture

Commercial revenue is influenced by:

```text
Demand

×

Price

×

Conversion

×

Volume

↓

Gross Revenue

↓

Discounts / Allowances

↓

Net Commercial Revenue

↓

Cost-to-Serve

↓

Commercial Contribution
```

Revenue growth must therefore be analyzed alongside economic quality.

---

# 1.14 Price Concept

A **Price** represents the commercial amount requested for a defined offering under specified conditions.

Price requires context such as:

- Product.
- variant.
- quantity.
- customer.
- channel.
- geography.
- currency.
- validity period.

There is rarely one universal price independent of context.

---

# 1.15 Base Price

The **Base Price** provides the starting commercial value for an offering.

Example:

```text
Product:
Wooden Engraved Photo Frame

Base Retail Price:
₹X
```

Additional pricing logic may adjust this amount.

---

# 1.16 List Price

List Price represents a formally published or configured standard selling price.

List Price may differ from:

- Contract price.
- promotional price.
- marketplace price.
- negotiated price.

---

# 1.17 Net Selling Price

The actual commercial selling price may be:

```text
List Price

-

Discounts

+

Approved Charges

=

Net Selling Price
```

This becomes a key input into commercial profitability.

---

# 1.18 Price Book

A **Price Book** groups pricing appropriate to a commercial context.

Examples:

- Retail Price Book.
- Amazon Price Book.
- Flipkart Price Book.
- Meesho Price Book.
- Corporate Price Book.
- Wholesale Price Book.
- Offline Store Price Book.

Each Price Book requires:

- Identity.
- ownership.
- currency.
- applicability.
- effective period.
- governance state.

---

# 1.19 Price Book Hierarchy

The Canon supports structured price relationships.

Example:

```text
Enterprise Base Price

↓

Channel Price Book

↓

Customer / Segment Price

↓

Approved Deal Exception
```

The hierarchy ensures price derivation remains understandable.

---

# 1.20 Customer-Specific Pricing

Some customers may legitimately receive:

- Contract pricing.
- volume pricing.
- corporate pricing.
- negotiated terms.

Customer-specific pricing must define:

- Customer.
- eligible products.
- price/discount.
- effective period.
- approval.
- conditions.

---

# 1.21 Segment Pricing

Pricing may differ by governed customer segment.

Examples:

- Retail.
- Corporate.
- reseller.
- wholesale.
- franchise.
- partner.

Segment pricing must remain commercially justified and legally appropriate.

---

# 1.22 Channel Pricing

Different channels may have different economics.

Example:

```text
Shopify Price

Marketplace Price

Corporate Price

Offline Price
```

Differences may reflect:

- Marketplace commission.
- payment fees.
- shipping model.
- acquisition cost.
- service expectations.

Channel price differences require commercial rationale.

---

# 1.23 Marketplace Economics

Marketplace pricing must consider:

```text
Selling Price

-

Platform Fees

-

Commission

-

Shipping / Fulfillment Cost

-

Discount Funding

-

Taxes / Applicable Charges

-

Product Cost

=

Commercial Contribution
```

High marketplace revenue may be economically weak if these costs are ignored.

---

# 1.24 Discount Architecture

Discounts may include:

- Percentage discount.
- fixed amount.
- volume discount.
- customer-specific discount.
- campaign discount.
- coupon.
- bundle discount.
- negotiated discount.
- service-recovery discount.

Every discount should have:

- Type.
- reason.
- authority.
- eligibility.
- validity.
- economic impact.

---

# 1.25 Discount Principle

Discount is not merely a selling tool.

It is a transfer of economic value from the enterprise to the customer.

Therefore every material discount must be economically understood.

---

# 1.26 Discount Authority

Discount permissions may follow levels such as:

```text
Standard Discount
Automatic / Pre-Approved

↓

Manager Discount
Requires Approval

↓

Exceptional Discount
Senior Approval

↓

Below-Floor Deal
Restricted / Executive Authority
```

Exact thresholds may evolve.

The authority architecture remains permanent.

---

# 1.27 Price Floor

A **Price Floor** defines the lowest price normally permitted under commercial policy.

Price floors may consider:

- Product cost.
- channel cost.
- shipping.
- target contribution.
- strategic context.

Selling below a floor requires explicit exception authority.

---

# 1.28 Margin Floor

A margin floor may protect minimum economic contribution.

Example:

```text
Net Selling Price

-

Variable Commercial Cost

=

Contribution

↓

Minimum Acceptable Contribution Threshold
```

The enterprise must know when revenue becomes economically destructive.

---

# 1.29 Promotion Architecture

Promotions may include:

- Coupon campaigns.
- seasonal offers.
- bundles.
- buy-more-save-more.
- customer acquisition offers.
- marketplace events.

A promotion requires:

- Objective.
- eligible products.
- eligible customers/channels.
- discount mechanism.
- effective period.
- budget where applicable.
- margin impact.
- success criteria.

---

# 1.30 Promotion Economics

Promotions should evaluate:

```text
Incremental Sales

×

Incremental Margin

-

Promotion Cost

-

Cannibalization

=

Promotion Economic Value
```

A promotion that increases orders but reduces overall contribution may not be successful.

---

# 1.31 Bundle Pricing

Bundles may combine several products.

Example:

```text
Lamp
+
Keychain
+
Card

↓

Bundle Price
```

Bundle pricing should consider:

- Combined standalone value.
- production cost.
- packaging cost.
- promotional objective.
- minimum margin.

---

# 1.32 Volume Pricing

Volume pricing may apply to:

- Corporate orders.
- reseller purchases.
- wholesale transactions.

Example:

```text
1–9 units
Standard

10–49 units
Volume Tier 1

50–99 units
Volume Tier 2

100+
Custom Commercial Review
```

Volume discount must reflect real economic efficiencies or strategic value.

---

# 1.33 Quantity Breaks

Quantity breaks must preserve:

- Minimum quantity.
- maximum quantity.
- applicable price.
- effective period.
- customer/segment eligibility.

Overlapping or conflicting quantity tiers should be prevented.

---

# 1.34 Commercial Terms

Commercial value is broader than price.

Terms may include:

- Payment terms.
- delivery terms.
- free shipping.
- setup fee.
- personalization fee.
- packaging.
- credit period.
- return conditions.

Deal economics must consider all material terms.

---

# 1.35 Deal Economics

A commercial deal should be evaluated as:

```text
Selling Price

-

Discount

-

Product Cost

-

Variable Production Cost

-

Packaging

-

Shipping

-

Channel Fees

-

Other Commercial Costs

=

Deal Contribution
```

This provides a more realistic view than revenue alone.

---

# 1.36 Deal Profitability

Deals may be categorized:

- Highly Attractive.
- Acceptable.
- Low Margin.
- Strategic Exception.
- Uneconomic.

The exact thresholds are business-governed.

---

# 1.37 Strategic Exception

An otherwise weak deal may be intentionally approved for reasons such as:

- Strategic customer acquisition.
- market entry.
- relationship development.
- inventory liquidation.
- promotional learning.

Strategic exceptions must remain explicit.

They must not become hidden normal pricing.

---

# 1.38 Commercial Approval Architecture

Commercial decisions may require different authority depending on:

- Discount level.
- deal value.
- margin.
- customer type.
- payment terms.
- risk.
- strategic importance.

Canonical model:

```text
Standard Deal

↓

Automated Policy Check

↓

Exception?

No → Continue

Yes → Approval Routing
```

---

# 1.39 Price Exception

A Price Exception occurs when the proposed deal falls outside normal commercial policy.

Examples:

- Below standard price.
- excess discount.
- unusual free service.
- special payment term.
- below margin floor.

Exceptions require:

- Reason.
- requester.
- approver.
- economic analysis.
- validity.
- audit history.

---

# 1.40 Approval Expiry

Commercial approvals may expire.

Example:

A special quoted price approved for a customer today may not remain valid indefinitely.

Approvals should define:

- Effective from.
- effective until.
- quantity or scope.

---

# 1.41 Quote Economics

A quotation should expose enough information to evaluate:

- Sell price.
- discount.
- estimated cost.
- margin.
- taxes where relevant.
- shipping.
- payment terms.

This prevents quotations from becoming detached from profitability.

---

# 1.42 Quote-to-Order Integrity

Canonical principle:

```text
Approved Quote

↓

Customer Acceptance

↓

Order

↓

Commercial Terms Preserved
```

An accepted order should not silently differ from the approved quote.

---

# 1.43 Revenue Quality

Revenue quality evaluates whether revenue is economically and operationally attractive.

Potential dimensions include:

- Margin.
- discount rate.
- payment quality.
- return rate.
- fulfillment complexity.
- customer support burden.
- repeat potential.

Not all revenue is equally valuable.

---

# 1.44 Revenue Quality Categories

Future classifications may include:

- High-Quality Revenue.
- Healthy Revenue.
- Low-Margin Revenue.
- Strategic Revenue.
- At-Risk Revenue.
- Destructive Revenue.

These categories must be based on governed criteria.

---

# 1.45 Commercial Contribution

The Domain supports contribution-oriented management.

Example:

```text
Revenue
₹1,000

-

Commercially Relevant Variable Costs
₹650

=

Commercial Contribution
₹350
```

Finance remains authoritative for accounting profit.

Commercial Contribution supports selling decisions.

---

# 1.46 Contribution vs Accounting Profit

The Domain permanently distinguishes:

```text
Commercial Contribution

≠

Final Accounting Profit
```

Commercial Contribution may support:

- Pricing.
- deal approval.
- channel optimization.

Finance determines final accounting results.

---

# 1.47 Customer Profitability

Future intelligence may evaluate customer economics across:

- Revenue.
- discounts.
- product mix.
- returns.
- support burden.
- payment behavior.
- repeat orders.

Customer profitability must be governed carefully and not used as an excuse for unfair treatment.

---

# 1.48 Product Commercial Performance

A product may be evaluated through:

- Sales volume.
- price realization.
- discount rate.
- gross/contribution margin.
- production complexity.
- return or complaint rate.

This supports pricing and portfolio decisions.

---

# 1.49 Price Realization

**Price Realization** measures how much of intended commercial price is actually achieved.

Example:

```text
Average Net Selling Price

÷

Reference / List Price

=

Price Realization
```

This can reveal excessive discounting.

---

# 1.50 Discount Leakage

Discount Leakage occurs when value is lost through:

- Uncontrolled discounting.
- unauthorized coupons.
- overlapping promotions.
- incorrect pricing.
- avoidable price exceptions.

Commercial Intelligence should surface leakage.

---

# 1.51 Margin Leakage

Margin Leakage may result from:

- Discounts.
- underestimated shipping.
- incorrect cost.
- excessive marketplace fee.
- rework.
- free services.
- pricing errors.

Revenue growth should be analyzed for margin leakage.

---

# 1.52 Price Consistency

Price consistency does not mean every customer receives the same price.

It means pricing differences are governed and explainable.

---

# 1.53 Price Waterfall

A future Price Waterfall may show:

```text
List Price

↓

Base Discount

↓

Promotion

↓

Customer Adjustment

↓

Channel Adjustment

↓

Net Selling Price

↓

Commercial Costs

↓

Contribution
```

This makes value leakage visible.

---

# 1.54 Commercial Segmentation

Commercial analysis may segment by:

- Product.
- channel.
- customer type.
- geography.
- order size.
- occasion.
- campaign.

Segmentation must use governed enterprise dimensions.

---

# 1.55 Pricing Periods

Prices may have:

- Effective-from date.
- effective-to date.
- seasonal validity.
- campaign validity.

Historical orders must preserve the applicable price context at transaction time.

---

# 1.56 Currency Architecture

Future enterprise expansion may require multiple currencies.

Pricing must then distinguish:

- Price currency.
- transaction currency.
- reporting currency.
- exchange-rate context.

Finance remains authoritative for financial conversion rules.

---

# 1.57 Regional Pricing

Future regional pricing may consider:

- Local costs.
- taxes.
- market conditions.
- distribution.
- currency.
- customer expectations.

Regional pricing must remain governed and legally compliant.

---

# 1.58 Revenue Forecasting

Commercial forecasting may estimate:

- Revenue.
- order value.
- product mix.
- discount levels.
- channel contribution.
- gross commercial margin.

Forecasts remain predictions.

---

# 1.59 Pricing Intelligence

Pricing Intelligence may analyze:

- Price realization.
- discount distribution.
- margin by price band.
- conversion response.
- channel economics.
- promotion performance.
- exception frequency.

---

# 1.60 Promotion Intelligence

Promotion analysis may evaluate:

- Incremental orders.
- revenue uplift.
- margin effect.
- customer acquisition.
- repeat purchase.
- cannibalization.

A successful promotion must be defined by business objective, not merely order volume.

---

# 1.61 Discount Intelligence

Discount Intelligence may answer:

- Which teams/channels discount most?
- Which discounts improve conversion?
- Which discounts damage margin?
- Where are exceptions becoming normal?

This enables disciplined commercial management.

---

# 1.62 Price Elasticity

Future advanced analytics may estimate how demand changes as price changes.

Price elasticity must be treated as an analytical estimate.

It is not a universal constant.

---

# 1.63 Dynamic Pricing

Future systems may support dynamic pricing under explicit rules.

Potential inputs:

- Demand.
- capacity.
- inventory.
- seasonality.
- channel economics.

However, dynamic pricing requires strict:

- governance.
- fairness.
- transparency where appropriate.
- floor controls.
- human authority.

---

# 1.64 AI-Assisted Pricing

AI may assist with:

- Price recommendations.
- discount recommendations.
- margin-risk detection.
- promotion optimization.
- customer/channel analysis.
- anomaly detection.

AI recommendations remain governed suggestions.

---

# 1.65 AI Pricing Authority Boundary

AI may not independently:

- Remove approved price floors.
- create discriminatory pricing policies.
- approve strategic price exceptions.
- redefine financial cost.
- change material pricing strategy.
- hide discount rationale.

Human authority remains permanent.

---

# 1.66 Commercial Fairness

Pricing strategy must remain consistent with:

- Law.
- customer trust.
- legitimate business differentiation.
- non-discriminatory principles where applicable.

Personal attributes must not become uncontrolled pricing variables.

---

# 1.67 GiftHatke Commercial Architecture

GiftHatke has multiple commercial contexts, including:

- Shopify.
- Amazon.
- future Flipkart.
- future Meesho.
- offline sales.
- corporate/B2B.
- customized quotations.

The Domain must allow these channels to operate under controlled but differentiated economics.

---

# 1.68 GiftHatke Retail Pricing

Retail pricing may consider:

```text
Product Cost

+

Production Effort

+

Personalization Cost

+

Packaging

+

Shipping / Channel Cost

+

Target Contribution

=

Commercial Price Basis
```

Final price may also reflect:

- Brand positioning.
- customer value.
- competitive conditions.

---

# 1.69 GiftHatke Marketplace Pricing

Marketplace pricing must account for:

- Commission.
- platform fees.
- shipping.
- marketplace promotions.
- payment/settlement economics.
- returns where relevant.

A marketplace product should not be assumed profitable merely because its selling price matches Shopify.

---

# 1.70 GiftHatke Corporate Pricing

Corporate/B2B pricing may use:

- Quantity tiers.
- customization complexity.
- packaging requirement.
- shipping quantity.
- payment terms.
- repeat potential.

B2B quotations should expose contribution economics before approval.

---

# 1.71 GiftHatke Personalized Product Pricing

Personalized products may require additional pricing dimensions such as:

- Personalization complexity.
- artwork/design work.
- materials.
- size.
- engraving area.
- finishing.
- packaging.
- rush requirement.

These inputs must remain manageable without creating excessive pricing complexity.

---

# 1.72 GiftHatke Rush Pricing

Future rush-order pricing may recognize expedited production cost or capacity impact.

Any rush charge should have:

- Clear conditions.
- operational feasibility.
- commercial rationale.

---

# 1.73 GiftHatke Bundle Pricing

GiftHatke bundles may combine:

- Lamps.
- keychains.
- cards.
- hampers.
- packaging.

Bundle economics must calculate combined cost and intended contribution.

---

# 1.74 GiftHatke Discount Guardrails

Discount guardrails should help prevent:

- Excessive manual discounts.
- marketplace over-discounting.
- overlapping coupons.
- below-margin quotations.
- inconsistent corporate offers.

---

# 1.75 GiftHatke Commercial Approval Example

Example:

```text
Corporate Quote

↓

100 Personalized Lamps

↓

Commercial Calculation

↓

Margin Above Standard Floor?
YES

↓

Within Sales Authority?
YES

↓

Quote Approved
```

Alternative:

```text
Margin Below Standard Floor

↓

Manager / Executive Review

↓

Strategic Justification

↓

Approved or Rejected
```

# ENTERPRISE REVENUE MANAGEMENT, PRICING & COMMERCIAL INTELLIGENCE CANON
## Stage 2 — Commercial Entity Model, Price Architecture & Revenue Structure Canon

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain** requires a permanent entity model defining how the enterprise represents:

- Prices.
- Price books.
- pricing rules.
- discounts.
- promotions.
- commercial terms.
- deal economics.
- approvals.
- price exceptions.
- contribution.
- revenue quality.
- commercial forecasts.
- pricing intelligence.

Stage 1 established the domain foundation, authority boundaries, and commercial philosophy.

Stage 2 now establishes the canonical commercial information architecture.

The objective is to ensure that every future GiftHatkeOS implementation can answer:

- What price applies?
- Why does that price apply?
- Which discount changed it?
- Which commercial policy allowed it?
- What margin was expected?
- Who approved the exception?
- What was the final transaction economics?
- Can the historical decision be reconstructed?

---

# 2.2 Commercial Entity Principles

The Domain follows permanent entity-model principles.

---

## Context Before Price

A price has no complete meaning without its commercial context.

---

## Version Before History

Historical prices and commercial rules must remain tied to the version active at transaction time.

---

## Rule Before Exception

Standard pricing must be known before an exception can be identified.

---

## Economics Before Approval

Material commercial decisions require sufficient profitability context.

---

## Transaction Truth Before Recalculation

Historical orders preserve actual transaction economics.

They must not be silently repriced using current rules.

---

## Ownership Before Modification

Material commercial entities require accountable ownership.

---

# 2.3 Canonical Commercial Entity Landscape

The permanent entity architecture includes:

| Entity | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Commercial Product Reference | Links pricing to sellable offering |
| Commercial Offering | Defines what is being priced |
| Price | Defines commercial amount |
| Base Price | Defines reference starting price |
| List Price | Defines standard published/configured price |
| Net Selling Price | Represents final commercial selling price |
| Price Book | Groups prices for a context |
| Price Book Entry | Connects offering to price |
| Pricing Rule | Defines price-selection or adjustment logic |
| Price Condition | Defines when a pricing rule applies |
| Price Adjustment | Represents price increase/decrease |
| Discount | Represents commercial concession |
| Discount Rule | Defines automated discount logic |
| Promotion | Defines temporary commercial campaign |
| Promotion Eligibility | Defines who/what qualifies |
| Coupon | Defines code-driven promotional entitlement |
| Bundle Price | Defines commercial price for combined offering |
| Quantity Tier | Defines volume-based price |
| Customer Price Agreement | Defines negotiated/customer-specific pricing |
| Channel Price | Defines channel-specific commercial price |
| Regional Price | Defines geography-specific price |
| Price Floor | Defines minimum normal sell price |
| Margin Floor | Defines minimum commercial contribution |
| Commercial Term | Defines non-price deal term |
| Quote | Represents proposed commercial offer |
| Quote Line | Represents individual priced offer item |
| Deal | Represents commercial transaction opportunity |
| Deal Economics Record | Calculates expected commercial economics |
| Commercial Approval | Records authorization |
| Price Exception | Records deviation from policy |
| Revenue Quality Record | Evaluates quality of revenue |
| Price Waterfall | Explains price-to-contribution journey |
| Commercial Contribution Record | Represents commercial contribution |
| Price Realization Record | Measures achieved price |
| Commercial Forecast | Projects future commercial outcomes |
| Pricing Insight | Represents analytical interpretation |
| Pricing Recommendation | Represents suggested commercial action |
| Commercial Risk | Represents risk to revenue or margin |
| Commercial Audit Record | Preserves evidence |

---

# 2.4 Commercial Product Reference

## Purpose

Connects the Revenue Management Domain to the Product Domain.

It may reference:

- Product.
- variant.
- SKU.
- bundle.
- service.
- personalization option.

Product ownership remains with the Product Domain.

Revenue Management uses the reference to assign commercial economics.

---

# 2.5 Commercial Offering

A **Commercial Offering** represents the precise sellable configuration being priced.

It may include:

- Product.
- variant.
- quantity.
- personalization level.
- packaging.
- service level.
- channel.
- region.

Example:

```text id="commercial-offering-example"
Product:
Acrylic LED Lamp

Variant:
Couple Design

Personalization:
Photo + Names

Packaging:
Gift Box

Channel:
Shopify
```

This gives pricing sufficient context.

---

# 2.6 Price Entity

The **Price** represents a monetary amount attached to a defined commercial context.

A Price should include:

- Price ID.
- amount.
- currency.
- tax treatment reference where relevant.
- effective-from date.
- effective-to date.
- source/owner.
- status.
- version.

---

# 2.7 Price Status Model

Canonical states:

```text id="price-status"
Draft

↓

Reviewed

↓

Approved

↓

Active

↓

Superseded / Expired

↓

Archived
```

Only approved active prices should normally be used for new transactions.

---

# 2.8 Base Price Entity

The Base Price represents the foundational commercial reference for a sellable offering.

It may serve as the starting point for:

- Channel adjustment.
- customer pricing.
- promotions.
- negotiated discount.

Example:

```text id="base-price-structure"
Base Price

↓

Channel Adjustment

↓

Promotion

↓

Customer Discount

↓

Net Selling Price
```

---

# 2.9 List Price Entity

List Price represents the standard advertised or configured commercial price.

It must preserve:

- Product/Offering.
- currency.
- applicability.
- validity.
- version.

List Price does not necessarily equal actual transaction price.

---

# 2.10 Net Selling Price Entity

Net Selling Price represents the commercially realized transaction price before or after specified charge treatment according to policy.

It may be derived through:

```text id="net-selling-price"
List / Reference Price

+

Price Adjustments

-

Discounts

+

Commercial Charges

=

Net Selling Price
```

The precise formula must be certified.

---

# 2.11 Price Book Entity

A **Price Book** groups commercial prices for a specific context.

Potential examples:

- GiftHatke Retail.
- Shopify.
- Amazon.
- Flipkart.
- Meesho.
- Corporate.
- Wholesale.
- Offline.

A Price Book contains:

- Price Book ID.
- name.
- currency.
- owner.
- applicability.
- priority.
- effective period.
- status.

---

# 2.12 Price Book Entry

A Price Book Entry connects:

```text id="price-book-entry"
Price Book

+

Commercial Offering

↓

Price
```

It should preserve:

- Offering reference.
- price.
- currency.
- validity.
- quantity basis if relevant.
- version.

---

# 2.13 Price Book Priority

Where multiple books could apply, selection must be deterministic.

Possible hierarchy:

```text id="price-book-priority"
Customer-Specific Agreement

↓

Contract / Segment Price

↓

Channel Price Book

↓

Regional Price Book

↓

Enterprise Default
```

The exact hierarchy may evolve.

The rule is that selection must remain explainable.

---

# 2.14 Pricing Rule Entity

A **Pricing Rule** defines logic that selects, modifies, or validates price.

Examples:

- Apply marketplace price.
- Apply volume tier.
- add rush charge.
- apply corporate contract price.
- block price below floor.

A Pricing Rule contains:

- Rule ID.
- definition.
- priority.
- conditions.
- action.
- effective period.
- owner.
- status.
- version.

---

# 2.15 Price Condition Entity

A Price Condition defines when a rule applies.

Conditions may include:

- Product.
- product category.
- customer.
- segment.
- channel.
- geography.
- quantity.
- date.
- promotion.
- personalization complexity.

Conditions must be deterministic and auditable.

---

# 2.16 Pricing Rule Precedence

When multiple rules apply:

```text id="pricing-precedence"
Eligible Rules Identified

↓

Priority Evaluated

↓

Conflict Checked

↓

Applicable Rule Set Determined

↓

Price Calculated
```

Rule conflicts must not produce unpredictable transaction prices.

---

# 2.17 Price Adjustment Entity

A Price Adjustment represents a controlled change to a base/reference price.

Examples:

- Rush surcharge.
- customization surcharge.
- region adjustment.
- channel adjustment.
- service fee.

Adjustments may be:

- Positive.
- negative.

Each requires:

- Type.
- value.
- reason.
- source rule.
- applicability.

---

# 2.18 Discount Entity

A **Discount** represents a commercial concession reducing price.

A Discount contains:

- Discount ID.
- type.
- amount or percentage.
- reason.
- eligibility.
- owner.
- validity.
- approval requirement.
- stacking behavior.

---

# 2.19 Discount Types

Canonical categories may include:

- Standard Discount.
- Customer Discount.
- Volume Discount.
- Promotional Discount.
- Coupon Discount.
- Bundle Discount.
- Negotiated Discount.
- Service Recovery Discount.
- Strategic Discount.

---

# 2.20 Discount Rule Entity

A Discount Rule determines when a discount can apply.

Example:

```text id="discount-rule"
IF
Corporate Order Quantity ≥ 50

AND
Product Eligible

THEN
Apply Approved Volume Discount Tier
```

Rules must preserve:

- Conditions.
- value.
- maximum permitted discount.
- validity.
- authority.

---

# 2.21 Discount Stacking

The architecture must explicitly define whether discounts may combine.

Possible states:

- Stackable.
- Exclusive.
- Stackable with limit.
- Requires approval.

Example:

```text id="discount-stacking"
Coupon

+

Marketplace Promotion

+

Manual Discount

↓

Conflict / Cap Evaluation
```

Uncontrolled stacking is prohibited.

---

# 2.22 Promotion Entity

A **Promotion** represents a temporary commercial initiative.

Contains:

- Promotion ID.
- name.
- objective.
- owner.
- eligible products.
- channels.
- customer eligibility.
- mechanism.
- validity period.
- budget where applicable.
- approval state.

---

# 2.23 Promotion Lifecycle

Canonical states:

```text id="promotion-lifecycle"
Proposed

↓

Economics Reviewed

↓

Approved

↓

Scheduled

↓

Active

↓

Completed

↓

Performance Reviewed

↓

Archived
```

---

# 2.24 Promotion Eligibility

Eligibility may depend on:

- Customer.
- customer segment.
- channel.
- product.
- product category.
- minimum quantity.
- minimum order value.
- region.
- date.

Eligibility rules must be explicit.

---

# 2.25 Coupon Entity

A Coupon should contain:

- Code.
- value/type.
- promotion relationship.
- valid period.
- minimum order.
- product eligibility.
- channel.
- usage limit.
- customer usage limit.
- stacking rule.
- status.

---

# 2.26 Coupon Lifecycle

```text id="coupon-lifecycle"
Created

↓

Approved

↓

Active

↓

Redeemed / Partially Used

↓

Expired / Disabled

↓

Archived
```

Coupon usage must remain traceable.

---

# 2.27 Bundle Price Entity

Bundle Price defines pricing for a defined product combination.

It should preserve:

- Bundle composition.
- standard combined value.
- bundle price.
- discount value.
- expected contribution.
- validity.

Example:

```text id="bundle-price"
Lamp ₹X
+
Keychain ₹Y
+
Card ₹Z

Standard Combined Value
₹A

Bundle Price
₹B
```

---

# 2.28 Quantity Tier Entity

Quantity Tier defines commercial pricing by ordered quantity.

Contains:

- Minimum quantity.
- maximum quantity.
- applicable price or discount.
- eligible offering.
- customer segment.
- effective period.

Tiers must not overlap ambiguously.

---

# 2.29 Customer Price Agreement

A Customer Price Agreement represents negotiated pricing for an identified customer or account.

Contains:

- Customer.
- products.
- prices/discounts.
- quantity requirements.
- validity.
- payment terms.
- approval.
- contract reference where relevant.

Customer-specific pricing must not become invisible manual knowledge.

---

# 2.30 Channel Price Entity

A Channel Price represents pricing designed for a particular sales channel.

Examples:

- Shopify.
- Amazon.
- offline.
- corporate.

It may reflect:

- Channel commission.
- fulfillment cost.
- payment fees.
- promotional expectations.

---

# 2.31 Regional Price Entity

Regional Price may apply to:

- Country.
- state.
- economic region.
- market.

It must preserve:

- Currency.
- region.
- validity.
- commercial rationale.
- legal compliance.

---

# 2.32 Price Floor Entity

Price Floor defines a minimum normal transaction price.

Contains:

- Offering.
- floor value.
- effective period.
- basis.
- authority.
- exception policy.

Below-floor transactions become Price Exceptions.

---

# 2.33 Margin Floor Entity

Margin Floor defines minimum acceptable commercial economics.

It may be represented as:

- Amount.
- percentage.
- contribution threshold.

Example:

```text id="margin-floor"
Net Selling Price

-

Commercially Relevant Costs

=

Contribution

↓

Must Meet Approved Floor
```

---

# 2.34 Commercial Term Entity

A Commercial Term represents non-price deal conditions.

Examples:

- Payment terms.
- delivery commitment.
- free shipping.
- customization included.
- credit period.
- setup fee waived.

Terms can materially affect deal economics.

---

# 2.35 Commercial Term Classification

Terms may be classified as:

- Standard.
- Negotiable.
- Restricted.
- Exceptional.

Authority requirements vary by classification.

---

# 2.36 Quote Entity

A **Quote** represents a proposed commercial offer.

Contains:

- Quote ID.
- customer.
- currency.
- validity.
- line items.
- discounts.
- charges.
- taxes where applicable.
- payment terms.
- approval status.
- total.

---

# 2.37 Quote Line Entity

Quote Line contains:

- Offering.
- quantity.
- reference price.
- adjustments.
- discounts.
- net line price.
- expected commercial contribution.

Line-level economics support transparent deal evaluation.

---

# 2.38 Quote Lifecycle

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="quote-lifecycle"
Draft

↓

Priced

↓

Economics Evaluated

↓

Approval if Required

↓

Issued

↓

Accepted / Rejected / Expired

↓

Converted to Order
```

---

# 2.39 Quote Versioning

Material quote changes create versions.

Examples:

- Price changed.
- quantity changed.
- discount changed.
- terms changed.

Customer acceptance must connect to the accepted version.

---

# 2.40 Quote-to-Order Relationship

Canonical relationship:

```text id="quote-order-relationship"
Approved Quote Version

↓

Customer Acceptance

↓

Order

↓

Transaction Commercial Terms
```

The order must preserve the actual accepted price and conditions.

---

# 2.41 Deal Entity

A **Deal** represents a commercial opportunity requiring economic evaluation.

Deal may relate to:

- B2B order.
- corporate contract.
- reseller arrangement.
- strategic customer.
- large custom project.

---

# 2.42 Deal Economics Record

The Deal Economics Record evaluates expected commercial outcome.

Possible components:

- Gross selling value.
- discount.
- net selling value.
- product cost.
- customization cost.
- packaging.
- shipping.
- channel fees.
- payment-cost implications.
- contribution.
- margin percentage.

---

# 2.43 Deal Economics Formula

Canonical structure:

```text id="deal-economics"
Gross Price

-

Discounts

+

Commercial Charges

=

Net Selling Price

-

Relevant Variable Costs

=

Commercial Contribution
```

Finance remains authoritative for accounting profitability.

---

# 2.44 Commercial Approval Entity

A Commercial Approval records authorization for a material commercial decision.

Contains:

- Approval ID.
- requested action.
- requester.
- approver.
- approval authority.
- economics.
- reason.
- decision.
- timestamp.
- expiry.
- conditions.

---

# 2.45 Commercial Approval States

```text id="commercial-approval-states"
Not Required

Pending

Approved

Approved With Conditions

Rejected

Expired

Revoked
```

---

# 2.46 Approval Threshold Model

Approvals may be triggered by:

- Discount percentage.
- deal value.
- margin.
- below-floor pricing.
- unusual payment terms.
- free service value.
- strategic exception.

Thresholds remain business-configurable.

---

# 2.47 Price Exception Entity

A **Price Exception** records deviation from standard commercial policy.

Contains:

- Standard price.
- proposed price.
- difference.
- discount.
- margin.
- reason.
- customer.
- transaction.
- requester.
- approver.
- validity.

---

# 2.48 Price Exception Lifecycle

```text id="price-exception-lifecycle"
Exception Detected

↓

Business Reason Captured

↓

Economics Evaluated

↓

Authority Determined

↓

Approved / Rejected

↓

Transaction Executed if Approved

↓

Exception Audited
```

---

# 2.49 Strategic Exception Entity

Strategic exceptions should identify explicit rationale such as:

- Market entry.
- strategic account.
- launch.
- liquidation.
- pilot.
- relationship investment.

The exception must remain visible separately from normal pricing.

---

# 2.50 Price Waterfall Entity

The **Price Waterfall** explains how reference price becomes realized economics.

Canonical structure:

```text id="price-waterfall-entity"
List Price

↓

Standard Discount

↓

Promotion

↓

Customer Adjustment

↓

Manual Exception

↓

Net Selling Price

↓

Channel Cost

↓

Fulfillment / Variable Cost

↓

Commercial Contribution
```

The waterfall provides commercial transparency.

---

# 2.51 Commercial Contribution Record

A Commercial Contribution Record represents contribution economics for:

- Order.
- order line.
- quote.
- deal.
- customer.
- channel.
- product.

The calculation must preserve the exact commercial-cost basis used.

---

# 2.52 Revenue Quality Record

A Revenue Quality Record may evaluate a transaction using:

- Contribution.
- discount.
- payment behavior.
- return/refund burden.
- rework.
- service burden.
- strategic value.

It may classify revenue as:

- High Quality.
- Healthy.
- Low Margin.
- Strategic.
- At Risk.
- Destructive.

Exact criteria must be governed.

---

# 2.53 Price Realization Record

Price Realization measures achieved commercial value compared with a governed reference.

Example:

```text id="price-realization-record"
Net Selling Price

÷

Reference Price

=

Price Realization
```

The reference price must always be explicit.

---

# 2.54 Discount Leakage Record

Discount Leakage may record:

- Expected discount.
- actual discount.
- excess discount.
- cause.
- transaction.
- owner.

Leakage intelligence helps distinguish intended commercial strategy from uncontrolled value loss.

---

# 2.55 Margin Leakage Record

- Excess discount.
- cost increase.
- unpriced customization.
- free shipping.
- high rework.
- incorrect marketplace economics.
- pricing defect.

---

- discount.

- channel mix.
- product mix.
- assumptions.
- confidence.
- version.

Forecasts remain predictions, not actual commercial results.

---

A Pricing Insight represents an analytical interpretation.

Example:

```text id="pricing-insight"
Observation:

Insight:
Contribution increased only 4% because promotional discount and fees rose.
```

The insight must preserve evidence.

- reduce discount.

- review cost basis.

- Margin erosion.
- excessive discounting.
- price inconsistency.
- channel conflict.
- promotion overuse.
- outdated costs.
- below-floor selling.
- customer concentration.

---

- Price created.
- Price changed.
- Discount approved.
- Promotion launched.
- Exception granted.
- floor revised.
- quote approved.
- customer agreement changed.

# ENTERPRISE REVENUE MANAGEMENT, PRICING & COMMERCIAL INTELLIGENCE CANON
## Stage 3 — Pricing Lifecycle, Commercial Operations & Revenue Governance Operating Model Canon

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain** requires a permanent operating model defining how enterprise pricing, discounts, promotions, quotes, deals, approvals, revenue quality, and commercial performance operate through their complete lifecycle.

Stages 1–2 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Commercial boundaries.
- Pricing philosophy.
- Price Books.
- Discounts.
- Promotions.
- Quotes.
- Deal Economics.
- Commercial approvals.
- Commercial entity architecture.

Stage 3 defines how these entities operate together as a governed commercial system.

The objective is to ensure that commercial decisions are:

- Consistent.
- Timely.
- Profitable.
- Explainable.
- Auditable.
- Customer-appropriate.
- Policy-controlled.

The permanent operating sequence is:

```text id="commercial-operating-sequence"
Commercial Need

↓

Applicable Pricing Context

↓

Price Calculation

↓

Economics Evaluation

↓

Policy Validation

↓

Approval if Required

↓

Customer Offer

↓

Accepted Transaction

↓

Commercial Outcome

↓

Performance Review
```

---

# 3.2 Commercial Operating Philosophy

The Domain follows permanent operating principles.

---

## Standard Before Exception

Normal commercial rules should handle most business.

Exceptions should remain exceptional.

---

## Price Before Negotiation

Commercial teams should understand the approved starting price before negotiation begins.

---

## Economics Before Commitment

A deal should be evaluated economically before the organization commits to it.

---

## Authority Before Concession

Discounts and special terms must respect approval boundaries.

---

## Transaction Integrity Before Revenue

Customer acceptance must preserve the approved commercial terms.

---

## Outcome Before Assumption

A deal expected to be profitable should later be evaluated against actual economics where practical.

---

## Learning Before Repetition

Repeated exceptions or weak promotions should influence future pricing policy.

---

The certified commercial lifecycle is:

```text id="enterprise-commercial-lifecycle"
Market / Customer Need

↓

Offering Selected

↓

Commercial Context Identified

↓

Applicable Price Determined

↓

Adjustments / Discounts Evaluated

↓

Commercial Economics Calculated

↓

Policy & Floor Validation

↓

Approval if Required

↓

Quote / Offer Issued

↓

Customer Decision

↓

Order Created

↓

Transaction Executed

↓

Commercial Outcome Measured

↓

Pricing Intelligence

↓

Policy Improvement
```

---

# 3.4 Price Creation Lifecycle

New prices follow:

```text id="price-creation-lifecycle"
Pricing Need Identified

↓

Commercial Analysis

↓

Price Proposed

↓

Cost / Margin Context Reviewed

↓

Owner Review

↓

Approval

↓

Effective Period Assigned

↓

Activated

↓

Monitored
```

A price should not become active solely because someone edited a value in a product record.

---

# 3.5 Price Review Lifecycle

Existing prices require periodic or trigger-based review.

Triggers may include:

- Cost change.
- margin deterioration.
- competitor movement where legitimately considered.
- demand change.
- channel fee change.
- product redesign.
- new packaging.
- exchange-rate movement.
- strategic repositioning.

Canonical flow:

```text id="price-review-lifecycle"
Active Price

↓

Trigger / Scheduled Review

↓

Commercial Economics

↓

Market / Customer Context

↓

Retain / Revise

↓

Approval

↓

New Version
```

---

# 3.6 Price Activation

Before activation, price governance should confirm:

- Offering exists.
- amount valid.
- currency valid.
- applicability defined.
- effective date valid.
- required approval complete.
- floor checks complete.
- conflicts evaluated.

Only then should the price become available for new transactions.

---

Prices may expire because of:

- Contract end.
- promotion end.
- seasonal period.
- planned revision.
- customer agreement termination.

Expired prices must remain available historically but unavailable for new transactions unless explicitly renewed.

```text id="price-supersession"
Old Price
Active Until Effective Boundary

↓

New Price
Active From Effective Boundary
```

Historical transactions preserve the old price.

Future eligible transactions use the new price.

- effective period.

```text id="quote-operating-lifecycle"
Revised Version if Needed

↓

Accepted / Rejected / Expired
```

---

# 3.29 Quote Preparation

Quote preparation should include:

- Customer.
- offering.
- quantity.
- price.
- discount.
- charges.
- payment terms.
- delivery terms.
- validity.

Internal economics may additionally include:

- Estimated cost.
- contribution.
- margin.

---

# 3.30 Quote Version Control

When negotiation changes material terms:

```text id="quote-version-control"
Quote v1

↓

Negotiation

↓

Quote v2

↓

Customer Acceptance

↓

Accepted Version Locked
```

The order must reference the accepted version.

---

# 3.31 Quote Approval

Approval may be required when:

- Discount above authority.
- below-floor price.
- unusual payment term.
- low margin.
- high-value deal.
- strategic exception.

---

# 3.32 Quote Expiration

Quotes should have governed validity.

An expired quote may require:

- Price revalidation.
- cost revalidation.
- renewed approval.

This prevents outdated commercial offers from remaining open indefinitely.

---

# 3.33 Quote-to-Order Conversion

Canonical transaction:

```text id="quote-to-order-conversion"
Accepted Quote Version

↓

Commercial Integrity Validation

↓

Order Created

↓

Price + Discount + Terms Snapshot Preserved

↓

Quote Marked Converted
```

The conversion must not silently alter commercial terms.

---

# 3.34 Deal Lifecycle

Larger or strategic commercial opportunities follow:

```text id="deal-lifecycle"
Opportunity

↓

Commercial Scope

↓

Pricing

↓

Economics

↓

Negotiation

↓

Approval

↓

Commitment

↓

Transaction

↓

Outcome Review
```

---

# 3.35 Deal Economics Review

Before approval, material deals should evaluate:

- Revenue.
- discount.
- contribution.
- margin.
- payment terms.
- fulfillment cost.
- risk.
- strategic value.

---

# 3.36 Commercial Profitability Tiers

Deals may be classified:

- Highly Attractive.
- Healthy.
- Low Margin.
- Strategic Exception.
- Uneconomic.

Classification should support decision making, not automatically replace human judgment.

---

# 3.37 Uneconomic Deal Handling

When a proposed deal fails commercial requirements:

```text id="uneconomic-deal"
Proposed Deal

↓

Margin / Floor Failure

↓

Commercial Warning

↓

Options:
Reprice
Reduce Scope
Change Terms
Seek Strategic Exception
Reject
```

The system should help users improve the deal before simply blocking it where appropriate.

---

# 3.38 Commercial Approval Lifecycle

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="commercial-approval-lifecycle"
Exception / Approval Trigger

↓

Request Created

↓

Economics Attached

↓

Authority Identified

↓

Reviewer Decision

↓

Approved / Conditional / Rejected

↓

Expiry / Conditions Applied

↓

Audit Preserved
```

---

# 3.39 Approval Routing

Approval routing may consider:

- Discount.
- contribution.
- order value.
- customer type.
- channel.
- payment terms.
- strategic importance.

Exact thresholds remain configurable.

---

# 3.40 Conditional Approval

Approvals may include conditions.

Examples:

- Minimum quantity.
- Advance payment.
- specific validity period.
- no further discount.
- fixed customization scope.

Conditions must become enforceable transaction controls where appropriate.

---

# 3.41 Approval Expiry

Expired approvals cannot automatically authorize later transactions.

The pricing context may have changed.

Revalidation may be necessary.

---

# 3.42 Approval Revocation

An approval may be revoked if:

- Pricing error discovered.
- commercial circumstances materially changed.
- fraud/security concern.
- customer conditions changed.

Transactions already contractually committed require appropriate legal/business handling.

---

# 3.43 Price Exception Lifecycle

The permanent Price Exception lifecycle is:

```text id="price-exception-operation"
Policy Deviation Detected

↓

Exception Classified

↓

Reason Captured

↓

Economic Impact Calculated

↓

Approval Authority Determined

↓

Approved / Rejected

↓

Transaction

↓

Exception Reviewed
```

---

# 3.44 Exception Categories

Possible categories:

- Discount exception.
- below-floor price.
- unusual free service.
- non-standard payment term.
- special channel pricing.
- strategic account exception.
- promotion override.

---

# 3.45 Exception Recurrence Management

Repeated exceptions should trigger policy review.

Example:

```text id="exception-recurrence"
Same Product
+
Same Customer Type
+
Repeated Manual Discount

↓

Pattern Detected

↓

Standard Pricing Review Required
```

A repeated exception may indicate poor commercial master data.

---

```text id="transaction-pricing"
Commercial Context

↓

Price Calculation

↓

Discount

↓

Approval Evidence

↓

Final Transaction Price

↓

Transaction Snapshot

↓

Order
```

The resulting transaction price becomes historical commercial truth.

---

# 3.47 Commercial Snapshot

The transaction snapshot should preserve where relevant:

- Price.
- Price Book.
- price version.
- promotion.
- coupon.
- manual discount.
- approval.
- quantity tier.
- commercial terms.

Future rule changes must not alter this historical snapshot.

---

# 3.48 Revenue Quality Lifecycle

Revenue quality follows:

```text id="revenue-quality-lifecycle"
Transaction

↓

Revenue

↓

Commercial Contribution

↓

Operational Outcome

↓

Payment / Refund / Rework Context

↓

Revenue Quality Assessment
```

Revenue quality may evolve as post-sale outcomes become known.

---

# 3.49 Commercial Contribution Lifecycle

Expected contribution may be calculated:

- At quote.
- at order.
- after actual fulfillment.
- after settlement.

This allows comparison between:

```text id="expected-actual-contribution"
Expected Contribution

vs

Actual Commercial Outcome
```

---

# 3.50 Expected vs Actual Economics

Differences may arise because of:

- Material-cost variation.
- rework.
- shipping increase.
- platform fee changes.
- returns/refunds.
- production complexity.

This creates commercial-learning opportunities.

---

# 3.51 Revenue Leakage Operating Model

```text id="revenue-leakage"

↓

Actual Commercial Outcome

↓

Unexpected Value Loss

↓

Leakage Cause

↓

Action
```

Potential causes:

- Unauthorized discount.
- incorrect pricing.
- forgotten charge.
- coupon stacking.
- system defect.

---

# 3.52 Margin Leakage Operating Model

Margin leakage analysis may identify:

- Cost increases.
- price not revised.
- discount overuse.
- free customization.
- excessive rework.
- marketplace fees.
- high fulfillment cost.

---

# 3.53 Price Realization Operations

Price Realization can be monitored by:

- Product.
- customer.
- sales channel.
- salesperson/team where appropriate.
- period.
- promotion.

The Performance Management Domain governs final KPI certification.

---

```text id="commercial-forecast-operating-model"
+

Current Pipeline / Demand

Price Assumptions
```
