```text id="commercial-forecast-operating-model"
Discount Assumptions

Product / Channel Mix
```

# 3.55 Price Change Impact Analysis

Before a major price change, the enterprise may analyze:

- Expected volume impact.
- revenue impact.
- margin impact.
- channel impact.
- customer impact.
- strategic risk.

A price change should not be evaluated on margin percentage alone.

```text id="promotion-impact-analysis"
Base Sales Expectation

vs

Promotion Scenario

Incremental Revenue

Incremental Contribution
```

Failure states may include:

- invalid currency.
- expired agreement.

- discount.

```text id="smp1-commercial-operation"
Migration
```

# ENTERPRISE REVENUE MANAGEMENT, PRICING & COMMERCIAL INTELLIGENCE CANON
## Stage 4 — Pricing Services, Commercial Execution & Revenue Management Service Architecture Canon

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain** requires a permanent service architecture that converts certified pricing concepts, commercial rules, discounts, promotions, approvals, and deal economics into executable enterprise capability.

Stages 1–3 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Commercial entity architecture.
- Price and discount structures.
- Quote and deal economics.
- Pricing lifecycle.
- Approval and exception operating models.
- Commercial outcome review.

Stage 4 defines the services responsible for:

- Price resolution.
- Price Book management.
- pricing-rule execution.
- discount application.
- promotion execution.
- quote pricing.
- deal-economics evaluation.
- margin protection.
- commercial approvals.
- transaction snapshots.
- revenue-quality evaluation.
- pricing intelligence.

The objective is to ensure commercial execution remains:

- Deterministic.
- Governed.
- Traceable.
- Economically aware.
- Auditable.
- Technology-independent.

---

# 4.2 Commercial Service Philosophy

The service architecture follows permanent principles.

---

## Offering Before Pricing

A service must know precisely what is being sold before selecting a price.

---

## Context Before Resolution

Pricing depends on governed commercial context.

---

## Policy Before Manual Override

Standard pricing policy executes before an exception is considered.

---

## Economics Before Approval

Material concessions require sufficient economic analysis.

---

## Validation Before Commitment

Final transaction pricing must pass relevant policy and authority controls.

---

## Historical Truth Before Recalculation

Once a commercial transaction is committed, its transaction-time pricing context becomes immutable historical truth except through governed correction.

---

## Explainability Before Optimization

The platform must be able to explain how a price was produced.

---

# 4.3 Canonical Commercial Service Landscape

The permanent service landscape includes:

| Service | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Commercial Offering Service | Resolve sellable commercial configuration |
| Price Management Service | Govern prices |
| Price Book Service | Govern contextual price collections |
| Pricing Context Service | Assemble pricing inputs |
| Pricing Rule Service | Execute pricing logic |
| Price Resolution Service | Determine applicable price |
| Price Adjustment Service | Apply governed adjustments |
| Discount Management Service | Govern discounts |
| Discount Eligibility Service | Determine discount applicability |
| Discount Stacking Service | Resolve discount combinations |
| Promotion Management Service | Govern promotions |
| Promotion Execution Service | Apply promotional logic |
| Coupon Service | Validate and redeem coupons |
| Quantity Pricing Service | Apply volume tiers |
| Customer Pricing Service | Apply negotiated pricing |
| Channel Pricing Service | Apply channel-specific pricing |
| Regional Pricing Service | Apply geographic pricing |
| Price Floor Service | Enforce minimum price |
| Margin Protection Service | Enforce commercial contribution rules |
| Commercial Terms Service | Govern non-price terms |
| Quote Pricing Service | Price quotations |
| Deal Economics Service | Evaluate transaction economics |
| Commercial Approval Service | Govern pricing authority |
| Price Exception Service | Manage policy deviations |
| Transaction Pricing Snapshot Service | Preserve transaction-time pricing |
| Price Waterfall Service | Explain price realization |
| Revenue Quality Service | Evaluate commercial quality |
| Commercial Contribution Service | Calculate contribution economics |
| Pricing Intelligence Service | Generate pricing insight |
| Commercial Risk Service | Identify revenue/margin risks |
| Commercial Audit Service | Preserve commercial evidence |

---

# 4.4 Commercial Offering Service

## Purpose

Resolves the exact commercial configuration to be priced.

Inputs may include:

- Product.
- variant.
- quantity.
- dimensions.
- personalization level.
- packaging.
- service options.
- channel.
- region.

Canonical flow:

```text id="commercial-offering-service"
Customer Request

↓

Product Structure

↓

Variant / Personalization / Service Context

↓

Commercial Offering
```

The service does not redefine Product master data.

It consumes certified Product information.

---

# 4.5 Price Management Service

## Purpose

Governs price records throughout their lifecycle.

Capabilities:

- Create Price.
- review Price.
- approve Price.
- activate Price.
- supersede Price.

## Discount Validation

# 4.54 Transaction Boundary — Price Resolution

Canonical transaction:

```text id="price-resolution-transaction"
Pricing Context Built

↓

Eligible Prices Identified

↓

Priority Applied

↓

Rules Applied

↓

Discounts Applied

↓

Floor / Margin Checks

↓

Approval Validation

↓

Final Price Returned
```

A partial failure must not return an apparently final price.

---

# 4.55 Transaction Boundary — Coupon Redemption

Coupon redemption must protect against:

- Duplicate use.
- concurrency.
- transaction failure after reservation.

Possible lifecycle:

```text id="coupon-redemption-transaction"
Coupon Validated

↓

Usage Reserved

↓

Order Commit

↓

Redemption Confirmed
```

If order commit fails, reservation must be safely released where appropriate.

---

# 4.56 Transaction Boundary — Commercial Approval

```text id="commercial-approval-transaction"
Approval Request

↓

Authority Validation

↓

Decision

↓

Conditions Recorded

↓

Audit Commit

↓

Approval Becomes Available
```

No transaction should use an approval before it is committed.

---

# 4.57 Idempotency

Repeated commercial requests must not unintentionally create:

- Duplicate approvals.
- duplicate coupon redemptions.
- duplicate Price Exceptions.
- duplicate quote conversions.
- duplicate promotions.

---

# 4.58 Concurrency Governance

Concurrency is especially important for:

- Coupon redemption.
- limited promotion allocation.
- Quote conversion.
- price changes.
- approval usage.

The system must preserve deterministic state under simultaneous transactions.

---

# 4.59 Price Change Concurrency

When a price changes while a customer is transacting:

The platform must apply an explicit policy such as:

- Transaction uses currently committed cart/quote price for a defined validity window.

or:

- Reprice before final commitment.

The policy must remain consistent and auditable.

---

# 4.60 Commercial Failure Classification

Potential failures include:

## Configuration Failure

No valid price or contradictory rule.

## Eligibility Failure

Customer/order not eligible for discount.

## Policy Failure

Price or margin below allowed threshold.

## Authority Failure

Required approval unavailable.

## Economic Data Failure

Required cost basis missing.

## Concurrency Failure

Coupon or promotion allocation changed.

## Integration Failure

Required Product, Customer, Finance, or Order service unavailable.

---

# 4.61 Failure Response Principles

The system should:

- Fail safely.
- explain the reason.
- preserve context.
- provide a governed next step.

It should never silently:

- Set price to zero.
- remove an approval requirement.
- ignore a floor.
- invent a cost.

---

# 4.62 Commercial Caching

Future standalone architecture may cache:

- Price Books.
- active pricing rules.
- customer agreements.
- channel pricing.

Caching must respect:

- Effective dates.
- version.
- invalidation.
- priority.

A changed price must not remain stale indefinitely because of cache behavior.

---

# 4.63 Effective-Time Architecture

Pricing is strongly time-dependent.

Services must correctly evaluate:

- Current time.
- effective from.
- effective until.
- quote validity.
- agreement validity.
- promotion validity.

Historical time must be handled separately from current pricing.

---

# 4.64 Currency Handling

Pricing services must preserve:

- Source currency.
- transaction currency.
- rounding.

If exchange conversion is required, Finance provides authoritative rate governance.

Pricing services must not invent exchange rates.

---

# 4.65 Tax Boundary

Pricing may provide pre-tax or tax-inclusive commercial amounts depending on configuration.

Tax calculation remains governed by Finance/Tax architecture.

Revenue Management must preserve the selected tax-treatment context.

---

# 4.66 Security & Access

Commercial services require authorization.

Examples:

- Sales may view price.
- managers may request discount.
- authorized managers may approve.
- only commercial administrators may modify Price Books.

Security Domain owns technical authorization enforcement.

---

# 4.67 Sensitive Commercial Information

Information such as:

- Margin floors.
- cost basis.
- strategic customer pricing.
- executive price approvals.

may require restricted visibility.

A sales user may need a permitted selling price without visibility into every internal cost component.

# 4.94 SMP1 Service Preservation Requirement

During **SMP1**, the standalone runtime may introduce dedicated:

- Pricing APIs.
- rules engine.
- promotion engine.
- commercial approval services.
- pricing cache.

But the first requirement is preservation of certified transaction truth.

Canonical rule:

```text id="smp1-commercial-service-rule"
New Commercial Service Technology

+

Same Certified Business Meaning

=

Valid Standalone Migration
```

---

# 4.95 SMP1 Historical Price Protection

The standalone pricing service must never take migrated historical orders and reapply today's price logic as though they were current transactions.

Historical order price remains historical truth.

---

# 4.96 Standalone v1.0 Service Foundation

Standalone v1.0 should support a durable foundation for:

- Transaction pricing.
- price history.
- discount history.
- channel context.
- commercial snapshots.
- auditability.

More advanced:

- Price Books.
- promotion engine.
- CPQ.
- AI pricing.

may evolve progressively according to implementation priorities.

---

# 4.97 ERP9 Service Integration

After standalone v1.0 certification, ERP9 may implement richer:

- Commercial Settings.
- Price Books.
- discount rules.
- customer groups.
- channel pricing.
- approval thresholds.

These should use the certified service architecture rather than creating isolated pricing logic.

---

# 4.98 ERP10 Service Certification

ERP10 should validate:

- Price-resolution correctness.
- discount correctness.
- approval enforcement.
- quote/order integrity.
- commercial snapshots.
- margin visibility.
- historical traceability.
- commercial-service usability.

---

# 4.99 Commercial Service Observability

The standalone architecture should monitor:

- Price-resolution failures.
- pricing-rule conflicts.
- floor breaches.
- margin-assessment failures.
- approval errors.
- coupon redemption failures.
- expired pricing used.
- stale cache.
- quote conversion failures.

Commercial services themselves must be operationally trustworthy.

---

# 4.100 Service Quality Standards

The commercial service architecture must prioritize:

## Correctness

The right price is calculated.

## Determinism

Equivalent valid context produces explainable output.

## Traceability

The platform can explain the result.

## Timeliness

Pricing is available when required for selling.

## Historical Integrity

Past transactions remain unchanged.

## Security

Sensitive commercial information is appropriately controlled.

## Resilience

Commercial failures do not produce dangerous fallback pricing.

---

# 4.101 Permanent Service Standards

The Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain permanently follows:

- Offering before price.
- Context before resolution.
- Policy before override.
- Deterministic rules before transaction.
- Economics before approval.
- Floor protection before concession.
- Committed pricing before order execution.
- Historical truth before recalculation.
- Explainability before optimization.
- Safe failure before arbitrary pricing.
- Human authority before strategic commercial automation.

---

# ENTERPRISE REVENUE MANAGEMENT, PRICING & COMMERCIAL INTELLIGENCE CANON
## Stage 5 — Commercial Governance, Pricing Authority, Margin Protection & Revenue Excellence Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain** requires a permanent governance framework defining who may create, approve, modify, override, interpret, and retire enterprise pricing and commercial policies.

Stages 1–4 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Commercial entity architecture.
- Pricing and revenue operating model.
- Pricing services.
- Discount and promotion execution.
- Quote and deal economics.
- Commercial approvals.
- Margin-protection services.

Stage 5 establishes the permanent authority, accountability, and governance model protecting enterprise commercial integrity.

The objective is to ensure that:

- Prices do not change arbitrarily.
- Discounts remain controlled.
- Margin floors cannot be silently bypassed.
- Promotions remain economically governed.
- Strategic exceptions remain explicit.
- Commercial authority is separated from technical capability.
- Revenue growth remains profitable.
- Pricing decisions remain reconstructable.
- AI assists commercial judgment without becoming uncontrolled pricing authority.

The central principle is:

> **Commercial freedom must exist inside governed economic boundaries.**

---

# 5.2 Commercial Governance Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Business Strategy Before Price Mechanics

Pricing exists to support enterprise strategy.

A pricing engine does not decide the strategy.

---

## Authority Before Concession

The ability to technically enter a discount does not create commercial authority to grant it.

---

## Margin Before Revenue Vanity

Revenue growth must be evaluated alongside economic contribution.

---

## Policy Before Exception

Normal pricing should be governed by standard policy.

Exceptions must remain visible.

---

## Evidence Before Approval

Material concessions require sufficient economic context.

---

## Customer Value Before Automatic Discounting

Discounting should not become the default response to commercial negotiation.

---

## Historical Integrity Before Repricing

Past transactions preserve their commercial truth.

---

## Human Accountability Before Autonomous Pricing

AI may recommend.

Humans remain accountable for material commercial policy.

---

# 5.3 Commercial Governance Layers

The permanent commercial governance framework operates across eight layers.

---

# Layer 1 — Commercial Strategy Governance

Controls:

- Pricing strategy.
- positioning.
- revenue objectives.
- channel strategy.
- commercial segmentation.

---

# Layer 2 — Price Governance

Controls:

- Base Prices.
- Price Books.
- pricing rules.
- effective periods.
- price versions.

---

# Layer 3 — Discount & Promotion Governance

Controls:

- Discount policy.
- coupon policy.
- promotion economics.
- stacking.
- limits.

---

# Layer 4 — Margin & Floor Governance

Controls:

- Price floors.
- margin floors.
- contribution requirements.
- below-floor exceptions.

---

# Layer 5 — Deal & Quote Governance

Controls:

- Quote economics.
- deal profitability.
- commercial terms.
- negotiation authority.

---

# Layer 6 — Commercial Exception Governance

Controls:

- Price exceptions.
- strategic exceptions.
- unusual terms.
- override authority.

---

# Layer 7 — Revenue Intelligence Governance

Controls:

- Price Realization.
- Revenue Quality.
- margin leakage.
- commercial forecasts.
- pricing recommendations.

---

# Layer 8 — Audit & Commercial Integrity Governance

Controls:

- Price history.
- discount history.
- approvals.
- exceptions.
- transaction snapshots.
- commercial decision evidence.

---

# 5.4 Canonical Commercial Governance Roles

The permanent role architecture includes:

- Enterprise Commercial Authority.
- Pricing Owner.
- Product Commercial Owner.
- Sales Authority.
- Commercial Analyst.
- Promotion Owner.
- Deal Owner.
- Finance Authority.
- Customer Account Owner.
- Commercial Approver.
- Commercial Auditor.
- Commercial Administrator.

These roles may be fulfilled by different organizational positions depending on enterprise scale.

---

# 5.5 Enterprise Commercial Authority

Responsibilities include:

- Maintaining enterprise pricing governance.
- Defining commercial-policy standards.
- Resolving cross-domain pricing conflicts.
- Governing major exception principles.
- Reviewing commercial maturity.
- Approving enterprise-level pricing architecture.

This authority does not replace:

- Finance.
- Product.
- Sales.
- Marketing.

It coordinates commercial economics across them.

---

# 5.6 Pricing Owner

The Pricing Owner is accountable for:

- Price architecture.
- Price Book integrity.
- price review.
- pricing rule governance.
- price-version integrity.

The Pricing Owner should understand:

- Customer value.
- costs.
- channels.
- product economics.
- market context.

---

# 5.7 Product Commercial Owner

May be responsible for commercial economics of a product or product family.

Responsibilities may include:

- Price recommendation.
- margin review.
- promotion suitability.
- channel economics.
- lifecycle commercial analysis.

Product lifecycle authority remains with the Product Domain.

---

# 5.8 Sales Authority

Sales owns:

- Commercial negotiation.
- customer engagement.
- opportunity progression.
- deal execution.

Sales authority to concede price must remain explicitly bounded.

Example:

```text id="sales-authority-boundary"
Sales Can Negotiate

BUT

Only Within
Approved Commercial Authority
```

---

# 5.9 Finance Authority

Finance remains authoritative for:

- Cost definitions.
- accounting revenue.
- margin definitions.
- financial profitability.
- tax-related financial treatment.

Revenue Management may use these concepts for pricing decisions.

It must not redefine them independently.

---

# 5.10 Promotion Owner

Responsible for:

- Promotion objective.
- target audience.
- offer design.
- expected commercial outcome.
- monitoring.
- post-promotion review.

Marketing may own campaign execution.

Commercial governance protects the economics.

---

# 5.11 Deal Owner

Responsible for:

- Commercial opportunity.
- customer requirements.
- quote structure.
- negotiation.
- approval coordination.
- transaction outcome.

The Deal Owner cannot independently waive governance controls outside granted authority.

---

# 5.12 Commercial Approver

A Commercial Approver may approve only within explicitly delegated authority.

Approval must be based on:

- Commercial context.
- economics.
- policy deviation.
- strategic rationale.
- risk.

An approver should not approve a deal merely because a request was escalated.

---

# 5.13 Commercial Auditor

Responsible for independent review of:

- Pricing changes.
- discounts.
- exceptions.
- approval compliance.
- price history.
- transaction snapshots.

Audit does not itself create commercial policy.

---

# 5.14 Commercial Administrator

May technically maintain:

- Price Books.
- rules.
- discount configurations.
- approval thresholds.

Technical administration does not automatically confer commercial decision authority.

This separation is permanent.

---

# 5.15 Pricing Authority Matrix

The Canon establishes decision-right separation.

| Commercial Decision | Primary Authority |
|---|---|
| Pricing strategy | Commercial / Executive Authority |
| Product commercial positioning | Product + Commercial |
| Cost basis | Finance |
| Standard price | Pricing Authority |
| Channel price | Pricing / Channel Authority |
| Discount policy | Commercial Authority |
| Promotion mechanics | Marketing + Commercial |
| Manual discount | Sales within delegated authority |
| Below-floor exception | Higher Commercial Authority |
| Strategic deal | Executive / Designated Authority |
| Transaction execution | Order/Sales systems |
| Historical commercial correction | Governed authority |
| Commercial audit | Audit |

---

# 5.16 Separation of Duties

High-impact commercial operations should separate:

- Requester.
- approver.
- executor.
- auditor.

Example:

```text id="commercial-separation-duty"
Sales Requests
20% Discount

↓

Manager Approves

↓

System Applies Approved Discount

↓

Audit Preserves Evidence
```

One user should not automatically control every step in high-risk commercial decisions.

---

# 5.17 Price Creation Governance

New standard prices require:

- Commercial rationale.
- product relationship.
- cost context.
- market/value context.
- effective period.
- owner.
- approval.

The system should prevent anonymous ungoverned price creation.

---

# 5.18 Price Change Governance

Material price changes follow:

```text id="price-change-governance"
Change Proposed

↓

Reason

↓

Economic Impact

↓

Affected Channels / Customers

↓

Historical Impact Reviewed

↓

Approval

↓

Future Effective Date

↓

New Version
```

---

# 5.19 Price Change Impact Analysis

Before approval, the enterprise may evaluate:

- Expected margin.
- demand impact.
- customer reaction.
- channel consistency.
- contract commitments.
- promotion interactions.

A price change can affect far more than one number.

---

# 5.20 Emergency Price Change

Rare situations may require rapid price change due to:

- Material-cost shock.
- regulatory change.
- critical pricing defect.
- marketplace issue.

Emergency changes still require:

- authority.
- reason.
- effective time.
- audit evidence.

Urgency does not remove governance.

---

# 5.21 Price Book Governance

Each Price Book requires:

- Business purpose.
- owner.
- channel/segment scope.
- currency.
- effective dates.
- certification/approval.

Unused or conflicting Price Books should be reviewed and rationalized.

---

# 5.22 Pricing Rule Governance

Pricing Rules require:

- Clear purpose.
- owner.
- conditions.
- precedence.
- effective period.
- test evidence where critical.
- version.

Rule changes must not silently alter existing transactions.

---

# 5.23 Discount Governance

Discount policy should define:

- Permitted discount types.
- default limits.
- approval thresholds.
- stacking rules.
- product exclusions.
- channel restrictions.
- strategic exceptions.

Discounts must remain visible as an economic concession.

---

# 5.24 Discount Authority Ladder

Example governance:

```text id="discount-authority-ladder"
Pre-Approved Discount
Automatic

↓

Sales-Level Discount
Within Delegated Limit

↓

Manager Discount
Requires Approval

↓

Senior Commercial Exception

↓

Executive Strategic Exception
```

The exact percentages remain configurable.

The authority hierarchy is permanent.

---

# 5.25 Discount Reason Governance

Manual discounts should use governed reasons such as:

- Volume.
- strategic customer.
- competitive negotiation.
- service recovery.
- inventory liquidation.
- approved campaign support.

Free-text explanation may supplement the reason.

It should not replace structured classification.

---

# 5.26 Discount Leakage Governance

The enterprise should monitor:

- Unauthorized discounts.
- repeated manual adjustments.
- high average discount.
- unusual discount patterns.
- overlapping promotions.

Leakage investigation should remain evidence-based.

---

# 5.27 Coupon Governance

Coupon governance controls:

- Who can create codes.
- Discount value.
- eligible products.
- validity.
- stacking.
- usage caps.
- customer limits.
- channels.

Expired or unauthorized coupons must not remain usable because of poor technical controls.

---

# 5.28 Promotion Governance

Every material Promotion should define:

- Business objective.
- commercial owner.
- marketing owner where applicable.
- eligible audience.
- offer.
- cost.
- expected contribution.
- duration.
- success criteria.

---

# 5.29 Promotion Approval Governance

Approval should consider:

- Margin.
- potential cannibalization.
- channel conflict.
- operational capacity.
- customer expectations.
- financial budget where relevant.

Promotion governance is therefore cross-domain.

---

# 5.30 Promotion Guardrails

Promotions may be restricted by:

- Minimum price.
- margin floor.
- maximum combined discount.
- excluded products.
- inventory availability.
- channel.
- quantity.

This prevents campaigns from accidentally creating uneconomic transactions.

---

# 5.31 Promotion Effectiveness Governance

Post-promotion review should compare:

- Expected outcome.
- actual revenue.
- contribution.
- redemption.
- customer acquisition.
- repeat behavior where relevant.
- operational impact.

A promotion should not be labeled successful only because it increased order count.

---

# 5.32 Price Floor Governance

Price floors require:

- Business rationale.
- underlying cost/economic basis.
- owner.
- effective period.
- review cadence.

Price floors should be updated when material economics change.

---

# 5.33 Margin Floor Governance

Margin floors protect minimum commercial economics.

They may vary by:

- Product.
- channel.
- customer segment.
- strategic context.

Any floor variation requires explicit policy.

---

# 5.34 Below-Floor Governance

A below-floor deal is a controlled exception.

Canonical flow:

```text id="below-floor-governance"
Proposed Price

↓

Floor Breach

↓

Economic Impact

↓

Strategic Rationale

↓

Authorized Decision

↓

Approved / Rejected
```

No user should bypass this simply by modifying the final order amount.

---

# 5.35 Margin Protection Governance

Margin protection should consider:

- Price.
- discount.
- cost.
- packaging.
- shipping.
- marketplace fees.
- rework expectation.
- service cost where material.

This creates more realistic commercial control.

---

# 5.36 Unknown Cost Governance

If required cost information is missing or untrusted:

The system may classify economics as:

- Not Assessable.
- Preliminary.
- High Risk.

For material deals, absence of cost data may require stronger approval.

---

# 5.37 Cost Change Governance

When significant cost changes occur:

```text id="cost-change-commercial-governance"
Cost Change

↓

Affected Products

↓

Current Margin

↓

Price Impact

↓

Commercial Review

↓

Price / Supplier / Product Decision
```

Prices should not become disconnected from economic reality.

---

# 5.38 Quote Governance

Quotes require:

- Customer.
- version.
- commercial validity.
- approved pricing.
- terms.
- approval evidence where relevant.

A quote sent to a customer becomes a meaningful commercial commitment.

It requires stronger governance than an internal draft.

---

# 5.39 Quote Negotiation Governance

Negotiation may modify:

- Price.
- quantity.
- scope.
- payment terms.
- delivery terms.

Material changes require:

- Updated economics.
- new version.
- new approval if limits crossed.

---

# 5.40 Quote Validity Governance

Expired Quotes may not automatically convert to Orders.

Commercial conditions may have changed.

The system should require revalidation.

---

# 5.41 Quote-to-Order Integrity

The accepted Quote version becomes the commercial source for the Order.

Canonical rule:

```text id="quote-order-integrity"
Accepted Commercial Promise

=

Order Commercial Truth
```

Any difference requires an explicit governed amendment.

---

# 5.42 Deal Governance

Material deals require balanced consideration of:

- Revenue.
- margin.
- strategic value.
- customer relationship.
- capacity.
- payment risk.
- operational feasibility.

High revenue alone does not justify a deal.

---

# 5.43 Deal Authority Governance

Large or unusual deals may require joint authority across:

- Sales.
- Commercial.
- Finance.
- Operations.
- Executive leadership.

This is especially important when commercial terms create operational or cash-flow risk.

---

# 5.44 Strategic Deal Governance

Strategic exceptions may be accepted for:

- Market entry.
- marquee customer.
- new product launch.
- long-term account value.
- excess inventory.
- pilot program.

The strategic value must be explicit.

Repeated "strategic" exceptions without evidence indicate governance failure.

---

# 5.45 Commercial Terms Governance

Non-price terms require governance because they may have economic impact.

Examples:

- Extended payment.
- free shipping.
- setup waiver.
- expedited delivery.
- custom packaging.
- free customization.

A deal with a healthy unit price can still be uneconomic due to its terms.

---

# 5.46 Payment-Term Governance

Extended credit terms may affect:

- Cash flow.
- collection risk.
- financing cost.
- customer exposure.

Finance or Credit authority must participate where relevant.

---

# 5.47 Free-Service Governance

"Free" services must remain visible economically.

Examples:

- Design work.
- shipping.
- gift packaging.
- rush production.

A zero customer charge does not mean zero enterprise cost.

---

# 5.48 Exception Governance

Every material commercial exception requires:

- Exception type.
- reason.
- impact.
- owner.
- approver.
- validity.
- evidence.
- transaction link.

Exceptions must remain searchable and reportable.

---

# 5.49 Exception Frequency Governance

The enterprise should monitor:

- Exceptions by product.
- channel.
- customer.
- salesperson.
- reason.
- approver.

High recurrence may indicate:

- Broken standard price.
- poor market fit.
- weak sales discipline.
- incorrect cost assumptions.

---

# 5.50 Exception Normalization Rule

A repeated exception should not silently become standard practice.

Instead:

```text id="exception-normalization"
Repeated Exception

↓

Pattern Review

↓

Either:
Change Standard Policy

or
Enforce Existing Policy
```

---

# 5.51 Revenue Quality Governance

Revenue Quality should evaluate more than sales value.

Potential factors:

- Contribution.
- discount.
- payment.
- returns.
- rework.
- support burden.
- strategic value.

Revenue quality classification must be transparent and governed.

---

# 5.52 Revenue Quality Authority Boundary

Revenue Management defines commercial interpretation.

Finance remains authoritative for formal accounting results.

Customer and relationship decisions remain within their relevant domains.

---

# 5.53 Price Realization Governance

Price Realization must use an explicit reference such as:

- List Price.
- standard Price Book.
- approved benchmark price.

Without a clear denominator, Price Realization is meaningless.

---

# 5.54 Revenue Leakage Governance

Revenue leakage investigation should ask:

- Was a discount authorized?
- Was a charge omitted?
- Was the wrong Price Book used?
- Did a coupon stack incorrectly?
- Did the system miscalculate?

The goal is control improvement.

Not automatic blame.

---

# 5.55 Margin Leakage Governance

Margin leakage may be assigned to cause categories such as:

- Pricing.
- discount.
- material cost.
- production inefficiency.
- shipping.
- marketplace fee.
- rework.
- return/refund.

This supports cross-domain accountability.

---

# 5.56 Commercial Performance Governance

Commercial measures may include:

- Revenue.
- Price Realization.
- average discount.
- contribution.
- exception rate.
- promotion effectiveness.
- revenue quality.

Domain 30 remains responsible for final KPI governance.

---

# 5.57 Channel Pricing Governance

Different channels may legitimately have different economics.

Each channel price should be governed against:

- Fees.
- fulfillment cost.
- returns.
- competition.
- customer expectations.
- brand strategy.

---

# 5.58 Channel Conflict Governance

Potential conflicts include:

- Marketplace price materially undercutting direct price.
- wholesale terms leaking into retail.
- incompatible promotions.
- regional price inconsistencies.

These require explicit commercial review.

---

# 5.59 Customer-Specific Pricing Governance

Customer agreements require:

- Account identity.
- scope.
- validity.
- price/discount.
- quantity.
- approval.
- terms.

Account-specific prices must not exist only in employee memory or messaging history.

---

# 5.60 Customer Pricing Fairness

Customer-specific pricing may legitimately differ based on:

- Volume.
- contract.
- service requirement.
- channel.
- strategic relationship.

Sensitive personal attributes must not become uncontrolled pricing factors.

---

# 5.61 Regional Pricing Governance

Regional differentiation should consider legitimate factors such as:

- Currency.
- logistics.
- market conditions.
- taxation.
- distribution.

Legal and fairness requirements remain binding.

---

# 5.62 Dynamic Pricing Governance

Dynamic pricing requires especially strong governance.

It must define:

- Eligible products.
- eligible channels.
- minimum price.
- maximum price.
- adjustment factors.
- frequency.
- prohibited variables.
- oversight.

---

# 5.63 Dynamic Pricing Safeguards

The system must prevent:

- Unbounded price movement.
- price below approved floor.
- unauthorized discrimination.
- unexplained price changes.
- instability from feedback loops.

---

# 5.64 AI Pricing Governance

AI may assist with:

- Price recommendations.
- margin-risk detection.
- elasticity estimates.
- promotion analysis.
- deal suggestions.

AI output is advisory unless explicitly governed otherwise.

---

# 5.65 AI Recommendation Governance

Material AI recommendations should expose:

- Data used.
- current price.
- recommended price.
- expected effect.
- confidence.
- major assumptions.
- risks.

This allows commercial authorities to evaluate the recommendation.

---

# 5.66 AI Authority Boundary

AI may not independently:

- Override price floors.
- approve below-floor deals.
- create strategic customer pricing.
- redefine Finance cost.
- activate major promotions.
- make discriminatory pricing decisions.
- rewrite historical transactions.

Human commercial authority remains permanent.

---

# 5.67 Commercial Fairness Governance

Pricing must remain aligned with:

- Applicable law.
- contractual obligations.
- legitimate differentiation.
- customer trust.

Commercial optimization must not justify abusive or deceptive practices.

---

# 5.68 Commercial Transparency

Internally, material pricing should be explainable.

The system should be capable of answering:

- Which price applied?
- Which rules modified it?
- Which discount applied?
- Which approval authorized it?
- What economics were expected?

---

# 5.69 Historical Commercial Integrity

A historical transaction preserves:

- Transaction price.
- discount.
- terms.
- channel.
- approval context.
- applicable price version.

Later configuration changes do not rewrite historical commercial truth.

---

# 5.70 Commercial Correction Governance

If a transaction pricing record is genuinely incorrect:

```text id="commercial-correction"
Evidence

Correction Authority

Correction / Adjustment
```

```text id="gift-rush-governance"
Customer Will Pay More

≠

Operational Capacity Exists
```

Production authority must confirm feasibility before commitment.

# ENTERPRISE REVENUE MANAGEMENT, PRICING & COMMERCIAL INTELLIGENCE CANON
## Stage 6 — Commercial Events, Pricing Synchronization & Revenue Coordination Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain** requires a permanent event-driven coordination model defining how material commercial changes propagate across the enterprise.

Stages 1–5 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Commercial entity architecture.
- Pricing and revenue operating model.
- Pricing services.
- Commercial governance and authority.

Stage 6 defines how commercial state changes become:

- Verified events.
- Pricing synchronization signals.
- Approval triggers.
- Revenue-protection alerts.
- Cross-domain coordination mechanisms.
- Audit evidence.

The objective is to ensure that important commercial changes are not trapped inside isolated systems.

They must become trusted enterprise signals without transferring ownership away from the authoritative domain.

---

# 6.2 Commercial Event Philosophy

A **Commercial Event** represents a verified change in pricing, deal, promotion, approval, revenue-quality, or commercial-governance state.

Examples:

- Price Activated.
- Price Superseded.
- Discount Approved.
- Promotion Started.
- Coupon Redeemed.
- Quote Accepted.
- Price Floor Breached.
- Commercial Exception Approved.
- Margin Risk Detected.

Commercial Events communicate certified business facts or governed analytical states.

---

# 6.3 Commercial Event Principles

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## State Before Event

A commercial change must first become authoritative before it is published.

---

## Meaning Before Transport

The event's business meaning matters more than whether it travels through:

- Queue.
- webhook.
- event bus.
- API.
- stream.

---

## Source Ownership

Revenue Management publishes commercial meaning.

It does not take ownership of Product, Order, Finance, CRM, or other source-domain facts.

---

## Idempotency

Repeated delivery must not create duplicate:

- discounts.
- approvals.
- coupon redemptions.
- price changes.
- quote conversions.

---

## Effective-Time Awareness

Pricing events must preserve when the change becomes commercially effective.

---

## Traceability

Material commercial events must remain auditable.

---

## Minimum Necessary Information

Sensitive:

- Margin.
- cost.
- customer agreement.
- price floor.

must only be exposed to appropriate consumers.

---

# 6.4 Canonical Commercial Event Landscape

The permanent event architecture includes the following categories.

---

# Price Lifecycle Events

Examples:

- Price Proposed.
- Price Approved.
- Price Activated.
- Price Superseded.
- Price Expired.
- Price Retired.

- Pricing Rule Retired.

---

- Discount Created.
- Discount Activated.
- Manual Discount Requested.
- Manual Discount Approved.
- Discount Rejected.
- Discount Applied.

---

# Promotion Events

Examples:

- Promotion Proposed.
- Promotion Approved.
- Promotion Scheduled.
- Promotion Activated.
- Promotion Paused.
- Promotion Completed.
- Promotion Performance Reviewed.

---

# Coupon Events

Examples:

- Coupon Created.

- Coupon Limit Reached.
- Coupon Expired.
- Coupon Disabled.

# Quote Events

Examples:

- Quote Created.

- Recurring Price Exception Detected.

# Margin & Revenue Events

# 6.5 Commercial Event Envelope

A material event may include:

- Event ID.
- Event type.
- event version.
- timestamp.
- effective timestamp.
- source service/domain.
- commercial object ID.
- product/offering reference.
- customer/account reference where appropriate.
- channel.
- price or adjustment context where authorized.
- approval reference.
- correlation ID.
- classification.
- audit reference.

The exact technical schema may evolve.

The business semantics must remain permanent.

---

# 6.6 Event Publication Lifecycle

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="commercial-event-publication"
Commercial Action

↓

Policy / Authority Validation

↓

Authoritative State Commit

↓

Audit Evidence

↓

Commercial Event Published

↓

Authorized Consumers
```

Events must not announce a price or approval before it becomes authoritative.

---

# 6.7 Price Activation Synchronization

When a price becomes active:

```text id="price-activation-sync"
Price Approved

↓

Effective Time Reached

↓

Price Activated

↓

Pricing Cache Invalidated

↓

Commerce Channels Updated

↓

Quote / Pricing Services Use New Price

↓

Audit Preserved
```

Historical orders remain unaffected.

---

# 6.8 Future-Effective Price Changes

A future-effective price may be approved before its activation date.

Canonical sequence:

```text id="future-effective-price"
Price v2 Approved Today

↓

Scheduled

↓

Old Price Remains Active

↓

Effective Date Arrives

↓

Price v2 Activated
```

Approval time and effective time must remain distinct.

---

# 6.9 Price Supersession Coordination

When a Price is superseded:

- New transactions use the new valid price.
- Existing accepted quotes follow their governed validity rules.
- Historical transactions remain unchanged.

The platform must not rewrite old order economics.

---

# 6.10 Price Book Synchronization

Price Book changes may affect:

- Commerce.
- Sales.
- Quotes.
- marketplaces.
- offline sales.
- pricing APIs.

Canonical coordination:

```text id="pricebook-sync"
Price Book Updated

↓

Validation

↓

New Version Activated

↓

Relevant Pricing Consumers Updated

↓

Cache / Projection Refresh
```

---

# 6.11 Pricing Rule Synchronization

When a rule changes:

```text id="pricing-rule-sync"
Rule Revision Approved

↓

New Version Created

↓

Effective Period Defined

↓

Pricing Engine Updated

↓

Conflict Check

↓

New Transactions Use Updated Rule
```

Prior transactions remain connected to previous rule context.

---

# 6.12 Discount Approval Coordination

When a manual discount is requested:

```text id="discount-approval-event"
Discount Request

↓

Authority Evaluation

↓

Approval Workflow

↓

Approved / Rejected Event

↓

Sales / Quote Context Updated
```

Approval itself does not mean a discount has been used.

Application remains a separate state.

---

# 6.13 Discount Applied Event

When a discount is actually applied:

The event should connect where appropriate to:

- Transaction.
- quote.
- approved authority.
- discount reason.
- resulting price.

This allows the enterprise to distinguish:

```text id="discount-authorized-applied"
Discount Approved

from

Discount Actually Used
```

---

# 6.14 Promotion Synchronization

Promotion activation may coordinate:

- Shopify/commerce.
- marketplace connectors.
- coupon systems.
- Marketing.
- Reporting.
- Performance Management.

Canonical model:

```text id="promotion-sync"
Promotion Approved

↓

Scheduled

↓

Activated

↓

Eligible Systems Updated

↓

Transactions Use Promotion

↓

Promotion Performance Monitored
```

---

# 6.15 Promotion Pause Event

A promotion may be paused due to:

- Margin deterioration.
- operational overload.
- technical defect.
- inventory shortage.
- budget exhaustion.

The pause must synchronize quickly enough to prevent continued unintended concessions.

---

# 6.16 Promotion Completion Coordination

At completion:

```text id="promotion-completion"
Promotion Ends

↓

Eligibility Disabled

↓

Outstanding Transactions Handled by Policy

↓

Commercial Results Finalized

↓

Performance Review Triggered
```

---

# 6.17 Coupon Redemption Events

Coupon redemption requires strong event integrity.

Canonical flow:

```text id="coupon-redemption-event"
Coupon Eligibility Confirmed

↓

Usage Reserved

↓

Order Commit

↓

Coupon Redemption Confirmed

↓

Redemption Event Published
```

A failed Order must not leave an incorrect confirmed redemption unless policy explicitly requires it.

---

# 6.18 Coupon Limit Coordination

When usage limit is reached:

```text id="coupon-limit-event"
Final Eligible Redemption

↓

Usage Limit Reached

↓

Coupon State Updated

↓

Commerce Systems Informed

↓

Further Redemptions Blocked
```

Concurrency safety is mandatory.

---

# 6.19 Quote Event Coordination

Quote lifecycle events may coordinate:

- Sales.
- CRM.
- Workflow.
- Commercial approvals.
- Order Management.

Example:

```text id="quote-coordination"
Quote Approved

↓

Sales Notified

↓

Quote Issued

↓

Customer Accepts

↓

Quote Accepted Event

↓

Order Conversion
```

---

# 6.20 Quote Revision Coordination

A material revision must:

- Create a new version.
- invalidate or supersede the previous active proposal as policy requires.
- trigger new approval if authority thresholds changed.

The accepted version must remain unambiguous.

---

# 6.21 Quote Expiration Event

Quote expiry may trigger:

- Sales notification.
- customer follow-up.
- repricing requirement.
- approval invalidation where linked.

An expired quote should not silently remain executable.

---

# 6.22 Quote-to-Order Event

Canonical sequence:

```text id="quote-to-order-event"
Quote Accepted

↓

Validity Check

↓

Approval Conditions Check

↓

Transaction Commercial Snapshot

↓

Order Created

↓

Quote Converted Event
```

This ensures the Order inherits the accepted commercial truth.

---

# 6.23 Deal Coordination

A large Deal may involve:

- Sales.
- Finance.
- Operations.
- Production.
- Commercial leadership.

Deal events coordinate these domains without removing their authority.

---

# 6.24 Deal Economics Event

A **Deal Economics Evaluated** event may indicate:

- Economics assessed.
- margin state.
- approval requirement.
- risk level.

Sensitive details should only be available to authorized consumers.

---

# 6.25 Strategic Exception Coordination

Strategic exception approval may notify:

- Deal Owner.
- Finance.
- relevant executive authority.
- Order/Quote service.

It should preserve the strategic rationale.

---

# 6.26 Approval Condition Coordination

Example:

```text id="approval-condition-event"
Deal Approved With Conditions

Conditions:
100-unit minimum
50% advance
No additional coupon

↓

Quote Service

↓

Order Service

↓

Payment / Commercial Validation
```

Conditions must not remain passive text.

---

# 6.27 Price Floor Breach Event

When proposed price falls below floor:

```text id="price-floor-event"
Calculated Price

↓

Price Floor Check

↓

BREACH

↓

Price Exception Created

↓

Approver Notified

↓

Transaction Held
```

The breach itself must not automatically mean misconduct.

It is a commercial-control event.

---

# 6.28 Margin Floor Breach Event

A margin-floor breach may coordinate:

- Sales.
- Commercial management.
- Finance.
- executive approval for strategic cases.

If cost data is untrusted, the system should communicate that instead of producing a false margin breach.

---

# 6.29 Revenue Leakage Coordination

A Revenue Leakage event may trigger:

- Commercial investigation.
- pricing configuration review.
- coupon review.
- transaction review.
- audit review.

Example:

```text id="revenue-leakage-event"
Expected Price

↓

Actual Commercial Value

↓

Unexpected Loss

↓

Leakage Signal

↓

Investigation
```

---

# 6.30 Margin Leakage Coordination

Potential downstream consumers:

- Commercial.
- Finance.
- Production.
- Procurement.
- Shipping.

Example:

A margin decline may originate from:

- Excess discount.
- material-cost increase.
- rework.
- shipping cost.

Cross-domain evidence is essential.

---

# 6.31 Revenue Quality Event

If Revenue Quality deteriorates materially, the event may trigger review of:

- Channel.
- products.
- promotions.
- customer terms.
- fulfillment burden.

The system should not treat all high-revenue activity as healthy automatically.

---

# 6.32 Price Realization Event

Material deterioration in Price Realization may indicate:

- Discount overuse.
- stronger promotional mix.
- contract pricing.
- channel shift.

The event triggers analysis.

It does not itself prove commercial failure.

---

# 6.33 Channel Commercial Coordination

Commercial events may synchronize with specific channels.

Examples:

- Amazon Price Changed.
- Shopify Promotion Activated.
- Corporate Price Agreement Updated.

External channel APIs are execution mechanisms.

GiftHatkeOS remains the governed source of internal commercial meaning where designed as authoritative.

---

# 6.34 External Marketplace Failure Handling

If a channel fails to receive an intended price update:

```text id="marketplace-sync-failure"
Internal Price Activated

↓

Marketplace Update Fails

↓

Synchronization Exception

↓

Operations / Commercial Alert

↓

Retry / Manual Resolution

↓

State Reconciled
```

The enterprise must know when internal and external prices diverge.

---

# 6.35 Channel Price Drift Event

Price Drift means external price differs unexpectedly from governed internal pricing.

Possible causes:

- Marketplace promotion.
- stale integration.
- manual channel edit.
- failed update.

Material drift should trigger investigation.

---

# 6.36 Product Coordination

Product events may affect pricing.

Examples:

- Product Activated.
- Variant Created.
- Product Retired.
- Product Specification Changed.

Revenue Management may react by:

- requiring a price.
- reviewing affected prices.
- retiring Price Book entries.

Product retains authoritative product ownership.

---

# 6.37 Cost Change Coordination

Finance or Procurement may publish cost-related changes.

Canonical flow:

```text id="cost-change-event"
Material Cost Increased

↓

Affected Product Economics Identified

↓

Margin Recalculated

↓

Commercial Risk Event

↓

Pricing Review
```

A cost change should not automatically change customer price without commercial authority.

---

# 6.38 Production Coordination

Production may publish:

- Personalization complexity.
- rush feasibility.
- production-cost or capacity signals where governed.

Revenue Management may consume these for:

- Rush pricing.
- custom quote economics.
- margin assessment.

---

# 6.39 Shipping Coordination

Shipping changes may affect:

- Free-shipping economics.
- delivery charges.
- corporate quote contribution.
- regional pricing.

Commercial terms remain governed separately from shipping execution.

---

# 6.40 CRM Coordination

Customer and account changes may affect:

- Customer agreements.
- segment pricing.
- account-specific terms.

Example:

```text id="crm-pricing-coordination"
Customer Agreement Updated

↓

Commercial Eligibility Re-Evaluated

↓

Customer Pricing Context Updated
```

CRM remains authoritative for customer identity.

---

# 6.41 Sales Coordination

Sales consumes commercial events such as:

- Quote Approved.
- Discount Rejected.
- Price Exception Approved.
- Customer Agreement Expiring.

The system should present actionable next steps.

---

# 6.42 Finance Coordination

Finance may consume:

- Transaction price.
- discount.
- commercial contribution context.
- approval.

Revenue Management consumes authoritative:

- cost.
- tax.
- currency rules.

Financial accounting remains within Finance.

---

# 6.43 Marketing Coordination

Marketing may consume:

- Promotion Activated.
- Promotion Paused.
- Promotion Completed.

Revenue Management may consume:

- Campaign performance.
- acquisition results.

Commercial and Marketing events jointly support promotion evaluation.

---

# 6.44 Workflow Coordination

Commercial events can trigger certified workflows.

Example:

```text id="commercial-workflow-event"
Below-Floor Request

↓

Commercial Approval Workflow

↓

Decision

↓

Pricing Context Updated

↓

Transaction Continues / Stops
```

Revenue Management owns commercial policy.

Workflow owns execution mechanics.

---

# 6.45 Notification Coordination

Notifications may include:

- Quote approval required.
- promotion ending.
- Price Book expiring.
- margin floor breached.
- commercial exception overdue.

Notifications should remain:

- Relevant.
- role-specific.
- material.
- actionable.

---

# 6.46 Performance Management Coordination

Domain 30 may consume commercial state for KPIs such as:

- Average Discount.
- Price Realization.
- Exception Rate.
- Revenue Quality.
- Promotion Effectiveness.

Commercial events provide governed source signals.

Performance Management governs KPI meaning and scorecards.

---

# 6.47 Data Governance Coordination

Domain 29 may publish:

- Cost data untrusted.
- product mapping broken.
- customer classification changed.

Commercial systems should respond appropriately.

Example:

```text id="commercial-data-trust"
Cost Data Trust Degraded

↓

Affected Margin Assessments Identified

↓

Contribution Confidence Reduced

↓

Commercial Approver Warned
```

---

# 6.48 Security Coordination

Security governs access to:

- Cost.
- margin floors.
- strategic pricing.
- account-specific prices.
- approval details.

Commercial Events must honor the same sensitivity.

---

# 6.49 Integration/API Coordination

External systems may consume events through:

- APIs.
- webhooks.
- event buses.
- queues.
- connectors.

Integration technology may evolve.

Canonical business event meaning remains fixed.

---

# 6.50 Orchestration Model

Orchestration is appropriate for controlled commercial processes.

Example — Strategic Deal Approval:

```text id="strategic-deal-orchestration"
Deal Submitted

↓

Economics Evaluation

↓

Commercial Approval

↓

Finance Review if Required

↓

Operational Feasibility

↓

Final Decision

↓

Quote Authorization
```

---

# 6.51 Choreography Model

Choreography is appropriate when domains independently respond to a fact.

Example:

**Promotion Activated**

may cause:

- Commerce to apply offer.
- Marketing to begin campaign.
- Reporting to track performance.
- Operations to anticipate demand.

No single coordinator needs to control every reaction.

---

# 6.52 Event Ordering

Commercial event ordering is critical.

Example:

```text id="commercial-event-ordering"
Price Approved

↓

Price Activated

↓

Price Available for Transactions
```

A transaction must not use a price before its activation event/state.

---

# 6.53 Event Deduplication

Consumers must protect against duplicates.

A repeated:

- CouponRedeemed.
- QuoteConverted.
- DiscountApplied.

must not create additional economic impact.

---

# 6.54 Event Replay

Future systems may replay events to:

- Rebuild pricing projections.
- reconstruct audit state.
- validate migration.
- rebuild commercial analytics.

Replay must preserve:

- Effective-time rules.
- version context.
- historical ordering.

---

# 6.55 Event Versioning

Commercial event evolution requires:

- Explicit schema version.
- semantic compatibility.
- documented change.

Changing payload structure must not silently change commercial meaning.

---

# 6.56 Event Correlation

Correlation IDs may connect:

```text id="commercial-event-correlation"
Deal

↓

Quote

↓

Approval

↓

Discount

↓

Order

↓

Commercial Outcome
```

This creates end-to-end commercial traceability.

---

# 6.57 Commercial Failure Events

Potential failure events include:

- Price Resolution Failed.
- Pricing Rule Conflict.
- Discount Validation Failed.
- Coupon Redemption Failed.
- Approval Synchronization Failed.
- External Price Update Failed.

Failures must remain visible.

---

# 6.58 Retry Architecture

Safe retry flow:

```text id="commercial-event-retry"
Processing Failure

↓

Failure Recorded

↓

Retry

↓

Idempotency Check

↓

Successful Processing
```

Retry must never duplicate economic state.

---

# 6.59 Dead-Letter Governance

Unprocessable commercial events may enter a controlled exception queue.

Each entry should preserve:

- Event.
- error.
- impacted commercial object.
- severity.
- retry attempts.
- owner.
- resolution.

Critical commercial events must never disappear silently.

---

# 6.60 Reconciliation After Failure

Following synchronization failure, the platform may compare:

```text id="commercial-state-reconcile"
Authoritative Internal State

vs

External Consumer State

↓

Difference

↓

Reconciliation

↓

Resolution
```

This is especially important for marketplace prices and promotions.

---

# 6.61 Event Security

Event security requires:

- Authenticated producers.
- authorized consumers.
- encryption where appropriate.
- classification-aware payloads.
- auditability.

---

# 6.62 Commercial Privacy

Customer-specific events should expose only information necessary for the consuming function.

A pricing event generally does not need unrelated personal customer information.

---

# 6.63 Event Auditability

Material commercial events should preserve:

- Actor or authority.
- object.
- prior state.
- new state.
- effective time.
- reason where applicable.
- correlation.
- audit reference.

---

# 6.64 Commercial Automation

Events may support low-risk automation.

Examples:

- Activate scheduled price.
- expire coupon.
- invalidate pricing cache.
- notify quote owner.
- create promotion review task.

Automation should execute approved policy.

---

# 6.65 Human Approval Boundary

Automation must not independently:

- Approve below-floor deals.
- grant strategic discounts.
- redefine price floors.
- approve major promotions.
- create discriminatory pricing policy.
- alter accepted historical transaction prices.

Human authority remains permanent.

---

AI may consume governed commercial events to identify:

- Margin risk.
- anomalous discounts.
- price realization trends.
- promotion performance.
- channel economics.

AI may publish:

- Pricing Insight Generated.
- Pricing Recommendation Generated.

These are not authoritative price-change events.

```text id="ai-pricing-event-boundary"

≠

Price Changed
```

A separate governed approval and price-change process is required.

Failures can be identified and reconciled.

The Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain permanently follows:

- State before event.
- effective time before transaction.
- business meaning before transport.
- authority before commercial consequence.
- idempotency before retry.
- transaction truth before synchronization.
- minimum necessary disclosure before distribution.
- reconciliation after failure.
- evidence before automated consequence.
- human authority before strategic commercial automation.

# ENTERPRISE REVENUE MANAGEMENT, PRICING & COMMERCIAL INTELLIGENCE CANON
## Stage 7 — Commercial Experience, Pricing Workspace & Revenue Command Center Canon

---

# 7.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Revenue Management, Pricing & Commercial Intelligence Domain** requires a permanent experience architecture through which commercial teams, managers, finance stakeholders, executives, analysts, and future AI-assisted systems interact with pricing and revenue decisions.

Stages 1–6 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Commercial entity architecture.
- Pricing lifecycle.
- Pricing and revenue services.
- Commercial governance.
- Commercial events and synchronization.

Stage 7 defines how pricing, discounts, quotes, deal economics, margin protection, commercial approvals, and Revenue Intelligence become visible, understandable, navigable, and actionable.

The objective is not merely to display prices.

The objective is to create a commercial operating experience that helps users answer:

- What price should apply?
- Why does it apply?
- What discount is permitted?
- Is the deal economically healthy?
- Does approval exist?
- What commercial risk is present?
- What requires management attention?
- What can the business learn from the outcome?

---

# 7.2 Commercial Experience Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Price With Context

A number alone is insufficient.

Users should understand:

- Price Book.
- validity.
- channel.
- customer context.
- discount.
- applicable terms.

---

## Decision Before Data Overload

Commercial interfaces should surface what is needed to make a decision.

---

## Standard Path Before Exception Path

The normal selling experience should remain simple.

Complex governance should become visible when the transaction requires it.

---

## Economics Before Concession

Before a material discount is granted, authorized users should understand commercial impact.

---

## Guardrail Before Block

Where possible, the platform should help users improve an uneconomic deal rather than merely rejecting it.

---

## Evidence Before Approval

Approvers require enough context to make accountable decisions.

---

## History Before Assumption

Users should be able to inspect relevant pricing and approval history.

---

## Role Before Visibility

Sensitive cost, margin, and strategic-price information must remain role-appropriate.

---

# 7.3 Enterprise Commercial Experience Landscape

The permanent experience architecture includes:

- Revenue Management Command Center.
- Executive Commercial Command Center.
- Pricing Workspace.
- Price Book Workspace.
- Pricing Rule Workspace.
- Discount Management Workspace.
- Promotion Workspace.
- Coupon Workspace.
- Quote Workspace.
- Deal Economics Workspace.
- Commercial Approval Workspace.
- Price Exception Workspace.
- Margin Protection Workspace.
- Channel Economics Workspace.
- Customer Pricing Workspace.
- Commercial Intelligence Workspace.
- Commercial Risk Workspace.
- Revenue Quality Workspace.
- Commercial Governance Workspace.
- Commercial Audit Workspace.

---

# 7.4 Revenue Management Command Center

The Revenue Management Command Center provides an enterprise-wide view of commercial health.

It may summarize:

## Pricing

- Active Price Books.
- upcoming price changes.
- pricing conflicts.
- stale prices.

## Discounts

- Average discount.
- manual discount volume.
- unusual discount patterns.
- approval backlog.

## Margin

- Deals below margin target.
- margin leakage.
- products with deteriorating economics.

## Promotions

- Active campaigns.
- promotion performance.
- promotion margin risk.

## Revenue Quality

- Healthy revenue.
- low-margin revenue.
- strategic revenue.
- destructive revenue.

## Risk

- Below-floor requests.
- channel price drift.
- commercial exceptions.
- missing cost context.

The Command Center answers:

> Where is commercial value being created, and where is it being lost?

---

# 7.5 Executive Commercial Command Center

Leadership requires a concise view of:

- Revenue growth.
- Price Realization.
- contribution.
- margin trend.
- channel economics.
- major commercial risks.
- promotion performance.
- strategic deals.
- Revenue Quality.

Canonical view:

```text id="executive-commercial-command"
Revenue

↓

Price Realization

↓

Discount

↓

Contribution

↓

Channel Economics

↓

Commercial Risk

↓

Executive Decision Required
```

The executive interface should prioritize material economic signals rather than transaction-level noise.

---

# 7.6 Executive Attention Model

Commercial issues may be categorized:

- Informational.
- Monitor.
- Management Attention.
- Executive Decision Required.

Examples of Executive Decision Required:

- Major strategic below-floor deal.
- severe margin erosion.
- significant channel conflict.
- large price-strategy revision.

Routine discount approvals should not flood executive attention.

---

# 7.7 Pricing Workspace

The Pricing Workspace provides authorized users with controlled price-management capability.

It may show:

- Offering.
- current price.
- Price Book.
- effective period.
- previous price.
- upcoming price.
- owner.
- approval state.
- margin context where permitted.

Users may:

- Propose price.
- review price.
- compare history.
- schedule new price.
- request approval.

---

# 7.8 Price Detail Experience

A Price detail page should answer:

- What is the price?
- What is being priced?
- Which Price Book?
- Which currency?
- Who owns it?
- When is it effective?
- What price did it replace?
- What rules depend on it?

This supports commercial transparency.

---

# 7.9 Price History Experience

Users should be able to inspect:

```text id="price-history-experience"
Price v1
₹X
Jan–Mar

↓

Price v2
₹Y
Apr–Jun

↓

Price v3
₹Z
Jul onward
```

Historical transactions remain connected to the appropriate historical version.

---

# 7.10 Price Change Experience

When proposing a price change, users may see:

- Current price.
- proposed price.
- percentage change.
- cost context.
- expected margin.
- affected channels.
- active agreements.
- active promotions.
- potential commercial risk.

This helps avoid isolated price changes.

---

# 7.11 Price Book Workspace

The Price Book Workspace may display:

- Price Book name.
- channel/segment.
- currency.
- validity.
- owner.
- entries.
- conflicts.
- status.

Users may:

- Add prices.
- revise entries.
- schedule activation.
- compare books.
- retire obsolete entries.

---

# 7.12 Price Book Comparison Experience

Example:

```text id="pricebook-comparison"
Product              Shopify    Amazon    Corporate

Acrylic Lamp         ₹X         ₹Y        Tiered
Photo Frame          ₹A         ₹B        Tiered
```

Comparison should allow users to investigate why prices differ.

The goal is not automatic uniformity.

It is explainable differentiation.

---

# 7.13 Pricing Rule Workspace

Authorized users may manage:

- Rule name.
- purpose.
- conditions.
- priority.
- action.
- version.
- effective period.

A rule simulation capability may show:

```text id="pricing-rule-simulation"
Input:
Amazon
Acrylic Lamp
Quantity 2

↓

Applicable Rules:
Amazon Price Book
Festival Promotion

↓

Expected Price:
₹X
```

Simulation helps detect configuration errors before activation.

---

# 7.14 Pricing Conflict Experience

When rules conflict, users should see:

- Conflicting rules.
- priorities.
- affected products/channels.
- why automatic resolution failed.
