# ENTERPRISE CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SERVICE MANAGEMENT & SUPPORT OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation & Enterprise Customer Service Scope

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** establishes the permanent enterprise architecture for how the organization:

- Receives customer support requests.
- manages complaints.
- resolves service issues.
- coordinates returns and refunds.
- manages escalations.
- protects customer satisfaction.
- supports post-sale communication.
- tracks service commitments.
- measures service quality.
- improves retention.
- manages customer recovery.
- preserves complete service history.
- uses AI responsibly in customer support.

The Domain exists to ensure that customer service becomes a governed enterprise capability rather than a collection of disconnected:

- Calls.
- emails.
- WhatsApp messages.
- marketplace complaints.
- informal notes.
- employee memory.

Its permanent mission is:

> Resolve customer needs accurately, quickly, fairly, and consistently while preserving customer trust, operational accountability, commercial discipline, and enterprise learning.

---

# 1.2 Domain Mission

The Domain governs the complete post-sale service relationship.

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="customer-service-lifecycle"
Customer Need / Issue

↓

Service Request

↓

Classification

↓

Ownership

↓

Investigation

↓

Resolution

↓

Customer Communication

↓

Verification

↓

Closure

↓

Learning / Retention
```

The objective is not merely to "close tickets."

The objective is to produce a valid customer outcome.

---

# 1.3 Customer Service Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Customer Context Before Response

Support should understand:

- Customer.
- order.
- product.
- personalization.
- payment.
- shipment.
- previous interactions.

before responding where relevant.

---

## Resolution Before Closure

A Case should not be considered successful merely because its status became closed.

---

## Ownership Before Handoff

Every active issue requires accountable ownership.

---

## Evidence Before Blame

Customer complaints must be investigated against available evidence.

---

## Recovery Before Defensiveness

When the enterprise genuinely fails, service operations should prioritize appropriate recovery.

---

## Fairness Before Concession

Customer recovery should be fair and governed.

Not every complaint automatically warrants a refund.

---

## Communication Before Silence

Where resolution takes time, customers should receive appropriate status communication.

---

## Root Cause Before Recurrence

Recurring service problems must feed operational improvement.

---

## Human Judgment Before Irreversible Automation

AI may assist.

High-impact customer decisions remain governed.

---

# 1.4 Domain Objectives

The Domain permanently supports:

- Customer trust.
- Fast response.
- accurate resolution.
- clear ownership.
- consistent service.
- escalation discipline.
- complaint visibility.
- returns coordination.
- refund coordination.
- post-sale customer care.
- retention.
- service quality.
- operational learning.
- Customer Success.
- executive service visibility.

---

# 1.5 Domain Boundary

The Domain owns:

- Customer service cases.
- service requests.
- complaints.
- support queues.
- escalation.
- service commitments.
- customer-resolution workflow.
- customer recovery coordination.
- case communication.
- service-quality intelligence.
- Customer Success operations.
- customer health and retention intelligence where appropriately governed.

It does **not** replace:

- CRM.
- Order Management.
- Shipping.
- Finance.
- Quality.
- Sales.
- Commercial Governance.
- Product.

Canonical relationship:

```text id="service-domain-boundary"
CRM
Owns Customer Relationship Identity

↓

Customer Service
Owns Service Case & Resolution

↓

Operational Domains
Own Root Business Facts

↓

Customer Service
Coordinates Customer Outcome
```

---

# 1.6 Relationship With CRM

CRM remains authoritative for:

- Customer identity.
- contact details.
- account relationship.
- customer history.
- segmentation.

Customer Service owns:

- Support Cases.
- complaints.
- resolutions.
- service interactions.
- escalations.

Canonical distinction:

```text id="crm-service-boundary"
Customer
→ CRM

Customer Issue
→ Customer Service
```

---

# 1.7 Relationship With Order Management

Order Management owns:

- Order.
- order line.
- order status.
- fulfillment requirements.

Customer Service may investigate:

- Missing order.
- incorrect item.
- delayed order.
- cancellation.
- modification request.

It coordinates the resolution but does not independently rewrite Order truth.

---

# 1.8 Relationship With Shipping

Shipping owns:

- Shipment.
- carrier.
- tracking.
- dispatch.
- delivery events.

Customer Service consumes this information when resolving:

- Delayed delivery.
- lost parcel.
- damaged delivery.
- incorrect shipment.

---

# 1.9 Relationship With Finance

Finance owns:

- Payment.
- refund accounting.
- credit note.
- financial adjustment.

Customer Service may:

- Request refund.
- recommend service credit.
- communicate approved refund status.

It must not create uncontrolled financial transactions.

---

# 1.10 Relationship With Quality

Quality owns:

- Defect assessment.
- quality standards.
- non-conformance.
- corrective quality action.

Customer Service may capture a complaint such as:

- Product damaged.
- engraving incorrect.
- personalization defective.

Quality determines technical quality facts where required.

---

# 1.11 Relationship With Commercial Governance

Domain 31 governs:

- Discounts.
- service recovery concessions.
- commercial approval.
- Price Exceptions.

Customer Service may propose:

- Recovery discount.
- replacement.
- goodwill offer.

Commercial authority remains governed.

---

# 1.12 Relationship With Product

Product owns:

- Product definition.
- specification.
- variant.
- lifecycle.

Customer complaints can become Product intelligence.

Customer Service does not independently change Product standards.

---

# 1.13 Core Enterprise Capabilities

The permanent capability landscape includes:

| Capability | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Case Management | Manage customer issues |
| Service Request Management | Handle structured customer requests |
| Complaint Management | Govern complaints |
| Case Routing | Assign correct ownership |
| Queue Management | Manage support workload |
| SLA Management | Govern service commitments |
| Escalation Management | Handle unresolved/high-impact issues |
| Communication Management | Coordinate customer updates |
| Investigation Management | Establish service facts |
| Resolution Management | Define customer outcome |
| Return Coordination | Manage return requests |
| Replacement Coordination | Manage replacement fulfillment |
| Refund Coordination | Coordinate financial recovery |
| Service Recovery | Govern goodwill/remediation |
| Customer Success | Support customer outcomes and retention |
| Customer Health | Identify relationship risk |
| Retention Management | Reduce avoidable customer loss |
| Service Quality | Measure support effectiveness |
| Knowledge Support | Reuse known resolutions |
| Service Intelligence | Analyze support patterns |
| AI-Assisted Support | Improve support efficiency |
| Service Audit | Preserve service evidence |

---

# 1.14 Customer Service Case

A **Case** represents a governed customer issue or support requirement requiring investigation, action, communication, or resolution.

A Case should contain:

- Case ID.
- Customer.
- contact.
- source/channel.
- issue type.
- related Order/Product where applicable.
- priority.
- owner.
- status.
- service commitment.
- communication history.
- resolution.

---

# 1.15 Case Sources

Cases may originate through:

- Phone.
- email.
- WhatsApp.
- website.
- Shopify.
- Amazon.
- marketplace.
- social media.
- internal employee.
- in-person interaction.

The architecture should unify these into a single service model where practical.

---

# 1.16 Omnichannel Service Principle

Different channels should not create separate customer realities.

Canonical goal:

```text id="omnichannel-service"
WhatsApp

Email

Phone

Marketplace

Website

↓

Unified Customer Service Case
```

The exact technical integration may evolve.

---

# 1.17 Service Request

A **Service Request** is a customer request that may not represent a failure.

Examples:

- Order-status question.
- invoice request.
- personalization clarification.
- address update.
- product usage question.

Service Requests should remain distinguishable from complaints where useful.

---

# 1.18 Complaint

A **Complaint** represents customer dissatisfaction regarding:

- Product.
- service.
- delivery.
- communication.
- payment.
- personalization.
- staff interaction.
- policy.

Complaints require:

- Clear classification.
- acknowledgment.
- investigation.
- resolution.
- outcome.

---

# 1.19 Complaint Principle

A complaint is not automatically proof that the enterprise failed.

It is a verified customer expression requiring appropriate investigation.

Canonical model:

```text id="complaint-model"
Customer Complaint

↓

Evidence Collection

↓

Business Facts

↓

Finding

↓

Resolution
```

---

# 1.20 Complaint Categories

Potential categories include:

- Order Issue.
- Personalization Issue.
- Product Quality.
- Production Error.
- Delivery Delay.
- Shipping Damage.
- Missing Item.
- Wrong Item.
- Payment Issue.
- Refund Issue.
- Communication Issue.
- Marketplace Issue.
- Service Experience.

---

# 1.21 Service Priority

Cases may carry priority based on:

- Customer impact.
- urgency.
- promised date.
- financial impact.
- reputational risk.
- number of affected customers.

Potential levels:

- Low.
- Normal.
- High.
- Urgent.
- Critical.

Priority should reflect business impact rather than the emotional intensity of a message alone.

---

# 1.22 Case Severity

Priority and Severity are distinct.

Severity may represent objective impact such as:

- Minor inconvenience.
- material customer impact.
- fulfillment failure.
- major financial/reputational impact.
- systemic incident.

---

# 1.23 Case Status Model

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="case-status-model"
New

↓

Acknowledged

↓

Assigned

↓

In Progress

↓

Waiting on Customer
or
Waiting on Internal Action

↓

Resolved

↓

Customer Verification where needed

↓

Closed
```

Additional states may include:

- Escalated.
- Reopened.
- Cancelled.

---

# 1.24 Resolution vs Closure

Permanent distinction:

## Resolved

The enterprise believes an acceptable solution has been provided.

## Closed

The case lifecycle is complete according to policy.

A Case must not be closed simply to improve support metrics.

---

# 1.25 Case Ownership

Every active Case requires:

- Named owner.

or:

- Accountable queue/team.

Ownership must always be determinable.

"Someone is handling it" is not sufficient enterprise control.

---

# 1.26 Queue Management

Support queues may organize work by:

- Issue type.
- channel.
- marketplace.
- customer segment.
- priority.
- product.
- language.

Queues must support:

- Visible workload.
- assignment.
- aging.
- escalation.

---

# 1.27 Case Routing

Canonical routing:

```text id="case-routing"
New Case

↓

Classification

↓

Priority

↓

Required Skill / Domain

↓

Correct Queue / Owner
```

Routing may be automated within governed rules.

---

# 1.28 Service-Level Commitment

An SLA or service commitment defines expected:

- First response.
- investigation.
- resolution.
- customer update.

Different Case types may have different commitments.

---

# 1.29 SLA Principle

SLA targets exist to create predictable service.

They should not encourage superficial responses designed only to stop the clock.

---

# 1.30 First Response

The first response should ideally:

- Acknowledge the customer.
- confirm the issue.
- communicate ownership or next step.
- request genuinely missing information.

It should not repeatedly ask customers to provide information the enterprise already possesses.

---

# 1.31 Response Time

Response-time measurement may begin from:

- Case creation.

and end at:

- meaningful initial response.

Automated acknowledgments may be tracked separately from human/service resolution.

---

# 1.32 Resolution Time

Resolution Time measures how long the Case remains unresolved.

The architecture should distinguish:

- Total elapsed time.
- customer waiting time.
- internal processing time.

This helps diagnose service delays fairly.

---

# 1.33 Waiting on Customer

A Case may legitimately pause certain service timers while waiting for:

- Customer photo.
- clarification.
- confirmation.
- address.

Such pauses must remain visible and governed.

---

# 1.34 Internal Dependency

Cases may depend on:

- Production.
- Quality.
- Shipping.
- Finance.
- Inventory.
- Sales.

The customer-facing Case must retain one service owner even while internal tasks are delegated.

---

# 1.35 Investigation

Service investigation may gather:

- Order record.
- personalization submission.
- production record.
- QC result.
- shipping event.
- payment record.
- previous communications.

The objective is to establish an evidence-backed service finding.

---

# 1.36 Investigation Finding

Potential findings include:

- Enterprise Error Confirmed.
- Customer Input Issue.
- Carrier Issue.
- Marketplace Issue.
- No Defect Found.
- Shared Responsibility.
- Unable to Determine.

The finding should remain separate from the customer-resolution decision.

---

# 1.37 Resolution

A resolution is the business response to the Case.

Examples:

- Information provided.
- Order corrected.
- replacement.
- partial refund.
- full refund.
- service credit.
- apology.
- delivery intervention.
- no commercial remedy required.
- policy explanation.

---

# 1.38 Resolution Principle

The "right" resolution depends on:

```text id="resolution-principle"
Verified Facts

+

Customer Impact

+

Policy

+

Commercial Authority

+

Operational Feasibility

=

Customer Resolution
```

---

# 1.39 Replacement

A replacement may be appropriate when:

- Product defective.
- wrong product sent.
- personalization error attributable to enterprise.
- shipping damage.

Replacement requires coordination with:

- Orders.
- Production.
- Inventory.
- Shipping.

---

# 1.40 Refund

Refunds may be:

- Full.
- partial.
- shipping-only.
- adjustment.

Customer Service may recommend or initiate governed workflow.

Finance remains authoritative for financial execution.

---

# 1.41 Return

Return coordination may include:

- Eligibility.
- reason.
- return authorization.
- logistics.
- receipt.
- inspection.
- refund/replacement outcome.

Personalized goods may require specific policy treatment.

---

# 1.42 Customer Recovery

**Customer Recovery** addresses situations where customer trust has been damaged.

Potential recovery actions:

- Priority remake.
- expedited shipping.
- discount.
- credit.
- personal manager follow-up.
- apology.

Recovery should be proportionate to impact.

---

# 1.43 Service Recovery Governance

Recovery actions may require approval depending on:

- Monetary value.
- customer impact.
- margin.
- precedent.
- policy.

Customer Service must not create uncontrolled commercial concessions.

---

# 1.44 Goodwill

Goodwill may be granted even where contractual failure is unclear.

Goodwill should have:

- Reason.
- value.
- authority.
- customer context.

This makes relationship investment visible.

---

# 1.45 Escalation

Cases may escalate due to:

- SLA breach.
- customer impact.
- repeated failure.
- unresolved internal dependency.
- legal/reputational risk.
- high-value customer.
- executive attention requirement.

---

# 1.46 Escalation Lifecycle

```text id="service-escalation"
Case

↓

Escalation Trigger

↓

Higher Authority / Specialist

↓

Priority Review

↓

Resolution Plan

↓

Customer Communication
```

Escalation transfers attention.

It should not make the original Case lose ownership.

---

# 1.47 Functional Escalation

Functional escalation moves the issue to specialist expertise.

Examples:

- Quality.
- Finance.
- Shipping.
- Production.

---

# 1.48 Hierarchical Escalation

Hierarchical escalation raises management attention because of:

- Risk.
- delay.
- value.
- customer impact.

These escalation types should remain distinguishable.

---

# 1.49 Reopened Case

A Case may reopen if:

- Resolution failed.
- customer reports recurrence.
- promised action not completed.
- new evidence changes the finding.

Reopen history must remain visible.

---

# 1.50 Repeat Contact

Repeat contacts for the same issue should ideally connect to the existing Case.

This prevents:

- Duplicate work.
- contradictory replies.
- fragmented customer history.

---

# 1.51 Case Merge

Duplicate Cases may be merged where appropriate.

The original evidence and communications must remain preserved.

---

# 1.52 Parent and Child Cases

Large incidents may generate multiple customer Cases linked to a common parent issue.

Example:

```text id="parent-child-case"
Courier Disruption

↓

Parent Service Incident

↓

Customer Case A
Customer Case B
Customer Case C
```

This enables coordinated resolution.

---

# 1.53 Service Incident

A **Service Incident** represents a broader issue affecting multiple customers.

Examples:

- Shipment carrier disruption.
- payment outage.
- production defect batch.
- marketplace synchronization failure.

Individual customer Cases may link to it.

---

# 1.54 Customer Communication

All material communication should preserve:

- Channel.
- timestamp.
- sender.
- recipient.
- message context.
- Case association.

Communication history should support continuity even when ownership changes.

---

# 1.55 Communication Tone Governance

The enterprise should communicate:

- Clearly.
- respectfully.
- accurately.
- without unnecessary blame.
- without promises outside authority.

Customer-facing users should not promise:

- Refund.
- delivery.
- remake.
- compensation.

unless they have authority or validated feasibility.

---

# 1.56 Internal Note vs Customer Message

Permanent distinction:

## Internal Note

For internal investigation and coordination.

## Customer Communication

Visible to customer.

Internal notes must not accidentally be exposed externally.

---

# 1.57 Customer Consent and Preferences

Support communication should respect:

- Communication preference.
- applicable consent.
- privacy requirements.

Marketing consent remains separate from necessary service communication.

---

# 1.58 Customer Success

Customer Success expands beyond reactive complaint handling.

Its purpose is to help customers achieve successful outcomes with the business relationship.

For GiftHatke, this may include:

- Ensuring personalization details are complete.
- preventing order mistakes.
- proactive delivery communication.
- B2B account follow-up.
- repeat gifting support.

---

# 1.59 Reactive Support vs Customer Success

Canonical distinction:

```text id="support-vs-success"
Customer Support
Responds to Problems

Customer Success
Helps Prevent Problems
and
Build Ongoing Value
```

Both belong within the broader Domain but remain distinct capabilities.

---

# 1.60 Customer Health

Customer Health may reflect:

- Order success.
- unresolved issues.
- repeat purchase.
- complaints.
- relationship engagement.
- B2B activity.

Customer Health is an analytical construct.

It is not a moral judgment of the customer.

---

# 1.61 Customer Health States

Possible states:

- Healthy.
- Monitor.
- At Risk.
- Recovery Required.
- Insufficient Evidence.

Exact criteria must be governed.

---

# 1.62 Retention Risk

Retention Risk may increase due to:

- Repeated complaints.
- delayed resolution.
- order failures.
- refunds.
- poor communication.
- declining engagement.

This can trigger Customer Success action.

---

# 1.63 Churn

Where meaningful for repeat or B2B customers, churn may represent:

- Relationship inactivity.
- lost corporate account.
- significant decline in purchasing.

For one-time gifting customers, simplistic subscription-style churn definitions may not be appropriate.

---

# 1.64 Customer Win-Back

Win-back activity may support:

- Former B2B accounts.
- dissatisfied repeat customers.
- lapsed high-value relationships.

Commercial offers used for win-back must remain governed by Domain 31.

---

# 1.65 Post-Resolution Follow-Up

Some Cases may require follow-up after resolution.

Examples:

- Replacement delivered.
- refund completed.
- corporate customer recovery.
- major complaint.

Follow-up verifies the resolution produced the intended customer outcome.

---

# 1.66 Customer Satisfaction

Possible service feedback may include:

- CSAT.
- case feedback.
- complaint resolution satisfaction.

Feedback should be voluntary and proportionate.

---

# 1.67 CSAT Boundary

Customer satisfaction scores are useful but imperfect.

They may be influenced by:

- Product outcome.
- policy.
- delivery.
- representative interaction.

They should not automatically become an individual employee punishment mechanism.

---

# 1.68 Service Quality

Service Quality may evaluate:

- Response timeliness.
- resolution accuracy.
- communication quality.
- reopen rate.
- escalation.
- customer outcome.

Quality must balance speed and correctness.

---

# 1.69 First Contact Resolution

First Contact Resolution may be useful where applicable.

However:

```text id="fcr-principle"
Fast One-Contact Closure

≠

Successful Resolution
```

Complex issues may appropriately require investigation.

---

# 1.70 Case Reopen Rate

High Reopen Rate may indicate:

- Incomplete resolution.
- premature closure.
- communication failure.
- operational follow-through failure.

This becomes a service-quality signal.

---

# 1.71 Escalation Rate

High escalation may indicate:

- Complex case mix.
- insufficient frontline authority.
- training gaps.
- process weakness.

It should not automatically be interpreted as poor employee performance.

---

# 1.72 Service Backlog

Backlog should be analyzed by:

- Priority.
- age.
- owner.
- category.
- dependency.

Total case count alone may be misleading.

---

# 1.73 Aging

Cases may be grouped:

- New.
- due soon.
- overdue.
- severely overdue.

Aging helps prioritize attention.

---

# 1.74 SLA Breach

A breach may trigger:

- Manager attention.
- escalation.
- customer update.
- root-cause review.

The system must distinguish breaches caused by:

- Internal delay.
- waiting on customer.
- external dependency.

---

# 1.75 Service Knowledge

Common issues and resolutions should become reusable knowledge.

Examples:

- How to submit personalization.
- delivery-status explanation.
- refund policy.
- care instructions.
- common troubleshooting.

This reduces repeated manual work.

---

# 1.76 Knowledge Article Boundary

The Knowledge Domain owns the enterprise knowledge architecture.

Customer Service consumes and contributes service knowledge.

Approved customer-facing guidance should be governed and versioned.

---

# 1.77 Service Templates

Templates may support:

- Acknowledgment.
- delay update.
- replacement confirmation.
- refund update.
- resolution.

Templates must not cause robotic responses where specific customer context matters.

---

# 1.78 Service Automation

Automation may assist with:

- Case creation.
- classification.
- routing.
- acknowledgment.
- reminders.
- SLA alerts.
- knowledge suggestions.

Automation should remove repetitive work without hiding unresolved customer needs.

---

# 1.79 AI-Assisted Support

AI may assist with:

- Case summarization.
- classification.
- routing.
- draft responses.
- knowledge retrieval.
- sentiment/context identification.
- suggested resolutions.
- recurring-issue detection.

---

# 1.80 AI Support Authority Boundary

AI may not independently make high-impact decisions such as:

- Approve significant refund.
- approve major compensation.
- accuse customer of fraud.
- permanently reject a legitimate claim.
- modify financial records.
- alter historical service evidence.

Human authority remains governed.

---

# 1.81 AI Response Grounding

AI-generated support responses should be grounded in:

- Customer Case.
- Order.
- policy.
- product.
- shipping.
- authorized knowledge.

AI must not invent:

- Delivery promises.
- refund completion.
- inventory availability.
- replacement status.

---

# 1.82 AI Confidence

Where AI suggests classification or resolution, uncertainty should remain visible where material.

Example:

```text id="ai-case-confidence"
Suggested Category:
Shipping Damage

Confidence:
Moderate

Reason:
Customer reports broken acrylic after delivery

Action:
Agent Review
```

---

# 1.83 Sentiment Intelligence

Sentiment may help prioritize customer attention.

It must not become the sole basis for:

- Case validity.
- compensation.
- escalation.

A calm customer can have a severe issue.

An angry customer can have a low-severity issue.

---

# 1.84 Service Fraud and Abuse Boundary

The enterprise may identify suspicious support patterns such as:

- repeated unsupported refund requests.
- coupon/recovery abuse.
- contradictory claims.

Such signals require investigation.

They are not proof of wrongdoing.

---

# 1.85 Customer Vulnerability & Fairness

Where customers may require additional accessibility or service support, the enterprise should provide reasonable treatment consistent with applicable policy and law.

Service optimization must not penalize customers simply because they require more assistance.

---

# 1.86 GiftHatke Service Architecture

GiftHatke Customer Service must support a personalized-product environment where many service issues depend on:

- Customer-submitted personalization.
- manufacturing.
- QC.
- packaging.
- shipping.

Canonical context:

```text id="gift-service-context"
Customer

↓

Order

↓

Personalization

↓

Production

↓

Quality

↓

Shipping

↓

Service Case
```

---

# 1.87 GiftHatke Personalization Support

Potential cases include:

- Photo not received.
- text missing.
- name spelling clarification.
- customer approval pending.
- requested design correction.

These should connect to the Personalization workflow rather than exist as isolated conversations.

---

# 1.88 GiftHatke Personalization Complaint

Example:

```text id="gift-personalization-complaint"
Customer Says:
Name Engraved Incorrectly

↓

Check Submitted Personalization

↓

Check Production Record

↓

Check QC

↓

Determine Cause

↓

Resolve
```

The system should establish whether the discrepancy arose from:

- Customer submission.
- internal transcription.
- production.
- design interpretation.

---

# 1.89 GiftHatke Production Complaint

Potential issues:

- Engraving defect.
- acrylic scratch.
- printing error.
- incorrect dimensions.
- incomplete item.

Customer Service coordinates with Production and Quality.

---

# 1.90 GiftHatke Shipping Complaint

Potential cases:

- Shipment delayed.
- package damaged.
- delivery marked complete but not received.
- wrong address.
- courier issue.

Shipping remains authoritative for shipment facts.

---

# 1.91 GiftHatke Marketplace Support

Marketplace Cases may originate from:

- Amazon.
- future Flipkart.
- future Meesho.

The system should preserve:

- Marketplace Order ID.
- channel.
- marketplace communication context.
- internal Case.

---

# 1.92 GiftHatke Corporate/B2B Support

Corporate customers may require:

- Dedicated Case handling.
- bulk-order tracking.
- invoice support.
- delivery coordination.
- post-delivery issue management.
- repeat-order follow-up.

Account context from CRM should remain visible.

---

# 1.93 GiftHatke Customer Success Executive Workspace

A frontline Customer Success Executive should eventually see:

```text id="gift-customer-success-workspace"
Today's New Cases

↓

Urgent Customer Issues

↓

Orders Awaiting Customer Details

↓

Shipping Delays

↓

Refund / Replacement Follow-Ups

↓

Cases Waiting on Internal Teams

↓

Customers Requiring Follow-Up
```

This creates a manageable daily operating queue.

---

# 1.94 GiftHatke Proactive Customer Success

The Domain should eventually support proactive actions such as:

- Contact customer when personalization is incomplete.
- inform customer before a known delay.
- follow up after a significant service recovery.
- remind B2B customer of approved repeat-order arrangements.

This reduces avoidable complaints.

---

# 1.95 GiftHatke Customer Recovery

Example:

```text id="gift-customer-recovery"
Enterprise Error Confirmed

↓

Customer Impact Assessed

↓

Possible Recovery:
Remake
Priority Production
Refund
Discount
Goodwill

↓

Commercial / Finance Approval if Required

↓

Customer Communication

↓

Outcome Verification
```

---

# 1.96 GiftHatke Refund Boundary

Customer Service may initiate a refund request.

Finance must confirm execution.

The customer-facing Case should show:

- Requested.
- approved.
- processing.
- completed.

The service representative must not claim a refund is completed before authoritative confirmation.

---

# 1.97 GiftHatke Replacement Boundary

A replacement requires:

```text id="gift-replacement"
Replacement Approved

↓

Order / Production Task

↓

Production

↓

QC

↓

Shipping

↓

Customer Follow-Up
```

The Case remains linked through the full recovery process.

---

# 1.98 GiftHatke Service Recovery Discount

If the resolution includes a future discount:

Domain 31 governs:

- Value.
- eligibility.
- expiry.
- approval.

Customer Service owns the customer-recovery context.

---

# 1.99 GiftHatke Service Intelligence

Potential service intelligence includes:

- Complaint rate by product.
- complaint rate by channel.
- personalization issue rate.
- delivery complaint rate.
- replacement rate.
- refund rate.
- reopen rate.
- average resolution time.
- customer-recovery outcome.

---

# 1.100 Product Complaint Feedback Loop

Canonical loop:

```text id="product-complaint-feedback"
Customer Complaints

↓

Pattern Detected

↓

Quality / Product Investigation

↓

Root Cause

↓

Product / Process Improvement

↓

Future Complaint Reduction
```

This turns support into enterprise learning.

---

# 1.101 Shipping Complaint Feedback Loop

Repeated shipping complaints may trigger review of:

- Carrier.
- packaging.
- address validation.
- dispatch process.
- service promise.

---

# 1.102 Personalization Complaint Feedback Loop

Recurring personalization errors may indicate weakness in:

- Intake form.
- asset mapping.
- customer confirmation.
- design workflow.
- production handoff.

Support intelligence should expose these patterns.

---

# 1.103 Service Performance Indicators

Potential measures include:

- Case volume.
- First Response Time.
- Resolution Time.
- SLA compliance.
- reopen rate.
- escalation rate.
- CSAT.
- refund rate.
- replacement rate.
- complaint recurrence.

Final KPI governance belongs to Domain 30.

---

# 1.104 Customer Success Indicators

Potential measures include:

- Repeat-order health.
- unresolved high-value accounts.
- service recovery success.
- B2B retention.
- proactive intervention success.

Exact definitions must be governed.

---

# 1.105 Service Analytics Boundary

Domain 32 defines service meaning.

Domain 30 governs KPI architecture.

Domain 7 Reporting & BI presents the information.

Canonical relationship:

```text id="service-analytics-boundary"
Customer Service
Defines Service Meaning

↓

Performance Management
Defines KPIs

↓

Reporting & BI
Presents Performance
```

---

# 1.106 Service Auditability

The platform should answer:

- Who reported the issue?
- when?
- what Order was affected?
- who owned the Case?
- what evidence was reviewed?
- what finding was reached?
- what resolution was approved?
- what was communicated?
- was the resolution completed?

This creates service integrity.

---

# 1.107 Customer Communication Audit

Material customer messages should remain attached to:

- Case.
- timestamp.
- channel.
- sender.

This enables continuity and dispute reconstruction.

---

# 1.108 Privacy & Data Minimization

Service Cases may contain:

- Contact information.
- address.
- images.
- Order information.
- complaint details.

Access must follow:

- Role.
- need-to-know.
- privacy classification.

Unnecessary sensitive information should not be copied into Case notes.

---

# 1.109 Service Retention

Case records may require retention based on:

- Legal.
- business.
- complaint.
- financial.
- warranty.
- customer relationship requirements.

Domain 29 governs Information Lifecycle principles.

---

# 1.110 Technology Independence

The Domain may eventually be implemented through:

- CRM service modules.
- Helpdesk platforms.
- omnichannel support systems.
- ticketing systems.
- contact-center tools.
- custom service applications.
- AI support assistants.

No vendor becomes the Customer Service architecture.

The Canon remains authoritative.

---

# 1.111 SMP1 Relevance

During **SMP1**, the standalone platform should preserve existing customer-service-relevant business history where available, including:

- Customer.
- Order.
- personalization.
- fulfillment.
- financial relationship.
- notes or existing support evidence.

Migration must not fabricate historical Cases that never existed.

---

# 1.112 SMP1 Service Continuity Rule

Canonical rule:

```text id="smp1-service-continuity"
Certified Existing Customer / Order History

↓

Standalone Migration

↓

Service Context Preserved

↓

Future Unified Customer Service
```

The standalone platform may introduce a much stronger service architecture after migration without redesigning historical facts.

---

# 1.113 Standalone v1.0 Foundation

Standalone v1.0 should provide enough reliable business context to support future Service Management:

- Stable Customer IDs.
- Order IDs.
- personalization relationships.
- shipping relationships.
- financial references.
- timestamps.
- role access.

Full advanced helpdesk capability need not exist at the first migration cutover unless included in certified scope.

---

# 1.114 ERP9 Relevance

After standalone certification, ERP9 may expand configurable service master data such as:

- Case categories.
- escalation reasons.
- service priorities.
- recovery policies.
- ownership settings.

These must implement this Canon.

---

# 1.115 ERP10 Relevance

ERP10 final enterprise polish should validate:

- Support usability.
- Case ownership.
- escalation clarity.
- Order/service context.
- resolution traceability.
- customer-recovery governance.
- service auditability.

---

# 1.116 Future Customer Service Evolution

The Domain supports future evolution toward:

- Unified omnichannel support.
- advanced Customer Success.
- predictive service.
- proactive issue prevention.
- conversational AI.
- automated case triage.
- customer-health analytics.
- intelligent service recovery.

Advanced automation remains subordinate to governance.

---

# 1.117 Permanent Domain Principles

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** permanently follows:

- Customer context before response.
- ownership before handoff.
- evidence before blame.
- resolution before closure.
- communication before silence.
- fairness before concession.
- root cause before recurrence.
- service recovery before defensiveness where failure is confirmed.
- trusted facts before automated response.
- human accountability before irreversible customer decisions.

---

# ENTERPRISE CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SERVICE MANAGEMENT & SUPPORT OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 2 — Service Entity Model, Case Architecture & Customer Relationship Service Structure Canon

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** requires a permanent information architecture defining how the enterprise represents:

- Customer Cases.
- Service Requests.
- Complaints.
- Investigations.
- resolutions.
- customer communications.
- escalations.
- returns.
- refunds.
- replacements.
- service recovery.
- Customer Success activity.
- customer health.
- retention risk.
- service knowledge.
- service incidents.
- service audit evidence.

Stage 1 established the Domain foundation, service philosophy, authority boundaries, and high-level service lifecycle.

Stage 2 defines the canonical entity architecture that future GiftHatkeOS implementations must preserve even as technologies change.

The objective is to ensure that every service interaction can answer:

- Who is the customer?
- What happened?
- What business object is affected?
- What is the issue?
- Who owns it?
- What evidence exists?
- What has been communicated?
- What action is pending?
- What resolution was approved?
- Was the customer outcome actually completed?

---

# 2.2 Service Entity Principles

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Customer Before Case Fragmentation

Service interactions should remain connected to the authoritative Customer relationship.

---

## Case Before Conversation Fragmentation

Multiple communications concerning the same issue should normally remain connected to the same Case.

---

## Evidence Before Finding

A service finding should emerge from verified context.

---

## Finding Before Resolution

The business should distinguish what happened from what it chooses to do about it.

---

## Resolution Before Closure

A Case is not complete merely because an action was recorded.

---

## Parent Context Before Child Task

Internal tasks remain subordinate to the customer-facing Case.

---

## Version Before Historical Mutation

Material policy, resolution, and communication history must remain reconstructable.

---

# 2.3 Canonical Service Entity Landscape

The permanent service entity architecture includes:

| Entity | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Customer Service Case | Governs customer issue lifecycle |
| Service Request | Represents structured support request |
| Complaint | Represents customer dissatisfaction |
| Case Category | Classifies issue type |
| Case Priority | Represents urgency/attention |
| Case Severity | Represents objective impact |
| Case Status | Represents lifecycle state |
| Case Owner | Defines accountability |
| Service Queue | Groups operational workload |
| Case Assignment | Records ownership transitions |
| Service SLA | Defines service commitment |
| SLA Clock | Tracks timing obligations |
| Service Interaction | Represents communication/contact |
| Customer Message | Customer-visible communication |
| Internal Case Note | Internal service context |
| Case Attachment | Connects evidence/assets |
| Case Relationship | Links Case to enterprise objects |
| Investigation | Governs fact-finding |
| Evidence Record | Captures supporting evidence |
| Investigation Finding | Records evaluated conclusion |
| Resolution | Defines intended customer outcome |
| Resolution Action | Represents work needed to resolve |
| Return Request | Governs returned-goods flow |
| Replacement Request | Governs replacement flow |
| Refund Request | Governs financial recovery request |
| Goodwill / Recovery Request | Governs customer recovery concession |
| Service Escalation | Represents increased attention/authority |
| Service Incident | Represents broader multi-customer issue |
| Parent/Child Case Link | Connects related Cases |
| Case Merge Record | Preserves duplicate consolidation |
| Case Reopen Record | Preserves reopen history |
| Service Commitment | Represents promise made to customer |
| Customer Follow-Up | Governs post-resolution contact |
| Customer Health Record | Represents relationship-health state |
| Retention Risk Record | Represents potential customer loss |
| Customer Success Action | Represents proactive relationship action |
| Service Knowledge Reference | Links approved guidance |
| Service Template | Represents controlled reusable communication |
| Customer Feedback Record | Captures service feedback |
| Service Quality Record | Evaluates service effectiveness |
| Service Risk | Represents support/customer risk |
| Service Audit Record | Preserves service evidence |

---

# 2.4 Customer Service Case

The **Customer Service Case** is the central operational entity of the Domain.

A Case should contain:

- Case ID.
- Customer reference.
- contact reference.
- source channel.
- Case type.
- category.
- priority.
- severity.
- current owner.
- current queue.
- current status.
- related Order/Product/Shipment where applicable.
- SLA.
- created time.
- last activity.
- resolution.
- closure information.

Canonical topology:

```text id="case-topology"
Customer

↓

Case

↓

Issue Context

↓

Investigation

↓

Resolution

↓

Customer Outcome
```

---

# 2.5 Case Identity

Every Case requires a stable unique identity.

This supports:

- Cross-channel continuity.
- audit.
- escalation.
- reopen history.
- reporting.
- references in internal workflows.

Case IDs must remain stable across platform migration.

---

# 2.6 Case Type

Case Type may classify the broad business purpose.

Examples:

- Question.
- Service Request.
- Complaint.
- Return.
- Refund.
- Replacement.
- Customer Success Follow-Up.
- Marketplace Support.
- B2B Support.

Case Type is broader than Case Category.

---

# 2.7 Case Category

A Case Category provides structured issue classification.

Potential hierarchy:

```text id="case-category-hierarchy"
Order Issue

→ Order Status
→ Modification
→ Cancellation

Personalization

→ Missing Input
→ Wrong Text
→ Wrong Image
→ Approval Delay

Product Quality

→ Damage
→ Scratch
→ Engraving Error
→ Printing Error

Shipping

→ Delay
→ Damage
→ Lost
→ Wrong Delivery
```

Categories should remain governable rather than becoming uncontrolled free text.

---

# 2.8 Case Subcategory

Subcategories allow more specific service intelligence without overloading users.

Example:

```text id="case-subcategory"
Category:
Shipping

Subcategory:
Delayed Delivery
```

Subcategories should remain optional where unnecessary.

---

# 2.9 Case Priority Entity

Priority represents how quickly the enterprise should act.

Priority may consider:

- Customer impact.
- urgency.
- deadline.
- financial exposure.
- reputational exposure.

Potential values:

- Low.
- Normal.
- High.
- Urgent.
- Critical.

---

# 2.10 Case Severity Entity

Severity represents objective service impact.

Potential values:

- Minor.
- Moderate.
- Major.
- Severe.
- Critical.

Priority and Severity may differ.

Example:

A low-value but wedding-day personalization failure may have high Priority due to irreversibility.

---

# 2.11 Case Status Entity

The canonical lifecycle includes:

```text id="case-status-entity"
New

↓

Acknowledged

↓

Assigned

↓

In Progress

↓

Waiting on Customer
or
Waiting on Internal Team

↓

Resolved

↓

Verification / Follow-Up if Required

↓

Closed
```

Additional governed states:

- Escalated.
- Reopened.
- Cancelled.

---

# 2.12 Status Transition Integrity

Not every status may transition directly to every other status.

Example:

```text id="case-status-transition"
New
→ Assigned

Assigned
→ In Progress

In Progress
→ Waiting / Resolved

Resolved
→ Closed / Reopened
```

Controlled transitions improve auditability.

---

# 2.13 Case Owner

The Case Owner represents accountable service responsibility.

The owner may be:

- Named employee.
- service team.
- queue.

However, accountability must remain determinable.

---

# 2.14 Case Assignment

A **Case Assignment** records:

- Previous owner.
- new owner.
- timestamp.
- reason.
- assigning actor.

This preserves handoff history.

---

# 2.15 Ownership Transfer

Canonical transfer:

```text id="case-owner-transfer"
Current Owner

↓

Handoff Reason

↓

New Owner Accepts / Assignment Commits

↓

Case Ownership Changes
```

The Case should never enter an unowned state unintentionally.

---

# 2.16 Service Queue Entity

A Queue may group Cases by:

- Function.
- channel.
- marketplace.
- priority.
- category.
- B2B/customer segment.

Examples:

- General Support.
- Personalization Support.
- Shipping Issues.
- Refunds.
- Corporate Accounts.
- Amazon Support.

---

# 2.17 Queue Membership

Queue membership should be based on:

- Role.
- skill.
- authorization.
- workload.

Technical queue membership does not necessarily confer authority to approve refunds or discounts.

---

# 2.18 Service Request Entity

A **Service Request** represents a request for assistance without necessarily asserting service failure.

Examples:

- Send invoice.
- update address.
- clarify personalization.
- provide order status.

A Service Request may be represented as a specialized Case type or related entity.

The business meaning must remain preserved.

---

# 2.19 Complaint Entity

A **Complaint** represents explicit dissatisfaction.

It should contain:

- Complaint ID.
- related Case.
- complaint category.
- customer allegation/statement.
- impact.
- date received.
- finding.
- resolution.

Complaint and Case may be one-to-one or one-to-many depending on technical design.

---

# 2.20 Complaint Statement

The original customer complaint should remain distinguishable from internal interpretation.

Example:

```text id="complaint-statement"
Customer Statement:
"Name is wrong on the lamp."

Internal Finding:
Customer entered different spelling in submitted form.
```

This distinction protects factual integrity.

---

# 2.21 Case Relationship Entity

A Case may relate to:

- Customer.
- Order.
- Order Line.
- Product.
- Personalization Asset.
- Production Job.
- QC record.
- Shipment.
- Payment.
- Refund.
- Quote.
- Marketplace Order.

The relationship should be explicit rather than hidden in free text.

---

# 2.22 Multi-Object Case Context

Some Cases may require several related records.

Example:

```text id="multi-object-case"
Case

↓

Order #123

↓

Order Line:
Acrylic Lamp

↓

Personalization Asset

↓

Production Job

↓

Shipment
```

This creates complete operational context.

---

# 2.23 Service Interaction Entity

A **Service Interaction** represents a communication or contact event.

Types may include:

- Incoming message.
- outgoing response.
- phone call.
- internal callback.
- marketplace message.
- social contact.

Each Interaction should preserve:

- timestamp.
- channel.
- direction.
- actor.
- recipient/sender.
- related Case.

---

# 2.24 Customer Message

A **Customer Message** represents communication visible to the customer.

It may contain:

- Text.
- attachment references.
- channel.
- timestamp.
- sending agent/system.
- delivery status where available.

---

# 2.25 Internal Case Note

An Internal Case Note may record:

- Investigation observations.
- coordination context.
- next step.
- internal reasoning.

It must be clearly distinguished from customer-visible communication.

---

# 2.26 Internal Note Security

Internal Notes may contain sensitive operational information.

Access should follow role-based controls.

They must never be unintentionally exposed externally.

---

# 2.27 Case Attachment

Attachments may include:

- Customer photo.
- damaged-product image.
- invoice.
- carrier evidence.
- personalization reference.
- screenshot.

Attachments should link to Digital Asset Management where appropriate.

---

# 2.28 Evidence Record

An **Evidence Record** represents information used during investigation.

Potential sources:

- Customer image.
- submitted personalization.
- production record.
- QC record.
- shipment scan.
- payment record.
- conversation.

Evidence should preserve source and integrity context.

---

# 2.29 Investigation Entity

An Investigation records:

- Issue to investigate.
- responsible investigator/team.
- evidence reviewed.
- hypotheses.
- findings.
- status.
- timestamps.

Not every simple Case requires a complex Investigation entity.

Complex complaints may.

---

# 2.30 Investigation Lifecycle

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="investigation-lifecycle"
Investigation Required

↓

Evidence Collected

↓

Facts Reviewed

↓

Possible Causes Considered

↓

Finding Established

↓

Investigation Closed
```

---

# 2.31 Investigation Finding

Potential findings include:

- Enterprise Error Confirmed.
- Customer Input Mismatch.
- Production Error.
- Carrier Error.
- Marketplace Error.
- Product Defect.
- No Defect Found.
- Shared Responsibility.
- Unable to Determine.

These should remain governed classifications.

---

# 2.32 Finding Confidence

Where evidence is incomplete, the finding may include:

- Confirmed.
- Probable.
- Inconclusive.

The enterprise should not manufacture certainty.

---

# 2.33 Resolution Entity

A **Resolution** defines the service outcome chosen for a Case.

It should preserve:

- Resolution type.
- reason.
- decision authority.
- action required.
- customer communication.
- effective/completion state.

---

# 2.34 Resolution Types

Potential resolution types:

- Information Provided.
- Correction.
- Replacement.
- Refund.
- Partial Refund.
- Return.
- Service Credit.
- Recovery Discount.
- Expedited Fulfillment.
- Policy Explanation.
- No Remedy Required.

---

# 2.35 Resolution Action

A Resolution may require one or more execution actions.

Example:

```text id="resolution-action"
Resolution:
Replacement

Actions:

Create Replacement Job

↓

Production

↓

QC

↓

Shipment

↓

Customer Follow-Up
```

Resolution and execution must remain distinct.

---

# 2.36 Resolution Completion

A Resolution becomes complete only when required actions are completed.

Example:

Refund approved is not the same as refund completed.

---

# 2.37 Customer Verification

Some Cases may require customer confirmation.

Examples:

- Replacement received.
- corrected personalization accepted.
- issue resolved.

Verification may be explicit or inferred by policy.

---

# 2.38 Return Request Entity

A Return Request should preserve:

- Customer.
- Order/Line.
- reason.
- eligibility.
- authorization.
- return method.
- received status.
- inspection.
- outcome.

---

# 2.39 Return Lifecycle

```text id="return-lifecycle"
Requested

↓

Eligibility Evaluated

↓

Authorized / Rejected

↓

Return In Transit

↓

Received

↓

Inspected

↓

Refund / Replacement / Other Outcome

↓

Closed
```

---

# 2.40 Personalized Goods Return Context

Personalized items may have restricted return eligibility.

The Case architecture should distinguish:

- Product defect.
- enterprise personalization error.
- customer-supplied incorrect details.
- change-of-mind request.

Policy remains governed by applicable commercial/legal rules.

---

# 2.41 Replacement Request Entity

A Replacement Request should contain:

- Original Order.
- affected line.
- replacement reason.
- approval.
- production requirement.
- shipping requirement.
- status.

---

# 2.42 Replacement Lifecycle

```text id="replacement-lifecycle"
Requested

↓

Approved

↓

Replacement Order / Job Created

↓

Production

↓

QC

↓

Shipment

↓

Delivered

↓

Outcome Verified
```

---

# 2.43 Refund Request Entity

A Refund Request represents a request for financial recovery.

It contains:

- Related Case.
- Order/payment.
- requested amount.
- refund reason.
- approval.
- Finance reference.
- status.

---

# 2.44 Refund Lifecycle

```text id="refund-lifecycle"
Requested

↓

Eligibility / Authority Review

↓

Approved / Rejected

↓

Finance Processing

↓

Refund Executed

↓

Customer Informed

↓

Case Updated
```

---

# 2.45 Refund Status Integrity

Possible states:

- Requested.
- Under Review.
- Approved.
- Rejected.
- Processing.
- Completed.
- Failed.
- Cancelled.

Customer Service must not claim "Completed" until Finance confirms authoritative completion.

---

# 2.46 Goodwill / Recovery Request

A Goodwill or Recovery Request represents non-standard customer recovery such as:

- Coupon.
- future discount.
- free shipping.
- upgrade.
- gift addition.

It should contain:

- Reason.
- requested value.
- authority.
- expiry.
- customer relationship.

---

# 2.47 Commercial Recovery Relationship

Canonical relationship:

```text id="commercial-recovery"
Service Case

↓

Recovery Need

↓

Domain 31 Commercial Governance

↓

Approved Recovery Instrument

↓

Customer Communication
```

---

# 2.48 Service Escalation Entity

An Escalation records:

- Case.
- escalation type.
- reason.
- severity.
- destination.
- timestamp.
- expected action.
- resolution.

---

# 2.49 Escalation Types

Canonical types:

- Functional.
- Hierarchical.
- SLA.
- Legal/Compliance.
- Reputational.
- Executive.

Exact classifications may evolve.

---

# 2.50 Escalation State

Possible states:

- Open.
- Acknowledged.
- Actioned.
- Resolved.
- Cancelled.

Escalation does not replace Case status.

---

# 2.51 Service Incident Entity

A Service Incident represents a systemic issue affecting multiple customers or Cases.

Examples:

- Carrier outage.
- payment gateway failure.
- batch production defect.
- marketplace integration outage.

---

# 2.52 Incident-to-Case Relationship

Canonical topology:

```text id="incident-case-topology"
Service Incident

↓

Affected Cases

↓

Individual Customer Resolutions
```

One Incident can explain many Cases.

Each customer still requires appropriate handling.

---

# 2.53 Parent Case

A Parent Case may coordinate:

- Family of related Cases.
- enterprise customer issue with multiple Orders.
- systemic B2B issue.

Parent Cases should not obscure child-level customer obligations.

---

# 2.54 Child Case

A Child Case retains:

- Own Customer impact.
- actions.
- status.
- resolution.

even when linked to common Parent context.

---

# 2.55 Case Merge Record

When duplicate Cases are merged, preserve:

- Primary Case.
- merged Case IDs.
- reason.
- timestamp.
- prior communications.

Nothing material should disappear.

---

# 2.56 Reopened Case Record

A Reopen Record should preserve:

- Previous resolution.
- reopen reason.
- new evidence.
- timestamp.
- owner.

This helps analyze premature closure.

---

# 2.57 Service Commitment Entity

A **Service Commitment** represents a promise made to the customer.

Examples:

- Callback by date.
- replacement dispatch by date.
- refund update tomorrow.
- investigation result by date.

Commitments should be tracked.

---

# 2.58 Commitment Lifecycle

```text id="service-commitment-lifecycle"
Commitment Made

↓

Due Date

↓

Completed / Missed / Revised

↓

Customer Updated
```

Missed commitments are important service-quality events.

---

# 2.59 Commitment Authority

A service representative should only make commitments within:

- Actual authority.
- operational feasibility.

The platform should discourage unrealistic promises.

---

# 2.60 Customer Follow-Up Entity

Follow-Up may preserve:

- Customer.
- Case.
- reason.
- due date.
- owner.
- outcome.

Examples:

- Confirm replacement.
- check refund receipt.
- B2B recovery follow-up.

---

# 2.61 Follow-Up Types

Potential types:

- Resolution Verification.
- Customer Recovery.
- Relationship Follow-Up.
- B2B Success Review.
- Win-Back.

---

# 2.62 Customer Success Action

A Customer Success Action represents proactive activity intended to improve customer outcome.

Examples:

- Request missing personalization before delay.
- notify customer about potential shipping issue.
- confirm repeat corporate requirements.
- check satisfaction after major recovery.

---

# 2.63 Customer Success Action Lifecycle

```text id="customer-success-action"
Opportunity / Risk Identified

↓

Action Planned

↓

Owner Assigned

↓

Customer Contact / Internal Action

↓

Outcome Recorded
```

---

# 2.64 Customer Health Record

A Customer Health Record may contain:

- Customer/account.
- health state.
- contributing indicators.
- date.
- confidence.
- owner/reviewer.

Health may be especially relevant for repeat and B2B customers.

---

# 2.65 Customer Health Inputs

Potential inputs:

- Recent complaints.
- unresolved Cases.
- repeat purchase.
- delivery success.
- payment quality.
- B2B engagement.
- customer feedback.

The scoring method must remain explainable.

---

# 2.66 Retention Risk Record

Retention Risk may contain:

- Customer.
- risk level.
- contributing reasons.
- value/relationship context.
- recommended action.
- owner.
- state.

---

# 2.67 Retention Risk States

Possible states:

- Low.
- Monitor.
- At Risk.
- Critical.
- Insufficient Evidence.

These are relationship-risk states, not judgments of customer worth.

---

# 2.68 Win-Back Entity

A Win-Back activity may relate to:

- Lapsed corporate account.
- previously dissatisfied repeat customer.

It may contain:

- reason for lapse.
- prior history.
- recovery plan.
- outcome.

Commercial offers remain governed by Domain 31.

---

# 2.69 Customer Feedback Record

Feedback may capture:

- CSAT.
- free-text feedback.
- survey response.
- rating.
- related Case.
- timestamp.

Feedback must not overwrite the Case finding.

---

# 2.70 Service Quality Record

A Service Quality Record may evaluate:

- Case handling.
- communication.
- process adherence.
- resolution quality.
- follow-through.

This is distinct from employee performance evaluation.

---

# 2.71 Service Risk Entity

Potential service risks:

- High backlog.
- SLA breach.
- repeated product complaint.
- refund backlog.
- carrier issue.
- unresolved B2B issue.
- systemic personalization failure.

Service Risk may connect to Enterprise Risk governance.

---

# 2.72 Service Knowledge Reference

A Case may reference approved knowledge such as:

- Policy.
- SOP.
- troubleshooting guide.
- refund guidance.
- product-care instructions.

Knowledge remains governed by the Enterprise Knowledge Domain.

---

# 2.73 Service Template Entity

A Service Template may define reusable customer communication.

It should include:

- Template ID.
- purpose.
- channel.
- language.
- version.
- approval state.

Templates should support customization.

---

# 2.74 Template Versioning

If policy changes, older communications should remain associated with the template version used at that time where relevant.

---

# 2.75 Case Communication Thread

The Case should support a chronological service timeline.

Example:

```text id="case-communication-thread"
09:00 Customer Email

09:05 Automated Acknowledgment

09:30 Agent Response

11:00 Internal Shipping Update

11:15 Customer Update

15:00 Resolution Confirmed
```

This enables continuity.

---

# 2.76 Case Timeline

The Case Timeline may combine:

- Communication.
- assignments.
- status changes.
- escalations.
- evidence.
- resolutions.
- internal actions.

This becomes the complete customer-service narrative.

---

# 2.77 Case Activity Entity

A generic Case Activity may represent:

- Note.
- phone call.
- email.
- assignment.
- status change.
- task.
- escalation.
- customer response.

The exact technical model may use specialized entities or an event timeline.

Business meaning must remain preserved.

---

# 2.78 Case Task Entity

Internal actions may become Case Tasks.

Examples:

- Ask Production to inspect job.
- request carrier investigation.
- confirm Finance refund.

Tasks should preserve:

- Owner.
- due date.
- status.
- Case relationship.

---

# 2.79 Case Task Boundary

A Case Task does not replace the Case.

Canonical distinction:

```text id="case-task-boundary"
Customer Problem
→ Case

Internal Work
→ Case Task
```

---

# 2.80 Internal Dependency Entity

A Case may depend on another Domain.

Dependency may record:

- Domain.
- required action.
- owner.
- due state.
- returned result.

This supports visible internal coordination.

---

# 2.81 Dependency States

Possible states:

- Requested.
- acknowledged.
- in progress.
- completed.
- blocked.
- cancelled.

The service owner remains responsible for the customer communication.

---

The Case itself remains channel-aware.

This supports reconciliation.
