# ENTERPRISE CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SERVICE MANAGEMENT & SUPPORT OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 3 — Service Lifecycle, Case Operations & Customer Success Operating Model Canon

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** requires a permanent operating model defining how customer Cases, complaints, service requests, investigations, escalations, resolutions, refunds, replacements, recovery actions, and proactive Customer Success activities move through their complete lifecycle.

Stages 1–2 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Service scope.
- Customer/Case boundaries.
- Service entity architecture.
- Complaint, investigation, and resolution structures.
- Returns, refunds, replacements, and recovery entities.
- Customer Success, Customer Health, and service audit entities.

Stage 3 defines how those entities work together as one governed service operating system.

The permanent objective is:

> Every customer issue must move from intake to accountable resolution through a clear, evidence-backed, customer-aware operating model.

---

# 3.2 Service Operating Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Intake Before Action

Customer needs must first be captured in a coherent service context.

---

## Classification Before Routing

Correct categorization improves ownership and resolution.

---

## Ownership Before Investigation

A Case must have accountable responsibility.

---

## Evidence Before Decision

Service findings and remedies require appropriate facts.

---

## Action Before Resolution Claim

A planned remedy is not yet a completed resolution.

---

## Customer Outcome Before Closure

Case closure must reflect a completed service lifecycle.

---

## Follow-Up Before Forgetting

Material recovery Cases may require post-resolution verification.

---

## Learning Before Recurrence

Recurring service problems should influence process, Product, Quality, Shipping, and Customer Success improvements.

---

# 3.3 Enterprise Service Lifecycle

The certified service lifecycle is:

```text id="enterprise-service-lifecycle"
Customer Need / Issue

↓

Case Intake

↓

Identity & Context Resolution

↓

Classification

↓

Priority / Severity

↓

Ownership / Routing

↓

Acknowledgment

↓

Investigation / Internal Coordination

↓

Finding

↓

Resolution Decision

↓

Resolution Execution

↓

Customer Communication

↓

Outcome Verification

↓

Closure

↓

Learning / Customer Success Follow-Up
```

---

# 3.4 Case Intake Lifecycle

Case intake begins when a customer need enters through:

- Email.
- phone.
- WhatsApp.
- website.
- marketplace.
- social channel.
- employee-created Case.
- B2B account contact.

Canonical flow:

```text id="case-intake-lifecycle"
Incoming Interaction

↓

Existing Case Search

↓

Customer Identification

↓

Business Context Link

↓

New Case or Existing Case Update
```

The system should minimize unnecessary duplicate Cases.

---

# 3.5 Existing Case Detection

Before creating a new Case, the platform should consider whether:

- The same Order is already under investigation.
- the same complaint is already open.
- the customer is replying to an existing thread.
- the marketplace message relates to an existing Case.

Duplicate detection should aid agents without incorrectly merging unrelated issues.

---

# 3.6 Customer Identity Resolution

At intake:

```text id="customer-identity-resolution"
Email / Phone / Marketplace Identity

↓

Customer Match

↓

Confidence Evaluation

↓

Canonical Customer Linked
```

If no confident match exists, the Case may remain temporarily unmatched.

The system must not force an incorrect customer identity.

---

# 3.7 Business Context Resolution

After customer identification, relevant context may be linked:

- Order.
- Order Line.
- Product.
- Personalization.
- Shipment.
- Payment.
- Quote.
- previous Case.

This gives agents sufficient context before responding.

---

# 3.8 Case Classification Lifecycle

Classification may follow:

```text id="case-classification"
Customer Message

↓

Broad Case Type

↓

Category

↓

Subcategory if Needed

↓

Priority / Severity
```

Classification may be:

- Human selected.
- rules-assisted.
- AI suggested.

Authority and audit boundaries remain explicit.

---

# 3.9 Misclassification Handling

If a Case was classified incorrectly:

- Classification may be corrected.
- prior classification remains auditable where material.
- routing may be updated.

Incorrect initial classification must not permanently distort service history.

---

# 3.10 Priority Assignment

Priority considers:

- Customer impact.
- urgency.
- committed date.
- commercial/reputational exposure.
- systemic impact.

Priority should be reassessed if circumstances change.

---

# 3.11 Severity Assignment

Severity reflects objective impact.

Example:

```text id="priority-severity-example"
Customer Message:
Very Angry

Issue:
Minor Packaging Question

Severity:
Low

Priority:
Normal
```

Conversely:

```text id="critical-calm-example"
Customer Message:
Calm

Issue:
Wedding Gift Wrong Name
Event Tomorrow

Severity:
Major

Priority:
Urgent
```

---

# 3.12 Queue Routing

Routing may consider:

- Case category.
- channel.
- customer/account type.
- marketplace.
- required expertise.
- language.
- priority.

Canonical flow:

```text id="queue-routing"
Case Classified

↓

Eligible Queue

↓

Available / Qualified Owner

↓

Assignment
```

---

# 3.13 Ownership Acceptance

Where operationally appropriate, assignment may require owner acknowledgment.

This helps prevent Cases from appearing assigned while no one is actually managing them.

---

# 3.14 First Response Lifecycle

After Case creation:

```text id="first-response-lifecycle"
Case Created

↓

Owner / Queue

↓

Context Reviewed

↓

Meaningful Acknowledgment

↓

Next Step Communicated
```

A purely automated receipt confirmation should remain distinguishable from meaningful service response.

---

# 3.15 Customer Information Requests

The customer may need to provide:

- Photo.
- Order reference.
- clarification.
- delivery confirmation.

The platform should only request information genuinely missing from enterprise records.

Repeated requests for already-available information create poor service.

---

# 3.16 Waiting on Customer Lifecycle

When customer input is required:

```text id="waiting-on-customer"
Information Requested

↓

Case Status:
Waiting on Customer

↓

Reminder if Appropriate

↓

Customer Responds

↓

Case Returns to Active Work
```

---

# 3.17 Customer Non-Response

If the customer does not respond:

The platform may:

- Send reminder.
- pause certain SLA clocks.
- eventually close according to policy.

Closure must preserve the reason:

**Closed — Customer Input Not Received**

rather than implying the issue was resolved.

---

# 3.18 Internal Investigation Lifecycle

When service facts are unclear:

```text id="internal-investigation"
Case

↓

Evidence Needed

↓

Relevant Domains Queried

↓

Evidence Collected

↓

Finding Established
```

Not every Case needs formal investigation.

Simple information requests may resolve immediately.

---

# 3.19 Internal Coordination

Cases may require action from:

- Production.
- Quality.
- Shipping.
- Finance.
- Sales.
- Inventory.
- Commercial Management.

Customer Service coordinates the customer outcome while authoritative operational facts remain in their respective domains.

---

# 3.20 Internal Task Creation

A Case may generate internal tasks such as:

- Inspect production record.
- confirm shipment.
- validate refund.
- recreate product.
- verify personalization.

Canonical structure:

```text id="case-internal-task"
Customer Case

↓

Internal Task

↓

Domain Owner

↓

Task Result

↓

Case Updated
```

---

# 3.21 Internal Task SLA

Internal tasks may have due dates based on the customer-facing service commitment.

This prevents internal departments from treating service dependencies as open-ended requests.

---

# 3.22 Internal Task Escalation

If an internal dependency is overdue:

```text id="internal-task-escalation"
Dependency Due

↓

No Completion

↓

Internal Reminder

↓

Escalation

↓

Customer Service Owner Informed
```

The customer-facing Case owner remains responsible for communication.

---

# 3.23 Investigation Evidence Review

Evidence may include:

- Customer submission.
- personalization form.
- production records.
- QC evidence.
- delivery scan.
- photographs.
- Finance records.

Evidence should be interpreted in context.

---

# 3.24 Finding Lifecycle

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="finding-lifecycle"
Evidence

↓

Initial Hypothesis

↓

Validation

↓

Finding

↓

Confidence
```

Possible outcome:

- Confirmed.
- probable.
- inconclusive.

---

# 3.25 Finding vs Responsibility

A finding should describe what occurred.

It should not automatically assign blame.

Example:

**Finding:** Personalization text in production differs from submitted customer text.

Responsibility determination may require separate process analysis.

---

# 3.26 Resolution Decision Lifecycle

Once facts are sufficient:

```text id="resolution-decision"
Finding

+

Customer Impact

+

Policy

+

Authority

+

Operational Feasibility

↓

Resolution Decision
```

---

# 3.27 Standard Resolutions

Predefined policy may allow frontline agents to resolve common Cases such as:

- Provide information.
- correct delivery information before dispatch.
- resend invoice.
- request missing personalization.

No unnecessary approval should be required for low-risk standard outcomes.

---

# 3.28 Controlled Resolutions

Controlled outcomes may include:

- Refund.
- replacement.
- significant discount.
- free service.
- rush remake.
- compensation.

These may require authorization.

---

# 3.29 Resolution Approval

Canonical flow:

```text id="resolution-approval"
Proposed Resolution

↓

Authority Check

↓

Within Authority?
YES → Proceed

NO → Approval Workflow
```

Service speed should not require abandonment of commercial and financial governance.

---

# 3.30 Resolution Execution

After approval:

```text id="resolution-execution"
Resolution Approved

↓

Execution Actions Created

↓

Operational Domains Act

↓

Completion Confirmed

↓

Customer Updated
```

---

# 3.31 Replacement Operating Model

Replacement lifecycle:

```text id="replacement-operating-model"
Replacement Decision

↓

Replacement Request

↓

Order / Production Creation

↓

Personalization Revalidation

↓

Production

↓

Quality Check

↓

Shipment

↓

Delivery Confirmation

↓

Case Resolution
```

For personalized goods, the replacement should verify the personalization before reproduction.

---

# 3.32 Replacement Priority

Replacement priority may consider:

- Event deadline.
- original service failure.
- customer impact.
- production capacity.

Priority must remain operationally feasible.

---

# 3.33 Replacement Quality Control

A replacement resulting from a quality or production failure may require enhanced QC.

This prevents repeated failure.

---

# 3.34 Refund Operating Model

Canonical flow:

```text id="refund-operating-model"
Refund Proposed

↓

Eligibility / Authority

↓

Refund Request

↓

Finance Processing

↓

Authoritative Confirmation

↓

Customer Notification

↓

Case Completion
```

---

# 3.35 Partial Refund

Partial refunds require explicit:

- Amount.
- reason.
- approval.
- remaining customer obligation/outcome.

The platform must preserve why the amount was partial.

---

# 3.36 Refund Failure Handling

If refund execution fails:

- Case remains unresolved.
- Finance failure state becomes visible.
- customer receives appropriate update.
- retry/escalation occurs.

Approval does not equal financial completion.

---

# 3.37 Return Operating Model

Canonical flow:

```text id="return-operating-model"
Return Requested

↓

Eligibility

↓

Return Authorization

↓

Customer Instructions

↓

Item Returned

↓

Receipt / Inspection

↓

Refund / Replacement Decision

↓

Completion
```

---

# 3.38 Personalized Return Decision

Personalized goods require evidence-based policy application.

Possible outcomes depend on:

- Defect.
- production error.
- customer-provided incorrect details.
- transit damage.
- change of mind.
- applicable law/policy.

---

# 3.39 Customer Recovery Operating Model

When customer trust is materially damaged:

```text id="customer-recovery-operating-model"
Service Failure / Severe Experience

↓

Customer Impact

↓

Resolution

↓

Recovery Need Evaluated

↓

Recovery Action Approved

↓

Customer Communication

↓

Follow-Up

↓

Relationship Outcome
```

---

# 3.40 Recovery Options

Possible recovery actions include:

- Priority remake.
- expedited shipping.
- refund.
- discount.
- future coupon.
- goodwill item.
- account-manager follow-up.

The strongest recovery is not automatically the largest monetary concession.

---

# 3.41 Recovery Proportionality

Recovery should consider:

- Failure severity.
- customer inconvenience.
- irreversibility.
- relationship.
- commercial policy.

Overcompensation can create inconsistent policy.

Undercompensation can damage trust.

---

# 3.42 Goodwill Operating Model

Goodwill may be used where:

- Responsibility is uncertain.
- customer impact is genuine.
- relationship value justifies a gesture.

Goodwill remains clearly categorized as such.

---

# 3.43 Escalation Operating Model

Canonical escalation:

```text id="escalation-operating-model"
Trigger

↓

Escalation Type

↓

Destination

↓

Acknowledgment

↓

Action Plan

↓

Service Owner Communication

↓

Escalation Resolution
```

---

# 3.44 SLA Escalation

A Case approaching SLA breach may trigger:

- Warning.
- reassignment.
- manager attention.
- customer status update.

Escalation should occur before failure where practical.

---

# 3.45 Functional Escalation

Functional escalation is used when specialized expertise is required.

Examples:

- Finance.
- Legal.
- Quality.
- Production Engineering.

---

# 3.46 Hierarchical Escalation

Hierarchical escalation occurs when:

- authority insufficient.
- Case unresolved too long.
- customer/reputational impact high.

---

# 3.47 Executive Escalation

Executive escalation should remain rare and material.

Examples:

- Major corporate account risk.
- systemic customer incident.
- legal/reputational issue.
- repeated severe failure.

---

# 3.48 Customer Escalation Communication

When a Case is escalated, the customer should receive appropriate communication without internal organizational complexity being unnecessarily exposed.

The important message is:

- Ownership remains.
- issue is receiving required attention.
- next step/timeline where known.

---

# 3.49 Case Reopen Lifecycle

```text id="case-reopen-lifecycle"
Resolved / Closed Case

↓

Customer Reports Issue Persists

↓

Reopen Reason

↓

New Evidence / Failed Resolution

↓

Owner Reassigned

↓

Investigation / Resolution Continues
```

---

# 3.50 Repeated Reopen

Repeated reopen patterns may indicate:

- Poor resolution quality.
- unresolved operational root cause.
- premature closure.
- communication misunderstanding.

These should trigger quality review.

---

# 3.51 Case Merge Operating Model

Duplicate Cases may be merged when:

- Same customer.
- same issue.
- same business context.

Canonical flow:

```text id="case-merge-operating-model"
Duplicate Detected

↓

Agent Review

↓

Primary Case Selected

↓

Messages / Evidence Linked

↓

Duplicate Closed as Merged
```

---

# 3.52 Parent/Child Case Operations

Parent/Child Cases are appropriate where:

- One systemic issue creates multiple customer consequences.
- one B2B incident affects multiple Orders.

Parent closure must not automatically close unresolved Child Cases.

---

# 3.53 Service Incident Lifecycle

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="service-incident-lifecycle"
Systemic Problem Detected

↓

Incident Created

↓

Affected Customers / Cases Identified

↓

Operational Owner Assigned

↓

Customer Communication Strategy

↓

Underlying Incident Resolved

↓

Individual Cases Completed

↓

Post-Incident Review
```

---

# 3.54 Major Incident Customer Communication

During broad incidents, communication should be:

- Consistent.
- timely.
- fact-based.
- not over-promising.

Customers may receive common updates while retaining individual Case handling.

---

# 3.55 Case Communication Lifecycle

Canonical communication model:

```text id="case-communication-lifecycle"
New Information / Decision

↓

Determine Customer Relevance

↓

Prepare Accurate Message

↓

Authority / Policy Check if Needed

↓

Send

↓

Record Interaction
```

---

# 3.56 Communication Timing

Customer updates may be required when:

- Case acknowledged.
- investigation delayed.
- dependency blocks resolution.
- escalation occurs.
- resolution approved.
- action completed.

Silence should not become the default during long-running Cases.

---

# 3.57 Communication Consistency

Multiple agents interacting with the same customer should use the Case timeline to avoid:

- Contradictory information.
- duplicate questions.
- repeated explanations.

---

# 3.58 Promise Management

Every promise to the customer should be realistic.

Examples:

- "We will update you tomorrow."
- "Replacement will dispatch by Friday."

Promises should create Service Commitments where material.

---

# 3.59 Commitment Monitoring

Canonical flow:

```text id="service-commitment-monitoring"
Commitment

↓

Due Time

↓

Completed?
YES → Record Completion

NO → Alert / Escalate / Update Customer
```

---

# 3.60 Missed Commitment

A missed commitment can itself become:

- Service-quality issue.
- escalation trigger.
- recovery consideration.

The system should not hide it by changing the original due date after failure.

---

# 3.61 Case Aging Operations

Open Cases should be reviewed according to age and status.

Potential categories:

- New.
- Active.
- approaching SLA.
- overdue.
- severely overdue.

Waiting states should remain separately visible.

---

# 3.62 Backlog Management

Managers should analyze backlog by:

- Priority.
- age.
- category.
- queue.
- dependency.
- customer impact.

Canonical goal:

```text id="backlog-management"
Backlog

↓

Prioritize by Risk + Urgency + Age

↓

Assign Capacity

↓

Resolve Old / High-Risk Cases
```

---

# 3.63 Workload Balancing

Case routing may consider current workload.

However, pure case counts can mislead.

One complex B2B complaint may require more effort than many simple status requests.

---

# 3.64 Service Capacity Management

Managers may consider:

- Incoming volume.
- backlog.
- average complexity.
- SLA risk.
- agent availability.

Domain 15 Scheduling/Resource Management may support broader capacity architecture.

---

# 3.65 Daily Service Operations

A daily service review should focus on:

```text id="daily-service-operations"
Critical Cases

↓

SLA Risk

↓

Overdue Cases

↓

Refund / Replacement Blockers

↓

Waiting Internal Dependencies

↓

Important Customer Follow-Ups
```

---

# 3.66 Weekly Service Review

A weekly review may include:

- Case volume.
- backlog.
- reopen rate.
- escalations.
- recurring categories.
- service incidents.
- B2B risks.

---

# 3.67 Monthly Service Review

Monthly management review may include:

- SLA performance.
- service quality.
- complaint patterns.
- Product/service root causes.
- recovery outcomes.
- Customer Health trends.
- operational improvement actions.

---

# 3.68 Case Closure Lifecycle

Before closure, the platform should validate where applicable:

- Resolution selected.
- required actions complete.
- refund/replacement confirmed.
- open internal tasks resolved or appropriately detached.
- customer communication sent.
- follow-up requirement assessed.

---

# 3.69 Closure Reason

Closure should capture reason such as:

- Resolved.
- customer confirmed.
- no response.
- duplicate/merged.
- request cancelled.
- no remedy required.

This improves analytical accuracy.

---

# 3.70 Closure Quality Control

Certain high-impact Cases may require:

- supervisor review.
- Quality review.
- completion evidence.

Not every simple Case needs secondary approval.

---

# 3.71 Customer Follow-Up Lifecycle

For important Cases:

```text id="customer-follow-up-lifecycle"
Resolution Completed

↓

Follow-Up Due

↓

Customer Contact

↓

Outcome:
Satisfied / Additional Help / No Response

↓

Case / Customer Health Updated
```

---

# 3.72 Customer Feedback Collection

Feedback may be requested after:

- Resolution.
- replacement.
- refund.
- major support interaction.

Requests should remain proportionate and not annoy customers.

---

# 3.73 Feedback Handling

Negative feedback may:

- Reopen Case.
- create follow-up.
- trigger quality review.

Positive feedback may contribute to service-learning and employee recognition according to HCM governance.

---

# 3.74 Customer Success Operating Model

Customer Success is proactive.

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="customer-success-operating-model"
Customer Risk / Opportunity

↓

Context

↓

Success Action

↓

Customer Engagement

↓

Outcome

↓

Relationship Health Updated
```

---

# 3.75 Proactive Missing-Personalization Workflow

For GiftHatke:

```text id="missing-personalization-proactive"
Order Received

↓

Personalization Incomplete

↓

Risk Detected

↓

Customer Success Task

↓

Contact Customer

↓

Details Received

↓

Production Ready
```

This prevents a future complaint.

---

# 3.76 Proactive Delay Workflow

When a delay is known before the customer complains:

```text id="proactive-delay-workflow"
Delay Risk Confirmed

↓

Affected Customers Identified

↓

Proactive Communication

↓

Revised Expectation / Recovery if Needed

↓

Customer Follow-Up
```

Proactive transparency can preserve trust.

---

# 3.77 B2B Customer Success Lifecycle

Corporate account Customer Success may include:

- Post-order review.
- delivery confirmation.
- complaint follow-up.
- repeat-order planning.
- relationship-risk identification.

---

# 3.78 Customer Health Review

Customer Health may be recalculated after:

- Successful purchase.
- repeated complaints.
- major recovery.
- B2B inactivity.
- successful follow-up.

Changes should remain explainable.

---

# 3.79 Customer Health Action Threshold

Health states may trigger actions.

Example:

```text id="customer-health-action"
Healthy
→ Routine

Monitor
→ Review

At Risk
→ Customer Success Action

Recovery Required
→ Priority Relationship Management
```

These are decision-support states.

---

# 3.80 Retention Risk Operating Model

Canonical flow:

```text id="retention-risk-operating-model"
Risk Signal

↓

Evidence

↓

Customer Context

↓

Risk Classification

↓

Retention Action

↓

Outcome
```

---

# 3.81 Win-Back Operating Model

For suitable customers:

```text id="winback-operating-model"
Lapsed / Lost Relationship

↓

Cause Reviewed

↓

Appropriate Win-Back Strategy

↓

Commercial Approval if Offer Needed

↓

Customer Contact

↓

Outcome
```

---

# 3.82 Service Knowledge Feedback Loop

Common Cases should improve enterprise knowledge.

```text id="service-knowledge-loop"
Repeated Question / Issue

↓

Knowledge Gap Identified

↓

Article / SOP Updated

↓

Agents Use Better Guidance

↓

Future Handling Improves
```

---

# 3.83 Service-to-Quality Feedback

Confirmed quality complaints should flow toward Quality Management.

```text id="service-quality-feedback"
Customer Complaint

↓

Confirmed Defect

↓

Quality Record

↓

Root Cause / CAPA

↓

Process Improvement
```

---

# 3.84 Service-to-Product Feedback

Repeated Product-related Cases may trigger:

- Product review.
- design change.
- packaging change.
- instruction improvement.

Customer Service provides evidence.

Product retains lifecycle authority.

---

# 3.85 Service-to-Production Feedback

Recurring production mistakes may trigger:

- SOP review.
- training.
- process control.
- QC changes.

Customer complaint history becomes operational intelligence.

---

# 3.86 Service-to-Shipping Feedback

Repeated delays/damage may trigger:

- Carrier review.
- packaging review.
- shipping-rule changes.
- customer communication improvement.

---

# 3.87 Service-to-Finance Feedback

Repeated refund failures or payment Cases may reveal:

- financial workflow issues.
- payment integration issues.
- policy confusion.

---

# 3.88 Root Cause Feedback Loop

Canonical enterprise loop:

```text id="service-root-cause-loop"
Service Cases

↓

Recurring Pattern

↓

Root Cause Analysis

↓

Corrective Action

↓

Operational Improvement

↓

Complaint Reduction
```

---

# 3.89 Service Quality Operating Model

Service quality should evaluate:

- Correctness.
- timeliness.
- ownership.
- communication.
- policy compliance.
- customer outcome.

It must not optimize speed at the expense of resolution quality.

---

# 3.90 First Response Quality

A fast first response is insufficient if it:

- Ignores the issue.
- contains incorrect information.
- requests already-known data.
- makes unsupported promises.

Response quality and response time are distinct.

---

# 3.91 Resolution Quality

A quality resolution should be:

- Factually correct.
- complete.
- authorized.
- feasible.
- communicated.
- executed.

---

# 3.92 Customer Satisfaction vs Service Quality

CSAT and service quality are related but not identical.

A correct policy decision may receive low CSAT.

A friendly but incorrect response may receive high CSAT temporarily.

Both must be interpreted carefully.

---

# 3.93 SLA Management Operating Model

SLA management should track:

- First response.
- next update.
- resolution.
- commitment.

Where clocks pause, pause reasons must be explicit.

---

# 3.94 SLA At-Risk State

Before breach:

```text id="sla-at-risk"
Remaining SLA Time

↓

Risk Threshold

↓

SLA At Risk

↓

Owner / Manager Alert
```

Prevention is better than post-breach reporting.

---

# 3.95 SLA Breach Lifecycle

```text id="sla-breach-lifecycle"
SLA Due

↓

Not Completed

↓

Breach Recorded

↓

Customer Impact Reviewed

↓

Escalation / Recovery if Required

↓

Root Cause Review
```

The original breach must remain in history.

---

# 3.96 Service Exception Handling

Exceptions may include:

- No Customer identity.
- missing Order.
- conflicting evidence.
- unavailable internal owner.
- Finance outage.
- marketplace data unavailable.

The Case must remain active with clear exception state.

---

# 3.97 No-Order Case

A customer may contact service without an identifiable Order.

The system should support:

```text id="no-order-case"
Customer Contact

↓

No Order Match

↓

Case Created

↓

Identity / Order Investigation

↓

Resolution
```

No Order ID should be fabricated.

---

# 3.98 Unsupported Claim

If evidence cannot validate a customer's claim:

The service should:

- Explain available finding appropriately.
- apply policy.
- preserve respectful communication.
- avoid accusing the customer without evidence.

---

# 3.99 Fraud/Abuse Investigation

Suspicious patterns may trigger separate risk investigation.

Canonical distinction:

```text id="service-abuse-boundary"
Suspicious Pattern

↓

Investigation

≠

Automatic Fraud Finding
```

---

# 3.100 Service Automation Operating Model

Low-risk operations may be automated:

- Case creation.
- acknowledgment.
- routing.
- reminders.
- SLA warnings.
- knowledge suggestions.
- status synchronization.

Automation should execute policy, not invent outcomes.

---

# 3.101 AI-Assisted Case Triage

AI may suggest:

- Category.
- priority.
- routing.
- summary.

Low-risk suggestions may be automatically applied where governed.

High-impact classification remains reviewable.

---

# 3.102 AI-Assisted Response Drafting

Canonical flow:

```text id="ai-response-drafting"
Case Context

+

Approved Knowledge

↓

AI Draft

↓

Agent Review / Policy Validation

↓

Customer Message
```

For higher-risk Cases, human review remains required.

---

# 3.103 AI-Assisted Resolution Suggestion

AI may suggest possible actions.

It must show:

- Supporting facts.
- relevant policy.
- confidence.
- uncertainty.

A suggestion is not an approved Resolution.

---

# 3.104 AI Escalation Assistance

AI may detect:

- repeated unresolved contact.
- SLA risk.
- severe customer impact.
- probable systemic issue.

It may recommend escalation.

Authority remains governed.

---

# 3.105 AI Customer Health Assistance

AI may help identify relationship risk from:

- repeated Cases.
- delivery failures.
- declining engagement.

Such outputs remain analytical signals, not definitive customer judgments.

---

# 3.106 AI Safety Boundary

AI may not independently:

- issue material refund.
- approve replacement with major cost.
- accuse customer of fraud.
- close severe complaint without review.
- override statutory rights.
- fabricate operational status.
- promise delivery without verified feasibility.

---

# 3.107 GiftHatke Daily Customer Success Operating Model

A future GiftHatke daily workspace should prioritize:

```text id="gift-daily-cs-model"
Critical Customer Cases

↓

Orders Blocked by Missing Personalization

↓

Shipping Problems

↓

Refunds Awaiting Finance

↓

Replacements in Production

↓

Overdue Internal Dependencies

↓

Customer Follow-Ups
```

---

# 3.108 GiftHatke Personalization Issue Lifecycle

Canonical flow:

```text id="gift-personalization-issue"
Customer Reports Error

↓

Retrieve Submitted Personalization

↓

Retrieve Production Output Context

↓

Compare

↓

Finding

↓

Correction / Replacement / Policy Resolution

↓

Customer Follow-Up
```

---

# 3.109 GiftHatke Missing Asset Operations

For missing customer images/details:

```text id="gift-missing-asset-operations"
Order Not Production Ready

↓

Customer Success Task

↓

Customer Contact

↓

Asset Received

↓

Order Updated

↓

Production Continues
```

---

# 3.110 GiftHatke Wrong Personalization Operations

If the wrong personalization was produced:

- Verify customer-submitted source.
- verify production input.
- verify approval evidence if applicable.
- determine finding.
- trigger remake/refund as appropriate.

This preserves fairness to both customer and operations team.

---

# 3.111 GiftHatke Product Damage Operations

Canonical flow:

```text id="gift-product-damage"
Damage Reported

↓

Customer Photo / Evidence

↓

Shipping vs Production Damage Assessment

↓

Resolution

↓

Replacement / Refund / Other

↓

Quality / Shipping Feedback
```

---

# 3.112 GiftHatke Delivery Delay Operations

```text id="gift-delivery-delay"
Customer Reports Delay

↓

Shipment Tracking

↓

Carrier Status

↓

Promised Date Context

↓

Resolution / Escalation

↓

Customer Update
```

---

# 3.113 GiftHatke Marketplace Complaint Operations

Marketplace complaint lifecycle may include:

- Import Case/message.
- link marketplace Order.
- investigate internally.
- respond within marketplace rules.
- preserve internal service history.

External marketplace status should synchronize without replacing internal Case ownership.

---

# 3.114 GiftHatke B2B Service Operations

Corporate Cases may require coordination across:

- Customer Success.
- Sales.
- Production.
- Shipping.
- Finance.

One B2B Case owner should maintain the account-facing communication.

---

# 3.115 GiftHatke Corporate Escalation

High-value corporate issues may escalate based on:

- Quantity affected.
- delivery deadline.
- event/business importance.
- repeat relationship.
- financial exposure.

High account value alone should not override factual service policy, but it may change attention priority.

---

# 3.116 GiftHatke Replacement Remake

For personalization failures:

```text id="gift-replacement-remake"
Replacement Approved

↓

Correct Personalization Reconfirmed

↓

Priority Production Job

↓

Enhanced QC

↓

Shipping

↓

Customer Confirmation
```

---

# 3.117 GiftHatke Refund Follow-Through

Customer Success must track refund until:

**Finance confirms execution.**

The Case should not close at "refund requested."

---

# 3.118 GiftHatke Recovery Discount Follow-Through

If a future coupon is offered:

- Coupon must be created through Commercial Governance.
- customer receives correct validity.
- Case records the recovery.
- future usage may be traceable.

---

# 3.119 GiftHatke Proactive Shipping Communication

If Shipping identifies a material delay before customer contact:

```text id="gift-proactive-shipping"
Delay Confirmed

↓

Affected Orders

↓

Customer Success Cases / Actions

↓

Proactive Message

↓

Resolution Expectations
```

This reduces avoidable inbound complaints.

---

# 3.120 GiftHatke Event-Date Sensitivity

Personalized gifts may be tied to:

- Birthday.
- anniversary.
- wedding.
- festival.

Where event date is legitimately known, it may influence service Priority because delayed delivery may become irreversible.

It should not automatically create impossible operational promises.

---

# 3.121 GiftHatke Service-to-Production Feedback

Example:

```text id="gift-service-production-feedback"
Repeated Engraving Complaints

↓

Pattern Confirmed

↓

Production / Quality Review

↓

Machine / SOP / Training Investigation

↓

Corrective Action
```

---

# 3.122 GiftHatke Service-to-Personalization Feedback

Repeated missing customer details may indicate that intake experience needs improvement.

Support should feed evidence back to:

- Personalization.
- Order.
- UX/process design.

---

# 3.123 GiftHatke Service-to-Product Feedback

A product with:

- high complaint rate.
- repeated breakage.
- difficult personalization.
- high replacements.

may require Product review.

---

# 3.124 Service Event Readiness

The operating model produces canonical future events such as:

- CaseCreated.
- CaseAssigned.
- CaseAcknowledged.
- SLAAtRisk.
- CaseEscalated.
- FindingConfirmed.
- ResolutionApproved.
- RefundCompleted.
- ReplacementDelivered.
- CaseReopened.
- CaseClosed.

Formal event architecture follows in later stages.

---

# 3.125 Service Observability

The platform should monitor:

- Unassigned Cases.
- aging backlog.
- SLA risk.
- overdue internal dependencies.
- unresolved escalations.
- failed refund/replacement coordination.
- communication failures.
- integration outages.

Service operations themselves must be observable.

---

# 3.126 Service Failure States

Potential system failures include:

- Customer match failure.
- Order lookup failure.
- internal task delivery failure.
- message send failure.
- refund integration failure.
- marketplace sync failure.

Failures must remain visible.

---

# 3.127 Safe Failure Principle

The system must not:

- Mark refund complete when Finance is unavailable.
- mark shipment delivered when tracking failed.
- close Case because a dependent service errored.
- send invented status to customer.

Unknown state must remain unknown.

---

# 3.128 SMP1 Operating Preservation

During **SMP1**, historical customer, Order, shipment, personalization, and financial relationships must remain usable for future service operations.

The migration may introduce new Case processes after cutover.

It must not invent historical workflows that did not exist.

---

# 3.129 SMP1 Service Transition

Canonical transition:

```text id="smp1-service-transition"
Certified Existing Business Context

↓

Standalone Migration

↓

Stable Customer / Order Relationships

↓

Formal Service Management Introduced

↓

Future Customer Service History Native to Standalone
```

---

# 3.130 SMP1 No-Redesign Rule

Permanent rule:

```text id="smp1-service-no-redesign"
Standalone Migration

≠

Permission to Alter Historical Customer / Order Facts
```

New service processes may improve future operations while preserving baseline truth.

---

# 3.131 Standalone v1.0 Operating Foundation

Standalone v1.0 should provide:

- Reliable Customer identity.
- Order navigation.
- personalization relationships.
- shipment status.
- financial references.
- role controls.
- audit history.

# ENTERPRISE CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SERVICE MANAGEMENT & SUPPORT OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 4 — Service Management Services, Case Execution & Customer Success Service Architecture Canon

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** requires a permanent service architecture that turns certified Case, complaint, investigation, resolution, escalation, return, refund, replacement, recovery, and Customer Success concepts into executable enterprise capability.

Stages 1–3 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Service entity architecture.
- Case lifecycle.
- Customer support operating model.
- investigation and findings.
- resolution execution.
- refund, return, and replacement coordination.
- proactive Customer Success.
- service-quality and escalation operations.

Stage 4 defines the service layer responsible for:

- Case intake.
- identity and context resolution.
- classification.
- routing.
- ownership.
- SLA execution.
- investigation.
- communication.
- resolution.
- escalation.
- refund/replacement coordination.
- Customer Success actions.
- service knowledge.
- customer health.
- service intelligence.
- audit.

The objective is to ensure that Customer Service execution remains:

- Reliable.
- explainable.
- governed.
- cross-domain aware.
- auditable.
- resilient.
- technology-independent.

---

# 4.2 Service Architecture Philosophy

The permanent service architecture follows:

---

## Customer Context Before Automation

Service execution should consume relevant business context before acting.

---

## Case State Before Workflow

Service orchestration must operate against an authoritative Case state.

---

## Ownership Before Delegation

Internal tasks may be distributed.

Customer accountability remains anchored to the Case.

---

## Evidence Before Resolution

High-impact resolutions require adequate facts.

---

## Authority Before Recovery

Refunds, concessions, and replacements must respect governance.

---

## Completion Before Closure

Execution services must distinguish:

- Approved action.
- action in progress.
- completed action.

---

## Safe Failure Before False Assurance

If a dependent service fails, the platform must not invent success.

---

# 4.3 Canonical Service Landscape

The permanent service architecture includes:

| Service | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Case Intake Service | Create and normalize incoming Cases |
| Customer Identity Resolution Service | Match incoming contact to Customer |
| Case Context Service | Attach Orders, Shipments, Products, etc. |
| Case Classification Service | Determine Case type/category |
| Priority & Severity Service | Evaluate urgency and impact |
| Case Routing Service | Select queue/owner |
| Case Ownership Service | Govern assignment and transfer |
| Queue Management Service | Manage support workload |
| SLA Management Service | Track service commitments |
| Case Interaction Service | Govern customer/internal interactions |
| Customer Communication Service | Send governed customer messages |
| Internal Note Service | Record internal context |
| Case Attachment Service | Manage Case evidence/assets |
| Investigation Service | Coordinate fact-finding |
| Evidence Service | Govern supporting evidence |
| Finding Service | Record investigation outcome |
| Resolution Management Service | Define service resolution |
| Resolution Execution Service | Coordinate operational completion |
| Return Service | Coordinate return workflow |
| Replacement Service | Coordinate remake/replacement |
| Refund Coordination Service | Coordinate financial refund workflow |
| Recovery Service | Govern goodwill/service recovery |
| Escalation Service | Govern service escalation |
| Service Incident Service | Manage systemic customer issues |
| Commitment Service | Track promises to customers |
| Follow-Up Service | Manage post-resolution follow-up |
| Customer Success Service | Govern proactive success actions |
| Customer Health Service | Maintain relationship-health state |
| Retention Risk Service | Identify relationship risk |
| Knowledge Assistance Service | Surface approved service knowledge |
| Service Quality Service | Evaluate handling quality |
| Service Risk Service | Identify operational service risk |
| Service Intelligence Service | Analyze patterns |
| Service Audit Service | Preserve evidence |

---

# 4.4 Case Intake Service

## Purpose

Normalize service requests arriving through multiple channels.

Potential sources:

- Email.
- WhatsApp.
- website.
- phone/manual entry.
- marketplace.
- social channel.
- internal employee.

Canonical flow:

```text id="case-intake-service"
Incoming Contact

↓

Normalize Message / Metadata

↓

Existing Case Check

↓

Customer Identity Resolution

↓

Create or Update Case

↓

Audit
```

---

# 4.5 Intake Normalization

The service should normalize:

- Channel.
- sender/contact.
- timestamp.
- message direction.
- external reference.
- attachments.
- marketplace/order identifiers.

Normalization must not strip source evidence.

---

# 4.6 Existing Case Detection Service

Before creating a new Case, the platform may check:

- Thread reference.
- Order.
- customer.
- recent open Cases.
- marketplace ticket reference.

Potential outcomes:

- Attach to existing Case.
- suggest merge.
- create new Case.

Automatic merge should remain conservative.

---

# 4.7 Customer Identity Resolution Service

## Purpose

Resolve incoming contact to the authoritative CRM Customer.

Inputs may include:

- Email.
- phone.
- marketplace identity.
- Order ID.
- account reference.

Canonical outcomes:

- Matched.
- probable match requiring review.
- unmatched.

---

# 4.8 Identity Confidence

A match should expose confidence where ambiguity exists.

The service must not automatically merge customer identities based on weak similarity.

---

# 4.9 Case Context Service

## Purpose

Attach authoritative operational context.

Possible relationships:

- Order.
- Order Line.
- Product.
- Personalization.
- Production Job.
- QC.
- Shipment.
- Payment.
- Refund.
- Quote.

Canonical flow:

```text id="case-context-service"
Case

↓

Known Customer

↓

Relevant Business Records

↓

Context Snapshot / References

↓

Agent View
```

---

# 4.10 Context Freshness

The Case interface may cache context.

However, operational status such as:

- Shipment status.
- refund state.
- production state.

must preserve freshness indicators where relevant.

---

# 4.11 Case Classification Service

## Purpose

Assign:

- Case type.
- category.
- subcategory.

Classification may use:

- Rules.
- keywords.
- historical patterns.
- AI suggestions.
- agent selection.

---

# 4.12 Classification Confidence

For AI/rules-assisted classification, the result may carry:

- High confidence.
- medium confidence.
- low confidence.

Low-confidence Cases may require agent review.

---

# 4.13 Priority & Severity Service

## Purpose

Evaluate:

- Service urgency.
- objective impact.

Inputs may include:

- promised event date.
- Case category.
- customer impact.
- Order value.
- number of customers affected.
- SLA state.
- systemic incident.

Priority rules must remain transparent.

---

# 4.14 Priority Recalculation

Priority may change when:

- New evidence arrives.
- delivery deadline approaches.
- Case becomes systemic.
- executive/account risk emerges.

Priority history must remain auditable.

---

# 4.15 Case Routing Service

## Purpose

Determine the correct queue and owner.

Potential routing inputs:

- Category.
- channel.
- marketplace.
- customer type.
- language.
- required skill.
- current workload.

Canonical flow:

```text id="case-routing-service"
Case

↓

Routing Criteria

↓

Eligible Queues

↓

Skill + Availability

↓

Assignment
```

---

# 4.16 Routing Guardrails

The service must not route Cases to users lacking:

- required permissions.
- required functional capability.
- applicable marketplace access.

---

# 4.17 Case Ownership Service

## Purpose

Govern:

- Assignment.
- transfer.
- acceptance.
- reassignment.
- owner history.

A Case should not become orphaned during transfer.

---

# 4.18 Ownership Transfer Transaction

```text id="ownership-transfer-service"
Current Owner

↓

Transfer Requested

↓

New Owner / Queue Validated

↓

Assignment Committed

↓

Audit

↓

Notifications
```

---

# 4.19 Queue Management Service

## Purpose

Manage operational Case workload.

Capabilities may include:

- Queue membership.
- Case counts.
- aging.
- priority.
- assignment.
- workload balancing.

Queue logic should account for complexity where possible, not only raw volume.

---

# 4.20 SLA Management Service

## Purpose

Track service commitments.

Potential timers:

- First response.
- next update.
- resolution.
- internal dependency.

The service must understand:

- start time.
- pause conditions.
- resume.
- breach.
- SLA version.

---

# 4.21 SLA Clock Service

Canonical lifecycle:

```text id="sla-clock-service"
Clock Starts

↓

Active

↓

Pause if Governed

↓

Resume

↓

Due

↓

Completed / Breached
```

Historical SLA performance must use the applicable SLA version.

---

# 4.22 SLA At-Risk Service

The service may calculate:

- Remaining time.
- Case complexity.
- owner state.
- dependencies.

and publish:

**SLA AT RISK**

before breach.

---

# 4.23 SLA Breach Service

On breach:

- Record breach.
- notify owner/manager.
- evaluate escalation.
- preserve original due time.

The platform must never erase a breach by resetting the clock.

---

# 4.24 Case Interaction Service

## Purpose

Record all material Case interactions.

Types:

- Incoming email.
- outgoing email.
- call.
- WhatsApp message.
- marketplace response.
- system communication.

Each interaction must link to the Case timeline.

---

# 4.25 Customer Communication Service

## Purpose

Send authorized customer-facing communication.

Capabilities:

- Draft/send response.
- use approved template.
- attach Case context.
- record delivery result where available.
- preserve communication history.

---

# 4.26 Communication Validation

Before sending high-impact messages, the service may validate:

- Refund status.
- shipment state.
- replacement feasibility.
- approval.

Example:

```text id="communication-validation"
Draft:
"Your refund has been completed."

↓

Finance Status:
Processing

↓

Send Blocked / Corrected
```

This prevents false assurance.

---

# 4.27 Internal Note Service

## Purpose

Record internal information that should not be customer-visible.

It must enforce visibility separation from Customer Messages.

---

# 4.28 Case Attachment Service

## Purpose

Manage attachments and evidence links.

Potential files:

- Customer photo.
- damaged product image.
- invoice.
- shipping proof.
- personalization reference.

The service should integrate with Digital Asset Management rather than duplicating uncontrolled file storage.

---

# 4.29 Evidence Service

## Purpose

Each evidence item may preserve:

- Source.
- timestamp.
- linked business object.
- creator/system.
- integrity metadata.
- classification.

---

# 4.30 Investigation Service

## Purpose

Coordinate structured Case investigation.

Capabilities:

- Open investigation.
- define question.
- request evidence.
- assign internal tasks.
- track hypotheses.
- record finding.
- close investigation.

---

# 4.31 Investigation Task Integration

The service may create tasks for:

- Production.
- Quality.
- Shipping.
- Finance.

Canonical boundary:

```text id="investigation-task-integration"
Customer Service
Owns Investigation Need

↓

Workflow / Task Engine
Executes Internal Work

↓

Domain Returns Evidence / Result

↓

Customer Service
Records Finding
```

---

# 4.32 Finding Service

## Purpose

Record the evaluated conclusion.

A Finding should preserve:

- Classification.
- evidence references.
- confidence.
- investigator.
- timestamp.

- Confirmed.
- probable.
- inconclusive.

---

# 4.33 Resolution Management Service

## Purpose

Select and authorize intended customer outcome.

Potential resolutions:

- Information provided.
- correction.
- replacement.
- refund.
- partial refund.
- recovery credit.
- no remedy required.

---

# 4.34 Resolution Eligibility

Resolution rules may depend on:

- Finding.
- policy.
- Order status.
- product type.
- customer impact.
- commercial authority.
- legal requirements.

---

# 4.35 Resolution Authority Service

High-impact resolutions may require authority checks.

Example:

```text id="resolution-authority-service"
Proposed:
Full Refund

↓

Agent Authority:
Up to ₹X

↓

Request Exceeds Authority

↓

Approval Required
```

---

# 4.36 Resolution Execution Service

## Purpose

Translate approved resolution into completed operational outcome.

Example:

```text id="resolution-execution-service"
Approved Resolution:
Replacement

↓

Create Replacement Request

↓

Production / Order

↓

QC

↓

Shipment

↓

Completion Confirmation

↓

Case Resolved
```

---

# 4.37 Resolution State Model

Possible states:

- Proposed.
- approved.
- executing.
- completed.
- failed.
- cancelled.

This prevents "approved" from being mistaken for "completed."

---

# 4.38 Return Service

## Purpose

Coordinate:

- Eligibility.
- authorization.
- return instructions.
- receipt.
- inspection.
- downstream outcome.

It consumes Product, Order, Shipping, and policy context.

---

# 4.39 Return Authorization

The service may issue a governed return reference.

This reference should link:

- Case.
- Order Line.
- return status.

---

# 4.40 Replacement Service

## Purpose

Coordinate replacement/remake execution.

Responsibilities may include:

- Validate approval.
- confirm personalization.
- create replacement Order/Job.
- assign priority.
- monitor QC.
- monitor shipment.
- return completion to Case.

---

# 4.41 Replacement Idempotency

Repeated service calls must not create duplicate replacement Orders.

A stable Resolution/Replacement ID should protect against this.

---

# 4.42 Refund Coordination Service

## Purpose

Coordinate refund lifecycle without taking over Finance authority.

Canonical flow:

```text id="refund-coordination-service"
Refund Request

↓

Eligibility / Approval

↓

Finance Refund Command

↓

Finance Processing

↓

Authoritative Result

↓

Case Updated
```

---

# 4.43 Refund Coordination Boundary

Customer Service may say:

- "Refund approved."
- "Refund processing."
- "Refund completed."

only according to authoritative Finance state.

---

# 4.44 Refund Failure Handling

If Finance returns failure:

- Case remains active.
- failure reason preserved.
- retry/escalation may occur.
- customer update generated if appropriate.

---

# 4.45 Recovery Service

## Purpose

Govern Customer Recovery actions beyond base resolution.

Potential actions:

- Coupon.
- discount.
- goodwill.
- expedited handling.
- added item.

The service integrates with Domain 31 for commercial authorization.

---

# 4.46 Recovery Authorization

Canonical boundary:

```text id="recovery-authorization"
Customer Service
Defines Recovery Need

↓

Commercial Governance
Defines Permitted Economic Concession

↓

Customer Service
Communicates Recovery
```

---

# 4.47 Escalation Service

## Purpose

Create and manage:

- Functional.
- hierarchical.
- SLA.
- legal.
- reputational.
- executive escalations.

The service should preserve:

- Trigger.
- destination.
- action owner.
- state.
- result.

---

# 4.48 Escalation Rule Service

Escalation triggers may include:

- SLA At Risk.
- SLA breached.
- critical severity.
- repeated reopen.
- high account impact.
- systemic issue.

Automatic escalation may occur within certified rules.

---

# 4.49 Escalation Closure

Closing an escalation does not automatically close the Case.

The Case resolution state remains authoritative.

---

# 4.50 Service Incident Service

## Purpose

Manage systemic issues affecting multiple Cases.

Capabilities:

- Create Incident.
- define scope.
- link affected Cases.
- identify operational owner.
- publish common updates.
- track root cause.
- close Incident.

# 4.51 Affected Customer Identification

- Shipment disruption.
- production defect batch.
- payment outage.

This can enable proactive service.

---

# 4.52 Incident Communication Coordination

The communication must still preserve channel and delivery evidence.

---

# 4.53 Commitment Service

Capabilities:

- Create Commitment.
- define due time.
- owner.
- status.
- completion.
- missed commitment alert.

# 4.54 Commitment Validation

Before creating a promise such as:

"Replacement will dispatch tomorrow"

the service may verify:

- Production feasibility.
- shipping cutoff.
- authorization.

This reduces impossible promises.

---

- At Risk.

- Insufficient Evidence.

- Credit score.
- moral judgment.

It is Customer Success decision support.

# 4.65 Service Quality Service

# 4.73 Case Validation Architecture

- valid category.

```text id="closure-validation"

Required Replacement Complete?

Open Critical Tasks?

Required Customer Message Sent?

Close or Block
```

```text id="case-create-transaction"
↓

Normalize

↓

↓

Case Created

↓

Initial Interaction Recorded

↓

SLA Started
```

```text id="resolution-approval-transaction"
Authority Checked

↓

Decision

Conditions Recorded

Audit Commit

↓

Execution Enabled
```

# 4.78 Transaction Boundary — Replacement Creation

```text id="replacement-create-transaction"
Approved Replacement

↓

Idempotency Check

↓

Replacement Request Created

↓

Order / Production Command

↓

Link Stored

↓

Case Updated
```

---

# 4.79 Transaction Boundary — Refund Request

```text id="refund-request-transaction"
Approved Refund

↓

Refund Request Created

↓

Finance Command

↓

Finance Reference Stored

↓

Case Status Updated
```

---

# 4.80 Idempotency

Repeated service calls must not create:

- Duplicate Cases from same source event.
- duplicate refunds.
- duplicate replacements.
- duplicate escalations.
- duplicate follow-up actions.

---

# 4.81 Concurrency Governance

Concurrency matters when:

- Two agents answer same Case.
- two managers reassign Case.
- refund and replacement decisions happen simultaneously.
- Case is closing while customer replies.

The system must preserve a coherent authoritative state.

---

# 4.82 Concurrent Customer Reply

If the customer replies while Case closure is in progress:

Policy should determine whether:

- Closure is blocked.
- Case reopens automatically.
- new interaction is appended before final decision.

Customer communication must never disappear.

---

# 4.83 Case Locking vs Optimistic Concurrency

Technical implementation may use:

- Record locks.
- optimistic version checks.
- event sequencing.

The Canon requires state consistency, not a specific technology.

---

# 4.84 Service Failure Classification

Potential failure classes:

## Identity Failure

Customer cannot be reliably matched.

## Context Failure

Order/Shipment unavailable.

## Routing Failure

No eligible owner.

## Communication Failure

Message delivery failed.

## Dependency Failure

Finance/Shipping/Production unavailable.

## Policy Failure

Resolution not permitted.

## Authority Failure

Approval missing.

## Integration Failure

Marketplace or external service unavailable.

---

# 4.85 Safe Failure Response

The platform should:

- Preserve Case state.
- record error.
- communicate internal next step.
- avoid invented customer-facing claims.

It should not automatically close a Case because a dependency failed.

---

# 4.86 Retry Architecture

Safe retry:

```text id="service-retry"
Operation Failed

↓

Failure Recorded

↓

Retry Eligible?

↓

Idempotency Check

↓

Retry

↓

State Reconciled
```

---

# 4.87 Dead-Letter / Exception Queue

Unprocessable service events/actions may enter a controlled exception queue.

Examples:

- Failed marketplace message.
- refund synchronization failure.
- replacement integration failure.

Each item needs:

- Case.
- failure.
- owner.
- severity.
- retry history.

---

# 4.88 Case Caching

Case-list views may use caching.

Caching must respect:

- Ownership changes.
- status changes.
- new customer replies.
- SLA state.
- escalation.

Stale cache must not hide urgent service work.

---

# 4.89 Search Index Synchronization

A future search index may contain Case data.

Updates must synchronize:

- Case status.
- customer identity.
- Order references.
- category.
- owner.

Search is secondary to authoritative Case storage.

---

# 4.90 Security Architecture

Service actions require role-based authorization.

Examples:

- Agent can respond.
- supervisor can reassign.
- authorized manager can approve selected recovery.
- Finance can complete refund.
- auditor can inspect history.

---

# 4.91 Sensitive Service Data

Restricted information may include:

- Customer contact.
- address.
- internal notes.
- refund details.
- complaint evidence.
- high-value account context.

Visibility must follow business need.

---

Service Management integrates with:

| Domain | Purpose |
|---|---|
| CRM | Customer identity and relationship |
| Orders | Order truth |
| Personalization | Customer input and assets |
| Production | Manufacturing state |
| Quality | Defect facts |
| Shipping | Shipment truth |

| Notifications | Alerts |
| Knowledge | SOP/policy |
| Data Governance | Trust/classification |
| Performance Management | KPI governance |
| AI | Triage/assistance |

---

# 4.93 CRM Integration

CRM provides:

- Customer ID.
- account.
- contact details.
- relationship context.

Service provides:

- Case history.
- service-risk/customer-health signals where appropriate.

---

Customer Service may query:

- Order status.
- items.
- dates.
- personalization state.

Order changes require Order Management commands, not direct service-record mutation.

---

# 4.95 Personalization Integration

Service may query:

- Submitted text.
- images.

- source.

This is critical for personalization disputes.

---

# 4.96 Production Integration

Production provides:

- Job status.
- manufacturing evidence.

- completion.

Customer Service must not fabricate production commitments.

---

# 4.97 Quality Integration

Quality may receive confirmed defect Cases.

Quality returns:

- assessment.
- non-conformance.
- corrective action context.

Customer Service converts this into customer resolution.

---

# 4.98 Shipping Integration

Shipping provides:

- Tracking.
- dispatch.
- delivery.
- carrier exception.

Customer Service communicates based on authoritative Shipping data.

---

# 4.99 Finance Integration

Finance provides:

- Payment status.
- refund status.
- credit-note status where relevant.

Service manages customer-facing resolution coordination.

---

# 4.100 Commercial Integration

Commercial Domain governs:

- Recovery discounts.
- goodwill coupons.
- exceptional concessions.

Customer Service provides the reason and customer context.

---

# 4.101 Workflow Integration

Internal service tasks and approvals may execute through Workflow.

Canonical boundary:

```text id="service-workflow-boundary"
Customer Service
Determines Needed Action

↓

Workflow
Routes / Tracks Execution

↓

Source Domain
Performs Action

↓

Customer Service
Updates Customer Case
```

---

# 4.102 Notification Integration

Notifications may communicate:

- New urgent Case.
- SLA At Risk.
- escalation.
- refund failure.
- replacement completion.
- customer reply.

Notifications must remain actionable.

# 4.103 Knowledge Integration

Knowledge service should surface the correct:

- Policy.
- SOP.
- troubleshooting.
- customer-facing guidance.

Outdated knowledge should not be silently suggested.

---

# 4.104 Data Governance Integration

Case services depend on trusted:

- Customer.
- Order.
- Shipment.
- payment.
- product.

If source trust is degraded, service agents should see the uncertainty.

---

# 4.105 Performance Management Integration

Domain 30 may govern service KPIs such as:

- First Response Time.
- Resolution Time.
- SLA Compliance.
- Reopen Rate.
- Escalation Rate.
- Service Recovery Success.

Domain 32 defines service business meaning.

# 4.106 AI-Assisted Case Service

AI may support:

- Summarization.
- classification.
- routing.
- knowledge suggestions.
- draft responses.
- resolution suggestions.

# 4.109 AI Grounding Requirement

AI responses must ground claims in:

- Current Order state.
- current Shipment state.
- approved refund state.
- certified policy.
- Case evidence.

AI must not invent completion.

---

AI may recommend:

- replacement.
- refund.
- apology.
- escalation.

But material execution requires human/policy authority.

It must not automatically classify a customer as fraudulent without governed investigation.

- fast-moving Orders.
- direct web sales.
- marketplaces.
- B2B.
- production and shipping dependencies.

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** permanently follows:

- authority before recovery.
