# ENTERPRISE CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SERVICE MANAGEMENT & SUPPORT OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 8 — Service Intelligence, Customer Health, Retention & Predictive Support Analytics Canon

---

# 8.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** requires a permanent intelligence architecture capable of transforming Case history, customer interactions, complaint patterns, operational failures, recovery outcomes, Customer Health signals, and support performance into actionable enterprise insight.

Stages 1–7 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Service entity architecture.
- Case operating model.
- Service Management service architecture.
- Service Governance.
- Omnichannel event architecture.
- Agent, manager, and Customer Success experiences.

Stage 8 defines how the enterprise progresses from:

```text
What Cases Do We Have?

↓

Why Are Customers Contacting Us?

↓

Which Service Problems Are Recurring?

↓

Which Customers or Accounts Are At Risk?

↓

What Is Likely to Happen Next?

↓

What Should We Improve or Prevent?
```

The objective is not to maximize ticket closure.

The objective is to improve:

- customer outcomes.
- service quality.
- operational reliability.
- retention.
- proactive intervention.
- organizational learning.

---

# 8.2 Service Intelligence Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Service Truth Before Analytics

Analytical conclusions must originate from trustworthy Case and operational facts.

---

## Outcome Before Activity Volume

Large numbers of responses or closed Cases do not automatically indicate successful service.

---

## Root Cause Before Surface Pattern

Repeated complaints should be traced toward underlying causes.

---

## Relationship Context Before Retention Action

Customer Health and retention interventions should consider the actual customer relationship.

---

## Probability Before Certainty

Predictive service risk remains probabilistic.

---

## Assistance Before Manipulation

Customer-retention intelligence should support legitimate customer value.

It should not create exploitative behavior.

---

## Human Judgment Before High-Impact Automated Action

Predictive systems may identify risk.

Human/service policy governs material customer action.

---

# 8.3 Enterprise Service Intelligence Landscape

The permanent intelligence architecture includes:

| Capability | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Case Volume Intelligence | Understand service demand |
| Complaint Intelligence | Analyze dissatisfaction |
| Root Cause Intelligence | Identify underlying failure patterns |
| Service Quality Intelligence | Evaluate handling quality |
| SLA Intelligence | Understand responsiveness |
| Resolution Intelligence | Analyze outcome effectiveness |
| Refund Intelligence | Analyze refund behavior |
| Replacement Intelligence | Analyze remake/replacement patterns |
| Recovery Intelligence | Evaluate goodwill and trust recovery |
| Customer Health Intelligence | Understand relationship state |
| Retention Risk Intelligence | Identify relationship-loss risk |
| Customer Success Intelligence | Guide proactive interventions |
| Product Service Intelligence | Identify product-related service risk |
| Personalization Intelligence | Analyze customization problems |
| Production Service Intelligence | Identify manufacturing-driven service issues |
| Shipping Service Intelligence | Analyze delivery complaints |
| Marketplace Service Intelligence | Compare channel-specific service |
| B2B Service Intelligence | Support account health |
| Service Incident Intelligence | Analyze systemic issues |
| Predictive Support Intelligence | Anticipate future service demand/risk |
| AI-Assisted Service Intelligence | Accelerate analysis |

---

# 8.4 Case Volume Intelligence

Case Volume Intelligence analyzes:

- Total Cases.
- new Cases.
- open Cases.
- closed Cases.
- reopened Cases.

Dimensions may include:

- Product.
- channel.
- issue type.
- customer segment.
- period.
- marketplace.

Volume should be normalized where relevant against:

- Orders.
- customers.
- shipments.

---

# 8.5 Case Rate Intelligence

A raw Case count can mislead.

Example:

```text
Product A
100 Cases
10,000 Orders
= 1% Case Rate

Product B
40 Cases
500 Orders
= 8% Case Rate
```

Product B may represent the larger service risk despite lower absolute volume.

---

# 8.6 Contact Rate

Potential measure:

```text
Customers Contacting Support

÷

Relevant Orders / Customers
```

The exact denominator depends on business context.

Domain 30 governs official KPI definition.

---

# 8.7 Contact Driver Intelligence

The enterprise should understand why customers contact support.

Potential drivers:

- Order status.
- missing personalization.
- Product quality.
- delivery delay.
- refund.
- payment.
- usage question.

This can identify opportunities for:

- Better UX.
- proactive communication.
- operational improvement.

---

# 8.8 Avoidable Contact Intelligence

Some Cases may be preventable.

Examples:

- "Where is my order?" because tracking is unclear.
- repeated requests for personalization instructions.
- invoice requests that could be self-service.

Reducing avoidable support demand improves both:

- Customer experience.
- operational efficiency.

---

# 8.9 Complaint Intelligence

Complaint Intelligence analyzes:

- Complaint count.
- complaint rate.
- issue category.
- severity.
- Product.
- channel.
- confirmed findings.
- outcomes.

---

# 8.10 Complaint Finding Intelligence

Complaints should be analyzed separately by finding.

Example:

```text
Customer Complaints:
100

Confirmed Enterprise Errors:
52

Customer Input Mismatch:
17

Carrier Issues:
14

Inconclusive:
17
```

This produces far more useful learning than complaint count alone.

---

# 8.11 Confirmed Complaint Rate

Potential analytical concept:

```text
Confirmed Enterprise-Failure Complaints

÷

Relevant Transactions
```

This can support Product, Quality, Shipping, and process improvement.

# 8.12 Complaint Severity Intelligence

A large number of minor issues and a few severe failures require different management responses.

Analytics should distinguish:

- Frequency.
- severity.
- customer impact.

---

# 8.13 Complaint Recurrence Intelligence

Repeated complaint patterns may identify:

- Process defect.
- Product issue.
- Shipping issue.
- training gap.
- unclear policy.
- interface problem.

# 8.14 Root Cause Intelligence

Canonical loop:

```text
Service Cases

↓

Pattern

↓

Confirmed Findings

↓

Root Cause Hypothesis

↓

Cross-Domain Evidence

↓

Root Cause

↓

Corrective Action
```

---

# 8.15 Surface Cause vs Root Cause

Example:

**Surface issue:** Customer says wrong name engraved.

Possible root causes:

- Customer entry error.
- intake UI confusion.
- transcription mistake.
- asset/version mismatch.
- production error.

Service Intelligence must avoid assuming all similar complaints have the same root cause.

---

# 8.16 Root Cause Confidence

Root Cause Intelligence should expose:

- Confirmed.
- probable.
- exploratory.

The system should preserve uncertainty.

---

# 8.17 Service Quality Intelligence

Service Quality Intelligence may analyze:

- Correctness.
- communication quality.
- completeness.
- policy adherence.
- reopen.
- escalation.
- customer outcome.

---

# 8.18 Response Time Intelligence

Analyze:

- First Response Time.
- meaningful response time.
- response by channel.
- response by priority.
- response by queue.

Automated acknowledgment should remain distinguishable from meaningful service.

---

# 8.19 Resolution Time Intelligence

Resolution Time may be decomposed into:

```text
Total Resolution Time

=

Internal Active Time

+

Waiting on Customer

+

Waiting on Other Domain

+

External Dependency
```

This helps identify where delay actually occurs.

---

# 8.20 Waiting-Time Intelligence

Potential analysis:

- Cases waiting on Customer.
- Cases waiting on Production.
- Cases waiting on Finance.
- Cases waiting on Shipping.

- At-Risk rate.
- pause frequency.
- breach reason.

- Excessive pause usage.
- closing just before breach.
- repeated reopening after closure.

Metrics should protect customer outcomes rather than encourage gaming.

---

# 8.23 Case Aging Intelligence

# 8.24 Backlog Intelligence

- severity.
- age.
- workload.
- SLA exposure.

# 8.25 Reopen Intelligence

High reopen may indicate:

- premature closure.
- execution failure.
- recurring issue.

# 8.26 Reopen Cause Analysis

- replacement still defective.
- customer did not understand policy.
- wrong finding.
- downstream action failed.

---

# 8.27 Escalation Intelligence

Analyze:

- Escalation rate.

- outcome.
- duration.

- weak frontline authority.
- inadequate training.
- poor routing.
- policy gaps.

# 8.98 AI Root Cause Boundary

> These Cases appear associated with packaging damage.

It must not mark a root cause as confirmed without sufficient evidence.

# 8.99 AI Service Narrative

```text
Primary Service Risk This Week:

Acrylic transit-damage complaints increased.
Most confirmed Cases originated from two shipping lanes.
Replacement completion remains healthy.
Packaging review recommended.
```

# 8.100 AI Hallucination Protection

AI must not invent:

- Customer complaints.
- refund completion.
- replacement status.
- Order history.
- Customer Health evidence.
- confirmed root cause.

---

# 8.101 AI Causal Boundary

Correlation is not automatically causation.

Example:

Higher complaint rate during a promotion may result from:

- Greater volume.
- rushed production.
- new customers.
- Shipping pressure.

Analysis must investigate.

---

# 8.102 AI Fairness Boundary

Customer Health or retention models must not use inappropriate sensitive traits for differential treatment.

Legitimate service behavior/context should drive intervention.

the standalone migration must document those gaps.

```text
Historical Information Missing

Begin Reliable Capture Post-Cutover
```

# ENTERPRISE CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SERVICE MANAGEMENT & SUPPORT OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 9 — Service Migration, Case Reconciliation, Validation, Testing & Customer Operations Certification Canon

---

# 9.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** requires a permanent assurance architecture proving that customer-service history, Case relationships, complaints, communications, refunds, replacements, recovery actions, escalations, Customer Success activity, and service intelligence remain valid whenever:

- Helpdesk technology changes.
- CRM service modules change.
- messaging platforms change.
- marketplace integrations change.
- the underlying ERP is migrated.
- customer identity models are modernized.
- AI-assisted support systems are introduced.

Stages 1–8 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Service entity model.
- Case operating model.
- Service Management service architecture.
- governance and authority.
- service events and omnichannel coordination.
- service workspace and Customer Success experience.
- Service Intelligence and predictive support analytics.

Stage 9 establishes the permanent framework for:

- Service migration.
- historical service preservation.
- customer-Case reconciliation.
- communication reconciliation.
- refund/replacement reconciliation.
- SLA validation.
- service-policy migration.
- Customer Success validation.
- omnichannel testing.
- security validation.
- business acceptance.
- customer-operations certification.

The central principle is:

> **Technology may change, but customer history, service commitments, resolution truth, and customer-impact evidence must not silently change with it.**

---

# 9.2 Service Migration Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Customer History Before Reformatting

Historical service activity must remain understandable after migration.

---

## Meaning Before Ticket Mapping

Mapping one ticket field into another is insufficient if the business meaning changes.

---

## Original Interaction Before Reconstructed Narrative

Historical customer messages remain the primary source where available.

---

## Resolution Truth Before Status Conversion

A migrated Case marked "Closed" must not lose the fact that a refund or replacement was still pending.

---

## Relationship Before Record Count

Customer, Order, Case, and operational relationships matter more than simply matching record counts.

---

## Evidence Before Certification

Service migration must be demonstrably correct.

---

## No Fabrication Before Completeness

Historical gaps must remain gaps rather than being filled with invented events.

---

# 9.3 Migration Scope

Potential migration scope includes:

- Customers.
- contacts.
- Cases.
- Service Requests.
- Complaints.
- categories.
- priorities.
- severity.
- statuses.
- queues.
- assignments.
- SLAs.
- communications.
- call logs.
- attachments.
- internal notes.
- investigations.
- evidence.
- findings.
- resolutions.
- returns.
- replacements.
- refunds.
- recovery actions.
- escalations.
- Service Incidents.
- commitments.
- follow-ups.
- Customer Success actions.
- Customer Health.
- retention risk.
- service knowledge references.
- service-quality reviews.
- service audit history.

---

# 9.4 Service Migration Inventory

Before migration, build an inventory of service-relevant objects.

Each may capture:

- Object ID.
- object type.
- business meaning.
- source system.
- owner.
- active/historical state.
- customer relationship.
- Order relationship.
- target representation.
- migration method.
- reconciliation method.
- certification status.

---

# 9.5 Source Classification

Historical information may be classified as:

- Authoritative Customer Record.
- Authoritative Order/Transaction Record.
- Native Service Case.
- Communication Evidence.
- Internal Operational Note.
- Derived Service Analytics.
- Reconstructed Historical Context.
- Unstructured Historical Evidence.

This classification determines how it may be treated.

---

# 9.6 Customer Identity Migration

Customer Service depends on stable customer identity.

Migration must preserve:

- Customer ID mapping.
- contact details where legitimate.
- account relationships.
- marketplace identity relationships where available.

Duplicate identity resolution must be governed.

---

# 9.7 Customer Merge Reconciliation

If multiple legacy customer records map to one canonical Customer:

```text id="customer-merge-reconciliation"
Legacy Customer A

+

Legacy Customer B

↓

Canonical Customer

↓

All Cases / Orders / Communications Preserved
```

No service history should disappear because of identity consolidation.

---

# 9.8 Unmatched Customer Migration

Some historical service interactions may not map confidently to a canonical Customer.

They should remain:

- Unmatched.
- partially matched.
- pending review.

The migration must not guess identity.

---

# 9.9 Case Identity Preservation

Existing native Case IDs should be preserved or permanently mapped.

This supports:

- Audit.
- support references.
- cross-system traceability.
- historical navigation.

---

# 9.10 Case Semantic Mapping

Each Case field must be mapped by meaning.

Example:

```text id="case-semantic-mapping"
Legacy:
ticket_status = "done"

Actual Meaning:
Agent finished internal work

Target:
Cannot automatically map to
Case Closed

unless closure semantics match
```

Semantic equivalence matters more than label similarity.

---

# 9.11 Case Status Mapping

Legacy statuses may map into:

- New.
- active.
- waiting.
- resolved.
- closed.
- cancelled.

Where semantics are ambiguous:

- preserve original status.
- record mapped analytical status separately if necessary.

---

# 9.12 Priority Migration

Legacy priority should be preserved where meaningful.

If the target uses a different priority scale:

```text id="priority-migration"
Legacy:
P1 / P2 / P3

↓

Document Mapping

↓

Target:
Critical / High / Normal
```

The mapping must be explicit.

---

# 9.13 Severity Migration

If the legacy system did not distinguish Priority from Severity:

Do not fabricate historical Severity.

The target may store:

**Severity: Unknown / Not Historically Captured**

---

# 9.14 Category Migration

Historical category migration should preserve:

- Original category.
- target category.
- mapping rationale.

If categories are redesigned for future operations, old Cases should not silently appear as though they were originally created under the new taxonomy.

---

# 9.15 Analytical Reclassification

The system may later analytically reclassify historical Cases.

Permanent distinction:

```text id="analytical-reclassification"
Original Operational Category

≠

Later Analytical Category
```

Both may coexist.

---

# 9.16 Queue Migration

Historical queue data should preserve:

- Queue name.
- ownership context.
- date.
- assignment history.

New queue architecture may differ.

Historical records should not be rewritten to imply future organizational structure existed in the past.

---

# 9.17 Assignment Migration

Where assignment history exists, preserve:

- Agent/team.
- assignment time.
- transfer history.

If only final owner exists, do not invent full assignment history.

---

# 9.18 SLA Migration

Historical SLA migration must preserve:

- SLA target.
- applicable version.
- start.
- pause.
- breach.
- completion.

Only where source evidence exists.

---

# 9.19 No-Retroactive-SLA Rule

Permanent rule:

```text id="no-retro-sla"
New SLA Policy

Must NOT

Be Applied as Historical Truth
to Old Cases
```

New policies may be used for comparative analytics only if clearly labeled.

---

# 9.20 SLA Gap Policy

If legacy support lacked formal SLA tracking:

The target must not fabricate:

- response timers.
- breach events.
- pause events.

Historical timestamps may support later analysis, but operational SLA history remains absent.

---

# 9.21 Communication Migration

Customer communications must preserve where available:

- Original text.
- sender.
- recipient.
- timestamp.
- channel.
- attachments.
- Case relationship.

---

# 9.22 Communication Ordering

Migration must preserve chronological order.

Example:

```text id="communication-ordering"
Customer Message

↓

Agent Reply

↓

Customer Reply

↓

Internal Update

↓

Resolution Message
```

Incorrect ordering can materially distort service history.

---

# 9.23 Channel Preservation

Historical messages should preserve:

- Email.
- WhatsApp.
- marketplace.
- phone.
- website.
- social.

A unified timeline must not erase original channel provenance.

---

# 9.24 Email Thread Migration

Where email thread identifiers exist:

- Preserve them.
- maintain Case relationship.

If threads cannot be reconstructed reliably, do not create false thread structure.

---

# 9.25 WhatsApp Migration

Where historical WhatsApp service messages are legitimately available:

Preserve:

- message timestamp.
- sender/recipient.
- attachment reference.
- Case/order relationship if known.

Privacy and retention policies remain binding.

---

# 9.26 Marketplace Communication Migration

Marketplace history may preserve:

- marketplace Order.
- message ID.
- channel.
- response.
- timestamp.

External marketplace history may be incomplete.

Limitations must be documented.

---

# 9.27 Phone Interaction Migration

Legacy call logs may preserve:

- Call time.
- direction.
- agent.
- outcome.

If call content was not recorded, the migration must not invent transcript content.

---

# 9.28 Internal Note Migration

Internal Notes should preserve:

- Original text.
- author.
- timestamp.
- visibility classification.

Historical note visibility must not accidentally become customer-visible.

---

# 9.29 Attachment Migration

Attachments may include:

- Customer images.
- damaged-product evidence.
- personalization screenshots.
- shipment proof.

Migration must preserve:

- Case association.
- source.
- access classification.
- integrity where feasible.

---

# 9.30 Personalization Evidence Migration

For GiftHatke, historical service assurance should preserve links to:

- Submitted text.
- submitted photos.
- approved design.
- production asset.

This is essential for personalization dispute reconstruction.

---

# 9.31 Investigation Migration

Where native Investigation records exist, preserve:

- Investigation question.
- evidence.
- owner.
- finding.
- confidence.

If investigation existed only as informal notes, preserve the notes rather than creating a fictional formal investigation.

---

# 9.32 Finding Migration

Historical findings should remain distinguishable from customer statements.

Example:

```text id="finding-migration"
Customer Statement:
"Product was damaged before delivery."

Finding:
Carrier Damage Probable
```

These must not be merged into one text field without semantics.

---

# 9.33 Finding Confidence Migration

If confidence level was not historically captured, it should remain:

- Not Captured.

Do not infer certainty retrospectively.

---

# 9.34 Resolution Migration

Historical Resolution should preserve:

- Resolution type.
- decision.
- completion state.
- customer communication.
- related refund/replacement.

---

# 9.35 Resolution-State Migration

A common migration risk is mapping:

**Approved Replacement**

to:

**Resolved**

even though replacement was never produced.

The target must distinguish:

- decision.
- execution.
- completion.

---

# 9.36 Refund Migration

Historical Refund records should preserve:

- Case.
- Order.
- amount.
- reason where known.
- approval.
- Finance state.
- completion date.

---

# 9.37 Refund Reconciliation

Canonical reconciliation:

```text id="refund-reconciliation"
Service Refund Record

↓

Finance Refund Record

↓

Payment / Transaction Reference

↓

Amounts + Status Compared
```

Material discrepancies require investigation.

---

# 9.38 Refund-State Reconciliation

The migration should specifically distinguish:

- Requested.
- approved.
- processing.
- completed.
- failed.

This prevents false customer-history claims.

---

# 9.39 Replacement Migration

Replacement history should preserve:

- Original Order.
- replacement reason.
- approval.
- replacement Order/Job.
- QC where available.
- shipment.
- delivery.

---

# 9.40 Replacement Reconciliation

Verify:

```text id="replacement-reconciliation"
Service Case

↓

Replacement Request

↓

Replacement Production / Order

↓

Shipment

↓

Final Delivery State
```

---

# 9.41 Repeat Replacement Migration

Where one Case created multiple replacements:

All replacements should remain distinguishable.

This is an important service-quality signal.

---

# 9.42 Return Migration

Return history should preserve:

- Return authorization.
- original Order.
- return reason.
- receipt.
- inspection.
- final outcome.

---

# 9.43 Recovery Migration

Historical Customer Recovery may preserve:

- Goodwill.
- coupon.
- discount.
- expedited service.
- recovery notes.

Commercial instruments must reconcile with Domain 31 where available.

---

# 9.44 Recovery Concession Reconciliation

If a Case shows:

**20% recovery discount**

the migration should reconcile against:

- coupon/discount record.
- validity.
- customer.
- actual usage if relevant.

---

# 9.45 Escalation Migration

Historical escalations should preserve where available:

- Type.
- reason.
- owner.
- time.
- outcome.

A manager CC'd on an email is not automatically a formal historical escalation unless the system treated it as one.

---

# 9.46 Service Incident Migration

Historical systemic issues may be preserved when native incident records exist.

If they did not exist, later grouping of Cases into an analytical incident must be labeled as reconstructed analysis.

---

# 9.47 Commitment Migration

Historical customer promises may be migrated if explicit data exists.

Examples:

- callback date.
- replacement dispatch promise.
- refund-update commitment.

Do not infer promises from vague conversation.

---

# 9.48 Follow-Up Migration

Historical follow-ups should preserve:

- due date.
- owner.
- customer contact.
- outcome.

If only the final message exists, don't fabricate a formal scheduled follow-up.

---

# 9.49 Customer Success Action Migration

Formal historical Customer Success actions should be preserved where they existed.

Reactive support activity should not automatically be relabeled as proactive Customer Success.

---

# 9.50 Customer Health Migration

If Customer Health did not exist historically:

Do not fabricate historical health scores.

Future standalone systems may calculate new health states based on preserved history and clearly label them as post-migration analytical assessments.

---

# 9.51 Retention Risk Migration

The same principle applies to Retention Risk.

Historical model output must remain tied to:

- Model.
- version.
- timestamp.

New models must not overwrite old predictions.

---

# 9.52 Service Knowledge Migration

Knowledge references may preserve:

- Article.
- version.
- usage.
- Case relationship.

If article history is unavailable, preserve current knowledge separately rather than invent historical versions.

---

# 9.53 Service Template Migration

Historical template usage may be preserved where available.

Communication itself remains more important than knowing whether a template generated it.

---

# 9.54 Quality Review Migration

Historical Service Quality reviews may preserve:

- Reviewer.
- Case.
- finding.
- coaching/process note.
- date.

These remain distinct from HCM performance records.

---

# 9.55 Service Audit Migration

Audit history should preserve material actions such as:

- Case creation.
- status change.
- ownership change.
- refund approval.
- replacement approval.
- escalation.
- closure.
- reopen.

---

# 9.56 Historical Audit Integrity

Where source audit history exists, it must not be flattened into only final state.

Final state alone cannot reconstruct service decisions.

---

# 9.57 Service Reconciliation Framework

Canonical sequence:

```text id="service-reconciliation-framework"
Certified Legacy Service State

↓

Target Standalone Service State

↓

Compare

↓

Difference Detected?

NO
→ PASS

YES
↓

Classify Difference

↓

Correct / Approve / Document

↓

Re-Test
```

---

# 9.58 Reconciliation Difference Classes

Potential classes:

- Exact Match.
- Expected Representation Difference.
- Approved Technical Transformation.
- Approved Business Correction.
- Legacy Defect.
- Migration Defect.
- Historical Data Gap.
- Unexplained Difference.

Material unexplained differences block certification.

---

# 9.59 Record Count Reconciliation

Counts may be compared for:

- Customers.
- Cases.
- communications.
- refunds.
- replacements.
- escalations.

Record-count equality is necessary in some scenarios but insufficient by itself.

---

# 9.60 Relationship Reconciliation

The platform must verify relationships such as:

```text id="service-relationship-reconciliation"
Customer

↓

Case

↓

Order

↓

Refund / Replacement

↓

Communication
```

A record migrated without its relationship may be operationally useless.

---

# 9.61 Customer-to-Case Reconciliation

Validate:

- All Cases map to correct Customer where known.
- unmatched Cases remain explicitly unmatched.

Incorrect customer linkage is a critical migration defect.

---

# 9.62 Case-to-Order Reconciliation

Validate:

- Correct Order.
- Order Line.
- Product.

especially for:

- Refunds.
- replacements.
- personalization disputes.

---

# 9.63 Communication-to-Case Reconciliation

Validate:

- Message count.
- timestamps.
- channel.
- direction.
- Case assignment.

---

# 9.64 Refund Aggregate Reconciliation

Compare:

- Number of refund Cases.
- refund amounts.
- completed refunds.
- failed/pending refunds.

Finance remains authoritative for actual financial amounts.

---

# 9.65 Replacement Aggregate Reconciliation

Compare:

- Replacement requests.
- replacement Orders/jobs.
- delivered replacements.
- repeat replacements.

---

# 9.66 Service Category Reconciliation

Compare legacy and target category distribution after mapped transformation.

Large unexpected changes may indicate mapping defects.

---

# 9.67 Channel Reconciliation

Compare service activity by:

- Shopify/direct.
- Amazon.
- future Flipkart.
- future Meesho.
- WhatsApp.
- email.
- B2B.

Channel identity must remain intact.

---

# 9.68 B2B Account Reconciliation

For corporate accounts validate:

- Account.
- Orders.
- Cases.
- commitments.
- recovery.
- follow-up.

---

# 9.69 GiftHatke Personalization Reconciliation

Validate historical personalization Cases against:

- Customer-submitted text.
- Product.
- Order.
- production-used data where available.

---

# 9.70 GiftHatke Shipping Reconciliation

Validate:

- Case.
- Shipment.
- tracking/reference.
- delivery state.
- complaint/resolution.

---

# 9.71 Service Test Architecture

The permanent testing model includes:

1. Customer Identity Testing.
2. Case Creation Testing.
3. Case Relationship Testing.
4. Routing Testing.
5. Ownership Testing.
6. SLA Testing.
7. Communication Testing.
8. Investigation Testing.
9. Resolution Testing.
10. Refund Testing.
11. Replacement Testing.
12. Return Testing.
13. Escalation Testing.
14. Incident Testing.
15. Customer Success Testing.
16. Security Testing.
17. Omnichannel Testing.
18. Migration Reconciliation.
19. Business Acceptance Testing.

---

# 9.72 Customer Identity Testing

Validate:

- Exact match.
- multiple contact methods.
- ambiguous match.
- unmatched customer.
- merged Customer.

The system must not silently link a Case to the wrong person.

---

# 9.73 Case Creation Testing

Tests should verify:

- Correct Case ID.
- source channel.
- interaction.
- Customer relation.
- SLA start.
- audit record.

---

# 9.74 Duplicate Intake Testing

Simulate duplicate inbound delivery.

Expected:

```text id="duplicate-intake-test"
Same Message Received Twice

↓

One Authoritative Interaction

↓

No Duplicate Case
```

unless business context requires separate Case creation.

---

# 9.75 Case Relationship Testing

Validate Case links to:

- Customer.
- Order.
- Product.
- Shipment.
- Refund.
- Replacement.

---

# 9.76 Routing Testing

Test:

- Correct category.
- correct queue.
- permissions.
- workload behavior.
- no eligible queue.

No-routing scenarios must fail visibly.

---

# 9.77 Ownership Testing

Validate:

- Assignment.
- reassignment.
- transfer.
- ownership history.
- no orphaned Case.

---

# 9.78 Status Transition Testing

Test allowed and prohibited transitions.

Example:

```text id="status-transition-test"
New → Assigned
PASS

New → Closed
without Resolution
BLOCK
```

where policy requires Resolution.

---

# 9.79 SLA Testing

Tests include:

- Start.
- pause.
- resume.
- At Risk.
- breach.
- completion.
- applicable SLA version.

---

# 9.80 SLA Pause Abuse Testing

Attempt to pause SLA using invalid internal-delay reason.

Expected:

- Block or require valid governed reason.

---

# 9.81 Communication Testing

Validate:

- Email send.
- message recording.
- delivery failure.
- reply capture.
- channel identity.
- attachments.

---

# 9.82 Communication Truth Testing

Controlled case:

```text id="communication-truth-test"
Finance Refund:
Processing

Agent Draft:
"Refund completed"

Expected:
Warning / Block according to policy
```

---

# 9.83 Omnichannel Thread Testing

Test one customer contacting through:

- Email.
- WhatsApp.
- marketplace.

The platform should preserve individual channels while providing coherent Case continuity.

---

# 9.84 Internal Note Privacy Testing

Validate that Internal Notes:

- Are not exposed to customer portal.
- are not included in customer messages.
- respect role access.

---

# 9.85 Investigation Testing

Validate:

- Investigation creation.
- evidence.
- internal tasks.
- finding.
- confidence.

---

# 9.86 Personalization Evidence Testing

GiftHatke controlled case:

```text id="personalization-evidence-test"
Submitted:
RIYA

Production:
RINA

Expected:
Internal mismatch visible
```

---

# 9.87 Finding Testing

Validate distinct states:

- Confirmed.
- probable.
- inconclusive.

The system must not force a confirmed outcome where evidence is insufficient.

---

# 9.88 Resolution Testing

Validate:

- Standard Resolution.
- controlled Resolution.
- authority.
- conditions.
- execution state.
- completion.

---

# 9.89 Closure Validation Testing

Attempt closure when:

- Refund still processing.
- replacement not shipped.
- critical task open.

Expected:

- Block or controlled exception according to policy.

---

# 9.90 Refund Testing

Test:

- Request.
- approval.
- Finance execution.
- failure.
- retry.
- completion.
- customer update.

---

# 9.91 Refund Idempotency Testing

Repeat same refund command.

Expected:

- One refund.
- no duplicate financial movement.

---

# 9.92 Replacement Testing

Test:

- Approval.
- personalization revalidation.
- replacement job creation.
- QC.
- shipment.
- delivery.
- Case completion.

---

# 9.93 Replacement Idempotency Testing

Repeated command must not create duplicate replacement jobs.

---

# 9.94 Repeat Replacement Testing

Second replacement should trigger required enhanced review where policy applies.

---

# 9.95 Return Testing

Validate:

- Eligibility.
- authorization.
- return receipt.
- inspection.
- refund/replacement decision.

---

# 9.96 Personalized Return Testing

Test:

- Enterprise defect.
- customer-input error.
- change of mind.

Expected outcomes should follow configured policy and applicable law.

---

# 9.97 Recovery Testing

Validate:

- Service Recovery need.
- approval.
- Domain 31 commercial instrument.
- customer communication.
- completion.

---

# 9.98 Commercial Recovery Reconciliation Testing

Verify recovery coupon/discount matches:

- Correct customer.
- correct value.
- correct validity.
- Case reference.

---

# 9.99 Escalation Testing

Test:

- Functional escalation.
- SLA escalation.
- manager escalation.
- executive escalation.
- closure of escalation independent of Case.

---

# 9.100 Incident Testing

Validate:

- Incident creation.
- affected Case linking.
- proactive customer identification.
- common communication.
- Incident resolution.
- individual Case completion.

---

# 9.101 Commitment Testing

Test customer promises:

- Create.
- due date.
- completion.
- missed commitment.
- alert.

---

# 9.102 Follow-Up Testing

Validate:

- Follow-up scheduled.
- owner.
- due date.
- completion.
- customer outcome.

---

# 9.103 Customer Success Testing

Test proactive workflows such as:

- Missing personalization.
- known shipping delay.
- B2B recovery follow-up.

---

# 9.104 Customer Health Testing

Validate:

- Input evidence.
- health state.
- explainability.
- confidence.
- update after new service event.

---

# 9.105 Retention Risk Testing

Test that:

- Risk recommendation appears.
- no automatic discount occurs unless policy separately authorizes it.

---

# 9.106 Service Intelligence Testing

Validate:

- Case rates.
- complaint findings.
- reopen.
- SLA.
- Product complaint analytics.
- channel analysis.

Each output must trace to source service records.

---

# 9.107 AI Service Testing

AI-assisted systems require testing for:

- Case grounding.
- no fabricated Order status.
- no fabricated refund status.
- no invented root cause.
- recommendation/authority separation.
- permission-aware responses.

---

# 9.108 AI High-Risk Boundary Testing

Prompt AI to:

- approve refund.
- accuse customer of fraud.
- promise impossible delivery.

Expected:

- AI does not independently execute unauthorized action.

---

# 9.109 Security Testing

Validate permissions for:

- Case access.
- internal notes.
- refund details.
- customer data.
- escalation.
- audit.
- configuration.

---

# 9.110 Cross-Customer Privacy Testing

Ensure one customer's Case data is not exposed to another account through:

- Search.
- customer portal.
- marketplace integration.
- AI assistant.

---

# 9.111 Audit Testing

Validate that material actions preserve:

- Actor.
- time.
- prior state.
- new state.
- reason where required.

---

# 9.112 Performance Testing

Service systems should be tested for:

- Case list performance.
- Customer lookup.
- Order lookup.
- timeline retrieval.
- message send.
- search.
- high-volume intake.

Correctness remains the priority.

---

# 9.113 Load Testing

Peak support load may occur during:

- Festival campaigns.
- carrier disruptions.
- marketplace incidents.

The service architecture should remain operational.

---

# 9.114 Failure-Recovery Testing

Simulate:

- CRM unavailable.
- Order service unavailable.
- Finance refund unavailable.
- marketplace API unavailable.
- email provider unavailable.

The Case must remain coherent and visible.

---

# 9.115 Message Delivery Failure Testing

If outbound delivery fails:

Expected:

- Message failure state.
- agent notification.
- customer not falsely marked informed.

---

# 9.116 Search Reconciliation Testing

- Status change.
- ownership change.
- customer merge.

---

# 9.117 Event Replay Testing

Replay historical service events.

Expected:

- Case projections rebuild.
- no duplicate customer messages.
- no new refunds.
- no duplicate replacements.

---

- complex complaint.
- refund.
- replacement.
- B2B Case.
- marketplace Case.
- personalization Case.
- reopened Case.
- severe escalation.

- replacements.
- open Cases.
- closed Cases.
- communication counts.

- find Customer.

- respond.
- request internal action.
- process replacement.
- track refund.
- escalate.
- follow up.
- close Case.

---

# 9.131 Certification Gates

The permanent customer-operations certification gates are:

## Gate 1 — Service Inventory

All critical service objects identified.

## Gate 2 — Semantic Mapping

Source and target meanings validated.

## Gate 3 — Customer Identity Integrity

Cases linked correctly.

## Gate 4 — Case Relationship Integrity

Orders, shipments, refunds, and replacements preserved.

## Gate 5 — Communication Integrity

Customer interaction history remains coherent.

## Gate 6 — Resolution Integrity

Decision, execution, and completion remain distinct.

## Gate 7 — Refund/Replacement Integrity

Recovery operations reconcile.

## Gate 8 — SLA & Escalation Integrity

Service commitments remain valid.

## Gate 9 — Privacy, Security & Audit

Sensitive data and authority protected.

## Gate 10 — Business Acceptance

Service users approve operational readiness.

---

# 9.132 Certification States

Possible outcomes:

- Fully Certified.
- Certified With Controlled Exceptions.
- Not Certified.

Material unresolved customer-history or Resolution discrepancies block full certification.

---

# 9.133 Controlled Exceptions

Examples:

- Old WhatsApp history unavailable.
- historical assignment history missing.
- legacy SLA never existed.
- old attachments unavailable.
- marketplace conversation partially inaccessible.
- historical Customer Health not available.

Each requires:

- Description.
- scope.
- risk.
- treatment.
- owner.
- approval.

---

# 9.134 Legacy Service Defects

Migration may expose:

- Incorrect Customer linkage.
- duplicate Case.
- Case closed while refund pending.
- inconsistent Resolution.
- missing communication.

Legacy defects should not be blindly copied purely to achieve equality.

---

# 9.135 Legacy Defect Treatment

Canonical process:

```text id="legacy-service-defect-treatment"
Legacy Defect Identified

↓

Evidence Captured

↓

Customer / Business Impact Assessed

↓

Preserve Historical Fact?

Correct Current State?

↓

Governed Decision

↓

Audit
```

---

# 9.136 Customer Commitment Protection

If migration occurs while active Cases exist:

All outstanding commitments must remain visible after cutover.

Examples:

- Refund pending.
- replacement promised.
- callback due.
- customer waiting for response.

---

# 9.137 Active Case Cutover

Canonical active-Case migration:

```text id="active-case-cutover"
Open Legacy Case

↓

Full Current State Snapshot

↓

Interactions + Dependencies

↓

Target Case Created

↓

Owner Assigned

↓

SLA / Commitment Context Preserved

↓

Cutover Verified
```

---

# 9.138 Active Case Dual-Authority Risk

During cutover, the same Case must not be actively managed independently in two systems.

One platform must be authoritative.

---

# 9.139 Active Customer Communication Cutover

Inbound channels must be switched carefully so that messages are not:

- Lost.
- duplicated.
- routed to legacy inbox only.

---

# 9.140 Active Refund Cutover

A refund already processing during migration must not be reissued.

The target should import:

- Existing refund ID.
- status.
- Finance relationship.

---

# 9.141 Active Replacement Cutover

A replacement already in Production must remain linked to:

- Current Case.
- production job.
- shipment workflow.

It must not be recreated.

---

# 9.142 Active Escalation Cutover

Open escalations must preserve:

- Reason.
- owner.
- due action.
- Case context.

---

# 9.143 SMP1 Mandatory Service Assurance

Stage 9 is binding for **SMP1** wherever customer-service-relevant data is migrated.

SMP1 cannot declare service continuity successful merely because:

- Customers imported.
- Orders imported.
- old notes exist.

It must ensure service context required for future support remains trustworthy.

---

```text id="smp1-service-migration"
Certified Apps Script Business Baseline

↓

Service-Relevant Data Inventory

↓

Customer / Order Mapping

↓

Historical Communication Preservation

↓

Standalone Identity & Relationship Model

↓

Migration

↓

Reconciliation

↓

Operational Acceptance

↓

Standalone Customer Operations Certification
```

---

# 9.145 SMP1 Historical Case Rule

If Apps Script does not contain formal Case Management:

```text id="smp1-historical-case-rule"
Historical Notes / Messages

↓

Preserve as Historical Evidence

NOT

Fabricate Complete Case Lifecycle
```

New Cases become native standalone records after cutover.

---

# 9.146 SMP1 No-Redesign Rule

Permanent rule:

```text id="smp1-service-redesign-rule"
Migration

≠

Permission to Rewrite Historical Customer Experience
```

New Customer Service processes may improve future operations.

Historical facts remain preserved.

```text id="smp1-service-cutover-authority"
Authoritative
```

# 9.149 SMP1 Rollback Requirement

Rollback planning must protect:

- Customer replies received after cutover.
- refunds initiated.
- replacements created.
- escalations.
- promises made.

Rollback cannot simply discard new customer-service activity.

# ENTERPRISE CUSTOMER SUCCESS, SERVICE MANAGEMENT & SUPPORT OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 10 — Final Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Certification Canon

---

# 10.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Customer Success, Service Management & Support Operations Domain** is hereby consolidated into one final authoritative enterprise specification.

Stages 1–9 established:

- Domain foundation.
- Service entity architecture.
- Case lifecycle and operating model.
- Service Management service architecture.
- Resolution authority and governance.
- Service events and omnichannel synchronization.
- Agent and Customer Success experience architecture.
- Service Intelligence and predictive support analytics.
- Service migration, reconciliation, testing, and certification.

Stage 10 formally certifies the Domain as the permanent GiftHatkeOS architecture for:

- Customer support.
- Customer Success.
- complaint handling.
- Case Management.
- service requests.
- returns.
- refunds.
- replacements.
- escalations.
- Customer Recovery.
- service commitments.
- Customer Health.
- retention risk.
- support intelligence.
- post-sale relationship operations.

The Domain exists to ensure that customer-service activity remains:

- Customer-centered.
- fact-based.
- accountable.
- fast.
- fair.
- governed.
- cross-domain aware.
- measurable.
- auditable.
- technically portable.

---

# 10.2 Final Canon Mission

The permanent mission is:

> **Resolve customer needs accurately, fairly, and efficiently while protecting customer trust, operational accountability, commercial discipline, and long-term relationship value.**

The Domain must enable the enterprise to answer:

- Who needs help?
- What happened?
- What business object is affected?
- Who owns the Case?
- What evidence exists?
- What is the current finding?
- What Resolution is appropriate?
- Who may authorize it?
- Has the Resolution actually been completed?
- Has the customer been informed?
- Is the customer relationship now healthy?
- What should the enterprise learn from the Case?

---

# 10.3 Certified Permanent Principles

The Domain permanently follows:

- Customer context before response.
- Case before fragmented conversations.
- ownership before handoff.
- evidence before finding.
- finding before Resolution.
- authority before customer promise.
- operational completion before closure.
- fairness before arbitrary concession.
- communication before silence.
- root cause before recurrence.
- proactive action before avoidable complaint.
- service truth before analytics.
- probability before predictive certainty.
- human accountability before irreversible automation.

---

# 10.4 Certified Domain Boundary

The Domain permanently owns:

- Customer Service Cases.
- Service Requests.
- Complaints.
- service queues.
- service ownership.
- service SLAs.
- investigations.
- service findings.
- Resolutions.
- Return coordination.
- Replacement coordination.
- Refund coordination.
- Customer Recovery.
- escalations.
- customer-service communication.
- service incidents.
- Customer Success actions.
- Customer Health.
- Retention Risk.
- Service Intelligence.
- service-quality evidence.

It does **not** replace:

- CRM.
- Orders.
- Product.
- Personalization.
- Production.
- Quality.
- Shipping.
- Finance.
- Commercial Governance.
- Legal.
- Data Governance.

Canonical relationship:

```text
CRM
Owns Customer Identity

↓

Orders / Operational Domains
Own Business Facts

↓

Customer Service
Owns Customer Case & Resolution Coordination

↓

Finance / Shipping / Production / Commercial
Execute Authoritative Domain Actions

↓

Customer Service
Owns Customer Communication & Outcome Continuity
```

---

# 10.5 Certified Relationship With CRM

CRM remains authoritative for:

- Customer identity.
- contact data.
- account.
- relationship context.

Domain 32 owns:

- Customer Service Case.
- Complaint.
- Resolution.
- Customer Success activity.
- service history.

Permanent distinction:

```text
Customer Relationship
→ CRM

Customer Service Issue
→ Domain 32
```

---

# 10.6 Certified Relationship With Order Management

Order Management owns:

- Order.
- Order Line.
- order lifecycle.
- transaction commitment.

Customer Service may:

- Investigate.
- request authorized correction.
- coordinate cancellation.
- link refund/replacement.

It must not silently alter Order truth.

---

# 10.7 Certified Relationship With Personalization

Personalization remains authoritative for:

- Customer-submitted text.
- images.
- assets.
- approvals.
- production-ready personalization.

Domain 32 consumes this evidence when resolving personalization-related Cases.

---

# 10.8 Certified Relationship With Production

Production owns:

- Manufacturing Job.
- production status.
- remake feasibility.
- operational execution.

Customer Service may coordinate replacements but cannot invent production commitments.

---

# 10.9 Certified Relationship With Quality

Quality owns:

- Defect assessment.
- non-conformance.
- corrective action.
- QC evidence.

Customer Service owns the customer-facing complaint and Resolution coordination.

---

# 10.10 Certified Relationship With Shipping

Shipping owns:

- Shipment.
- tracking.
- dispatch.
- delivery.
- carrier exception.

Customer Service communicates only from authoritative Shipping facts.

---

# 10.11 Certified Relationship With Finance

Finance remains authoritative for:

- Payment.
- refund execution.
- financial adjustment.
- credit-note state where applicable.

Customer Service may:

- request.
- coordinate.
- communicate.

Permanent rule:

```text
Refund Approved

≠

Refund Completed
```

---

# 10.12 Certified Relationship With Commercial Governance

Domain 31 governs:

- Discounts.
- coupons.
- commercial concessions.
- recovery offers.

Domain 32 governs:

- Why Customer Recovery is needed.
- the customer-service context.
- follow-through.

---

# 10.13 Certified Relationship With Product

Product owns:

- Product definition.
- specifications.
- lifecycle.

Domain 32 provides:

- Complaint patterns.
- service burden.
- customer-impact evidence.

Product decisions remain with Product Governance.

---

The permanent service entity model includes:

- Customer Service Case.
- Service Request.
- Complaint.
- Case Category.
- Case Priority.
- Case Severity.
- Case Status.
- Case Owner.
- Service Queue.

- Service SLA.

- Case Attachment.
- Evidence Record.
- Investigation.
- Finding.
- Resolution.
- Resolution Action.

- Replacement Request.
- Refund Request.
- Recovery Request.
- Service Escalation.
- Service Incident.
- Service Commitment.
- Customer Follow-Up.
- Customer Success Action.
- Customer Health Record.
- Retention Risk Record.
- Customer Feedback.
- Service Quality Record.
- Service Risk.
- Service Audit Record.

# 10.15 Certified Service Entity Topology

The permanent topology is:

```text
Customer

↓

Case

↓
```

Every Case requires a stable identity.

Case identity must remain valid across:

The permanent lifecycle is:

```text

↓
```
