# 1.15 Manufacturing Performance

Manufacturing Performance should not be represented by one universal number.

It may include:

- Throughput.
- Schedule Adherence.
- Cycle Time.
- Downtime.
- Yield.
- Rework.
- Scrap.
- Capacity.

---

# 1.16 Throughput

**Throughput** represents useful Production output completed over time.

Potential units:

- Jobs/day.
- units/hour.
- orders/day.

The correct unit depends on the process.

---

# 1.17 Throughput vs Activity

Permanent distinction:

```text id="throughput-vs-activity"
Machine Running

≠

Customer-Ready Output Produced
```

Activity without useful output may still represent operational loss.

---

# 1.18 Throughput Rate

Conceptual model:

```text id="throughput-rate"
Completed Good Output

÷

Time Period

=

Throughput Rate
```

---

# 1.19 Production Completion

Completed output should align with Domain 3 Production truth.

Domain 34 does not redefine when a Job is operationally complete.

---

# 1.20 Cycle Time

Cycle Time represents the elapsed or active time required to complete relevant manufacturing work.

The system may distinguish:

- Process time.
- queue time.
- waiting time.
- total elapsed time.

---

# 1.21 Process Time

Process Time represents actual productive processing activity.

Examples:

- Laser cutting.
- engraving.
- sublimation printing.
- assembly.

---

# 1.22 Queue Time

Queue Time represents work waiting before a process begins.

Large queues may reveal:

- Bottleneck.
- poor scheduling.
- missing inputs.

---

# 1.23 Waiting Time

Waiting may occur because of:

- Material.
- personalization.
- machine.
- approval.
- labor.
- Quality.
- previous process.

---

# 1.24 Total Lead Time

Conceptually:

```text id="manufacturing-lead-time"
Queue Time

+

Process Time

+

Waiting Time

+

Transfer Time

=

Manufacturing Lead Time
```

---

# 1.25 Standard Cycle Time

A Standard Cycle Time represents expected duration under normal conditions.

Standards should be:

- Product/process specific.
- versioned.
- evidence-based.

---

# 1.26 Actual Cycle Time

Actual Cycle Time should be captured from real Production execution where technically feasible.

---

# 1.27 Cycle-Time Variance

Canonical relationship:

```text id="cycle-time-variance"
Actual Cycle Time

-

Standard Cycle Time

=

Cycle-Time Variance
```

---

# 1.28 Variance Interpretation

Positive variance does not automatically mean operator failure.

Potential causes:

- Material issue.
- rework.
- machine problem.
- unusual Product complexity.
- inaccurate standard.
- rush interruption.

---

# 1.29 Production Adherence

Production Adherence compares:

- Planned Production.
- scheduled Production.
- actual Production.

---

# 1.30 Schedule Adherence

Conceptual question:

> Did Production happen when the enterprise expected it to happen?

---

# 1.31 Schedule Miss

Potential causes:

- Material shortage.
- missing personalization.
- machine downtime.
- capacity overload.
- Quality issue.
- priority changes.

---

# 1.32 Production Plan vs Schedule

Permanent distinction:

```text id="plan-vs-schedule"
Production Plan
=
What Should Be Produced

Production Schedule
=
When / Where It Should Be Produced

Actual
=
What Was Produced
```

---

# 1.33 Work Center

A Work Center may represent:

- Laser.
- sublimation.
- assembly.
- QC.
- packaging.
- design/personalization preparation.

Domain 3 remains authoritative for Work Center master data.

---

# 1.34 Work-Center Performance

Potential dimensions:

- Throughput.
- cycle time.
- queue.
- downtime.
- rework.
- available capacity.

---

# 1.35 Work-Center Queue

A persistent queue at one Work Center may indicate:

- Bottleneck.
- upstream overproduction.
- downstream delay.

---

# 1.36 Machine Utilization

Utilization may measure:

```text id="machine-utilization"
Machine Busy Time

÷

Available Scheduled Time
```

But utilization alone is not a manufacturing-excellence objective.

---

# 1.37 Utilization Trap

Running every machine at maximum utilization can create:

- Excess WIP.
- queues.
- overproduction.

Therefore utilization must be interpreted with flow.

---

# 1.38 Availability

Equipment Availability considers whether the machine/resource was available when scheduled to produce.

---

# 1.39 Downtime

Downtime represents periods when Production cannot proceed due to:

- Machine failure.
- maintenance.
- setup.
- missing material.
- no operator.
- utility issue.

Not all downtime belongs to Equipment Domain.

Cause classification is important.

---

# 1.40 Planned Downtime

Examples:

- Preventive maintenance.
- planned cleaning.
- scheduled setup.

---

# 1.41 Unplanned Downtime

Examples:

- Breakdown.
- power failure.
- unexpected tool issue.

---

# 1.42 Downtime Cause

Every meaningful downtime record should ideally capture:

- Cause.
- start.
- end.
- affected resource.
- affected Production.

---

# 1.43 Production Loss

Production Loss represents lost output potential.

Potential categories:

- Availability Loss.
- performance loss.
- quality loss.
- waiting loss.
- setup loss.
- planning/material loss.

---

# 1.44 Loss Tree

Canonical concept:

```text id="manufacturing-loss-tree"
Available Production Opportunity

↓

Availability Loss

↓

Performance Loss

↓

Quality Loss

↓

Useful Output
```

GiftHatke may use a simplified version appropriate to its scale.

---

# 1.45 Setup Time

Setup Time may include:

- Loading files.
- changing material.
- adjusting jig.
- changing machine settings.
- cleaning/preparation.

---

# 1.46 Changeover

Changeover represents switching from one Product/process configuration to another.

---

# 1.47 Changeover Optimization

The enterprise may reduce lost time by:

- Product sequencing.
- standardized setup.
- tooling preparation.
- grouped similar jobs.

---

# 1.48 Setup vs Production Time

Permanent distinction:

```text id="setup-production-time"
Setup
=
Prepare Resource

Run Time
=
Produce Output
```

Both consume capacity differently.

---

# 1.49 Batch Size

Batch size affects:

- Setup frequency.
- WIP.
- responsiveness.
- lead time.

Large batches are not always better.

---

# 1.50 Batch Tradeoff

Canonical relationship:

```text id="batch-tradeoff"
Larger Batch

↓

Fewer Setups

BUT

More WIP / Longer Wait for Other Jobs
```

---

# 1.51 Work-In-Progress

WIP represents Production that has started but is not finished.

---

# 1.52 WIP Visibility

The enterprise should understand:

- Quantity.
- process stage.
- age.
- owner/work center.
- blockage.

---

# 1.53 Excess WIP

Excess WIP can:

- Hide delays.
- increase handling.
- increase damage risk.
- increase confusion.

---

# 1.54 WIP Age

A Job waiting unusually long should become visible.

---

# 1.55 Queue Management

Queue Management should identify:

- Jobs waiting.
- priority.
- age.
- expected processing time.

---

# 1.56 Flow Time

Flow Time measures how long work takes to move through the entire Production system.

---

# 1.57 Flow Efficiency

Conceptual relationship:

```text id="flow-efficiency"
Value-Adding Process Time

÷

Total Flow Time

=

Flow Efficiency
```

Exact KPI governance belongs to Domain 30.

---

# 1.58 Bottleneck

A Bottleneck is the resource/process limiting overall system throughput.

---

# 1.59 Bottleneck Identification

Potential signals:

- Persistent queue.
- high utilization.
- late jobs.
- downstream starvation.
- capacity overload.

---

# 1.60 Bottleneck Principle

Permanent rule:

```text id="bottleneck-principle"
Improve Constraint

Before

Optimizing Non-Constraint
```

when the objective is overall flow.

---

# 1.61 Bottleneck Shift

After improving one bottleneck, another resource may become the new constraint.

Continuous monitoring is required.

---

# 1.62 Starvation

A Work Center is starved when it has capacity but lacks:

- Material.
- work.
- required input.

---

# 1.63 Blocking

A process may be blocked because downstream capacity is unavailable.

---

# 1.64 Material-Induced Production Loss

Production may lose time because:

- Material not available.
- wrong material.
- material quality failure.

Domain 2/Quality own operational truth.

Domain 34 analyzes the Production impact.

---

# 1.65 Personalization-Induced Production Loss

GiftHatke may lose Production time when:

- Photo missing.
- text incomplete.
- approval pending.
- artwork correction required.

This should be visible separately from machine inefficiency.

---

# 1.66 Quality Loss

Quality loss may include:

- Scrap.
- rework.
- failed QC.
- remake.

Domain 4 remains authoritative for defect classification.

---

# 1.67 Yield

Yield represents usable output relative to input.

Conceptually:

```text id="production-yield"
Good Output

÷

Total Output / Input Basis

=

Yield
```

---

# 1.68 Material Yield

For sheet materials such as Acrylic/MDF, Yield may reflect:

- usable Product output.
- material input.

---

# 1.69 Process Yield

Process Yield may reflect:

- Units entering process.
- units exiting acceptable.

---

# 1.70 Scrap

Scrap represents unusable material/output that cannot reasonably continue as intended.

---

# 1.71 Scrap Cause

Potential causes:

- Cutting error.
- engraving error.
- print defect.
- breakage.
- wrong personalization.
- material defect.

---

# 1.72 Scrap vs Rework

Permanent distinction:

```text id="scrap-vs-rework"
Scrap
=
Cannot Be Recovered as Intended

Rework
=
Requires Additional Processing to Become Acceptable
```

---

# 1.73 Rework

Rework consumes:

- Capacity.
- labor.
- machine time.
- material.
- lead time.

It should not be hidden inside normal Production activity.

---

# 1.74 Rework Loop

Canonical flow:

```text id="rework-loop"
Production

↓

Quality Failure

↓

Rework Required

↓

Additional Processing

↓

Reinspection
```

---

# 1.75 First-Pass Quality

First-Pass Performance asks:

> How much output passes the intended process without rework?

---

# 1.76 First-Pass Quality Boundary

Domain 34 may analyze First-Pass performance.

Domain 4 owns the authoritative Quality acceptance criteria.

---

# 1.77 Replacement Production

Customer-service replacements create real manufacturing workload.

These should be separately identifiable where useful.

---

# 1.78 Replacement Capacity Impact

The enterprise should be able to understand:

- How much capacity is used by replacement/remake work?

---

# 1.79 Rush Production

Rush Jobs may disrupt normal sequencing.

They should be visibly classified.

---

# 1.80 Rush Impact

Potential impacts:

- Additional setup.
- rescheduling.
- delayed normal Jobs.
- overtime.

---

# 1.81 Priority Change Loss

Frequent priority changes may create operational instability.

The Domain should detect this pattern.

---

# 1.82 Production Stability

Production Stability means output is reasonably predictable over time.

Indicators may include:

- Stable cycle times.
- manageable WIP.
- predictable quality.
- low unplanned interruption.

---

# 1.83 Process Variation

Variation may occur due to:

- Product complexity.
- material.
- machine.
- operator method.
- environment.
- inconsistent standard work.

---

# 1.84 Common vs Special Cause

Where useful, the enterprise may distinguish:

- Common recurring variation.
- special unusual event.

This supports better corrective action.

---

# 1.85 Standard Work

Standard Work describes the expected consistent operating method.

It may include:

- Sequence.
- setup.
- key quality checks.
- safety steps.
- standard time.

---

# 1.86 Standard Work Governance

Standards should be:

- Approved.
- versioned.
- accessible.
- trainable.
- auditable.

---

# 1.87 Standard Work vs Work Instruction

Detailed instructions may live in:

- Knowledge.
- Document Management.
- Production.

Domain 34 focuses on consistency and performance against the standard.

---

# 1.88 Standard Deviation / Variation Analytics

Future systems may use statistical analysis to detect instability.

Advanced statistics should only be used where:

- Data quality.
- process volume.

support meaningful interpretation.

---

# 1.89 Takt Concept

Where useful, **Takt Time** may represent the pace required to meet demand.

Conceptually:

```text id="takt-concept"
Available Production Time

÷

Required Customer Demand

=

Required Pace
```

For highly customized, low-volume Products, this may be used selectively.

---

# 1.90 Takt vs Cycle Time

Canonical distinction:

```text id="takt-vs-cycle"
Takt
=
Required Demand Pace

Cycle Time
=
Actual Process Pace
```

---

# 1.91 Takt Applicability Boundary

GiftHatke should not force high-volume manufacturing metrics onto every custom Product.

Use only where operationally meaningful.

---

# 1.92 OEE-Style Intelligence

Future equipment-intensive operations may use OEE-style thinking based on:

- Availability.
- Performance.
- Quality.

---

# 1.93 OEE Boundary

OEE is not mandatory as one universal GiftHatke KPI.

The Canon preserves the underlying concepts while allowing an appropriately scaled implementation.

---

# 1.94 Availability Loss

Potential causes:

- Breakdown.
- maintenance.
- setup.
- operator unavailable.

---

# 1.95 Performance Loss

Potential causes:

- Slower-than-standard run.
- micro-stops.
- poor process flow.

---

# 1.96 Quality Loss

Potential causes:

- Scrap.
- rework.
- defective units.

---

# 1.97 Micro-Stop

Short interruptions may materially reduce output even when not recorded as major downtime.

Future systems may capture them where technically practical.

---

# 1.98 Production Constraint

A Production Constraint may be:

- Machine.
- labor skill.
- Quality.
- Material.
- personalization.
- packaging.

---

# 1.99 Constraint Ownership

The cause determines which Domain owns the corrective action.

Example:

```text id="constraint-ownership"
Material Constraint
→ Inventory / Procurement

Machine Constraint
→ Asset Management

Quality Constraint
→ Quality

Flow / Process Constraint
→ Production / Manufacturing Excellence
```

---

# 1.100 Production Loss Classification

Potential high-level loss categories:

- Equipment Loss.
- Material Loss.
- Quality Loss.
- Planning Loss.
- Waiting Loss.
- Setup Loss.
- Process Performance Loss.
- Workforce Availability Loss.
- System/Information Loss.

---

# 1.101 Information Loss

Production may be delayed because:

- Wrong file.
- missing design.
- inaccessible information.
- incorrect Job instructions.

This should remain separately classifiable.

---

# 1.102 Production Delay Classification

Delay can be caused by:

- Upstream.
- internal process.
- downstream.

This distinction improves root-cause analysis.

---

# 1.103 Root Cause Analysis

Manufacturing root-cause analysis may use:

- Evidence.
- process timeline.
- Production events.
- Quality evidence.
- machine evidence.

---

# 1.104 Root Cause vs Symptom

Example:

```text id="manufacturing-root-cause"
Symptom:
Laser Queue Too Long

Possible Root Cause:
Unexpected Rework Load
or
Poor Scheduling
or
Machine Downtime
```

The queue itself is not necessarily the root cause.

---

# 1.105 Corrective Action

Corrective Action may involve:

- Process change.
- maintenance.
- training.
- Supplier change.
- Production standard change.
- planning parameter change.

Ownership remains with relevant Domain.

---

# 1.106 Preventive Improvement

The Domain should prioritize changes that prevent recurrence, not merely recover today's delay.

---

# 1.107 Continuous Improvement

Canonical improvement loop:

```text id="continuous-improvement-loop"
Observe Performance

↓

Identify Loss

↓

Find Root Cause

↓

Design Improvement

↓

Implement

↓

Measure Result

↓

Standardize if Successful
```

---

# 1.108 Improvement Opportunity

Potential sources:

- Repeated downtime.
- high rework.
- long queues.
- repeated late Jobs.
- high setup time.
- low material yield.

---

# 1.109 Improvement Prioritization

Potential factors:

- Customer impact.
- throughput impact.
- frequency.
- cost.
- risk.
- feasibility.

---

# 1.110 Improvement Hypothesis

Before change, define:

- Problem.
- proposed cause.
- expected improvement.

This enables evidence-based learning.

---

# 1.111 Improvement Baseline

Every material improvement should record:

- Before-state.

Without baseline, improvement claims are weak.

---

# 1.112 Improvement Outcome

After implementation, compare:

- Before.
- after.
- expected.
- actual.

---

# 1.113 Improvement Standardization

If successful:

- Standard Work.
- Production parameters.
- training.
- relevant system configuration.

should be updated through governed channels.

---

# 1.114 Unsuccessful Improvement

A change that fails should remain part of organizational learning.

It should not be erased.

---

# 1.115 Visual Factory Concept

The manufacturing environment should make operational state visible.

Potential displays:

- Jobs waiting.
- current bottleneck.
- machine state.
- QC backlog.
- daily output.
- urgent exceptions.

---

# 1.116 Visual Management Principle

The purpose is:

- Faster recognition.
- faster response.

not dashboard decoration.

---

# 1.117 Andon-Style Alert Concept

Future implementation may support immediate visible signals for:

- Machine down.
- Quality stop.
- Material shortage.
- urgent Production blockage.

GiftHatke may implement this digitally rather than through traditional factory hardware.

---

# 1.118 Stop-the-Process Authority

Where serious Quality or safety risk exists:

Authorized users/processes should be able to stop Production.

Quality/EHS authority boundaries remain intact.

---

# 1.119 Daily Production Review

A daily Manufacturing Excellence review may focus on:

- Output.
- missed Jobs.
- bottleneck.
- downtime.
- quality/rework.
- urgent improvement actions.

---

# 1.120 Weekly Manufacturing Review

Weekly review may include:

- Throughput trend.
- cycle-time variance.
- Work-Center performance.
- bottlenecks.
- downtime causes.
- rework.
- improvement actions.

---

# 1.121 Monthly Excellence Review

Monthly review may include:

- Capacity.
- process stability.
- material yield.
- chronic losses.
- improvement benefits.
- equipment constraints.

---

# 1.122 Manufacturing Performance Board

A future management board may show:

- Planned vs Actual Output.
- Throughput.
- Bottleneck.
- Downtime.
- Rework.
- Scrap.
- WIP.
- Critical Improvement Actions.

---

# 1.123 Production Loss Pareto

The enterprise may rank major loss causes.

Example:

```text id="loss-pareto"
Total Lost Hours

1. Machine Downtime
2. Missing Personalization
3. Rework
4. Material Shortage
5. Setup
```

---

# 1.124 Loss Pareto Boundary

A Pareto ranking identifies frequency/impact.

It does not by itself prove root cause.

---

# 1.125 Work-Center Comparison

Future analytics may compare:

- Laser A vs Laser B.
- different shifts.
- Product families.

Comparisons must adjust for Product complexity where relevant.

---

# 1.126 Complexity-Adjusted Performance

Highly customized Products may naturally require more time.

The enterprise should avoid unfair comparisons based solely on raw units/hour.

---

# 1.127 Product Complexity

Potential complexity dimensions:

- Number of personalization elements.
- engraving area.
- material type.
- assembly complexity.
- revision needs.

---

# 1.128 Production Mix

Different Product mix can materially affect throughput.

Therefore:

```text id="production-mix-effect"
Same Order Count

≠

Same Production Workload
```

---

# 1.129 GiftHatke Manufacturing Model

GiftHatke manufacturing is characterized by:

- High personalization.
- relatively small batches.
- mixed Products.
- variable complexity.
- event-driven peaks.
- B2B bulk Jobs.
- shared equipment.

Therefore Manufacturing Excellence must emphasize:

- Flow.
- bottleneck visibility.
- mix-aware capacity.
- quality-at-source.
- personalization readiness.

---

# 1.130 GiftHatke Laser Operations

Laser operations may involve:

- Cutting.
- engraving.
- Product setup.
- file preparation.
- material positioning.

---

# 1.131 GiftHatke Laser Loss Categories

Potential laser losses:

- Setup.
- machine downtime.
- wrong file.
- material not ready.
- rework.
- cleaning.
- excessive changeover.

---

# 1.132 GiftHatke Laser Performance

Potential analytical dimensions:

- Jobs/hour.
- Laser minutes/unit.
- setup time.
- rework.
- machine availability.

---

# 1.133 GiftHatke Acrylic Yield

Acrylic performance may analyze:

- Planned sheet use.
- actual sheet use.
- scrap.
- nesting effectiveness.

---

# 1.134 GiftHatke MDF/Wood Yield

Similarly for:

- MDF.
- wood.
- other sheet materials.

---

# 1.135 GiftHatke Sublimation Operations

Potential loss areas:

- Printer downtime.
- reprints.
- color/print defects.
- setup.
- media wastage.

---

# 1.136 GiftHatke Personalization Preparation

Before Production, potential delays include:

- Customer details incomplete.
- image unusable.
- artwork pending.
- revision required.

This is a critical upstream manufacturing readiness stage.

---

# 1.137 GiftHatke Personalization-Ready State

Canonical distinction:

```text id="gift-personalization-ready"
Order Confirmed

↓

Personalization Complete?

NO
→ Not Production Ready

YES
→ Production Ready
```

---

# 1.138 GiftHatke Design Revision Load

Repeated design revisions consume real operational capacity.

Future systems should be able to measure them.

---

# 1.139 GiftHatke Assembly Operations

Some Products may require:

- Base assembly.
- hardware.
- electronics.
- packaging preparation.

Assembly can become a separate bottleneck.

---

# 1.140 GiftHatke QC Operations

Quality checks should be included in manufacturing flow.

QC backlog can delay finished output even when manufacturing itself is complete.

---

# 1.141 GiftHatke Packaging Operations

Packaging may become:

- Work Center.
- constraint.
- quality-control point.

---

# 1.142 GiftHatke Replacement/Rework Production

Replacement Jobs should be visible separately from:

- Normal customer Production.

This enables understanding of hidden quality/service cost.

---

# 1.143 GiftHatke Rush Job Classification

Rush Jobs should preserve:

- Reason.
- priority.
- impact on schedule.

---

# 1.144 GiftHatke Festival Manufacturing

Festival periods may increase:

- Setup pressure.
- WIP.
- rush work.
- overtime.
- defect risk.

Manufacturing Excellence should monitor these as a distinct operational condition.

---

# 1.145 GiftHatke Rakhi Production

Potential Rakhi operations include:

- Component preparation.
- engraving.
- assembly.
- packaging.

The flow should be analyzed end to end.

---

# 1.146 GiftHatke Corporate Bulk Production

Large B2B Orders may benefit from:

- Batch optimization.
- standard work.
- dedicated material staging.
- planned QC.

---

# 1.147 GiftHatke Custom B2B Production

Corporate personalization may increase:

- Design complexity.
- setup.
- sample/approval cycles.

The business should distinguish standard bulk work from highly customized bulk work.

---

# 1.148 GiftHatke Work-In-Progress Board

A future WIP board may show:

```text id="gift-wip-board"
Awaiting Personalization

↓

Ready for Laser

↓

Laser In Progress

↓

Assembly

↓

QC

↓

Packaging

↓

Ready to Ship
```

---

# 1.149 GiftHatke Blocked Job

A blocked Job should show:

- Stage.
- reason.
- age.
- owner.
- required action.

---

# 1.150 GiftHatke Production Aging

Older-than-expected WIP should become visible before customer delay occurs.

---

# 1.151 GiftHatke Bottleneck Example

```text id="gift-bottleneck-example"
Laser:
80% Utilization

Assembly:
55%

QC:
145% Required Load

↓

True Bottleneck:
QC
```

Buying another laser would not fix this specific problem.

# 1.152 GiftHatke Loss Example — Missing Personalization

```text id="gift-missing-personalization-loss"
Production Jobs Waiting:
24

Cause:
Customer Personalization Missing

↓

Manufacturing Lost Flow

but

Not Machine Performance Failure
```

# 1.153 GiftHatke Loss Example — Rework

```text id="gift-rework-loss"
Engraving Jobs:
100

Rework:
8

↓

Additional Laser Capacity Consumed
```

# 1.154 GiftHatke Loss Example — Supplier Material

```text id="gift-material-loss"
Production Ready Jobs:
40

Blocked:
12

Planning / Procurement Constraint
```

# 1.155 GiftHatke Improvement Example — Laser Setup

Before:

- Frequent Product-by-Product material changes.

Improvement:

- Group compatible jobs.

Possible outcome:

- Reduced setup.
- increased throughput.

---

# 1.156 GiftHatke Improvement Example — Design Preparation

Problem:

- Jobs reaching Production with missing/incorrect design files.

Improvement:

- Strong Production-readiness gate.

Expected effect:

- Lower waiting.
- lower wrong-personalization rework.

---

# 1.157 GiftHatke Improvement Example — QC at Source

Problem:

- Defect discovered only at final QC.

Improvement:

- Add early check after critical engraving step.

Potential effect:

- Lower downstream rework.

# 1.158 GiftHatke Improvement Example — Packaging

Problem:

- Finished Jobs wait for packaging.

Improvement:

- Stage packaging materials based on Production plan.

Potential effect:

- Lower finished-goods queue time.

# 1.159 Industrial Operations Risk

Potential manufacturing risks include:

- Chronic bottleneck.
- equipment dependence.
- excessive rework.
- unstable Production standards.
- high WIP.
- poor yield.
- missing skills.
- information failures.

# 1.160 Single-Machine Risk

# 1.161 Manufacturing Risk Horizon

Risk may be:

- Immediate.
- near-term.
- structural.

# 1.162 Production Exception

- Cycle Time > threshold.
- WIP age high.
- repeated rework.
- bottleneck overload.
- abnormal downtime.
- yield drop.

# 1.163 Exception Ownership

- Owner.
- cause classification.
- due action.

# 1.164 Production Escalation

Critical operational problems may escalate when:

- Customer commitments at risk.
- repeated defect.
- severe machine downtime.
- safety concern.

- What changed?
- where?
- why?
- what is constraining output?
- what should improve first?

- Time.
- Product family.
- Work Center.
- season.

- standards needing recalibration.

# 1.168 Downtime Intelligence

- Frequency.
- duration.
- cause.
- machine.
- Production impact.

---

# 1.169 Rework Intelligence

May identify:

- Product.
- process.
- defect.
- source.
- capacity consumed.

# 1.170 Scrap Intelligence

May analyze:

- Material.
- process.
- defect.
- value context.

# 1.171 WIP Intelligence

# 1.172 Bottleneck Intelligence

# 1.173 Predictive Manufacturing Intelligence

Future systems may predict:

- Machine downtime.
- cycle-time risk.
- Production delay.
- bottleneck.
- quality/rework risk.

# 1.174 Predictive Production Delay

- Current WIP.
- resource capacity.
- Product complexity.
- material readiness.
- machine state.

# 1.175 Predictive Quality Risk

- Product.
- material.
- process history.

# 1.176 AI-Assisted Manufacturing Excellence

- Loss categorization.
- root-cause suggestions.

- Production summaries.
- improvement recommendations.
- anomaly detection.

```text id="ai-manufacturing-explanation"
QC Queue

Confidence:
High
```

# 1.179 AI Hallucination Boundary

- Machine status.
- Production quantity.
- QC result.
- Material availability.
- downtime.
- Job completion.

# 1.180 Manufacturing Data Requirements

The Domain depends on trustworthy:

- Production Job.
- Work Center.
- Product.
- timestamps.
- status changes.
- machine/resource identity.
- Quality outcomes.
- material usage.
- downtime.

# 1.181 Missing Data

the system must not present high-precision performance analytics.

# 1.182 Manufacturing Data Quality

Domain 29 governs data quality standards.

Domain 34 should expose confidence limitations.

---

# 1.183 Manufacturing Event Readiness

Future events may include:

- JobStarted.
- JobCompleted.
- JobBlocked.
- WorkCenterQueueChanged.
- MachineDown.
- SetupStarted.
- SetupCompleted.

- ScrapRecorded.

- ImprovementImplemented.

# 1.184 Technology Independence

- ERP Production modules.

# 1.185 Manufacturing Excellence Maturity

Permanent progression:

```text id="manufacturing-maturity"
Reactive Production

↓

Visible Production

↓

Measured Production

↓

Stable Standardized Production

↓

Continuous Improvement

↓

Predictive / Intelligent Industrial Operations
```

# 1.186 Reactive Production

Characteristics:

- Problems discovered late.
- limited measurement.
- priorities change constantly.
- rework hidden.

Not the target state.

# 1.187 Visible Production

Characteristics:

- WIP visible.
- bottlenecks visible.
- downtime captured.
- blocked Jobs identified.

- Production Jobs.

- statuses.

- Work Centers.
- Quality relationships.

# 1.193 SMP1 Historical Measurement Rule

If Apps Script does not contain reliable historical:

- Cycle Time.
- downtime.
- WIP events.
- setup times.

SMP1 must not fabricate these measures.

---

# 1.194 SMP1 No-Fabrication Principle

Canonical rule:

```text id="smp1-manufacturing-no-fabrication"
Historical Manufacturing Telemetry Missing

↓

Preserve Available Production Facts

↓

Document Measurement Gaps

↓

Begin Reliable Shop-Floor Measurement
Post-Cutover
```

---

# 1.195 SMP1 Event Reconstruction Boundary

Historical Production states may be imported.

Synthetic detailed event sequences should not be presented as original history unless they can be reliably derived and clearly identified as reconstructed.

# ENTERPRISE MANUFACTURING EXCELLENCE & INDUSTRIAL OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 2 — Manufacturing Performance, Work Center, Loss, WIP & Improvement Entity Model Canon

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Manufacturing Excellence & Industrial Operations Domain** requires a permanent entity architecture defining how the enterprise represents:

- Manufacturing Performance.
- Production flow.
- Work Centers.
- machine/resource performance.
- Production states.
- Work-In-Progress.
- queue and blocked work.
- cycle times.
- standards.
- setups.
- changeovers.
- downtime.
- Production Loss.
- Yield.
- Scrap.
- Rework.
- bottlenecks.
- constraints.
- process variation.
- Industrial Exceptions.
- Continuous Improvement.
- manufacturing intelligence.

Stage 1 established the Domain foundation, Manufacturing Excellence philosophy, operational scope, and authority boundaries.

Stage 2 establishes the canonical information model required to make manufacturing performance:

- Measurable.
- comparable.
- explainable.
- traceable.
- auditable.
- continuously improvable.

The central objective is:

> **Every material manufacturing outcome should be traceable through what was planned, what resource was used, what actually happened, what time and material were consumed, what losses occurred, what quality outcome resulted, and what improvement followed.**

---

# 2.2 Manufacturing Entity Principles

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Production Truth Before Performance Interpretation

Manufacturing Excellence consumes authoritative Production execution records.

It does not invent alternative Production completion states.

---

## Time State Before Efficiency Metric

Performance metrics should originate from reliable:

- Start.
- stop.
- queue.
- downtime.
- completion.

evidence.

---

## Resource Identity Before Comparison

Machine or Work-Center performance cannot be interpreted without knowing which resource actually executed the work.

---

## Good Output Before Gross Activity

Completed acceptable output matters more than machine activity alone.

---

## Loss Cause Before Loss Allocation

Lost time or material must be classified before assigning organizational responsibility.

---

## Original Event Before Derived Metric

Cycle time, utilization, and throughput are derived.

Underlying Production events remain the evidence.

---

## Version Before Historical Mutation

Standards and classifications used at one point in time must remain reconstructable later.

---

# 2.3 Canonical Manufacturing Excellence Entity Landscape

The permanent entity model includes:

| Entity | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Manufacturing Performance Record | Captures performance context |
| Production Performance Period | Defines analytical time scope |
| Work Center | Represents manufacturing function/resource group |
| Resource | Represents machine/person/team/tool context |
| Resource Capability | Defines what resource can perform |
| Resource Availability | Defines usable manufacturing capacity |
| Production Job Performance | Performance view of Production Job |
| Operation Performance | Performance of individual process step |
| Production Event | Represents operational state change |
| Production State Interval | Represents duration in a state |
| Standard Work | Defines approved execution method |
| Production Standard | Defines expected operational performance |
| Standard Cycle Time | Defines expected process duration |
| Standard Setup Time | Defines expected setup duration |
| Standard Yield | Defines expected good-output ratio |
| Actual Cycle Time | Captures realized time |
| Setup Record | Captures setup activity |
| Changeover Record | Captures Product/process transition |
| Queue Record | Captures waiting before execution |
| WIP Record | Represents unfinished Production |
| WIP Aging Record | Tracks age of unfinished work |
| Blocked Job Record | Represents inability to proceed |
| Production Delay | Represents delayed manufacturing progression |
| Downtime Record | Captures resource/process downtime |
| Downtime Reason | Controlled reason classification |
| Micro-Stop Record | Captures short interruption where relevant |
| Production Loss | Represents lost productive potential |
| Loss Category | Classifies Production Loss |
| Yield Record | Represents good output vs input |
| Scrap Record | Represents unrecoverable output/material loss |
| Scrap Reason | Controlled Scrap classification |
| Rework Record | Represents additional corrective processing |
| Rework Reason | Controlled Rework classification |
| First-Pass Record | Represents right-first-time processing |
| Production Constraint | Represents manufacturing limiting condition |
| Bottleneck Record | Represents identified throughput constraint |
| Starvation Record | Represents resource waiting for upstream input |
| Blocking Record | Represents upstream stoppage due to downstream constraint |
| Capacity Performance Record | Represents planned vs realized capacity |
| Production Adherence Record | Represents Plan/Schedule vs Actual |
| Manufacturing Exception | Represents material abnormal condition |
| Root Cause Investigation | Represents structured cause analysis |
| Improvement Opportunity | Represents potential process improvement |
| Improvement Initiative | Represents governed improvement effort |
| Improvement Hypothesis | Defines expected improvement logic |
| Improvement Baseline | Defines before-state |
| Improvement Experiment | Records controlled change/test |
| Improvement Outcome | Captures measured result |
| Standardization Record | Records adoption of successful improvement |
| Manufacturing Risk | Represents industrial operational risk |
| Manufacturing Insight | Represents analytical observation |
| Manufacturing Recommendation | Represents suggested improvement |
| Manufacturing Audit Record | Preserves change/action history |

# 2.4 Manufacturing Performance Record

A Manufacturing Performance Record may represent:

- Product.
- Production Job.
- Work Center.
- Resource.
- period.
- planned quantity.
- actual good quantity.
- Scrap.
- Rework.
- cycle time.
- downtime.
- throughput.

It is a derived operational performance view.

Possible periods:

- Shift.
- Day.
- Week.
- month.
- campaign.
- Production batch.

The period must be explicit when comparing performance.

# 2.6 Work Center Entity

A **Work Center** represents a logical manufacturing capability.

GiftHatke examples:

- Personalization Preparation.
- Laser.
- Sublimation.
- Assembly.
- QC.
- Packaging.

Domain 3 remains authoritative for the Production Work-Center master.

Domain 34 extends it with performance semantics.

Each Work Center should have stable identity.

Potential fields:

- Work Center ID.
- name.
- capability.
- location.
- active status.
- owning operational function.

---

# 2.8 Resource Entity

A Resource may represent:

- Machine.
- equipment.
- workstation.
- team.
- specialized labor capacity.

Resource identity supports finer performance measurement.

---

# 2.9 Work Center vs Resource

Permanent distinction:

```text id="work-center-resource"
Work Center:
Laser Department

Resources:
Laser Machine A
Laser Machine B
```

A Work Center can contain multiple Resources.

---

# 2.10 Resource Capability

Resource Capability may define:

- Supported processes.
- materials.
- size limits.
- Product types.
- operational restrictions.

---

# 2.11 Resource Availability

Resource Availability may include:

- Planned working time.
- maintenance.
- outage.
- reservation.
- available operational time.

Domain 26 remains authoritative for equipment availability events where applicable.

---

# 2.12 Production Job Performance

A **Production Job Performance** record links Manufacturing Excellence analytics to authoritative Domain 3 Production Job.

Potential data:

- Job ID.
- Product.
- quantity.
- due date.
- release time.
- first start.
- completion.
- good quantity.
- Scrap.
- Rework.
- total elapsed time.

# 2.13 Operation Performance

A Production Job may contain multiple operations.

Example:

```text id="operation-performance"
Production Job

↓

Personalization Prep

↓

Laser

↓

Assembly

↓

QC

↓

Packaging
```

Each operation may have separate performance state.

---

# 2.14 Operation Sequence

Operation records should preserve:

- Planned sequence.
- actual sequence.
- skipped/repeated process where authorized.

This helps identify Rework and flow disruption.

---

# 2.15 Production Event

Canonical Production Events may include:

- JobReleased.
- JobQueued.
- JobStarted.
- JobPaused.
- JobBlocked.
- JobResumed.
- JobCompleted.
- OperationStarted.
- OperationCompleted.

These provide the basis for time analysis.

# 2.16 Production Event Identity

Every event should preserve:

- Event ID.
- Production Job.
- Operation.
- timestamp.
- actor/system.
- resource.
- state.
- source.

# 2.17 Production State Interval

A State Interval derives duration between events.

Example:

```text id="production-state-interval"
Queued:
09:00–09:45

Processing:
09:45–10:20

Waiting QC:
10:20–11:10

QC:
11:10–11:20
```

Potential states:

- Queued.
- Setup.
- Processing.
- Paused.
- Blocked.
- Waiting Material.
- Waiting Personalization.
- Waiting QC.
- Rework.
- Completed.

If timestamps are missing:

- Duration should remain unknown.

Do not invent it.

- expected timing.

```text id="equipment-process-downtime"
Machine Ready
```

# 2.80 Bottleneck Confidence

# 2.83 Starvation Record

Represents resource idle because required upstream work/input is unavailable.

Potential causes:

- Material shortage.
- no released Jobs.
- missing personalization.

---

# 2.84 Blocking Record

Represents inability of upstream Production to continue because downstream cannot accept work.

Example:

- QC backlog blocks more production.

---

# 2.85 Capacity Performance Record

May compare:

- Planned capacity.
- available capacity.
- consumed capacity.
- productive capacity.
- lost capacity.

---

# 2.86 Capacity Consumption

Capacity consumption may include:

- Productive run time.
- Setup.
- Rework.
- waiting tied to resource.

Different analyses may classify these differently.

---

# 2.87 Realized Capacity

Realized capacity reflects what was genuinely usable, not theoretical installed capacity.

---

# 2.88 Production Adherence Record

May capture:

- Planned quantity.
- scheduled quantity.
- actual completed quantity.
- due time.
- actual completion.

---

# 2.89 Schedule Change Record

- Original schedule.

# 2.90 Priority Change Record

- Original priority.

The **Enterprise Manufacturing Excellence & Industrial Operations Domain** permanently follows:

- Production truth before performance interpretation.
- resource identity before comparison.
- original event before derived metric.
- good output before activity.
- Standard Work before variance analysis.
- waiting classification before efficiency blame.

- Rework before hidden capacity consumption.
- Bottleneck evidence before optimization.
- Root Cause before improvement.

- versioning before historical mutation.
- human authority before high-impact industrial action.

- **ERP10**
- Version 1.1 and later releases.
- MES implementations.
- shop-floor systems.
- Work-Center Management.
- Loss Analysis.
- WIP Management.
- Industrial Analytics.
- Continuous Improvement.
- Digital Manufacturing.
- AI-assisted Manufacturing Excellence.
- future enterprise expansion.

The entity architecture defined here is permanent at the business-semantics level. Future MES platforms, machine telemetry systems, industrial databases, IoT platforms, work-center applications, optimization engines, and AI manufacturing systems may evolve, but every implementation must preserve certified Production truth, event/time integrity, Work-Center and Resource identity, WIP, Production Loss, Scrap/Rework, bottleneck, improvement lineage, versioning, auditability, and human operational authority established by this Canon.

# ENTERPRISE MANUFACTURING EXCELLENCE & INDUSTRIAL OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 3 — Manufacturing Excellence Lifecycle, Shop-Floor Control & Continuous Improvement Operating Model Canon

---

# 3.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Manufacturing Excellence & Industrial Operations Domain** requires a permanent operating model defining how Production performance, Work-In-Progress, Work Centers, Resource states, Downtime, Rework, Scrap, Bottlenecks, Production Loss, Root Cause, and Improvement Initiatives move through a governed Manufacturing Excellence lifecycle.

Stages 1–2 established:

- Domain foundation.
- manufacturing excellence philosophy.
- canonical performance entity model.
- Work Center and Resource semantics.
- WIP, Loss, Scrap, Rework, Bottleneck, and Improvement entities.

Stage 3 defines how these entities operate together in:

- Daily shop-floor control.
- production-flow management.
- exception handling.
- WIP control.
- Downtime response.
- Quality-loss response.
- Bottleneck management.
- Production recovery.
- continuous improvement.
- operational review.

The permanent objective is:

> **Create a disciplined operating system in which Production problems become visible early, work remains controlled through the shop floor, losses are classified correctly, constraints are actively managed, and improvements are verified before becoming Standard Work.**

---

# 3.2 Manufacturing Excellence Operating Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

- Readiness before release.
- flow before local utilization.
- visible WIP before hidden queue.
- standard before variance.
- loss classification before corrective action.
- containment before escalation.
- bottleneck before non-constraint optimization.
- Root Cause before permanent change.
- controlled experiment before standardization.
- measured outcome before improvement claim.
- safety and Quality before throughput pressure.

---

# 3.3 Canonical Manufacturing Excellence Lifecycle

The certified operating lifecycle is:

```text
Production Requirement / Schedule

↓

Production Readiness

↓

Job Release

↓

Queue / WIP

↓

Setup

↓

Processing

↓

Quality / Internal Checks

↓

Completion

↓

Performance Capture

↓

Loss / Variance Detection

↓

Containment

↓

Root Cause

↓

Improvement

↓

Validation

↓

Standardization

↓

Continuous Monitoring
```

---

# 3.4 Shop-Floor Control Cycle

The operating cycle should continuously answer:

- What work is ready?
- What work is waiting?
- What is blocked?
- What is running?
- What failed?
- What is late?
- What requires intervention?
- What is the current bottleneck?

---

# 3.5 Production Readiness Gate

Before a Job enters active Production, the system/process should determine whether required prerequisites are available.

Potential checks include:

- Material Ready.
- Personalization Ready.
- Design/Instruction Ready.
- Resource Ready.
- required Quality prerequisites complete.

---

# 3.6 Readiness States

Potential states:

```text
NOT READY

READY WITH CONDITION

READY
```

A Job should not appear executable merely because an Order exists.

---

# 3.7 Material Readiness

Material readiness must be based on authoritative Inventory availability/reservation.

Potential failures include:

- Material missing.
- wrong specification.
- quarantined Material.
- insufficient quantity.

---

# 3.8 Personalization Readiness

For GiftHatke, this may require:

- Customer image.
- name/text.
- dimensions.
- approved artwork where applicable.

---

# 3.9 Instruction Readiness

Production requires correct:

- Job instructions.
- design file.
- Product specification.
- approved personalization.

---

# 3.10 Resource Readiness

Resource readiness may consider:

- Machine availability.
- maintenance.
- capability.
- operator/skill availability where required.

---

# 3.11 Conditional Readiness

A Job may be conditionally ready when a non-blocking dependency remains.

Conditions should be visible rather than silently ignored.

---

# 3.12 Job Release

Once readiness and scheduling conditions are satisfied:

```text
Production Job

↓

Released to Shop Floor
```

Domain 3 remains authoritative for Production release.

Domain 34 monitors flow and performance after release.

---

# 3.13 Release Discipline

Production should avoid releasing excessive work purely to keep every resource busy.

Too much released work can increase:

- WIP.
- queue time.
- confusion.
- handling.

---

# 3.14 Controlled WIP Principle

Permanent rule:

```text
Release Work at a Rate
the System Can Actually Process
```

not:

```text
Release Everything Immediately
```

---

# 3.15 Queue Entry

When Job reaches a Work Center:

- Queue entry time should be captured where practical.
- priority should remain visible.

---

# 3.16 Queue Prioritization

Queue sequencing may consider:

- Customer due date.
- Rush status.
- Product family.
- setup optimization.
- material readiness.
- downstream constraints.

---

# 3.17 Queue Stability

Constant arbitrary reordering should be discouraged.

Priority changes should be controlled.

---

# 3.18 Rush Job Handling

Canonical flow:

```text
Rush Request

↓

Impact Check

↓

Authority

↓

Priority Change

↓

Affected Jobs Identified
```

---

# 3.19 Rush Impact Visibility

A rush Job should expose:

- Additional setup.
- delayed normal work.
- capacity impact.
- affected commitments.

---

# 3.20 Setup Lifecycle

Canonical flow:

```text
Previous Job Complete

↓

Setup Required?

↓

Setup Start

↓

Material / Tool / File Preparation

↓

Setup Complete

↓

Production Start
```

---

# 3.21 Setup Readiness

Preparation can begin before machine becomes free where practical.

This may reduce changeover.

---

# 3.22 Setup Standardization

Repeated setup activity should follow approved Standard Work where possible.

---

# 3.23 Changeover Control

Changeover should be tracked separately from productive run time when meaningful.

---

# 3.24 Job Start

A Job should transition to active processing only when real processing begins.

Queue time should not be included as productive run time.

---

# 3.25 Active Processing

During processing, relevant events may include:

- Start.
- Pause.
- Resume.
- completion.
- Scrap.
- Rework.
- operational alert.

---

# 3.26 Pause Handling

A pause should be classified.

Potential reasons:

- Material.
- Machine.
- Quality.
- Personalization.
- Information.
- operator.
- downstream blocking.

---

# 3.27 Pause vs Downtime

A Production Job can be paused without the machine being broken.

This distinction is mandatory for correct loss analysis.

---

# 3.28 Job Blocking

Canonical flow:

```text
Dependency Missing

↓

Job Blocked

↓

Cause Classified

↓

Owner Assigned

↓

Resolution

↓

Job Resumed
```

---

# 3.29 Blocked Job Aging

Blocked Jobs should be monitored by:

- Age.
- due date.
- customer impact.
- severity.

---

# 3.30 Block Escalation

A block should escalate if:

- Customer commitment is threatened.
- wait time exceeds threshold.
- multiple Jobs share same cause.
- critical Production resource becomes idle.

---

# 3.31 Material Block Workflow

```text
Material Missing

↓

Inventory / Procurement Review

↓

Expected Availability

↓

Can Job Wait?

YES → Controlled Hold
NO → Escalation / Replan
```

---

# 3.32 Personalization Block Workflow

```text
Customer Input Missing

↓

Production Block

↓

Customer Success / Personalization Owner

↓

Input Resolved

↓

Production Ready
```

---

# 3.33 Quality Hold Workflow

When Quality requires a stop:

```text
Quality Concern

↓

Job / Batch Hold

↓

Investigation

↓

Disposition

↓

Resume / Rework / Scrap
```

Domain 4 remains authoritative for Quality disposition.

---

# 3.34 Machine Failure Workflow

Canonical operating sequence:

```text
Machine Failure

↓

Machine State = Down

↓

Affected Jobs Paused

↓

Maintenance / Asset Response

↓

Capacity Impact

↓

Recovery / Reallocation

↓

Production Resumes
```

---

# 3.35 Downtime Detection

Downtime should be identified as close to occurrence as practical.

---

# 3.36 Downtime Classification

Potential high-level causes:

- Planned Maintenance.
- unplanned breakdown.
- utilities.
- setup.
- operator availability.
- process issue.

Only true equipment unavailability should be counted as Equipment Downtime.

---

# 3.37 Downtime Response

The response should consider:

- Expected duration.
- affected Jobs.
- alternate resource.
- customer impact.
- maintenance owner.

---

# 3.38 Downtime Escalation

Critical escalation may occur when:

- Bottleneck resource fails.
- long customer queue is affected.
- peak season is active.
- no alternate resource exists.

---

# 3.39 Downtime Recovery

Once machine returns:

- Resource state updated.
- Job queue recalculated.
- recovery plan considered.

---

# 3.40 Post-Downtime Recovery Plan

Possible responses:

- Resume original order.
- prioritize critical Jobs.
- overtime.
- alternate resource.
- revised schedule.

---

# 3.41 WIP Control

WIP should be continuously visible by:

- Work Center.
- stage.
- age.
- priority.
- block state.

---

# 3.42 WIP Aging

A Job that exceeds expected stage duration becomes an exception candidate.

---

# 3.43 WIP Age Severity

Potential states:

- Normal.
- Monitor.
- Late.
- Critical.

---

# 3.44 Excess WIP

Excess WIP may indicate:

- Upstream overproduction.
- bottleneck.
- scheduling imbalance.
- downstream capacity issue.

---

# 3.45 WIP Reduction

Potential responses:

- Restrict release.
- prioritize bottleneck flow.
- stop feeding downstream constraint.
- rebalance resources.

---

# 3.46 Flow Control

The shop-floor objective is controlled movement through all operations.

---

# 3.47 Flow Interruption

A flow interruption may arise from:

- Material.
- machine.
- approval.
- Quality.
- capacity.
- information.

---

# 3.48 Starvation Detection

A Resource is starved when it has capacity but no process-ready input.

---

# 3.49 Starvation Response

Potential actions:

- Resolve upstream block.
- pull alternate ready Job.
- review release sequencing.

---

# 3.50 Blocking Detection

Blocking occurs when downstream cannot accept output.

---

# 3.51 Blocking Response

Potential actions:

- Slow/restrict upstream release.
- expand downstream capacity.
- resolve downstream Quality/packaging issue.

---

# 3.52 Bottleneck Detection

The operating model should identify constraints using evidence such as:

- Persistent queue.
- high required load.
- late Jobs.
- downstream starvation.
- high WIP age.

---

# 3.53 Bottleneck Confirmation

Before declaring a structural bottleneck, review:

- Duration.
- recurrence.
- Product mix.
- temporary outages.

---

# 3.54 Bottleneck Management Cycle

```text
Identify Constraint

↓

Protect Constraint

↓

Reduce Avoidable Loss at Constraint

↓

Exploit Available Capacity

↓

Support Constraint

↓

Measure

↓

Constraint Shift?
```

---

# 3.55 Protect the Bottleneck

Critical bottleneck resources should avoid unnecessary:

- Waiting Material.
- missing files.
- preventable setup.
- non-priority work.

---

# 3.56 Bottleneck Queue Discipline

The constraint queue should contain:

- Ready work.
- correct priorities.
- valid inputs.

---

# 3.57 Non-Bottleneck Discipline

Non-constraints should not overproduce merely to maximize utilization.

---

# 3.58 Bottleneck Shift

After successful improvement:

- New limiting resource should be identified.
- Prior assumptions updated.

---

# 3.59 Production Completion

A Job/operation may complete when Domain 3 execution rules are satisfied.

Domain 34 captures performance consequences.

---

# 3.60 Good Output Capture

Completion analysis should distinguish:

- Produced quantity.
- good accepted quantity.
- Scrap.
- Rework.

---

# 3.61 Partial Completion

If Job completes partially:

- Remaining quantity should remain visible.
- performance should not assume full completion.

---

# 3.62 Quality Check Integration

Quality checks may occur:

- In-process.
- final.

The operating model should not wait until final QC to detect every possible defect if earlier control is practical.

---

# 3.63 Quality-at-Source Principle

Permanent rule:

```text
Detect Defect
as Close as Practical
to the Process That Created It
```

---

# 3.64 First-Pass Flow

Good first-pass output should flow forward without Rework.

---

# 3.65 Rework Workflow

```text
Defect / Process Failure

↓

Rework Required

↓

Rework Operation Created

↓

Capacity Consumed

↓

Reinspection

↓

Pass / Further Action
```

---

# 3.66 Rework Priority

Rework may compete with normal Production.

The priority should be governed based on:

- Customer commitment.
- existing delay.
- service recovery.
- available capacity.

---

# 3.67 Rework Capacity Visibility

Rework must be visible as separate capacity consumption.

---

# 3.68 Rework Escalation

Repeated Rework for:

- Same Product.
- same process.
- same defect.

should trigger Root Cause review.

---

# 3.69 Scrap Workflow

```text
Unrecoverable Output

↓

Scrap Recorded

↓

Reason Classified

↓

Material / Quantity Captured

↓

Cause Review if Material
```

---

# 3.70 Scrap Containment

If abnormal Scrap appears:

- Pause affected process where appropriate.
- investigate before continuing uncontrolled production.

---

# 3.71 Scrap Reuse

Reusable offcuts should not be falsely classified as unrecoverable Scrap.

---

# 3.72 Yield Monitoring

Yield should be monitored by:

- Product.
- Material.
- Work Center.
- process.

---

# 3.73 Yield Degradation

Material decline in Yield should create an investigation trigger.

---

# 3.74 Cycle-Time Monitoring

Actual cycle time should be compared with applicable Standard.

---

# 3.75 Cycle-Time Exception

A variance may be generated when:

- Absolute or percentage difference exceeds configured tolerance.

---

# 3.76 Cycle-Time Investigation

Before changing Standard, determine whether variance arose from:

- Product complexity.
- machine.
- Material.
- Rework.
- incorrect Standard.
- process instability.

---

# 3.77 Standard Calibration

If actual stable performance differs persistently from Standard:

- Standard may require review.

Do not simply manipulate the Standard to make performance appear compliant.

---

# 3.78 Production Adherence Review

Compare:

- Planned.
- scheduled.
- completed.

---

# 3.79 Missed Schedule Investigation

Potential cause categories:

- Planning.
- Material.
- capacity.
- Quality.
- machine.
- personalization.
- priority change.

---

# 3.80 Schedule Recovery

Potential actions:

- Reprioritize.
- add approved capacity.
- reschedule.
- escalate customer risk.

---

# 3.81 Daily Shop-Floor Control

The daily process should focus on:

```text
What Must Ship / Finish?

↓

What Is Blocked?

↓

What Is the Bottleneck?

↓

What Is Down?

↓

What Is Aging?

↓

What Requires Immediate Action?
```

---

# 3.82 Start-of-Day Review

Potential review items:

- Today's Production plan.
- carryover WIP.
- material readiness.
- critical machines.
- urgent Orders.
- current bottleneck.

---

# 3.83 Intra-Day Review

For fast-moving operations, lightweight reviews may occur when:

- Major machine stops.
- WIP spike occurs.
- critical customer Job blocks.

---

# 3.84 End-of-Day Review

Potential review:

- Planned vs Actual.
- incomplete Jobs.
- Downtime.
- Scrap/Rework.
- unresolved blockers.
- carryover risk.

---

# 3.85 Daily Accountability

Every critical unresolved issue should have:

- Owner.
- next action.
- due time.

---

# 3.86 Weekly Manufacturing Review

Weekly review may include:

- Throughput.
- Schedule Adherence.
- Work-Center queues.
- Downtime.
- Rework.
- Scrap.
- bottlenecks.
- Improvement Initiatives.

---

# 3.87 Monthly Excellence Review

Monthly review may focus on:

- Structural Bottlenecks.
- chronic Production Loss.
- Standard accuracy.
- capacity effectiveness.
- improvement results.

---

# 3.88 Production Loss Review

Loss should be reviewed by:

- Category.
- time.
- quantity.
- customer impact.
- recurrence.

---

# 3.89 Loss Pareto

The enterprise may rank highest-impact losses.

Example:

```text
1. Missing Personalization
2. QC Rework
3. Laser Downtime
4. Material Shortage
5. Setup
```

---

# 3.90 Loss Response Principle

The largest measurable loss should receive attention, but:

- Safety.
- severe customer impact.
- regulatory Quality issues.

may take priority even when volume is lower.

---

# 3.91 Manufacturing Exception Queue

A controlled queue should include:

- Bottleneck exceptions.
- WIP Aging.
- Cycle-Time Variance.
- Downtime.
- Rework spikes.
- Scrap spikes.
- readiness failures.

---

# 3.92 Exception Ownership

Each exception should have:

- Owner.
- severity.
- due response.
- status.

---

# 3.93 Exception Triage

Potential categories:

- Immediate Containment.
- investigate.
- monitor.
- improvement candidate.

---

# 3.94 Exception Aging

Long-running unresolved exceptions should escalate.

---

# 3.95 Exception Closure

Close only when:

- Condition resolved.
- accepted through authority.
- no longer material.

---

# 3.96 Containment vs Root Cause

Permanent distinction:

```text
Containment
=
Stop Immediate Damage

Root Cause Action
=
Prevent Recurrence
```

Both may be required.

---

# 3.97 Root Cause Investigation Trigger

Root Cause review may be mandatory for:

- Repeated Scrap.
- repeated Rework.
- recurring Downtime.
- recurring late Jobs.
- chronic bottleneck.
- serious Quality issue.

---

# 3.98 Root Cause Investigation Lifecycle

```text
Problem Defined

↓

Evidence Collected

↓

Possible Causes

↓

Cause Tested

↓

Root Cause Confirmed / Inconclusive

↓

Corrective Action
```

---

# 3.99 Root Cause Evidence

Evidence may include:

- Production timeline.
- Quality findings.
- machine records.
- operator notes.
- Material records.
- job files.
- system events.

---

# 3.100 No-Blame Root Cause Principle

The initial investigation should focus on:

- Process.
- system.
- conditions.

rather than assume personal fault.

---

# 3.101 Corrective Action

A corrective action addresses the cause of a known issue.

Potential actions:

- Repair machine.
- revise process.
- improve Material control.
- change readiness gate.
- improve training.
- revise Work Instruction.

---

# 3.102 Preventive Action

Preventive action addresses an identified risk before failure occurs.

---

# 3.103 Improvement Opportunity Lifecycle

```text
Opportunity Identified

↓

Impact Estimated

↓

Priority Assigned

↓

Improvement Initiative
```

---

# 3.104 Improvement Initiative Lifecycle

```text
Define Problem

↓

Establish Baseline

↓

Create Hypothesis

↓

Design Experiment

↓

Run Pilot

↓

Measure Outcome

↓

Adopt / Modify / Reject

↓

Standardize if Successful
```

---

# 3.105 Baseline Requirement

Before improvement, capture relevant before-state.

Examples:

- Cycle time.
- Setup time.
- Rework.
- WIP.
- Throughput.

---

# 3.106 Improvement Target

Targets should be:

- Specific.
- measurable.
- operationally meaningful.

---

# 3.107 Pilot Principle

Where feasible, test changes on controlled scope before enterprise-wide adoption.

---

# 3.108 Experiment Control

Define:

- Product scope.
- Work Center.
- duration.
- expected outcome.

---

# 3.109 Improvement Measurement

Compare:

```text
Baseline

vs

Pilot Result

vs

Target
```

---

# 3.110 Improvement Outcome Review

Possible outcomes:

- Successful.
- partially successful.
- inconclusive.
- no improvement.
- harmful.

---

# 3.111 Improvement Standardization

A successful improvement may update:

- Standard Work.
- Production Standard.
- sequence.
- training.
- system configuration.

---

# 3.112 Standardization Authority

Changes to approved Production standards require appropriate operational authority.

---

# 3.113 Improvement Rollback

If improvement harms:

- Quality.
- Safety.
- throughput.
- customer outcomes.

rollback should be available.

---

# 3.114 Improvement Learning

Failed experiments remain useful evidence.

They should not disappear from organizational memory.

---

# 3.115 Standard Work Review

Standard Work should be reviewed when:

- Process changes.
- new equipment introduced.
- Product changes.
- repeated variance appears.
- successful improvement adopted.

---

# 3.116 Standard Work Deviation

Deviation from Standard Work may be:

- Authorized.
- emergency.
- unintentional.

The context matters.

---

# 3.117 Emergency Deviation

Emergency deviation may be required during:

- Equipment failure.
- urgent recovery.
- Supply disruption.

It should remain temporary and auditable.

---

# 3.118 Production Control Board

A daily board may show:

- Plan vs Actual.
- current WIP.
- blocked Jobs.
- machine state.
- Bottleneck.
- critical Quality issue.
- Production loss.
- action owners.

---

# 3.119 Visual Factory Principle

Operational state should be understandable quickly without requiring deep report analysis.

---

# 3.120 Shop-Floor Status Colors

If visual states use color, they should also include text/icon semantics.

Accessibility and clarity remain required.

---

# 3.121 Andon-Style Escalation

A critical operational signal may immediately identify:

- What stopped.
- why.
- who owns response.

---

# 3.122 Stop-Production Workflow

Where serious Quality or safety concern exists:

```text
Issue Raised

↓

Authorized Stop

↓

Affected Jobs Held

↓

Investigation / Control

↓

Restart Authorized
```

---

# 3.123 Restart Discipline

Restart should only occur when:

- Cause controlled sufficiently.
- relevant authority approves where required.

---

# 3.124 Work-Center Operating Model

Each Work Center should maintain visibility into:

- Queue.
- active Jobs.
- Resource state.
- setup.
- exceptions.
- output.

---

# 3.125 Work-Center Handoff

When a Job completes one operation:

- downstream readiness should be checked.
- Job should not disappear between Work Centers.

---

# 3.126 Internal Handoff Integrity

Canonical flow:

```text
Operation Completed

↓

Output Accepted

↓

Next Operation Ready?

YES → Queue Next Work Center
NO → Controlled Waiting / Block
```

---

# 3.127 Shift Handoff

If multiple shifts exist:

Open:

- WIP.
- exceptions.
- machine conditions.
- priorities.

should be handed over explicitly.

---

# 3.128 Production Scheduling Interaction

Domain 34 may recommend:

- Queue sequencing.
- bottleneck protection.

Domain 3 owns execution scheduling.

---

# 3.129 Planning Interaction

Domain 34 sends actual performance intelligence to Domain 33:

- Real cycle time.
- realized capacity.
- bottleneck.
- Production loss.

---

# 3.130 Quality Interaction

Domain 34 consumes Quality facts to understand:

- Rework.
- Scrap.
- first-pass flow.

Domain 4 governs defect disposition.

---

# 3.131 Maintenance Interaction

Domain 34 consumes:

- Machine downtime.
- maintenance schedules.

Domain 26 governs Asset maintenance.

---

# 3.132 Customer Service Interaction

Replacement/remake work from Domain 32 should be visible as:

- Production demand.
- capacity use.
- Quality-loss consequence where relevant.

---

# 3.133 Supply Chain Interaction

Material Shortage causing Production block should feed:

- Domain 33 planning.
- Domain 2 Procurement/Inventory.

---

# 3.134 Manufacturing Risk Review

Risks may include:

- Critical-machine dependency.
- chronic QC bottleneck.
- unstable Yield.
- high replacement load.
- excessive WIP.
- untrained critical process.

---

# 3.135 Risk Mitigation

Potential mitigation:

- alternate Resource.
- training.
- buffer.
- process redesign.
- maintenance.
- Quality improvement.

---

# 3.136 Manufacturing Knowledge Capture

Important learning should preserve:

- What happened.
- Root Cause.
- what changed.
- whether it worked.

---

# 3.137 GiftHatke Shop-Floor Flow

Canonical GiftHatke flow may be:

```text
Order / Job Released

↓

Personalization Preparation

↓

Material Ready

↓

Laser / Sublimation

↓

Assembly

↓

QC

↓

Packaging

↓

Production Complete
```

Product routes may vary.

---

# 3.138 GiftHatke Personalization Gate

A personalized Job should not enter downstream Production if critical personalization input is missing.

---

# 3.139 GiftHatke Personalization Queue

Potential queue states:

- Awaiting customer input.
- design pending.
- approval pending.
- ready.

---

# 3.140 GiftHatke Laser Queue

Laser queue should prioritize:

- Ready work.
- valid files.
- correct Material.
- customer due dates.
- setup efficiency.

---

# 3.141 GiftHatke Laser Changeover

Potential changeovers:

- Acrylic thickness.
- wood/MDF.
- engraving/cutting mode.
- fixture/jig.

---

# 3.142 GiftHatke Laser Bottleneck Protection

If Laser is constraint:

Avoid sending it Jobs with:

- missing file.
- unverified Material.
- unresolved personalization.

---

# 3.143 GiftHatke Sublimation Flow

Potential flow:

```text
Design Ready

↓

Print

↓

Transfer / Process

↓

Inspection

↓

Assembly / Packaging
```

# ENTERPRISE MANUFACTURING EXCELLENCE & INDUSTRIAL OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 4 — Manufacturing Excellence Services, Shop-Floor Execution Intelligence & Industrial Optimization Architecture Canon

---

# 4.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Manufacturing Excellence & Industrial Operations Domain** requires a permanent service architecture defining how Production execution facts are transformed into:

- Manufacturing Performance.
- Work-Center intelligence.
- WIP visibility.
- Cycle-Time analysis.
- Downtime intelligence.
- Scrap/Rework intelligence.
- Bottleneck detection.
- Production Loss analysis.
- Root Cause support.
- Improvement recommendations.
- Industrial optimization.
- governed shop-floor actions.

Stages 1–3 established:

- Domain foundation.
- manufacturing entity architecture.
- Shop-Floor Control lifecycle.
- WIP, Loss, Bottleneck, and Improvement operating model.

Stage 4 establishes the permanent service and execution-intelligence architecture required to make Manufacturing Excellence operational across:

- Production.
- Quality.
- Asset Management.
- Inventory.
- Supply Chain Planning.
- Workforce.
- Customer Service.
- Analytics.
- AI.

The permanent objective is:

> **Transform authoritative shop-floor events into timely manufacturing intelligence and governed improvement actions without allowing analytical or optimization services to override Production, Quality, Safety, Maintenance, or Workforce authority.**

---

# 4.2 Manufacturing Service Architecture Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Authoritative Production State Before Performance Service

Manufacturing Excellence services consume Production truth.

They do not redefine whether a Job is:

- Released.
- active.
- completed.
- cancelled.

---

## Event Before Derived Metric

Cycle Time, Throughput, WIP Age, and Downtime should derive from evidence.

---

## Work Center Before Aggregate Factory Number

Performance should remain explainable by operational location/resource.

---

## Loss Classification Before Optimization

The system should understand where Production capability is being lost before recommending improvement.

---

## Constraint Before Schedule Optimization

Optimization must not improve local activity while worsening system flow.

---

## Recommendation Before Execution

Manufacturing Excellence may recommend:

- resequencing.
- capacity change.
- process improvement.

Execution remains governed through authoritative domains.

---

## Safe Failure Before False Precision

Missing event data should lower confidence rather than generate invented performance.

---

# 4.3 Canonical Service Landscape

The permanent service landscape includes:

| Service | Primary Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Manufacturing Context Service | Resolve manufacturing scope and references |
| Production Event Service | Consume/canonicalize Production events |
| Operation Timeline Service | Build operation timelines |
| Job Performance Service | Calculate Job-level performance |
| Work Center Performance Service | Analyze Work-Center results |
| Resource State Service | Maintain analytical resource-state view |
| Production Readiness Intelligence Service | Evaluate execution readiness context |
| WIP Service | Maintain WIP analytical state |
| WIP Aging Service | Detect aging work |
| Queue Intelligence Service | Analyze queue health |
| Cycle-Time Service | Calculate actual cycle time |
| Standard Comparison Service | Compare Actual vs Standard |
| Setup Intelligence Service | Analyze setup time |
| Changeover Intelligence Service | Analyze changeovers |
| Downtime Intelligence Service | Analyze lost operational time |
| Production Loss Service | Classify Production losses |
| Throughput Service | Calculate useful output flow |
| Yield Intelligence Service | Analyze usable output |
| Scrap Intelligence Service | Analyze unrecoverable material/output loss |
| Rework Intelligence Service | Analyze corrective processing |
| First-Pass Performance Service | Analyze right-first-time execution |
| Schedule Adherence Service | Compare Schedule vs Actual |
| Capacity Realization Service | Analyze realized capacity |
| Constraint Service | Represent manufacturing constraints |
| Bottleneck Detection Service | Identify flow-limiting resource |
| Manufacturing Exception Service | Manage abnormal conditions |
| Root Cause Support Service | Assemble causal evidence |
| Improvement Opportunity Service | Identify improvement candidates |
| Improvement Experiment Service | Evaluate controlled changes |
| Improvement Outcome Service | Compare baseline vs result |
| Manufacturing Recommendation Service | Generate action suggestions |
| Manufacturing Optimization Service | Evaluate flow/process alternatives |
| Manufacturing Reconciliation Service | Compare derived state with sources |
| Manufacturing Audit Service | Preserve protected action history |
| Industrial AI Service | Assist analysis and recommendations |

## Purpose

Potential references:

- Production Job.
- Product.
- Operation.
- Work Center.
- Resource.
- Batch.
- Production Schedule.

```text id="smp1-no-fake-metrics"
Missing Historical Timestamps

↓

Do Not Invent Cycle Time / Downtime

↓

Start Reliable Measurement Post-Cutover
```

- Modular monolith.

It does not need premature microservices.

Canonical service boundaries should nevertheless remain explicit.
