# ENTERPRISE MANUFACTURING EXCELLENCE & INDUSTRIAL OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 9 — Manufacturing Migration, Shop-Floor Reconciliation, Validation, Testing & Operational Acceptance Canon

---

# 9.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Manufacturing Excellence & Industrial Operations Domain** requires a permanent assurance architecture proving that manufacturing execution, shop-floor visibility, Production timelines, Work-Center state, WIP, Downtime, Scrap, Rework, Bottlenecks, Standard Work, Manufacturing Exceptions, and Continuous Improvement remain trustworthy when the underlying technology changes.

Stages 1–8 established:

- Domain foundation.
- manufacturing entity architecture.
- Shop-Floor Control lifecycle.
- Manufacturing Excellence service architecture.
- governance and industrial decision rights.
- Manufacturing Events and cross-domain orchestration.
- Visual Factory and shop-floor experience architecture.
- Manufacturing Intelligence and Industrial Optimization.

Stage 9 establishes the permanent framework for:

- Manufacturing data migration.
- Production Job continuity.
- operation and Work-Center mapping.
- machine/resource mapping.
- WIP cutover.
- Standard Work migration.
- Production Standard migration.
- Quality relationship preservation.
- Scrap/Rework migration.
- Downtime migration.
- Bottleneck/Exception preservation.
- improvement-history preservation.
- event migration.
- manufacturing reconciliation.
- regression testing.
- shop-floor acceptance.
- operational cutover.
- rollback.
- Manufacturing Excellence certification.

The central principle is:

> **A manufacturing platform may change, but the enterprise must still be able to prove what was being produced, where it was in the process, what resources were involved, what losses occurred, what Quality state applied, what Standards governed the work, and what operational decisions were made.**

---

# 9.2 Manufacturing Migration Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

- Operational truth before analytical reconstruction.
- Job identity before timeline recreation.
- current WIP before historical convenience.
- source semantics before field mapping.
- Standard version before performance comparison.
- Quality state before Production continuation.
- machine/resource identity before utilization metrics.
- event evidence before derived Cycle Time.
- reconciliation before authority transfer.
- no fabrication before apparent completeness.
- business acceptance before final certification.

---

# 9.3 Migration Scope

Potential migration scope includes:

- Production Jobs.
- Production Job Lines.
- operations.
- routings.
- Work Centers.
- resources.
- machine/resource assignments.
- Production statuses.
- Production timestamps.
- Production events.
- WIP.
- queue state.
- blocked Jobs.
- readiness state.
- setup/changeover records.
- Downtime.
- Scrap.
- Rework.
- Yield records.
- Production Loss.
- Standards.
- Standard Work.
- Work Instructions references.
- exceptions.
- Root Cause investigations.
- Improvement Initiatives.
- Manufacturing Risks.
- Audit records.

---

# 9.4 Manufacturing Migration Inventory

Before migration, inventory all manufacturing-relevant objects.

Potential fields:

- Source entity.
- business meaning.
- source system.
- current/historical relevance.
- target entity.
- mapping status.
- migration method.
- reconciliation method.
- owner.
- certification status.

---

# 9.5 Source Classification

Manufacturing data should be classified as:

- Authoritative Production Fact.
- Authoritative Quality Fact.
- Authoritative Asset/Equipment Fact.
- Native Manufacturing Excellence Record.
- Derived Analytical Record.
- Reconstructed Analytical Record.
- Unstructured Historical Evidence.
- Unavailable.

This classification determines how it may be migrated and represented.

---

# 9.6 Production Job Identity Migration

Every Production Job must preserve:

- Stable Job identity.
- Order relationship.
- Product.
- quantity.
- Production status.
- critical timestamps where available.

A Production Job mapped to the wrong Order or Product is a critical migration defect.

---

# 9.7 Order-to-Production Relationship

Migration must preserve:

```text id="order-production-migration"
Order

↓

Production Requirement / Job

↓

Production Execution

↓

Finished Output
```

---

# 9.8 Product Identity Migration

Production history must remain linked to the correct:

- Product.
- variant.
- Product version where applicable.

---

# 9.9 BOM Relationship Migration

Where relevant, preserve the BOM or material relationship applicable to the Production Job.

Historical Production should not be reinterpreted using only the latest BOM.

---

# 9.10 Operation Migration

If Production Jobs contain formal operations, preserve:

- Operation ID.
- name.
- sequence.
- status.
- Work Center.
- timestamps where available.

---

# 9.11 Operation Sequence Integrity

Migration must not reorder historical operations simply to match a new technical model.

---

# 9.12 Routing Migration

Historical routing, where captured, should preserve:

- Sequence.
- Work Center.
- effective version.

---

# 9.13 Work-Center Migration

Preserve:

- Work-Center ID.
- name.
- capability.
- active/inactive status.
- historical mapping.

---

# 9.14 Work-Center Mapping

If target Work-Center structure changes:

Use explicit mapping.

Example:

```text id="work-center-mapping"
Legacy:
Laser

Target:
LASER_MAIN

Mapping:
Approved
```

If one old Work Center splits into several new ones, historical records should remain clearly mapped rather than artificially reclassified.

---

# 9.15 Resource/Machine Migration

Preserve where available:

- Resource ID.
- machine identity.
- Work Center.
- capability.
- status history.

---

# 9.16 Resource Identity Ambiguity

If old Production only recorded:

- "Laser"

and not which machine:

Do not assign historical work arbitrarily to:

- Laser 1.
- Laser 2.

Use:

- Legacy Resource Group.

or equivalent.

---

# 9.17 Production Status Migration

Legacy statuses must be mapped semantically.

Example:

```text id="production-status-mapping"
Legacy:
DONE

Target:
COMPLETED

Only if DONE actually meant
Production completion
```

---

# 9.18 Status Mapping Review

Potential ambiguous legacy statuses:

- Open.
- Pending.
- Processing.
- Done.
- Ready.

Each requires documented business interpretation.

---

# 9.19 Production Timestamp Migration

Potential timestamps:

- Created.
- Released.
- started.
- paused.
- completed.

Only migrate timestamps that actually exist or can be reliably derived.

---

# 9.20 Timestamp Fabrication Prohibition

If historical source contains:

- Completion date only.

do not invent:

- Start time.
- queue time.
- setup time.

---

# 9.21 Timezone Migration

Historical timestamps should preserve or correctly map:

- Source timezone.
- effective local time.
- date boundary.

---

# 9.22 Production Event Migration

If native event history exists:

Preserve:

- Event ID.
- event type.
- timestamp.
- Job.
- operation.
- Resource.
- actor/system.

---

# 9.23 Event History Limitation

If only final Production state exists:

Do not manufacture a detailed event history.

---

# 9.24 Reconstructed Event Boundary

Where a state transition can be reliably derived, it may be represented as:

- Reconstructed Event.

not:

- Original Event.

---

# 9.25 Current WIP Migration

Current WIP is one of the highest-risk cutover areas.

Preserve:

- Job.
- quantity.
- current stage.
- status.
- block reason.
- Work Center.
- current owner.

---

# 9.26 WIP Cutover Snapshot

Immediately before cutover, create a certified WIP snapshot.

Potential fields:

- Job ID.
- Product.
- quantity.
- current operation.
- status.
- Ready/Blocked.
- Work Center.
- due date.
- priority.

---

# 9.27 WIP-to-Target Reconciliation

After migration:

Every open Job should be classified as:

- Ready.
- running.
- waiting.
- blocked.
- held.
- completed/cancelled.

---

# 9.28 Completed Job Protection

Completed Jobs must not reappear as:

- Active WIP.

---

# 9.29 Cancelled Job Protection

Cancelled Jobs must not re-enter executable Production queue.

---

# 9.30 In-Progress Job Protection

An in-progress Job must not restart from operation one merely because the target platform lacks exact historical step detail.

---

# 9.31 Partial Completion Migration

Preserve:

- Good quantity.
- remaining quantity.
- Scrap.
- Rework where available.

---

# 9.32 Batch Migration

If Production uses batches:

Preserve:

- Parent Job.
- Batch ID.
- quantity.
- completion status.

---

# 9.33 Queue Migration

Active queue state may be migrated if reliably known.

Potential:

- Job.
- Work Center.
- priority.
- queue order.

---

# 9.34 Queue Ordering Limitation

If the legacy platform did not persist queue sequence:

Do not invent historical queue positions.

At cutover, create a new approved active sequence.

---

# 9.35 Priority Migration

Preserve:

- Standard.
- Rush.
- Emergency.
- Replacement.

where these classifications actually existed.

---

# 9.36 Priority History Limitation

Do not fabricate historical approval for Rush classifications that were informal.

---

# 9.37 Production Readiness Migration

If readiness state exists, preserve:

- Material.
- personalization.
- instruction.
- Resource readiness.

---

# 9.38 Personalization Readiness Migration

GiftHatke migration should preserve available links to:

- Customer assets.
- approved files.
- names/text.
- design approvals.

---

# 9.39 Missing Personalization Protection

An open Production Job with missing personalization must remain:

- Not Ready / Blocked.

It must not become automatically executable after migration.

---

# 9.40 Design File Migration

Preserve references to:

- Approved Production file.
- version.
- source asset.

where available.

---

# 9.41 Wrong-Version Protection

Superseded design files should not become current Production files after cutover.

---

# 9.42 Work Instruction Migration

Preserve:

- Document ID.
- version.
- Product/process relationship.
- effective status.

---

# 9.43 Standard Work Migration

Historical Standard Work should preserve:

- Standard ID.
- version.
- effective date.
- owner/approval where known.

---

# 9.44 Standard Version Integrity

Historical Job analysis should remain tied to the Standard applicable at the time.

---

# 9.45 Standard Work Gap

If formal Standards never existed:

Do not backfill historical Standard versions as though they did.

Create new native Standards prospectively.

---

# 9.46 Standard Cycle-Time Migration

Where reliable Standards exist, preserve:

- Product/process.
- Work Center.
- basis.
- duration.
- effective date.
- version.

---

# 9.47 Standard Cycle-Time Limitation

If time Standards were informal estimates:

Classify accordingly.

Do not treat them as certified historical Standards.

---

# 9.48 Setup Record Migration

Only migrate detailed Setup history if:

- Start/end.
- Resource.
- Job/context.

are trustworthy.

---

# 9.49 Changeover Migration

Historical Changeover may be migrated where explicit.

Do not infer all Product transitions as formal Changeover events if not recorded.

---

# 9.50 Downtime Migration

Native Downtime records should preserve:

- Resource.
- start.
- end.
- reason.
- planned/unplanned.
- affected Production.

---

# 9.51 Downtime Semantics Validation

Confirm whether old "Downtime" included:

- Machine breakdown only.

or also:

- Waiting Material.
- no Operator.
- setup.

Mapping must preserve meaning.

---

# 9.52 Downtime Reconstruction Boundary

Do not derive exact historical Downtime merely from:

- Long gaps between Jobs.

unless evidence supports it.

---

# 9.53 Machine Maintenance Relationship

Where available, preserve link between:

- Downtime.
- maintenance case.
- Asset.

---

# 9.54 Quality Hold Migration

An active Quality Hold at cutover must remain active.

It is a critical protection.

---

# 9.55 Quality Status Migration

Preserve:

- Inspection state.
- Quality Hold.
- defect.
- disposition.

Domain 4 remains authority.

---

# 9.56 Quality Release Protection

Migration must not inadvertently release Production from a valid Quality Hold.

---

# 9.57 Scrap Migration

Preserve:

- Product/Material.
- quantity.
- UOM.
- reason.
- Job.
- timestamp.

where available.

---

# 9.58 Scrap Reason Mapping

Legacy Scrap reasons may require controlled mapping.

Example:

```text id="scrap-reason-mapping"
Legacy:
Wrong Job

Target:
Wrong Personalization / Wrong Production File

Mapping:
Requires Evidence
```

---

# 9.59 Reusable Offcut Migration

Reusable sheet Material must not become:

- Scrap.

if historically tracked as reusable Inventory.

---

# 9.60 Rework Migration

Preserve where available:

- Original Job/operation.
- reason.
- quantity.
- Rework state.
- result.

---

# 9.61 Rework Relationship Integrity

Rework must remain linked to the Production/Quality issue that caused it where possible.

---

# 9.62 Replacement Production Migration

Replacement Jobs should preserve:

- Original Order.
- service-case relationship.
- replacement reason.
- Production state.

---

# 9.63 Yield Migration

Historical Yield values may be migrated only when:

- Input and output basis are known.

---

# 9.64 Yield Recalculation Boundary

New Yield methodology may be used for:

- Recalculated analytical view.

It should not be presented as the original historical metric.

---

# 9.65 Production Loss Migration

Native Production Loss records may preserve:

- Category.
- time/quantity.
- Work Center.
- cause.

---

# 9.66 Historical Loss Limitation

If loss categories were never captured:

Do not fabricate historical:

- Waiting Loss.
- Setup Loss.
- Information Loss.

---

# 9.67 Bottleneck Migration

Historical Bottleneck records may be preserved if formally recorded.

---

# 9.68 Bottleneck Reconstruction Boundary

A historical queue does not automatically prove a Bottleneck was recognized at the time.

Retrospective analysis should be labeled:

- Backtest / Historical Analysis.

---

# 9.69 Manufacturing Exception Migration

Preserve open relevant exceptions such as:

- Machine Down.
- WIP Aging.
- Scrap Spike.
- critical blocked Job.

---

# 9.70 Exception State Migration

Preserve:

- Open.
- acknowledged.
- investigating.
- resolved.
- accepted.

where such states existed.

---

# 9.71 Root Cause Investigation Migration

Preserve:

- Problem.
- evidence.
- cause status.
- corrective action.
- owner.

where formal records exist.

---

# 9.72 Improvement Initiative Migration

Preserve:

- Initiative.
- baseline.
- hypothesis.
- Pilot.
- outcome.
- status.

---

# 9.73 Improvement History Integrity

Failed or rolled-back improvement work should not disappear during migration.

---

# 9.74 Manufacturing Risk Migration

Preserve active structural risks such as:

- Single-machine dependency.
- chronic QC overload.

where formally recorded.

---

# 9.75 Manufacturing Audit Migration

Historical audit should preserve material:

- Standard change.
- status correction.
- priority change.
- Quality/Maintenance release.
- improvement decision.

---

# 9.76 Manufacturing Reconciliation Framework

Canonical sequence:

```text id="manufacturing-reconciliation-framework"
Certified Source Manufacturing State

↓

Migrated Target State

↓

Compare

↓

Difference

↓

Classify

↓

Correct / Accept / Document

↓

Re-Test

↓

Certify
```

---

# 9.77 Difference Classes

Potential:

- Exact Match.
- Expected Representation Difference.
- Approved Technical Transformation.
- Approved Business Correction.
- Legacy Defect.
- Historical Data Gap.
- Migration Defect.
- Unexplained Difference.

Material unexplained differences block certification.

---

# 9.78 Job Count Reconciliation

Compare:

- Total Jobs.
- completed.
- cancelled.
- open.
- blocked.

where meaningful.

---

# 9.79 Job Relationship Reconciliation

Validate:

```text id="job-relationship-reconciliation"
Order

↓

Production Job

↓

Product

↓

Operation / Work Center

↓

Output
```

---

# 9.80 Open-WIP Reconciliation

Every active Job from source must be accounted for in target.

This is a critical certification gate.

---

# 9.81 Quantity Reconciliation

Validate:

- Planned quantity.
- produced quantity.
- Good Output.
- remaining.
- Scrap.
- Rework.

---

# 9.82 Work-Center Reconciliation

Validate:

- Work-Center mappings.
- active queues.
- Jobs assigned.

---

# 9.83 Resource Reconciliation

Validate:

- Machine identity.
- current availability.
- maintenance state.

where available.

---

# 9.84 Quality Reconciliation

Validate:

- Active Holds.
- failed checks.
- Rework requirements.
- release states.

---

# 9.85 Inventory/Material Reconciliation

Validate Production-related:

- Material issues.
- returns.
- Scrap.
- remaining reservations.

Domain 2 remains authoritative.

---

# 9.86 Personalization Reconciliation

For open GiftHatke Jobs, validate:

- Correct customer asset.
- correct personalization text.
- Production-ready status.
- approved file.

---

# 9.87 Production File Reconciliation

Spot-check:

- Job.
- Product.
- approved production file.
- version.

This is especially important for personalized manufacturing.

---

# 9.88 Standard Reconciliation

Validate:

- Current Standard.
- effective version.
- Work-Center relationship.

---

# 9.89 Downtime Reconciliation

For active downtime at cutover:

Validate:

- Resource.
- current state.
- maintenance linkage.
- affected Jobs.

---

# 9.90 Scrap/Rework Reconciliation

Validate:

- Quantity.
- reason.
- Job.
- Quality link.

---

# 9.91 Replacement Reconciliation

Validate:

- Replacement Job.
- original Order.
- service case.
- current status.

---

# 9.92 Manufacturing Exception Reconciliation

Open critical exceptions must remain visible after cutover.

---

# 9.93 GiftHatke Laser Reconciliation

Validate:

- Laser Work Center.
- machine identities.
- open Laser Jobs.
- current queue.
- machine availability.

---

# 9.94 GiftHatke Acrylic Reconciliation

Validate:

- thickness.
- sheet size.
- issued Material.
- Scrap/offcuts.
- open Jobs.

---

# 9.95 GiftHatke Sublimation Reconciliation

Validate:

- Relevant Production Jobs.
- Resource.
- Reprint/Rework where captured.

---

# 9.96 GiftHatke QC Reconciliation

Validate:

- QC queue.
- Quality Holds.
- Rework returns.
- completed QC.

---

# 9.97 GiftHatke Packaging Reconciliation

Validate:

- Jobs awaiting packaging.
- packaging-material blocks.
- completion state.

---

# 9.98 GiftHatke Corporate Batch Reconciliation

Validate:

- Sample approval.
- batch quantities.
- production status.
- QC status.

# 9.99 Manufacturing Test Architecture

The permanent testing model includes:

1. Master Data Tests.
2. Production Job Tests.
3. Operation Tests.
4. Work-Center Tests.
5. Resource Tests.
6. Readiness Tests.
7. WIP Tests.
8. Queue Tests.
9. Production Event Tests.
10. Cycle-Time Tests.
11. Standard Tests.
12. Setup/Changeover Tests.
13. Downtime Tests.
14. Scrap Tests.
15. Rework Tests.
16. Quality Integration Tests.
17. Bottleneck Tests.
18. Manufacturing Exception Tests.
19. Improvement Tests.
20. AI/Optimization Tests.
21. Migration/Reconciliation Tests.
22. Shop-Floor Acceptance Tests.

---

# 9.100 Production Job Creation Test

Validate:

- Job identity.
- Order relationship.
- Product.
- quantity.

---

# 9.101 Production Job State Test

Test lifecycle:

```text id="production-job-state-test"
Created

↓

Released

↓

Started

↓

Completed
```

Expected:

- Valid state transitions.
- audit preserved.

---

# 9.102 Invalid State Transition Test

Attempt:

```text id="invalid-production-transition-test"
Completed

↓

Started
```

Expected:

- Rejected or governed correction path.

---

# 9.103 Partial Completion Test

Example:

```text id="partial-completion-test"
Planned:
100

Good Completed:
70

Scrap:
5

Remaining:
25
```

Expected:

- Job not falsely marked fully complete unless business rules allow appropriate terminal state.

---

# 9.104 Cancellation Test

Cancel active Job.

Expected:

- No further normal execution.
- prior history preserved.
- material/capacity relationships reconciled.

---

# 9.105 Work-Center Assignment Test

Validate Job routes to correct Work Center.

---

# 9.106 Resource Capability Test

Attempt incompatible Resource assignment.

Expected:

- Rejected or warning according to certified control.

---

# 9.107 Material Readiness Test

If required Material unavailable:

Expected:

- Not Ready / Blocked.

---

# 9.108 Quarantined Material Test

Quarantined Material should not satisfy Production readiness unless Quality-authorized disposition allows it.

---

# 9.109 Personalization Readiness Test

For personalized Job without required photo/text:

Expected:

- Not Production Ready.

---

# 9.110 Artwork Approval Test

Where approval required:

Unapproved file must not become active Production file.

---

# 9.111 Wrong-File Protection Test

Assign superseded design file.

Expected:

- Prevented or clearly blocked under configured control.

---

# 9.112 Production Start Test

Start valid ready Job.

Expected:

- Event generated.
- WIP updated.
- timeline begins.

---

# 9.113 Production Pause Test

Pause Job.

Expected:

- reason required where policy says so.
- state/timeline updated.

---

# 9.114 Block Job Test

Block due to Material shortage.

Expected:

- Block reason.
- owner.
- age.
- exception linkage.

---

# 9.115 Resume Test

Resolve block.

Expected:

- Block interval closes.
- Job returns to appropriate active/queue state.

---

# 9.116 Job Completion Test

Complete Job.

Expected:

- WIP closes.
- output updated.
- downstream state available.
- no duplicate completion.

---

# 9.117 Completion Idempotency Test

Repeat same completion command/event.

Expected:

- no duplicate Good Output.

---

# 9.118 Queue Entry Test

Released Job enters correct Work-Center queue.

---

# 9.119 Queue Priority Test

Validate:

- Priority.
- due date.
- governed queue order.

---

# 9.120 Rush Priority Test

Apply Rush.

Expected:

- authority captured.
- affected Jobs visible.
- audit preserved.

---

# 9.121 Unauthorized Rush Test

Operator without authority attempts to change priority.

Expected:

- Denied.

---

# 9.122 WIP Aging Test

Age exceeds threshold.

Expected:

- WIP Aging Exception.

---

# 9.123 Completed-WIP Removal Test

Complete Job.

Expected:

- removed from active WIP after synchronization.

---

# 9.124 Stale WIP Reconciliation Test

Force projection mismatch.

Expected:

- Reconciliation identifies discrepancy.
- projection corrected.

---

# 9.125 Production Event Deduplication Test

Replay JobStarted.

Expected:

- one start transition.

---

# 9.126 Out-of-Order Event Test

Deliver:

- JobCompleted.
- then JobStarted.

Expected:

- no invalid active state.
- reconciliation required if needed.

---

# 9.127 Event Replay Test

Replay historical events.

Expected:

- derived views rebuilt.
- no operational side effects repeated.

---

# 9.128 Cycle-Time Calculation Test

Example:

```text id="cycle-time-calculation-test"
Start:
10:00

End:
10:25

Expected Active Cycle:
25 Minutes
```

subject to certified pause semantics.

---

# 9.129 Missing Start Test

Completion exists without valid Start.

Expected:

- Cycle Time unavailable or low confidence.

Not fabricated.

---

# 9.130 Standard Version Test

Job executed under Standard v2.

After v3 published:

Historical comparison should remain against v2.

---

# 9.131 Cycle-Time Variance Test

Validate:

- Standard.
- Actual.
- variance.

---

# 9.132 Setup Test

Capture:

- Setup Start.
- Setup End.

Expected:

- Setup duration separate from run time.

---

# 9.133 Changeover Test

Switch Product family.

Expected:

- Changeover recorded where configured.

---

# 9.134 Machine Downtime Test

Machine Down.

Expected:

- Resource unavailable.
- active Job paused/affected.
- capacity impact visible.

---

# 9.135 Waiting-vs-Downtime Test

Machine operational but no Material.

Expected:

- Waiting/Starvation.

Not:

- Equipment Breakdown.

---

# 9.136 Planned Maintenance Test

Maintenance window should be:

- Planned Downtime.

not unplanned failure.

---

# 9.137 Machine Recovery Test

Return to service.

Expected:

- Resource readiness updated.
- affected queue recalculated.

---

# 9.138 Scrap Test

Record Scrap.

Expected:

- Quantity.
- UOM.
- reason.
- Job.
- Yield impact.

---

# 9.139 Reusable Offcut Test

Record reusable Acrylic offcut.

Expected:

- Not counted as true Scrap.
- passed to relevant Inventory process where implemented.

---

# 9.140 Rework Test

Quality failure creates Rework.

Expected:

- Rework operation.
- capacity consumption.
- reinspection requirement.

---

# 9.141 Repeat Rework Test

Rework fails again.

Expected:

- second Rework cycle remains visible.
- not overwritten.

---

# 9.142 First-Pass Test

Output requiring Rework:

Expected:

- Not first-pass successful even if later accepted.

---

# 9.143 Quality Hold Test

Apply Hold.

Expected:

- Production blocked.
- cannot continue normal completion.

---

# 9.144 Unauthorized Quality Release Test

Production user attempts to remove Quality Hold.

Expected:

- Denied.

---

# 9.145 Safety Stop Test

Apply Safety Stop.

Expected:

- Production stops.
- optimization cannot override it.

---

# 9.146 Unauthorized Restart Test

Attempt restart before release.

Expected:

- Denied.

---

# 9.147 Bottleneck Detection Test

Controlled scenario:

```text id="bottleneck-test"
Laser:
Required 18h
Available 24h

QC:
Required 31h
Available 16h

Expected:
QC = Bottleneck
```

# 9.148 Bottleneck Shift Test

Increase QC capacity.

Create Laser overload.

Expected:

- Bottleneck shifts to Laser.

# 9.149 WIP Release Control Test

Excess WIP at downstream Work Center.

Expected:

- Recommendation or control according to policy.

---

# 9.150 Manufacturing Exception Test

Trigger:

- Scrap Spike.

Expected:

- one correlated active exception.
- owner.
- severity.

# 9.151 Exception Deduplication Test

Repeat same condition.

Expected:

- no uncontrolled duplicate exceptions.

---

# 9.152 Root Cause Workflow Test

Validate:

```text id="root-cause-test"
Exception

↓

Investigation

↓

Evidence

↓

Cause Status

↓

Corrective Action
```

# 9.153 Improvement Pilot Test

Validate:

- Baseline.
- hypothesis.
- Pilot scope.
- outcome.
- approval.

---

# 9.154 Improvement Standardization Test

Successful Pilot accepted.

Expected:

- New Standard version.
- effective date.
- previous version retained.

---

# 9.155 Improvement Rollback Test

- Rollback.
- prior safe Standard available.
- evidence retained.

# 9.156 Shop-Floor Permission Test

Validate role boundaries for:

- Start/Complete.
- priority.
- Standard change.
- Quality release.
- risk acceptance.

---

# 9.157 Audit Test

Protected actions should preserve:

- actor.
- time.
- prior state.
- new state.
- reason.

---

# 9.158 Manufacturing Search Test

Validate search for:

- Job.
- Order.
- Product.
- Work Center.
- exception.

---

# 9.159 Manufacturing Command Center Test

Validate current:

- WIP.
- machine.
- Bottleneck.
- critical exceptions.

against source state.

# 9.160 Visual Factory Stale-State Test

Break integration.

Expected:

- Stale/partial-data warning.

Not false green status.

# 9.161 Offline Event Test

Capture permitted local event offline.

Reconnect.

Expected:

- synchronization.
- deduplication.
- conflict handling.

# 9.162 Event-Storm Test

Expected:

- system remains stable.
- no duplicate state.
- critical events prioritized.

# 9.163 Load Test

Peak scenarios may include:

- mass B2B release.

- WIP.
- queues.
- events.
- dashboards.

# 9.164 AI Root Cause Test

Provide insufficient evidence.

Expected:

- Suggested/uncertain cause.

Not false confirmation.

# 9.165 AI Hallucination Test

Ask AI:

- "Which Laser failed at 11:00?"

when no evidence exists.

Expected:

- Reports insufficient data.

# 9.166 AI Resequencing Test

AI suggests sequence.

- Recommendation only.

- Infeasible / blocked.

# 9.168 AI Quality Constraint Test

- Blocked.

# 9.192 Certification Gates

The permanent Manufacturing Operational Certification Gates are:

## Gate 1 — Production Identity Integrity

Jobs, Products, Orders, and quantities map correctly.

## Gate 2 — Active WIP Integrity

Every open Job is correctly represented.

## Gate 3 — Work-Center/Resource Integrity

Current routing and resource identity are valid.

## Gate 4 — Quality/Safety Integrity

Holds, Stops, and releases remain enforced.

## Gate 5 — Standard Work Integrity

Current Standards and versions remain valid.

## Gate 6 — Loss Integrity

Scrap/Rework/Downtime semantics are trustworthy.

## Gate 7 — Event & Synchronization Integrity

State changes synchronize without duplication.

## Gate 8 — Manufacturing Intelligence Integrity

Derived metrics and Bottlenecks use trustworthy evidence.

## Gate 9 — Governance, Security & Audit

Authority boundaries remain intact.

## Gate 10 — Shop-Floor Business Acceptance

Operational users certify usability and correctness.

# 9.194 Critical Certification Blockers

- Missing active WIP.
- wrong Job/Product linkage.
- completed Jobs reopened.
- active Quality Hold lost.
- active Safety Stop bypassed.
- wrong Production file.
- machine state materially incorrect.
- Scrap/Rework quantities corrupted.
- duplicate Production execution.
- unexplained current-state difference.

These block full certification.

- Historical setup detail unavailable.
- old machine identity unavailable.
- historical downtime incomplete.
- historical Cycle Time cannot be calculated.
- informal old Standards unavailable.

- Scope.
- reason.
- business impact.
- risk.
- treatment.
- owner.
- approval.

# ENTERPRISE MANUFACTURING EXCELLENCE & INDUSTRIAL OPERATIONS CANON
## Stage 10 — Final Enterprise Manufacturing Excellence & Industrial Operations Certification Canon

---

# 10.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Manufacturing Excellence & Industrial Operations Domain** is hereby consolidated into one final authoritative enterprise specification.

Stages 1–9 established:

- Domain foundation and industrial-operating scope.
- Manufacturing Performance, Work Center, Loss, WIP, and Improvement entity architecture.
- Shop-Floor Control and Continuous Improvement operating model.
- Manufacturing Excellence services and Industrial Optimization architecture.
- Manufacturing Governance, Standard Work control, and industrial decision rights.
- Manufacturing Events, synchronization, workflows, and cross-domain orchestration.
- Manufacturing Operations Workspace, Visual Factory, and shop-floor UX.
- Manufacturing Intelligence, OEE-style analytics, predictive operations, and optimization.
- migration, reconciliation, testing, and operational acceptance.

Stage 10 formally certifies Domain 34 as the permanent GiftHatkeOS architecture for:

- Manufacturing Excellence.
- Industrial Operations.
- shop-floor visibility.
- Production Flow Management.
- Work-Center performance.
- Resource-state intelligence.
- WIP control.
- Queue Management.
- Cycle-Time Management.
- Setup and Changeover Management.

- Yield.
- Scrap.

- Schedule Adherence.
- Realized Capacity.
- Standard Work.
- Root Cause Investigation.
- Continuous Improvement.
- Visual Factory.
- Predictive Manufacturing.
- Industrial Optimization.
- AI-assisted manufacturing operations.

The Domain exists to ensure that manufacturing becomes:

- Visible.
- measurable.
- stable.
- explainable.
- continuously improvable.
- Quality-controlled.
- safety-governed.
- auditable.
- technologically portable.

---

# 10.2 Final Canon Mission

The permanent mission is:

> **Measure, control, stabilize, and continuously improve how manufacturing work is executed so that customer demand is converted into reliable good output with minimal avoidable waiting, rework, scrap, downtime, instability, and capacity loss.**

The Domain must enable the enterprise to answer:

- What is running?
- What is waiting?
- What is blocked?
- What is late?
- Which machine or Work Center is constraining flow?
- How much capacity is being lost?
- Why?
- How much output is truly good?
- Where is Rework occurring?
- Where is Scrap occurring?
- Which Standards are inaccurate?
- Which processes are unstable?
- Which improvement should be prioritized?
- Did the improvement actually work?
- Which manufacturing risks are emerging?
- What action is recommended?
- Who has authority to act?

---

The Domain permanently follows:

- Safety before output.
- Quality before schedule pressure.
- Production truth before performance interpretation.
- readiness before release.
- flow before local utilization.
- good output before activity.
- visible WIP before hidden queue.
- Standard before variance.
- cause before blame.
- loss classification before optimization.
- Bottleneck before non-constraint improvement.
- containment before escalation.

- baseline before improvement claim.
- Pilot before Standardization.
- event evidence before derived metric.
- constraint before industrial optimization.
- recommendation before execution.
- reconciliation before certification.
- human authority before high-impact autonomous industrial action.

- timestamp.
- source.
- entity reference.
- correlation.
- version where relevant.

# 10.17 Certified Event Replay Safety

Permanent rule:

```text
Replay Manufacturing Events

≠

Repeat Physical Production
```

Rebuilds may restore projections.

They must not repeat real-world side effects.

---

# 10.18 Certified Production Timeline

Canonical Production flow:

```text
Released

↓

Queued

↓

Setup

↓

Processing

↓

Waiting / Blocked

↓

Rework if Required

↓

QC

↓

Packaging

↓

Completed
```

- Material readiness.
- Personalization readiness.
- instruction readiness.
- Resource readiness.
- Quality prerequisites.

```text
Order Confirmed

≠

Production Ready
```

when required:

- Photo.
- name/text.
- design.
- approval.

remains incomplete.

---

# 10.21 Certified Job Release Discipline

The enterprise should avoid releasing excessive Production merely to keep resources busy.

Excess release can create:

- WIP.
- queues.
- handling.
- confusion.
- longer Lead Time.

---

# 10.22 Certified WIP

WIP represents real unfinished Production.

It should preserve:

- Job.
- current stage.
- quantity.
- age.
- priority.
- block state.

# 10.23 Certified WIP Integrity

---

# 10.24 Certified WIP Aging

# 10.25 Certified Queue Management

Queues should distinguish:

- Ready work.
- blocked work.
- conditional work.

---

# 10.26 Certified Queue Prioritization

- Customer due date.
- Rush authority.
- Product family.
- setup efficiency.
- Bottleneck protection.
- readiness.

---

# 10.27 Certified Priority Governance

Permanent distinction:

```text
Normal Priority

≠

Rush

≠

Emergency

≠

Replacement / Recovery
```

Priority changes require governed reason.

# 10.28 Certified Setup

Setup is capacity-consuming preparation activity distinct from Productive Run Time.

---

# 10.29 Certified Changeover

Changeover represents transition between Product/process configurations.

- Material change.
- fixture/jig.
- Product family.
- machine setting.

---

# 10.30 Certified Batch Tradeoff

Permanent relationship:

```text
Larger Batch
→ Fewer Changeovers

BUT

Potentially
→ More WIP / Longer Waiting
```

# 10.31 Certified Cycle Time

Cycle Time must remain semantically clear.

Possible forms:

- Active Process Time.
- Operation Elapsed Time.
- Total Manufacturing Lead Time.

They are not interchangeable.

# 10.32 Certified Standard Cycle Time

- Evidence-based.
- Product/process-aware.
- versioned.
- effective-dated.

```text
Actual Cycle Time

-

Applicable Standard Cycle Time

=

Cycle-Time Variance
```

# 10.34 Certified Variance Interpretation

Potential causes include:

- Product complexity.
- Rework.
- Material.
- machine.
- wrong Standard.
- queue interruption.

# 10.35 Certified Manufacturing Lead Time

Total flow may include:

- Queue.
- setup.
- processing.
- waiting.
- Rework.
- QC.
- Packaging.

---

# 10.36 Certified Flow Principle

The enterprise should improve:

- End-to-end flow.

not simply maximize each local resource's activity.

---

# 10.37 Certified Throughput

Throughput represents useful Good Output over time.

---

# 10.38 Certified Good Output

Good Output aligns with authorized Quality acceptance.

---

# 10.39 Certified Gross vs Good Output

Permanent distinction:

```text
Gross Produced

≠

Good Accepted Output
```

---

# 10.40 Certified Utilization

# 10.41 Certified Utilization Trap

100% Resource utilization can create:

- Queues.
- excess WIP.
- overproduction.

Therefore:

```text
Maximum Utilization
≠
Maximum System Performance
```

---

# 10.42 Certified Availability

Availability describes whether a Resource was available when required/scheduled.

---

# 10.43 Certified Downtime

Downtime should distinguish:

- Planned Maintenance.
- unplanned failure.
- operational waiting.
- setup.

---

# 10.44 Certified Equipment vs Waiting Loss

```text
Machine Broken
=
Equipment Downtime

Machine Ready but No Material
=
Waiting / Starvation
```

---

# 10.45 Certified Production Loss

High-level Loss categories include:

- Availability Loss.
- Performance Loss.
- Quality Loss.
- Setup Loss.
- Waiting Loss.
- Material Loss.
- Planning Loss.
- Information Loss.
- Workforce Availability Loss.

---

# 10.46 Certified Honest Loss Classification

Misclassifying loss corrupts:

- Root Cause.
- Maintenance decisions.
- Capacity assumptions.
- improvement priorities.

---

# 10.47 Certified Yield

Yield represents usable output relative to an explicit input basis.

---

# 10.48 Certified Scrap

Scrap represents unrecoverable Material/output loss.

---

# 10.49 Certified Reusable Offcuts

For GiftHatke sheet materials:

```text
Reusable Offcut

≠

Scrap
```

where reuse is operationally valid.

---

# 10.50 Certified Rework

Rework represents additional corrective processing required to make output acceptable.

- time.
- machine capacity.
- labor.
- Material.

# 10.51 Certified Rework Visibility

Rework must not disappear into normal Production activity.

---

# 10.52 Certified First-Pass Performance

---

# 10.53 Certified Replacement Production

Permanent distinction:

```text
Rework
=
Correct Existing Output

Replacement Production
=
Create New Recovery Output
```

Both consume capacity.

---

# 10.54 Certified Quality-Loss Propagation

Canonical relationship:

```text
Defect

↓

Rework / Scrap

↓

Additional Capacity Consumption

↓

Queue / WIP Growth

↓

Schedule Risk

↓

Customer Impact
```

# 10.55 Certified Bottleneck

---

# 10.56 Certified Bottleneck Evidence

- Persistent queue.
- WIP accumulation.
- required capacity > available capacity.
- downstream starvation.
- recurring lateness.

---

# 10.57 Certified Temporary vs Structural Bottleneck

Bottlenecks should be classified as:

- Temporary.
- seasonal.
- structural.

where evidence supports it.

---

# 10.58 Certified Bottleneck Principle

Permanent rule:

```text
Improve the Constraint

Before

Optimizing Non-Constraints
```

when total system flow is the objective.

---

# 10.59 Certified Bottleneck Shift

Improving one constraint may reveal another.

Manufacturing Excellence is therefore continuous.

---

# 10.60 Certified Capacity

Capacity should distinguish:

- Installed.
- scheduled.
- available.
- realized.
- productive.

---

# 10.61 Certified Realized Capacity

---

# 10.62 Certified Capacity Loss Bridge

Conceptually:

```text
Installed Capacity

-

Maintenance

-

Downtime

-

Setup

-

Rework

-

Starvation / Waiting

=

Effective Productive Capacity
```

# 10.63 Certified Schedule Adherence

Schedule Adherence compares:

- What was scheduled.
- what actually occurred.

---

# 10.64 Certified Schedule Miss Causes

Potential:

- Material.
- machine.
- Quality.
- Personalization.
- Capacity.
- Priority change.
- incorrect Standard.

# 10.65 Certified Rush Work

Rush work should preserve:

- authority.
- displacement impact.

```text
What Must Finish?

↓

What Is Ready?

↓

What Is Running?

↓

What Is Blocked?

↓

What Is Aging?

↓

What Is the Bottleneck?

↓

What Requires Action?
```

# 10.68 Certified Daily Manufacturing Review

Daily review should focus on:

- Plan vs Actual.
- carryover.
- critical blocks.
- machine issues.
- Quality issues.
- Bottleneck.
- customer-critical risk.
- immediate actions.

# 10.69 Certified Weekly Review

Weekly review may focus on:

- Throughput.
- WIP.
- Downtime.
- Rework.
- Scrap.
- Bottlenecks.
- Improvement Initiatives.

# 10.70 Certified Monthly Manufacturing Excellence Review

Monthly review may focus on:

- Chronic losses.

- Manufacturing Risk.

- Jobs running.

- output.

# 10.73 Certified Andon-Style Control

# 10.74 Certified Stop-Work Authority

conditions exist.

# 10.76 Certified Unauthorized Restart Prohibition

- Safety Stop.

- accessible.

```text
Acknowledged

↓

Investigated

↓

Action Planned

↓
```

```text
↓

Downtime

↓

Queue Growth

↓

Schedule Delay

↓

Customer Risk
```

```text
Containment
≠
Permanent Corrective Action
```

# 10.87 Certified Root Cause States

- Inconclusive.

- system.
- Standard.
- equipment.
- materials.
- workload.
- instructions.

# 10.89 Certified Workforce Boundary

# 10.129 Certified Recommendation Outcome Learning

- decision.
- action.
- actual outcome.

# ENTERPRISE INNOVATION, RESEARCH & CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT CANON
## Stage 1 — Domain Foundation, Innovation Scope, Research Architecture & Enterprise Improvement Model Canon

---

# 1.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Innovation, Research & Continuous Improvement Domain** establishes the permanent architecture for how GiftHatkeOS discovers opportunities, captures ideas, investigates problems, researches alternatives, tests hypotheses, runs experiments, evaluates evidence, scales successful innovations, rejects unsuccessful ideas responsibly, and preserves organizational learning.

This Domain exists because an enterprise should not improve only when:

- Something breaks.
- Customer complaints increase.
- competitors move first.
- costs become unacceptable.
- a manager happens to remember an idea.

Innovation and improvement must become durable enterprise capabilities.

The permanent objective is:

> **Create a governed system through which ideas, research, experiments, lessons, and improvement opportunities are converted into evidence-backed business decisions and reusable organizational knowledge.**

---

# 1.2 Domain Mission

The permanent mission is:

> **Enable GiftHatkeOS to discover, evaluate, test, learn from, and responsibly scale better products, processes, technologies, business models, and operational practices without confusing ideas with evidence or experiments with approved production standards.**

The Domain must enable the enterprise to answer:

- What should we improve?
- What new opportunities are emerging?
- Which ideas are worth investigating?
- What evidence supports an idea?
- What assumptions remain unproven?
- What experiment should be run?
- What outcome would count as success?
- What risks exist?
- Who may approve a Pilot?
- Did the Pilot work?
- Were there negative side effects?
- Should the innovation be scaled?
- Should the experiment be stopped?
- What did we learn?
- Has the same idea already been tested?
- Which innovations actually generated value?
- Which failed ideas should not be repeated?
- Which research should influence Product, Production, Marketing, Sales, or platform architecture?

---

# 1.3 Innovation Philosophy

The Domain permanently follows:

---

## Problem Before Solution

Start with:

- Need.
- problem.
- opportunity.

before becoming attached to a proposed solution.

---

## Evidence Before Confidence

An attractive idea is not automatically a good business decision.

---

## Hypothesis Before Experiment

Experiments should state what is expected to happen.

---

## Small Test Before Large Commitment

Where practical, validate uncertainty through controlled Pilots before major investment.

---

## Learning Before Success Theatre

An experiment that disproves an assumption may still create valuable enterprise knowledge.

---

## Baseline Before Improvement Claim

Without understanding the current state, improvement claims are weak.

---

## Customer and Business Value Before Novelty

Innovation is not valuable merely because it is new.

---

## Safety, Quality, Privacy and Compliance Before Experiment Speed

Experiments remain subject to enterprise governance.

---

## Reversibility Before Irreversible Commitment

Higher uncertainty should generally favor more reversible experiments.

---

## Knowledge Preservation Before Repetition

The enterprise should remember what it already tested and learned.

---

Permanent distinction:

```text id="innovation-vs-improvement"
Continuous Improvement
=
Improve an Existing Product, Process or Capability

Innovation
=
Explore Potentially New
Products, Processes, Technologies,
Business Models or Ways of Creating Value
```

Both belong in Domain 35.

- Risk levels.

- experimentation methods.

# 1.15 Opportunity

An **Opportunity** represents:

> A business situation where improvement, innovation, experimentation, or further investigation may create value.

Examples:

- Excessive customization delay.
- new gifting category.
- reusable packaging concept.
- AI-assisted artwork preparation.
- improved laser nesting.
- B2B self-service personalization portal.

- competitor observation.
- supplier innovation.
- technology change.
- analytics.
- AI insights.
- management strategy.

# 1.17 Problem

A **Problem** is a verified or suspected undesirable condition requiring understanding.

Example:

> Personalized LED lamp Orders spend too much time waiting for artwork preparation.

---

# 1.18 Opportunity vs Problem

Permanent distinction:

```text id="opportunity-vs-problem"
Problem
=
Something undesirable exists

Opportunity
=
A possibility exists to create additional value
```

An innovation may address either.

---

# 1.19 Problem Statement

A useful Problem Statement should describe:

- Who/what is affected.
- Current condition.
- evidence.
- impact.

It should avoid assuming the solution.

---

# 1.20 Poor Problem Statement

Example:

> We need AI.

This is not a sufficiently defined business problem.

---

# 1.21 Better Problem Statement

Example:

> Artwork preparation for personalized lamp Orders averages 18 minutes and delays Production readiness during peak periods.

This creates something measurable to investigate.

---

# 1.22 Idea

An **Idea** represents a proposed possible response to:

- Opportunity.
- problem.
- strategic objective.

---

# 1.23 Idea Is Not Evidence

Permanent rule:

```text id="idea-not-evidence"
Idea

≠

Validated Solution
```

---

# 1.24 Idea Capture

An Idea may contain:

- Title.
- description.
- source.
- related Problem/Opportunity.
- expected benefit.
- initial assumptions.
- owner.
- date.

---

# 1.25 Idea Sources

Ideas may come from:

- Employees.
- Customers.
- partners.
- suppliers.
- managers.
- research.
- AI systems.

---

# 1.26 Open Idea Culture

Authorized employees should be able to contribute improvement ideas without requiring formal project paperwork at the initial capture stage.

---

# 1.27 Idea Quality

The system may guide contributors to explain:

- What is the problem?
- what is the proposed idea?
- who benefits?
- why might it help?

---

# 1.28 Duplicate Idea Detection

Before starting new research, the enterprise should identify whether:

- Similar Idea.
- previous experiment.
- prior failed approach.

already exists.

---

# 1.29 Idea Clustering

Related ideas may be grouped into:

- Themes.
- Opportunities.
- problem areas.

---

# 1.30 Innovation Theme

A Theme may represent a broad area such as:

- Faster Personalization.
- Production Automation.
- Sustainable Packaging.
- Corporate Gifting.
- AI-Assisted Operations.

---

# 1.31 Innovation Funnel

Canonical flow:

```text id="innovation-funnel"
Opportunity / Problem

↓

Ideas

↓

Screening

↓

Research

↓

Hypothesis

↓

Experiment / Prototype

↓

Pilot

↓

Evaluation

↓

Adopt / Scale / Reject / Defer
```

Not every Idea should proceed through the entire funnel.

---

# 1.32 Idea Screening

Initial screening may evaluate:

- Relevance.
- potential value.
- obvious feasibility.
- duplication.
- risk.
- strategic alignment.

---

# 1.33 Early Rejection

An Idea may be rejected early if:

- Duplicative.
- clearly infeasible.
- legally unacceptable.
- strategically irrelevant.
- insufficient potential value.

Rejection reason should be preserved.

---

# 1.34 Deferred Idea

Some ideas may be valuable but premature.

State:

- Deferred.

should preserve:

- Reason.
- potential review trigger.

---

# 1.35 Research Request

A Research Request asks for structured investigation into an uncertainty.

Examples:

- Can a new acrylic supplier reduce cost without affecting Quality?
- Can AI reduce artwork-preparation time?
- Would UV printing expand Product capability?
- Is reusable premium gift packaging commercially viable?

---

# 1.36 Research Question

A good Research Question should be:

- Specific.
- answerable.
- decision-relevant.

---

# 1.37 Research Programme

A larger strategic topic may contain multiple Research Projects.

Example:

```text id="research-programme-example"
Programme:
Automation of Personalized Production

Projects:
1. AI Artwork Preparation
2. Automated Image Quality Checking
3. Laser Job Sequencing
4. Customer Self-Service Preview
```

---

# 1.38 Research Project

A Research Project may contain:

- Question.
- scope.
- owner.
- methodology.
- sources.
- findings.
- limitations.
- conclusion.

---

# 1.39 Research Evidence

Evidence may include:

- Internal operational data.
- Customer interviews.
- Supplier information.
- Market research.
- technical testing.
- academic/public research.
- Prototype results.
- Pilot data.

---

# 1.40 Evidence Quality

Evidence should be evaluated by:

- Relevance.
- reliability.
- recency.
- sample quality.
- reproducibility where applicable.
- conflict with other evidence.

---

# 1.41 Evidence vs Opinion

Permanent distinction:

```text id="evidence-vs-opinion"
Evidence
=
Supports a conclusion

Opinion
=
A viewpoint that may require validation
```

Both may be captured, but must not be confused.

---

# 1.42 Source Provenance

Research evidence should preserve:

- Source.
- date.
- author/provider where relevant.
- context.
- relationship to conclusion.

---

# 1.43 Conflicting Evidence

Research may produce conflicting findings.

The system should preserve:

- Both sides.
- confidence.
- unresolved questions.

---

# 1.44 Research Limitation

Every material research conclusion may specify limitations such as:

- Small sample.
- limited timeframe.
- uncertain supplier information.
- incomplete market data.

---

# 1.45 Assumption

An **Assumption** represents something believed to be true but not yet sufficiently validated.

Example:

> Customers will accept self-service personalization without sales assistance.

---

# 1.46 Assumption Register

Important initiatives should identify assumptions concerning:

- Customer behavior.
- demand.
- technology.
- cost.
- operations.
- adoption.
- Quality.
- suppliers.

---

# 1.47 Critical Assumption

A Critical Assumption is one whose failure could invalidate:

- Business Case.
- Experiment.
- initiative.

---

# 1.48 Assumption Status

Potential states:

- Untested.
- partially supported.
- validated.
- invalidated.
- uncertain.

---

# 1.49 Hypothesis

A **Hypothesis** converts an assumption into a testable proposition.

Example:

```text id="innovation-hypothesis"
If customers upload personalization
through a guided self-service flow,

then manual artwork-preparation time
will decrease by at least 30%,

without increasing order-error rate.
```

---

# 1.50 Hypothesis Components

A useful hypothesis may identify:

- Intervention/change.
- expected outcome.
- target population/process.
- measurable success condition.

---

# 1.51 Hypothesis Falsifiability

A hypothesis should be capable of being proven wrong.

A statement that cannot fail is weak for experimentation.

---

# 1.52 Experiment

An **Experiment** is a controlled attempt to test uncertainty.

---

# 1.53 Experiment Purpose

Experiments should be designed to:

- Learn.

not merely to demonstrate that a preferred idea was correct.

---

# 1.54 Experiment Scope

Experiment should define:

- Hypothesis.
- test group/scope.
- duration.
- method.
- metrics.
- risks.
- success criteria.
- stop criteria.

---

# 1.55 Minimum Useful Experiment

Permanent principle:

> Use the smallest sufficiently reliable test capable of reducing the important uncertainty.

---

# 1.56 Experiment Risk

Risk may include:

- Customer impact.
- Quality.
- Safety.
- privacy.
- cost.
- operational disruption.
- reputational impact.

---

# 1.57 Experiment Environment

Potential environments:

- Sandbox.
- laboratory/test environment.
- internal process Pilot.
- limited Customer Pilot.
- controlled Production Pilot.

---

# 1.58 Experiment Isolation

Experiments should avoid altering enterprise-wide authoritative processes before approval.

---

# 1.59 Experiment Control Group

Where meaningful, an Experiment may compare:

- Existing process.
- experimental process.

Not every business experiment requires a formal statistical control group.

---

# 1.60 Success Criteria

Success criteria should be defined before results where practical.

Example:

```text id="experiment-success-criteria"
Artwork Automation Pilot

Success:
Preparation Time -30% or more

AND

Order Error Rate does not materially increase
```

---

# 1.61 Failure Criteria

A Pilot should also define unacceptable outcomes.

Examples:

- Quality defects increase.
- customer complaints increase.
- Production delay worsens.
- privacy risk appears.

---

# 1.62 Stop Criteria

Experiments may require immediate stop if:

- Safety risk.
- material Quality risk.
- legal/compliance concern.
- severe customer harm.

---

# 1.63 Prototype

A **Prototype** represents an early representation intended to test:

- Feasibility.
- desirability.
- usability.
- technical concept.

---

# 1.64 Prototype Is Not Production

Permanent distinction:

```text id="prototype-not-production"
Prototype

≠

Production-Ready Solution
```

---

# 1.65 Prototype Types

Potential:

- Product sample.
- UI mockup.
- workflow prototype.
- machine fixture.
- Packaging prototype.
- software proof of concept.

---

# 1.66 Proof of Concept

A Proof of Concept asks:

> Can this technically work?

It does not necessarily answer:

- Will customers want it?
- Is it economically viable?
- Can it scale?

---

# 1.67 Pilot

A **Pilot** tests a sufficiently mature concept in limited real operational conditions.

---

# 1.68 Pilot vs Prototype

Permanent distinction:

```text id="prototype-vs-pilot"
Prototype
=
Test Concept

Pilot
=
Test Limited Real-World Operation
```

---

# 1.69 Pilot Scope

A Pilot may be constrained by:

- Customer segment.
- Product.
- location.
- Work Center.
- channel.
- duration.
- transaction volume.

---

# 1.70 Pilot Authority

Higher-impact Pilots require appropriate:

- Business.
- Product.
- Production.
- Quality.
- Legal.
- Security.

approval depending on scope.

---

# 1.71 Pilot Rollback

A Pilot should be reversible where practical.

---

# 1.72 Feasibility

Feasibility may include:

- Technical Feasibility.
- Operational Feasibility.
- Commercial Feasibility.
- Financial Feasibility.
- Legal/Compliance Feasibility.
- Security/Privacy Feasibility.
- Supply Chain Feasibility.

---

# 1.73 Technical Feasibility

Question:

> Can we build or operate it reliably?

---

# 1.74 Operational Feasibility

Question:

> Can the team actually use and support it in normal operations?

---

# 1.75 Commercial Feasibility

Question:

> Does it create sufficient Customer/market value?

---

# 1.76 Financial Feasibility

Question:

> Does the expected benefit justify investment and operating cost?

Finance remains authoritative for formal financial measures.

---

# 1.77 Compliance Feasibility

Domain 24 should review where innovation affects:

- Contracts.
- regulations.
- consumer rights.
- legal obligations.

---

# 1.78 Security & Privacy Feasibility

Domains 28 and 29 govern security/privacy where experiments involve:

- Customer data.
- employee data.
- AI.
- new integrations.

---

# 1.79 Operational Readiness

Before Pilot scaling, assess:

- Process.
- team.
- documentation.
- support.
- system.
- training.
- monitoring.

---

# 1.80 Business Case

A Business Case may summarize:

- Problem/Opportunity.
- evidence.
- proposed solution.
- expected benefits.
- costs.
- risks.
- assumptions.
- alternatives.
- recommendation.

---

# 1.81 Business Case Boundary

Business Case is:

- Decision support.

not guaranteed outcome.

---

# 1.82 Innovation Investment Levels

Potential stages:

```text id="innovation-investment-ladder"
Idea
→ Minimal Cost

Research
→ Small Investment

Prototype
→ Controlled Investment

Pilot
→ Moderate Investment

Scale
→ Major Commitment
```

Evidence requirements should rise with commitment.

---

# 1.83 Progressive Evidence Principle

Permanent rule:

```text id="progressive-evidence"
Higher Investment / Risk

↓

Higher Evidence Requirement
```

---

# 1.84 Innovation Portfolio

The enterprise may maintain a Portfolio of:

- Ideas.
- Research.
- Experiments.
- Pilots.
- scale candidates.

---

# 1.85 Portfolio Purpose

The Portfolio should prevent:

- Too many simultaneous experiments.
- duplicated work.
- scattered investment.
- innovation without ownership.

---

# 1.86 Innovation Categories

Potential categories include:

- Product Innovation.
- Manufacturing Innovation.
- Customer Experience Innovation.
- Supply Chain Innovation.
- Commercial Innovation.
- Marketing Innovation.
- Technology Innovation.
- Process Improvement.
- Sustainability Innovation.
- Business Model Innovation.

---

# 1.87 Innovation Horizon

Possible horizons:

- Incremental.
- Adjacent.
- Transformational.

This classification should guide risk expectations.

---

# 1.88 Incremental Innovation

Examples:

- Reduce Laser setup time.
- improve Packaging process.
- simplify customer artwork upload.

---

# 1.89 Adjacent Innovation

Examples:

- New corporate-gifting workflow.
- new Product category.
- new manufacturing technology closely related to existing capability.

---

# 1.90 Transformational Innovation

Examples:

- Significantly different business model.
- highly automated personalization platform.
- new manufacturing paradigm.

Transformational initiatives require stronger governance and experimentation.

---

# 1.91 Continuous Improvement

Continuous Improvement focuses on repeated smaller enhancements to existing operations.

---

# 1.92 Improvement Opportunity Sources

May originate from:

- Manufacturing losses.
- Customer complaints.
- employee friction.
- workflow delays.
- duplicate data entry.
- Quality defects.
- Inventory errors.

---

# 1.93 Continuous Improvement Loop

Canonical:

```text id="continuous-improvement-domain35"
Observe

↓

Define Problem

↓

Baseline

↓

Find Cause / Opportunity

↓

Test Change

↓

Measure

↓

Standardize

↓

Monitor
```

---

# 1.94 Improvement Ownership

Improvement may be owned by:

- Business team.
- Process Owner.
- Manufacturing Excellence.
- Customer Success.
- Finance.
- Technology.

depending on scope.

---

# 1.95 Improvement vs Routine Fix

A one-time correction is not necessarily Continuous Improvement.

Improvement should reduce recurrence or improve the underlying system.

---

# 1.96 Root Cause Integration

Domain 35 may consume Root Cause findings from:

- Domain 4.
- Domain 32.
- Domain 34.
- Domain 14.

to generate improvement opportunities.

---

# 1.97 Lessons Learned

A **Lesson Learned** captures reusable knowledge from:

- Successful experiment.
- failed experiment.
- research.
- project.
- incident.
- improvement.

---

# 1.98 Positive Lesson

Example:

> Grouping similar acrylic jobs reduces Laser setup without causing meaningful delivery delay.

---

# 1.99 Negative Lesson

Example:

> Customer self-service preview created more confusion than the manual process for complex B2B designs.

Negative learning should be preserved.

---

# 1.100 Lesson Evidence

Lessons should reference:

- Source Initiative.
- evidence.
- context.
- date.

---

# 1.101 Knowledge Reuse

Before starting similar innovation:

Search:

- Prior Research.
- Pilots.
- failed Ideas.
- Lessons Learned.

---

# 1.102 Innovation Decision

Possible decisions:

- Proceed to Research.
- Prototype.
- Pilot.
- Scale.
- Adopt.
- Defer.
- Reject.
- Stop.
- Revisit.

---

# 1.103 Decision Evidence

A material decision should preserve:

- Evidence.
- assumptions.
- risks.
- decision maker.
- rationale.

---

# 1.104 Reject Decision

Rejected Ideas should retain:

- Why rejected.
- evidence.
- date.

A rejection is not necessarily permanent.

---

# 1.105 Stop Decision

An active Experiment may be stopped when:

- hypothesis disproven.
- costs exceed value.
- unacceptable risk.
- stronger alternative appears.

---

# 1.106 Scale Decision

Scaling requires stronger evidence than beginning a Pilot.

---

# 1.107 Adoption

Adoption means innovation becomes an approved enterprise capability/process.

It should transition into the owning operational Domain.

---

# 1.108 Operational Handoff

Canonical:

```text id="innovation-operational-handoff"
Validated Innovation

↓

Adoption Decision

↓

Owning Business Domain

↓

Implementation

↓

Operational Standard

↓

Performance Monitoring
```

---

# 1.109 Innovation Does Not Own Permanent Operations

Once adopted:

The owning operational Domain becomes authoritative.

Domain 35 preserves:

- Innovation history.
- evidence.
- lessons.

---

# 1.110 Research-to-Decision Traceability

Canonical:

```text id="research-decision-lineage"
Research Question

↓

Evidence

↓

Finding

↓

Hypothesis

↓

Experiment

↓

Result

↓

Decision
```

---

# 1.111 Innovation Risk

Innovation inherently contains uncertainty.

Risk categories may include:

- Technical.
- financial.
- operational.
- Customer.
- Quality.
- Safety.
- legal.
- security.
- privacy.
- strategic.

---

# 1.112 Risk vs Uncertainty

Permanent distinction:

```text id="risk-vs-uncertainty"
Known Potential Adverse Outcome
=
Risk

What We Do Not Yet Understand
=
Uncertainty
```

Research reduces uncertainty.

---

# 1.113 Innovation Risk Acceptance

Higher-risk experiments require stronger authority.

---

# 1.114 Experiment Blast Radius

Every Pilot should understand:

- How many Customers?
- How many Orders?
- Which systems?
- Which Production processes?
- Which data?

may be affected.

---

# 1.115 Reversibility

Innovations may be classified:

- Easily reversible.
- reversible with cost.
- difficult to reverse.
- irreversible.

Evidence requirements should increase with irreversibility.

---

# 1.116 Technology Scouting

Technology Scouting systematically investigates emerging capabilities relevant to the enterprise.

Examples:

- New printing technology.
- new Laser equipment.
- AI personalization tools.
- vision inspection.
- automated Packaging.

---

# 1.117 Technology Signal

A Technology Signal may contain:

- Technology.
- source.
- maturity.
- possible use.
- risks.
- relevance.

---

# 1.118 Technology Maturity

Potential classification:

- Experimental.
- emerging.
- proven.
- mainstream.
- declining.

---

# 1.119 Technology Hype Control

New technology should not be adopted simply because:

- It is popular.
- competitors mention it.
- AI recommends it.

Business value and evidence remain required.

---

# 1.120 Technology Feasibility Trial

Example:

```text id="technology-feasibility-trial"
Technology:
Computer Vision QC

Question:
Can it reliably detect engraving alignment defects?

Prototype:
Historical image set

Success:
Detection accuracy sufficient for assisted review

Boundary:
Does not automatically replace human QC
```

---

# 1.121 Trend Scouting

Potential trends:

- Customer personalization behavior.
- marketplace changes.
- materials.
- gifting trends.
- manufacturing technology.
- sustainability expectations.

---

# 1.122 Market Signal

A Market Signal is not automatically forecast truth.

It may generate:

- Research Opportunity.

---

# 1.123 Customer Discovery

Customer research may use:

- Interviews.
- surveys.
- support tickets.
- Order behavior.
- Product reviews.

---

# 1.124 Customer Research Ethics

Research involving customers must respect:

- Privacy.
- consent where required.
- honest communication.
- fair treatment.

---

# 1.125 Employee Discovery

Employees often understand:

- Process friction.
- workarounds.
- recurring errors.

Their insights should be usable as innovation inputs.

---

# 1.126 Supplier Innovation

Suppliers may propose:

- Materials.
- Components.
- processes.
- Packaging.
- technologies.

These should undergo independent evaluation.

---

# 1.127 Partner Innovation

Partners may contribute:

- Logistics.
- platform.
- Production.
- technology.

innovations.

---

# 1.128 Competitive Intelligence Boundary

Competitive information may inform innovation.

It should be acquired and used legally and ethically.

---

# 1.129 Research Ethics

Research must not rely on:

- Stolen confidential information.
- unauthorized access.
- deceptive collection practices.

---

# 1.130 Innovation Metrics

Potential operational measures include:

- Ideas submitted.
- ideas researched.
- Experiment cycle time.
- Pilot success.
- adoption rate.
- learning captured.
- realized improvement.

Domain 30 governs official KPI definitions.

---

# 1.131 Idea Count Trap

A high number of Ideas does not automatically mean strong innovation.

---

# 1.132 Experiment Success-Rate Trap

A very high Pilot success rate may indicate:

- Experiments are too safe.
- failed experiments are hidden.
- teams only test obvious improvements.

---

# 1.133 Failure as Learning

A well-run failed experiment may be valuable if it:

- Invalidates a costly assumption early.
- prevents larger bad investment.
- produces reusable knowledge.

---

# 1.134 Innovation Throughput

Potential question:

> How efficiently does the enterprise convert worthwhile Opportunities into validated learning?

Not merely:

> How many Ideas were submitted?

---

# 1.135 Research Cycle Time

The enterprise may monitor how long important uncertainties remain unresolved.

---

# 1.136 Experiment Cycle Time

Reducing time from:

- Hypothesis.
- test.
- result.

can accelerate learning.

---

# 1.137 Innovation Bottleneck

Potential Bottlenecks:

- Approval.
- lack of evidence.
- technical resources.
- Pilot capacity.
- decision delay.

---

# 1.138 Innovation Portfolio Balance

Portfolio may balance:

- Small operational improvements.
- adjacent opportunities.
- strategic experiments.

---

# 1.139 Resource Competition

Innovation work competes with:

- Daily operations.
- Production.
- platform development.

Capacity should be allocated deliberately.

---

# 1.140 Innovation Budget Boundary

Finance owns:

- Budget.
- accounting.
- financial approvals.

Domain 35 manages Innovation demand and evidence for investment decisions.

---

# 1.141 Innovation Prioritization

Potential dimensions:

- Business value.
- Customer value.
- strategic alignment.
- risk reduction.
- evidence strength.
- feasibility.
- effort.
- learning value.

---

# 1.142 Priority Score Boundary

A scoring model may support ranking.

It should not replace management judgment.

---

# 1.143 Evidence Confidence

Potential states:

- Low.
- Moderate.
- High.
- Insufficient.

---

# 1.144 Confidence Evolution

Confidence may progress:

```text id="innovation-confidence-evolution"
Idea
Low

↓

Research
Moderate

↓

Pilot
Higher

↓

Scaled Operation
Evidence-Based
```

Not every Initiative follows this exact pattern.

---

# 1.145 Innovation Stage Gates

Potential Gates:

## Gate 1 — Opportunity Validity

Is the Problem/Opportunity meaningful?

## Gate 2 — Research Sufficiency

Do we understand enough to test?

## Gate 3 — Experiment Readiness

Is the test safe and useful?

## Gate 4 — Pilot Evidence

Did it work in limited operation?

## Gate 5 — Adoption Readiness

Is it ready for operational ownership?

---

# 1.146 Gate Flexibility

Small improvements should not require the same bureaucracy as:

- Major system change.
- new technology.
- high-risk Product innovation.

Governance should be proportional.

---

# 1.147 Fast-Lane Improvements

Low-risk reversible improvements may use accelerated:

```text id="fast-lane-improvement"
Opportunity

↓

Small Test

↓

Evidence

↓

Process Owner Approval

↓

Standardize
```

---

# 1.148 Strategic Innovation Path

Higher-risk initiatives may require:

```text id="strategic-innovation-path"
Strategic Opportunity

↓

Research

↓

Business Case

↓

Prototype

↓

Pilot

↓

Executive Review

↓

Project / Product Programme
```

---

# 1.149 Innovation Portfolio States

Potential:

- Proposed.
- Screening.
- Researching.
- Prototyping.
- Experimenting.
- Piloting.
- Ready for Adoption.
- Scaling.
- Deferred.
- Rejected.
- Closed.

---

# 1.150 Innovation Ownership

Every active material Initiative requires:

- Owner.

Ideas without owners may remain backlog rather than active work.

---

# 1.151 Decision Owner

A different person may own:

- Research.

versus:

- Scale decision.

---

# 1.152 Cross-Functional Innovation

Innovation may require contributors from:

- Product.
- Production.
- Marketing.
- Sales.
- Customer Success.
- Finance.
- Technology.
- Quality.

---

# 1.153 Innovation Council

As GiftHatke grows, a governance forum may review:

- Strategic Ideas.
- Portfolio priorities.
- Pilots.
- scale decisions.
- innovation risks.

This need not become excessive bureaucracy.

---

# 1.154 Innovation Review Cadence

Potential:

## Weekly

- Active experiment blockers.

## Monthly

- Portfolio.
- Pilot outcomes.
- new opportunities.

## Quarterly

- Strategic innovation themes.
- technology scouting.
- innovation investment.

---

# 1.155 Research Review

Research should be reviewed for:

- Question answered?
- evidence sufficient?
- limitations?
- recommended next step?

---

# 1.156 Experiment Review

Experiment review should ask:

- Did it test the Hypothesis?
- Was execution valid?
- Did metrics behave as expected?
- Were there confounders?
- What was learned?

---

# 1.157 Pilot Review

Pilot review should consider:

- Customer impact.
- operational impact.
- Quality.
- cost context.
- adoption difficulty.
- scalability.

---

# 1.158 Scale Readiness

Before scaling:

- Process defined.
- technology reliable.
- support available.
- training considered.
- governance established.
- monitoring ready.

---

# 1.159 Innovation Handoff Checklist

Potential:

- Final design.
- owning Domain.
- Standard/Process.
- documentation.
- training.
- support.
- configuration.
- monitoring.
- rollback.

---

# 1.160 Post-Adoption Review

After scale:

Review:

- Did expected value materialize?
- Were assumptions correct?
- Did unintended effects appear?

---

# 1.161 Innovation Benefit Realization

Potential benefits:

- Revenue.
- Customer value.
- Quality.
- speed.
- capacity.
- cost reduction.
- risk reduction.
- employee effort reduction.
- sustainability.

---

# 1.162 Benefit Attribution

Do not automatically attribute all improvement after rollout to the innovation.

Preserve causal caution.

---

# 1.163 Innovation Failure Categories

Potential:

- Problem not real.
- Customer value insufficient.
- Technology failed.
- operations could not support.
- economics weak.
- compliance issue.
- adoption failure.
- timing wrong.

---

# 1.164 Failure Taxonomy

Failure classification helps the enterprise understand whether:

- Idea was wrong.
- execution was poor.
- conditions changed.

---

# 1.165 Kill Criteria

Strategic initiatives should define when to stop investing.

This reduces escalation of commitment.

---

# 1.166 Sunk-Cost Discipline

Prior investment alone is not sufficient reason to continue a weak Initiative.

---

# 1.167 Revisit Criteria

A rejected/deferred Idea may reopen when:

- Technology improves.
- cost changes.
- Customer behavior changes.
- new evidence emerges.

---

# 1.168 Innovation Memory

Every significant Initiative should preserve:

- Problem.
- Idea.
- assumptions.
- evidence.
- Experiment.
- outcome.
- decision.
- lessons.

---

# ENTERPRISE INNOVATION, RESEARCH & CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT CANON
## Stage 2 — Innovation Opportunity, Research, Hypothesis, Experiment, Pilot & Learning Entity Model Canon

---

# 2.1 Purpose

The **Enterprise Innovation, Research & Continuous Improvement Domain** requires a permanent entity architecture defining how the enterprise represents:

- Problems.
- Opportunities.
- Ideas.
- Research Questions.
- Research Projects.
- Evidence.
- Assumptions.
- Hypotheses.
- Experiments.
- Prototypes.
- Proofs of Concept.
- Pilots.
- Feasibility assessments.
- Business Cases.
- Innovation Decisions.
- Improvement Initiatives.
- Lessons Learned.
- Innovation Risks.
- Portfolio items.
- Adoption and Scale decisions.

Stage 1 established:

- Domain scope.
- Innovation philosophy.
- Research architecture.
- Experimentation doctrine.
- Continuous Improvement model.
- GiftHatke-specific innovation context.

Stage 2 establishes the permanent information model that allows every significant innovation journey to remain:

- Traceable.
- explainable.
- comparable.
- auditable.
- searchable.
- reusable.
- technologically portable.

The central objective is:

> **Preserve the complete chain from Problem or Opportunity through Idea, Research, Assumption, Hypothesis, Experiment, Result, Decision, Adoption, and Lesson so the enterprise can understand not only what it changed, but why it changed it and what evidence justified the decision.**

---

# 2.2 Innovation Entity Principles

The Domain permanently follows:

- Problem before proposed solution.
- Opportunity before project commitment.
- source before interpretation.
- evidence before conclusion.
- assumption before certainty.
- Hypothesis before Experiment.
- Experiment before scale.
- baseline before Improvement result.
- result before decision.
- decision before operational adoption.
- Lesson before archival closure.
- version before historical mutation.
- lineage before summary.
- human authority before high-impact adoption.

---

# 2.3 Canonical Innovation Entity Landscape

The permanent entity architecture includes:

| Entity | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Innovation Opportunity | Represents potential value creation |
| Innovation Problem | Represents undesirable current condition |
| Opportunity Source | Records origin of Opportunity |
| Idea | Represents proposed solution/concept |
| Idea Submission | Preserves original Idea intake |
| Idea Theme | Groups related Ideas |
| Idea Cluster | Groups similar/duplicate concepts |
| Innovation Portfolio Item | Represents managed innovation work |
| Research Request | Requests structured investigation |
| Research Question | Defines decision-relevant uncertainty |
| Research Programme | Groups related Research Projects |
| Research Project | Organizes structured investigation |
| Research Method | Describes research approach |
| Research Source | Identifies source of evidence |
| Research Evidence | Preserves evidence |
| Evidence Assessment | Evaluates evidence quality |
| Research Finding | Represents supported observation |
| Research Limitation | Records uncertainty/constraint |
| Assumption | Represents unverified belief |
| Critical Assumption | Represents high-impact uncertainty |
| Hypothesis | Represents testable proposition |
| Hypothesis Metric | Defines measurement |
| Experiment | Represents controlled test |
| Experiment Variant | Represents tested alternative |
| Experiment Cohort | Represents subject/process population |
| Experiment Metric | Defines measured outcome |
| Experiment Baseline | Defines comparison state |
| Success Criterion | Defines success threshold |
| Failure Criterion | Defines unacceptable result |
| Stop Criterion | Defines early termination condition |
| Experiment Result | Records measured outcome |
| Experiment Exception | Records abnormal test condition |
| Prototype | Represents early solution representation |
| Proof of Concept | Tests technical feasibility |
| Pilot | Tests limited real-world operation |
| Pilot Scope | Defines Pilot boundaries |
| Pilot Result | Captures Pilot outcomes |
| Feasibility Assessment | Evaluates viability |
| Technical Feasibility | Assesses technical viability |
| Operational Feasibility | Assesses business-operating viability |
| Commercial Feasibility | Assesses market/customer viability |
| Financial Feasibility | Assesses economics |
| Compliance Feasibility | Assesses legal/regulatory viability |
| Security/Privacy Feasibility | Assesses information risk |
| Business Case | Consolidates decision evidence |
| Innovation Risk | Represents uncertainty/risk |
| Risk Mitigation | Represents risk response |
| Innovation Decision | Records governed decision |
| Decision Option | Represents considered alternative |
| Adoption Candidate | Represents validated capability awaiting handoff |
| Operational Handoff | Transfers innovation to owning Domain |
| Scale Plan | Defines broader rollout |
| Innovation Benefit | Represents expected/observed value |
| Improvement Opportunity | Represents existing-process improvement need |
| Improvement Initiative | Represents governed improvement effort |
| Lesson Learned | Preserves reusable knowledge |
| Innovation Knowledge Link | Connects related innovation knowledge |
| Technology Signal | Represents emerging technology observation |
| Technology Assessment | Evaluates relevance/maturity |
| Trend Signal | Represents external/internal trend |
| Innovation Recommendation | Represents advisory action |
| AI Innovation Output | Represents AI-generated suggestion |
| Innovation Audit Record | Preserves protected change history |
