# ENTERPRISE BUSINESS CONTINUITY, DISASTER RECOVERY & OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE CANON
## Stage 5 — Resilience Governance, Recovery Authority, RTO/RPO Policy, Backup Control & Crisis Decision Rights Canon

---

# 5.1 Purpose

Stage 5 defines who may set resilience policy, declare continuity mode, activate recovery, choose restore points, authorize failover, accept recovery Risk, and return critical services to normal operation.

The objective is:

> **Ensure resilience decisions are made by the correct authority, within defined business tolerances, with explicit control over recovery targets, backup integrity, data loss, and restoration authority.**

---

# 5.2 Governance Philosophy

Permanent principles:

- Business owners define business tolerance.
- Technical teams implement recovery capability.
- Recovery authority must be explicit.
- RTO/RPO are business commitments, not engineering guesses.
- Faster recovery cannot override data integrity.
- Backup existence does not prove recoverability.
- Emergency does not eliminate Security or audit.
- AI may advise but does not own recovery authority.

---

# 5.3 Resilience Governance Layers

Canonical:

```text id="resilience-governance-stage5"
Business Owner
        ↓
Resilience / Service Authority
        ↓
Technical Recovery Authority
        ↓
Recovery Operators

Material Exception
        ↓
Executive / Governance Authority
```

---

# 5.4 Business Owner Authority

The Business Owner should approve or validate:

- Service criticality
- acceptable disruption
- RTO
- business fallback
- return-to-normal readiness

for their Service.

---

# 5.5 Technical Authority

Technical authority owns:

- backup implementation
- restore procedure
- recovery infrastructure
- failover execution
- technical validation

but does not independently redefine business tolerance.

---

# 5.6 Data Authority

Where recovery affects important data:

Data authority should validate:

- integrity
- reconciliation expectations
- privacy/data-governance controls

---

# 5.7 Security Authority

Security retains authority over:

- cyber containment
- emergency credentials
- compromised systems
- secure recovery

Recovery urgency cannot casually override Security controls.

---

# 5.8 Executive Authority

Executive/Domain 37 governance becomes relevant when disruption creates:

- material financial impact
- major customer impact
- prolonged business interruption
- exceptional Risk
- strategic decision requirement

---

# 5.9 Criticality Approval

Criticality classification should be approved by:

- business/service ownership

with technical input.

Technology alone must not classify every technical dependency as business-critical.

---

# 5.10 RTO Governance

RTO should consider:

- customer impact
- operating cost
- revenue exposure
- dependency chain
- recovery capability
- cost of higher resilience

---

# 5.11 RPO Governance

RPO should consider:

- transaction frequency
- data reconstruction ability
- financial impact
- customer impact
- legal/compliance exposure

---

# 5.12 No Arbitrary RTO/RPO

Permanent:

```text id="no-arbitrary-rto-stage5"
RTO / RPO
must be
Business-Justified
```

Not copied blindly from enterprise best-practice templates.

---

# 5.13 RTO/RPO Approval

A Recovery Objective record should preserve:

- target
- rationale
- business owner
- technical feasibility
- approval/effective date

---

# 5.14 Recovery Objective Exception

If technical architecture cannot meet approved RTO/RPO:

Create:

- Resilience Gap
- Risk
- remediation or accepted exception

Do not quietly change the target.

---

# 5.15 Cost vs Recovery Decision

Permanent:

```text id="cost-recovery-stage5"
Lower RTO / Lower RPO

Usually Means

Higher Cost / Complexity
```

The business decides whether the extra resilience is justified.

---

# 5.16 Backup Governance

Backup policy should define:

- protected data/system
- frequency
- retention
- storage
- encryption
- owner
- test expectation

---

# 5.17 Backup Ownership

Technical team may operate backups.

Business/Data owner determines what data is materially required.

---

# 5.18 Backup Failure Escalation

Backup failure severity depends on:

- Service criticality
- available valid restore points
- RPO exposure
- duration of protection gap

---

# 5.19 Backup Failure Authority

Routine backup retry may be automated.

Prolonged loss of recoverability may require:

- Service owner
- executive escalation

depending on Risk.

---

# 5.20 Backup Deletion Authority

Deletion of protected backups should follow:

- retention policy
- authorization
- immutability/security controls where applicable

---

# 5.21 Restore Authority

Restore authority should be defined based on impact.

Routine test restore:

- technical authority.

Production destructive restore:

- stronger recovery authority.

---

# 5.22 Destructive Restore

Permanent:

```text id="destructive-restore-governance-stage5"
Restore Capability
≠
Authority to Overwrite Production
```

---

# 5.23 Restore Decision Evidence

Before destructive restore, consider:

- failure cause
- current authoritative state
- candidate restore point
- expected data loss
- newer legitimate transactions
- reconciliation plan
- Security state

---

# 5.24 Restore Point Selection Authority

Technical team may recommend.

Material production restore selection should follow defined recovery authority.

---

# 5.25 Corruption Scenario

If latest backup may contain corruption:

Authority may choose an older clean Restore Point.

The expected data gap must be explicit.

---

# 5.26 Data-Loss Acceptance

If recovery necessarily loses data beyond normal tolerance:

The required business authority must explicitly accept or reject that exposure.

---

# 5.27 Data-Loss Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="data-loss-stage5"
Technically Recoverable
≠
Business-Acceptable Data Loss
```

---

# 5.28 Continuity Invocation Authority

Define who may declare:

- continuity mode
- major degraded operation
- formal DR activation

according to severity.

---

# 5.29 Invocation Threshold

Potential factors:

- outage duration
- criticality
- affected customer volume
- data integrity concern
- fallback availability

---

# 5.30 DR Activation Authority

Technical recovery may begin within pre-authorized policy.

High-impact actions still require the applicable authority.

---

# 5.31 Failover Authority

Automated failover may be allowed where:

- pre-approved
- deterministic
- tested

Manual/high-impact failover requires explicit authority.

---

# 5.32 Failback Authority

Return from alternate environment should require:

- synchronization
- validation
- business readiness

---

# 5.33 Authority Switch Governance

Critical rule:

```text id="authority-switch-governance-stage5"
Technical Traffic Switch
≠
Automatic Business Authority Switch
```

The authoritative writer state must be explicit.

---

# 5.34 Return-to-Normal Authority

Business owner or delegated recovery authority should confirm that:

- critical workflows function
- reconciliation is acceptable
- conditions are controlled

before continuity mode is closed.

---

# 5.35 Return With Conditions

If service returns with unresolved non-critical issues:

Conditions require:

- owner
- severity
- deadline
- Risk treatment

---

# 5.36 Critical Exception

A critical unresolved recovery exception may block return to normal.

Examples:

- missing Orders
- incorrect stock
- security compromise
- broken identity permissions

---

# 5.37 Risk Acceptance During Recovery

Risk may be accepted temporarily only by appropriate authority.

Acceptance should record:

- Risk
- duration
- mitigation
- expiry/review
- authority

---

# 5.38 Temporary Risk Acceptance

Permanent:

```text id="temporary-risk-stage5"
Temporary Recovery Exception
≠
Permanent Control Removal
```

---

# 5.39 Crisis Decision Rights

A crisis should have clear decision categories:

- invoke continuity
- prioritize Services
- activate workaround
- restore
- failover
- accept data loss
- accept residual Risk
- communicate externally
- return to normal

---

# 5.40 Crisis Command Structure

Minimum practical structure:

- Recovery Lead
- Technical Recovery Lead
- Business Owner
- Security/Data authority where needed
- Executive escalation authority

---

# 5.41 Recovery Lead Authority

Recovery Lead may coordinate and prioritize within established policy.

They do not automatically gain unlimited:

- financial
- legal
- Security
- corporate

authority.

---

# 5.42 Service Recovery Priority

When multiple Services fail:

Prioritize according to:

- criticality
- dependencies
- customer/business impact
- recovery feasibility

---

# 5.43 Recovery Priority Conflict

If two critical Services compete for limited recovery resources:

Escalate according to business impact and executive authority where necessary.

---

# 5.44 Customer Communication Authority

Routine outage updates may be pre-approved.

Material external communications may require:

- Business
- Legal
- executive

review depending on impact.

---

# 5.45 Supplier Continuity Authority

Activation of:

- alternate supplier
- outsourced production
- emergency carrier

may require Procurement/Finance authority according to cost and contract impact.

---

# 5.46 Facility Continuity Authority

Moving business activity to alternate facility may require:

- operational
- Security
- Finance
- executive

approval according to materiality.

---

# 5.47 Equipment Continuity Authority

Use of alternate equipment or outsourced production should preserve:

- Product/Quality requirements
- cost authority
- customer commitments

---

# 5.48 Manual Workaround Authority

Workarounds should be:

- pre-approved where possible

or:

- explicitly authorized during disruption.

---

# 5.49 Workaround Change Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="workaround-change-stage5"
Emergency Workaround
≠
Authority to Permanently Redesign Workflow
```

---

# 5.50 Offline Record Governance

Continuity records must have:

- responsible user
- temporary ID
- timestamp
- reconciliation owner

---

# 5.51 Reconciliation Authority

Reconciliation execution may be operational.

Material unresolved discrepancies may require:

- business owner
- Finance
- Data
- other Domain authority

depending on record type.

---

# 5.52 Financial Reconciliation

Domain 6 controls financial truth.

Recovery teams cannot invent accounting adjustments purely to make reconciliation totals match.

---

# 5.53 Inventory Reconciliation

Domain 2 controls stock semantics.

Recovery reconciliation must use legitimate movement/adjustment authority.

---

# 5.54 Order Reconciliation

Domain 1 controls Order state.

Offline Orders become authoritative only through valid reconciliation.

---

# 5.55 Shipping Reconciliation

Domain 5 controls Shipment/Fulfillment truth.

Carrier evidence should reconcile to proper shipment records.

---

# 5.56 Recovery Test Governance

Tests should have:

- scope
- owner
- approved procedure
- success criteria
- evidence

---

# 5.57 Test Authority

Routine backup restore tests may be technical.

Tests that disrupt production require stronger operational authority.

---

# 5.58 Failed Test Governance

Failed recovery test should produce:

- remediation
- owner
- Risk
- retest requirement

---

# 5.59 Test Exception Acceptance

A failed critical recovery capability should not be marked acceptable without explicit Risk treatment.

---

# 5.60 Resilience Policy Change

Changes to:

- criticality
- RTO/RPO
- backup policy
- recovery authority

should be versioned and approved appropriately.

---

# 5.61 Domain 14 Authority Boundary

Domain 14 can detect/respond operationally.

Domain 38 determines continuity/recovery policy.

---

# 5.62 Domain 28 Authority Boundary

Security may block restoration of a compromised environment until containment requirements are satisfied.

---

# 5.63 Domain 29 Authority Boundary

Data governance may restrict:

- Restore Point
- retention
- privacy treatment
- recovered-data usage

---

# 5.64 Domain 36 Boundary

Resilience remediation requiring implementation becomes a Project under Domain 36.

---

# 5.65 Domain 37 Boundary

Material continuity decisions may escalate to Domain 37.

Domain 38 does not invent new corporate authority.

---

# 5.66 AI Recovery Authority Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="ai-recovery-authority-stage5"
AI Recommendation
≠
Restore Approval
≠
Failover Approval
≠
Data-Loss Acceptance
≠
Return-to-Normal Approval
```

---

# 5.67 AI Assistance

AI may help:

- explain recovery options
- compare Restore Points
- identify dependency impact
- summarize Risk

but actual authority remains human/rule-based.

---

# 5.68 Automated Recovery Authority

Automation may perform pre-authorized actions such as:

- backup
- health check
- service restart
- tested failover

within defined policy.

---

# 5.69 Automation Guardrails

Automated actions should define:

- trigger
- allowed environment
- maximum impact
- rollback behavior
- audit

---

# 5.70 No Blind Destructive Automation

Production-destructive recovery should not occur through unrestricted automation.

---

# 5.71 SMP1 Governance Relevance

SMP1 requires explicit recovery authority for:

- migration rollback
- restore
- Cutover failure
- authority switch
- standalone recovery testing

---

# 5.72 SMP1 Cutover vs Recovery Authority

Domain 36 governs planned Cutover.

Domain 38 governs operational recovery architecture.

Some authorities may overlap but the contexts remain distinct.

---

# 5.73 SMP1 Rollback Authority

Rollback criteria should define:

- who can trigger
- what target state
- allowable data gap
- reconciliation requirement

---

# 5.74 SMP1 Restore Authority

Standalone recovery must identify who may authorize:

- production Restore Point
- destructive rollback
- service authority restoration

---

# 5.75 SMP1 Apps Script Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="apps-script-fallback-stage5"
Apps Script Reference Baseline
≠
Approved Failover Target
```

unless deliberately engineered, tested, and formally governed.

---

# 5.76 SMP1 Business Architecture Protection

Recovery procedures must restore the same certified business semantics.

They cannot use emergency recovery as a route to introduce workflow redesign.

---

# 5.77 SMP1 Certification Requirement

Before standalone v1.0 certification, confirm:

- recovery authority documented
- backup responsibility defined
- restore authority defined
- Return-to-Normal authority defined
- rollback authority defined
- recovery test evidence exists

---

# 5.78 ERP9 / ERP10 Governance

ERP9/ERP10 should inherit the same recovery authority model.

Do not invent separate DR governance per release.

---

# 5.79 Version 1.1 Governance

Version 1.1 extends the same resilience authority architecture.

---

# 5.80 Small-Team Practicality

GiftHatke may combine several recovery roles.

For material recovery decisions, compensate with:

- explicit record
- clear authority
- second review where practical
- audit

---

# 5.81 Anti-Bureaucracy Principle

Routine safe recovery should not require executive approval for every step.

Authority should scale with:

- impact
- Risk
- irreversibility
- data loss
- financial/customer exposure

---

# 5.82 Resilience Governance Anti-Patterns

The Canon rejects:

- engineers setting business RTO alone
- arbitrary zero-data-loss promises
- uncontrolled production restores
- automatic failover without validation
- emergency authority becoming permanent
- closing continuity mode before reconciliation
- ignoring failed restore tests
- treating Apps Script as an automatic DR site
- executive approval for every backup operation
- recovery procedures changing business semantics

---

# 5.83 Critical Governance Invariants

1. Business owner defines business recovery tolerance.
2. Technical capability does not alone determine RTO/RPO.
3. Restore capability ≠ restore authority.
4. Technical recovery ≠ business acceptance.
5. Data-loss exposure requires explicit business treatment.
6. Emergency authority remains bounded.
7. Domain-specific authority remains preserved.
8. Return-to-normal requires appropriate validation.
9. AI has no independent recovery authority.
10. SMP1 recovery authority cannot bypass TITAN LOCK architecture protections.

---

# 5.84 Stage 5 Certification

Stage 5 permanently establishes the minimum implementation-grade governance architecture for:

- Service criticality approval
- RTO/RPO governance
- resilience gaps
- backup policy authority
- backup failure escalation
- restore authority
- Restore Point selection
- data-loss acceptance
- continuity invocation
- DR activation
- failover/failback authority
- Authority Switch governance
- Return-to-Normal authority
- recovery Risk acceptance
- crisis Decision Rights
- recovery prioritization
- communication/supplier/facility/equipment authority
- manual Workarounds
- reconciliation authority
- recovery testing
- cross-domain authority preservation
- AI/automation boundaries
- SMP1 rollback/restore/recovery authority
- ERP9/ERP10/Version 1.1 reuse
- anti-overengineering controls

This is sufficient to govern real recovery decisions for standalone v1.0 without creating an unnecessary enterprise crisis-management bureaucracy.

# ENTERPRISE BUSINESS CONTINUITY, DISASTER RECOVERY & OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE CANON
## Stage 6 — Resilience Events, Continuity Workflow, Automated Recovery, Escalation & Cross-Domain Recovery Orchestration Canon

---

# 6.1 Purpose

Stage 6 defines how disruption Events, continuity invocation, recovery actions, automated responses, escalations, validation, reconciliation, and Return-to-Normal are coordinated across GiftHatkeOS.

The objective is:

> **Ensure disruption and recovery actions propagate reliably across technical and business Domains without duplicate recovery actions, false recovery states, lost transactions, or accidental authority changes.**

---

# 6.2 Resilience Event Principle

A resilience Event records something that occurred.

Examples:

- ServiceDegraded
- ServiceUnavailable
- BackupFailed
- ContinuityInvoked
- RecoveryStarted
- RestoreCompleted
- RecoveryValidationPassed
- ReconciliationCompleted
- AuthoritySwitched
- ContinuityClosed

Permanent:

```text id="event-command-stage6-d38"
Event
≠
Command
≠
Recovery Approval
```

---

# 6.3 Canonical Event Envelope

Minimum:

- Event ID
- Event Type
- affected Service/System
- actor/source
- occurrence time
- recording time
- correlation ID
- causation ID
- severity
- schema version
- security context

---

# 6.4 Event Integrity

Resilience Events should be:

- immutable
- traceable
- ordered where required
- replay-safe
- auditable

---

# 6.5 Idempotency

Repeated processing must not duplicate:

- recovery invocation
- restore execution
- temporary transaction import
- authority switch
- reconciliation completion

---

# 6.6 Replay Safety

Permanent:

```text id="replay-stage6-d38"
Replay AuthoritySwitched
≠
Switch Authority Again
```

---

# 6.7 Disruption Workflow

Canonical:

```text id="disruption-flow-stage6"
Disruption Detected

↓

Service Impact Evaluated

↓

Within Normal Incident Tolerance?

YES
→ Domain 14 Incident Handling

NO
→ Continuity Assessment
```

---

# 6.8 Continuity Invocation Workflow

```text id="continuity-invocation-stage6"
Service Impact Exceeds Tolerance

↓

Authority Validated

↓

Continuity Plan Selected

↓

Continuity Mode Declared

↓

Business / Technical Actions Triggered
```

---

# 6.9 DR Activation Workflow

Canonical:

```text id="dr-activation-stage6"
Recovery Required

↓

DR Plan Identified

↓

Authority / Preconditions Checked

↓

Recovery Environment Prepared

↓

Restore / Failover Executed
```

---

# 6.10 Continuity Invocation Event

Potential:

```text id="continuity-event-stage6"
ContinuityInvoked
```

This Event should trigger only after the invocation Decision actually exists.

---

# 6.11 Service Degradation Workflow

A degraded Service may trigger:

- user notification
- workload reduction
- manual fallback readiness
- dependency impact evaluation

---

# 6.12 Service Failure Workflow

Critical failure may trigger:

- Incident escalation
- continuity assessment
- recovery plan lookup
- leadership notification

---

# 6.13 Dependency Propagation

If a dependency fails:

```text id="dependency-propagation-stage6"
Dependency Failed

↓

Affected Services Identified

↓

Criticality Evaluated

↓

Recovery / Workaround Routes Activated
```

---

# 6.14 Cross-Service Impact

One failed component may affect multiple Services.

The system should avoid creating unrelated duplicate recovery cases when one underlying cause exists.

---

# 6.15 Recovery Correlation

Use common:

- Incident ID
- Recovery ID
- correlation ID

to associate related recovery activity.

---

# 6.16 Backup Failure Workflow

Canonical:

```text id="backup-failure-stage6"
Backup Failed

↓

Retry Allowed?

YES
→ Retry

↓

Recovery Protection Window Threatened?

YES
→ Escalate Resilience Risk
```

---

# 6.17 Backup Success Event

Potential:

```text id="backup-success-stage6"
BackupCompleted
```

Backup success does not automatically mean:

- RestorePointValidated.

---

# 6.18 Restore Point Validation Workflow

```text id="restorepoint-stage6"
Backup Available

↓

Integrity Check

↓

Recoverability / Test Evidence

↓

Restore Point Validated
```

---

Potential:

```text id="recovery-selection-stage6"
Recovery Needed

↓

Candidate Restore Points

↓

↓

Restore Point Selected

↓

Authority Confirmed
```

---

High-impact restore should follow:

```text id="destructive-restore-stage6"
Restore Requested

↓

Current State Snapshot Where Possible

↓

Impact / Data-Loss Assessment

↓

Required Authority

↓

Execute Restore

↓

Validate
```

---

# 6.21 Restore Execution Event

Potential:

- RestoreStarted
- RestoreCompleted
- RestoreFailed

---

# 6.22 Restore Failure

Restore failure should:

- preserve current recovery state
- create Recovery Exception
- prevent false readiness
- allow alternate Restore Point/procedure

---

Where supported:

```text id="failover-stage6"
Primary Unavailable

↓

Failover Eligibility

↓

Secondary Activated

↓

Technical Validation

↓

Business Validation

↓

Authority State Confirmed
```

---

# 6.24 Failover Event

Potential:

```text id="failover-event-stage6"
FailoverCompleted
```

This does not alone mean:

- BusinessRecovered.

# 6.25 Failback Workflow

Canonical:

```text id="failback-stage6"
↓

State Synchronization

↓

Validation

↓

Failback Authority

↓

Traffic / Writer Switch

↓

Reconciliation

↓

Close Alternate Mode
```

```text id="manual-workaround-stage6"
Transactions Reconciled

↓

Workaround Closed
```

# 6.27 Temporary Transaction Event

```text id="temporary-record-stage6"
ContinuityTransactionRecorded
```

It should contain enough information for later reconciliation.

---

Canonical:

```text id="reconciliation-stage6"
Temporary Records

↓

Duplicate Check
```

# 6.29 Duplicate Protection

Reconciliation must use:

- stable temporary IDs
- business keys
- idempotency keys

where appropriate.

# 6.30 Reconciliation Exception

- duplicate Order
- missing Customer
- invalid stock movement
- conflicting Shipment
- mismatched payment state

---

# 6.31 Financial Reconciliation Workflow

Financial discrepancies route to Domain 6.

Recovery automation cannot independently create accounting fixes merely to balance totals.

---

# 6.32 Inventory Reconciliation Workflow

Offline Inventory movements must flow into valid Domain 2 movement logic.

---

# 6.33 Production Reconciliation Workflow

Offline Production states must preserve:

- actual work completed
- traceability
- personalization correctness

---

# 6.34 Shipping Reconciliation Workflow

Carrier actions performed during downtime should reconcile into Domain 5 records.

---

# 6.35 Recovery Validation Workflow

Canonical:

```text id="validation-workflow-stage6"
Technical Validation

↓

Data Validation

↓

Security Validation

↓

Business Validation

↓

PASS / PASS WITH CONDITIONS / FAIL
```

---

# 6.36 Validation Failure

If any mandatory validation fails:

- return-to-normal cannot be falsely recorded.

---

# 6.37 Conditional Validation

PASS WITH CONDITIONS should create:

- Recovery Exception
- owner
- Risk
- due point

---

# 6.38 Authority Switch Workflow

Canonical:

```text id="authority-switch-stage6"
Current Writer Identified

↓

Target Writer Validated

↓

Pending Transactions Reconciled

↓

Authority Switch Approved

↓

Writer State Changed

↓

Audit Event Recorded
```

---

# 6.39 Writer State

Potential states:

```text id="writer-state-stage6"
PRIMARY
SECONDARY
READ ONLY
DISABLED
```

---

# 6.40 Dual-Writer Protection

The orchestration layer should detect:

- multiple systems claiming PRIMARY authority

and raise a critical exception.

---

# 6.41 Return-to-Normal Workflow

```text id="return-normal-stage6"

↓

Reconciliation Acceptable

↓

↓

ReturnToNormal

↓

Continuity Closed
```

---

# 6.42 Return-to-Normal Event

Potential:

```text id="return-event-stage6"
NormalOperationsRestored
```

Only emit after actual business recovery approval.

---

# 6.43 Post-Recovery Workflow

After closure:

```text id="post-recovery-stage6"
Recovery Closed

↓

Post-Incident Review

↓

Lessons

↓

Resilience Actions

↓

Retest / Improvement
```

---

# 6.44 RTO Breach Event

Potential:

```text id="rto-breach-stage6"
RecoveryObjectiveMissed
```

---

# 6.45 RPO Breach Event

If recovered data exceeds acceptable loss tolerance:

- escalate according to business impact.

---

# 6.46 Recovery Objective Breach

Breach may result in:

- Risk acceptance
- remediation Project
- architecture improvement
- business tolerance reassessment

---

# 6.47 Crisis Escalation Workflow

Canonical:

```text id="crisis-escalation-stage6"
Recovery Impact Increases

↓

Current Authority Insufficient

↓

Executive / Domain 37 Escalation

↓

Decision

↓

Recovery Continues
```

---

# 6.48 Escalation Reasons

Examples:

- prolonged outage
- data loss beyond RPO
- major customer impact
- financial exposure
- regulatory/security impact
- unavailable recovery path

---

# 6.49 Security Incident Recovery

For cyber disruption:

```text id="security-recovery-stage6"
Security Incident

↓

Containment / Isolation

↓

Clean Recovery Decision

↓

Restore

↓

Credential / Security Validation

↓

Business Validation
```

---

# 6.50 No Unsafe Auto-Restore

If compromise may persist in backups:

Do not blindly restore the newest backup.

---

# 6.51 Supplier Failure Workflow

```text id="supplier-failure-stage6"
Supplier Failed

↓

Affected Services Identified

↓

Alternate Route Available?

YES
→ Activate Controlled Fallback

NO
→ Degraded / Suspended Service + Escalation
```

---

# 6.52 Facility Failure Workflow

Potential orchestration:

- assess access
- identify alternate workspace/production
- activate remote capability
- reroute production
- communicate

---

# 6.53 Equipment Failure Workflow

Potential:

```text id="equipment-failure-stage6"
Critical Machine Failed

↓

Repair Estimate

↓

Alternate Capacity?

YES
→ Reallocate / Outsource

NO
→ Reprioritize Orders / Escalate
```

---

# 6.54 Event Ordering

Where ordering matters:

Example:

```text id="event-order-stage6"
RestoreCompleted
must precede
RecoveryValidationPassed
```

unless a different valid recovery path exists.

---

# 6.55 Eventual Consistency

Cross-Domain recovery may not be transactionally atomic.

Use:

- Events
- idempotency
- reconciliation
- status tracking

rather than pretending all systems commit simultaneously.

---

# 6.56 Workflow Failure

Permanent:

```text id="workflow-failure-stage6-d38"
Recovery Workflow Failure
≠
Recovery Success
```

---

# 6.57 Dead-Letter / Exception Handling

Unprocessable recovery Events should enter:

- controlled exception queue
- owner
- recovery context
- retry/reconciliation path

---

# 6.58 Retry Safety

Retries must not:

- repeat destructive restore
- duplicate offline transaction imports
- repeat authority switch

without explicit protection.

---

# 6.59 Concurrency Protection

Protect:

- Restore Point selection
- continuity state
- authority state
- reconciliation completion
- Return-to-Normal Decision

from conflicting simultaneous actions.

---

# 6.60 Notification Orchestration

Domain 9 may deliver:

- outage alert
- continuity invocation
- recovery status
- customer communication
- resolution notification

---

# 6.61 Notification Severity

Use proportional levels such as:

- informational
- operational
- critical

Avoid broadcasting every recovery step to everyone.

---

# 6.62 Monitoring Orchestration

Domain 14 may trigger resilience workflows from:

- health checks
- availability alerts
- database failures
- infrastructure incidents

---

# 6.63 Workflow Orchestration

Domain 11 may execute:

- recovery checklists
- approval routing
- reconciliation workflows
- post-incident Actions

Domain 38 defines resilience meaning.

---

# 6.64 Data Orchestration

Domain 29 may validate:

- recovered-data integrity
- retention/privacy
- critical dataset handling

---

# 6.65 Project Orchestration

If repeated recovery weaknesses require engineering change:

```text id="resilience-project-stage6"
Resilience Gap

↓

Remediation Required

↓

Domain 36 Project / Change
```

---

# 6.66 Governance Orchestration

Domain 37 handles only material decisions exceeding recovery authority.

Routine recovery remains within Domain 38/technical operations.

---

# 6.67 SMP1 Event Model

Critical SMP1 resilience Events may include:

- StandaloneBackupCompleted
- StandaloneRestoreTestStarted
- StandaloneRestoreTestPassed
- MigrationRollbackInvoked
- StandaloneRecoveryStarted
- StandaloneRecoveryValidated
- StandaloneAuthorityRestored

```text id="smp1-cutover-failure-stage6"
Assess Severity

NO
```

# 6.69 SMP1 Rollback Event

Potential:

```text id="smp1-rollback-stage6"
MigrationRollbackAuthorized
```

# 6.70 SMP1 Rollback Safety

Capture and reconcile legitimate changes.

```text id="smp1-restore-test-stage6"
Backup Created

Permissions Validated

Critical Workflows Tested

↓

Result Recorded
```

# 6.72 SMP1 Recovery Certification Evidence

Before standalone v1.0 certification, Event/evidence chain should demonstrate:

```text id="smp1-recovery-evidence-stage6"
Backup
→ Restore
→ Validation
→ Reconciliation
→ Recovery Acceptance
```

---

# 6.73 SMP1 Apps Script Boundary

The Apps Script baseline may receive:

- no automatic production authority

during standalone recovery unless separately engineered and certified.

---

# 6.74 SMP1 Architecture Protection

Recovery orchestration must restore:

- certified business behavior.

Emergency mode cannot become hidden redesign.

---

# 6.75 ERP9 / ERP10 Reuse

ERP9/ERP10 should reuse:

- backup/recovery Events
- validation
- reconciliation
- escalation

rather than new recovery workflows.

---

# 6.76 Version 1.1 Reuse

Same architecture extends to future releases.

---

# 6.77 AI Event Assistance

AI may:

- summarize event timeline
- identify likely failed dependency
- suggest recovery procedure
- flag unresolved reconciliation

---

# 6.78 AI Recovery Orchestration Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="ai-boundary-stage6-d38"
AI Suggestion
≠
Restore Command
≠
Authority Switch
≠
Recovery Acceptance
```

---

# 6.79 Automated Recovery

Automation may execute pre-authorized deterministic responses such as:

- restart
- retry backup
- health-check
- failover

when policy allows.

---

# 6.80 Automation Kill Switch

High-impact automated recovery should support:

- disable/suspend control
- manual intervention

where technically appropriate.

---

# 6.81 Automation Audit

Automated recovery actions must record:

- service identity
- trigger
- action
- result
- timestamp

---

# 6.82 Human Override

Authorized operators may override automation when:

- automation is unsafe
- recovery context changed
- incorrect dependency assumptions exist

with audit.

---

# 6.83 Recovery State Projection

A lightweight operational view should derive:

```text id="recovery-projection-stage6"
Affected Service
Current Mode
Recovery Phase
Latest Successful Step
Critical Blocker
Next Action
Authority State
```

---

# 6.84 Reconciliation State Projection

Should show:

- temporary records
- matched
- imported
- exceptions
- unresolved critical items

---

# 6.85 No False Green

A recovered Service must not show normal/healthy merely because:

- infrastructure responded.

Business validation matters.

---

# 6.86 Standalone Minimum Implementation

For standalone v1.0, event/workflow capability only needs:

- outage → continuity routing
- backup failure routing
- restore workflow
- validation
- reconciliation
- authority switch
- Return-to-Normal
- recovery audit

No sophisticated enterprise orchestration bus is required specifically for Domain 38.

---

# 6.87 Advanced Capabilities That Can Wait

Later, if justified:

- automated regional disaster orchestration
- advanced chaos engineering
- multi-site crisis workflows
- predictive recovery optimization
- fully autonomous remediation

---

# 6.88 Anti-Overengineering Rule

Permanent:

> **Resilience orchestration must make SMP1 and standalone recovery reliable and understandable; it must not create another platform programme before standalone v1.0 is delivered.**

---

# 6.89 Critical Event & Workflow Invariants

1. Event ≠ Command.
2. Backup success ≠ Restore Point validation.
3. Restore completion ≠ recovery acceptance.
4. Retry must not duplicate destructive actions.
5. Manual transactions require idempotent reconciliation.
6. Authority switching must be explicit and auditable.
7. Workflow failure must never fabricate recovery success.
8. Domain authority remains preserved during crisis.
9. AI/automation cannot independently accept recovery or material data loss.
10. SMP1 recovery orchestration must preserve the certified business architecture and prevent uncontrolled dual authority.

---

# 6.90 Stage 6 Certification

Stage 6 permanently establishes the minimum implementation-grade orchestration architecture for:

- resilience Events
- Event integrity/idempotency
- disruption routing
- continuity invocation
- DR activation
- dependency propagation
- backup failure handling
- Restore Point selection
- destructive restore
- failover/failback
- manual Workarounds
- reconciliation
- recovery validation
- Authority Switching
- Return-to-Normal
- RTO/RPO breach escalation
- crisis escalation
- Security/supplier/facility/equipment recovery
- workflow failures/retries/concurrency
- notifications/monitoring
- cross-Domain recovery orchestration
- SMP1 Cutover failure/rollback
- standalone restore testing
- AI/automation boundaries
- anti-overengineering controls

This is sufficient to orchestrate real continuity and recovery safely for standalone v1.0 without introducing unnecessary enterprise-scale recovery complexity.

**Stage 6 Status: ✅ CERTIFIED**

**Enterprise Canon Position: Domain 38 — IN PROGRESS (6/10 stages certified).**

**Total Fully Certified Domains: 37**

# ENTERPRISE BUSINESS CONTINUITY, DISASTER RECOVERY & OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE CANON
## Stage 7 — Resilience Command Center, Recovery Workspace, Continuity Dashboard & Crisis Operations UX Canon

---

# 7.1 Purpose

Stage 7 defines the minimum human experience required to manage disruption, continuity mode, backup/restore status, recovery execution, reconciliation, critical dependencies, and Return-to-Normal decisions.

The objective is:

> **Give operators and business owners a clear, calm, evidence-based view of what is broken, what remains operational, what recovery step is active, what is blocked, and who has authority to act—without building a complex crisis-management platform.**

---

# 7.2 UX Philosophy

Permanent principles:

- Critical Service impact before infrastructure noise.
- Current recovery state before historical logs.
- Actions before dashboards.
- business validation before technical Green.
- exceptions before routine detail.
- authority before destructive controls.
- clear sequencing before excessive telemetry.
- reconciliation before declaring full recovery.

---

# 7.3 Core UX Areas

Minimum:

- Resilience Home
- Active Incident / Continuity Workspace
- Critical Service View
- Recovery Workspace
- Backup Health View
- Restore Point View
- Dependency View
- Manual Workaround View
- Reconciliation View
- Recovery Validation View
- Resilience Test View
- Recovery Action View
- Audit Timeline

---

# 7.4 Resilience Home

Should answer immediately:

- Are any critical Services disrupted?
- Is continuity mode active?
- Are backups healthy?
- Is a recovery currently running?
- Are there unresolved critical recovery Risks?
- Is business reconciliation outstanding?

---

# 7.5 Resilience Home Example

```text id="resilience-home-stage7"
CRITICAL SERVICES

Healthy:
6

Degraded:
1

Unavailable:
0

CONTINUITY MODE:
ACTIVE

ACTIVE RECOVERY:
Order Management

BACKUP HEALTH:
NORMAL

CRITICAL RECOVERY EXCEPTIONS:
0
```

---

# 7.6 Critical Service Card

Minimum:

```text id="critical-service-card-stage7"
ORDER MANAGEMENT

Status:
DEGRADED

Criticality:
CRITICAL

RTO:
Defined Business Target

Current Outage:
34 Minutes

Fallback:
ACTIVE

Owner:
Assigned
```

---

# 7.7 Criticality Visibility

Criticality should be visible without becoming decorative.

Suggested labels:

- CRITICAL
- HIGH
- STANDARD
- LOW

---

# 7.8 Service vs System UX

The user should be able to distinguish:

```text id="service-system-stage7"
Business Service:
Order Management

Affected Technology:
Standalone ERP Database
```

This prevents infrastructure failure from being confused with complete business failure.

---

# 7.9 Active Continuity Workspace

For an active continuity invocation show:

- affected Services
- start time
- current phase
- Recovery Lead
- current workaround
- top blocker
- latest Decision
- next action

---

# 7.10 Continuity State

Show clearly:

```text id="continuity-state-stage7"
NORMAL
DEGRADED
CONTINUITY MODE
RECOVERING
VALIDATING
```

---

# 7.11 Current Recovery Phase

The UI should clearly identify whether recovery is in:

- Assessment
- Restore
- Technical Validation
- Business Validation
- Reconciliation
- Return-to-Normal Review

---

# 7.12 Recovery Step Indicator

Example:

```text id="recovery-step-stage7"
RECOVERY

✓ Recovery Environment Ready
✓ Database Restored
✓ Application Started
→ Business Validation
○ Reconciliation
○ Return to Normal
```

---

# 7.13 Recovery Lead View

Recovery Lead should see:

- current status
- active owners
- blockers
- decisions required
- elapsed time
- critical exceptions

Not every low-level log line.

---

# 7.14 Technical Recovery View

Technical users may additionally see:

- failed components
- Restore Point
- recovery environment
- technical checks
- service logs/links

---

# 7.15 Business Owner View

Business Owner should focus on:

- service availability
- fallback capability
- customer impact
- business validation
- reconciliation
- Return-to-Normal decision

---

# 7.16 Executive View

Executive users should see only material information:

- critical Services affected
- duration
- major business impact
- recovery confidence
- critical Risk
- Decision required

---

# 7.17 No Crisis Dashboard Theatre

The Canon rejects dashboards optimized for:

- hundreds of graphs
- CPU metrics
- raw log volume

when the real question is:

> Can the business safely operate?

---

# 7.18 Backup Health View

Should show:

- protected system
- last successful backup
- current backup state
- retention status
- latest validated Restore Point

---

# 7.19 Backup Health Example

```text id="backup-health-stage7"
DATABASE BACKUP

Last Successful:
08:00

Latest Valid Restore Point:
08:00

Current Backup:
SUCCESS

Restore Test:
PASS
```

---

# 7.20 Backup Failure UX

A failed critical backup should show:

- failure time
- reason
- protection gap
- current valid Restore Point
- Risk

---

# 7.21 Backup Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="backup-boundary-stage7"
Backup Successful
≠
Restore Proven
```

The UX should display both separately.

---

# 7.22 Restore Point View

Show candidate Restore Points with:

- timestamp
- integrity state
- validation/test status
- expected data gap
- corruption concern

---

# 7.23 Restore Point Comparison

Example:

```text id="restore-point-comparison-stage7"
08:00
VALIDATED
Expected Data Gap: 15 min

08:15
UNTESTED
Possible Corruption Risk

Recommended:
08:00
```

Recommendation does not equal approval.

---

# 7.24 Destructive Restore Warning

Before production overwrite:

Show clearly:

- target system
- selected Restore Point
- expected data loss
- newer data at Risk
- required authority

---

# 7.25 Destructive Action UX

Controls such as:

- Restore Production
- Switch Primary Writer
- Failback

must not resemble routine buttons.

They require proper authority validation.

---

# 7.26 Dependency View

Should show critical Service dependencies and current health.

Example:

```text id="dependency-view-stage7"
ORDER MANAGEMENT

Identity        HEALTHY
Database        FAILED
Inventory       HEALTHY
Customer Data   HEALTHY
```

---

# 7.27 Dependency Impact

Selecting a failed dependency should show:

- affected Services
- Workarounds
- recovery sequence
- downstream impact

---

# 7.28 Single Point of Failure

If relevant:

```text id="spof-stage7"
SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE

Dependency:
Primary Database

Mitigation:
Backup + Restore

No Live Secondary Configured
```

This is useful truth—not automatically a failure.

---

# 7.29 Manual Workaround View

When continuity workaround is active, show:

- affected Service
- start time
- approved procedure
- temporary records captured
- reconciliation pending
- owner

---

# 7.30 Offline Transaction UX

Example:

```text id="offline-transaction-stage7"
TEMPORARY ORDER

Reference:
OFFLINE-ORDER-00017

Customer:
Recorded

Production Status:
Not Started

Reconciliation:
PENDING
```

---

# 7.31 Workaround Warning

Permanent:

> **Temporary records are not yet authoritative ERP records until reconciled.**

---

# 7.32 Workaround Exit

The UI should show when it is safe to stop fallback operation.

Stopping too early can lose transactions.

---

# 7.33 Reconciliation Workspace

Should answer:

- How many temporary records exist?
- How many matched?
- How many imported?
- Which conflicts remain?
- Are any critical records unresolved?

---

# 7.34 Reconciliation Example

```text id="reconciliation-view-stage7"
OFFLINE ORDERS

Captured:
24

Matched / Imported:
22

Exceptions:
2

Critical:
0

Status:
IN PROGRESS
```

---

# 7.35 Duplicate Warning

If temporary record matches existing ERP transaction:

Flag:

```text id="duplicate-warning-stage7"
POTENTIAL DUPLICATE

Do Not Import Automatically
```

---

# 7.36 Reconciliation Exception View

Show:

- temporary record
- authoritative record
- conflict
- recommended treatment
- required Domain authority

---

# 7.37 Financial Reconciliation UX

Financial discrepancies should visibly route to:

- Domain 6

rather than offer arbitrary recovery adjustment.

---

# 7.38 Inventory Reconciliation UX

Stock conflicts should surface:

- expected movement
- authoritative stock state
- required valid adjustment/movement path

---

# 7.39 Production Reconciliation UX

Show:

- work actually completed
- ERP-recorded state
- personalization/order reference
- discrepancy

---

# 7.40 Shipping Reconciliation UX

Show:

- carrier action
- tracking number
- authoritative Shipment state
- reconciliation result

---

# 7.41 Recovery Validation Workspace

Should provide separate sections:

- Technical
- Data
- Security
- Business

---

# 7.42 Validation Example

```text id="validation-view-stage7"
RECOVERY VALIDATION

Technical:
PASS

Data:
PASS

Security:
PASS

Business:
PENDING

Overall:
NOT YET RECOVERED
```

---

# 7.43 No False Green

Permanent:

```text id="false-green-stage7"
Infrastructure Green
+
Business Validation Pending

=
NOT FULLY RECOVERED
```

---

# 7.44 Business Validation View

For each critical workflow show:

- test/check
- result
- evidence
- tester/owner

---

# 7.45 Critical Workflow Example

```text id="business-validation-stage7"
ORDER WORKFLOW

Create Order:
PASS

Load Order:
PASS

Inventory Reservation:
PASS

Production Handoff:
PASS

Shipment Creation:
PASS
```

---

# 7.46 Recovery Exception View

Recovery Exceptions should show:

- severity
- affected Service
- business impact
- owner
- treatment
- whether Return-to-Normal is blocked

---

# 7.47 Critical Exception

Critical exception should be unmistakable.

Example:

```text id="critical-exception-stage7"
CRITICAL RECOVERY EXCEPTION

3 Orders Missing

Return to Normal:
BLOCKED
```

---

# 7.48 Return-to-Normal Workspace

Should summarize:

- service recovery
- validation
- reconciliation
- exceptions
- required authority

---

# 7.49 Return-to-Normal Example

```text id="return-normal-view-stage7"
RETURN TO NORMAL REVIEW

Service:
Order Management

Technical:
PASS

Business:
PASS

Reconciliation:
COMPLETE

Critical Exceptions:
0

Decision:
READY
```

---

# 7.50 Conditional Return UX

If returning with conditions:

Clearly show:

- outstanding condition
- owner
- Risk
- due point

---

# 7.51 Recovery Timeline

A concise timeline may show:

```text id="recovery-timeline-stage7"
09:02 Service Failed
09:08 Continuity Invoked
09:15 Workaround Started
09:34 Restore Started
10:11 Restore Completed
10:24 Validation Started
```

---

# 7.52 Audit vs Operational Timeline

Operational timeline surfaces major recovery events.

Full audit history remains separately available.

---

# 7.53 RTO UX

Show:

- target RTO
- elapsed time
- target status

where a legitimate target exists.

---

# 7.54 RTO Example

```text id="rto-example-stage7"
RTO Target:
2 Hours

Elapsed:
1h 22m

Status:
WITHIN TARGET
```

---

# 7.55 RPO UX

For recovery show:

- target RPO
- selected Restore Point
- expected/actual data exposure

---

# 7.56 Unknown Target

If no target exists:

Show:

- NOT DEFINED

rather than arbitrary zero.

---

# 7.57 Resilience Test Workspace

Should show:

- test type
- scope
- target
- actual recovery time
- result
- exceptions
- Actions

---

# 7.58 Failed Test UX

Example:

```text id="failed-test-stage7"
RESTORE TEST

Result:
FAIL

Reason:
Application configuration incomplete

Action:
Create complete recovery configuration package

Retest:
REQUIRED
```

---

# 7.59 Failed Tests Are Valuable

Do not visually bury failed DR tests.

They identify real resilience gaps before a disaster.

---

# 7.60 Resilience Action View

Show:

- source
- remediation
- owner
- priority
- due status
- retest dependency

---

# 7.61 Supplier Continuity View

For critical suppliers show:

- supplier
- supported Service
- current availability
- alternate route
- fallback status

---

# 7.62 Equipment Continuity View

For material production equipment show:

- equipment
- outage
- repair estimate
- alternate capacity
- affected Orders where appropriate

---

# 7.63 Facility Continuity View

Show:

- affected facility
- Services impacted
- alternative operating location/capability
- estimated restoration

Only if business need warrants it.

---

# 7.64 Notifications

Use Domain 9 for material events such as:

- continuity invoked
- critical Service down
- recovery phase change
- business validation needed
- critical reconciliation exception
- return to normal

---

# 7.65 Notification Fatigue

Do not send leadership a notification for every:

- backup execution
- technical retry
- validation sub-step

unless critical.

---

# 7.66 Search

Users should be able to find:

- continuity plan
- DR procedure
- latest Restore Point
- last restore test
- dependency
- active recovery
- Resilience Action

---

# 7.67 Permission UX

Protected actions should show actual authority state.

Example:

```text id="permission-stage7"
RESTORE PRODUCTION

Required Authority:
Recovery Administrator + Business Approval

Your Authority:
INSUFFICIENT
```

---

# 7.68 Confidentiality

Sensitive recovery information may include:

- infrastructure details
- credentials/security procedures
- cyber incident data

Access should remain role-based.

---

# 7.69 Mobile Experience

Mobile should focus on:

- current disruption
- recovery status
- approvals
- critical alerts
- Return-to-Normal review

---

# 7.70 Desktop Experience

Desktop supports:

- recovery operations
- dependency analysis
- Restore Point comparison
- reconciliation
- test evidence

---

# 7.71 Accessibility

Use:

- clear text status
- accessible labels
- keyboard navigation
- sufficient contrast

Never rely solely on color.

---

# 7.72 SMP1 Resilience Command Center

For standalone migration, the command center should focus on:

- current authoritative system
- latest source snapshot
- backup state
- rollback point
- migration/reconciliation status
- Cutover/recovery state
- critical blockers

---

# 7.73 SMP1 Cutover Failure UX

Example:

```text id="smp1-cutover-failure-stage7"
SMP1 CUTOVER

Status:
FAILED VALIDATION

Issue:
Inventory reconciliation mismatch

Current Authority:
Apps Script Legacy

Standalone:
NOT AUTHORITATIVE

Decision:
REPAIR OR ROLLBACK
```

---

# 7.74 SMP1 Authority State

During Cutover/Recovery display clearly:

```text id="smp1-authority-state-stage7"
AUTHORITATIVE WRITER

Apps Script:
READ ONLY

Standalone:
PRIMARY
```

or the actual current state.

---

# 7.75 SMP1 Dual-Writer Warning

Example:

```text id="dual-writer-warning-stage7"
CRITICAL

Multiple systems appear writable.

Apps Script:
WRITE ENABLED

Standalone:
PRIMARY

Immediate Review Required
```

---

# 7.76 SMP1 Restore Test Workspace

Before certification, evidence should show:

- backup selected
- environment rebuilt
- data restored
- application started
- permissions validated
- critical workflows passed

---

# 7.77 SMP1 Recovery Readiness

Potential:

```text id="smp1-recovery-readiness-stage7"
STANDALONE RECOVERY READINESS

Backup:
PASS

Restore:
PASS

Business Validation:
PASS

Reconciliation:
PASS

Rollback Procedure:
PASS

Critical Exceptions:
0
```

---

# 7.78 Apps Script Baseline UX

Apps Script should be visibly labeled after standalone certification as appropriate:

- Reference Baseline
- Historical
- Read-Only

not silently presented as equivalent live production authority.

---

# 7.79 ERP9 / ERP10 Reuse

ERP9 and ERP10 resilience views should reuse the same recovery UX.

No release-specific DR dashboard is required.

---

# 7.80 Version 1.1 Reuse

Future platform evolution extends the same workspace.

---

# 7.81 AI Recovery Assistant

Potential capabilities:

- summarize current recovery
- explain which dependency failed
- retrieve correct procedure
- compare Restore Points
- summarize reconciliation exceptions

---

# 7.82 AI Provenance

AI recovery summaries should indicate the records/events they rely upon where appropriate.

---

# 7.83 AI Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="ai-boundary-stage7-d38"
AI Says Restore Is Best
≠
Restore Approved

AI Says Service Is Healthy
≠
Business Validation Passed
```

---

# 7.84 No Autonomous Crisis UI

Do not make the interface appear as if AI is:

- Recovery Lead
- business approver
- Return-to-Normal authority

---

# 7.85 Data Freshness

Show timestamps for:

- Service status
- Backup status
- dependency health
- reconciliation state

during active recovery.

---

# 7.86 Stale Recovery Data

If telemetry becomes stale:

Show:

```text id="stale-recovery-data-stage7"
STATUS UNKNOWN

Last Confirmed:
12 Minutes Ago
```

not GREEN.

---

# 7.87 Error State

If monitoring data is unavailable:

Show unavailable/unknown.

Do not assume:

- service healthy
- backup healthy
- reconciliation complete.

---

# 7.88 No-Data Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="no-data-stage7-d38"
No Recovery Test Record
≠
Recovery Capability Proven
```

---

# 7.89 Implementation Priority

### Must Have for Standalone v1.0

- Resilience Home
- Active Recovery Workspace
- Backup Health
- Restore Point
- recovery phase/status
- Business Validation
- Reconciliation
- Authority State
- Return-to-Normal
- Test Evidence
- Audit

### Later

- advanced crisis collaboration
- geographic resilience maps
- sophisticated supplier resilience visualization
- automated simulation dashboards
- AI predictive outage interfaces

---

# 7.90 Anti-Overengineering Rule

Permanent:

> **The resilience UX must help GiftHatke recover the business quickly and safely; it must not become a large crisis-management application before SMP1 and standalone v1.0 are delivered.**

---

# 7.91 Critical UX Invariants

1. Business Service status must remain distinct from infrastructure status.
2. Backup success ≠ restore proven.
3. Restore completed ≠ business recovered.
4. Temporary records remain visibly non-authoritative until reconciled.
5. Critical Recovery Exceptions must be prominent.
6. Authority state must remain explicit.
7. Dual-writer conditions must be treated as critical.
8. Stale/unknown data must not appear healthy.
9. AI remains visibly advisory.
10. SMP1 resilience UX must protect certified business semantics and the authoritative-system boundary.

---

# 7.92 Stage 7 Certification

Stage 7 permanently establishes the minimum implementation-grade experience for:

- Resilience Home
- Critical Service status
- active Continuity Workspace
- recovery phases
- Recovery Lead/business/executive views
- Backup Health
- Restore Point comparison
- destructive recovery warnings
- dependency impact
- manual Workarounds
- offline transactions
- reconciliation
- technical/data/security/business validation
- Recovery Exceptions
- Return-to-Normal
- recovery timeline
- RTO/RPO visibility
- resilience testing
- supplier/equipment/facility continuity
- permission/confidentiality handling
- SMP1 Cutover/rollback/authority UX
- standalone recovery readiness
- Apps Script reference-state representation
- AI assistant boundaries
- stale/error/no-data handling
- anti-overengineering controls

This is sufficient to make Domain 38 operationally usable during real disruption and SMP1 recovery without introducing unnecessary enterprise crisis-management complexity.

**Stage 7 Status: ✅ CERTIFIED**

**Enterprise Canon Position: Domain 38 — IN PROGRESS (7/10 stages certified).**

# ENTERPRISE BUSINESS CONTINUITY, DISASTER RECOVERY & OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE CANON
## Stage 8 — Resilience Analytics, Recovery Performance, Dependency Risk & Predictive Continuity Intelligence Canon

---

# 8.1 Purpose

Stage 8 defines the minimum analytics and intelligence architecture required to understand whether GiftHatke's continuity and recovery controls are actually effective.

The objective is:

> **Provide clear resilience intelligence on Service risk, backup health, recovery performance, dependency exposure, and readiness without creating artificial resilience scores or excessive operational reporting.**

---

# 8.2 Analytics Philosophy

Permanent principles:

- Recovery capability before policy documentation.
- Tested restore before backup count.
- business impact before infrastructure volume.
- dependency risk before cosmetic availability.
- actual recovery time before assumed RTO compliance.
- unresolved recovery gaps before optimistic readiness.
- trend before isolated snapshots.
- evidence before prediction.

---

# 8.3 Core Analytics Landscape

Minimum intelligence areas:

- Critical Service Resilience
- RTO Performance
- RPO Performance
- Backup Health
- Restore Capability
- Recovery Performance
- Dependency Risk
- Single-Point-of-Failure Exposure
- Continuity Invocation Trends
- Manual Workaround Effectiveness
- Reconciliation Performance
- Recovery Exception Intelligence
- Resilience Test Performance
- Recovery Readiness
- Predictive Resilience Intelligence

---

# 8.4 Critical Service Resilience

For each Critical Service, track at minimum:

- criticality
- recovery targets
- current dependency Risk
- backup coverage
- latest restore test
- unresolved resilience gaps

---

# 8.5 Resilience Status

A practical status may be:

```text id="service-resilience-stage8"
READY
READY WITH CONDITIONS
AT RISK
NOT READY
UNKNOWN
```

This should be evidence-driven.

---

# 8.6 No Artificial Resilience Score

Permanent:

```text id="resilience-score-stage8"
Resilience = 87%
```

should not be invented unless a defensible and useful methodology exists.

---

# 8.7 RTO Performance

Compare:

```text id="rto-performance-stage8"
Actual Recovery Time

vs

Approved RTO
```

---

# 8.8 RTO Compliance

Potential categories:

- Within Target
- Target Missed
- Not Tested
- Not Defined

---

# 8.9 RTO Trend

Track whether recovery performance is:

- improving
- stable
- deteriorating

over successive valid tests/incidents.

---

# 8.10 RTO Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="rto-boundary-stage8"
No Recovery Event
≠
RTO Proven
```

---

# 8.11 RPO Performance

Compare:

- actual recovered point
- failure time
- approved RPO

where measurable.

---

# 8.12 Data-Loss Exposure

Track actual or estimated:

- data gap

during recovery.

---

# 8.13 RPO Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="rpo-boundary-stage8"
Successful Restore
≠
RPO Target Met
```

---

# 8.14 Backup Health

Track:

- last successful backup
- backup failure rate
- protection gap
- retention health
- latest usable Restore Point

---

# 8.15 Backup Coverage

Should answer:

- Which critical data is protected?
- Which is not?
- Which backup has not been validated?

---

# 8.16 Backup Success Rate

Useful operational metric:

```text id="backup-success-rate-stage8"
Successful Backup Executions
/
Expected Backup Executions
```

But success rate alone does not prove recoverability.

---

# 8.17 Restore Test Coverage

Track:

- Services/systems with validated restore
- Services/systems never tested
- overdue tests

---

# 8.18 Restore Success Rate

Potentially measure:

- successful restore tests
- failed restore tests
- conditional passes

---

# 8.19 Restore Failure Analysis

Repeated failure may indicate:

- incomplete configuration
- stale procedure
- corrupt backups
- missing dependencies
- permission problems

---

# 8.20 Recovery Duration

Track recovery time by phase where useful:

- environment preparation
- restore
- technical validation
- business validation
- reconciliation

---

# 8.21 Recovery Bottleneck

This helps identify whether recovery delay is caused by:

- technology
- data
- authority
- business validation
- dependency
- reconciliation

---

# 8.22 Technical vs Business Recovery Time

Permanent distinction:

```text id="technical-business-recovery-stage8"
Technical Recovery Time
≠
Business Recovery Time
```

---

# 8.23 Recovery Exception Intelligence

Track:

- open exceptions
- critical exceptions
- age
- recurring type
- owner

---

# 8.24 Exception Recurrence

Repeated exception categories may indicate:

- systemic recovery weakness.

---

# 8.25 Dependency Risk Analytics

Track:

- failed dependencies
- degraded dependencies
- critical shared dependencies
- Services affected per dependency

---

# 8.26 Dependency Concentration

If many Critical Services depend on one:

- vendor
- database
- identity platform
- network provider

this is important resilience exposure.

---

# 8.27 Single Point of Failure Analytics

Track known critical SPOFs and their treatment:

- accepted
- workaround
- redundancy
- mitigation Project

---

# 8.28 SPOF Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="spof-boundary-stage8"
Single Point of Failure
≠
Automatic Architecture Failure
```

The business may consciously accept some SPOFs.

---

# 8.29 Supplier Resilience Intelligence

For critical suppliers, potentially track:

- outage frequency
- duration
- alternate route availability
- affected Services

---

# 8.30 Facility Resilience Intelligence

Where relevant, track:

- facility dependency
- outage history
- alternate operating capability

---

# 8.31 Equipment Resilience Intelligence

For critical production equipment, track:

- failure history
- repair duration
- alternate capacity
- business impact

---

# 8.32 Continuity Invocation Analytics

Track material continuity invocations by:

- Service
- cause
- duration
- fallback used
- outcome

---

# 8.33 Invocation Frequency

Repeated continuity activation may indicate:

- underlying architectural weakness
- supplier instability
- poor operational controls

---

# 8.34 Manual Workaround Effectiveness

Track:

- transactions captured
- errors
- duplicates
- reconciliation duration
- user issues

---

# 8.35 Workaround Boundary

A workaround with high reconciliation error may not be a reliable continuity mechanism.

---

# 8.36 Reconciliation Analytics

Track:

- temporary records
- matched
- imported
- duplicates
- unresolved exceptions
- completion time

---

# 8.37 Reconciliation Quality

Potential:

```text id="reconciliation-quality-stage8"
Temporary Records
→
Successfully Reconciled
```

with unresolved exceptions explicitly visible.

---

# 8.38 Duplicate Rate

Repeated duplicate reconciliation may indicate:

- weak temporary identifiers
- unclear operational procedure
- missing idempotency controls

---

# 8.39 Recovery Objective Gaps

Track Services where:

```text id="recovery-gap-stage8"
Required RTO/RPO
<
Current Proven Capability
```

These are resilience gaps.

---

# 8.40 Gap Treatment

Each material gap may have:

- accepted Risk
- remediation
- Project
- revised business tolerance

---

# 8.41 Resilience Test Analytics

Track:

- tests planned
- tests completed
- pass
- conditional pass
- fail
- retest overdue

---

# 8.42 Test Coverage

Should identify which Critical Services have never had recovery capability tested.

---

# 8.43 Failed Test Aging

A critical failed test that remains unresolved for a long period should stay visible.

---

# 8.44 Remediation Performance

Track Resilience Actions:

- open
- overdue
- completed
- retest status

---

# 8.45 Plan Freshness

Track whether continuity/DR Plans became stale after:

- architecture changes
- supplier changes
- business workflow changes

---

# 8.46 Stale Plan Risk

Permanent:

```text id="stale-plan-stage8"
Document Exists
≠
Plan Is Current
```

---

# 8.47 Backup Age Risk

If no recent valid backup exists:

Show actual protection exposure.

---

# 8.48 Restore Point Age

Track age of latest validated Restore Point for critical systems.

---

# 8.49 Recovery Readiness

A practical readiness summary may consider:

- Recovery Objectives defined
- backup coverage
- latest valid Restore Point
- current DR Plan
- successful recent test
- unresolved critical gaps

---

# 8.50 Readiness Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="readiness-boundary-stage8"
Plan Approved
≠
Recovery Ready
```

---

# 8.51 Executive Resilience View

Executives should see:

- Critical Services not ready
- major recovery gaps
- material supplier/SPOF exposure
- failed critical tests
- major investment decisions required

not detailed backup logs.

---

# 8.52 Operational Resilience View

Operators may see:

- failed backups
- stale Restore Points
- overdue tests
- recovery exceptions
- plan freshness

---

# 8.53 Trend Intelligence

Useful trends may include:

- backup failure trend
- recovery duration
- RTO misses
- critical recovery gaps
- failed-test recurrence

---

# 8.54 Root-Cause Intelligence

Post-incident data may identify recurring causes such as:

- cloud/vendor outage
- configuration drift
- human error
- equipment failure
- network failure
- security incident

---

# 8.55 Root Cause Boundary

Correlation should not be represented as confirmed Root Cause without evidence.

---

# 8.56 Predictive Service Risk

Future systems may estimate risk of Service disruption using:

- dependency health
- recent failures
- backup gaps
- infrastructure health
- supplier reliability

---

# 8.57 Predictive Recovery Delay

Potential predictors:

- stale DR Plan
- failed recent restore test
- unresolved dependency
- untested configuration
- large reconciliation backlog

---

# 8.58 Predictive Data-Loss Risk

May consider:

- backup frequency
- backup failures
- transaction rate
- replication health

---

# 8.59 Prediction Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="prediction-boundary-stage8-d38"
Predicted Outage / Recovery Delay
≠
Actual Event
```

---

# 8.60 Prescriptive Resilience

Future systems may recommend:

- run restore test
- increase backup frequency
- remediate SPOF
- renew alternate supplier
- update DR Plan

---

# 8.61 Prescriptive Boundary

Recommendation does not approve:

- investment
- destructive change
- Risk acceptance

---

# 8.62 Scenario Analysis

Future capability may model:

- primary database failure
- cloud outage
- internet outage
- laser machine failure
- carrier outage
- key supplier failure

---

# 8.63 Scenario Example

```text id="scenario-example-stage8"
Scenario:
Primary ERP Database Unavailable

Affected Services:
Orders
Inventory
Production
Shipping

Fallback:
Limited Offline Operation

Expected Recovery:
Restore-Based
```

---

# 8.64 Business Impact Simulation

Advanced future analysis may estimate:

- Orders delayed
- revenue exposure
- customer impact
- production backlog

during different outage durations.

---

# 8.65 Cost-of-Resilience Intelligence

Future decision support may compare:

```text id="resilience-cost-stage8"
Cost of Additional Resilience

vs

Expected Business Impact of Outage
```

This supports rational investment.

---

# 8.66 No Zero-Risk Objective

Permanent:

> **The goal is not to eliminate all operational Risk; it is to keep Risk within acceptable business tolerance.**

---

# 8.67 AI Resilience Intelligence

AI may assist with:

- summarizing readiness gaps
- detecting recurring failure themes
- comparing test results
- explaining dependency impact
- suggesting remediation priorities

---

# 8.68 AI Grounding

AI must rely on:

- actual backup records
- test evidence
- recovery Events
- dependency data
- approved Recovery Objectives

---

# 8.69 AI False Confidence

AI must not claim:

> Disaster recovery is guaranteed.

Recovery is always subject to real operating conditions.

---

# 8.70 AI Prediction Confidence

Where predictive capability exists:

Expose uncertainty and relevant supporting evidence.

---

# 8.71 SMP1 Resilience Analytics

For SMP1, focus strictly on:

- backup readiness
- restore test
- recovery validation
- rollback readiness
- reconciliation
- authority state
- critical recovery exceptions

---

# 8.72 SMP1 Readiness Summary

Example:

```text id="smp1-readiness-stage8"
STANDALONE RECOVERY

Backup:
READY

Restore Test:
PASS

Critical Workflows:
PASS

Reconciliation:
PASS

Rollback:
READY

Critical Recovery Gaps:
0
```

---

# 8.73 SMP1 Restore Performance

Measure actual restore rehearsal:

- start
- technical restoration
- business validation
- reconciliation completion

---

# 8.74 SMP1 Recovery Gap

If standalone cannot yet meet the approved business Recovery Objective:

The gap must remain visible before certification.

---

# 8.75 SMP1 Architecture Drift

Resilience analytics should not encourage a different business workflow purely because recovery is easier.

The certified architecture remains authoritative.

---

# 8.76 SMP1 Apps Script Metric Boundary

Do not count the retained Apps Script reference baseline as:

- secondary recovery capability

unless it is deliberately engineered and tested as one.

---

# 8.77 ERP9 / ERP10 Analytics Reuse

ERP9 and ERP10 should reuse:

- criticality
- Recovery Objective
- backup
- test
- recovery-gap

analytics.

---

# 8.78 Version 1.1 Reuse

Future releases extend the same resilience intelligence model.

---

# 8.79 Historical Analytics Integrity

Do not fabricate historical:

- RTO achievement
- restore success
- backup availability
- continuity duration

where the data was not captured.

---

# 8.80 No-Data Boundary

Permanent:

```text id="no-data-boundary-stage8-d38"
No Recorded Recovery Failure
≠
Recovery Capability Proven
```

---

# 8.81 Metric Lineage

Material resilience metrics should identify:

- source
- calculation
- time range
- target
- current data freshness

---

# 8.82 Auditability

Users should be able to drill from:

```text id="auditability-stage8-d38"
2 Critical Services Not Ready
```

to the actual Services and failed/missing controls.

---

# 8.83 Minimum KPI Set

For standalone v1.0, a small set is enough:

- Critical Services without defined Recovery Objectives
- failed critical backups
- Services without validated Restore Point
- failed/overdue critical restore tests
- open critical recovery gaps
- unresolved recovery exceptions
- latest standalone recovery-test result

---

# 8.84 Metrics That Can Wait

Later if genuinely useful:

- sophisticated availability modelling
- predictive outage scoring
- Monte Carlo resilience simulation
- supplier reliability scoring
- automated cost-of-downtime modelling
- AI recovery optimization

---

# 8.85 Anti-Overengineering Rule

Permanent:

> **Resilience analytics must show whether GiftHatke can actually recover. It must not become a separate BI or reliability-science programme before standalone v1.0.**

---

# 8.86 Critical Analytics Invariants

1. Backup count ≠ recoverability.
2. RTO target ≠ achieved recovery time.
3. Restore success ≠ RPO compliance.
4. Technical recovery time ≠ business recovery time.
5. Plan existence ≠ current readiness.
6. Single Point of Failure ≠ automatic unacceptable Risk.
7. No recorded failure ≠ capability proven.
8. Prediction ≠ actual disruption.
9. AI insight ≠ recovery evidence.
10. SMP1 resilience analytics must measure real standalone recoverability without treating the Apps Script reference baseline as automatic failover.

---

# 8.87 Stage 8 Certification

Stage 8 permanently establishes the minimum implementation-grade analytics and intelligence architecture for:

- Critical Service resilience
- RTO/RPO performance
- backup health
- Restore Point coverage
- restore-test performance
- recovery duration
- recovery bottlenecks
- Recovery Exceptions
- dependency concentration
- single-point-of-failure exposure
- supplier/facility/equipment resilience
- continuity invocation trends
- Workaround effectiveness
- reconciliation quality
- resilience gaps
- test/remediation performance
- plan freshness
- Recovery Readiness
- executive/operational resilience views
- predictive/prescriptive intelligence
- scenario analysis
- cost-of-resilience decision support
- AI resilience assistance
- SMP1 backup/restore/rollback analytics
- ERP9/ERP10/Version 1.1 reuse
- metric lineage and historical integrity

This is sufficient to determine whether standalone v1.0 is genuinely recoverable and operationally safe without introducing unnecessary resilience analytics complexity.
